chapters.name: Mathematics & Computational Tools
chapters.context: This chapter tests your ability to apply analytic geometry, single-variable calculus, vector operations, and computational tools (spreadsheets and structured programming) to engineering problems.

subtopics.name: Analytic Geometry
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you use analytic geometry constantly — computing slopes and grades for road profiles, finding distances between survey points, resolving force components with trig, solving oblique triangles for property boundaries, and working with conic sections in highway curve design. If a problem gives you coordinates, angles, or a line equation, this is your toolkit.

lessons.name: Straight Lines & Quadratics
lessons.application: Civil engineers work with straight lines constantly — from defining road alignments and grade slopes, to establishing property boundaries in surveying, to plotting stress-strain relationships in materials testing. The quadratic formula shows up any time a parabolic curve is involved: vertical curves in highway design, projectile trajectories in dynamics, and cable sag calculations. On the FE, expect direct questions asking you to find a slope, a distance between two points, or the roots of a quadratic. These are fast-solve questions if you know the formulas — free points.

lessons.name: Logarithms
lessons.application: Logarithms show up across multiple FE Civil topics — computing the time for a contaminant to decay to safe levels in environmental engineering, finding the number of compounding periods in engineering economics, and working with the pH scale in water quality. On the FE, log questions tend to be algebra problems: simplify an expression using log rules, change bases, or solve an equation where the unknown is in the exponent. The formulas are all in the handbook — the skill is knowing which identity to apply.

lessons.name: Right Triangle Trigonometry
lessons.application: Civil engineers use right triangle trig constantly — resolving cable forces into horizontal and vertical components, computing slope distances on graded roads, sizing retaining wall footings, and laying out survey lines. On the FE exam, any time you see an angle paired with a force or a length, you're reaching for SOH-CAH-TOA. This is foundational for statics, surveying, and structural problems throughout the test.

lessons.name: Law of Sines & Law of Cosines
lessons.application: Civil engineers encounter oblique triangles — triangles with no right angle — when surveying irregular property boundaries, computing forces in non-orthogonal truss members, or triangulating positions from two known points. The Law of Sines and Law of Cosines let you solve any triangle when you can't drop a clean perpendicular. On the FE exam, if the given triangle isn't a right triangle, one of these two laws is your only path forward.

lessons.name: Unit Circle & Trig Identities
lessons.application: Trig identities show up on the FE whenever a problem needs simplification before you can solve it — combining force components at different angles, converting between sin and cos in vibration equations, or simplifying expressions in calculus-based derivations. The unit circle ties angles to coordinates, giving you exact values for common angles without a calculator. On the FE exam, knowing your reference angles and a handful of identities saves real time.

lessons.name: Circles & Conic Sections
lessons.application: Conic sections appear in civil engineering more than you'd expect — circular curves on highway alignments, parabolic profiles for vertical road curves, and elliptical arches in bridge design. On the FE exam, you need to recognize the standard equation of a circle, identify its center and radius, and know the basic forms of parabolas and ellipses. Most FE problems stick to circles, but an occasional parabola or ellipse shows up in the math section.

subtopics.name: Single-Variable Calculus
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you rely on calculus every time you compute the area under a load diagram, find where shear is zero (and moment is maximum) on a beam, or determine the rate of change of flow in a storm drain. Differentiation and integration are the backbone of structural analysis, earthwork volumes, and hydraulic design.

lessons.name: Derivatives & Derivative Rules
lessons.application: Civil engineers use derivatives any time they need a rate of change — the slope of a deflection curve to find beam rotation, the rate of flow change in a pipe to detect surges, or the velocity of a settling particle in a sedimentation tank. On the FE, derivative questions are usually 'apply the right rule' problems: you see a function, pick the correct derivative rule from the handbook table, and crank through the algebra. The chain rule shows up the most because the FE loves composite functions like sin(3x²) or e^(-0.5t).

lessons.name: Applications of Derivatives
lessons.application: Civil engineers use max/min analysis constantly — finding where bending moment is maximum along a beam, optimizing the dimensions of a channel for maximum flow, or locating the peak elevation on a vertical highway curve. Inflection points tell you where a beam changes from bending one way to the other. On the FE, these problems are formulaic: take the derivative, set it equal to zero, solve, and use the second derivative to classify. They're free points if you don't make sign errors.

lessons.name: Integral Calculus
lessons.application: Civil engineers integrate constantly — computing the area under a load diagram to find total force, calculating earthwork volumes from cross-section data, finding the total flow through a culvert over time, or determining the deflection of a beam from its moment equation. The FE gives you a function and asks for an antiderivative or a definite integral. You have the integral table in the handbook, so the real skill is recognizing which formula fits and applying substitution or integration by parts when it doesn't match directly.

lessons.name: L'Hopital's Rule
lessons.application: L'Hopital's Rule is a one-trick tool — but it appears on the FE almost every cycle. Whenever you plug a limit value into a fraction and get 0/0 or ∞/∞, you differentiate the top and bottom separately and try the limit again. Civil engineers encounter these indeterminate forms when analyzing boundary conditions in hydraulics (flow at a critical depth transition), evaluating limiting cases in structural deflection formulas, and checking asymptotic behavior of decay functions. It's a fast 1-2 minute problem if you recognize the setup.

subtopics.name: Vector Operations
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, vectors are how you resolve forces on structural connections, compute the moment of a force about a point, and determine resultant loads on a structure. Dot products find the angle between forces; cross products give you moment arms in three dimensions.

lessons.name: Vector Basics & Unit Vectors
lessons.application: Vectors are the language of forces in civil engineering. Every time you draw a free body diagram — resolving a cable tension into horizontal and vertical components, adding wind loads on a structure, or combining soil pressure resultants — you're doing vector math. Unit vectors let you express direction independently of magnitude, which is essential for writing force equilibrium equations in 2D and 3D. On the FE, vector basics show up directly in statics and dynamics problems. If you can add, subtract, and normalize vectors quickly, you'll save time on at least 5-10 questions.

lessons.name: Dot Product & Angle Between Vectors
lessons.application: The dot product is how civil engineers find the angle between two forces, compute the component of one force along another direction, and check whether two vectors are perpendicular. In structural analysis, you use it to find the projection of a load onto a member axis. In surveying, it helps find the angle between two traverse legs. On the FE, dot product questions are quick if you know the two formulas — the component formula and the cosine formula — and when to use each.

lessons.name: Cross Product & Applications
lessons.application: The cross product gives civil engineers a vector perpendicular to two other vectors — and its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram they form. In practice, you use it to compute the moment of a force about a point ($\vec{M} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$), find the area of a triangular region defined by two edge vectors, and determine the direction of a normal to a surface. On the FE, cross product questions appear in statics (moment calculations) and occasionally in surveying (area from coordinates). Know the determinant formula and the right-hand rule.

subtopics.name: Computational Tools
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you build spreadsheets for earthwork, quantity takeoffs, and load combinations, and you trace logic in macros and analysis scripts. The FE tests order of operations in cell formulas, relative vs. absolute references when a formula is copied, and reading short pseudocode (if-then-else and loops).

lessons.name: Spreadsheet Computations
lessons.application: Civil engineers live in spreadsheets — earthwork volume tables, quantity takeoffs, load combinations, rebar schedules, and cost estimates are all built from cell formulas. The FE tests whether you can read a formula, apply the correct order of operations, and predict what happens to relative vs. absolute references when a formula is copied. These are quick points if you know the rules cold.

lessons.name: Structured Programming
lessons.application: Whether you script earthwork calcs, automate a hydraulic spreadsheet with a macro, or just read someone else's analysis routine, you need to trace structured logic. The FE keeps it conceptual: given a short block of pseudocode with an if-then-else or a loop, predict the output or count the iterations. No language syntax to memorize — just sequence, selection, and iteration.

lessons.name: Numerical Methods: Root-Finding
lessons.application: When an equation cannot be solved in closed form, engineers find roots numerically. As a civil engineer you use these methods inside spreadsheets and solvers to find, for example, the depth that satisfies a nonlinear flow equation. On the FE, expect to apply one iteration of Newton's method and to know the requirement that makes bisection work.

chapters.name: Probability & Statistics
chapters.context: This chapter covers probability distributions, statistical inference, and regression — foundational tools for engineering data analysis.

subtopics.name: Descriptive Statistics
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you compute means and standard deviations every time you evaluate concrete cylinder break tests, assess traffic count data, or summarize soil boring results. You fit regression curves to field data constantly — correlating SPT blow counts with soil shear strength, developing stage-discharge relationships, or establishing IDF curves for stormwater design. The spread in your data and the strength of your correlations tell you whether a design value is reliable.

lessons.name: Measures of Central Tendency & Dispersion
lessons.application: Civil engineers compute means and standard deviations constantly — averaging concrete cylinder break strengths to verify a pour meets spec, computing the standard deviation of traffic counts to size turn lanes, or summarizing soil boring data across a site. When you report a value to a client, the spread tells you whether you need more samples or whether the data is tight enough to design on. On the FE, expect straightforward “find the mean” or “find the standard deviation” questions where the only trap is which formula to use.

lessons.name: Linear Regression & Correlation
lessons.application: Civil engineers fit regression lines to field data constantly — correlating SPT blow counts with soil shear strength, developing stage-discharge curves for stream gauges, or establishing relationships between traffic speed and density. The regression equation lets you predict one variable from another, and the correlation coefficient tells you how much to trust that prediction. On the FE, expect problems that give you summary statistics ($\Sigma x$, $\Sigma y$, $\Sigma xy$, etc.) and ask for the slope, intercept, or $R^2$.

subtopics.name: Probability
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, probability distributions drive design — the 100-year flood follows a log-Pearson Type III distribution, traffic arrivals follow a Poisson distribution, and concrete strengths are modeled as normal. Expected values show up when comparing alternatives in benefit-cost analyses or compositing soil properties from multiple borings. You pick design values directly from these distributions.

lessons.name: Probability Distributions
lessons.application: Civil engineers deal with probability every time they design for uncertainty — sizing a culvert for the 100-year storm, estimating the chance that fewer than 3 out of 20 concrete cylinders fail spec, or determining whether observed traffic accidents at an intersection are statistically unusual. The FE tests your ability to compute basic probabilities, apply the binomial distribution for discrete pass/fail scenarios, and use the normal distribution with z-scores to find areas under the curve.

lessons.name: Expected Value & Weighted Averages
lessons.application: Civil engineers use expected values when comparing alternatives under uncertainty — weighting each outcome by its probability to decide between bridge repair strategies, estimating the average number of vehicle arrivals at a toll plaza per hour, or computing the expected cost of a project with multiple risk scenarios. On the FE, expect problems that hand you a probability table and ask for $E(X)$, or that combine independent random variables and ask for the resulting mean or standard deviation.

subtopics.name: Inferential Statistics
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, confidence intervals tell you how much to trust your field data — reporting a soil friction angle as 32° ± 3° at 95% confidence directly affects foundation design. Hypothesis testing tells you whether differences are real or noise: does a new concrete mix meet spec? Did a pavement treatment actually reduce accidents? These tools turn raw data into engineering decisions.

lessons.name: Confidence Intervals & Estimation
lessons.application: Civil engineers build confidence intervals every time they report field data with a margin of error — stating that a soil’s friction angle is 32° ± 3° at 95% confidence, or that the mean 28-day concrete strength is 4,200 ± 150 psi. That range directly affects design safety factors and whether you need more samples. On the FE, expect problems that give you sample data and ask you to construct an interval or determine the required sample size.

lessons.name: Hypothesis Testing & Goodness of Fit
lessons.application: Civil engineers run hypothesis tests whenever a specification is on the line — testing whether concrete strength meets the design minimum, whether a new traffic signal actually reduced accident rates, or whether soil compaction data matches the Proctor target. The test gives you a yes/no decision backed by statistics, not gut feeling. Chi-square goodness of fit shows up when you need to check whether observed data matches a theoretical distribution (uniform arrivals, Poisson failures, normal distribution). On the FE, expect problems that give you sample data, a claimed value, and ask you to compute the test statistic or make a reject/fail-to-reject decision.

chapters.name: Ethics & Prof. Practice
chapters.context: This chapter tests your understanding of professional obligations, codes of ethics, the licensure process, and broader responsibilities like intellectual property and sustainability. The FE Handbook (pp. 4-13) includes the NCEES Model Rules of Professional Conduct, Model Law definitions and licensure requirements, grounds for disciplinary action, intellectual property categories, and societal considerations. Most exam questions are scenario-based — they describe a situation and ask what the engineer should do.

subtopics.name: Professional Conduct
subtopics.application: The NCEES Model Rules (pp. 4-5) define three tiers of obligations: to the public, to employers and clients, and to other licensees. Public safety is always the paramount duty — it overrides client wishes, budget pressures, and employer directives. The FE tests this with scenario questions where you must identify the correct course of action when obligations conflict.

lessons.name: Obligations to the Public
lessons.application: Every section of the NCEES Model Rules starts with one idea: public safety comes first. On the FE, ethics questions test whether you can identify which obligation takes priority when two rules collide — and the answer is almost always "protect the public." Civil engineers sign and seal plans for bridges, buildings, and water systems that directly affect human life, so the exam checks that you know the ten rules in Section A cold, especially the hierarchy: public safety > employer loyalty > personal interest.

lessons.name: Obligations to Employers, Clients & Other Licensees
lessons.application: Sections B and C of the Model Rules govern how you deal with the people you work for and the people you work alongside. On the FE, these rules show up as conflict-of-interest scenarios, confidentiality dilemmas, and questions about professional competence boundaries. Civil engineers constantly juggle multiple clients, subconsultants, and government agencies — the exam checks that you know where the ethical lines are when money, loyalty, and professional reputation are in play.

subtopics.name: Licensure & Law
subtopics.application: The Model Law (pp. 6-10) defines who can call themselves a Professional Engineer, what constitutes the practice of engineering, the FE-to-PE licensure path, and what gets your license revoked. On the FE, expect questions about education and experience requirements, what an Engineer Intern can and cannot do, and which actions constitute grounds for disciplinary action.

lessons.name: Definitions & Practice of Engineering
lessons.application: The Model Law definitions tell you who counts as an engineer, what counts as engineering, and what "responsible charge" actually means. On the FE, these definitions show up as boundary questions — is this person allowed to do this work? Does this activity require a license? Civil engineers deal with these boundaries constantly: when a technician prepares drawings under your supervision, when you coordinate with surveyors, or when someone without a license calls themselves an "engineer." The exam tests whether you know exactly where the legal lines are drawn.

lessons.name: Licensure Path & Disciplinary Action
lessons.application: The licensure path is the roadmap every engineer follows from student to PE — and the FE exam you're studying for is one of the checkpoints on it. The exam tests whether you know the sequence (education → FE → experience → PE) and the requirements at each stage. It also tests the flip side: what gets your license taken away. Civil engineers work on public infrastructure where mistakes can be catastrophic, so the board has broad power to discipline licensees for fraud, incompetence, misconduct, and even felony convictions unrelated to engineering. Knowing these grounds helps you spot the violation in scenario questions.

subtopics.name: Contracts & Liability
subtopics.application: Engineering services are delivered under contracts, and engineers carry legal responsibility for their work. You should know what makes a contract enforceable (offer, acceptance, consideration), how contract types and project delivery methods allocate cost risk, and how professional liability turns on the standard of care and the four elements of negligence. The FE tests these as scenario questions on contracts, delivery methods, and liability.

lessons.name: Engineering Contracts
lessons.application: Almost every engineering service is delivered under a contract — between owner and engineer, owner and contractor, or engineer and subconsultant. As a civil engineer you should recognize what makes an agreement legally binding, how different contract types shift cost risk, and how projects are delivered. The FE tests these as scenario questions about contract elements, payment types, and project delivery methods.

lessons.name: Professional Liability
lessons.application: Engineers can be held legally responsible when their work causes harm. As a civil engineer you should understand the standard of care you are measured against, what a plaintiff must prove to win a negligence claim, and how time limits and contract clauses affect your exposure. The FE tests these as scenario questions about liability, negligence, and the standard of care.

subtopics.name: Broader Responsibilities
subtopics.application: Beyond the code of conduct, engineers must understand intellectual property protections (patents, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets) and sustainability principles (life-cycle analysis, environmental stewardship). The handbook covers these on pp. 12-13. Expect 1-2 questions asking which IP protection applies to a given scenario or which practice qualifies as sustainable design.

lessons.name: Intellectual Property, Sustainability & Societal Considerations
lessons.application: Engineers create valuable designs, methods, and innovations — and need to know how to protect them. The FE tests whether you can distinguish between patents, trademarks, copyrights, and trade secrets, and pick the right protection for a given scenario. It also tests sustainability principles: life-cycle analysis, resource conservation, and the "triple bottom line" of economic, environmental, and social impact. Civil engineers make decisions every day that affect ecosystems, public health, and long-term resource use — from choosing materials for a highway to designing a stormwater system that minimizes pollution.

chapters.name: Engineering Economics
chapters.context: This chapter tests your ability to evaluate the economic viability of engineering projects using time-value-of-money principles, cost analysis, and depreciation methods.

subtopics.name: Time Value of Money
subtopics.application: Time value of money is the foundation of every infrastructure investment decision. When a city asks whether to replace a bridge now for $8M or do major rehabilitation in 10 years for $12M, you convert both options to present worth at the appropriate discount rate. On the FE, you need the nine standard interest factors and the skill to read factor tables quickly (pp. 229, 232–236).

lessons.name: Equivalence & Interest Factors
lessons.application: Every engineering economics problem on the FE boils down to moving money through time. You'll convert a lump sum today into its future equivalent, spread a present cost into equal annual payments, or discount a series of future cash flows back to the present. The nine standard interest factors are the tools — and the factor tables in the handbook (pp. 232–236) are your shortcut. Civil engineers use these constantly: sizing a sinking fund for bridge replacement, calculating loan payments on equipment, or comparing the annual cost of two pavement alternatives. If you can read a cash flow diagram and pick the right factor, these are fast points.

lessons.name: Present Worth, Future Worth & Annual Worth Analysis
lessons.application: When a DOT compares two bridge rehabilitation options with different lifespans and costs, they need a common basis for comparison. Present worth converts everything to today's dollars, future worth projects everything to a target date, and annual worth spreads everything into equivalent yearly costs. The FE tests whether you can pick the right method, apply the correct factors from the tables, and compare alternatives using MARR as the decision threshold. These are the bread-and-butter problems of engineering economics — expect at least one on exam day.

subtopics.name: Cost & Economic Analysis
subtopics.application: Civil engineers compare alternatives constantly — asphalt vs. concrete over a 30-year life, pump station upgrade vs. status quo, highway widening vs. new interchange. The FE tests whether you can classify costs correctly, find break-even points, compute benefit-cost ratios, and use decision trees to handle uncertainty (pp. 230–231).

lessons.name: Cost Types & Break-Even Analysis
lessons.application: Before you can compare alternatives or run an economic analysis, you need to classify costs correctly. The FE tests whether you can separate fixed from variable costs, recognize sunk costs (and ignore them in decisions), and find the break-even point where two alternatives switch from one being cheaper to the other. Civil engineers use break-even analysis constantly — deciding when to buy vs. rent equipment, choosing between two construction methods at different volumes, or determining whether a capital investment pays for itself within the project timeline. Expect at least one cost-classification or break-even problem on the exam.

lessons.name: Benefit-Cost Analysis & Decision Trees
lessons.application: Public-sector projects live or die by the benefit-cost ratio. When a DOT evaluates a highway interchange, a flood control levee, or a new transit line, the deciding metric is whether public benefits outweigh government costs. The FE tests two skills: computing the conventional B/C ratio and using incremental analysis to choose between mutually exclusive alternatives (you cannot simply pick the highest individual B/C). Decision trees add probability to the picture — you compute expected values at chance nodes and pick the best path at decision nodes. Civil engineers at agencies like USACE, FHWA, and municipal public works use B/C analysis on nearly every capital project, and decision trees show up whenever outcomes depend on uncertain factors like traffic growth, flood frequency, or construction delays.

lessons.name: Rate of Return (IRR)
lessons.application: Decision-makers often want a project's return expressed as a percentage rather than a present worth. As a civil engineer you compute the internal rate of return (IRR) and compare it against a minimum acceptable rate (MARR) to accept or reject projects. On the FE, expect to define the IRR, apply the accept/reject rule, and solve a simple single-cash-flow IRR.

subtopics.name: Depreciation & Finance
subtopics.application: Depreciation determines the book value of infrastructure assets like treatment plants, fleet vehicles, and heavy equipment. The FE tests straight-line and MACRS methods, the inflation-adjusted interest rate, and basic bond/capitalized-cost calculations (pp. 230–231).

lessons.name: Depreciation, Taxation & Inflation
lessons.application: Every capital asset a civil engineering firm owns — excavators, survey equipment, vehicles, even software — loses value over time, and the IRS lets you deduct that loss. The FE tests whether you can compute depreciation using straight-line and MACRS methods, calculate book value, and understand how depreciation affects taxable income. Inflation shows up when you need to convert between real and nominal dollars or adjust an interest rate for purchasing power erosion. These topics tie directly to after-tax cash flow analysis and project justification. Expect at least one depreciation or inflation-adjusted problem on exam day, and the MACRS table is provided right in the handbook (p. 231).

chapters.name: Statics
chapters.context: This chapter tests your ability to analyze forces, moments, and equilibrium in rigid body systems.

subtopics.name: Forces & Equilibrium
subtopics.application: Every structural analysis starts with resolving forces into components and writing equilibrium equations. Whether you are finding the reactions of a simply supported bridge girder, combining dead load, live load, and wind on a building connection, or checking the overturning stability of a retaining wall, the process is the same: draw the free body diagram, resolve forces, and apply ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0.

lessons.name: Force Systems & Resultants
lessons.application: Civil engineers resolve force systems every time they combine dead load, live load, and wind on a structural connection, or find the net effect of soil pressure on a retaining wall. The FE tests whether you can break a force into x and y components, find the resultant of multiple concurrent forces, and compute the moment of a force about a point. These are the building blocks — every equilibrium, truss, and beam problem starts here. The handbook gives you the formulas on p. 94, but the exam tests whether you can apply them quickly with direction cosines, geometry-based resolution, and the cross product.

lessons.name: Equilibrium & Free Body Diagrams
lessons.application: Every structural analysis on the FE starts the same way: draw the free body diagram, identify all forces and reactions, then write the equilibrium equations. Whether you are finding the reactions of a simply supported beam, checking a cantilever retaining wall, or analyzing forces at a bolted connection, the process is the same three equations: $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$, $\sum M = 0$. The FE tests whether you can draw a correct FBD, identify the right number and type of support reactions, and solve for unknowns. Getting the FBD wrong means every calculation afterward is wrong.

subtopics.name: Trusses & Friction
subtopics.application: Civil engineers analyze trusses when designing roof systems, pedestrian bridges, and transmission towers. Method of joints gives you all member forces; method of sections lets you cut straight to the one member you need to size. Friction governs the sliding stability of retaining walls, the traction of vehicles on road surfaces, and belt-driven equipment loads.

lessons.name: Trusses: Method of Joints & Sections
lessons.application: Trusses are one of the highest-frequency statics topics on the FE Civil. You will see roof trusses, bridge trusses, and transmission towers. The exam tests two methods: method of joints (write equilibrium at each joint to find all member forces) and method of sections (cut through the truss and use equilibrium on one side to find specific member forces). It also tests whether you can spot zero-force members instantly. The handbook (p. 97) defines both methods and the zero-force member rules. Knowing when to use joints vs. sections saves critical time on exam day.

lessons.name: Friction
lessons.application: Friction problems on the FE test whether you understand the difference between static and kinetic friction, can identify when impending motion occurs, and can apply the belt friction and screw-jack formulas. Civil engineers check friction when designing retaining walls against sliding, analyzing braking forces on highway grades, and sizing belt-driven equipment. The handbook (pp. 96–97) covers static friction ($F \leq \mu_s N$), screw-jack mechanics, and belt friction. Expect one friction problem on the exam — it is usually straightforward if you set up the normal force correctly.

lessons.name: Frames & Machines
lessons.application: Not every structure is a truss of two-force members. As a civil engineer you analyze frames (stationary structures that support loads) and machines (assemblies that transmit or modify forces), both of which contain multi-force members. On the FE, expect to recognize two-force members, analyze a simple frame or lever by dismembering it, and apply the mechanical advantage of a machine.

subtopics.name: Section Properties
subtopics.application: Centroids locate the neutral axis of composite beam cross-sections and the point of application of distributed loads. Moments of inertia control how much a beam bends and where it fails in flexure. You compute these for composite sections using the parallel axis theorem — built-up steel columns, reinforced concrete T-beams, and timber box beams all require combining individual shape properties about a common axis.

lessons.name: Centroids of Composite Shapes
lessons.application: Centroids locate the neutral axis of beam cross-sections, the point of application of distributed loads, and the center of pressure on submerged surfaces. On the FE, you will decompose a composite shape into simple rectangles, triangles, or circles, look up each piece’s area and centroid from the handbook tables (pp. 98–100), and combine them using the weighted-average formula. The most common exam setup is a T-beam, an L-shape, or a plate with holes. If you can split a shape into pieces and take a weighted average, these are fast points.

lessons.name: Area Moments of Inertia
lessons.application: The moment of inertia (second moment of area) controls how much a beam bends and where it fails in flexure. On the FE, you will look up $I$ for simple shapes from the handbook tables, then combine them using the parallel axis theorem for composite sections. This comes up in beam bending stress ($\sigma = My/I$), beam deflection, and column buckling. The parallel axis theorem is the single most important formula in this lesson — forgetting the $Ad^2$ term is the most common mistake on the exam.

chapters.name: Dynamics
chapters.context: This chapter tests kinematics, kinetics, energy methods, and momentum principles for particles and rigid bodies.

subtopics.name: Kinematics
subtopics.application: Kinematics describes motion without worrying about forces — how fast, how far, what path. Civil engineers use it to derive stopping sight distance on highways, predict projectile trajectories for debris analysis, and calculate the motion of rotating machinery components.

lessons.name: Particle Kinematics
lessons.application: Civil engineers use particle kinematics to derive stopping sight distance on highways, predict how far debris travels after a blast, and calculate the trajectory of water leaving a spillway. On the FE, expect straightforward plug-and-chug with the constant acceleration equations and projectile motion — know which formula connects the variables you're given.

lessons.name: Rigid Body Kinematics & Mass Moments of Inertia
lessons.application: Rigid body kinematics governs anything that rotates — construction crane booms swinging loads, gate valves opening under hydraulic pressure, and rotating equipment on foundations. Mass moment of inertia determines how resistant a body is to angular acceleration, which directly affects vibration analysis of bridge decks and seismic response of buildings. On the FE, expect rotation about a fixed axis and parallel-axis theorem problems using the standard shape table.

subtopics.name: Kinetics & Energy
subtopics.application: Kinetics connects forces to the motion they cause. Civil engineers use Newton's second law to compute dynamic forces from earthquake ground acceleration on a building, impact forces on bridge barriers, and work-energy methods to size pump motors, design guardrails for crash energy absorption, and calculate power requirements for construction equipment.

lessons.name: Force & Acceleration
lessons.application: Newton's second law is how civil engineers compute dynamic forces — earthquake ground acceleration on a building mass, impact forces when a vehicle strikes a bridge barrier, or the forces on a crane boom during a sudden lift. These dynamic forces often exceed static loads and control the design. On the FE, expect ΣF = ma applied to particles and simple rigid body problems with given accelerations.

lessons.name: Work, Energy & Power
lessons.application: Work-energy methods let civil engineers determine how much energy a guardrail must absorb in a vehicle crash, size a pump motor by computing the power needed to lift water, or calculate the energy dissipated by a hydraulic jump in a spillway. On the FE, these problems often skip the force-acceleration approach entirely — if you know positions and speeds but not time, energy methods are faster.

subtopics.name: Momentum & Vibrations
subtopics.application: Impulse-momentum methods handle short-duration forces like vehicle impacts on bridge piers and water jets on turbine blades. Vibration analysis ensures pedestrian bridges don't resonate with footfalls, buildings don't amplify earthquake motion, and machine foundations don't vibrate excessively.

lessons.name: Impulse & Momentum
lessons.application: Impulse-momentum methods handle short-duration forces that are hard to model with F = ma directly — a vehicle slamming into a bridge pier, a water jet striking a turbine blade, or a pile driver hitting a foundation pile. On the FE, expect conservation of momentum for collisions and the coefficient of restitution to distinguish elastic from plastic impacts.

lessons.name: Vibrations & Natural Frequency
lessons.application: Civil engineers check natural frequencies to ensure a pedestrian bridge doesn't resonate with walking footfalls, a building doesn't amplify earthquake ground motion, or a machine foundation doesn't vibrate excessively. If the forcing frequency matches the natural frequency, even small loads cause dangerously large oscillations. On the FE, expect basic natural frequency calculations and understanding of resonance — rarely anything beyond undamped free vibration.

chapters.name: Mechanics of Materials
chapters.context: This chapter tests internal forces, stress-strain analysis, deformations, and stability of structural members.

subtopics.name: Stress, Strain & Material Behavior
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you compute stresses and deformations to check whether structural members are safe and serviceable — axial stress in columns, torsional shear in shafts, and material properties from stress-strain curves. These fundamentals underpin every structural calculation.

lessons.name: Axial Stress, Strain & Deformation
lessons.application: Civil engineers compute axial stress and deformation constantly — checking whether a steel rod can carry a suspension load, sizing a concrete column for gravity forces, or estimating how much a bridge hanger elongates under traffic. Thermal deformation matters too: expansion joints in bridges and buildings exist because steel and concrete grow with temperature. On the FE, axial stress problems are the most straightforward mechanics questions — direct σ = P/A and δ = PL/AE with occasional thermal twists.

lessons.name: Torsion
lessons.application: Civil engineers encounter torsion in spandrel beams loaded eccentrically, in auger piles during installation, and in any shaft transmitting power — pump stations, turbine foundations, and mechanical equipment. The FE handbook formula τ = Tc/J is the torsion equivalent of σ = Mc/I for bending. On the FE, expect straightforward plug-and-chug: given a torque and shaft dimensions, find the maximum shear stress or the angle of twist.

lessons.name: Stress-Strain Diagrams & Material Behavior
lessons.application: The stress-strain curve is how civil engineers evaluate a material before using it in design — it reveals the yield strength for steel column sizing, the modulus of elasticity for deflection calculations, and whether a material fails gradually (ductile) or suddenly (brittle). Concrete is brittle; mild steel is ductile — this distinction drives every seismic detailing decision. On the FE, expect questions that ask you to identify curve features (proportional limit, yield point, ultimate strength) or compute E from the slope.

subtopics.name: Beams
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you design beams by constructing shear and moment diagrams, computing bending and shear stresses from internal forces, and checking deflections against serviceability limits. From floor joists to bridge girders, beam analysis is the most frequently tested mechanics topic.

lessons.name: Shear & Moment Diagrams
lessons.application: Shear and moment diagrams are the first step in designing every beam a civil engineer touches — from a simple floor joist to a continuous bridge girder. The maximum moment tells you how much flexural reinforcement or what steel section you need, and the maximum shear tells you where to place stirrups or stiffen a web. On the FE, expect problems that give you a loaded beam and ask for the maximum shear, maximum moment, or the moment at a specific location.

lessons.name: Bending & Shear Stresses in Beams
lessons.application: Once you know the moment and shear at a cross-section, the next question is: what stresses does the material actually see? Bending stress σ = Mc/I determines whether a steel wide-flange beam has enough section modulus, whether a concrete beam needs more tension reinforcement, or whether a timber joist is overstressed. Transverse shear stress τ = VQ/Ib governs where you place stirrups in concrete and controls web thickness in plate girders. On the FE, expect both formulas with given M, V, and section properties.

lessons.name: Beam Deflections
lessons.application: Deflection limits often control beam design more than strength — a floor beam might be strong enough but deflect so much that the ceiling cracks or feels bouncy underfoot. Building codes limit deflection to L/360 for live load and L/240 for total load. Civil engineers use the deflection tables in the FE handbook to check serviceability without deriving anything. On the FE, expect problems that give you a beam configuration and ask for the maximum deflection or slope using the tables on pp. 140–141.

lessons.name: Transformed Sections & Plastic Moment
lessons.application: Real beams are not always one material or limited to elastic behavior. As a civil engineer you analyze composite beams (steel-reinforced wood, concrete with rebar) using the transformed-section method, and you size steel beams using the plastic moment that develops when the whole section yields. On the FE, expect to compute the modular ratio, apply it to composite bending stress, and find the plastic moment.

subtopics.name: Combined Loading & Stability
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, real members experience combined stresses — axial plus bending, shear plus torsion. You find principal stresses and maximum shear using Mohr's circle, and check slender columns against Euler buckling to prevent sudden stability failures.

lessons.name: Combined Stresses & Mohr's Circle
lessons.application: Real structural members rarely see just one type of stress. A bridge pier experiences axial compression from dead load plus bending from lateral wind. A shaft in a pump station sees torsion and bending simultaneously. Civil engineers combine these stresses and find the principal stresses to check the actual failure condition — the material doesn't know it's seeing "bending plus shear," it just sees stress at a point. Mohr's circle gives a graphical way to find principal stresses, maximum shear stress, and stresses on any rotated plane. On the FE, expect problems that give σx, σy, and τxy and ask for principal stresses or max shear stress.

lessons.name: Column Buckling
lessons.application: Buckling is a sudden, catastrophic failure mode — a steel column can buckle well below its material yield strength if it's too slender. Civil engineers use Euler's formula to determine the critical load for steel wide-flange columns in buildings, bracing members in trusses, and temporary shoring during construction. The effective length factor K depends entirely on how the column ends are connected, and getting K wrong can mean the difference between a safe design and a collapse. On the FE, expect Euler's formula problems where you identify K from end conditions and compute the critical load or critical stress.

chapters.name: Materials
chapters.context: This chapter covers mechanical properties of materials, material testing methods, thermal and processing effects, concrete mix design and curing, aggregates, asphalt, wood and masonry, composite materials, and corrosion — the core materials topics tested on the FE Civil exam.

subtopics.name: Mechanical Properties & Testing
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you interpret tensile test results to verify that steel meets specifications, check Brinell hardness to estimate tensile strength in the field, review Charpy impact data to ensure bridge steel won't become brittle in cold climates, and evaluate fracture toughness to assess crack tolerance. Understanding stress-strain behavior, thermal processing, and phase diagrams lets you predict how materials perform under real-world loading and environmental conditions.

lessons.name: Stress-Strain Behavior & Material Properties
lessons.application: Civil engineers select materials based on mechanical properties — choosing high-yield steel for seismic frames, ductile aluminum for lightweight roofing, or high-modulus concrete for stiff foundations. Understanding how elastic modulus, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility are defined from a tensile test lets you interpret mill certifications, compare materials, and verify that delivered materials meet your design specifications. On the FE, expect questions that require computing stress or strain from test data, finding elastic modulus, or converting between engineering and true values.

lessons.name: Hardness, Impact & Fatigue Testing
lessons.application: Civil engineers use material testing to verify that steel, concrete, and other materials meet project specifications. You’ll review Brinell hardness numbers to estimate tensile strength from a quick field test, check Charpy impact results to ensure bridge steel won’t become brittle in cold climates, and evaluate fatigue data for structures under cyclic loading like highway bridges and crane rails. Fracture toughness determines whether a cracked member fails catastrophically or can tolerate the crack until the next inspection. On the FE, expect BHN-to-TS conversions, fracture toughness calculations, and conceptual questions about fatigue.

lessons.name: Thermal Effects, Processing & Phase Diagrams
lessons.application: Civil engineers account for thermal expansion when designing bridges with expansion joints, sizing gaps between rail sections, and specifying bearing pads that allow movement. You also need to understand how steel is processed — why quenched and tempered steel is harder than hot-rolled, why cold-worked rebar has higher yield strength, and what happens to steel properties at elevated temperatures during a fire. Phase diagrams explain why different heat treatments produce different steel microstructures. On the FE, expect thermal expansion calculations and conceptual questions about heat treatment.

subtopics.name: Concrete Technology
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you specify and approve concrete mixes on nearly every project — setting the water-cement ratio for target strength, specifying air entrainment for freeze-thaw durability, evaluating 7-day and 28-day cylinder break results, and writing curing specifications. Getting these right is the difference between a durable structure and one that cracks, spalls, or fails to meet design strength.

lessons.name: Concrete Mix Design
lessons.application: Concrete mix design is central to virtually every civil engineering project. You specify the water-cement ratio to hit a target compressive strength, decide whether air entrainment is needed for freeze-thaw durability, and choose admixtures like superplasticizers when you need workable concrete without adding excess water. Getting the mix wrong means weak concrete, early cracking, or failed cylinder breaks — any of which can shut down a job site. On the FE, expect questions about the W/C ratio, its relationship to strength, and the effects of air entrainment and admixtures.

lessons.name: Concrete Curing & Strength Development
lessons.application: The curing process makes or breaks concrete performance. As a civil engineer, you write curing specifications, decide when forms can be stripped, and evaluate cylinder break results at 7 and 28 days to verify that the placed concrete meets the design strength. Understanding why moist curing matters, how strength develops over time, and why concrete is reinforced with steel gives you the foundation to manage concrete quality on every project. On the FE, expect questions about curing conditions, the 7-day to 28-day strength relationship, and why concrete needs reinforcement.

subtopics.name: Construction Materials
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you test and proportion the aggregates, asphalt, wood, and masonry that build roadways and structures — checking aggregate gradation, specific gravity, and absorption; verifying asphalt air voids, VMA, and VFA against mix-design targets; and accounting for wood moisture content and masonry mortar types. These material checks ensure pavements and assemblies meet specification and perform durably.

lessons.name: Aggregate Properties & Gradation
lessons.application: Aggregates make up 60--75% of concrete by volume and the bulk of asphalt mixes and base courses. As a civil engineer you specify and test their gradation, specific gravity, and absorption to proportion mixes correctly — too much absorption steals mix water, and a poorly graded aggregate wastes paste or binder. On the FE, expect to compute absorption, bulk specific gravity, and fineness modulus from lab data.

lessons.name: Asphalt Concrete Mix Design
lessons.application: Hot-mix asphalt (HMA) is aggregate bound by asphalt cement, and its performance is governed by volumetric properties — chiefly the air voids. As a civil engineer you check that a mix meets target air voids (about 4%), adequate voids in the mineral aggregate (VMA), and a reasonable voids-filled-with-asphalt (VFA). On the FE, expect to compute air voids and the VMA/VFA relationships from specific gravities.

lessons.name: Wood & Masonry
lessons.application: Wood and masonry are workhorse construction materials with behavior very different from steel and concrete. As a civil engineer you account for wood's moisture sensitivity and adjust its allowable stresses for service conditions, and you specify masonry units and mortar types to meet strength and durability needs. On the FE, expect to compute moisture content and to reason about adjustment factors, mortar types, and specified masonry strength.

subtopics.name: Composites & Material Selection
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you encounter composites in FRP bridge decks, carbon fiber wraps for column strengthening, and fiber-reinforced concrete. You also manage corrosion on every project with exposed metals — selecting coatings, specifying cathodic protection, and avoiding galvanic couples between dissimilar metals. The rule of mixtures lets you estimate composite properties, while the galvanic series guides material compatibility decisions.

lessons.name: Composite Materials
lessons.application: Civil engineers encounter composites in fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) bridge decks, carbon fiber wraps for strengthening concrete columns, and glass fiber reinforced concrete panels. Understanding the rule of mixtures lets you estimate a composite’s density, stiffness, and strength from the properties and volume fractions of its components — critical for evaluating whether an FRP alternative can replace a traditional steel or concrete member. On the FE, expect rule-of-mixtures calculations for modulus and density.

lessons.name: Corrosion & Material Selection
lessons.application: Civil engineers deal with corrosion on every project that involves metals in contact with water, soil, or dissimilar metals. You select coatings for bridge steel, specify cathodic protection for buried pipelines, and avoid connecting dissimilar metals (like aluminum flashing on a steel beam) without an insulating barrier. Understanding galvanic corrosion and the electrochemical series lets you predict which metal corrodes in a couple and design around it. On the FE, expect questions about anode/cathode identification, galvanic corrosion, and basic material comparison.

chapters.name: Fluid Mechanics
chapters.context: This chapter covers fluid properties, hydrostatic pressure and forces, Bernoulli's equation, pipe flow and head loss, the momentum equation, flow measurement devices, and dimensional analysis — the core fluid mechanics topics tested on the FE Civil exam.

subtopics.name: Fluid Properties & Statics
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you need fluid properties to size every hydraulic system. Density and specific weight let you compute hydrostatic forces on dams and retaining walls. Viscosity determines whether flow is laminar or turbulent in water mains. Manometers and pressure calculations are how you verify pressures in the field and on design drawings. Buoyancy governs whether a buried tank floats out of saturated ground.

lessons.name: Fluid Properties
lessons.application: Civil engineers need fluid properties for every hydraulic calculation. Density and specific weight let you compute hydrostatic forces on dams and retaining walls. Viscosity determines whether flow in a water main is laminar or turbulent, which controls friction losses and pipe sizing. Specific gravity lets you compare fluids to water quickly. On the FE, expect questions that require converting between density, specific weight, and specific gravity, or applying viscosity in a shear stress calculation.

lessons.name: Hydrostatic Pressure & Manometers
lessons.application: Civil engineers compute hydrostatic pressure to design water tanks, dams, and buried pipes. Gauge pressure at depth tells you the force on a valve or the water pressure at a fire hydrant. Manometers — U-tubes filled with a denser fluid like mercury — are a classic FE problem type where you step through each fluid column adding or subtracting γh. On the FE, expect problems that require computing pressure at a point, converting between gauge and absolute pressure, or analyzing a manometer.

lessons.name: Hydrostatic Forces & Buoyancy
lessons.application: Civil engineers calculate hydrostatic forces to design dams, gates, and lock chambers. The resultant force on a submerged surface acts at the center of pressure — not the centroid — which matters for computing overturning moments. Buoyancy governs whether a buried tank floats out of saturated ground, how much a barge settles under load, and the uplift on submerged foundations. On the FE, expect problems requiring the hydrostatic force on a flat surface, locating the center of pressure, or applying Archimedes’ principle.

subtopics.name: Fluid Dynamics
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, continuity and Bernoulli's equation are the first tools you reach for in any pipe or channel analysis. The Darcy-Weisbach equation gives you friction head loss for pipe sizing, and the momentum equation lets you compute forces at pipe bends and nozzles — which is how you design thrust blocks and restrained joints for water mains.

lessons.name: Continuity & Bernoulli’s Equation
lessons.application: The continuity equation and Bernoulli’s equation are the two most-used tools in hydraulic design. Continuity (Q = Av) tells you how velocity changes when a pipe transitions from one diameter to another. Bernoulli connects pressure, velocity, and elevation along a streamline — letting you determine if a hydrant will deliver adequate pressure or compute the velocity of a jet at a spillway. On the FE, these two equations often appear together in a single problem: use continuity to find the velocity, then Bernoulli to find the pressure.

lessons.name: Pipe Flow & Head Loss
lessons.application: Civil engineers size water mains, sewage force mains, and fire protection systems by computing head loss. The Darcy-Weisbach equation gives friction head loss in any pipe, while the Hazen-Williams equation is the shortcut for water-only systems. The Reynolds number tells you if flow is laminar or turbulent — which determines whether you read the Moody diagram for the friction factor or use the laminar formula directly. On the FE, expect problems that require computing head loss, finding the friction factor from the Moody diagram, or comparing flow regimes.

lessons.name: Momentum Equation
lessons.application: Civil engineers use the momentum equation to compute forces at pipe bends, tees, and reducers — which is how you design thrust blocks and restrained joints for water mains. It also gives the force on a bridge pier from river flow and the reaction force from a fire hose nozzle. On the FE, momentum problems typically involve a pipe bend at some angle, where you solve for the force components using the impulse-momentum principle.

subtopics.name: Flow Analysis & Measurement
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you measure flow to monitor treatment processes, calibrate hydraulic models, and verify stormwater controls. Pitot tubes, venturi meters, and orifice plates each exploit Bernoulli's principle to give you velocity or flow rate. Dimensional analysis and similitude let you build scale models of spillways and bridge decks that actually predict full-scale behavior.

lessons.name: Flow Measurement
lessons.application: Civil engineers measure flow to monitor water treatment, calibrate hydraulic models, and verify stormwater controls. Pitot tubes measure point velocity from stagnation pressure. Venturi meters and orifice plates measure flow rate in closed conduits using the Bernoulli principle with a calibration coefficient. On the FE, expect problems using the Pitot tube equation or computing flow through a venturi or orifice meter.

lessons.name: Dimensional Analysis & Similitude
lessons.application: Civil engineers use dimensional analysis when building physical models — a scale model of a spillway in a hydraulics lab or a wind tunnel model of a bridge deck. The Buckingham Pi theorem tells you how many dimensionless groups exist. Similitude rules (Reynolds, Froude) tell you which parameters to match so model results predict full-scale behavior. On the FE, expect problems using the Pi theorem to count dimensionless groups or applying Froude similitude to scale model results.

chapters.name: Surveying
chapters.context: This chapter covers angles, bearings, and distances; differential leveling; traverse computations; area and volume calculations; and horizontal and vertical curve design — the core surveying topics tested on the FE Civil exam.

subtopics.name: Measurement & Leveling
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, every project starts with measuring angles, distances, and elevations. You convert between bearings and azimuths, run level loops to establish grades for drainage, and close traverses to verify accuracy. Getting the survey wrong means the entire design is wrong — from building pad elevations to sewer inverts.

lessons.name: Angles, Distances & Bearings
lessons.application: Every civil engineering project starts with a survey — measuring angles and distances to establish property boundaries, construction staking, and control points. You need to convert between bearings (N 45° E) and azimuths (045°), and understand how angles are measured in the field. On the FE, expect problems converting bearings to azimuths, computing horizontal distances from slope measurements, and interpreting survey data.

lessons.name: Differential Leveling
lessons.application: Civil engineers use differential leveling to establish elevations for drainage design, building pad grades, road profiles, and sewer inverts. A level run gives you the elevation difference between benchmarks, and closing the loop back to a known point tells you the accuracy of your survey. On the FE, expect problems computing elevations using the Height of Instrument (HI) method, identifying BS and FS readings, and checking level loop closures.

subtopics.name: Area, Volume & Traverse
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you compute traverse closures to verify boundary surveys, use the coordinate method to determine property areas and impervious surface coverage, and calculate earthwork volumes for cut-and-fill estimating. These computations directly affect project costs, regulatory compliance, and legal property descriptions.

lessons.name: Traverse Computations
lessons.application: Civil engineers run traverses to establish control points on job sites and verify property boundary closures. You compute latitudes (north-south) and departures (east-west) for each course, check that the traverse closes, and distribute any error using the compass rule. A traverse that doesn’t close within tolerance means the survey data can’t be trusted for design or legal purposes. On the FE, expect problems computing latitudes and departures, finding closure error, and applying the compass rule adjustment.

lessons.name: Area Computations
lessons.application: Civil engineers compute areas for property plats, right-of-way acquisitions, impervious surface calculations in stormwater reports, and wetland delineation boundaries. The coordinate method (also called the shoelace formula) gives exact areas from survey coordinates. The trapezoidal rule and Simpson’s 1/3 rule approximate areas from equally spaced measurements. On the FE, expect problems using the coordinate method to compute the area of a polygon from its vertex coordinates.

lessons.name: Earthwork & Volume Computations
lessons.application: Civil engineers compute earthwork volumes to estimate project costs, balance cut and fill quantities, and verify contractor pay quantities. The average end area method is the workhorse for road and site grading projects — you compute cross-section areas at each station, then multiply by the distance between stations to get volume. On the FE, expect problems computing volumes using the average end area or prismoidal formula.

lessons.name: Coordinate Geometry & Systems
lessons.application: Modern surveying stores points as coordinates (easting, northing). As a civil engineer you compute a new point's coordinates from a known point and a measured course (forward computation), and recover the distance and direction between two known points (inverse computation). On the FE, expect to apply these and to understand plane coordinate systems like State Plane.

subtopics.name: Horizontal & Vertical Curves
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you design horizontal curves to provide adequate sight distance and superelevation for the design speed, and vertical curves to ensure stopping sight distance over crests and headlight illumination through sags. Curve geometry determines lane widths, right-of-way requirements, and grading quantities.

lessons.name: Horizontal Curves
lessons.application: Civil engineers design horizontal curves for road alignments that connect tangent sections. The curve geometry — radius, tangent distance, curve length, and external distance — determines lane widths, superelevation, and sight distance. On the FE, expect problems computing curve elements (R, T, L, E, M) from the degree of curve or intersection angle, and checking superelevation requirements.

lessons.name: Vertical Curves
lessons.application: Civil engineers design vertical curves — parabolic profiles that transition between road grades. Crest curves must provide adequate stopping sight distance over the top, and sag curves must allow headlight illumination. You compute elevations at any point on the curve using the PVC elevation, the grades, and the curve length. On the FE, expect problems finding the elevation at a specific station on a vertical curve, locating the high or low point, and selecting the minimum curve length for sight distance.

chapters.name: Water Resources & Env.
chapters.context: This is the highest-weighted chapter — covering open channel flow, hydrology, groundwater, and environmental engineering.

subtopics.name: Hydraulics
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you design open channels, storm sewers, and water distribution systems using Manning's equation, Hazen-Williams, and weir formulas. You classify flow as subcritical or supercritical using the Froude number, compute critical depth for channel transitions, and size pumps and pipes to deliver adequate pressure and flow while guarding against cavitation.

lessons.name: Open-Channel Flow & Manning's Equation
lessons.application: Civil engineers size every ditch, swale, culvert, and storm sewer using Manning's equation. You select the roughness coefficient based on channel lining, compute the hydraulic radius from the cross-section geometry, and solve for discharge or normal depth. On the FE, expect problems computing flow in rectangular or circular channels, selecting Manning's $n$, and applying the 1.486 conversion factor for US Customary units.

lessons.name: Specific Energy & Critical Flow
lessons.application: Civil engineers use specific energy to classify flow as subcritical or supercritical, design channel transitions, and analyze hydraulic jumps. Knowing the critical depth tells you whether your channel is operating safely above or below the energy minimum. On the FE, expect problems computing critical depth in rectangular channels, classifying flow with the Froude number, and finding conjugate depths across a hydraulic jump.

lessons.name: Hazen-Williams & Weir Formulas
lessons.application: Civil engineers use the Hazen-Williams equation to size water distribution mains and compute head loss in pipe networks. Weir formulas measure flow at treatment plants, streams, and detention pond outlets. On the FE, expect problems computing pipe velocity with Hazen-Williams, selecting the C coefficient for different pipe materials, and calculating discharge over rectangular or V-notch weirs.

lessons.name: Pumps & Water Distribution
lessons.application: Civil engineers size the pumps that move water through supply, distribution, and wastewater systems. On the FE, expect to compute the power a pump draws (accounting for efficiency), find the net positive suction head available to guard against cavitation, and relate pump head to the static lift plus friction losses of the system.

subtopics.name: Hydrology & Groundwater
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you estimate peak runoff using the Rational Method and SCS/NRCS curve number, predict hydrograph shapes with unit hydrograph theory, and evaluate groundwater flow with Darcy's law and well hydraulics. These methods drive the design of storm drains, detention ponds, dewatering systems, and water supply wells.

lessons.name: Rainfall-Runoff Methods
lessons.application: Civil engineers use the Rational Method to size storm drains for small catchments and the SCS/NRCS Curve Number method for larger watersheds and detention pond design. You pull rainfall data from intensity-duration-frequency curves, estimate the runoff coefficient or curve number from land cover and soil type, and compute the peak flow your drainage system must handle. On the FE, expect problems applying Q = CIA for the Rational Method and computing runoff depth from the SCS equation.

lessons.name: Hydrographs & Watershed Analysis
lessons.application: Civil engineers use hydrographs to predict the shape and timing of runoff — not just the peak flow, but how long the storm takes to arrive, peak, and recede. You need the full hydrograph to size detention ponds, route flows through a reservoir, and design outlet structures. Watershed characteristics like time of concentration and drainage area control how fast runoff reaches the outlet. On the FE, expect problems scaling unit hydrographs, computing time of concentration, and applying the hydrologic mass balance.

lessons.name: Groundwater & Wells
lessons.application: Civil engineers use Darcy's law to estimate seepage under dams, flow to dewatering systems, and contaminant transport through aquifers. Well hydraulics (Dupuit and Thiem equations) let you compute drawdown at a pumping well and determine whether pumping will affect neighboring properties. On the FE, expect problems computing Darcy velocity vs. seepage velocity, finding well discharge from drawdown data, and distinguishing confined from unconfined aquifer behavior.

subtopics.name: Water Quality & Treatment
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you evaluate water and wastewater treatment performance using BOD, dissolved oxygen models, and design parameters like overflow rate, F:M ratio, and solids residence time. You size clarifiers, filters, activated sludge basins, and disinfection systems; set chlorine doses and CT; and check hardness and contaminant levels against Safe Drinking Water Act and NPDES limits.

lessons.name: Water Quality & BOD
lessons.application: Civil engineers monitor BOD, dissolved oxygen, and other water quality parameters to evaluate treatment plant performance and assess the impact of discharges on receiving streams. The Streeter-Phelps model predicts how dissolved oxygen changes downstream of a wastewater outfall. On the FE, expect problems computing BOD at a given time, finding the critical oxygen deficit, and applying temperature corrections to rate constants.

lessons.name: Water & Wastewater Treatment
lessons.application: Civil engineers design and evaluate treatment processes for drinking water and wastewater. You size clarifiers based on overflow rate, compute the food-to-microorganism ratio for activated sludge, and determine solids residence time. On the FE, expect problems computing overflow rate for a settling basin, determining treatment efficiency, and applying activated sludge design parameters.

lessons.name: Drinking Water Treatment & Disinfection
lessons.application: Civil engineers design the conventional surface-water treatment train — coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, and disinfection — to turn raw water into safe drinking water. On the FE, expect to compute a filter loading rate, set a chlorine dose from demand plus required residual, and apply the CT concept for disinfection credit.

lessons.name: Drinking Water Standards & Hardness
lessons.application: Civil engineers design treatment to meet federal water-quality regulations and to deliver water of acceptable hardness. On the FE, expect to distinguish enforceable health-based standards from aesthetic ones, compute total hardness expressed as CaCO₃, and determine the removal efficiency a process must achieve to meet a discharge limit.

chapters.name: Structural Engineering
chapters.context: This chapter tests structural analysis, load combinations, and the design of reinforced concrete and steel members.

subtopics.name: Analysis & Load Combinations
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you solve member forces in trusses (method of joints and sections), compute deflections of determinate beams, trusses, and frames (unit-load / virtual work), classify structures as determinate or indeterminate (and handle a single redundant), build influence lines for moving loads, and apply ASCE 7 load combinations to size every member.

lessons.name: Determinacy & Stability
lessons.application: Before analyzing any structure, a civil engineer must determine whether it is stable and whether it is statically determinate or indeterminate. Counting members, reactions, and joints tells you if the structure has enough constraints or too many. If the count fails, the structure is a mechanism and will collapse. On the FE, expect problems classifying trusses and frames using the standard equations.

lessons.name: Truss Analysis: Joints & Sections
lessons.application: Finding member forces in a determinate truss is a bread-and-butter FE structural-analysis skill. The method of joints gets you forces at a connection; the method of sections cuts straight to one member without solving the whole truss. Knowing when to use each — and spotting zero-force members instantly — saves real time on the exam.

lessons.name: Deflection of Determinate Structures
lessons.application: The FE asks you to find how far a determinate beam, truss, or frame moves under load — for serviceability checks and to set up indeterminate analysis. The unit-load (virtual work) method is the general tool, and for common beams you simply look up a deflection formula. Both show up on the exam.

lessons.name: Elementary Indeterminate Structures
lessons.application: Real structures are usually statically indeterminate — continuous beams, fixed-end members, propped cantilevers. The FE keeps this elementary: count the degree of indeterminacy, then handle a single redundant with the force method (consistent deformations) or recall standard results like the propped-cantilever reaction and fixed-end moments.

lessons.name: Loads & Load Combinations
lessons.application: Every structural design begins with load combinations from ASCE 7. You factor dead, live, wind, snow, and seismic loads using prescribed multipliers to ensure adequate safety. LRFD (strength design) factors loads up and compares to nominal strength; ASD (allowable stress) uses unfactored loads against reduced allowable capacity. On the FE, expect problems computing the controlling factored load and applying live load reduction.

lessons.name: Influence Lines
lessons.application: Influence lines tell you where to place a moving load to produce the maximum structural response — maximum reaction, shear, or moment at a specific point. This is critical for bridge design where truck loads travel across a span. On the FE, expect problems using influence line ordinates to compute maximum effects from one or more concentrated loads.

subtopics.name: Reinforced Concrete Design
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you design reinforced concrete beams, columns, slabs, and footings on most building and infrastructure projects. You compute required flexural reinforcement using the Whitney stress block, check shear capacity and add stirrups when needed, and verify that columns can carry the factored axial load.

lessons.name: RC Beams: Flexure & Shear
lessons.application: Reinforced concrete beam design is the most heavily tested structural design topic on the FE. You compute the Whitney stress block depth to find moment capacity, then check whether the concrete alone can carry the shear or if stirrups are needed. On the FE, expect problems computing nominal moment capacity from given reinforcement, checking shear adequacy, and finding required stirrup spacing.

lessons.name: RC Columns
lessons.application: Reinforced concrete columns carry axial load and moment simultaneously. On the FE, the most common problem type is computing the maximum axial load capacity of a short tied column using the ACI formula. You also need to know the reinforcement ratio limits and the difference between tension-controlled and compression-controlled sections. Interaction diagrams appear in the handbook but are rarely tested numerically.

subtopics.name: Steel Design
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, steel design means selecting W-shapes from the AISC manual to resist the required loads. You check beams for flexure and lateral-torsional buckling, columns for axial capacity and slenderness, and tension members for yielding and rupture on the net section.

lessons.name: Steel Beams
lessons.application: Steel beam design per AISC 360-16 centers on checking flexural strength and lateral-torsional buckling (LTB). If the beam is fully braced, it reaches its full plastic moment. If the unbraced length exceeds a threshold, the capacity drops. On the FE, expect problems computing the plastic moment capacity, selecting beam sizes from AISC tables, and checking whether LTB reduces the available strength.

lessons.name: Steel Columns
lessons.application: Steel column design revolves around buckling. The critical stress depends on the slenderness ratio KL/r and whether the column buckles inelastically or elastically. The AISC Table 4-14 in the FE Handbook gives available critical stress directly from KL/r, making the design process a table lookup. On the FE, expect problems computing the slenderness ratio and the design compressive strength.

lessons.name: Steel Tension Members
lessons.application: Steel tension members (braces, truss chords, hangers) must be checked for two failure modes: yielding on the gross section and rupture on the net section through bolt holes. The controlling limit state — whichever gives the smaller design strength — governs. On the FE, expect problems computing net area with bolt holes, effective net area with the shear lag factor U, and determining which limit state controls.

chapters.name: Geotechnical Eng.
chapters.context: This chapter covers soil classification, phase relations, effective stress, consolidation, shear strength, permeability and seepage, slope stability, bearing capacity, lateral earth pressure, retaining walls, deep foundations, and soil improvement.

subtopics.name: Soil Properties & Classification
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you classify soils using USCS and AASHTO systems, compute phase relations from lab data (water content, unit weight, void ratio), and construct effective stress profiles through layered soil with a water table. These fundamentals underpin every geotechnical design calculation.

lessons.name: Phase Relations
lessons.application: Every soil sample is a mixture of solids, water, and air. Phase relations convert between the properties you measure in the lab (water content, unit weight) and the properties you need for design (void ratio, degree of saturation). On the FE, expect 2–3 problems that give you some soil properties and ask you to compute the others using the phase diagram relationships.

lessons.name: Soil Classification
lessons.application: Soil classification communicates subsurface conditions in a standard language. The Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) assigns a two-letter symbol based on grain size and plasticity. The AASHTO system rates soils for highway subgrade suitability. On the FE, expect problems that give sieve data and Atterberg limits and ask you to classify the soil or compute the coefficient of uniformity.

lessons.name: Effective Stress
lessons.application: Effective stress is the single most important concept in geotechnical engineering. It is the stress carried by the soil skeleton, and it controls strength, compressibility, and volume change. When a water table is present, you subtract the pore water pressure from the total stress to get the effective stress. On the FE, expect problems drawing stress profiles through layered soils with and without a water table.

subtopics.name: Consolidation & Shear Strength
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you predict how much a clay layer will settle under new loading using the consolidation e-log p curve, and you determine soil shear strength from triaxial tests to check foundation, slope, and retaining wall stability.

lessons.name: Consolidation & Settlement
lessons.application: When load is applied to saturated clay, water slowly squeezes out and the soil compresses over time — this is consolidation. You compute total settlement using the compression index and the e-log p curve, then predict how long it takes using the time factor. On the FE, expect problems computing settlement with the three consolidation cases and using the time factor table.

lessons.name: Shear Strength of Soils
lessons.application: Soil shear strength controls whether foundations, slopes, and retaining structures are stable. The Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion defines the maximum shear stress a soil can resist on any plane.
