On the FE, expect problems computing shear strength from given parameters, or extracting the friction angle from triaxial test results using the Mohr circle.

subtopics.name: Seepage & Slope Stability
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you use Darcy's law and flow nets to quantify seepage through dams and excavations, check the critical hydraulic gradient against quick (boiling) conditions, and compute the factor of safety of natural and engineered slopes — including the destabilizing effect of seepage after rainfall.

lessons.name: Permeability & Seepage
lessons.application: Water moving through soil controls dewatering, drainage, and the stability of dams, levees, and excavations. As a civil engineer you use Darcy's law to estimate flow, flow nets to quantify seepage under structures, and the critical hydraulic gradient to guard against quick (boiling) conditions. On the FE, expect to compute discharge, seepage quantity from a flow net, and the critical gradient.

lessons.name: Slope Stability
lessons.application: Embankments, cut slopes, levees, and natural hillsides can fail by sliding along a slip surface. As a civil engineer you compute a factor of safety comparing the soil's shearing resistance to the driving force of gravity. On the FE, expect the infinite-slope factor of safety for cohesionless soil, the effect of seepage, and the planar slip-surface factor of safety.

subtopics.name: Foundations & Earth Pressures
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you compute bearing capacity to size foundations, calculate lateral earth pressures to design retaining walls, and check walls for overturning, sliding, and bearing failure. These are the most common geotechnical design tasks in practice.

lessons.name: Bearing Capacity
lessons.application: Bearing capacity is the maximum pressure a foundation can apply to the soil before a shear failure occurs. Terzaghi’s equation uses bearing capacity factors that depend on the friction angle, plus contributions from cohesion, overburden, and footing width. On the FE, expect problems computing ultimate or allowable bearing capacity for strip footings with given Nc, Nq, and Nγ values.

lessons.name: Lateral Earth Pressure
lessons.application: Lateral earth pressure is the horizontal force that soil exerts on retaining walls, basement walls, and braced excavations. The pressure depends on wall movement: active (wall moves away), passive (wall pushes into soil), or at-rest (rigid wall, no movement). On the FE, expect problems computing the Rankine coefficients Ka, Kp, or K0 and the resulting force on a wall.

lessons.name: Retaining Wall Stability
lessons.application: Retaining wall design requires checking three failure modes: overturning about the toe, sliding along the base, and bearing capacity failure beneath the footing. Each check produces a factor of safety. On the FE, expect problems computing the FS against overturning or sliding, or finding the eccentricity and maximum base pressure under the wall.

subtopics.name: Deep Foundations & Soil Improvement
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you turn to deep foundations (piles, drilled shafts) when surface soils are too weak — combining end bearing and skin friction for capacity — and you improve weak ground by compaction (verified against a Proctor maximum) and chemical stabilization (lime for clays, cement for granular soils).

lessons.name: Deep Foundations
lessons.application: When near-surface soils are too weak or compressible to carry a structure on shallow footings, civil engineers use deep foundations — driven piles or drilled shafts — to transfer load to deeper, stronger soil or rock. On the FE, expect to combine end bearing and skin friction into a total pile capacity and to reason about when deep foundations are needed and how pile groups behave.

lessons.name: Compaction & Soil Improvement
lessons.application: Before building on or with soil, civil engineers densify and improve it. Compaction increases strength and reduces settlement, and is verified in the field against a laboratory maximum dry density. As a civil engineer you run Proctor tests, specify relative compaction, evaluate relative density of granular fills, and select stabilization methods. On the FE, expect relative compaction, relative density, and stabilization questions.

chapters.name: Transportation Eng.
chapters.context: This chapter covers highway geometric design, traffic engineering, travel demand planning, traffic control devices, flexible and rigid pavement design, and earthwork calculations.

subtopics.name: Geometric Design
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you design roads that let drivers see far enough to stop safely, transition smoothly between grades on vertical curves, and navigate horizontal curves at the design speed with proper superelevation. These geometric elements control safety, cost, and right-of-way requirements.

lessons.name: Stopping Sight Distance & PHF
lessons.application: Stopping sight distance (SSD) is the minimum distance a driver needs to see ahead to stop safely for an unexpected obstacle. It controls everything from vertical curve design to horizontal clearance requirements. The FE Handbook provides the SSD formula with a deceleration rate and grade adjustment, plus intersection sight distance (ISD) for stop-controlled approaches. Expect problems plugging into the SSD formula with or without grade, and computing the Peak Hour Factor from 15-minute traffic counts.

lessons.name: Vertical Curve Design
lessons.application: Vertical curves are parabolas that transition between two road grades. Crest curves must provide adequate sight distance over the hill; sag curves must illuminate the road with headlights at night. The FE Handbook gives separate formulas for crest and sag curves, each with S ≤ L and S > L cases. Expect problems computing minimum curve length from sight distance, finding the tangent offset at the PVI, or using the K-value to compare designs.

lessons.name: Horizontal Curve Design
lessons.application: Horizontal curves guide vehicles through direction changes on a roadway. The curve geometry is defined by the radius (R), degree of curve (D), and intersection angle (I). Engineers compute tangent length, curve length, and middle ordinate to lay out the curve in the field, then set the superelevation rate to counteract centrifugal force at the design speed. On the FE, expect problems converting between R and D, computing T and L, or finding the required superelevation.

subtopics.name: Traffic Engineering
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you time traffic signals to balance safety and efficiency, analyze traffic flow using the Greenshields model, evaluate freeway capacity and level of service, and measure crash rates to compare safety performance across locations.

lessons.name: Traffic Signal Timing
lessons.application: Traffic signal timing balances safety and efficiency at intersections. The yellow interval gives drivers time to stop or clear the intersection; the all-red clearance protects crossing traffic; and the pedestrian green ensures walkers can cross safely. The FE Handbook provides formulas for all three. Expect problems computing the yellow interval from approach speed and deceleration, the red clearance from intersection width, or the minimum pedestrian green time.

lessons.name: Traffic Flow & Crash Rates
lessons.application: Traffic flow theory describes the relationship between speed, density, and flow on a roadway. The Greenshields model assumes a linear speed-density relationship, which produces a parabolic flow-density curve with a single peak (maximum flow). Crash rate formulas let engineers compare the safety performance of intersections and road segments using a per-million-vehicle exposure rate. On the FE, expect problems finding maximum flow or speed from Greenshields, or computing RMEV/RMVM from crash and traffic data.

lessons.name: Freeway Capacity & Level of Service
lessons.application: Freeway capacity analysis converts a raw traffic volume into a per-lane passenger-car flow rate, then compares the resulting density to the LOS table to rate the facility from A (free flow) through F (breakdown). The conversion accounts for the peak hour factor (PHF), number of lanes, and the presence of heavy vehicles using the passenger car equivalent (PCE). On the FE, expect problems computing the heavy-vehicle adjustment factor, the demand flow rate, or determining the LOS from density.

subtopics.name: Planning & Traffic Operations
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you forecast travel with the four-step model and distribute trips between zones using the gravity model, and you apply the MUTCD to select signs, markings, and signals — installing a signal only when a warrant is met. These planning and operations tasks shape demand and safety before and after a road is built.

lessons.name: Travel Demand & Trip Distribution
lessons.application: Before a road or transit line is designed, planners forecast how many trips will use it and where they will go. As a civil engineer you apply the four-step travel demand model and use the gravity model to distribute trips among destination zones. On the FE, expect to identify the planning steps and to compute trips between zones with the gravity model.

lessons.name: Traffic Control Devices & Warrants
lessons.application: Signs, signals, and markings are how engineers communicate with drivers. As a civil engineer you apply the MUTCD to select and place these devices, recognize sign categories by shape and color, and understand that a traffic signal is installed only when a warrant is met. On the FE, expect conceptual questions on device categories and signal warrants.

subtopics.name: Pavement Design & Earthwork
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you design flexible pavement sections using the AASHTO structural number equation, design rigid (concrete) slabs that carry load by beam action, convert mixed axle loads to ESALs, and compute earthwork volumes between cross sections to estimate cut-and-fill quantities for highway construction.

lessons.name: Pavement Design (AASHTO)
lessons.application: The AASHTO method designs flexible (asphalt) pavements by computing the required Structural Number (SN) from traffic loading and soil support, then selecting layer thicknesses that provide that SN. Each layer contributes based on its structural coefficient and drainage condition. Load equivalency factors convert mixed axle loads to 18-kip equivalent single-axle loads (ESALs). On the FE, expect problems computing SN from given layers, solving for a missing layer thickness, or applying load equivalency factors.

lessons.name: Earthwork Volumes
lessons.application: Earthwork calculations determine how much soil must be excavated (cut) or placed (fill) along a highway corridor. Engineers compute volumes between cross sections using the average end area method or the more accurate prismoidal formula. These volumes drive project cost estimates and the mass haul diagram that optimizes where cut material is moved to fill areas. On the FE, expect problems applying both volume formulas and converting cubic feet to cubic yards.

lessons.name: Rigid Pavement Design
lessons.application: Highways and airfields use rigid (Portland cement concrete) pavement where heavy loads and long service life justify it. As a civil engineer you should understand how a rigid slab carries load differently from flexible asphalt, what the modulus of subgrade reaction represents, and why joints and dowels are used. On the FE, expect conceptual questions comparing rigid and flexible pavement and on joint function.

chapters.name: Construction Eng.
chapters.context: This chapter covers CPM scheduling, earned value analysis, project delivery methods, and construction safety.

subtopics.name: CPM Scheduling
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, CPM scheduling is how you plan and track construction projects. You identify activities, durations, and dependencies, then compute early/late start and finish times. The forward pass finds the earliest each activity can start; the backward pass finds the latest without delaying the project. Activities with zero total float form the critical path — any delay on the critical path delays the entire project.

lessons.name: CPM Scheduling Basics
lessons.application: The Critical Path Method (CPM) is how civil engineers plan and control construction projects. Every activity has a duration and dependencies on other activities. The network diagram shows the sequence, and the critical path identifies which activities control the project completion date. On the FE, expect problems involving precedence relationships, reading network diagrams, and understanding the difference between activity-on-node and activity-on-arrow notation.

lessons.name: Forward & Backward Pass
lessons.application: The forward pass computes the earliest each activity can start and finish; the backward pass computes the latest each can start and finish without delaying the project. Together they reveal total float and identify the critical path. On the FE, expect problems that give a small network and ask you to compute ES, EF, LS, or LF for specific activities using these two passes.

lessons.name: Float & Critical Path
lessons.application: Total float tells you how much an activity can slip without delaying the project. Free float tells you how much it can slip without affecting any successor. Activities with zero total float form the critical path — the longest chain through the network that controls the project duration. On the FE, expect problems computing total float, identifying critical activities, and distinguishing total float from free float.

subtopics.name: Earned Value Management
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer managing a project, earned value analysis lets you track cost and schedule performance simultaneously. BCWS is what you planned to spend, BCWP is the budgeted value of work completed, and ACWP is what you actually spent. Cost and schedule variances tell you if you are over/under budget and ahead/behind schedule. Performance indices (CPI, SPI) and forecasting formulas (ETC, EAC) predict total cost at completion.

lessons.name: Earned Value Analysis
lessons.application: Earned value analysis (EVA) tracks project performance by comparing three cost curves: what you planned to spend (BCWS), what the work is actually worth (BCWP), and what you actually spent (ACWP). The cost variance tells you if you are over or under budget; the schedule variance tells you if you are ahead or behind schedule. On the FE, expect problems computing CV and SV from given values, or interpreting what the signs mean.

lessons.name: Performance Indices & Forecasting
lessons.application: Performance indices (CPI and SPI) normalize the cost and schedule variances into ratios, making it easy to compare projects of different sizes. Forecasting formulas use the CPI to predict the total cost at completion (EAC) and the remaining cost (ETC). On the FE, expect problems computing CPI/SPI and using them to forecast the estimate at completion.

subtopics.name: Project Delivery & Safety
subtopics.application: As a civil engineer, you work within different project delivery systems — design-bid-build, design-build, and CM-at-risk — each allocating risk and responsibility differently. You also must understand OSHA construction safety requirements: excavation protection at 5 ft, fall protection at 6 ft, and PE-designed systems for excavations deeper than 20 ft. These topics appear as scenario-based questions on the FE.

lessons.name: Project Delivery Methods
lessons.application: Project delivery methods define how design and construction responsibilities are allocated between the owner, designer, and contractor. The choice affects cost risk, schedule control, and change-order authority. Design-bid-build is the traditional method; design-build combines responsibilities under one entity; CM-at-risk brings the contractor in early for cost input. On the FE, expect scenario-based questions asking you to identify which delivery method fits a given situation.

lessons.name: Construction Safety (OSHA)
lessons.application: OSHA regulations set minimum safety standards for construction sites. Civil engineers must understand these requirements because they affect design decisions (specifying trench protection, designing for erection sequences) and construction administration (reviewing safety plans, conducting site inspections). On the FE, expect scenario-based questions about excavation safety thresholds, fall protection requirements, and the engineer's responsibility during construction.

mathematics/straight-lines-quadratics.name: Straight Lines & Quadratics
mathematics/straight-lines-quadratics.application: Civil engineers work with straight lines constantly — from defining road alignments and grade slopes, to establishing property boundaries in surveying, to plotting stress-strain relationships in materials testing. The quadratic formula shows up any time a parabolic curve is involved: vertical curves in highway design, projectile trajectories in dynamics, and cable sag calculations. On the FE, expect direct questions asking you to find a slope, a distance between two points, or the roots of a quadratic. These are fast-solve questions if you know the formulas — free points.

content.body: Three forms of a line equation show up in the handbook. Know when to use each one.
Slope-Intercept Form

content.label: When you know slope and y-intercept

content.body: Point-Slope Form

content.label: When you know slope and one point

content.body: Slope from Two Points
Distance Between Two Points
Perpendicular Lines
Two lines are perpendicular if their slopes are negative reciprocals.
Quadratic Formula
For $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, the roots are:
On the exam, if a quadratic looks messy, check the discriminant first. If $b^2 - 4ac < 0$, there are no real roots — you can eliminate answers immediately.
The distance formula and the quadratic formula are both in the handbook. Don't waste time memorizing — know where to find them and practice using them fast.

problems.statement: A surveyor records two elevation points along a proposed road centerline: Point A at station $0{+}00$ with elevation $120.0\,\text{ft}$ and Point B at station $3{+}00$ with elevation $126.0\,\text{ft}$. What is the grade (slope) of the road between the two points?
problems.eli5: Station notation is just a way of writing distance in hundreds of feet — station 3+00 means 300 ft. Once you see that, it's just rise over run: 6 ft of rise over 300 ft of run = 0.02 = 2%. The trap is forgetting to convert stations to feet and using "3" instead of "300," which gives you 200% — obviously wrong but easy to do under pressure.
problems.hint: Convert the station numbers to feet before dividing.

steps.text: Convert stations to feet: Station $0{+}00 = 0\,\text{ft}$, Station $3{+}00 = 300\,\text{ft}$.

traps: Forgetting to convert station notation to feet
Confusing rise/run with run/rise

problems.statement: A property boundary runs from point $P(2, 3)$ to point $Q(8, 7)$. A utility easement must be laid perpendicular to this boundary through point $Q$. What is the slope of the easement line?
problems.eli5: First find the slope of the boundary line — rise over run gives you 2/3. Then flip it and negate it for the perpendicular slope: 2/3 becomes -3/2. The most common mistake is only flipping without negating (getting 3/2) or only negating without flipping (getting -2/3). You have to do both — flip AND negate.
problems.hint: Perpendicular means negative reciprocal — flip the fraction and change the sign.

Only taking the reciprocal without negating

problems.statement: A projectile is launched from a $5\,\text{m}$ high embankment with an initial vertical velocity of $12\,\text{m/s}$. Its height is modeled by $h(t) = -4.9t^2 + 12t + 5$. At what time does the projectile hit the ground?
problems.eli5: Set the height equation equal to zero and use the quadratic formula. You'll get two roots — one negative and one positive. Negative time doesn't make physical sense, so throw it away. The sneaky part: the negative root (-0.36) shows up as the 0.36 s choice without the minus sign. If you forget to check which root is physically valid, you might pick it. Always ask yourself: does my answer make sense in the real world?
problems.hint: Set $h(t) = 0$ and apply the quadratic formula. One of the two roots won't make physical sense.

traps: Selecting the negative root (appears as choice A without the minus sign)
Sign errors with the negative leading coefficient (a = -4.9)
Forgetting the embankment adds 5 m to initial height

mathematics/logarithms.name: Logarithms
mathematics/logarithms.application: Logarithms show up across multiple FE Civil topics — computing the time for a contaminant to decay to safe levels in environmental engineering, finding the number of compounding periods in engineering economics, and working with the pH scale in water quality. On the FE, log questions tend to be algebra problems: simplify an expression using log rules, change bases, or solve an equation where the unknown is in the exponent. The formulas are all in the handbook — the skill is knowing which identity to apply.

content.body: A logarithm answers the question: what power do I raise the base to in order to get this number?
Definition
Two Common Bases
$\ln x$ means base $e$ (natural log). $\log x$ means base 10 on the FE.
Base Change Formula
The most useful form: $\ln x = 2.302585 \cdot \log_{10} x$.
Key Identities
Most FE log problems boil down to one move: use the power rule to pull the exponent down, then solve the resulting linear equation.
There is no log rule for $\log(x + y)$. Students who try to split a sum inside a log lose easy points. Only products, quotients, and powers have rules.

problems.eli5: The power rule says you can pull the exponent out front: $\log(10^x) = x\log(10)$. And $\log_{10}(10) = 1$ because '10 to the what power gives 10? The answer is 1.' So the whole thing simplifies to just $x = 3.5$. The trap is overthinking it — some students try to compute $10^{3.5}$ and get confused. The log and the exponent with the same base just cancel.
problems.hint: What happens when the base of the log matches the base of the exponent?
traps: Computing 10^3.5 instead of recognizing the identity
Multiplying 10 by 3.5

problems.statement: A contaminant in a groundwater well decays according to $C = C_0 \cdot e^{-0.03t}$, where $t$ is in days. How many days until the concentration drops to 25% of its initial value?
problems.eli5: You need to 'undo' the exponential, and the natural log does exactly that — $\ln(e^{\text{something}}) = \text{something}$. So take $\ln$ of both sides to bring the exponent down. The main trap is forgetting to divide out $C_0$ first, or getting confused by the negatives. Both $\ln(0.25)$ and $-0.03$ are negative, so they cancel and $t$ comes out positive — which makes sense because time cannot be negative.
problems.hint: Divide both sides by $C_0$ first, then take the natural log to isolate $t$.

steps.text: Set $C = 0.25 C_0$ and divide both sides by $C_0$:
Take the natural log of both sides:

traps: Forgetting to divide by $C_0$ before taking the log
Sign error with the two negatives giving a negative time

problems.statement: Simplify the expression: $\log_2(32) - \log_2(4) + \log_2(8)$
problems.eli5: Three terms with the same base — combine them. Subtraction means divide, addition means multiply: $\log_2(32/4 \times 8) = \log_2(64)$. Then ask: 2 to the what power gives 64? Count the doublings: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 — that is 6. The trap is trying to evaluate each log separately and then doing regular arithmetic on the results without being careful. You can do it that way too ($5 - 2 + 3 = 6$), but combining first is faster and less error-prone. The sneaky distractor is 36 — which is what you get if you multiply the separate values ($5 \times 2 \times 3$) instead of adding them.
problems.hint: Combine the logs into a single log using the product and quotient rules before evaluating.

Misapplying the quotient rule order

mathematics/right-triangle-trig.name: Right Triangle Trigonometry
mathematics/right-triangle-trig.application: Civil engineers use right triangle trig constantly — resolving cable forces into horizontal and vertical components, computing slope distances on graded roads, sizing retaining wall footings, and laying out survey lines. On the FE exam, any time you see an angle paired with a force or a length, you're reaching for SOH-CAH-TOA. This is foundational for statics, surveying, and structural problems throughout the test.

content.body: A right triangle gives you three ratios relative to an angle $\theta$. Pick the ratio that connects what you know to what you need.
The Three Ratios
Remember: cos is "cozy" with the adjacent side (the one touching the angle). If you have the hypotenuse and want the opposite side, that's sine.
The biggest exam trap is mixing up which component gets sin vs cos when resolving forces. Always confirm your calculator is in degree mode.

problems.statement: A surveyor measures the angle of elevation to the top of a building as $35°$ from a point $50\,\text{m}$ away on level ground. What is the height of the building?
problems.eli5: You are standing 50 m from a building and looking up at $35°$. You know the ground distance (adjacent) and want the height (opposite) — that is tangent. Multiply 50 by $\tan(35°)$ and you are done. The trap is using sin or cos instead.
problems.hint: You know the adjacent side and want the opposite — which trig ratio connects those two?

steps.text: Identify the triangle: building height is opposite the 35° angle, the 50 m ground distance is adjacent.
Pick the ratio that connects opposite and adjacent:

traps: Using sin or cos instead of tan
Calculator in radian mode

problems.statement: A cable exerts a force of $12\,\text{kN}$ at $40°$ above the horizontal on a bridge anchor. What is the horizontal component of the force?
problems.eli5: "40 degrees above horizontal" means the angle is measured FROM the horizontal axis. The horizontal component is the side touching the angle — that's adjacent — so you use cosine. The classic trap is using sin for horizontal because it "feels" right. Remember: cos is cozy with the adjacent side.
problems.hint: The angle is measured from the horizontal axis — which side of the triangle is the horizontal component relative to that angle?

steps.text: The angle is measured from horizontal, so the horizontal component is adjacent to the angle.
Use cosine to find the adjacent (horizontal) component:

traps: Using sin instead of cos for the horizontal component
Dividing by cos instead of multiplying

problems.statement: An engineer stands at point A and measures the angle of elevation to the top of a tower as $25°$. She walks $30\,\text{m}$ closer to the tower to point B and measures the angle of elevation as $42°$. What is the height of the tower?
problems.eli5: This is a two-triangle problem. You set up tan equations from both positions — each has the same unknown height h but different distances. Write both equations, substitute one into the other, and solve for h. It looks nasty but it's just algebra after the two tan equations are set up. Don't try to shortcut — set up both equations first, then eliminate d.
problems.hint: Set up a separate tan equation from each observation point. Both share the same unknown height — eliminate the distance variable.

steps.text: Let h = tower height, d = horizontal distance from B to the base.

traps: Forgetting to add 30 m to the distance from A
Rounding intermediate values too early

mathematics/law-of-sines-cosines.name: Law of Sines & Law of Cosines
mathematics/law-of-sines-cosines.application: Civil engineers encounter oblique triangles — triangles with no right angle — when surveying irregular property boundaries, computing forces in non-orthogonal truss members, or triangulating positions from two known points. The Law of Sines and Law of Cosines let you solve any triangle when you can't drop a clean perpendicular. On the FE exam, if the given triangle isn't a right triangle, one of these two laws is your only path forward.

content.body: Two formulas cover every oblique triangle.
Law of Sines
Works when you have an angle and its opposite side plus one more piece.
Law of Cosines
Works when you have two sides and the included angle (SAS) or all three sides (SSS).
Decision tree: if you know a side-angle pair, start with Sines. If you know SAS or SSS, start with Cosines.
Watch out for the ambiguous case with Law of Sines (two possible triangles). The FE usually avoids it, but if you see SSA given, check whether a second solution exists.

problems.statement: In triangle ABC, angle $A = 40°$, angle $B = 75°$, and side $a = 18\,\text{m}$. What is the length of side $b$?
problems.eli5: You have a side and its opposite angle (a and A), plus another angle (B). That's a textbook Law of Sines setup. Cross-multiply to isolate b: multiply 18 by sin(75°)/sin(40°). The most common mistake is flipping the fraction and getting a smaller number instead of a bigger one.
problems.hint: You have a complete side-angle pair (a and A) — which law lets you use that directly?

steps.text: Identify the known pair: side a = 18 m is opposite angle A = 40°. We want side b opposite angle B = 75°.

traps: Flipping the sin ratio and getting a smaller answer
Using cos instead of sin

problems.statement: A surveyor measures two sides of a triangular lot as $85\,\text{m}$ and $110\,\text{m}$ with an included angle of $62°$. What is the length of the third side?
problems.eli5: When you see two sides and the angle between them, that is SAS — go straight to Law of Cosines. It is basically the Pythagorean theorem with a correction term ($-2ab\cos C$) for non-right triangles. The trap is forgetting to subtract that term, or accidentally using sine instead of cosine.
problems.hint: You know two sides and the included angle — which formula generalizes the Pythagorean theorem for non-right triangles?

steps.text: Two sides and included angle (SAS) → Law of Cosines.

traps: Adding the cosine term instead of subtracting
Using sin instead of cos in the formula

problems.statement: A triangular truss has sides $a = 6.0\,\text{m}$, $b = 8.0\,\text{m}$, and $c = 11.0\,\text{m}$. What is the measure of angle $C$ (the angle opposite the longest side)?
problems.eli5: When you have all three sides but no angles, rearrange the Law of Cosines to solve for cosine of the angle. The key insight: if the numerator comes out negative, the cosine is negative, which means the angle is obtuse (bigger than 90°). Don't panic when you see a negative — just hit inverse cosine on your calculator and it handles it. The trap is second-guessing the negative and subtracting from 180°.
problems.hint: Rearrange the Law of Cosines to isolate $\cos C$. What does a negative value of cosine tell you about the angle?

steps.text: All three sides known (SSS) → rearrange Law of Cosines to solve for the angle.

traps: Sign error using +c² in the numerator
Subtracting from 180° when cosine is negative

mathematics/unit-circle-trig-identities.name: Unit Circle & Trig Identities
mathematics/unit-circle-trig-identities.application: Trig identities show up on the FE whenever a problem needs simplification before you can solve it — combining force components at different angles, converting between sin and cos in vibration equations, or simplifying expressions in calculus-based derivations. The unit circle ties angles to coordinates, giving you exact values for common angles without a calculator. On the FE exam, knowing your reference angles and a handful of identities saves real time.

content.body: The unit circle maps every angle $\theta$ to coordinates $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ on a circle of radius 1. Memorize the key angles: $0°$, $30°$, $45°$, $60°$, $90°$ and their values — everything else follows by symmetry across quadrants.
Pythagorean Identity
Double-Angle Formulas
Don't memorize all identities — know the Pythagorean identity cold, and recognize when a double-angle or sum formula is being tested.

problems.statement: What is the exact value of $\cos 60°$?
problems.eli5: The unit circle point at $60°$ is $(1/2,\, \sqrt{3}/2)$. Cosine is always the x-coordinate, sine is the y-coordinate. The trap is mixing them up — $\sqrt{3}/2$ (the √3/2 choice) is the sine of $60°$, not the cosine. If you remember that $\cos 60° = 1/2$ and $\sin 60° = \sqrt{3}/2$, you have the most commonly tested pair down.
problems.hint: On the unit circle, cosine is the x-coordinate and sine is the y-coordinate at any angle.

steps.text: Recall the unit circle: at 60°, the coordinates are (1/2, √3/2).

traps: Confusing sin and cos (picking $\sqrt{3}/2$)
Mixing up 45° and 60° values

problems.statement: If $\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}$ and $\theta$ is in the second quadrant, what is $\cos\theta$?
problems.eli5: Plug $\sin\theta$ into the Pythagorean identity and solve for $\cos\theta$. You get $\pm 4/5$. Now the quadrant matters — in Q2, $x$ is negative, so cosine is negative. The trap is forgetting the quadrant and picking the positive root. Always check which quadrant you are in after solving.
problems.hint: Use $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ to find $|\cos\theta|$, then decide the sign based on the quadrant.
traps: Forgetting the sign from the quadrant
Confusing sin and cos values

problems.statement: If $\sin\theta = \frac{5}{13}$ and $\theta$ is in the first quadrant, what is the value of $\sin 2\theta$?
problems.eli5: This is a two-step problem. Step 1: use the Pythagorean identity to find $\cos\theta = 12/13$. Step 2: plug both into the double-angle formula $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$. The most common mistake is thinking "double angle" means "just double the sine" — it does not. You need both $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$. The second trap is forgetting the 2 out front.
problems.hint: The double-angle formula needs both $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ — find the missing one first with the Pythagorean identity.

steps.text: Find cos θ using the Pythagorean identity:

traps: Just doubling $\sin\theta$ without multiplying by $\cos\theta$
Forgetting the factor of 2

mathematics/circles-conics.name: Circles & Conic Sections
mathematics/circles-conics.application: Conic sections appear in civil engineering more than you'd expect — circular curves on highway alignments, parabolic profiles for vertical road curves, and elliptical arches in bridge design. On the FE exam, you need to recognize the standard equation of a circle, identify its center and radius, and know the basic forms of parabolas and ellipses. Most FE problems stick to circles, but an occasional parabola or ellipse shows up in the math section.

content.body: Circle
If the equation is in general form $x^2 + y^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0$, complete the square to convert to standard form.
Parabola

content.label: Vertical — sign of a sets direction

content.body: Ellipse
The key FE skill is converting from general form to standard form by completing the square — practice until it's automatic.

problems.statement: A circular retention pond is modeled by the equation $(x - 5)^2 + (y + 3)^2 = 64$. What are the center and radius of the pond?
problems.eli5: Read the center straight from the equation: $(x - 5)$ means $h = 5$, and $(y + 3)$ means $k = -3$ because $y + 3 = y - (-3)$. The number on the right is $r^2$, not $r$ — so take the square root. The two traps are getting the sign of $k$ wrong and forgetting to square-root the radius.
problems.hint: The sign inside the parentheses is opposite to the coordinate — $(y + 3)$ means $k = -3$. And 64 is $r^2$, not $r$.
traps: Flipping the sign of $k$
Giving $r^2$ instead of $r$

problems.statement: A tunnel cross-section is described by $x^2 + y^2 - 10x + 6y + 18 = 0$. What is the radius of the circular cross-section?
problems.eli5: Move the constant to the right side, then complete the square for both $x$ and $y$. For $x^2 - 10x$, half of 10 is 5, squared is 25 — add 25 to both sides. For $y^2 + 6y$, half of 6 is 3, squared is 9 — add 9 to both sides. Now you have standard form and can read off the radius. The trap is forgetting to add the completing-the-square values to both sides, or giving $r^2$ as the answer.
problems.hint: Group the x and y terms, then complete the square for each — remember to add the same values to both sides.

steps.text: Complete the square for both variables:

traps: Forgetting to add completing-the-square values to both sides
Giving $r^2$ instead of $r$

problems.statement: A vertical highway curve is modeled by $y = -0.004x^2 + 2.4x - 200$. At what horizontal distance $x$ does the curve reach its maximum elevation, and what is that elevation?
problems.eli5: For a parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$, the vertex is at $x = -b/(2a)$. Plug in $a = -0.004$ and $b = 2.4$ to get $x = 300$. Then substitute $x = 300$ back into the equation to get $y = 160$. The big trap is forgetting the 2 in the denominator and using $-b/a = 600$ instead. Always double-check by plugging the $x$ value back in.
problems.hint: The vertex of $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ is at $x = -b/(2a)$ — do not forget the 2 in the denominator.

steps.text: Since a = -0.004 < 0, the parabola opens downward — the vertex is the maximum.
Plug x = 300 back in to find y:

traps: Forgetting the 2 in the denominator and using -b/a
Reading the constant term as the max y value

mathematics/derivatives-rules.name: Derivatives & Derivative Rules
mathematics/derivatives-rules.application: Civil engineers use derivatives any time they need a rate of change — the slope of a deflection curve to find beam rotation, the rate of flow change in a pipe to detect surges, or the velocity of a settling particle in a sedimentation tank. On the FE, derivative questions are usually 'apply the right rule' problems: you see a function, pick the correct derivative rule from the handbook table, and crank through the algebra. The chain rule shows up the most because the FE loves composite functions like sin(3x²) or e^(-0.5t).

content.body: The derivative of $y = f(x)$ gives the instantaneous rate of change. The handbook has a full table of 27 derivative formulas — you don't memorize them, you look them up. But you do need to know which rule to apply.
Power Rule
Product Rule
Quotient Rule

content.label: lo d-hi minus hi d-lo over lo-lo

content.body: Chain Rule

content.label: Derivative of outer times derivative of inner

content.body: Common Derivatives
Almost every FE derivative problem is a chain rule problem in disguise. Ask yourself: is the argument anything other than plain $x$? If yes, chain rule.

The quotient rule is the #1 sign-error generator on the FE. The numerator is $v\,du - u\,dv$, not the other way around. A mnemonic: 'lo d-hi minus hi d-lo' — the denominator function ($v$, the 'lo') goes first.

problems.statement: Find the derivative of $f(x) = (3x + 5)^4$.
problems.eli5: The power rule says bring the exponent down and subtract one from the power. But the argument isn't just x — it's 3x + 5 — so you have to chain rule it. That means you also multiply by the derivative of the inside, which is 3. The most common mistake is forgetting that extra factor of 3. The choice $4(3x + 5)^3$ is exactly what you get if you skip the chain rule.
problems.hint: The argument isn't plain x — what extra factor does the chain rule add?

steps.text: Recognize this as a chain rule problem: the outer function is $u^4$ and the inner function is $u = 3x + 5$.
Multiply by the derivative of the inner function:

traps: Forgetting the chain rule and omitting the factor of 3
Leaving the exponent as 4 instead of reducing to 3

problems.statement: Find the derivative of $f(x) = x^2 e^{3x}$.
problems.eli5: Two functions multiplied together means product rule. The tricky part is that e^(3x) also needs the chain rule — its derivative is 3e^(3x), not just e^(3x). The choice e^{3x}(2x + x^2) is what you get if you forget that chain rule factor of 3 on the exponential. The choice 2xe^{3x} only differentiates the x² part and ignores the product rule entirely. Always ask: am I using BOTH terms of the product rule?
problems.hint: Two functions multiplied means product rule. And $e^{3x}$ needs the chain rule for its own derivative.

steps.text: Identify $u = x^2$ and $v = e^{3x}$. This needs the product rule.
Find each derivative: $du/dx = 2x$ and $dv/dx = 3e^{3x}$ (chain rule on the exponential).

traps: Forgetting the chain rule on e^(3x) (missing the factor of 3)
Only differentiating one factor and ignoring the product rule

problems.statement: Find the derivative of $f(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x^2 + 1}$.
problems.eli5: Quotient rule: 'lo d-hi minus hi d-lo over lo-lo.' The denominator function ($x^2 + 1$) goes first in the numerator — it multiplies the derivative of the top ($\cos x$). Then subtract the top ($\sin x$) times the derivative of the bottom ($2x$). The classic trap is flipping the subtraction order. The choice with a plus where there should be a minus (cos x term plus 2x sin x) is wrong. The choice with the terms in the wrong order entirely (2x sin x minus the cos x term) is also wrong. The mnemonic saves you: lo d-hi MINUS hi d-lo.
problems.hint: 'Lo d-hi minus hi d-lo over lo-lo' — the bottom function goes first in the numerator.

steps.text: Identify $u = \sin x$ and $v = x^2 + 1$. This needs the quotient rule.

traps: Flipping the subtraction order in the quotient rule numerator
Forgetting to square the denominator
Simplifying the denominator instead of leaving it as (x² + 1)²

mathematics/applications-derivatives.name: Applications of Derivatives
mathematics/applications-derivatives.application: Civil engineers use max/min analysis constantly — finding where bending moment is maximum along a beam, optimizing the dimensions of a channel for maximum flow, or locating the peak elevation on a vertical highway curve. Inflection points tell you where a beam changes from bending one way to the other. On the FE, these problems are formulaic: take the derivative, set it equal to zero, solve, and use the second derivative to classify. They're free points if you don't make sign errors.

content.body: To find where a function reaches its highest or lowest value, set the first derivative equal to zero and solve. The second derivative tells you which one it is.
Test for a Maximum
Test for a Minimum
Test for Inflection Point
$f''(a) = 0$ and $f''(x)$ changes sign through $x = a$.
Memory trick: second derivative negative means the curve frowns (concave down) — that's a max. Second derivative positive means the curve smiles (concave up) — that's a min.

The FE almost always gives you a polynomial or a simple function. Take the derivative, set it to zero, factor or use the quadratic formula, then plug critical points into the second derivative. Don't skip the second derivative test — some problems have both a max and a min.

problems.statement: Find the value of $x$ at which $f(x) = -2x^2 + 16x - 5$ reaches its maximum.
problems.eli5: Take the derivative, set it to zero, solve for $x$. That is it. The second derivative is $-4$, which is negative — concave down — so it is a max, not a min. Since the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward, so of course it is a max. The choice $x = 8$ is what you get if you forget the factor of 2 when differentiating $-2x^2$. Always double-check your power rule on the leading term.
problems.hint: Set $f'(x) = 0$ and solve. Is the parabola opening up or down?
traps: Forgetting the coefficient when differentiating $-2x^2$ (getting $-2x$ instead of $-4x$)
Reporting the max value of $f(x)$ instead of the $x$-location

problems.statement: A civil engineer models the cost per meter of a retaining wall as $C(h) = 3h^2 - 36h + 150$, where $h$ is the wall height in meters. What wall height minimizes the cost, and what is the minimum cost?
problems.eli5: Same process — derivative, set to zero, solve. You get $h = 6$. The second derivative is positive ($6 > 0$), so it is concave up — a minimum. The extra step is plugging $h = 6$ back into the original function to get the cost. The choice giving C = 150/m is the trap for students who find the right $h$ but give the constant term (150) as the cost instead of actually evaluating $C(6)$. Always plug back in.
problems.hint: After finding where $C'(h) = 0$, plug that value back into the original $C(h)$ to find the minimum cost.
traps: Giving the constant term as the min cost instead of evaluating C(6)
Arithmetic error in evaluating the quadratic at h = 6

problems.statement: A beam deflection curve is modeled by $y(x) = x^3 - 12x^2 + 36x$, where $x$ is in meters along the beam and $y$ is deflection. At what point does the curvature of the beam change direction (inflection point)?
problems.eli5: An inflection point is where the curve changes from bending one way to bending the other — concave up to concave down or vice versa. Set the SECOND derivative to zero, not the first. That is the most common mistake: students set y' = 0 and find critical points instead. The choices x = 2 m and x = 6 m are the critical points where y' = 0 — those are max/min locations, not inflection points. The inflection point is where y'' = 0 and actually changes sign.
problems.hint: Inflection points come from the second derivative, not the first. Set $y''(x) = 0$.

steps.text: Set the second derivative to zero:
Verify sign change: $y''(3) = -6 < 0$ and $y''(5) = 6 > 0$ — sign changes, confirming inflection point.

problems.handbookFormula: f''(a) = 0 \text{ and } f''(x) \text{ changes sign} \implies \text{inflection point}
traps: Setting y'(x) = 0 instead of y''(x) = 0 (finding critical points instead of inflection points)
Not verifying that y'' actually changes sign at the candidate point

mathematics/integral-calculus.name: Integral Calculus
mathematics/integral-calculus.application: Civil engineers integrate constantly — computing the area under a load diagram to find total force, calculating earthwork volumes from cross-section data, finding the total flow through a culvert over time, or determining the deflection of a beam from its moment equation. The FE gives you a function and asks for an antiderivative or a definite integral. You have the integral table in the handbook, so the real skill is recognizing which formula fits and applying substitution or integration by parts when it doesn't match directly.

content.body: Integration is the reverse of differentiation. On the FE, you either evaluate a definite integral (get a number) or find an indefinite integral (get a function + C). The handbook gives you 27 integral formulas — your job is pattern matching.
Indefinite Integral
Where $F'(x) = f(x)$. The $+C$ matters on the exam — wrong answer choices often omit it.
Power Rule for Integration
This is the workhorse. When $n = -1$, it becomes $\int \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln|x| + C$.
Integration by Parts

Use when the integrand is a product of two different types (e.g., $x\,e^x$, $x\,\sin x$). Pick $u$ using LIATE: Logs, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential — earlier in the list = better choice for $u$.
U-Substitution
If you see a composite function $f(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)$, let $u = g(x)$, then $du = g'(x)\,dx$. This converts the integral into $\int f(u)\,du$, which is usually a standard form.
Definite Integral
Find the antiderivative, plug in the upper limit, subtract the lower limit. No $+C$ needed — it cancels.
LIATE for integration by parts: Logs → Inverse trig → Algebraic → Trig → Exponential. Pick $u$ from whatever appears earliest in this list.

The FE handbook has the integral table on p. 50. You don't need to memorize all 27 formulas — but you DO need to recognize when substitution or by-parts is needed to get an integrand into a form that matches the table.

problems.statement: A retaining wall footing exerts a parabolically varying pressure on the soil given by $q(x) = 3x^2$ kPa, where $x$ is in meters from the toe. Find the total force per unit width over the first 2 m of the footing.
problems.eli5: Total force from a varying pressure is just the integral of the pressure function over the loaded length. Power rule: bring the exponent up by 1 and divide. The 3 and the 1/3 cancel perfectly here — clean answer, no tricks.
problems.hint: Integrate the pressure function from 0 to 2 using the power rule.

steps.text: Total force = area under the pressure curve:

traps: Forgetting to evaluate at both limits (plugging in only the upper bound)
Confusing pressure (kPa) with force (kN/m) — the integral of pressure over length gives force per unit width

problems.statement: Evaluate $\int_0^1 x\,e^{2x}\,dx$.
problems.eli5: You've got $x$ times $e^{2x}$ — two different types multiplied together, so it's integration by parts. LIATE says pick $u = x$ (algebraic) since it comes before exponential. Then $dv = e^{2x}\,dx$ and you integrate that to get $v$. Watch the factor of 1/2 from integrating $e^{2x}$ — that's where most errors happen.
problems.hint: LIATE: $x$ is algebraic (A), $e^{2x}$ is exponential (E). Algebraic comes first — let $u = x$.
traps: Forgetting the 1/2 factor when integrating $e^{2x}$ (the antiderivative is $\frac{e^{2x}}{2}$, not $e^{2x}$)
Picking $u$ and $dv$ backwards — if you let $u = e^{2x}$, the integral gets harder, not easier

problems.statement: Evaluate $\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^3 x\,\cos x\,dx$.
problems.eli5: Whenever you see $\sin^n x \cdot \cos x$ (or $\cos^n x \cdot \sin x$), it's screaming for u-sub. The $\cos x$ is the derivative of $\sin x$ — that's the $g'(x)$ that makes substitution work. After substituting, you're left with a basic power rule integral. Don't forget to change the limits when it's a definite integral.
problems.hint: Notice that $\cos x$ is the derivative of $\sin x$. Let $u = \sin x$.

steps.text: Recognize the pattern: $\sin^3 x \cdot \cos x = f(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)$ where $g(x) = \sin x$.

traps: Forgetting to change the integration limits when substituting (going back to $x$ limits with a $u$ antiderivative)
Mixing up which function is $u$ and which is $du$ — the one with the higher power ($\sin^3 x$) stays, its derivative ($\cos x\,dx$) becomes $du$

mathematics/lhopitals-rule.name: L'Hopital's Rule
mathematics/lhopitals-rule.application: L'Hopital's Rule is a one-trick tool — but it appears on the FE almost every cycle. Whenever you plug a limit value into a fraction and get 0/0 or ∞/∞, you differentiate the top and bottom separately and try the limit again. Civil engineers encounter these indeterminate forms when analyzing boundary conditions in hydraulics (flow at a critical depth transition), evaluating limiting cases in structural deflection formulas, and checking asymptotic behavior of decay functions. It's a fast 1-2 minute problem if you recognize the setup.

content.body: L'Hopital's Rule handles limits that produce the indeterminate forms $\frac{0}{0}$ or $\frac{\infty}{\infty}$. If direct substitution gives either form, differentiate the numerator and denominator separately — then try the limit again.
L'Hopital's Rule
You differentiate the numerator and denominator independently — this is NOT the quotient rule. You're replacing $f$ with $f'$ and $g$ with $g'$, then re-evaluating the limit.
When to Apply

Step 1: Plug in the limit value. If you get $\frac{0}{0}$ or $\frac{\infty}{\infty}$, apply L'Hopital's. If you get a real number, you're done — no rule needed. If you get $\frac{\text{nonzero}}{0}$, the limit is $\pm\infty$ (or DNE), not an indeterminate form.
Repeated Application

If after one round of differentiation the limit is still $\frac{0}{0}$ or $\frac{\infty}{\infty}$, apply the rule again. Keep going until you get a determinate form. Most FE problems resolve in 1-2 rounds.
Always check the form BEFORE differentiating. If direct substitution gives a real number, L'Hopital's doesn't apply — and using it anyway will give a wrong answer.
This is NOT the quotient rule. You differentiate the top alone and the bottom alone. Do not apply $\frac{f'g - fg'}{g^2}$ — that's for derivatives of fractions, not limits of fractions.

problems.statement: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x}$.
problems.eli5: Plug in $x = 0$ and you get $0/0$ — that is the signal to use L'Hopital's. Derivative of $\sin x$ is $\cos x$, derivative of $x$ is 1. Now plug in 0 again: $\cos(0) = 1$. Done in one round. This is probably the most classic L'Hopital's example you will ever see.
problems.hint: Direct substitution gives 0/0. Differentiate the numerator and denominator separately.

steps.text: Apply L'Hopital's — differentiate top and bottom:

traps: Trying to simplify sin x / x algebraically instead of just applying the rule
Applying the quotient rule instead of differentiating top and bottom independently

problems.statement: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{e^x - x - 1}{x^2}$.
problems.eli5: First try gives 0/0, so you differentiate top and bottom. But the second try also gives 0/0 — apply the rule again. Third try: e^x / 2 evaluated at 0 gives 1/2. Two rounds is the most the FE will usually ask for. If you're on round 3+, you probably made a derivative error earlier.
problems.hint: After the first application you still get 0/0. Apply L'Hopital's a second time.

steps.text: First round — differentiate top and bottom:

traps: Stopping after the first round when the result is still indeterminate
Forgetting to differentiate the constant -1 in e^x - 1 (its derivative is 0, which simplifies things)

problems.statement: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{e^x}{x}$.
problems.eli5: This is a trap problem. You see a fraction with $x \to 0$ and want to reach for L'Hopital's — but check the form first! $e^0 / 0 = 1/0$, which is NOT indeterminate. It is a 'blow up' form. The numerator is a finite nonzero number and the denominator goes to zero, so the function goes to $\pm\infty$. Since it goes to $+\infty$ from the right and $-\infty$ from the left, the limit DNE.
problems.hint: Before applying L'Hopital's, check: does direct substitution actually give 0/0 or ∞/∞?

steps.text: L'Hopital's Rule does NOT apply here.
Since left and right limits disagree, the two-sided limit does not exist.

problems.handbookPage: p. 48, L'Hopital's Rule (applies only to 0/0 or ∞/∞ forms)
traps: Blindly applying L'Hopital's without checking the indeterminate form — applying it here gives lim e^x/1 = 1, which is WRONG
Choosing ∞ instead of DNE — the one-sided limits must agree for the two-sided limit to exist

mathematics/vector-basics-unit-vectors.name: Vector Basics & Unit Vectors
mathematics/vector-basics-unit-vectors.application: Vectors are the language of forces in civil engineering. Every time you draw a free body diagram — resolving a cable tension into horizontal and vertical components, adding wind loads on a structure, or combining soil pressure resultants — you're doing vector math. Unit vectors let you express direction independently of magnitude, which is essential for writing force equilibrium equations in 2D and 3D. On the FE, vector basics show up directly in statics and dynamics problems. If you can add, subtract, and normalize vectors quickly, you'll save time on at least 5-10 questions.

content.body: A vector has both magnitude and direction. On the FE, vectors are usually written in component form using unit vectors $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$ along the $x$, $y$, $z$ axes.
Vector in Component Form
Magnitude of a Vector
Unit Vector
A unit vector points in the same direction as $\vec{A}$ but has magnitude 1. Multiply it by any scalar to get a vector of that length in that direction.
Vector Addition
Add component by component. Subtraction works the same way — subtract each component.
Scalar Multiplication
Multiplying a vector by a scalar $c$ scales every component: $c\vec{A} = cA_x\hat{i} + cA_y\hat{j} + cA_z\hat{k}$. If $c$ is negative, the vector reverses direction.
To express a force along a known direction: find the unit vector in that direction, then multiply by the force magnitude. This is how you resolve 3D forces into components: $\vec{F} = F\,\hat{u}$.
Don't confuse magnitude with a component. $|\vec{A}|$ uses the square root of the sum of squares. $A_x$ alone is just the projection onto the $x$-axis — it can be negative.

problems.statement: A surveyor measures a displacement of $\vec{d} = 30\hat{i} + 40\hat{j}$ meters from a benchmark. What is the total distance from the benchmark?
problems.eli5: Distance is the magnitude of the displacement vector. Square each component, add them, take the square root. This is a 3-4-5 right triangle scaled by 10 — if you recognize the Pythagorean triple you can skip the calculator entirely.
problems.hint: The total distance is the magnitude of the vector, not the sum of components.
traps: Adding components directly (30 + 40 = 70) instead of using the magnitude formula
Forgetting to square root — 900 + 1600 = 2500 is not the answer, √2500 = 50 is

problems.statement: A force acts along the direction from point $A(1, 2, 2)$ to point $B(4, 6, 2)$. What is the unit vector from $A$ to $B$?
problems.eli5: Two steps: first get the direction vector by subtracting coordinates (B − A), then divide every component by the magnitude. The choice 3î + 4ĵ + 0k̂ is the direction vector before normalizing — that's the most common mistake. Always check that your unit vector's magnitude equals 1: √(0.6² + 0.8²) = √(0.36 + 0.64) = 1. ✓
problems.hint: Subtract A from B to get the direction vector, then divide by its magnitude.
traps: Forgetting to divide by the magnitude — choice B is the raw direction vector, not the unit vector
Subtracting in the wrong order (A − B instead of B − A) — this reverses the direction

problems.statement: Three forces act on a gusset plate: $\vec{F}_1 = 500\hat{i} + 0\hat{j}$ N, $\vec{F}_2 = -200\hat{i} + 300\hat{j}$ N, and $\vec{F}_3 = 0\hat{i} - 400\hat{j}$ N. What is the magnitude of the resultant force?
problems.eli5: Vector addition is component-by-component — add all the x's together, add all the y's together. Then the resultant magnitude is √(Rx² + Ry²). The trap is adding magnitudes directly (500 + 360.6 + 400 ≈ 1261) — that only works if all forces point the same direction, which they never do in real problems. Here √100000 = 100√10 ≈ 316 N.
problems.hint: Add the x-components and y-components separately, then find the magnitude of the resultant vector.
traps: Adding magnitudes directly instead of adding components — forces in opposite directions partially cancel
Forgetting the negative signs on components — F₂ₓ = -200 and F₃ᵧ = -400 are critical

mathematics/dot-product-angle.name: Dot Product & Angle Between Vectors
mathematics/dot-product-angle.application: The dot product is how civil engineers find the angle between two forces, compute the component of one force along another direction, and check whether two vectors are perpendicular. In structural analysis, you use it to find the projection of a load onto a member axis. In surveying, it helps find the angle between two traverse legs. On the FE, dot product questions are quick if you know the two formulas — the component formula and the cosine formula — and when to use each.

content.body: The dot product takes two vectors and returns a scalar. It has two equivalent formulas — one for computing, one for finding angles.
Dot Product (Component Form)
Multiply matching components and add. This is the formula you use to compute the number.
Dot Product (Angle Form)
This is the formula you use to find the angle. Rearrange: $\cos\theta = \frac{\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}}{|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|}$.
Scalar Projection
This gives the signed length of $\vec{A}$'s shadow onto $\vec{B}$. Positive means same general direction, negative means opposite.
Perpendicularity Test
If $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = 0$, the vectors are perpendicular. This is the fastest way to check orthogonality.
Typical FE workflow: compute the dot product using components, compute both magnitudes, then plug into the angle formula to get $\cos\theta$, then $\theta = \cos^{-1}(\ldots)$.
The dot product always returns a scalar (a number), never a vector. If the answer has $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, or $\hat{k}$ in it, you're doing the cross product, not the dot product.

problems.statement: Given $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = -2\hat{i} + 5\hat{j}$, compute $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}$.
problems.eli5: Multiply matching components and add: x with x, y with y. That's it. The negative sign on B_x = -2 is critical — (3)(-2) = -6, not +6. Then add (4)(5) = 20. Total: 14. The choice -6 is just the first term without adding the second.
problems.hint: Multiply x-components together, multiply y-components together, then add.
traps: Dropping the negative sign: (3)(-2) = -6, not +6
Cross-multiplying components (A_x B_y) instead of matching (A_x B_x) — that's the cross product pattern

problems.statement: Find the angle between $\vec{A} = 1\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = 1\hat{i} + 1\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$.
problems.eli5: This is the standard three-step workflow: (1) compute the dot product with components, (2) compute both magnitudes, (3) divide and take inverse cosine. Vector A points along the x-axis, vector B points at 45° in the xy-plane — so the answer makes geometric sense. Always sanity-check your angle.
problems.hint: Use $\cos\theta = (\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}) / (|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|)$ and solve for $\theta$.
traps: Forgetting to compute magnitudes and dividing dot product by component sums instead
Getting $\cos\theta = 1/\sqrt{2}$ but reporting $\theta = 1/\sqrt{2}$ without taking $\cos^{-1}$

problems.statement: A force $\vec{F} = 300\hat{i} + 600\hat{j} - 300\hat{k}$ N acts at a joint. A structural member runs from the joint in the direction $\vec{d} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 1\hat{k}$. What is the component of the force along the member?
problems.eli5: The scalar projection tells you how much of the force acts along the member's axis. Compute the dot product (which mixes all three components), then divide by the magnitude of the direction vector — not the force vector. The 1500 N option is the raw dot product without dividing — the most common mistake. The 900 N option is the sum of force component magnitudes, which ignores direction entirely.
problems.hint: The component of F along d is (F · d) / |d| — divide by the magnitude of the direction, not the force.
traps: Using the raw dot product (1500) without dividing by |d| — the projection requires normalization
Dividing by |F| instead of |d| — you project onto the direction vector, not the force

mathematics/cross-product-applications.name: Cross Product & Applications
mathematics/cross-product-applications.application: The cross product gives civil engineers a vector perpendicular to two other vectors — and its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram they form. In practice, you use it to compute the moment of a force about a point ($\vec{M} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$), find the area of a triangular region defined by two edge vectors, and determine the direction of a normal to a surface. On the FE, cross product questions appear in statics (moment calculations) and occasionally in surveying (area from coordinates). Know the determinant formula and the right-hand rule.

content.body: The cross product takes two vectors and returns a new vector that is perpendicular to both. Its magnitude equals $|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|\sin\theta$.
Cross Product (Determinant Form)

content.latex: \vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ A_x & A_y & A_z \\ B_x & B_y & B_z \end{vmatrix}

content.body: Expand using cofactors: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = (A_yB_z - A_zB_y)\hat{i} - (A_xB_z - A_zB_x)\hat{j} + (A_xB_y - A_yB_x)\hat{k}$.
Magnitude of the Cross Product
This equals the area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors. Half of it gives the area of the triangle.
Moment of a Force
Where $\vec{r}$ is the position vector from point $O$ to the point where $\vec{F}$ is applied. The result is a moment vector — its magnitude is the torque, its direction is the axis of rotation.
Key Properties
$\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = -(\vec{B} \times \vec{A})$ — order matters. Reversing the order flips the sign. Also, $\vec{A} \times \vec{A} = \vec{0}$ — a vector crossed with itself is zero.
For the $\hat{j}$ component, the sign is NEGATIVE in the cofactor expansion. A common mnemonic: "+, −, +" for $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$ cofactors.
The cross product returns a vector, not a scalar. If the problem asks for the magnitude of the moment, compute the cross product first, then take its magnitude.

problems.statement: Compute $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$ where $\vec{A} = 1\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = 0\hat{i} + 1\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$.
problems.eli5: i × j = k — this is the right-hand rule in action. Point your fingers along x, curl them toward y, and your thumb points along z. This is one of those "just know it" results that saves time. The -1k̂ choice has the wrong sign — that would be j × i, the reversed order.
problems.hint: Use the determinant formula, or recall that i × j = k.
problems.handbookFormula: \vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ A_x & A_y & A_z \\ B_x & B_y & B_z \end{vmatrix}
traps: Reversing the order: B × A = -k, not +k
Thinking the cross product of perpendicular unit vectors is zero — that's the dot product (i · j = 0)

problems.statement: A force $\vec{F} = 0\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} - 50\hat{k}$ N (downward) is applied at point $P$. The position vector from the pivot $O$ to $P$ is $\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$ m. What is the moment $\vec{M}_O = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$?
problems.eli5: Moment = r × F. Set up the 3×3 determinant and expand carefully. The j component has the MINUS sign in front of the cofactor — so you get -(3·(-50) - 0) = -(-150) = +150. That negative-of-a-negative is where most people mess up. The distractor $200\hat{i} - 150\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$ flips all the signs — that is F × r (wrong order).
problems.hint: Set up the determinant with r in the second row and F in the third row. Watch the sign on the j cofactor.
traps: Forgetting the negative sign on the j cofactor — the pattern is +, −, + across the three components
Reversing r and F — moment is r × F, not F × r

problems.statement: Two edges of a triangular plot are defined by $\vec{u} = 4\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$ m and $\vec{v} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$ m. What is the area of the triangle?
problems.eli5: The cross product magnitude gives the parallelogram area. A triangle is half the parallelogram. So: compute the cross product, take the magnitude, divide by 2. The 12 m² choice is the parallelogram area without halving — the most common mistake. Since both vectors lie in the xy-plane, the cross product points purely in the k direction, which makes the magnitude easy.
problems.hint: Triangle area = ½|u × v|. Compute the cross product first, then take half its magnitude.
traps: Forgetting to divide by 2 — the cross product magnitude gives the parallelogram area, not the triangle area
Using the dot product instead of the cross product — the dot product gives a scalar related to $\cos\theta$, not an area

mathematics/spreadsheet-computations.name: Spreadsheet Computations
mathematics/spreadsheet-computations.application: Civil engineers live in spreadsheets — earthwork volume tables, quantity takeoffs, load combinations, rebar schedules, and cost estimates are all built from cell formulas. The FE tests whether you can read a formula, apply the correct order of operations, and predict what happens to relative vs. absolute references when a formula is copied. These are quick points if you know the rules cold.

content.body: A spreadsheet stores values in cells named by column-letter and row-number (A1, B2, C3). A cell that begins with an equals sign holds a formula: the cell displays the computed result, not the text. For example, if A1 = 2 and A2 = 3, then a cell containing =A1+A2 displays 5.
Order of Operations

Spreadsheets follow standard algebraic precedence (PEMDAS): parentheses first, then exponentiation (^), then multiplication and division (left to right), then addition and subtraction (left to right). So =2+3*4 is 14, not 20 — the multiplication happens before the addition. Use parentheses to force a different order: =(2+3)*4 is 20.
Relative vs. Absolute References

A plain reference like A1 is RELATIVE: when you copy the formula to another cell, the reference shifts by the same offset. Copy =A1*2 from C1 down to C2 and it becomes =A2*2. Putting a dollar sign in front of a coordinate LOCKS it (absolute): $A$1 never changes when copied, A$1 locks only the row, and $A1 locks only the column.

This is the single most-tested spreadsheet idea on the FE: a unit price in one fixed cell ($D$1) multiplied down a column of quantities. The quantity reference shifts row by row while the unit-price reference stays locked.
Common Functions

SUM(range) adds a range, AVERAGE(range) means the arithmetic mean, MAX/MIN return the largest/smallest, COUNT counts numeric cells, and ROUND(value, digits) rounds. The logical function IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false) returns one of two results based on a comparison — e.g., =IF(A1>=3000, "PASS", "FAIL").

Before copying a formula, ask which references must stay fixed (constants like a unit price, an interest rate, a γ value) and put $ on those. Everything that should move with the row/column stays relative.

The #1 spreadsheet error is forgetting the $ — the constant reference drifts when copied and every row below the first is wrong. The #2 error is order of operations: =A1+A2/A3 divides A2 by A3 first, it does NOT add A1+A2 before dividing.

problems.statement: A spreadsheet cell contains the formula =A1+A2*A3. The cells hold A1 = 2, A2 = 3, and A3 = 4. What value does the cell display?
problems.eli5: Spreadsheets follow PEMDAS, so multiplication happens before addition. Compute A2*A3 = 3*4 = 12 first, then add A1: 2 + 12 = 14. The 20 option is the classic mistake of working strictly left to right as (2+3)*4. The 9 option just adds all three. The 24 option multiplies all three.
problems.hint: Spreadsheets obey order of operations — do the multiplication before the addition.

steps.text: Apply precedence: multiplication before addition. Evaluate A2*A3 first.

traps: Evaluating left-to-right as (2+3)*4 = 20 instead of obeying precedence
Adding all three values (9) and ignoring the operators

problems.statement: Cell C1 contains the formula =A1*$B$1, where A1 = 5 and B1 = 10, so C1 displays 50. The formula in C1 is copied down into C2, and cell A2 = 8. What value does C2 display?
problems.eli5: When you copy down one row, the RELATIVE reference A1 shifts to A2, but the ABSOLUTE reference $B$1 stays locked. So C2 becomes =A2*$B$1 = 8 × 10 = 80. The 50 option assumes the A reference didn't move (it isn't locked, so it does). The 18 option adds instead of multiplies. The 800 option shifts or multiplies the locked reference by mistake.
problems.hint: A1 is relative (it shifts when copied); $B$1 is absolute (it stays put).

steps.text: Copying down one row shifts relative references down one row: A1 → A2.
The absolute reference $B$1 does not change.

traps: Thinking A1 stays fixed — it is relative and shifts to A2
Accidentally shifting the locked $B$1 reference

problems.statement: A cell contains =IF(A1>=10, A1*2, A1+5). Cell A1 holds the value 12. What does the cell display?
problems.eli5: IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false) checks the test first. Here A1>=10 asks 'is 12 at least 10?' — yes, so the function returns the TRUE result, A1*2 = 12 × 2 = 24. The choice 17 is the FALSE branch A1+5, which only applies if the test fails. The choice 1 is the mistake of treating TRUE as the literal number 1.
problems.hint: Evaluate the test (is A1 ≥ 10?) and return the matching branch.

steps.text: Because the test is TRUE, return the second argument: A1*2.

traps: Returning the FALSE branch (A1+5 = 17) even though the test passes
Treating the logical result TRUE as the number 1

mathematics/structured-programming.name: Structured Programming
mathematics/structured-programming.application: Whether you script earthwork calcs, automate a hydraulic spreadsheet with a macro, or just read someone else's analysis routine, you need to trace structured logic. The FE keeps it conceptual: given a short block of pseudocode with an if-then-else or a loop, predict the output or count the iterations. No language syntax to memorize — just sequence, selection, and iteration.

content.body: Structured programming builds every routine from three constructs: SEQUENCE (run statements in order), SELECTION (choose a path with IF-THEN-ELSE), and ITERATION (repeat with a loop). On the FE you trace these by hand, tracking each variable's value as the code runs.
Selection: IF-THEN-ELSE

A condition evaluates to TRUE or FALSE and decides which branch runs. Conditions chain with ELSE IF, and they are checked top to bottom — the FIRST true condition wins and the rest are skipped. Example: IF x > 10 THEN y = 1; ELSE IF x > 5 THEN y = 2; ELSE y = 3. With x = 7, the first test fails, the second (7 > 5) is true, so y = 2 and the final ELSE never runs.
Iteration: Loops

A counted FOR loop like FOR i = 1 TO 4 runs its body once for each value 1, 2, 3, 4 — that is 4 times (the endpoints are inclusive). A WHILE loop runs as long as its condition stays true and re-checks the condition before each pass; it stops the moment the condition is false.
Tracing a Loop

To trace, write the variables in a column and update them pass by pass. Example — total = 0; FOR i = 1 TO 4: total = total + i. After the passes total = 0+1+2+3+4 = 10. Accumulator problems (running sum or product) are the most common FE pseudocode question.
For a WHILE loop, the safest approach is a small trace table: list the variable, check the condition, update, repeat. Stop the instant the condition is false and read off the final value.

Off-by-one errors are the trap. FOR i = 1 TO N runs N times (inclusive), not N−1. And a WHILE loop checks its condition BEFORE the body, so the value that breaks the condition is the one left over at the end.

problems.statement: Trace this pseudocode: total = 0; FOR i = 1 TO 4: total = total + i. What is the value of total after the loop finishes?
problems.eli5: The loop runs for i = 1, 2, 3, 4 (inclusive endpoints), adding i to a running total each pass: 0+1+2+3+4 = 10. The 6 option stops at i = 3, the off-by-one error. The 15 option runs one extra pass to i = 5. The 4 option is just the number of iterations, not the sum.
problems.hint: FOR i = 1 TO 4 runs four times (1,2,3,4). Add each i to the running total.

steps.text: i = 4: total = 6 + 4 = 10. Loop ends (i would be 5, past 4).

traps: Stopping at i = 3 (off-by-one) for a total of 6
Reporting the iteration count (4) instead of the accumulated sum

problems.statement: Given the logic: IF x > 10 THEN y = 1; ELSE IF x > 5 THEN y = 2; ELSE y = 3. If x = 7, what is the value of y?
problems.eli5: Conditions are checked top to bottom and the first true one wins. x = 7 is not greater than 10 (first test fails), but 7 > 5 is true (second test), so y = 2 and the final ELSE is skipped. The value 1 would require x > 10. The value 3 would require both tests to fail (x ≤ 5).
problems.hint: Check conditions in order; the first TRUE branch runs and the rest are skipped.

steps.text: First test: x > 10 → 7 > 10 → FALSE. Skip y = 1.
Second test: x > 5 → 7 > 5 → TRUE. Set y = 2.
The remaining ELSE branch is skipped. y = 2.

traps: Falling through to the final ELSE (y = 3) instead of stopping at the first true test
Confusing the strict inequality (7 is not > 10)

problems.statement: Trace this WHILE loop: x = 1; WHILE x < 100: x = x * 2. What is the value of x when the loop stops?
problems.eli5: A WHILE loop keeps doubling as long as x < 100, and it stops the moment the condition fails. The sequence is 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32 → 64 → 128. When x = 64 the condition (64 < 100) is still true, so it doubles once more to 128. Now 128 < 100 is false, so the loop stops with x = 128. The choice 64 stops one pass too early. The choice 100 assumes the loop caps at the limit, which it does not.
problems.hint: Keep doubling while x < 100; the value that breaks the condition is the final value.

steps.text: At x = 64 the condition 64 < 100 is still true, so double once more: x = 128.
Now 128 < 100 is FALSE, so the loop exits with x = 128.

traps: Stopping at 64 because it is the last value below 100, forgetting the loop doubles it again
Assuming the result is capped at the limit value (100)

mathematics/numerical-methods.name: Numerical Methods: Root-Finding
mathematics/numerical-methods.application: When an equation cannot be solved in closed form, engineers find roots numerically. As a civil engineer you use these methods inside spreadsheets and solvers to find, for example, the depth that satisfies a nonlinear flow equation. On the FE, expect to apply one iteration of Newton's method and to know the requirement that makes bisection work.

content.body: A root of f(x) is a value where f(x) = 0. Two standard numerical methods find roots when algebra cannot: Newton's method (fast, needs the derivative) and bisection (robust, needs a sign change).
Newton's Method

content.label: Each iteration refines the estimate using the slope

content.body: Starting from an estimate $x_j$, Newton's method follows the tangent line to a better estimate. It converges quickly when the initial guess is near the root, but can fail if the guess is poor or the derivative is near zero.
Bisection Method

Bisection brackets a root in an interval $[a, b]$ where the function changes sign — that is, $f(a)\cdot f(b) < 0$ — then repeatedly halves the interval, keeping the half that still contains the sign change. It always converges but more slowly than Newton's method.
Newton's method is fast but needs a good starting guess and the derivative; bisection is slow but guaranteed to converge as long as the interval brackets a sign change.
Newton's method can diverge or oscillate if the initial estimate is far from the root or if f′(x) is near zero (a flat slope sends the next estimate far away).

problems.statement: Use one iteration of Newton's method to improve the estimate of a root of $f(x) = x^2 - 2$, starting from $x_0 = 1.5$. (Here $f'(x) = 2x$.) What is $x_1$?
problems.eli5: x₁ = x₀ − f(x₀)/f′(x₀). f(1.5) = 1.5² − 2 = 0.25; f′(1.5) = 2(1.5) = 3. So x₁ = 1.5 − 0.25/3 = 1.5 − 0.0833 = 1.417 (approaching √2 ≈ 1.4142). The 1.333 choice forgets to square (uses x-2 over 2). The 1.500 choice is just the starting value. The 1.250 choice over-corrects.
problems.hint: x₁ = x₀ − f(x₀)/f′(x₀); compute f and f′ at 1.5.

steps.text: Evaluate f and f′ at x₀ = 1.5:

traps: Forgetting to divide by the derivative
Adding instead of subtracting the correction

problems.statement: The bisection method can find a root in an interval $[a, b]$ only if which condition holds?

choices.text: The function changes sign over the interval: $f(a)\cdot f(b) < 0$
The function is positive at both ends
The derivative is zero somewhere in the interval
The interval is shorter than 1 unit

problems.eli5: Bisection relies on the Intermediate Value Theorem: if a continuous function has opposite signs at the two endpoints (f(a)·f(b) < 0), a root must lie between them. The "positive at both ends" option gives no guarantee of a root. The "derivative is zero" and "interval shorter than 1 unit" options are irrelevant to the bracketing requirement.
