problems.hint: What must be true about the function's sign at the two ends of the interval?

steps.text: Bisection brackets a root between sign changes.
A sign change means f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs.

traps: Thinking same-sign endpoints can bracket a root
Confusing the bisection requirement with a derivative condition

problems.statement: Under what condition is Newton's method most likely to FAIL to converge?

choices.text: When the initial estimate is far from the root or the derivative is near zero
When the initial estimate is very close to the root
When the function is a straight line

problems.eli5: Newton's method follows the tangent slope. A poor (far) starting guess or a near-zero derivative (a nearly flat tangent) throws the next estimate far away, so the method may diverge or oscillate. A close starting guess and a straight line (where it converges in one step) are ideal, not failures. A large derivative gives small, well-behaved steps.
problems.hint: The method uses the slope — what makes a tangent line send you far from the root?

steps.text: Newton's step is f(x)/f′(x); a near-zero f′ makes the step huge.
A far initial guess can also send iterations away from the root.
So poor guesses or near-zero derivatives cause failure.

traps: Assuming a close initial guess causes failure
Overlooking the near-zero-derivative problem

statistics/central-tendency-dispersion.name: Measures of Central Tendency & Dispersion
statistics/central-tendency-dispersion.application: Civil engineers compute means and standard deviations constantly — averaging concrete cylinder break strengths to verify a pour meets spec, computing the standard deviation of traffic counts to size turn lanes, or summarizing soil boring data across a site. When you report a value to a client, the spread tells you whether you need more samples or whether the data is tight enough to design on. On the FE, expect straightforward “find the mean” or “find the standard deviation” questions where the only trap is which formula to use.

content.body: Six descriptive statistics summarize any data set: three for center (mean, median, mode) and three for spread (range, variance, standard deviation). The FE gives you the formulas — your job is picking the right one and not mixing up population vs. sample.
Arithmetic Mean
Add every value, divide by the count. The weighted mean replaces equal weighting with specific weights $w_i$.
Median and Mode
The median is the middle value when data is sorted. For even $n$, average the two middle values. The mode is the value that appears most often — a set can have no mode, one mode, or multiple modes.
Variance and Standard Deviation
The only difference is the denominator: $N$ for a population, $n-1$ for a sample. The FE almost always uses the sample formula ($n-1$) — that’s Bessel’s correction.
Coefficient of Variation
A dimensionless measure of relative spread. Useful for comparing variability between data sets with different units or scales.
The number one trap on the FE: dividing by $n$ instead of $n-1$ for sample standard deviation. If the problem says “sample” or gives you a subset of data, use $n-1$.
Variance is standard deviation squared — and vice versa. Some problems give you $\sigma^2$ and ask for $\sigma$, or give $s$ and ask for $s^2$. Read the question twice.

TI-36X Pro: Enter data with [data], then [2nd][data] (stat) → 1-Var Stats. The output gives you six values: $n$ = number of data points, $\bar{x}$ = sample mean (arithmetic average), $s_x$ = sample standard deviation (uses $n-1$), $\sigma_x$ = population standard deviation (uses $n$), $\Sigma x$ = sum of all values, $\Sigma x^2$ = sum of all squared values. For the FE, you almost always want $\bar{x}$ and $s_x$. Ignore $\sigma_x$ unless the problem explicitly says “population.”

problems.statement: A geotechnical engineer collects five soil moisture content readings from a site: $12.3\%$, $14.1\%$, $11.8\%$, $13.5\%$, and $12.8\%$. What is the arithmetic mean moisture content?
problems.eli5: Just add them up and divide by 5. The trap here is the 64.50% option — that’s the sum, not the mean. Some students rush and pick the first number they compute. Also, don’t confuse this with the median (which would be 12.8 after sorting). The mean is 12.9 because you’re averaging all five readings equally.
problems.hint: Add all five values, then divide by the number of readings.

steps.text: TI-36X Pro: [data] → enter all 5 values → [2nd][data] (stat) → 1-Var Stats. Read $\bar{x} = 12.9$ (that’s your mean). You can ignore $s_x$ and $\sigma_x$ for this problem — it only asks for the mean.

traps: Picking the sum (64.5) instead of dividing by n
Confusing mean with median (the middle value after sorting is 12.8, not 12.9)

problems.statement: A quality control lab tests six concrete cylinders from a single pour and records compressive strengths (in psi): $4120$, $4250$, $4080$, $4310$, $4190$, $4150$. What is the sample standard deviation?
problems.eli5: This is the classic “compute the sample standard deviation” problem. The key word is sample — these 6 cylinders represent one pour, not the entire universe of concrete, so you divide by n−1 = 5, not n = 6. The 77.8 psi choice is what you’d get if you divided by n = 6 (population formula). The 7,267 choice is the variance, not the standard deviation — they’re hoping you forget to take the square root. The $230\,\text{psi}$ choice is just the range (max minus min), which is a different measure of spread entirely.
problems.hint: Use the sample formula — divide by $n - 1$, not $n$, then take the square root.

steps.text: TI-36X Pro: [data] → enter all 6 values → [2nd][data] (stat) → 1-Var Stats. Read $s_x = 85.2$ — that’s the sample standard deviation (uses $n-1$). Don’t accidentally read $\sigma_x$ — that’s the population version (uses $n$) and gives 77.8, which is the wrong answer here.

traps: Dividing by n instead of n−1 (gives 75.0 — the population std dev)
Reporting variance (s² = 6,753) instead of standard deviation

problems.statement: A transportation engineer measures traffic volumes at an intersection over three periods. The morning count is $520$ vehicles (counted over $2$ hours), the midday count is $870$ vehicles (counted over $5$ hours), and the evening count is $610$ vehicles (counted over $3$ hours). What is the weighted average hourly traffic volume?
problems.eli5: The trick is figuring out what the values and weights are. You’re not averaging the raw counts — you’re averaging the hourly rates, weighted by how long each period lasted. The 667 veh/hr choice is what you get if you just average the raw vehicle counts without converting to rates. The 212 veh/hr choice is the unweighted average of the three hourly rates — it treats the 2-hour morning period the same as the 5-hour midday period, which overweights the shorter observations. The 260 veh/hr choice is just the morning rate.
problems.hint: First convert each count to an hourly rate, then weight by the duration of each counting period.

steps.text: Convert raw counts to hourly rates:
Identify weights as the duration of each period:

traps: Averaging raw counts instead of hourly rates (gives 667)
Using unweighted average of rates instead of weighted average (gives 212)

statistics/linear-regression-correlation.name: Linear Regression & Correlation
statistics/linear-regression-correlation.application: Civil engineers fit regression lines to field data constantly — correlating SPT blow counts with soil shear strength, developing stage-discharge curves for stream gauges, or establishing relationships between traffic speed and density. The regression equation lets you predict one variable from another, and the correlation coefficient tells you how much to trust that prediction. On the FE, expect problems that give you summary statistics ($\Sigma x$, $\Sigma y$, $\Sigma xy$, etc.) and ask for the slope, intercept, or $R^2$.

content.body: Linear regression fits the best straight line through a scatter of data points. The FE gives you the formulas — your job is plugging in the summary statistics correctly and interpreting the result.
Least-Squares Regression Line
The regression line has the form $\hat{y} = a + bx$, where $b$ is the slope and $a$ is the y-intercept.

content.latex: b = \frac{n\sum x_i y_i - \sum x_i \sum y_i}{n\sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2}
content.label: Slope

content.body: The intercept formula is much simpler — once you have $b$, just plug in the means.
Correlation Coefficient

content.latex: r = \frac{n\sum x_i y_i - \sum x_i \sum y_i}{\sqrt{\left[n\sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2\right]\left[n\sum y_i^2 - (\sum y_i)^2\right]}}
content.label: Sample Correlation (r)

content.body: $r$ ranges from $-1$ to $+1$. Positive means both variables increase together; negative means one decreases as the other increases. The closer $|r|$ is to 1, the tighter the data fits the line.
Coefficient of Determination
$R^2$ tells you the fraction of variability in $y$ explained by $x$. If $R^2 = 0.85$, the regression explains 85% of the variation — the remaining 15% is unexplained scatter.
Residual
The residual is the vertical distance between an observed point and the regression line. Positive means the point is above the line; negative means below.

TI-36X Pro: Enter paired data with [data] (two columns: L1 = x, L2 = y), then [2nd][data] (stat) → LinReg (ax+b). The calculator gives you $a$ (slope), $b$ (intercept), and $r$ (correlation coefficient) instantly. This is the single biggest time-saver on regression problems.

Notice the numerator of $b$ and $r$ are identical: $n\sum x_i y_i - \sum x_i \sum y_i$. The slope formula just divides by the $x$-side denominator; the correlation formula divides by the geometric mean of both sides.
Don’t confuse $r$ and $R^2$. If a problem asks for the coefficient of determination, square $r$. If it asks for the correlation coefficient, don’t square it.

problems.statement: A hydrologist collects 5 paired measurements of rainfall depth ($x$, in cm) and runoff volume ($y$, in m³). The summary statistics are: $n = 5$, $\sum x = 30$, $\sum y = 120$, $\sum x_i y_i = 860$, $\sum x_i^2 = 220$. What is the slope of the least-squares regression line?
problems.eli5: Plug the five summary statistics into the slope formula. The numerator is $n\sum xy - \sum x \sum y$ and the denominator is $n\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2$. The 4.0 choice comes from dividing $\sum y$ by $\sum x$ ($120/30$) — that’s the ratio of totals, not the regression slope. The 24.0 choice is $\bar{y} = 120/5 = 24$, which is just the mean of $y$. The 0.286 choice is the reciprocal of the slope ($1/3.5$) — you probably flipped the fraction.
problems.hint: Use the slope formula with the five given summary statistics. Watch the order of terms in the numerator.

steps.latex: b = \frac{n\sum x_i y_i - \sum x_i \sum y_i}{n\sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2}

steps.text: TI-36X Pro: [data] → enter all 5 $(x, y)$ pairs in L1/L2 → [2nd][data] (stat) → LinReg → read the slope $b = 3.5$.

problems.handbookFormula: b = \frac{n\sum x_i y_i - \sum x_i \sum y_i}{n\sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2}
traps: Dividing Σy by Σx instead of using the regression formula (gives 4.0)
Flipping numerator and denominator (gives the reciprocal 0.286)

problems.statement: A structural engineer develops a regression model relating the age of a steel bridge ($x$, years) to its condition rating ($y$, scale 1–9). The correlation coefficient is $r = -0.92$. What percentage of the variation in condition rating is explained by bridge age?
problems.eli5: The question asks for “percentage of variation explained” — that’s $R^2$, not $r$. Square the correlation coefficient: $(-0.92)^2 = 0.846$. The negative sign disappears when you square. The 92% option is just $|r|$ expressed as a percentage — that’s the correlation, not the determination. The -84.6% option is impossible — $R^2$ is always positive (you can’t explain a negative percentage of variation). The 8.0% option comes from $1 - 0.92 = 0.08$ — confusing the complement of $r$ with the complement of $R^2$.
problems.hint: “Variation explained” means $R^2$. Square the correlation coefficient — the sign doesn’t matter.

steps.text: The coefficient of determination is $R^2 = r^2$.

traps: Reporting r (92%) instead of r² (84.6%) — confusing correlation with determination
Thinking R² can be negative because r is negative

problems.statement: A geotechnical engineer correlates Standard Penetration Test blow count ($x$) with undrained shear strength ($y$, in kPa). From 8 borings: $\bar{x} = 15$, $\bar{y} = 75$, and the regression slope is $b = 4.2$. Using the regression equation, what is the predicted shear strength for a blow count of $x = 20$?
problems.eli5: This is a two-step problem. First you need the intercept — they don’t give it to you directly, but you know the regression line passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, so $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x} = 75 - 4.2(15) = 12$. Then plug in $x = 20$: $\hat{y} = 12 + 4.2(20) = 96$. The 84 kPa option is $4.2 \times 20$ without adding the intercept — they forgot the $a$ term. The 75 kPa option is just $\bar{y}$ — the mean, not a prediction at $x = 20$. The 12 kPa option is the intercept itself, not the prediction.
problems.hint: First find the intercept using $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$, then plug $x = 20$ into the full equation $\hat{y} = a + bx$.
traps: Forgetting the intercept and computing only b × x (gives 84)
Reporting the mean ȳ as the prediction regardless of x (gives 75)

statistics/probability-distributions.name: Probability Distributions
statistics/probability-distributions.application: Civil engineers deal with probability every time they design for uncertainty — sizing a culvert for the 100-year storm, estimating the chance that fewer than 3 out of 20 concrete cylinders fail spec, or determining whether observed traffic accidents at an intersection are statistically unusual. The FE tests your ability to compute basic probabilities, apply the binomial distribution for discrete pass/fail scenarios, and use the normal distribution with z-scores to find areas under the curve.

content.body: This lesson covers three layers: counting methods (how many ways can something happen), discrete probability (binomial), and continuous probability (normal). The FE handbook gives you all the formulas — your job is recognizing which distribution fits the problem.
Permutations and Combinations
A permutation cares about order. A combination does not. Use permutations when arrangement matters (e.g., ranking), combinations when you’re just choosing a group.
TI-36X Pro: Type the value of $n$, then [PRB] → nPr or nCr, then type $r$ and press [=]. Example: 10 nCr 3 = 120. No manual factorials needed.
Laws of Probability

content.latex: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
content.label: Addition Rule

content.body: If events are mutually exclusive, $P(A \cap B) = 0$. If events are independent, $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$, so the multiplication rule simplifies to $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$.
Binomial Distribution
Use when you have $n$ independent trials, each with the same probability $p$ of success. The question asks for the probability of exactly $x$ successes.
Normal Distribution and Z-Scores

The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the bell curve. To find probabilities, convert any normal variable to a standard normal using the z-score, then look up the area in the unit normal table provided in the FE handbook.
In the handbook table: $F(z)$ = area from $-\infty$ to $z$, $R(z)$ = area from $z$ to $\infty$, $W(z)$ = area between $-z$ and $z$. Remember that $F(-z) = 1 - F(z)$.

Decision tree: Fixed number of trials with pass/fail outcome → Binomial. Continuous measurement with a bell-shaped spread → Normal. If the problem gives you $\mu$ and $\sigma$ and asks for a probability above or below some value, it’s always z-score.
The binomial formula uses $C(n, x)$, not $P(n, x)$. Order doesn’t matter when counting successes — 3 failures out of 10 is the same regardless of which 3 failed.

The FE handbook includes a full unit normal distribution table at the end of the statistics section. You do NOT need to memorize z-values — just know how to read the table. $F(z)$ gives you the left-tail area directly.

problems.statement: A project manager must select 3 inspectors from a pool of 8 qualified engineers to review a bridge deck pour. How many different inspection teams are possible?
problems.eli5: This is a straight combinations problem — you’re choosing a group, not ranking them, so order doesn’t matter. The choice 336 is the permutation $P(8,3)$ — that’s what you’d get if you cared about who was picked first, second, and third. The choice 24 is $4!$, which has nothing to do with this problem. The choice 512 is $8^3$, which would be the answer if each pick were independent with replacement.
problems.hint: Are you arranging the inspectors in order, or just picking a group? That tells you permutation vs. combination.

steps.text: Order doesn’t matter (a team is a team), so use combinations.

traps: Using permutations instead of combinations (gives 336)
Confusing C(8,3) with 8³ (gives 512)

problems.statement: A batch of 10 asphalt samples is tested, and historically $90\%$ of samples from this plant pass the Marshall stability test. What is the probability that exactly 8 of the 10 samples pass?
problems.eli5: The binomial formula has three pieces: the number of ways to arrange 8 passes and 2 failures ($C(10,8) = 45$), the probability of 8 passes ($0.9^8$), and the probability of 2 failures ($0.1^2$). You multiply all three. The 0.349 distractor is $P(X = 10) = 0.9^{10}$ — the probability of all 10 passing, not exactly 8. The 0.900 distractor is just $p$ itself, not a binomial calculation. The 0.387 distractor is $P(X = 9)$ — the probability of exactly 9 passing, not 8.
problems.hint: Identify $n$, $x$, $p$, and $q$, then plug into the binomial formula. Don’t forget the $C(n,x)$ term.
traps: Forgetting the C(n,x) term (gives only pˣqⁿ⁻ˣ, which is far too small)
Computing P(X = 9) instead of P(X = 8) (gives 0.349)

problems.statement: The 28-day compressive strength of a concrete mix is normally distributed with a mean of $4{,}500\,\text{psi}$ and a standard deviation of $300\,\text{psi}$. The specification requires a minimum strength of $4{,}000\,\text{psi}$. What percentage of cylinders are expected to fail the specification?
problems.eli5: You’re looking for the left-tail area — the percentage below 4,000 psi. First convert 4,000 to a z-score: it’s 1.67 standard deviations below the mean, so $z = -1.67$. The handbook table gives you $F(1.67) = 0.9525$, which is the area to the LEFT of positive 1.67. For the negative side, flip it: $1 - 0.9525 = 0.0475$, or 4.75%. The 95.25% option is $F(1.67)$ — that’s the percentage that PASSES, not fails. The 1.67% option is the z-score itself (1.67) misread as a probability. The 45.25% option treats it as if the mean were shifted or misreads the table.
problems.hint: Compute the z-score for $4{,}000$ psi, then use $F(-z) = 1 - F(z)$ to find the left-tail probability.

steps.text: Look up the area to the left of $z = -1.67$ using the symmetry rule:

traps: Reporting the pass rate (95.25%) instead of the fail rate
Confusing the z-score value (1.67) with a probability

statistics/expected-value-weighted-avera.name: Expected Value & Weighted Averages
statistics/expected-value-weighted-avera.application: Civil engineers use expected values when comparing alternatives under uncertainty — weighting each outcome by its probability to decide between bridge repair strategies, estimating the average number of vehicle arrivals at a toll plaza per hour, or computing the expected cost of a project with multiple risk scenarios. On the FE, expect problems that hand you a probability table and ask for $E(X)$, or that combine independent random variables and ask for the resulting mean or standard deviation.

content.body: Expected value is just a weighted average where the weights are probabilities. If you can build a table of outcomes and their probabilities, you can compute $E(X)$ in one line.
Expected Value (Discrete)
Multiply each outcome by its probability, then add. The result is the long-run average — not necessarily a value that can actually occur.
Variance from Expected Value
This shortcut avoids computing every $(x_k - \mu)^2$ term. First find $E(X^2) = \sum x_k^2 \cdot P(x_k)$, then subtract the square of the mean.
Linearity of Expectation
When you combine random variables, the expected value of the sum is the sum of the expected values — always, regardless of independence.

content.latex: E(a_1 X_1 + a_2 X_2 + \cdots + a_n X_n) = a_1 E(X_1) + a_2 E(X_2) + \cdots + a_n E(X_n)

content.body: Variance of Combinations
Variances add only if the random variables are independent. And the constants get squared.

content.latex: \text{Var}(a_1 X_1 + a_2 X_2 + \cdots + a_n X_n) = a_1^2\,\sigma_1^2 + a_2^2\,\sigma_2^2 + \cdots + a_n^2\,\sigma_n^2

content.body: The standard deviation of the combination is the square root of this sum — not the sum of the standard deviations.
Shortcut for variance: the $E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2$ form is almost always faster than computing deviations from the mean. Build two columns in your scratch work: $x \cdot P(x)$ and $x^2 \cdot P(x)$.
Standard deviations do NOT add directly. If you need the standard deviation of a sum of independent variables, add the variances first, then take the square root of the total.

problems.statement: A contractor estimates the following profit outcomes for a bridge rehabilitation project: best case 120,000 dollars (probability $0.25$), expected case 80,000 dollars (probability $0.50$), worst case 20,000 dollars (probability $0.25$). What is the expected profit?
problems.eli5: Multiply each outcome by its probability, then add. That’s it. The 80,000 dollars choice is the mode — the most likely single outcome — but that’s not the expected value. The expected value weights all outcomes by how likely they are. The 73,333 dollars choice is what you get if you just average the three profits without using the probabilities (simple mean of 120k, 80k, 20k). The 220,000 dollars choice is the sum of all profits without any probability weighting.
problems.hint: Multiply each profit by its probability and add the results.
traps: Picking the most likely outcome ($80,000) instead of computing the weighted sum
Taking the simple average of the three values instead of using the probabilities (gives $73,333)

problems.statement: A traffic sensor at a toll plaza records the number of trucks per minute during the morning peak. The probability distribution is: $x = 1$ with $P = 0.10$, $x = 2$ with $P = 0.30$, $x = 3$ with $P = 0.40$, $x = 4$ with $P = 0.20$. What is the variance of trucks per minute?
problems.eli5: Two-column scratch work makes this fast. Column 1: $x \cdot P(x)$ gives you $E(X) = 2.70$. Column 2: $x^2 \cdot P(x)$ gives you $E(X^2) = 8.10$. Then subtract: $8.10 - 2.70^2 = 0.81$. The 0.90 choice comes from a rounding or arithmetic slip. The 2.70 choice is $E(X)$ itself — the mean, not the variance. The 8.10 choice is $E(X^2)$, which is only the first half of the variance formula.
problems.hint: Use the shortcut $\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2$. Build two columns: $x \cdot P(x)$ and $x^2 \cdot P(x)$.
traps: Reporting E(X) as the answer instead of Var(X) (gives 2.70)
Reporting E(X²) without subtracting [E(X)]² (gives 8.10)

problems.statement: Two independent loads act on a bridge beam. Dead load $D$ has a mean of $50\,\text{kN}$ and standard deviation of $3\,\text{kN}$. Live load $L$ has a mean of $30\,\text{kN}$ and standard deviation of $8\,\text{kN}$. The total load is $T = D + L$. What is the standard deviation of the total load?
problems.eli5: This is the classic “standard deviations don’t add” trap. When you combine independent random variables, you add the variances (the squared standard deviations), then take the square root at the end. So it’s $\sqrt{3^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{73} = 8.54$. The 11.0 kN option is what you get if you add the standard deviations directly ($3 + 8 = 11$) — that’s the most common mistake. The 73 kN option is the variance, not the standard deviation — you forgot the square root. The 80.0 kN option is the mean of the total load ($50 + 30$), not its standard deviation.
problems.hint: Variances add (not standard deviations). Square first, add, then take the square root.

steps.text: The loads are independent, so variances add:

traps: Adding standard deviations directly instead of variances (gives 11.0)
Reporting variance (73) instead of standard deviation

statistics/confidence-intervals-estimati.name: Confidence Intervals & Estimation
statistics/confidence-intervals-estimati.application: Civil engineers build confidence intervals every time they report field data with a margin of error — stating that a soil’s friction angle is 32° ± 3° at 95% confidence, or that the mean 28-day concrete strength is 4,200 ± 150 psi. That range directly affects design safety factors and whether you need more samples. On the FE, expect problems that give you sample data and ask you to construct an interval or determine the required sample size.

content.body: A confidence interval gives a range around a sample statistic that’s likely to contain the true population parameter. The width depends on three things: the confidence level, the variability, and the sample size.
Confidence Interval — σ Known (Z)
When the population standard deviation $\sigma$ is known (rare in practice, common on the FE), use the z-based interval.
Confidence Interval — σ Unknown (t)
When you compute $s$ from your sample (the usual case), use the t-distribution with $v = n - 1$ degrees of freedom.
Common z Values
The FE handbook provides these on p. 75. Memorizing the 95% value ($z_{\alpha/2} = 1.960$) is enough — the rest are in the table: 90% → 1.645, 95% → 1.960, 99% → 2.576.
Sample Size
If you need a specific margin of error $e$ before collecting data, solve for $n$.
Always round $n$ up to the next whole number — you can’t test half a specimen.

Decision tree: Does the problem give you $\sigma$ (population std dev)? Use z. Does it give you $s$ (sample std dev)? Use t with $n-1$ degrees of freedom. The FE almost always tells you which one you have.
The margin of error is $z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma / \sqrt{n}$, NOT $z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma / n$. Forgetting the square root on $n$ is a classic exam mistake.
The FE handbook includes z-values on p. 75 and a t-distribution table. You do NOT need to memorize these — just know which table to use and how to read it.

problems.statement: A geotechnical lab tests 25 soil samples and measures a mean liquid limit of $\bar{x} = 42\%$. The population standard deviation is known to be $\sigma = 5\%$. What is the 95% confidence interval for the true mean liquid limit?
problems.eli5: This is the simplest confidence interval — they give you $\sigma$ directly, so use z. Plug into the formula: $42 \pm 1.96 \times (5/\sqrt{25})$. The $\sqrt{25} = 5$, so the standard error is $5/5 = 1.0$, and the margin is $1.96 \times 1.0 = 1.96$. The $(41.02\%,\; 42.98\%)$ distractor has too small a margin ($0.98$) — it halves the correct standard error instead of using $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 1.0$. The $(32.20\%,\; 51.80\%)$ distractor forgets to divide by $\sqrt{n}$ entirely (uses $1.96 \times 5 = 9.8$). The $(40.08\%,\; 43.92\%)$ distractor is a close distractor from a rounding variation (margin $1.92$).
problems.hint: The problem gives you $\sigma$ (not $s$), so use the z-interval. Don’t forget to divide $\sigma$ by $\sqrt{n}$.
traps: Dividing by n instead of √n (gives a much narrower interval)
Forgetting to divide by √n at all (gives a much wider interval)

problems.statement: An engineer tests 10 concrete cylinders and obtains a sample mean of $\bar{x} = 4{,}350\,\text{psi}$ with a sample standard deviation of $s = 120\,\text{psi}$. Using $t_{0.025,\,9} = 2.262$, what is the 95% confidence interval for the true mean strength?
problems.eli5: The key difference from P1: they give you $s$ (sample std dev), not $\sigma$ (population), so you must use the t-distribution. The degrees of freedom are $n - 1 = 9$, and they tell you $t = 2.262$. The interval $(4{,}276,\;4{,}424)$ uses $z = 1.960$ instead of the given t-value — that’s wrong because with only 10 samples and unknown $\sigma$, the z-interval is too narrow. The interval $(4{,}115,\;4{,}585)$ forgets to divide by $\sqrt{n}$, giving a margin of $\pm 235$; it also uses $z = 1.960$ instead of $t$ ($1.960 \times 120 = 235$). The interval $(4{,}323,\;4{,}377)$ divides by $n = 10$ instead of $\sqrt{10} = 3.162$.
problems.hint: The problem gives you $s$ (not $\sigma$) and a t-value — use the t-interval formula with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom.
traps: Using z = 1.960 instead of the given t-value (gives a narrower interval)
Dividing by n instead of √n (gives a much narrower interval)

problems.statement: A transportation engineer wants to estimate the mean daily traffic volume at an intersection within $\pm 200$ vehicles at 95% confidence. Historical data suggests a population standard deviation of $\sigma = 800$ vehicles. What is the minimum number of days the engineer must count?
problems.eli5: Work backwards from the confidence interval formula. You want the margin of error to be exactly 200, so set $z \cdot \sigma / \sqrt{n} = 200$ and solve for $n$. The trick is remembering to round UP, not to the nearest integer. If you need 61.47 days, 61 days isn’t enough — you need 62. The 61.47 option is the raw calculation before rounding — not a valid answer since you can’t have a fraction of a day. The value 8 comes from forgetting to square ($7.84$ rounded to 8). The value 16 comes from using $z = 1.0$ instead of $1.960$.
problems.hint: Rearrange the margin of error formula to solve for $n$. Remember to round up to the next whole number.

steps.text: Round up: $n = 62$ (always round up — you can’t count for 0.47 of a day).

traps: Forgetting to square the result (gives ~8 instead of 62)
Reporting the raw decimal (61.47) instead of rounding up to 62

statistics/hypothesis-testing-goodness-o.name: Hypothesis Testing & Goodness of Fit
statistics/hypothesis-testing-goodness-o.application: Civil engineers run hypothesis tests whenever a specification is on the line — testing whether concrete strength meets the design minimum, whether a new traffic signal actually reduced accident rates, or whether soil compaction data matches the Proctor target. The test gives you a yes/no decision backed by statistics, not gut feeling. Chi-square goodness of fit shows up when you need to check whether observed data matches a theoretical distribution (uniform arrivals, Poisson failures, normal distribution). On the FE, expect problems that give you sample data, a claimed value, and ask you to compute the test statistic or make a reject/fail-to-reject decision.

content.body: Hypothesis testing is a decision framework: assume the status quo ($H_0$) is true, then check whether your data is surprising enough to reject it. If it is, you switch to $H_1$. If not, you stick with $H_0$.
Null and Alternative Hypotheses

$H_0$ (null) is the default claim — usually "no difference" or "meets spec." $H_1$ (alternative) is what you’re trying to prove. The test never proves $H_0$ — you either reject it or fail to reject it.
One-tailed tests ($H_1: \mu > \mu_0$ or $H_1: \mu < \mu_0$) are used when you care about one direction. Two-tailed tests ($H_1: \mu \neq \mu_0$) are used when any deviation matters.
Type I and Type II Errors

Type I error ($\alpha$): rejecting $H_0$ when it’s actually true (false alarm). Type II error ($\beta$): failing to reject $H_0$ when it’s actually false (missed detection). The significance level $\alpha$ is the probability of a Type I error — you choose it before testing.
Z-Test Statistic (σ Known)
Use when the population standard deviation $\sigma$ is known. Compare $z$ to $z_{\alpha}$ (one-tailed) or $z_{\alpha/2}$ (two-tailed).
t-Test Statistic (σ Unknown)
Use when you only have the sample standard deviation $s$. Degrees of freedom: $v = n - 1$. Compare $t$ to $t_{\alpha,\,v}$ from the t-table.
Chi-Square Goodness of Fit

$O_i$ = observed count, $E_i$ = expected count under the theoretical model. Degrees of freedom: $v = k - 1$ (where $k$ is the number of categories). If $\chi^2 > \chi^2_{\alpha,\,v}$, the data doesn’t fit the model.

Decision rule cheat sheet: for z and t tests, reject $H_0$ when $|\text{test statistic}| > \text{critical value}$. For chi-square, reject when $\chi^2 > \chi^2_{\text{crit}}$. In both cases, "bigger means reject."

Failing to reject $H_0$ does NOT mean $H_0$ is true. It means you don’t have enough evidence to reject it. The FE loves distractor choices that say "the mean equals $\mu_0$" after a fail-to-reject result.

The FE handbook gives you z-tables (p. 72) and t-tables (p. 73). You do NOT need to memorize critical values — just know which table to use and how to read it based on $\alpha$ and degrees of freedom.

problems.statement: A materials engineer tests whether a new concrete mix meets the specified mean compressive strength of $\mu_0 = 4{,}000\,\text{psi}$. From 36 cylinders, she measures $\bar{x} = 4{,}120\,\text{psi}$ with a known population standard deviation of $\sigma = 360\,\text{psi}$. What is the test statistic?
problems.eli5: Plug straight into the z-test formula. The numerator is how far the sample mean is from the hypothesized mean ($4{,}120 - 4{,}000 = 120$). The denominator is the standard error ($360/\sqrt{36} = 60$). The 0.33 option divides the difference by $\sigma$ itself ($120/360$) — forgot to divide $\sigma$ by $\sqrt{n}$. The 12.0 option multiplies by $\sqrt{n}$ instead of dividing $\sigma$ by it — a unit mix-up. The 0.056 option scales the difference down by far too much, the wrong order of magnitude.
problems.hint: Compute $(\bar{x} - \mu_0)$ for the numerator and $\sigma / \sqrt{n}$ for the denominator.
traps: Dividing by σ instead of σ/√n (gives 0.33)
Forgetting to take the square root of n in the denominator

problems.statement: A geotechnical engineer claims the mean bearing capacity of a clay deposit exceeds $200\,\text{kPa}$. From 16 field tests: $\bar{x} = 218\,\text{kPa}$, $s = 30\,\text{kPa}$. The critical value for a one-tailed test at $\alpha = 0.05$ with 15 degrees of freedom is $t_{0.05,\,15} = 1.753$. What is the correct conclusion?

choices.text: Fail to reject $H_0$; insufficient evidence that $\mu > 200\,\text{kPa}$
Fail to reject $H_0$; the mean is exactly $200\,\text{kPa}$

problems.eli5: Two things to get right: compute the t-statistic, then compare it to the critical value. $t = 18/7.5 = 2.4$, which beats the threshold of 1.753, so you reject $H_0$. The "fail to reject" option gets the comparison backward — 2.4 is greater than 1.753, not less. The "$\mu \neq 200$" option uses the wrong alternative hypothesis — the engineer’s claim is $\mu > 200$ (one-tailed), not $\mu \neq 200$ (two-tailed). The "mean is exactly 200" option is a conceptual error — failing to reject $H_0$ doesn’t prove $H_0$ is true, and besides, we rejected anyway.
problems.hint: Compute the t-statistic first, then compare to the given critical value. The claim is one-tailed (greater than).

steps.text: Compare to the critical value: $t = 2.4 > t_{\text{crit}} = 1.753$.
Since $t > t_{\text{crit}}$, reject $H_0$. There is sufficient evidence that $\mu > 200\,\text{kPa}$.

traps: Mixing up one-tailed vs. two-tailed — the claim is "exceeds," so it’s one-tailed right
Thinking fail-to-reject means "the null is true" — it only means insufficient evidence

problems.statement: A traffic engineer models vehicle arrivals at an intersection as a uniform distribution across 4 time periods. Over 200 observations, the observed counts are: Period 1 = 60, Period 2 = 45, Period 3 = 55, Period 4 = 40. At $\alpha = 0.05$ with $\chi^2_{0.05,\,3} = 7.815$, should the engineer reject the uniform model?

choices.text: $\chi^2 = 5.0$; fail to reject the uniform model
$\chi^2 = 0.10$; fail to reject the uniform model

problems.eli5: Chi-square goodness of fit checks whether observed data matches a theoretical model. Under uniform distribution, you expect $200/4 = 50$ per period. Compute $(O - E)^2 / E$ for each cell and add them up. You get 5.0. Since $5.0 < 7.815$, the data doesn’t deviate enough to reject the model. The "$\chi^2 = 5.0$; reject the uniform model" choice gets the decision backward — when $\chi^2$ is LESS than the critical value, you fail to reject (the data fits well enough). The "$\chi^2 = 50.0$; reject" choice forgot to divide by $E$ — adding $(O-E)^2$ without dividing gives an inflated value of $100 + 25 + 25 + 100 = 250$ instead of 5.0, so any large un-normalized total is a sign $E$ was mishandled. The "$\chi^2 = 0.10$; fail to reject" choice divided $(O-E)$ by $E$ before squaring instead of after, which gives a tiny number.
problems.hint: Compute expected counts first ($200 / 4$), then apply $\sum (O - E)^2 / E$ and compare to the critical value.

steps.text: Under the uniform model, each expected count is:
Compare: $\chi^2 = 5.0 < 7.815 = \chi^2_{\text{crit}}$. Fail to reject $H_0$ — the uniform model is adequate.

traps: Forgetting to divide by Eᵢ in each term (gives a much larger χ²)
Rejecting when χ² < χ²_crit — the decision is "reject when big"

ethics/obligations-to-the-public.name: Obligations to the Public
ethics/obligations-to-the-public.application: Every section of the NCEES Model Rules starts with one idea: public safety comes first. On the FE, ethics questions test whether you can identify which obligation takes priority when two rules collide — and the answer is almost always "protect the public." Civil engineers sign and seal plans for bridges, buildings, and water systems that directly affect human life, so the exam checks that you know the ten rules in Section A cold, especially the hierarchy: public safety > employer loyalty > personal interest.

content.body: The NCEES Model Rules §240.15 Section A lists ten obligations every licensee owes to the public. You don't need to memorize them word-for-word — the exam tests whether you can apply the right rule to a scenario. Here's the framework.
The Cardinal Rule — Safety First

Rule A.1 is the foundation of everything: your $\textit{first and foremost}$ responsibility is to safeguard the health, safety, and welfare of the public. When any other obligation conflicts with this one, A.1 wins. Period.

If a question ever asks "what should the engineer do first?" and one answer involves protecting the public, that's almost certainly correct. The exam loves testing whether you'll prioritize public safety over client deadlines, employer pressure, or personal gain.
Seal Only What You Can Stand Behind

Rule A.2 says you only sign and seal documents that conform to accepted standards and safeguard public welfare. If your boss hands you plans that cut corners on a retaining wall design, you don't seal them — even if they're technically your project.
Blow the Whistle When It Matters

Rule A.3 is the whistleblower rule. If your professional judgment is overruled and public safety is at risk, you must notify your employer and the appropriate authority. Staying quiet to keep the peace is a violation.

Common exam trap: a question where the engineer disagrees with the client but public safety isn't actually at risk. In that case, A.3 doesn't apply — you don't blow the whistle over a design preference. The trigger is specifically "health, safety, or welfare of the public is endangered."
Honesty and Competence

Rules A.4 and A.5 cover truthfulness. All professional documents must include relevant information presented objectively and truthfully (A.4). Public opinions must be founded on adequate knowledge and competent evaluation (A.5). In short: don't guess, don't spin, and don't speak outside your expertise.
Disclosure, Fraud & Reporting

Rules A.6 through A.8 deal with transparency. If someone is paying you to say something publicly, disclose it (A.6). Don't partner with anyone engaged in fraud (A.7). And if you know another licensee is violating the rules, you must report it to the board (A.8).

Decision tree for "what should the engineer do?" questions: (1) Is public safety at risk? → Notify employer + authorities (A.3). (2) Is another licensee violating rules? → Report to the board (A.8). (3) Is the engineer being asked to act outside their competence? → Decline the work. (4) None of the above? → Look at Sections B or C.
Licensure Integrity

Rules A.9 and A.10 close out the section. Don't lie on behalf of an applicant seeking licensure (A.9), and comply with the licensing laws of every jurisdiction where you practice (A.10). These show up less often on the exam but are straightforward.

The exam typically gives you 2-3 ethics questions. They're fast points if you know the hierarchy: (1) public safety is paramount, (2) honesty and truthfulness always, (3) report violations to the board. Most wrong answers try to tempt you with "tell your supervisor and do nothing else" — that's almost never sufficient when safety is at stake.

problems.statement: A structural engineer discovers that the concrete mix specified by the client for a parking garage does not meet the minimum compressive strength required by the building code. The client insists on using the cheaper mix to stay within budget. What should the engineer do?

choices.text: Use the client's specified mix and note the deviation in the project file
Reduce the number of parking levels to compensate for the weaker concrete
Seal the plans but add a disclaimer limiting the engineer's liability
Refuse to seal the plans and notify the client that the design must meet code requirements

problems.eli5: This one is textbook Rule A.1 + A.2. The client wants to cut corners on concrete strength, but the building code exists to protect people. You can't seal plans that don't meet code — full stop. Using the client's mix and just noting the deviation in the project file is wrong because noting it doesn't fix the safety issue. Sealing the plans with a liability disclaimer is wrong because a disclaimer doesn't magically make unsafe concrete safe. Reducing the number of parking levels is creative but you can't just redesign around a code violation without the client's mix actually meeting requirements. The right move is to refuse to seal until the design is code-compliant.
problems.hint: Which obligation always takes priority when client requests conflict with public safety?

steps.text: Identify the core issue: the client wants to use a concrete mix that violates building code, which directly affects public safety.
Apply Rule A.1: the engineer's first and foremost responsibility is to safeguard the health, safety, and welfare of the public.
Apply Rule A.2: licensees shall only sign and seal documents that conform to accepted standards and safeguard public welfare.
The engineer cannot seal plans that violate the building code regardless of client pressure. The correct action is to refuse to seal and require code-compliant design.

problems.handbookFormula: \text{A.1: First and foremost responsibility is to safeguard the health, safety, and welfare of the public.}
traps: Thinking that documenting the deviation protects the engineer — it doesn't satisfy A.2
Believing a disclaimer shifts liability and makes sealing acceptable

problems.statement: A geotechnical engineer working for a consulting firm learns that a colleague at the same firm made a significant error in a soil bearing capacity report for a school building project. The colleague has already submitted the report to the client. The engineer raises the concern to the colleague, who dismisses it. What is the engineer's most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Notify the firm's management and, if the issue is not resolved, report to the licensing board
Contact the school district directly to warn them about the error
Do nothing further since the colleague is responsible for their own work
Anonymously post a warning on a public engineering forum

problems.eli5: This is the classic "escalation ladder" question. You already tried step one — talking to the colleague — and got shut down. The next step isn't to go rogue and call the school district directly or post online, and it definitely isn't to shrug and walk away saying the colleague is responsible for their own work. You escalate through proper channels: tell management, and if they don't fix it, report to the licensing board. The exam tests whether you know the correct order of escalation. It's always: direct conversation → management → board. Jumping straight to the board or the public is only correct when there's imminent danger and no time for the chain.
problems.hint: Think about the proper order of escalation when a colleague's error puts public safety at risk.

steps.text: Identify the issue: a material error in a bearing capacity report for a school — public safety is clearly at risk (Rule A.1).
The engineer already tried informal resolution by talking to the colleague (consistent with Rule C.4 — make a reasonable effort to inform another licensee of a material error).
Since the colleague dismissed the concern, the engineer must escalate. Rule A.3 requires notifying the employer and appropriate authority when public safety is endangered.
Rule A.8 requires reporting violations to the board if the issue is not resolved through the chain of command.
The proper sequence is: colleague → management → board. Skipping management to go directly to the client or public is premature.

problems.handbookFormula: \text{A.3: Notify employer and appropriate authority when public safety is endangered.}
traps: Going directly to the client before exhausting internal channels — the firm should have the opportunity to correct the error first
Assuming "the colleague is responsible for their own work" releases you from reporting obligations under A.8

problems.statement: A civil engineer employed by a state transportation department is also a member of the department's consultant selection committee. A close friend who owns an engineering firm asks the engineer to recommend their firm for an upcoming highway bridge project. The friend's firm is technically qualified. Which action most closely aligns with the NCEES Model Rules?

choices.text: Recommend the friend's firm since they are technically qualified and public safety is not at risk
Recuse from the selection process for this project and disclose the personal relationship to the committee
Evaluate all firms objectively and vote for whichever is most qualified, regardless of the personal relationship
Resign from the selection committee entirely to avoid any future conflicts of interest

problems.eli5: This question is sneaky because it mixes Section A (public obligations) with Section B (employer/client obligations). The friend's firm being qualified is a red herring — the issue isn't competence, it's conflict of interest. Rule B.8 is very specific: if you serve on a government body, you can't participate in decisions about contracts involving people you have a relationship with. The "just vote objectively" option sounds reasonable, but the rules say the appearance of bias is enough to require action. And resigning from the committee entirely is overkill — you don't need to quit the whole committee, just sit out this one decision. The right answer is always disclose + recuse.
problems.hint: Focus on what the rules say about conflicts of interest when serving on a government selection body — is objectivity alone sufficient?

steps.text: Identify the issue: the engineer has a personal relationship with a firm competing for a government contract — this is a conflict of interest.
Apply Rule B.6: licensees shall disclose all known or potential conflicts of interest that could influence or appear to influence their judgment.
Apply Rule B.8: licensees serving as members of a government body shall not participate in decisions with respect to professional services offered by a concern where they have a personal interest.

Even though the friend's firm is qualified, the engineer's participation in the selection creates an appearance of bias. Voting objectively without stepping back ("evaluate all firms objectively and vote for whichever is most qualified") isn't enough — the engineer must also recuse from this decision.
Resigning from the committee entirely is excessive — recusal from this specific project is sufficient; permanent resignation isn't required.

problems.handbookFormula: \text{B.8: Licensees serving on a government body shall not participate in decisions involving firms where they have a personal interest.}
traps: Believing that technical qualification of the friend's firm eliminates the conflict — the rules address appearance of influence, not just actual bias
Choosing "evaluate objectively" (C) because it sounds ethical — but the Model Rules require recusal, not just good intentions

ethics/obligations-employers-clients-pee.name: Obligations to Employers, Clients & Other Licensees
ethics/obligations-employers-clients-pee.application: Sections B and C of the Model Rules govern how you deal with the people you work for and the people you work alongside. On the FE, these rules show up as conflict-of-interest scenarios, confidentiality dilemmas, and questions about professional competence boundaries. Civil engineers constantly juggle multiple clients, subconsultants, and government agencies — the exam checks that you know where the ethical lines are when money, loyalty, and professional reputation are in play.

content.body: Sections B and C of Model Rules §240.15 cover two relationships: your obligations to employers and clients (B, 9 rules) and your obligations to other licensees (C, 4 rules). The exam tests these less often than Section A, but the questions tend to be trickier because the "right" answer isn't always obvious.
Stay in Your Lane

Rule B.1 is the competence rule: only take on assignments you're qualified for by education or experience. Rule B.2 backs it up — don't sign or seal anything outside your area of competence, or anything not prepared under your responsible charge. The exception is B.3: you can coordinate an entire project if each technical segment is signed by the specialist who prepared it.

"Responsible charge" is a term the exam loves. It means direct control and personal supervision. If you didn't prepare the work or directly supervise the person who did, you can't seal it — even if you reviewed it and it looks fine.
Confidentiality and Conflicts of Interest

Rule B.4 protects client information — don't reveal facts obtained in a professional capacity without consent, except when required by law. Rules B.5 through B.7 address money and loyalty: no gratuities from contractors (B.5), disclose all conflicts of interest (B.6), and don't accept payment from multiple parties on the same project without written consent from everyone (B.7).

Conflict-of-interest questions are the most common trap in Sections B and C. The exam tests whether you can spot the conflict — not whether the engineer is actually biased. Under B.6, even the appearance of a conflict requires disclosure.
Government Service

Rule B.8 is specific to engineers who serve on government bodies. If you sit on a selection committee or advisory board, you cannot participate in decisions about contracts involving your own firm or personal connections. The reverse also applies — your firm can't bid on work from a body where you serve. B.9 rounds out the section: don't use confidential information from your assignments for personal profit.
Obligations to Other Licensees

Section C has just four rules, all about professional integrity. Don't misrepresent your qualifications or exaggerate your role in past projects (C.1). Don't offer gifts or political contributions to secure work (C.2). Don't trash another licensee's reputation (C.3). And if you believe another licensee's work contains a material error that could affect public safety, make a reasonable effort to inform them (C.4).

Quick mental model for Sections B and C: Section B = "don't cheat the people who pay you." Section C = "don't cheat the people who do what you do." Both boil down to honesty, competence, and transparency.

When a question involves two licensees disagreeing, check whether public safety is at risk. If yes, escalate per A.3/A.8. If no, the answer is usually C.4 — make a reasonable effort to inform the other licensee directly.

problems.statement: A transportation engineer is offered a freelance assignment to design a roundabout intersection. The engineer has extensive experience with highway alignment and signalized intersections but has never designed a roundabout. According to the NCEES Model Rules, what should the engineer do?

choices.text: Decline the assignment because it falls outside the engineer's specific area of competence
Accept the assignment since highway intersection experience is close enough
Accept the assignment and learn roundabout design while working on the project
Accept the assignment but have a colleague review the final design

problems.eli5: Rule B.1 is blunt — you only take on work you're actually qualified for. "Close enough" doesn't cut it. Highway intersection design and roundabout design share some fundamentals, but roundabouts have their own geometry, sight-distance criteria, and capacity methods. Accepting and learning roundabout design on the job is wrong because it puts the project at risk. Accepting because highway intersection experience is "close enough" is wrong because adjacent experience isn't the same as specific competence. Accepting but having a colleague review the final design sounds safe but a peer review doesn't make you qualified — the person signing and sealing needs to be competent, not just the reviewer.
problems.hint: What does Rule B.1 say about the relationship between your qualifications and the assignments you accept?

steps.text: Identify the core issue: the engineer lacks specific experience in roundabout design, which is a distinct specialty within transportation engineering.
Apply Rule B.1: licensees shall undertake assignments only when qualified by education or experience in the specific technical fields involved.
General intersection experience does not satisfy the "specific technical fields" requirement for roundabout design — geometry, deflection angles, and capacity analysis differ significantly.
The engineer should decline unless they first obtain the necessary training or partner with a qualified specialist.

problems.handbookFormula: \text{B.1: Undertake assignments only when qualified by education or experience in the specific technical fields involved.}
traps: Assuming that experience in a related subfield (highway intersections) satisfies the "specific technical fields" requirement
Believing that having a colleague review the work compensates for the engineer's own lack of competence

problems.statement: A water resources engineer works for a consulting firm and is managing a stormwater design project for City A. A competing municipality, City B, approaches the same firm and asks the engineer to evaluate City A's stormwater system for potential deficiencies as part of a regulatory dispute between the two cities. What should the engineer do?

choices.text: Accept the City B assignment since the two projects involve different scopes of work
Disclose the conflict to both clients and only proceed if both provide written consent
Accept the City B assignment but keep all City A project files confidential
Decline the City B assignment outright because it creates an unresolvable conflict

problems.eli5: This one stacks three rules on top of each other. You've got confidential info from City A (B.4), you've got an obvious conflict of interest (B.6), and you'd be getting paid by two parties on related work (B.7). The accept-anyway option ignores the conflict entirely. The keep-files-confidential option tries to compartmentalize, but you can't un-know what you know from the City A project — and the rules require disclosure, not just self-discipline. The decline-outright option is too extreme — the Model Rules don't say you can never work for competing parties, they say you need full disclosure and written consent. The exam wants you to pick the answer that involves transparency and consent, not avoidance.
problems.hint: When two clients' interests overlap, what do the Model Rules require before you can serve both?

steps.text: Identify the issue: the engineer has confidential knowledge from City A's project that is directly relevant to City B's request — this is a clear conflict of interest.
Apply Rule B.4: licensees shall not reveal facts obtained in a professional capacity without prior consent.
Apply Rule B.6: licensees shall disclose all known or potential conflicts of interest that could influence their judgment or quality of service.

Apply Rule B.7: licensees shall not accept compensation from more than one party for services pertaining to the same subject matter unless circumstances are fully disclosed and agreed to in writing by all interested parties.
The correct action is full disclosure to both clients with written consent required before proceeding. Neither silence nor outright refusal is the best answer.

problems.handbookPage: p. 5, Model Rules §240.15 B.4, B.6, B.7
problems.handbookFormula: \text{B.7: Do not accept compensation from more than one party unless fully disclosed and agreed to in writing.}
traps: Thinking that different scopes of work eliminate the conflict — the engineer's knowledge from City A is the issue, not the project boundaries
Choosing to decline outright when disclosure + consent is the Model Rules' preferred resolution

problems.statement: An engineer at a large firm discovers that a senior partner has been listing a major bridge project on the firm's marketing materials as a past accomplishment. The senior partner served as project manager, but the bridge design was actually performed by a subconsultant who is no longer affiliated with the firm. The marketing materials do not mention the subconsultant. A prospective client is evaluating the firm for a similar bridge project based partly on this claimed experience. What is the most appropriate action under the Model Rules?

choices.text: Do nothing — the senior partner managed the project, so claiming it as the firm's work is acceptable
Report the senior partner directly to the licensing board for misrepresentation
Inform the senior partner that the marketing materials misrepresent the firm's role and should be corrected
Contact the prospective client directly to clarify the firm's actual role on the bridge project

problems.eli5: This is a C.1 + C.4 combo. The marketing materials exaggerate the firm's role — the partner managed the project but didn't do the bridge design. That's a misrepresentation under C.1, especially since it's being used to win new work ("presentations incidental to the solicitation of employment"). But you don't jump straight to the board or the client. Rule C.4 says make a reasonable effort to inform the licensee first. The "do nothing" option is wrong because "project manager" doesn't equal "performed the design." Reporting straight to the licensing board skips the direct conversation step. Contacting the prospective client goes outside the firm before trying to fix it internally. Start with the partner, then escalate if they refuse to correct it.
problems.hint: Before reporting to the board or contacting the client, what does Rule C.4 require you to do first?

steps.text: Identify the issue: the firm's marketing materials imply the firm performed the bridge design, when in fact a subconsultant did the technical work. This overstates the firm's in-house capability.

Apply Rule C.1: licensees shall not misrepresent or exaggerate their degree of responsibility in prior assignments. Presentations incidental to the solicitation of employment shall not misrepresent pertinent facts.
Apply Rule C.4: licensees shall make a reasonable effort to inform another licensee whose conduct contains a material issue. The senior partner should be notified first.

Going directly to the board (reporting the senior partner to the licensing board) skips the "reasonable effort to inform" step required by C.4. Going directly to the client (contacting the prospective client) bypasses internal resolution and may violate confidentiality (B.4).

The correct first step is to inform the senior partner and request a correction. If the partner refuses and a prospective client is being misled, escalation to management and potentially the board may follow.

problems.handbookFormula: \text{C.1: Shall not misrepresent or exaggerate degree of responsibility in prior assignments.}
traps: Assuming that project management equals design responsibility — the materials must accurately reflect who did the technical work
Jumping to the board before making a reasonable effort to inform the senior partner directly (C.4 requires the direct approach first)

ethics/definitions-practice-of-engineeri.name: Definitions & Practice of Engineering
ethics/definitions-practice-of-engineeri.application: The Model Law definitions tell you who counts as an engineer, what counts as engineering, and what "responsible charge" actually means. On the FE, these definitions show up as boundary questions — is this person allowed to do this work? Does this activity require a license? Civil engineers deal with these boundaries constantly: when a technician prepares drawings under your supervision, when you coordinate with surveyors, or when someone without a license calls themselves an "engineer." The exam tests whether you know exactly where the legal lines are drawn.

content.body: Model Law §110.20 defines the key terms that control who can practice engineering and what activities require licensure. The exam doesn't ask you to recite definitions — it gives you a scenario and tests whether you can figure out if a license is required or if someone is crossing a legal boundary.
Professional Engineer vs. Engineer Intern

A Professional Engineer (PE) is someone qualified by education, training, experience, and examination — and duly licensed by the board. An Engineer Intern (EI) has passed the FE exam and been certified by the board, but hasn't completed the experience requirements for full licensure yet. A PE can also be designated as licensed in a specific discipline based on additional education and examination.

The exam may test the difference between "certified" (EI status after passing the FE) and "licensed" (PE status after passing both FE and PE exams plus meeting experience requirements). These are not interchangeable terms.
What Is "Practice of Engineering"?

The Model Law defines it broadly: any service or creative work requiring engineering education, training, and experience that potentially impacts the health, safety, and welfare of the public. This includes design, planning, studies, drawings, specifications, and reviewing construction for compliance. It also includes teaching engineering design courses.

You're construed to be practicing engineering if you do any of these: (a) practice any discipline of engineering or hold yourself out as able to, (b) represent yourself as a PE by any means — verbal, sign, letterhead, card, advertisement, or (c) use a title that implies you're a PE.

The "holding out" clause is a common exam trap. You don't have to actually do engineering work to violate the law — just representing yourself as a PE when you're not licensed is enough. This includes business cards, LinkedIn titles, and verbal claims.
Responsible Charge

"Responsible charge" means direct control and personal supervision of engineering work. This is the standard for who can sign and seal documents. If you didn't personally prepare the work or directly supervise the person who did, you can't put your seal on it — even if you reviewed it thoroughly after the fact.
Other Key Definitions

A few more definitions show up on the exam. "Firm" means any business entity other than a sole proprietorship. "Signature" means a name, mark, or writing made with the intent to verify or authenticate — including electronic or digital signatures. "Disciplinary action" covers everything from reprimands and fines to suspension and revocation of a license.

When the exam asks whether someone needs a license, use this checklist: (1) Does the activity impact public health, safety, or welfare? (2) Does it require engineering education and judgment? (3) Is the person holding themselves out as an engineer? If yes to any of these, a license is required.

The Exemption Clause (§170.20) is worth knowing: employees working under a licensed PE's responsible charge don't need their own license, as long as the PE verifies the work and the employee isn't making final design decisions.

problems.statement: A recent engineering graduate has passed the FE exam and been certified as an Engineer Intern. The graduate's employer asks them to sign and seal a set of drainage plans for a residential subdivision. What should the graduate do?

choices.text: Decline to sign and seal because an Engineer Intern is not a licensed Professional Engineer
Sign and seal the plans but note "Engineer Intern" next to the signature
Sign and seal the plans since passing the FE exam demonstrates competence
Sign and seal the plans if a licensed PE in the firm reviews them first

problems.eli5: This is the certified vs. licensed distinction. Passing the FE gets you "certified" as an Engineer Intern — it's a milestone, not a license. You can't sign and seal anything as an EI, period. The "passing the FE demonstrates competence" option is wrong because the FE exam proves foundational knowledge, not authority to practice. The "note Engineer Intern next to the signature" option is wrong because adding "Engineer Intern" doesn't magically grant sealing authority. The "sign if a licensed PE reviews them first" option is tempting but backwards — the PE who supervised the work should be the one sealing, not the EI with a PE looking over their shoulder.
problems.hint: What's the difference between being certified as an Engineer Intern and being licensed as a Professional Engineer?

steps.text: Identify the key distinction: the graduate is a certified Engineer Intern (EI), not a licensed Professional Engineer (PE).
Under §110.20, certification as an EI means passing the FE exam — it does not grant licensure to practice independently.
Only a licensed PE can sign and seal engineering documents. An EI lacks the authority regardless of competence or supervision.
Even if a PE reviews the plans afterward, the EI cannot be the one to sign and seal — the PE who exercised responsible charge must seal the documents.

problems.handbookPage: p. 6, Model Law §110.20 A.2 (Engineer Intern), §110.20 A (Professional Engineer)
problems.handbookFormula: \text{Engineer Intern: certified by the board. Professional Engineer: licensed by the board.}
traps: Confusing EI certification with PE licensure — passing the FE is necessary but not sufficient for signing and sealing authority
Thinking that PE review of an EI's sealed documents makes the seal valid — only the PE can seal

problems.statement: A construction company hires a project manager with a degree in construction management but no engineering license. The project manager reviews structural shop drawings submitted by a steel fabricator, compares them to the engineer-of-record's design drawings, and flags discrepancies for the engineer to resolve. Is the project manager practicing engineering under the Model Law?

choices.text: Yes — reviewing structural drawings requires engineering judgment and therefore requires a license
Yes — the project manager is holding themselves out as able to practice engineering by reviewing technical documents
No — the project manager is comparing documents for compliance, not making final engineering design decisions, and works under an exemption
No — construction management is a separate profession and is never considered engineering

problems.eli5: This question tests whether you know the boundary between engineering and non-engineering work. The PM is doing a comparison task — lining up shop drawings against the engineer's design and saying "these don't match here." That's a compliance check, not a design decision. The Exemption Clause (§170.20 C) specifically allows unlicensed employees to do this kind of work under a PE's responsible charge, as long as they're not making final design decisions. The "engineering judgment" option (c1) is wrong because comparing documents isn't the same as exercising engineering judgment. The "holding themselves out" option (c2) is wrong because the PM isn't claiming to be an engineer. The "never considered engineering" option (c4) goes too far — it's not that construction management is never engineering, it's that this specific activity falls under the exemption.
problems.hint: Does the project manager's task involve final engineering design decisions, or is it a compliance comparison under someone else's responsible charge?

steps.text: Apply the definition of "practice of engineering" from §110.20 A.3: services requiring engineering education, training, and experience that impact public health, safety, and welfare.
The project manager is comparing shop drawings to design drawings and flagging discrepancies — this is a compliance check, not a design decision.
Apply the Exemption Clause §170.20 C: employees working under the responsible charge of a licensed PE can perform work that doesn't include final engineering designs or decisions.
The engineer-of-record makes the final design decisions when resolving the flagged discrepancies. The PM is functioning as a subordinate under the PE's responsible charge.

The "never considered engineering" option (c4) is too broad — some construction management activities could cross into engineering. The correct reasoning is the specific exemption, not a blanket exclusion.

problems.handbookPage: p. 6, Model Law §110.20 A.3 (Practice of Engineering); p. 11, §170.20 C (Exemption Clause)
problems.handbookFormula: \text{§170.20 C: Work of a subordinate under responsible charge that does not include final engineering designs or decisions.}
traps: Assuming that any review of structural documents automatically constitutes "practice of engineering" — the key is whether final design decisions are being made
Choosing D based on the job title rather than analyzing the specific activity against the Model Law definition

problems.statement: A software developer creates a mobile app that calculates beam deflections and recommends steel member sizes for residential deck construction. The app is marketed to homeowners as a "DIY structural design tool." The developer has no engineering license and the app does not involve any licensed engineer in its operation. Under the Model Law, which of the following best describes the developer's situation?

choices.text: The developer is not practicing engineering because software development is not an engineering discipline
The developer is not practicing engineering because the app is a tool and the homeowner makes the final decision
The developer is practicing engineering because the app provides structural design services that impact public safety, and the developer holds themselves out as able to provide engineering services
The developer is only violating trademark law by implying engineering services, not the Model Law

problems.eli5: This is a modern twist on an old rule. The Model Law doesn't care whether you deliver engineering through paper drawings or a mobile app — if you're creating a tool that performs structural design calculations and marketing it to the public, you're practicing engineering. The app recommends steel member sizes for structures people will stand on. That impacts public safety. And by marketing it as a "structural design tool," the developer is holding themselves out as providing engineering services (§110.20 A.3(a)). The "not an engineering discipline" choice is wrong because the issue isn't the developer's profession — it's the nature of the service the app provides. The "tool / homeowner makes the final decision" choice is wrong because the "final decision" excuse doesn't apply when the app is doing the engineering judgment. The trademark-only choice is too narrow — this goes beyond trademark issues into unlicensed practice.
problems.hint: Focus on what the app does (structural design calculations) and how it's marketed (as a design tool) — does the Model Law care about the medium of delivery?

steps.text: Apply the definition of "practice of engineering" from §110.20 A.3: any service or creative work requiring engineering education, training, and experience that potentially impacts the health, safety, and welfare of the public.
The app performs structural design calculations (beam deflection, member sizing) for construction — this directly impacts public safety and requires engineering judgment to create correctly.
Apply §110.20 A.3(a): an individual is construed to practice engineering if they practice any discipline of engineering or hold themselves out as able to do so.
Marketing a "structural design tool" to the public constitutes holding oneself out as able to provide engineering services — the developer is offering engineering judgment embedded in software.

The fact that the developer writes code rather than stamped drawings doesn't matter. The output is structural design recommendations that affect public safety. The medium doesn't change the nature of the service.

problems.handbookPage: p. 6, Model Law §110.20 A.3 (Practice of Engineering), §110.20 A.3(a)–(c) (construed to practice)
problems.handbookFormula: \text{§110.20 A.3(a): Practices any discipline of engineering or holds themselves out as able and entitled to practice.}
traps: Assuming that software development can never be "practice of engineering" — the Model Law focuses on the nature of the output, not the medium
Believing that shifting the final decision to the homeowner absolves the developer — the engineering judgment is embedded in the app's calculations

ethics/licensure-path-disciplinary-actio.name: Licensure Path & Disciplinary Action
ethics/licensure-path-disciplinary-actio.application: The licensure path is the roadmap every engineer follows from student to PE — and the FE exam you're studying for is one of the checkpoints on it. The exam tests whether you know the sequence (education → FE → experience → PE) and the requirements at each stage. It also tests the flip side: what gets your license taken away. Civil engineers work on public infrastructure where mistakes can be catastrophic, so the board has broad power to discipline licensees for fraud, incompetence, misconduct, and even felony convictions unrelated to engineering. Knowing these grounds helps you spot the violation in scenario questions.

content.body: Model Law §130.10 lays out the requirements for licensure, and §§150.10/150.30 list the grounds for disciplinary action. Together they form a complete picture: how you get your license and how you lose it.
The Licensure Ladder

Five general requirements apply to everyone seeking licensure: (1) good character and reputation, (2) meeting education criteria set by the board, (3) meeting experience criteria, (4) passing the required examinations, and (5) submitting five references acceptable to the board.
Engineer Intern → Professional Engineer

The path has two stages. First, become an Engineer Intern by graduating from an EAC/ABET-accredited program (or meeting the NCEES Engineering Education Standard) and passing the FE exam. Second, become a PE by passing the PE exam and completing four years of progressive engineering experience after your qualifying degree.

Experience credit for graduate degrees: a master's reduces the requirement to three years, a doctoral degree (with FE passed) to two years. But a degree used to satisfy education requirements can't also count as experience — no double-dipping. And graduate degree credit can't overlap with work experience credit.
Comity (Reciprocal Licensure)

Already licensed in another state? You can get licensed by comity if your credentials meet the new jurisdiction's standards. An active NCEES Council Record makes this straightforward — it's a pre-verified portfolio that most boards accept. Either way, you may still need to pass a jurisdiction-specific exam on local statutes and rules.
Grounds for Discipline — Licensees

Section 150.10 gives the board power to suspend, revoke, fine, or reprimand any licensee found guilty of a long list of offenses. The big categories: fraud or deceit in obtaining licensure, negligence or incompetence, felony conviction (even if unrelated to engineering), dishonesty-related misdemeanors, failure to comply with board rules, and practicing outside your area of competence.

The felony clause catches students off guard. A felony conviction of any kind — even one completely unrelated to engineering — is grounds for discipline. For misdemeanors, only those involving dishonesty or directly related to engineering practice qualify.
Grounds for Discipline — Unlicensed Individuals

Section 150.30 targets people who aren't licensed at all. The board can fine anyone who practices engineering without a license, uses the title "professional engineer" without authorization, presents someone else's license or seal, or uses an expired, suspended, or revoked license. Each day of continued violation counts as a separate offense.

For exam questions about discipline, ask two questions: (1) Is the person licensed? If yes, §150.10 applies. If no, §150.30 applies. (2) What did they do? Match it to the specific ground — fraud, incompetence, felony, unauthorized practice, or seal misuse. The answer usually maps cleanly to one provision.

The board considers several factors when setting fines: whether the amount is a deterrent, the severity and circumstances of the violation, the risk to the public, the economic benefit the violator gained, and consistency with past fines. The exam occasionally tests whether you know that fines scale with these factors.

problems.statement: An individual graduated from an EAC/ABET-accredited engineering program, passed the FE exam, and has been working as an Engineer Intern for two years under a licensed PE. The individual wants to apply for PE licensure. What is the most likely outcome?

choices.text: The application will be denied — the individual needs at least four years of progressive experience after the qualifying degree
The application will be approved — two years of experience is sufficient after passing the FE
The application will be denied — the individual must pass the PE exam before gaining experience
The application will be approved if the supervising PE writes a recommendation letter

problems.eli5: The licensure path is rigid on experience: four years after your bachelor's, three with a master's, two with a doctorate (if you passed the FE). This person has a bachelor's and two years — they're only halfway there. The "two years is sufficient" choice is wrong because two years is the doctoral track, not the bachelor's track. The "must pass the PE first" choice gets the order wrong — you can gain experience before passing the PE exam; in fact, that's the normal sequence. The "recommendation letter approves it" choice confuses references with the experience requirement. You need five references, but they don't let you skip years.
