traps: Swapping sine and cosine — cosine always goes with the adjacent side (the axis the angle is measured from)
Forgetting to set your calculator to degree mode — radian mode gives completely wrong trig values

problems.statement: A cable anchored to a retaining wall runs to a deadman anchor. The cable exerts a force of 1,300 N along a line that runs 5 m horizontally and 12 m vertically from the wall to the anchor point. What are the horizontal and vertical components of the cable force?
problems.eli5: When geometry gives you the direction instead of an angle, use the rise-over-run approach: find $R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$, then $F_x = (x/R) \times F$ and $F_y = (y/R) \times F$. The 5-12-13 triangle is one of the FE’s favorite right triangles — recognize it instantly. The choice $F_x = 1{,}200$ N, $F_y = 500$ N swaps the components (applies the vertical leg to the horizontal direction). The choice $F_x = 650$ N, $F_y = 650$ N splits the force evenly, which would only be correct at 45 degrees. The choice $F_x = 260$ N, $F_y = 1{,}040$ N uses the wrong denominator (divides by 25 and 5 instead of 13).
problems.hint: You do not need to find the angle. Use the geometry directly: $F_x = (x/R) \times F$ where $R$ is the distance from the wall to the anchor point.

steps.text: The cable runs 5 m horizontal and 12 m vertical. Find the hypotenuse distance:
4. The choice $F_x = 1{,}200$ N, $F_y = 500$ N swaps the legs — it applies the vertical leg (12) to the horizontal component and vice versa.

traps: Swapping the x and y legs when geometry is given — the horizontal leg goes with the horizontal component
Using the force magnitude as the denominator instead of the hypotenuse distance R

problems.statement: A construction crane has a 10 m boom that makes a 40-degree angle with the horizontal. A 5,000 N load hangs vertically from the boom tip. What is the moment of the load about the boom’s pivot point at the base?
problems.eli5: The load hangs straight down from the boom tip — it is a vertical force. To find the moment about the pivot, you need the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force’s line of action. Since the force is vertical, that perpendicular distance is the horizontal distance from the pivot to the tip, which is the boom length times cosine of the boom angle. The 50,000 N·m choice uses the full boom length as if the perpendicular distance equals the boom length (only true if the boom were horizontal). The 32,100 N·m choice uses sine instead of cosine, which gives the vertical projection of the boom — that is perpendicular to the boom, not to the force.
problems.hint: The force is vertical (gravity). The perpendicular distance to a vertical force is a horizontal distance. How far horizontally is the boom tip from the pivot?

steps.text: The load (5,000 N) acts vertically downward from the boom tip.
The horizontal distance from the pivot to the tip is the perpendicular distance to the vertical force:
The 50,000 N·m choice forgets the angle entirely: $5{,}000 \times 10 = 50{,}000$. This would only be correct if the boom were perfectly horizontal.
The 32,100 N·m choice uses $\sin 40\degree$ instead of $\cos 40\degree$, giving the vertical projection of the boom rather than the horizontal projection.

traps: Using the boom length directly as the moment arm instead of computing the perpendicular distance
Confusing sin and cos when finding the horizontal vs. vertical projection of the boom

statics/equilibrium-free-body-diagrams.name: Equilibrium & Free Body Diagrams
statics/equilibrium-free-body-diagrams.application: Every structural analysis on the FE starts the same way: draw the free body diagram, identify all forces and reactions, then write the equilibrium equations. Whether you are finding the reactions of a simply supported beam, checking a cantilever retaining wall, or analyzing forces at a bolted connection, the process is the same three equations: $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$, $\sum M = 0$. The FE tests whether you can draw a correct FBD, identify the right number and type of support reactions, and solve for unknowns. Getting the FBD wrong means every calculation afterward is wrong.

content.body: Equilibrium means an object is not accelerating. For a rigid body in static equilibrium, the sum of all forces and the sum of all moments about any point must both be zero.
Equilibrium Equations (2D)

Three equations, three unknowns maximum. If a problem has more than three unknown reaction forces, it is statically indeterminate and requires additional equations (compatibility conditions from Mechanics of Materials).
Free Body Diagrams
A free body diagram isolates the object from its supports and replaces each support with the reaction forces it provides. Getting this step right is the single most important skill in statics.

Common 2D supports: a roller provides 1 reaction (perpendicular to the surface), a pin provides 2 reactions ($R_x$ and $R_y$), and a fixed support provides 3 reactions ($R_x$, $R_y$, and a moment $M$).

The FE will not tell you to draw an FBD — it will just ask for reactions or forces. But your first step should always be sketching one. Mark every external force, every support reaction, and every applied moment before writing any equations.
Strategy for Solving

Start by summing moments about a point where two unknowns intersect — this eliminates them and gives you a single equation with one unknown. Then use the force sum equations to find the remaining reactions.
When choosing a moment point, pick a location where as many unknown forces as possible pass through that point. Their moment arms become zero, simplifying the equation.

A common FBD mistake: forgetting the direction of a roller reaction. A roller can only push, never pull. If your solution gives a negative roller reaction, recheck the problem setup — it usually means you drew the FBD wrong or made a sign error.

problems.statement: A simply supported beam spans 8 m. A single concentrated load of 12 kN acts 3 m from the left support (A). Support A is a pin and support B is a roller. What is the vertical reaction at support B?
problems.eli5: Sum moments about point A to eliminate both reactions at A. The only forces creating moments about A are the 12 kN load at 3 m and the roller reaction at B at 8 m. Set the sum to zero: $12 \times 3 = B_y \times 8$, so $B_y = 4.5$ kN. The 7.5 kN choice is the reaction at support A, not B — a classic trap where you solve correctly but report the wrong support. The 6.0 kN choice splits the load in half, which would only be right if the load were at midspan. The 12.0 kN choice puts the entire load on one support, ignoring equilibrium entirely.
problems.hint: Sum moments about the pin support to eliminate two unknowns at once. Be sure to report the reaction at B, not A.

steps.text: FBD: pin at A ($A_x$, $A_y$), roller at B ($B_y$), 12 kN load at 3 m from A.
The 12 kN load acts 3 m from A (clockwise), and $B_y$ acts 8 m from A (counterclockwise):
Check: $A_y = 12 - 4.5 = 7.5$ kN. The 7.5 kN choice is the reaction at A, not B.

traps: Reporting the reaction at the wrong support — read the question carefully to see which support it asks for
Splitting the load evenly between supports — this is only valid when the load is at midspan

problems.statement: A cantilever beam is 4 m long with a fixed support at the left end. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 3 kN/m over its entire length. What are the vertical reaction and the fixed-end moment at the support?
problems.eli5: A distributed load of 3 kN/m over 4 m has a total force of $3 \times 4 = 12$ kN, acting at the centroid of the load (midpoint of the beam = 2 m from the support). The vertical reaction equals the total load (12 kN). The fixed-end moment resists the moment of that resultant about the support: $M = 12 \times 2 = 24$ kN\cdot m. The 48 kN\cdot m choice uses the full beam length (4 m) as the moment arm instead of the centroid distance (2 m). The $R_y = 6$ kN, $M = 12$ kN\cdot m choice uses half the load as if only half the beam were loaded. The $R_y = 12$ kN, $M = 12$ kN\cdot m choice gets the reaction right but uses 1 m instead of 2 m for the moment arm.
problems.hint: Replace the distributed load with its resultant (total force at the centroid). Where does the centroid of a uniform load act?

steps.latex: W = 3 \times 4 = 12 \text{ kN, acting at the centroid (2 m from the fixed end)}

steps.text: The choice $R_y = 12$ kN, $M = 48$ kN\cdot m uses the full length 4 m as the moment arm: $12 \times 4 = 48$. The resultant acts at the centroid (2 m), not at the tip.

traps: Using the full beam length instead of the centroid distance for the moment arm of a distributed load
Forgetting that a fixed support has a moment reaction in addition to force reactions

problems.statement: A beam AB is 10 m long, supported by a pin at A and a roller at B. It carries a 20 kN concentrated load at 4 m from A and a 10 kN\cdot m counterclockwise couple applied at 7 m from A. What is the vertical reaction at A?
problems.eli5: This problem has both a force and a couple (pure moment). The couple has no net force — it only shows up in the moment equation, not the force equations. Sum moments about A to find $B_y$ first: the 20 kN load at 4 m creates a clockwise moment of 80, and the CCW couple adds 10 in the opposite direction. So $B_y = (80 - 10)/10 = 7$ kN. Then from $\sum F_y = 0$: $A_y = 20 - 7 = 13$ kN. The 12.0 kN choice ignores the couple entirely: $20 \times 6 / 10 = 12$. The 11.0 kN choice gets the couple sign wrong, subtracting it from the wrong side.
problems.hint: A couple contributes to the moment equation but not to the force equations. Sum moments about one support, then use $\sum F_y = 0$ to find the other reaction.

steps.text: FBD: pin at A ($A_x$, $A_y$), roller at B ($B_y$), 20 kN downward at 4 m from A, 10 kN\cdot m CCW couple at 7 m from A.
The 20 kN load at 4 m creates a CW moment ($-$), $B_y$ at 10 m creates a CCW moment ($+$), and the couple is CCW ($+$):
The 12.0 kN choice ignores the couple: $B_y = 80/10 = 8$, $A_y = 12$. The couple shifts 1 kN from B to A.

traps: Ignoring the couple in the moment equation — it contributes directly regardless of where it is located on the beam
Getting the sign of the couple wrong — a counterclockwise couple is positive if your convention is CCW positive

statics/trusses-joints-sections.name: Trusses: Method of Joints & Sections
statics/trusses-joints-sections.application: Trusses are one of the highest-frequency statics topics on the FE Civil. You will see roof trusses, bridge trusses, and transmission towers. The exam tests two methods: method of joints (write equilibrium at each joint to find all member forces) and method of sections (cut through the truss and use equilibrium on one side to find specific member forces). It also tests whether you can spot zero-force members instantly. The handbook (p. 97) defines both methods and the zero-force member rules. Knowing when to use joints vs. sections saves critical time on exam day.

content.body: A truss is a structure made of straight, two-force members connected at joints. Each member carries only axial force (tension or compression). All loads and reactions act at the joints.
Zero-Force Members

Two rules identify zero-force members without any calculation. Rule 1: if only two members meet at an unloaded joint, both are zero-force members. Rule 2: if three members meet at an unloaded joint and two are collinear, the third member is a zero-force member.
The FE loves to test zero-force member identification. Before doing any calculations, scan the truss for joints that match these two rules. It can eliminate unknowns and simplify the entire analysis.
Method of Joints

Isolate each joint as a free body. The forces acting on the joint are the member forces (along each member) and any external loads or reactions. Write two equilibrium equations per joint. Start at a joint with at most two unknown member forces.
Method of Sections

Cut through the truss so that the cut passes through the member whose force you need. Draw a free body diagram of one side of the cut. You have three equilibrium equations ($\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$, $\sum M = 0$), so you can solve for up to three unknown member forces.

Method of sections is faster when you need just one or two member forces in the middle of the truss. Method of joints is better when you need all member forces. On the FE, sections is almost always the faster path since the problem only asks for one member.
When assuming member forces, assume tension (pulling away from the joint). If the answer comes out negative, the member is in compression. Be consistent — mixing conventions leads to sign errors.

problems.statement: In a truss, joint C is where three members meet. Members AC and CE are collinear (both along the same horizontal line), and member CD connects vertically downward. No external load or reaction is applied at joint C. What can you conclude about the force in member CD?

choices.text: CD carries the same force as AC
CD carries half the force of CE

problems.eli5: This is a direct application of zero-force member Rule 2: when three members meet at an unloaded joint and two of them are collinear, the third is a zero-force member. AC and CE lie along the same horizontal line (collinear), so CD (the non-collinear member) carries zero force. No calculation needed. The choices that CD carries the same force as AC or half the force of CE assume CD shares load with the other members, but collinear members pass their force straight through the joint. The "cannot determine without calculating reactions" choice overthinks it — the zero-force rule gives the answer by inspection.
problems.hint: Three members meet at an unloaded joint. Two are collinear. What does the zero-force member rule say about the third?

steps.text: Joint C has three members: AC, CE (collinear along the horizontal), and CD (non-collinear, vertical).
No external load or support reaction is applied at joint C.
Zero-force member Rule 2: when three members meet at an unloaded joint and two are collinear, the third is a zero-force member.
Therefore CD is a zero-force member:

traps: Skipping the zero-force check and jumping straight into calculations
Assuming a member must carry load just because it is connected to the truss

problems.statement: A symmetric triangular truss has joints at A (bottom left, pin support), B (bottom right, roller support), and C (top center). The span AB is 6 m and C is 4 m directly above the midpoint of AB. A 10 kN downward load is applied at joint C. Using the method of joints at joint A, what is the force in member AC?
problems.eli5: At joint A, two member forces and the 5 kN upward reaction must balance. Since AB is horizontal, it has no vertical component — so member AC must carry the entire vertical load. The vertical component of the AC force equals 5 kN, and since AC runs from A(0,0) to C(3,4) (a 3-4-5 triangle), the full force is $5 \div (4/5) = 6.25$ kN. The negative sign in the tension convention means AC is in compression (pushing toward the joint). The 5 kN tension option confuses the vertical component with the total member force. The 3.75 kN tension option is actually the force in member AB, not AC.
problems.hint: At joint A, only member AC has a vertical component. Set $\sum F_y = 0$ at joint A to find the force in AC directly.

steps.text: Find reactions. By symmetry (load at midpoint):
Member AC runs from A(0,0) to C(3,4). Length = 5 (3-4-5 triangle). Direction cosines: $(3/5,\, 4/5)$.
At joint A, assume $F_{AC}$ is tension (pulling away from A along AC). Vertical equilibrium:
Negative means our tension assumption was wrong — AC is in compression. Force = 6.25 kN (C).

problems.handbookPage: p. 97, Plane Truss: Method of Joints
traps: Reporting the vertical component (5 kN) as the total member force instead of dividing by the direction cosine
Mixing up which member force the problem asks for — AC vs. AB

problems.statement: A truss spans 9 m with three equal 3 m panels. Bottom chord joints are A (left, pin support), B (3 m), C (6 m), and D (right, roller support at 9 m). Top chord joints are E (directly above B, height 4 m) and F (directly above C, height 4 m). A single 24 kN downward load acts at joint F. Using the method of sections, what is the force in bottom chord member BC?
problems.eli5: Method of sections lets you cut straight to the member you need without solving the entire truss. Cut through EF, EC, and BC, then take the left portion (joints A, B, E). To isolate the force in BC, sum moments about point E — both the EF and EC forces pass through E, so their moments vanish. The only forces with nonzero moments about E are the 8 kN support reaction at A and the unknown BC force. The reaction at A (8 kN upward) is 3 m to the left of E, creating a 24 kN\cdot m clockwise moment. Member BC is 4 m below E. Setting the moments equal: $F_{BC} \times 4 = 24$, so $F_{BC} = 6$ kN tension. The 8 kN tension choice confuses the support reaction with the member force. The 16 kN tension choice is the reaction at D.
problems.hint: Cut through the three members and sum moments about point E, where two of the three cut forces intersect.

steps.latex: \sum M_A = 0:\quad 24(6) = D_y(9) \quad \Rightarrow \quad D_y = 16 \text{ kN},\quad A_y = 8 \text{ kN}

steps.text: Cut through members EF, EC, and BC. Analyze the left portion (joints A, B, E).
Sum moments about E to eliminate $F_{EF}$ and $F_{EC}$ (both pass through E at (3, 4)):
$A_y = 8$ kN upward at A(0,0), which is 3 m left of E. This creates a CW moment about E:
$F_{BC}$ acts horizontally at height $y = 0$, which is 4 m below E. It creates a CCW moment:
Set the sum to zero and solve:

problems.handbookPage: p. 97, Plane Truss: Method of Sections
traps: Confusing support reactions with member forces — the 8 kN reaction is not the answer
Summing moments about the wrong point — choose a point where two unknown cut forces intersect to get one equation with one unknown

statics/friction.name: Friction
statics/friction.application: Friction problems on the FE test whether you understand the difference between static and kinetic friction, can identify when impending motion occurs, and can apply the belt friction and screw-jack formulas. Civil engineers check friction when designing retaining walls against sliding, analyzing braking forces on highway grades, and sizing belt-driven equipment. The handbook (pp. 96–97) covers static friction ($F \leq \mu_s N$), screw-jack mechanics, and belt friction. Expect one friction problem on the exam — it is usually straightforward if you set up the normal force correctly.

content.body: Friction resists the tendency of two surfaces to slide relative to each other. The maximum static friction force depends on the normal force and the coefficient of static friction.
Static Friction
The friction force $F$ can be anything from zero up to $\mu_s N$. It only equals $\mu_s N$ at the point of impending motion. Until then, friction adjusts to match the applied force.

Do not assume $F = \mu_s N$ unless the problem says the object is about to move or asks for the maximum force before sliding. If the object is stationary and not on the verge of moving, friction could be less than $\mu_s N$.
Belt Friction

$F_1$ is the tension on the tight side (direction of impending motion), $F_2$ is the tension on the slack side, $\mu$ is the coefficient of friction, and $\theta$ is the total angle of contact in radians. The exponential relationship means even a small $\mu$ over many wraps creates enormous holding force.
Screw Thread (Screw-Jack)

$P$ is the axial load, $r$ is the mean thread radius, $\alpha$ is the pitch angle, and $\phi = \arctan\mu$ where $\mu$ is the coefficient of friction. Use $+$ for tightening (raising the load) and $-$ for loosening (lowering the load).
For belt friction, always identify which side is the tight side ($F_1$) — it is the side in the direction the belt is trying to slip. The angle $\theta$ must be in radians, not degrees.

The handbook (p. 96) gives the belt friction formula with $F_1$ as the force in the direction of impending motion. If the problem describes a pulley or capstan, identify the tight and slack sides before plugging in.

problems.statement: A 500 N crate sits on a flat concrete floor. The coefficient of static friction between the crate and the floor is 0.40. What is the maximum horizontal force that can be applied to the crate before it begins to slide?
problems.eli5: On a flat floor, the normal force equals the weight (500 N). The maximum friction force before sliding is $\mu_s \times N = 0.40 \times 500 = 200$ N. The 500 N choice uses the full weight as the friction force, which would require $\mu_s = 1$. The 125 N choice divides weight by 4 instead of multiplying by 0.40. The 1,250 N choice divides the weight by the coefficient instead of multiplying.
problems.hint: On a flat surface, the normal force equals the weight. Maximum friction = $\mu_s \times N$.

steps.text: Normal force on a flat surface:
Any horizontal force less than 200 N will be resisted by friction. At exactly 200 N, the crate is on the verge of sliding.

traps: Forgetting that the normal force equals the weight only on a flat surface — on an incline, $N = W\cos\theta$
Dividing by $\mu$ instead of multiplying — getting 1,250 N instead of 200 N

problems.statement: A flat belt wraps 180 degrees around a pulley. The coefficient of friction between the belt and pulley is 0.30. If the tension on the slack side is 200 N, what is the maximum tension on the tight side before the belt slips?
problems.eli5: Belt friction is exponential, not linear — that is the key insight. The tight side tension equals the slack side times $e^{\mu\theta}$. With $\mu = 0.30$ and $\theta = \pi$ radians (180 degrees), you get $F_1 = 200 \times e^{0.30\pi} = 200 \times 2.566 = 513$ N. The 260 N option treats friction as a simple percentage add-on ($200 + 0.30 \times 200 = 260$), ignoring the exponential. The 320 N option uses 90 degrees ($\pi/2$) instead of 180 degrees ($\pi$) for the contact angle. The 200 N option assumes the belt cannot transmit any additional force through friction.
problems.hint: Convert the contact angle to radians before using the belt friction formula. 180 degrees = $\pi$ radians.

steps.text: TI-36X Pro: type $200 \times e^{(0.30 \times \pi)}$ and press $=$.

traps: Using degrees instead of radians for the contact angle — 180 degrees must become $\pi$ radians
Adding friction linearly ($F_2 + \mu F_2$) instead of using the exponential relationship

problems.statement: A block weighing 800 N rests on a ramp inclined at 25 degrees. The coefficient of static friction is 0.50. A horizontal force $P$ is applied to push the block up the ramp. What is the minimum value of $P$ to start the block moving upward?
problems.eli5: The tricky part is that the horizontal push $P$ does two things simultaneously: it has a component up the ramp ($P\cos 25\degree$) that helps push the block, but it also has a component into the ramp surface ($P\sin 25\degree$) that increases the normal force and therefore increases friction. You must account for both. Set up equilibrium along the ramp: the up-ramp component of $P$ must overcome the weight component down the ramp plus friction. Solving gives $P = 1{,}008$ N. The 338 N choice is just the weight component down the ramp ($800\sin 25\degree$), ignoring friction entirely. The 773 N choice forgets that $P$ increases the normal force, underestimating friction. The 400 N choice uses a flat-surface friction calculation ($\mu \times W$).
problems.hint: The horizontal force $P$ has components both along and perpendicular to the ramp. The perpendicular component increases the normal force, which increases friction.

steps.text: Resolve weight along and perpendicular to the ramp:
steps.latex: W_x = 800\sin 25\degree = 338 \text{ N (down ramp)}, \quad W_y = 800\cos 25\degree = 725 \text{ N (into surface)}

steps.text: Resolve $P$ along and perpendicular to the ramp:
steps.latex: P_x = P\cos 25\degree \text{ (up ramp)}, \quad P_y = P\sin 25\degree \text{ (into surface)}

steps.text: Normal force includes contributions from both weight and $P$:

traps: Forgetting that $P$ has a component perpendicular to the ramp that changes the normal force
Using the weight as the normal force — on an incline with a horizontal push, $N$ depends on both $W$ and $P$

statics/frames-machines.name: Frames & Machines
statics/frames-machines.application: Not every structure is a truss of two-force members. As a civil engineer you analyze frames (stationary structures that support loads) and machines (assemblies that transmit or modify forces), both of which contain multi-force members. On the FE, expect to recognize two-force members, analyze a simple frame or lever by dismembering it, and apply the mechanical advantage of a machine.

content.body: Frames and machines differ from trusses: they contain MULTI-FORCE members — members loaded at three or more points, which therefore carry shear and bending, not just axial force.
Two-Force vs. Multi-Force Members

A TWO-FORCE member is loaded at only two points; for equilibrium the two forces must be equal, opposite, and directed along the line joining the two points (pure axial). Any member loaded at three or more points is a MULTI-FORCE member, and its pin forces generally are NOT along the member.
Analyzing Frames & Machines

Dismember the structure and draw a free-body diagram of each member. At a connecting pin, the force one member exerts on another is equal and opposite (Newton's third law). Apply the equilibrium equations ($\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$, $\sum M = 0$) to each member to solve for pin and support reactions.
Machines & Mechanical Advantage

content.label: Lever: output force scales with the ratio of moment arms

content.body: Spot two-force members first — a straight, unloaded-between-pins member carries force along its axis, which immediately gives the direction of that pin force and simplifies the rest of the frame.
Do not treat a frame member loaded at three points as a two-force member. Only members loaded at exactly two points have their force directed along the member; multi-force members do not.

problems.statement: A straight, rigid member in a frame is pinned at each end and carries no load between the pins. In what direction does the force in this member act?

choices.text: Along the straight line connecting the two pins (axial)

problems.eli5: A member loaded at only two points is a two-force member: equilibrium requires the two forces to be equal, opposite, and collinear, so they act along the line joining the pins — purely axial. The "perpendicular to the member" and "at 45°" options contradict moment equilibrium. The "undetermined direction" option is wrong because the direction IS determined for a two-force member — it must be axial.
problems.hint: A member loaded at only two points is a two-force member — where must its forces line up?

steps.text: Loaded at only two points → two-force member.
Equilibrium forces the two forces to be equal, opposite, collinear.
So the force acts along the line between the two pins.

problems.handbookFormula: Two-force member: forces are equal, opposite, and collinear (axial)
traps: Assuming pin forces are perpendicular to the member
Treating a multi-force member as two-force

problems.statement: A lever (a simple machine) has an effort applied $300\text{ mm}$ from the pivot and a load located $50\text{ mm}$ from the pivot on the other side. If an effort of $100\text{ N}$ is applied, what load can be balanced?
problems.eli5: Take moments about the pivot: F_out × 50 = F_in × 300, so F_out = 100 × (300/50) = 100 × 6 = 600 N. The longer effort arm multiplies the force (mechanical advantage = 6). The 16.7 N distractor divides instead of multiplies. The 100 N distractor ignores the arms. The 300 N distractor uses only the effort-arm length.
problems.hint: Sum moments about the pivot: effort × effort arm = load × load arm.
traps: Dividing by the arm ratio instead of multiplying
Forgetting to take moments about the pivot

problems.statement: What distinguishes a frame from a truss in statics?

choices.text: A frame contains at least one multi-force member; a truss has only two-force members
A frame has only axial-force members; a truss has bending members
A frame is always moving; a truss is always stationary
There is no difference — the terms are interchangeable

problems.eli5: A truss is made entirely of two-force members (pure axial). A frame is a stationary structure that includes at least one multi-force member, which carries shear and bending in addition to axial force. The "only axial-force members" option reverses the definitions. The "always moving" option confuses frames with machines (machines move). The "no difference" option is false.
problems.hint: Think about whether the members carry only axial force or also bending.

steps.text: Frames include multi-force members (shear and bending).
So the frame is distinguished by its multi-force member(s).

traps: Swapping the truss and frame member definitions
Confusing a frame (stationary) with a machine (moving parts)

statics/centroids-composite-shapes.name: Centroids of Composite Shapes
statics/centroids-composite-shapes.application: Centroids locate the neutral axis of beam cross-sections, the point of application of distributed loads, and the center of pressure on submerged surfaces. On the FE, you will decompose a composite shape into simple rectangles, triangles, or circles, look up each piece’s area and centroid from the handbook tables (pp. 98–100), and combine them using the weighted-average formula. The most common exam setup is a T-beam, an L-shape, or a plate with holes. If you can split a shape into pieces and take a weighted average, these are fast points.

content.body: The centroid of a composite area is the area-weighted average of the centroids of its parts. Split the shape into simple pieces, find each piece’s area and centroid from the tables, then combine.
Composite Centroid Formula

content.latex: \bar{x} = \frac{\sum A_i\, x_i}{\sum A_i} \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{\sum A_i\, y_i}{\sum A_i}
content.label: Centroid of a Composite Area

content.body: $A_i$ is the area of each piece, and $(x_i, y_i)$ is the centroid of that piece measured from a chosen reference axis. For holes or cutouts, use negative area.
First Moment of Area

content.latex: Q_x = \sum A_i\, y_i = \bar{y}\, A \qquad Q_y = \sum A_i\, x_i = \bar{x}\, A
content.label: First Moment of Area

content.body: The first moment of area connects centroids to beam analysis. $Q$ appears in shear stress calculations ($\tau = VQ/Ib$) in Mechanics of Materials. For now, know that $Q$ is the numerator of the centroid formula.
Strategy for Composite Shapes

Step 1: Choose a reference axis (usually the bottom or left edge). Step 2: Split the shape into simple pieces (rectangles, triangles, circles). Step 3: For each piece, find area $A_i$ and centroid $(x_i, y_i)$ from the handbook tables. Step 4: Compute $\sum A_i x_i$, $\sum A_i y_i$, and $\sum A_i$. Step 5: Divide.
For shapes with holes, treat the hole as a piece with negative area. The formula still works — the hole’s contribution subtracts from both the numerator and the denominator.

The handbook (pp. 98–100) provides centroid locations for triangles, rectangles, circles, semicircles, and parabolic segments. You do not need to integrate — just look up the centroid and multiply by the area.

The most common mistake is measuring centroid distances from the wrong reference point. Pick one reference axis and stick with it for every piece. If you switch mid-problem, the weighted average will be wrong.

problems.statement: A T-shaped cross section has a top flange 120 mm wide and 20 mm thick, and a web 20 mm wide and 80 mm deep below the flange. What is the distance from the bottom of the section to the centroid?
problems.eli5: Split the T into two rectangles: the web (20 × 80 mm, centroid at 40 mm from the bottom) and the flange (120 × 20 mm, centroid at 90 mm from the bottom). Take the area-weighted average: $(1{,}600 \times 40 + 2{,}400 \times 90) / 4{,}000 = 70$ mm. The 50 mm choice is the geometric midpoint of the total 100 mm height, ignoring that the flange has more area and sits higher. The 90 mm choice is the centroid of the flange alone. The 65 mm choice is the simple average of the two centroids, $(40 + 90)/2 = 65$, ignoring the different areas.
problems.hint: Split the T into web and flange. Compute each area and centroid distance from the bottom, then take the weighted average.

steps.text: Web: 20 × 80 mm. Area and centroid from the bottom:
Flange: 120 × 20 mm. Sits on top of the web (bottom of flange at 80 mm):

problems.handbookPage: p. 95, Centroid of Area; pp. 98–100, Shape Properties
traps: Using the geometric midpoint of the overall height instead of the area-weighted centroid
Averaging the two centroid locations without weighting by area

problems.statement: A 300 mm wide by 200 mm tall steel plate has a single 60 mm diameter circular hole drilled with its center at 150 mm from the left edge and 150 mm from the bottom. What is the y-coordinate of the centroid of the remaining plate, measured from the bottom?
problems.eli5: Treat the hole as a piece with negative area. The full plate’s centroid is at $y = 100$ mm (center). The hole is above center at $y = 150$ mm. Removing material above the centroid pulls the centroid downward. The math: $\bar{y} = (60{,}000 \times 100 - 2{,}827 \times 150) / (60{,}000 - 2{,}827) = 97.5$ mm. The 100 mm choice ignores the hole entirely. The 102.5 mm choice adds the hole’s effect instead of subtracting, pushing the centroid the wrong direction.
problems.hint: Subtract the hole: use negative area for the circular cutout. Removing material above the original centroid shifts it downward.

steps.text: Full plate: $A = 300 \times 200 = 60{,}000$ mm², centroid at $y = 100$ mm.
The hole is above the plate’s center, so removing it shifts the centroid downward — consistent with our answer being less than 100 mm.

problems.handbookPage: p. 95, Centroid of Area; pp. 98–100, Shape Properties
traps: Ignoring the hole and reporting the centroid of the full plate (100 mm)
Adding the hole contribution instead of subtracting it — removing material above the centroid shifts it down, not up

problems.statement: A built-up steel section consists of three rectangles: a bottom flange (200 mm wide × 30 mm tall), a web (30 mm wide × 140 mm tall centered on the flange), and a top flange (150 mm wide × 30 mm tall centered on the web). The total height is 200 mm. What is the y-coordinate of the centroid measured from the bottom?
problems.eli5: Split the section into three rectangles: bottom flange ($A = 6{,}000$, $y = 15$), web ($A = 4{,}200$, $y = 100$), and top flange ($A = 4{,}500$, $y = 185$). The bottom flange is the widest piece with the most area, so it pulls the centroid below the geometric center. The weighted average gives 91.3 mm. The 100 mm choice is the geometric center of the 200 mm height. The 108.7 mm choice measures from the top instead of the bottom. The 75 mm choice only accounts for two of the three rectangles.
problems.hint: Three rectangles, three areas, three centroid locations. Take the weighted average from the bottom.
problems.handbookPage: p. 95, Centroid of Area; pp. 98–100, Shape Properties
traps: Using the geometric midpoint (100 mm) instead of the area-weighted centroid
Forgetting one of the three pieces — especially the web, which is easy to overlook

statics/area-moments-of-inertia.name: Area Moments of Inertia
statics/area-moments-of-inertia.application: The moment of inertia (second moment of area) controls how much a beam bends and where it fails in flexure. On the FE, you will look up $I$ for simple shapes from the handbook tables, then combine them using the parallel axis theorem for composite sections. This comes up in beam bending stress ($\sigma = My/I$), beam deflection, and column buckling. The parallel axis theorem is the single most important formula in this lesson — forgetting the $Ad^2$ term is the most common mistake on the exam.

content.body: The moment of inertia measures how an area’s material is distributed relative to an axis. The farther the material from the axis, the larger the moment of inertia and the stiffer the beam.
Moment of Inertia (Second Moment of Area)

content.latex: I_x = \int y^2\, dA \qquad I_y = \int x^2\, dA
content.label: Definition of Moment of Inertia

content.body: For standard shapes, the handbook tables (pp. 98–100) provide $I$ directly. For a rectangle about its centroidal axis: $I_{xc} = bh^3/12$. For a circle: $I_{xc} = \pi r^4/4$.
Parallel Axis Theorem

$\bar{I}_{xc}$ is the moment of inertia about the shape’s own centroidal axis, $A$ is the area, and $d$ is the perpendicular distance from the centroidal axis to the new axis. This theorem lets you move $I$ from one axis to a parallel one.

The parallel axis theorem only works from a centroidal axis to a non-centroidal axis (or vice versa). You cannot go directly from one non-centroidal axis to another — you must pass through the centroid first.
Polar Moment of Inertia
The polar moment $J$ is the sum of $I_x$ and $I_y$ about the same point. It appears in torsion problems ($\tau = Tr/J$).
Radius of Gyration
The radius of gyration is the distance from the axis at which the entire area could be concentrated to produce the same moment of inertia. It appears in column buckling formulas.

For composite sections: find the composite centroid first (Lesson 5), then apply the parallel axis theorem to each piece about the composite centroidal axis, and sum. You need the centroid before you can compute the composite $I$.
The handbook tables (pp. 98–100) give $I$ about centroidal axes for every standard shape. Do not compute integrals on the FE — look up the value and apply the parallel axis theorem if needed.

problems.statement: A rectangular cross section is 150 mm wide and 300 mm tall. What is the moment of inertia about its centroidal horizontal axis ($I_{xc}$)?
problems.eli5: For a rectangle, the centroidal moment of inertia is $bh^3/12$. The key is using the correct dimension for $h$ — it is the dimension perpendicular to the axis you are computing about. For $I_x$, $h$ is the height (300 mm) and $b$ is the width (150 mm). The choice $1.35 \times 10^9$ uses $bh^3/3$ instead of $bh^3/12$ — that is the moment of inertia about the base, not the centroid. The choice $8.44 \times 10^7$ swaps $b$ and $h$, computing $b^3h/12$ (moment of inertia about the vertical centroidal axis instead). The choice $6.75 \times 10^8$ doubles the correct value.
problems.hint: For a rectangle, $I_{xc} = bh^3/12$. Make sure $h$ is the dimension perpendicular to the axis.

steps.text: Rectangle: $b = 150$ mm (width), $h = 300$ mm (height). For $I_x$, $h$ is perpendicular to the x-axis.
The choice $1.350 \times 10^9$ uses $bh^3/3$, which is the moment of inertia about the base edge, not the centroid.
The choice $8.44 \times 10^7$ uses $b^3h/12 = 150^3 \times 300/12$, which is $I_y$ (about the vertical axis), not $I_x$.

traps: Using $bh^3/3$ (about the base) instead of $bh^3/12$ (about the centroid)
Swapping width and height — $h$ must be the dimension perpendicular to the axis of interest

problems.statement: A rectangular cross section is 50 mm wide and 100 mm tall. Using the parallel axis theorem, what is the moment of inertia about the bottom edge of the rectangle?
problems.eli5: The parallel axis theorem says $I = I_c + Ad^2$. First find the centroidal moment of inertia: $I_c = 50 \times 100^3/12 = 4.17 \times 10^6$. Then add the transfer term: $Ad^2 = (50 \times 100)(50^2) = 12.50 \times 10^6$. Total: $16.67 \times 10^6$ mm⁴. The $4.17 \times 10^6$ choice is just $I_c$ — it forgets the $Ad^2$ transfer term entirely. The $12.50 \times 10^6$ choice is the $Ad^2$ term alone without the centroidal $I_c$. These two errors are the most common parallel axis theorem mistakes on the FE.
problems.hint: The distance $d$ from the centroid to the base is half the height. Do not forget either term — both $I_c$ and $Ad^2$ contribute.

steps.text: Distance from centroid to the base:
Verification: the direct formula gives the same result: $bh^3/3 = 50 \times 100^3/3 = 16.67 \times 10^6$.

problems.handbookPage: p. 95, Parallel Axis Theorem; pp. 98–100, Shape Properties
traps: Forgetting the $Ad^2$ term and reporting only the centroidal value ($4.17 \times 10^6$)
Forgetting the centroidal $I_c$ term and reporting only $Ad^2$ ($12.50 \times 10^6$)

problems.statement: A T-shaped cross section has a top flange 120 mm wide × 20 mm thick and a web 20 mm wide × 80 mm deep below the flange. The composite centroid is at 70 mm from the bottom (found in the previous lesson). What is the moment of inertia of the composite section about its centroidal x-axis?
problems.eli5: For each piece, compute its own centroidal $I$ and then transfer it to the composite centroidal axis using the parallel axis theorem. The web’s centroid is 30 mm below the composite centroid, and the flange’s centroid is 20 mm above it. Add both transferred moments: $I = (I_{c,web} + A_{web} d_{web}^2) + (I_{c,flange} + A_{flange} d_{flange}^2) = 2.29 \times 10^6 + 1.04 \times 10^6 = 3.33 \times 10^6$ mm⁴. The $0.93 \times 10^6$ choice adds only the centroidal $I$ values without the $Ad^2$ transfer terms — the single most common parallel axis theorem mistake. The $2.40 \times 10^6$ choice includes only the $Ad^2$ terms without the centroidal $I$ values.
problems.hint: Apply the parallel axis theorem to each piece separately: $I_{piece} = I_{c,piece} + A_{piece} \times d_{piece}^2$, where $d$ is the distance from that piece’s centroid to the composite centroid.

steps.text: Web (20 × 80 mm): centroid at $y = 40$ mm, distance to composite centroid: $d = 70 - 40 = 30$ mm.
Flange (120 × 20 mm): centroid at $y = 90$ mm, distance to composite centroid: $d = 90 - 70 = 20$ mm.

The $0.93 \times 10^6$ distractor adds only the centroidal values: $853{,}333 + 80{,}000 = 933{,}333$. This misses the $Ad^2$ terms, which account for most of the composite $I$. The $2.40 \times 10^6$ distractor instead sums only the $Ad^2$ transfer terms ($1{,}440{,}000 + 960{,}000$) and drops the centroidal $I$ values.

problems.handbookPage: p. 95, Parallel Axis Theorem; pp. 98–100, Shape Properties
traps: Adding only the centroidal moments of inertia without the $Ad^2$ transfer terms
Using the distance from each piece to the base instead of to the composite centroid

dynamics/particle-kinematics.name: Particle Kinematics
dynamics/particle-kinematics.application: Civil engineers use particle kinematics to derive stopping sight distance on highways, predict how far debris travels after a blast, and calculate the trajectory of water leaving a spillway. On the FE, expect straightforward plug-and-chug with the constant acceleration equations and projectile motion — know which formula connects the variables you're given.

content.body: Kinematics describes motion without worrying about forces. For a particle moving in a straight line with constant acceleration, four equations cover everything.
Constant Acceleration (Rectilinear)

content.latex: s = s_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2} a t^2

content.body: Pick the equation that connects the three knowns to the one unknown. If time isn't involved, use the third equation.
Projectile Motion
Projectile motion splits into two independent directions: horizontal ($a_x = 0$) and vertical ($a_y = -g$). Use the same constant-acceleration equations in each direction separately.
Curvilinear Motion (Normal-Tangential)
When a particle follows a curved path, acceleration has two components: tangential (speeds up or slows down) and normal (changes direction).
The total acceleration magnitude is $a = \sqrt{a_t^2 + a_n^2}$.
Relative Motion
Works for position, velocity, and acceleration. Useful when two objects move in the same frame — like a car on a moving train.
Decision tree: no time in the problem? Use v² = v₀² + 2a(s − s₀). Curved path? Split into a_t and a_n. Two objects? Use relative motion.
The constant-acceleration equations ONLY work when a is constant. If acceleration varies with time or position, you need calculus (integrate a(t) to get v(t)).
Projectile problems almost always give you an angle and initial speed. Split into x and y immediately — never mix horizontal and vertical in the same equation.

problems.statement: A car traveling at $25 \text{ m/s}$ applies its brakes and decelerates uniformly at $5 \text{ m/s}^2$. What is the stopping distance?
problems.eli5: You've got initial speed, final speed (zero), and acceleration — no time. That's the signature for v² = v₀² + 2aΔs. Plug in, solve for s. The trap is forgetting the negative sign on acceleration (braking = negative), but since v = 0 you'd still get the right magnitude.
problems.hint: Which kinematic equation doesn't require time?
traps: Forgetting that deceleration means a is negative
Using s = v₀t + ½at² without first solving for t (works but takes longer)

problems.statement: A ball is launched from ground level at $20 \text{ m/s}$ at an angle of $60\degree$ above the horizontal. What is the maximum height reached? Use $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$.
problems.eli5: At the top of the arc, the vertical velocity is zero — that's your key. Decompose the launch velocity into vertical (v₀ sin θ), then use the no-time equation with v_y = 0. Common mistake: using the full 20 m/s instead of just the vertical component, which gives 20.4 m (the 20.4 m choice).
problems.hint: What is the vertical velocity at the highest point?
traps: Using v₀ = 20 m/s instead of v₀y = 20 sin 60° — gives 20.4 m (distractor D)
Mixing up sin and cos for the vertical component

problems.statement: A car travels along a circular curve of radius $200 \text{ m}$. At a certain instant, its speed is $30 \text{ m/s}$ and it is accelerating at $2 \text{ m/s}^2$ along the road. What is the magnitude of the car's total acceleration?
problems.eli5: On a curve, you have two accelerations at right angles: tangential (speeding up, given as 2) and normal (centripetal, v²/ρ). Since they're perpendicular, combine with Pythagorean theorem. Choosing just 4.5 means you forgot the tangential piece. Choosing 2.0 means you forgot the normal piece.
problems.hint: The car has two perpendicular acceleration components — tangential and normal. How do you combine perpendicular vectors?
traps: Reporting only a_n = 4.5 and ignoring tangential acceleration (distractor B)
Adding a_t + a_n = 6.5 instead of using Pythagorean theorem — they're perpendicular, not collinear

dynamics/rigid-body-kinematics-mass-moi.name: Rigid Body Kinematics & Mass Moments of Inertia
dynamics/rigid-body-kinematics-mass-moi.application: Rigid body kinematics governs anything that rotates — construction crane booms swinging loads, gate valves opening under hydraulic pressure, and rotating equipment on foundations. Mass moment of inertia determines how resistant a body is to angular acceleration, which directly affects vibration analysis of bridge decks and seismic response of buildings. On the FE, expect rotation about a fixed axis and parallel-axis theorem problems using the standard shape table.

content.body: When a body rotates rather than translates, you swap linear variables for angular ones. The same constant-acceleration structure applies.
Rotation About a Fixed Axis
These are the angular analogs of the linear kinematic equations. Swap $v \to \omega$, $a \to \alpha$, $s \to \theta$.
Relating Linear and Angular Quantities

content.latex: s = r\theta \qquad v = r\omega \qquad a_t = r\alpha
content.label: Arc length, velocity, tangential accel

content.body: Mass Moment of Inertia
Mass moment of inertia $I$ measures how mass is distributed relative to a rotation axis. Larger $I$ means harder to spin up.
For standard shapes (cylinder, sphere, rod, disk), use the table on handbook pp. 114–115 — don't derive from scratch.
Parallel-Axis Theorem

$I_c$ is the moment about the centroidal axis, $m$ is the total mass, and $d$ is the distance between the two parallel axes. Always transfer FROM the centroid — never between two arbitrary axes directly.
The parallel-axis theorem only works one direction: centroidal axis to any parallel axis. If you need to go from axis A to axis B, go A to centroid first, then centroid to B.
Angular velocity must be in rad/s for all formulas. If given rpm, convert: ω = rpm × 2π/60.
The FE Handbook gives mass MOI formulas for standard shapes on pp. 114–115. You don't need to memorize them — just know how to read the table and apply the parallel-axis theorem.

problems.statement: A wheel starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at $4 \text{ rad/s}^2$. What is its angular velocity after $5 \text{ s}$?
problems.eli5: This is the angular version of v = v₀ + at. Starts from rest (ω₀ = 0), constant angular acceleration, solve for ω. Just multiply α × t. The trap would be using the wrong equation — but this one is as direct as it gets.
problems.hint: What is the angular analog of v = v₀ + at?
traps: Confusing αt² (displacement equation) with αt (velocity equation) — gives 50 or 100
Forgetting to check units — if α were given in rpm/s you'd need to convert

problems.statement: A grinding wheel of radius $0.15 \text{ m}$ spins at $3{,}600 \text{ rpm}$. What is the tangential velocity at the rim?
problems.eli5: The key step is converting rpm to rad/s — multiply by 2π/60. Then it's just v = rω. The classic trap is forgetting the conversion: 3,600 × 0.15 = 540 m/s (the 540 m/s choice) is wrong because rpm isn't rad/s. The 1,696 m/s choice is 3,600 × 2π × 0.15 (forgetting to divide by 60).
problems.hint: What unit must angular velocity be in before using v = rω?
traps: Using rpm directly without converting to rad/s — gives 540 m/s (distractor C)
Multiplying by 2π but forgetting to divide by 60 — gives 1,696 m/s (distractor D)

problems.statement: A solid cylinder has mass $12 \text{ kg}$ and radius $0.2 \text{ m}$. Using the parallel-axis theorem, what is the mass moment of inertia about an axis parallel to the cylinder's longitudinal axis but located $0.5 \text{ m}$ from the center?
problems.eli5: Step 1: look up the centroidal MOI formula from the handbook table — for a solid cylinder about its axis, it's ½mR². Step 2: add md² where d is the distance to the new axis. The md² term (3.00) dominates here because the offset is large compared to the radius. Choosing 0.24 means you forgot the transfer. Choosing 3.00 means you forgot the centroidal term.
problems.hint: Look up I_c for a solid cylinder from the handbook table, then add the transfer term md².

steps.text: Centroidal MOI for solid cylinder about its longitudinal axis:

traps: Forgetting the md² term and reporting only I_c = 0.24 (distractor A)
Forgetting I_c and reporting only md² = 3.00 (distractor B)
Using mR² instead of ½mR² for the cylinder — gives wrong I_c

dynamics/force-and-acceleration.name: Force & Acceleration
dynamics/force-and-acceleration.application: Newton's second law is how civil engineers compute dynamic forces — earthquake ground acceleration on a building mass, impact forces when a vehicle strikes a bridge barrier, or the forces on a crane boom during a sudden lift. These dynamic forces often exceed static loads and control the design. On the FE, expect ΣF = ma applied to particles and simple rigid body problems with given accelerations.

content.body: Kinetics connects forces to the motion they cause. The foundation is Newton's second law: the net force on a body equals its mass times acceleration.
Newton's Second Law (Particle)
This is a vector equation. In practice, break it into components: $\sum F_x = ma_x$ and $\sum F_y = ma_y$. Always draw a free body diagram first.
Normal-Tangential Kinetics
For curved-path motion, apply Newton's law in tangential and normal directions separately.
Rigid Body Plane Motion
For a rigid body, you need both force and moment equations. The moment equation uses the mass moment of inertia about the center of mass.
$a_c$ is the acceleration of the mass center, $I_c$ is the mass moment of inertia about the mass center, and $\alpha$ is the angular acceleration.
Weight vs. Mass
On the FE, $g = 9.81$ m/s² (SI) or $32.2$ ft/s² (US customary). If given weight, divide by $g$ to get mass before using $F = ma$.
Always draw the FBD before writing equations. Include gravity, normal forces, friction, and applied forces. Miss one force and the entire answer is wrong.
Don't confuse mass and weight. If a problem says "a 500 N block," the mass is 500/9.81 = 50.97 kg. If it says "a 50 kg block," the weight is 50 × 9.81 = 490.5 N.
Most FE dynamics problems give you enough info to solve with ΣF = ma in one or two directions. If the problem involves rotation, add ΣM = Iα. Don't overcomplicate it.

problems.statement: A $80 \text{ kg}$ crate is pushed along a frictionless floor by a horizontal force of $240 \text{ N}$. What is the acceleration of the crate?
problems.eli5: This is the simplest possible ΣF = ma problem. One force, one direction, no friction. Just divide force by mass. The $0.33 \text{ m/s}^2$ choice comes from dividing mass by force (flipped). The $29.4 \text{ m/s}^2$ choice comes from accidentally using weight (80 × 9.81) as the force.
problems.hint: Only one horizontal force acts on the crate. Apply ΣF = ma directly.

steps.text: Frictionless floor, horizontal force — only horizontal equation matters:

traps: Dividing mass by force instead of force by mass
Unnecessarily involving weight or normal force when the surface is frictionless and the push is horizontal

problems.statement: A $500 \text{ N}$ block slides down a frictionless incline at $30\degree$. What is the block's acceleration along the incline? Use $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$.
problems.eli5: Two things trip people up here. First: the problem gives weight (500 N), not mass — divide by g to get mass. Second: only the component of weight along the incline drives the motion, which is W sin 30°. The normal component (W cos 30°) is balanced by the surface. If you skip the mass conversion and just do 500 sin 30° you get 250 (the 250 m/s² option) — that's a force, not an acceleration.
problems.hint: The block's weight is given in Newtons. What's the mass? Which component of weight acts along the incline?

steps.text: Component of weight along the incline:
Apply ΣF = ma along the incline:

traps: Using 500 N as mass instead of weight — must divide by g first
Using cos 30° instead of sin 30° for the component along the incline — gives 8.50
Reporting the force (250 N) as the acceleration

problems.statement: A uniform disk of mass $10 \text{ kg}$ and radius $0.3 \text{ m}$ is mounted on a frictionless axle at its center. A tangential force of $15 \text{ N}$ is applied at the rim. What is the angular acceleration of the disk?
problems.eli5: Three steps: find I from the handbook table (½mR² for a disk), find the torque (force × radius), then divide torque by I. The 33.3 rad/s² choice comes from dividing the raw force by I (15/0.45) — forgetting to convert force to torque by multiplying by the radius. The 5.0 rad/s² choice comes from using I = mR² (forgetting the ½), giving 4.5/0.9. The 50 rad/s² choice comes from leaving the mass out of the inertia (using I = R² = 0.09), giving 4.5/0.09.
problems.hint: Find the disk's mass moment of inertia from the handbook table, compute the torque, then apply ΣM = Iα.

steps.text: Mass moment of inertia for a solid disk about its center:

traps: Using I = mR² instead of ½mR² for a solid disk — gives 33.3 rad/s²
Applying ΣF = ma instead of ΣM = Iα — this is a rotation problem, not translation
Forgetting to multiply the force by the radius to get torque

dynamics/work-energy-power.name: Work, Energy & Power
dynamics/work-energy-power.application: Work-energy methods let civil engineers determine how much energy a guardrail must absorb in a vehicle crash, size a pump motor by computing the power needed to lift water, or calculate the energy dissipated by a hydraulic jump in a spillway. On the FE, these problems often skip the force-acceleration approach entirely — if you know positions and speeds but not time, energy methods are faster.

content.body: When you know starting and ending positions but not time, energy methods bypass force-acceleration equations entirely.
Work-Energy Theorem
If no nonconservative forces act (no friction, no external work), this simplifies to conservation of energy: $T_1 + V_1 = T_2 + V_2$.
Kinetic Energy
Potential Energy
Work Done by Common Forces
Work is force times displacement in the direction of the force.
Power & Efficiency
Energy methods shine when you know two positions and need a speed (or vice versa) without caring about the path between them. If the problem gives you positions and heights, think energy first.
Don't forget to set a datum for gravitational PE. Heights above the datum are positive. If an object drops below your datum, V_g is negative.
Power = force × velocity. If a problem asks for the power required to maintain a constant speed against a resistive force, it's just P = Fv — one step.

problems.statement: A $5 \text{ kg}$ block slides from rest down a frictionless ramp, dropping $3 \text{ m}$ in elevation. What is its speed at the bottom? Use $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$.
problems.eli5: Conservation of energy: all the potential energy at the top converts to kinetic energy at the bottom. Set mgh = ½mv². Notice mass cancels — the answer is actually v = √(2gh) regardless of mass. That gives √(2 × 9.81 × 3) = 7.67 m/s. The 29.4 m/s option is just 2gh without the square root.
problems.hint: With no friction, potential energy at the top equals kinetic energy at the bottom.

steps.text: No friction — use conservation of energy:

traps: Forgetting to take the square root — 2gh = 58.86 (distractor D)
Thinking mass matters — it cancels out in this frictionless case
Computing mgh but forgetting to set T₁ = 0 (block starts from rest)

problems.statement: A pump lifts water at a rate of $0.05 \text{ m}^3\text{/s}$ through a height of $20 \text{ m}$. If the pump efficiency is $80\%$, what input power is required? Use $\rho_{water} = 1{,}000 \text{ kg/m}^3$ and $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$.
problems.eli5: First find the useful power — that's the rate of lifting water against gravity: mass flow rate × g × height. Then divide by efficiency to get the input power the motor must supply. The trap is stopping at 9.81 kW (the 9.81 kW choice) — that's the output power, not the input. Since the pump is only 80% efficient, the motor needs to deliver more.
problems.hint: Compute the useful power first (rate of work against gravity), then adjust for efficiency.
traps: Reporting P_out = 9.81 kW without dividing by efficiency (distractor B)
Multiplying by efficiency instead of dividing — gives 7.85 kW (distractor A)
Forgetting to convert flow rate to mass flow rate (need ρQ, not just Q)

problems.statement: A $10 \text{ kg}$ block is sliding at $8 \text{ m/s}$ on a horizontal surface with a coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k = 0.3$. How far does the block slide before stopping? Use $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$.
problems.eli5: Friction does negative work (removes kinetic energy). Start with the initial KE (½mv²), set it equal to the friction work (μmgd), and solve for d. Notice mass cancels again: d = v²/(2μg). The traps are using μ = 0.3 × 10 = 3 as the friction force (forgetting to multiply by g) or dividing by 2μg incorrectly.
problems.hint: All the kinetic energy is removed by friction work. Set ½mv² = μmgd and solve for d.
traps: Forgetting to multiply by g when computing the friction force — N = mg, not just m
Using v instead of v² in the kinetic energy — ½mv gives wrong units
Not recognizing that friction work is negative (removes energy from the system)

dynamics/impulse-and-momentum.name: Impulse & Momentum
dynamics/impulse-and-momentum.application: Impulse-momentum methods handle short-duration forces that are hard to model with F = ma directly — a vehicle slamming into a bridge pier, a water jet striking a turbine blade, or a pile driver hitting a foundation pile. On the FE, expect conservation of momentum for collisions and the coefficient of restitution to distinguish elastic from plastic impacts.

content.body: When forces act over a short time (impacts, explosions), impulse-momentum is easier than tracking acceleration. Momentum is always conserved when no external forces act.
Linear Impulse-Momentum

content.latex: m v_1 + \sum \int_{t_1}^{t_2} F \, dt = m v_2

content.body: The integral of force over time is the impulse. For a constant force: impulse $= F \Delta t$.
Conservation of Linear Momentum
Applies when external forces are negligible during the event (like a collision). Momentum before = momentum after.
Impact & Coefficient of Restitution
$e = 1$: perfectly elastic (KE conserved). $e = 0$: perfectly plastic (objects stick together). Most real impacts fall between.
For a perfectly plastic collision ($e = 0$), the objects move together after impact: $v_1' = v_2' = v'$.
Angular Impulse-Momentum
The angular version — moments produce angular impulse that changes angular momentum. Same structure as the linear case.

For perfectly plastic collisions, you only need conservation of momentum (one equation, one unknown). For other impacts, you need both momentum conservation AND the restitution equation (two equations, two unknowns).
The coefficient of restitution formula uses velocities NORMAL to the impact surface. For oblique impacts, tangential velocities don't change.

If a problem says "the objects stick together," that's e = 0 (perfectly plastic). Combine masses and use conservation of momentum. Don't try to conserve kinetic energy — it isn't conserved in plastic impacts.

problems.statement: A $2{,}000 \text{ kg}$ car traveling at $15 \text{ m/s}$ rear-ends a $1{,}000 \text{ kg}$ car at rest. The two cars lock bumpers and move together. What is their velocity immediately after impact?
problems.eli5: "Lock bumpers" = perfectly plastic = stick together. Total momentum before equals total momentum after, but now it's one combined mass. So 2,000 × 15 = 3,000 × v'. Simple division. The 7.5 m/s option comes from dividing by 4,000 instead of 3,000. The 15 m/s option assumes no speed change, which violates momentum conservation.
problems.hint: The cars stick together — combine their masses and use conservation of momentum.

steps.text: Perfectly plastic collision (stick together), so $v_1' = v_2' = v'$.

traps: Dividing by the wrong total mass
Trying to conserve kinetic energy — KE is NOT conserved in plastic collisions

problems.statement: A $2 \text{ kg}$ ball moving at $8 \text{ m/s}$ strikes a $2 \text{ kg}$ ball at rest. The coefficient of restitution is $e = 0.5$. What is the velocity of the striking ball after impact?
problems.eli5: Two equations, two unknowns. Momentum conservation gives you the sum of the final velocities, and the restitution equation gives you their difference. Add and subtract to solve. Equal masses make the algebra clean — the striking ball slows to 2 m/s and the struck ball picks up 6 m/s. The 4.0 m/s option assumes each ball gets half the original speed, which only happens at e = 1 for equal masses.
problems.hint: You need two equations: conservation of momentum and the restitution formula. Solve them simultaneously.

steps.text: Subtract to find the striking ball:

traps: Using only momentum conservation without the restitution equation — gives one equation with two unknowns
Flipping the restitution formula (swapping numerator and denominator)
Assuming kinetic energy is conserved — it's only conserved when e = 1

problems.statement: A $1{,}500 \text{ kg}$ vehicle traveling at $20 \text{ m/s}$ crashes into a barrier and comes to rest in $0.15 \text{ s}$. What is the average impact force on the vehicle?
problems.eli5: Impulse = change in momentum. The car goes from 20 m/s to 0, so the change in momentum is 1,500 × 20 = 30,000 kg·m/s. Divide by the impact time (0.15 s) to get the average force. The shorter the impact time, the bigger the force — that's why crumple zones extend the impact time to reduce force. The 30,000 N choice is just the momentum change without dividing by time.
problems.hint: Impulse equals change in momentum. What's the change in momentum, and over what time interval?
problems.handbookFormula: m v_1 + \int F \, dt = m v_2
traps: Reporting the momentum change (30,000) as the force — must divide by time
Using Δt = 1.5 s instead of 0.15 s — misreading the decimal
Forgetting that the vehicle stops (v₂ = 0), so the full 20 m/s is the velocity change

dynamics/vibrations-natural-frequency.name: Vibrations & Natural Frequency
dynamics/vibrations-natural-frequency.application: Civil engineers check natural frequencies to ensure a pedestrian bridge doesn't resonate with walking footfalls, a building doesn't amplify earthquake ground motion, or a machine foundation doesn't vibrate excessively. If the forcing frequency matches the natural frequency, even small loads cause dangerously large oscillations. On the FE, expect basic natural frequency calculations and understanding of resonance — rarely anything beyond undamped free vibration.

content.body: Vibration problems boil down to one question: what's the natural frequency, and is it close to anything that could excite it?
Undamped Free Vibration
$k$ is the spring stiffness (N/m) and $m$ is the mass (kg). The motion is $x(t) = x_0 \cos(\omega_n t) + \frac{\dot{x}_0}{\omega_n} \sin(\omega_n t)$.
Torsional Vibration
$k_t$ is the torsional stiffness and $I$ is the mass moment of inertia. For a solid round shaft: $k_t = GJ/L$ where $G$ is shear modulus, $J$ is polar moment, and $L$ is length.
Damping
Real systems have damping. The damping ratio $\zeta$ determines behavior:
$\zeta < 1$: underdamped (oscillates and decays). $\zeta = 1$: critically damped (fastest return, no oscillation). $\zeta > 1$: overdamped (slow return, no oscillation).
Forced Vibration & Resonance

When an external periodic force $F_0 \sin(\omega t)$ is applied, the steady-state amplitude peaks when the forcing frequency $\omega$ approaches $\omega_n$. This is resonance — the most dangerous condition in structural dynamics.
Most FE vibration questions just ask for the natural frequency. Find k (spring stiffness) and m (mass), plug into ω_n = √(k/m), and convert to Hz or period as needed.
Don't confuse ω_n (rad/s) with f_n (Hz). They differ by a factor of 2π. The exam will try to catch you mixing these up.
If a problem describes a system and asks "at what frequency will resonance occur," the answer is the natural frequency. Resonance = forcing frequency matches natural frequency.

problems.statement: A $50 \text{ kg}$ mass is attached to a spring with stiffness $k = 800 \text{ N/m}$. What is the natural frequency of the system?
problems.eli5: Two steps: compute ω_n in rad/s, then divide by 2π to get Hz. The biggest trap is stopping at 4.0 rad/s (the 4.0 rad/s choice) — that's ω_n, not f_n. The question asks for frequency, which is in Hz. Always check the units the question wants.
problems.hint: Compute ω_n = √(k/m) first, then convert from rad/s to Hz.
traps: Reporting ω_n = 4.0 rad/s as the answer without converting to Hz (distractor C)
Confusing ω_n (rad/s) with f_n (Hz) — they differ by a factor of 2π
Forgetting to take the square root of k/m

problems.statement: A machine weighing $2{,}000 \text{ N}$ sits on a mounting with spring stiffness $k = 50{,}000 \text{ N/m}$. The machine has a rotating imbalance that produces a periodic force. At what forcing frequency (in Hz) will resonance occur? Use $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$.
problems.eli5: Resonance = forcing frequency matches natural frequency. So the question is really "what's the natural frequency?" The twist is that weight is given (2,000 N) instead of mass — divide by g first. Then it's the standard ω_n = √(k/m) converted to Hz. The 5.0 Hz choice comes from using the weight as mass (skipping the /g step). The 15.7 rad/s choice is ω_n in rad/s.
problems.hint: Resonance occurs at the natural frequency. But first — is the 2,000 N a mass or a weight?
traps: Using weight (2,000 N) as mass — must divide by g to get kg
Stopping at ω_n in rad/s and not converting to Hz (distractor C)
Confusing spring stiffness with total force

problems.statement: A disk with mass moment of inertia $I = 0.5 \text{ kg}{\cdot}\text{m}^2$ is attached to a shaft with torsional stiffness $k_t = 500 \text{ N}{\cdot}\text{m/rad}$. What is the natural frequency of torsional vibration?
problems.eli5: Same structure as linear vibration — just swap k for k_t and m for I. Compute ω_n = √(k_t/I), then divide by 2π for Hz. The extra knowledge needed is knowing that torsional stiffness replaces spring stiffness and mass moment of inertia replaces mass. The 31.6 rad/s choice is ω_n in rad/s — right number, wrong unit.
problems.hint: Torsional vibration uses the same formula as linear vibration but with k_t and I instead of k and m.
traps: Reporting ω_n in rad/s instead of converting to Hz (distractor C)
Confusing mass moment of inertia (kg·m²) with area moment of inertia (m⁴) — different quantities
Forgetting that k_t = GJ/L when shaft properties are given instead of k_t directly

mechanics-materials/axial-stress-strain-.name: Axial Stress, Strain & Deformation
mechanics-materials/axial-stress-strain-.application: Civil engineers compute axial stress and deformation constantly — checking whether a steel rod can carry a suspension load, sizing a concrete column for gravity forces, or estimating how much a bridge hanger elongates under traffic. Thermal deformation matters too: expansion joints in bridges and buildings exist because steel and concrete grow with temperature. On the FE, axial stress problems are the most straightforward mechanics questions — direct σ = P/A and δ = PL/AE with occasional thermal twists.

content.body: Axial loading is the simplest stress state — a force pulling or pushing straight through the centroid of a cross-section.
Axial Stress
$P$ is the internal axial force (N or lb) and $A$ is the cross-sectional area (m² or in²). Tension is positive, compression is negative.
Axial Strain & Deformation
$E$ is the modulus of elasticity (Young's modulus). For steel, $E = 200$ GPa (29,000 ksi). For multi-segment bars, sum the deformations: $\delta_{total} = \sum \frac{P_i L_i}{A_i E_i}$.
Thermal Deformation
$\alpha$ is the coefficient of thermal expansion. If the member is restrained (can't expand freely), the prevented deformation creates thermal stress: $\sigma_t = E \alpha \Delta T$.
Hooke's Law (Uniaxial)
Valid only in the elastic range (below the proportional limit). This connects stress, strain, and modulus in one equation.

Three quantities, three formulas — if you know any two of stress, strain, and deformation, you can find the third. Decision tree: need stress? σ = P/A. Need deformation? δ = PL/AE. Need strain? ε = δ/L.
Watch the units. If E is in GPa and A is in mm², keep P in N and L in mm. Mixing m and mm is the most common source of wrong answers.
If a problem says "a steel rod" without giving E, use 200 GPa (or 29,000 ksi). The handbook's material properties table (p. 137) has values for common materials.

problems.statement: A steel rod has a circular cross-section with diameter $d = 20 \text{ mm}$ and carries a tensile load of $P = 15 \text{ kN}$. What is the axial stress in the rod?
problems.eli5: Just P/A — but the trap is computing the area wrong. You need A = πd²/4, not πd² or πd. Using diameter as radius gives A = π(20)² = 1,257 mm² and stress = 11.9 MPa (the 11.9 MPa choice). Using circumference instead of area gives πd = 62.8 and stress = 477 MPa (the 477 MPa choice). The correct area is π(20)²/4 = 314.2 mm².
problems.hint: Remember, the area of a circle uses diameter: A = πd²/4.
traps: Using diameter as radius in A = πr² — gives A = π(20)² = 1,257 mm², stress = 11.9 MPa (choice D)
Using circumference πd instead of area πd²/4 — gives 477 MPa (choice C)

problems.statement: A $2.5 \text{ m}$ long aluminum rod ($E = 70 \text{ GPa}$) has a rectangular cross-section of $30 \text{ mm} \times 50 \text{ mm}$ and carries an axial tensile load of $120 \text{ kN}$. What is the elongation of the rod?
problems.eli5: This is a straight δ = PL/AE plug-in, but the real test is unit consistency. If you work in N, mm, and MPa (which equals N/mm²), everything stays clean. The common disaster is mixing meters and millimeters — if you leave L in meters (2.5) but use A in mm², you're off by a factor of 1,000, giving about 0.00286 mm (nearest distractor 0.0286 mm). The 0.286 mm choice is off by a factor of 10 the same way, and the 28.6 mm choice is off by a factor of 10 in the other direction. Always convert everything to mm before plugging in.
problems.hint: Convert all lengths to the same unit (mm) before plugging into δ = PL/AE.
traps: Leaving L in meters while A is in mm² — off by 10³ (choice A)
Forgetting to convert kN to N or GPa to MPa — off by powers of 10
Mixing unit systems (m and mm) is the #1 source of wrong answers in deformation problems

problems.statement: A steel bar ($E = 200 \text{ GPa}$, $\alpha = 11.7 \times 10^{-6} \text{ /\degree C}$) is $1.0 \text{ m}$ long and rigidly fixed between two walls at $20\degree\text{C}$. The temperature rises to $70\degree\text{C}$. What is the compressive stress in the bar?
problems.eli5: The key insight: if a bar can't expand, the prevented expansion turns into compressive stress. You don't need the length or cross-section area — they cancel out. The formula simplifies to σ = EαΔT. The 58.5 MPa choice comes from using ΔT = 25 instead of 50 (maybe averaging temperatures instead of subtracting). The 0.585 mm choice is the free expansion in mm — that's a deformation, not a stress (wrong units entirely, which is the giveaway). The 23.4 MPa choice comes from using the wrong E or α.
problems.hint: If the bar can't move, the thermal deformation δt must be counteracted by an equal mechanical compression. Set δ_thermal = δ_mechanical.

steps.text: Since the bar is fully restrained, the walls prevent this expansion. The thermal stress is:

traps: Reporting the free expansion (0.585 mm) as the answer — that's deformation, not stress (choice C)
Using ΔT = 25°C (averaging instead of differencing temperatures) — gives half the answer (choice A)
Thinking you need the bar's cross-sectional area — it cancels out in σ = EαΔT

mechanics-materials/torsion.name: Torsion
mechanics-materials/torsion.application: Civil engineers encounter torsion in spandrel beams loaded eccentrically, in auger piles during installation, and in any shaft transmitting power — pump stations, turbine foundations, and mechanical equipment. The FE handbook formula τ = Tc/J is the torsion equivalent of σ = Mc/I for bending. On the FE, expect straightforward plug-and-chug: given a torque and shaft dimensions, find the maximum shear stress or the angle of twist.

content.body: Torsion is shear stress caused by a twisting moment. For circular shafts, the stress varies linearly from zero at the center to a maximum at the outer surface.
Torsional Shear Stress

content.label: Max shear stress in a circular shaft

content.body: $T$ is the applied torque, $c$ is the outer radius, and $J$ is the polar moment of inertia. For a solid circular shaft: $J = \frac{\pi d^4}{32}$. For a hollow shaft: $J = \frac{\pi (d_o^4 - d_i^4)}{32}$.
Angle of Twist
$G$ is the shear modulus (modulus of rigidity). For steel, $G = 80$ GPa. The relationship between $E$, $G$, and Poisson's ratio is $G = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)}$.
Thin-Walled Hollow Shafts

$t$ is the wall thickness and $A_m$ is the area enclosed by the median line of the wall (not the cross-sectional area of the material). Use this when the wall thickness is small compared to the radius ($t < 0.1r$).
Torsional Stiffness
The torque per radian of twist. Higher $GJ$ or shorter $L$ means a stiffer shaft.

Torsion formulas mirror bending formulas. τ = Tc/J is the rotational twin of σ = Mc/I. J replaces I, torque replaces moment, shear stress replaces normal stress. If you know bending, you already know torsion.
J is the POLAR moment of inertia (πd⁴/32), not the area moment of inertia I (πd⁴/64). J = 2I for circular sections. Using I instead of J halves your answer.
If a problem gives power P (watts) and rotational speed ω (rad/s), find torque first: T = P/ω. If speed is in rpm, convert: ω = rpm × 2π/60.

problems.statement: A solid circular shaft has a diameter of $50 \text{ mm}$ and is subjected to a torque of $T = 500 \text{ N}{\cdot}\text{m}$. What is the maximum shear stress in the shaft?
problems.eli5: Plug into τ = Tc/J. Two common mistakes: using d instead of c = d/2 (doubles your answer to 40.7 MPa), or using I = πd⁴/64 instead of J = πd⁴/32 (halves your answer to 10.2 MPa). Remember: torsion uses J (polar), not I (area moment). And c is the radius, not diameter.
problems.hint: What is J for a solid circular shaft? And is c the radius or the diameter?
traps: Using diameter instead of radius for c — doubles the stress (choice C)
Using I = πd⁴/64 instead of J = πd⁴/32 — halves the stress (choice A)

problems.statement: A solid steel shaft ($G = 80 \text{ GPa}$) is $1.5 \text{ m}$ long with a diameter of $40 \text{ mm}$. It transmits a torque of $300 \text{ N}{\cdot}\text{m}$. What is the angle of twist?
problems.eli5: Straight φ = TL/GJ, but the unit trap is real. Everything needs to be in mm, N, and MPa. If you leave L in meters (1.5), you get a wildly wrong answer. The 0.0448 rad option comes from using I instead of J (half the J means double the twist). The 0.0112 rad option comes from doubling J (e.g. using π/16 instead of π/32), which halves the twist. The 1.28 rad option comes from reporting the answer in degrees (1.28°) but mislabeling it as radians.
problems.hint: Make sure L is in mm and G is in MPa (= N/mm²) before plugging into φ = TL/GJ.
traps: Leaving L in meters while J is in mm⁴ — off by 10³
Using I instead of J — doubles the angle of twist (choice B)
Confusing radians and degrees — 0.0224 rad ≈ 1.28°, not the same number

problems.statement: A hollow circular steel shaft has an outer diameter of $80 \text{ mm}$ and an inner diameter of $60 \text{ mm}$. If the allowable shear stress is $\tau_{allow} = 60 \text{ MPa}$, what is the maximum torque the shaft can transmit?
problems.eli5: Same formula τ = Tc/J, but solve backwards for T. The hard part is computing J for a hollow shaft — it's π(d_o⁴ − d_i⁴)/32, not π(d_o² − d_i²). The 2.06 kN·m option comes from using c = d_o = 80 instead of c = 40 (doubles c, halves T). The 5.50 kN·m option comes from using J of a solid 80 mm shaft (ignoring the hollow core). The 8.25 kN·m option comes from combining both errors or an arithmetic mistake.
problems.hint: J for a hollow shaft subtracts the inner d⁴ from the outer d⁴. And c is the outer radius, not the outer diameter.
traps: Using c = d_o (diameter) instead of c = d_o/2 (radius) — halves the torque capacity (choice A)
Forgetting to subtract the inner term in J — using J_solid gives too much torque (choice C)
Subtracting diameters (d_o − d_i)⁴ instead of (d_o⁴ − d_i⁴) — completely wrong J

mechanics-materials/stress-strain-diagra.name: Stress-Strain Diagrams & Material Behavior
