The load duration factor C_D exceeds 1.0 for short-duration loads — about 1.6 for wind or seismic and 1.25 for a 7-day load — and drops below 1.0 (0.9) for permanent loads. So for a wind load, C_D ≈ 1.6 increases the allowable stress. The "C_D < 1.0, decreasing allowable stress" choice has the direction backwards. The "C_D = 1.0 for all load types" choice ignores duration effects. The "applies only to permanent dead loads" choice misstates where the factor applies.
problems.hint: Wood gets stronger (in allowable terms) for briefly applied loads — which direction does C_D move?

steps.text: Shorter load duration → higher allowable stress in wood.
Wind/seismic loads use C_D ≈ 1.6 (> 1.0); permanent loads use C_D = 0.9.
Therefore C_D > 1.0 for the wind load case, raising the allowable stress.

traps: Reversing the direction — assuming brief loads reduce capacity
Treating C_D as a constant 1.0 regardless of load duration

materials/composite-materials.name: Composite Materials
materials/composite-materials.application: Civil engineers encounter composites in fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) bridge decks, carbon fiber wraps for strengthening concrete columns, and glass fiber reinforced concrete panels. Understanding the rule of mixtures lets you estimate a composite’s density, stiffness, and strength from the properties and volume fractions of its components — critical for evaluating whether an FRP alternative can replace a traditional steel or concrete member. On the FE, expect rule-of-mixtures calculations for modulus and density.

content.body: A composite is made of two or more materials combined to get properties neither has alone — typically a strong, stiff fiber (glass, carbon, steel) embedded in a matrix (polymer, cement, metal) that holds shape and transfers load.
Rule of Mixtures — Density
$f_1$ and $f_2$ are the volume fractions of each constituent (they sum to 1). This is a straight weighted average by volume.
Rule of Mixtures — Elastic Modulus (Parallel to Fibers)

When load is applied parallel to the fibers, both components stretch by the same amount (isostrain condition: $\varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2$). The composite modulus is a volume-weighted average of the component moduli.
Isostrain Condition

Because the strains are equal, the stress in each phase is different: $\sigma_1 = E_1 \varepsilon$ and $\sigma_2 = E_2 \varepsilon$. The stiffer component (higher $E$) carries a proportionally larger share of the stress.
Perpendicular to Fibers (Isostress)
When load is perpendicular to the fibers, both components carry the same stress but strain differently. The resulting composite modulus is always lower than the isostrain value.

Parallel loading (isostrain) = additive formula = higher composite modulus. Perpendicular loading (isostress) = reciprocal formula = lower composite modulus. The FE almost always tests the parallel (isostrain) case.
The handbook (p. 123) gives the rule of mixtures for density, heat capacity, and Young’s modulus. It also explicitly states the isostrain condition for long-fiber composites.

problems.statement: A composite material consists of $30\%$ glass fibers ($\rho_f = 2{,}500 \text{ kg/m}^3$) by volume in a polymer matrix ($\rho_m = 1{,}200 \text{ kg/m}^3$). What is the density of the composite?
problems.eli5: Rule of mixtures for density: $\rho_c = f_f \rho_f + f_m \rho_m = 0.30 \times 2{,}500 + 0.70 \times 1{,}200 = 750 + 840 = 1{,}590$ kg/m³. The 1,850 kg/m³ option uses $f_m = 0.50$ instead of 0.70 (equal fractions). The 3,700 kg/m³ option adds the densities without weighting (2,500 + 1,200). The 1,200 kg/m³ option just uses the matrix density, ignoring the fibers.
problems.hint: The volume fractions must sum to 1. If fibers are 30%, the matrix is 70%.
traps: Forgetting to compute the matrix fraction as $(1 - f_{fiber})$ — using equal fractions gives 1,850 (choice B)
Adding densities without volume weighting — gives 3,700 (choice C)

problems.statement: A carbon fiber composite has $40\%$ carbon fibers ($E_f = 230 \text{ GPa}$) by volume in an epoxy matrix ($E_m = 3.5 \text{ GPa}$). What is the elastic modulus of the composite when loaded parallel to the fibers?
problems.eli5: Parallel to fibers = isostrain model: $E_c = f_f \times E_f + f_m \times E_m = 0.40 \times 230 + 0.60 \times 3.5 = 92 + 2.1 = 94.1$ GPa. The 5.8 GPa option uses the isostress (perpendicular) model: $1/E_c = 0.40/230 + 0.60/3.5$, giving $E_c \approx 5.8$ GPa. The 116.8 GPa option uses $f = 0.50/0.50$ instead of 0.40/0.60. The 233.5 GPa option adds the moduli without weighting.
problems.hint: Parallel loading means isostrain (equal strain) — use the additive rule of mixtures, not the reciprocal formula.
traps: Using the isostress (perpendicular) formula instead of isostrain — gives 5.8 GPa (choice B)
Using equal volume fractions (50/50) instead of 40/60 — gives 116.8 GPa (choice C)

problems.statement: A steel-fiber reinforced composite ($E_f = 200 \text{ GPa}$, $E_m = 3 \text{ GPa}$, $f_f = 0.25$) is loaded parallel to the fibers at a total composite stress of $100 \text{ MPa}$. What is the stress carried by the fibers?
problems.eli5: Under isostrain, both phases have the same strain. First find composite modulus: $E_c = 0.25(200) + 0.75(3) = 50 + 2.25 = 52.25$ GPa. Then find the common strain: $\varepsilon = \sigma_c / E_c = 100/52{,}250 = 0.001914$. Fiber stress: $\sigma_f = E_f \varepsilon = 200{,}000 \times 0.001914 = 383 \approx 384$ MPa. The fibers carry much more stress because they’re much stiffer. The 100 MPa choice assumes equal stress (isostress model, wrong for parallel loading). The 25 MPa choice scales by volume fraction: $100 \times 0.25$. The 200 MPa choice confuses fiber modulus with fiber stress.
problems.hint: Under isostrain, find the composite modulus first, then the common strain, then multiply by each phase’s modulus to get its stress.
traps: Assuming equal stress in both phases (isostress) — that’s the perpendicular model, gives 100 MPa (choice B)
Scaling the composite stress by volume fraction ($100 \times 0.25 = 25$) instead of by modulus ratio (choice C)

materials/corrosion-material-selection.name: Corrosion & Material Selection
materials/corrosion-material-selection.application: Civil engineers deal with corrosion on every project that involves metals in contact with water, soil, or dissimilar metals. You select coatings for bridge steel, specify cathodic protection for buried pipelines, and avoid connecting dissimilar metals (like aluminum flashing on a steel beam) without an insulating barrier. Understanding galvanic corrosion and the electrochemical series lets you predict which metal corrodes in a couple and design around it. On the FE, expect questions about anode/cathode identification, galvanic corrosion, and basic material comparison.

content.body: Corrosion is the electrochemical degradation of a metal. It requires four things: an anode (metal that corrodes), a cathode (metal that is protected), an electrolyte (water or moist soil), and an electrical connection between the two metals.
Galvanic Corrosion

When two dissimilar metals are in electrical contact in the presence of an electrolyte, the more electropositive (more active) metal becomes the anode and corrodes preferentially. The more noble metal becomes the cathode and is protected.
Anode & Cathode Reactions
At the anode, the metal loses electrons (oxidation) and dissolves into solution. Common cathode reactions include oxygen reduction: $\frac{1}{2}O_2 + 2e^- + H_2O \rightarrow 2OH^-$.
Galvanic Series & Material Selection

The galvanic series ranks metals from most active (anodic) to most noble (cathodic). In seawater: zinc and magnesium are very active (corrode first), while gold and platinum are noble (resist corrosion). Steel is moderately active, which is why we galvanize it (coat with zinc) — the zinc corrodes preferentially, protecting the steel.
Corrosion Prevention

Common strategies: protective coatings (paint, galvanizing), cathodic protection (sacrificial anodes or impressed current), material selection (stainless steel, FRP), and isolation (insulating gaskets between dissimilar metals).
Material Properties Comparison

The FE Handbook (p. 119) provides a table of metal properties including density, melting point, specific heat, electrical resistivity, and thermal conductivity. Use this table to compare materials for specific applications.
In a galvanic couple, the more active metal (higher on the activity series) is the ANODE and corrodes. Zinc protects steel because zinc is more active — it sacrifices itself.

The handbook (p. 116) describes the anode/cathode reactions for corrosion. The metals table (p. 119) provides property data for comparison questions. Know which common metals are more active (zinc, aluminum, steel) vs. more noble (copper, stainless steel, gold).

problems.statement: A steel bolt is used to connect an aluminum bracket to a copper grounding plate. All three metals are exposed to rainwater. Which metal will corrode first?
problems.eli5: In the galvanic series, aluminum is more active (more anodic) than both steel and copper. When dissimilar metals are in contact with an electrolyte (rainwater), the most active metal corrodes first. Order of activity (most to least): aluminum > steel > copper. So aluminum corrodes, and the copper and steel are cathodically protected. Steel would be the answer if aluminum weren’t present (steel is more active than copper). Copper is the most noble of the three — it’s protected. "All three corrode equally" is wrong because galvanic corrosion specifically accelerates corrosion of the most active metal while protecting the others.
problems.hint: In the galvanic series, the most active (anodic) metal in contact corrodes first. Rank: aluminum > steel > copper.

steps.text: Rank the metals by activity (most active first): aluminum > steel > copper
The most active metal (aluminum) becomes the anode and corrodes preferentially.
The steel and copper are cathodically protected by the aluminum.

traps: Thinking the smallest/thinnest metal corrodes first — corrosion is driven by electrochemical potential, not size
Confusing noble (cathode, protected) with active (anode, corrodes)

problems.statement: Galvanized steel is steel coated with a thin layer of zinc. If the zinc coating is scratched and the underlying steel is exposed to moisture, what happens?

choices.text: The zinc corrodes preferentially, continuing to protect the exposed steel
The exposed steel corrodes rapidly while the zinc is unaffected
Both metals corrode at equal rates
Neither metal corrodes because the coating is only scratched

problems.eli5: Zinc is more active (more anodic) than steel in the galvanic series. Even when the coating is scratched and steel is exposed, the zinc surrounding the scratch becomes the anode and corrodes sacrificially. The electrons flow from zinc to steel, keeping the steel cathodically protected. This is why galvanizing works even with scratches and cuts — unlike paint, which only provides a physical barrier. The "exposed steel corrodes while the zinc is unaffected" choice reverses the polarity. The "both corrode at equal rates" choice ignores the galvanic effect. The "neither corrodes" choice doesn’t understand that moisture + dissimilar metals = galvanic cell.
problems.hint: Zinc is more active than steel. In a galvanic couple, the more active metal corrodes to protect the less active one.

steps.text: Zinc is more active (more anodic) than steel in the galvanic series.
When both are exposed to moisture, a galvanic cell forms: zinc = anode, steel = cathode.
The zinc corrodes sacrificially, providing cathodic protection to the steel even at the scratch.

traps: Thinking the exposed metal (steel) corrodes because it’s unprotected — galvanic protection extends beyond the coating edge
Thinking corrosion only occurs under the coating, not at the scratch

problems.statement: An engineer is selecting a metal for a heat exchanger that will operate in a marine environment. The metal must have high thermal conductivity ($> 200 \text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$), low density ($< 5{,}000 \text{ kg/m}^3$), and good corrosion resistance. From the FE Handbook metals table, which metal best meets all three criteria?
problems.eli5: Check each criterion: Thermal conductivity > 200 W/(m·K): aluminum (236) ✔, copper (403) ✔, iron (83.5) ✘, titanium (22) ✘. This eliminates iron and titanium. Low density < 5,000 kg/m³: aluminum (2,698) ✔, copper (8,933) ✘. This eliminates copper. Only aluminum meets all three criteria. While copper has the best thermal conductivity, it’s too heavy. Titanium has excellent corrosion resistance but poor thermal conductivity. Iron fails both conductivity and density requirements and corrodes readily in marine environments.
problems.hint: Eliminate choices by checking each criterion one at a time. Start with the easiest to verify — thermal conductivity eliminates two options immediately.

steps.text: Check thermal conductivity (> 200 W/(m·K)): Al = 236 ✔, Cu = 403 ✔, Fe = 83.5 ✘, Ti = 22 ✘
Eliminate iron and titanium. Check density (< 5,000 kg/m³):
Aluminum meets all criteria: high conductivity, low density, and forms a protective oxide layer for corrosion resistance.

traps: Picking copper for its highest thermal conductivity without checking density — it’s too heavy (choice A)
Picking titanium for its corrosion resistance without checking conductivity — it’s a poor conductor (choice D)

fluid-mechanics/fluid-properties.name: Fluid Properties
fluid-mechanics/fluid-properties.application: Civil engineers need fluid properties for every hydraulic calculation. Density and specific weight let you compute hydrostatic forces on dams and retaining walls. Viscosity determines whether flow in a water main is laminar or turbulent, which controls friction losses and pipe sizing. Specific gravity lets you compare fluids to water quickly. On the FE, expect questions that require converting between density, specific weight, and specific gravity, or applying viscosity in a shear stress calculation.

content.body: Fluid mechanics starts with three linked properties: density, specific weight, and specific gravity. Know how to convert between them — the FE gives you one and asks for another.
Density, Specific Weight & Specific Gravity
Reference values for water at standard conditions: $\rho_w = 1{,}000 \text{ kg/m}^3$ (62.4 lbm/ft³), $\gamma_w = 9{,}810 \text{ N/m}^3$ (62.4 lbf/ft³).
Viscosity

Dynamic (absolute) viscosity $\mu$ has units of Pa·s or N·s/m². Kinematic viscosity $\nu$ has units of m²/s. For a thin fluid film with linear velocity profile: $\tau = \mu v / \delta$, where $v$ is the plate velocity and $\delta$ is the film thickness.
Surface Tension & Capillarity
Surface tension $\sigma$ is force per unit length at a fluid interface. Capillary rise depends on tube diameter $d$, contact angle $\beta$, and the fluid’s specific weight $\gamma$.
Specific gravity is dimensionless — it’s just the ratio to water. SG = 1.0 for water, SG = 13.6 for mercury, SG = 0.8–0.9 for oil. Multiply SG by 9,810 N/m³ to get specific weight in SI.
Don’t confuse dynamic viscosity ($\mu$, in Pa·s) with kinematic viscosity ($\nu$, in m²/s). The FE handbook uses both — check which one the problem gives you before plugging in.

problems.statement: A fluid has a specific gravity of $SG = 0.85$. What is its specific weight?
problems.eli5: Specific gravity is the ratio of the fluid’s density (or specific weight) to water’s. So $\gamma = SG \times \gamma_w = 0.85 \times 9{,}810 = 8{,}338.5$ N/m³. The 850 N/m³ choice just multiplies $0.85 \times 1{,}000$ and slaps on the wrong units. The 9,810 N/m³ choice is water’s specific weight ($SG = 1.0$). The 8,338 kg/m³ choice has the right number but wrong units — specific weight is force per volume (N/m³), not mass per volume (kg/m³).
problems.hint: Specific weight $= SG$ times the specific weight of water ($9{,}810$ N/m³ in SI).
traps: Confusing specific weight (N/m³) with density (kg/m³) — different units, related by $g$
Using $\rho_w = 1{,}000$ instead of $\gamma_w = 9{,}810$ when computing specific weight

problems.statement: A flat plate moves at $v = 0.5 \text{ m/s}$ over a $\delta = 2 \text{ mm}$ thick oil film with dynamic viscosity $\mu = 0.1 \text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$. The velocity profile in the film is linear. What is the shear stress on the plate?
problems.eli5: For a linear velocity profile, $dv/dy = v/\delta$. The unit trap is converting mm to m: $2$ mm $= 0.002$ m. So $\tau = \mu \times v/\delta = 0.1 \times 0.5/0.002 = 25$ Pa. The 0.05 Pa distractor omits the film thickness entirely, computing $\mu \times v = 0.1 \times 0.5 = 0.05$ (treating $\delta$ as 1 m). Note that using $\delta = 2$ m directly would give 0.025 Pa, not 0.05 Pa. The 250 Pa distractor uses $\delta = 0.0002$ m (converting mm to m incorrectly). The 0.25 Pa distractor uses $\delta = 0.2$ m.
problems.hint: For a linear velocity profile, $dv/dy = v/\delta$. Convert the film thickness to meters before dividing.
traps: Forgetting to convert mm to m for the film thickness — off by a factor of 1,000
Using kinematic viscosity $\nu$ instead of dynamic viscosity $\mu$ in the shear stress formula

problems.statement: A glass capillary tube with diameter $d = 1.5 \text{ mm}$ is inserted into water at 20°C. The surface tension of water is $\sigma = 0.0728 \text{ N/m}$, the contact angle is $\beta = 0\degree$, and $\gamma_w = 9{,}789 \text{ N/m}^3$. What is the approximate capillary rise?
problems.eli5: Plug into $h = 4\sigma \cos\beta / (\gamma d)$. With $\beta = 0\degree$, $\cos 0\degree = 1$. Convert $d = 1.5$ mm $= 0.0015$ m. Then $h = 4(0.0728)(1) / (9{,}789 \times 0.0015) = 0.2912 / 14.684 = 0.01983$ m $\approx 19.8$ mm. The 9.9 mm choice drops the factor of 4 — using $\sigma \cos\beta / (\gamma d)$ instead. The 39.7 mm choice uses the radius instead of the diameter (doubling the answer). The 4.95 mm choice uses 2 instead of 4 in the numerator.
problems.hint: The capillary rise formula uses diameter (not radius) in the denominator, and there’s a factor of 4 in the numerator.
traps: Dropping the factor of 4 in the numerator — gives half the correct answer
Using radius instead of diameter — doubles the answer
Forgetting to convert mm to m for the tube diameter

fluid-mechanics/hydrostatic-pressure.name: Hydrostatic Pressure & Manometers
fluid-mechanics/hydrostatic-pressure.application: Civil engineers compute hydrostatic pressure to design water tanks, dams, and buried pipes. Gauge pressure at depth tells you the force on a valve or the water pressure at a fire hydrant. Manometers — U-tubes filled with a denser fluid like mercury — are a classic FE problem type where you step through each fluid column adding or subtracting γh. On the FE, expect problems that require computing pressure at a point, converting between gauge and absolute pressure, or analyzing a manometer.

content.body: In a static fluid, pressure increases linearly with depth. There are no shear stresses, and pressure acts equally in all directions at a point (Pascal’s law).
Pressure Variation with Depth

content.latex: P_2 - P_1 = \gamma(z_1 - z_2) = \gamma h = \rho g h
content.label: Hydrostatic pressure difference

content.body: Pressure increases as you go deeper (lower $z$). The depth $h$ is measured from the free surface down to the point of interest.
Absolute vs. Gauge Pressure

Gauge pressure is zero at the free surface open to the atmosphere. Most civil engineering problems use gauge pressure unless the problem explicitly says “absolute.” Standard atmospheric pressure is 101.325 kPa (14.696 psi).
Manometers

For a U-tube manometer, start at the known pressure side and walk through each fluid column: add $\gamma h$ going down, subtract $\gamma h$ going up. When both columns have equal height: $P_0 = P_2 + (\gamma_2 - \gamma_1)h$.
Manometer trick: start at the side with the known pressure (often atmospheric = 0 gauge). Walk through each column — going DOWN adds pressure, going UP subtracts it. Each fluid gets its own γ.
The sign convention trips people up. If your datum is at the top, h is positive downward and pressure increases. Always be explicit about which direction is positive in your setup.

problems.statement: A water tank is open to the atmosphere. What is the gauge pressure at a depth of $h = 5 \text{ m}$ below the water surface? Use $\gamma_w = 9{,}810 \text{ N/m}^3$.
problems.eli5: Direct application of P = γh. P = 9,810 × 5 = 49,050 Pa = 49.05 kPa. This is gauge pressure because the surface is open to the atmosphere (P_gauge = 0 at surface). The 49,050 kPa choice forgets to convert Pa to kPa. The 150.4 kPa choice adds atmospheric pressure (making it absolute, not gauge). The 4.905 kPa choice divides by 10,000 instead of 1,000 when converting Pa to kPa.
problems.hint: Gauge pressure at the surface of an open tank is zero. At depth h, P_gauge = γh.
traps: Forgetting to convert Pa to kPa — gives 49,050 instead of 49.05
Adding atmospheric pressure when the problem asks for gauge pressure

problems.statement: A closed tank contains oil ($SG = 0.85$) with a gauge pressure of $20 \text{ kPa}$ on the oil surface. What is the absolute pressure at a point $3 \text{ m}$ below the surface? Use $\gamma_w = 9{,}810 \text{ N/m}^3$ and $P_{\text{atm}} = 101.3 \text{ kPa}$.
problems.eli5: Two things contribute to the pressure at depth: the surface pressure and the hydrostatic column. First, γ_oil = SG × γ_w = 0.85 × 9,810 = 8,338.5 N/m³. Hydrostatic pressure = 8,338.5 × 3 = 25,016 Pa = 25.0 kPa. Gauge pressure at depth = 20 + 25.0 = 45.0 kPa. Absolute = 101.3 + 45.0 = 146.3 kPa. The 45.0 kPa option gives gauge pressure, not absolute. The 121.3 kPa option adds atmospheric to the surface gauge pressure but forgets the hydrostatic column. The 150.8 kPa option uses γ_w instead of γ_oil.
problems.hint: Start with the surface gauge pressure, add the hydrostatic increase γh, then add atmospheric pressure to convert to absolute.
traps: Giving gauge pressure instead of absolute when the problem asks for absolute (choice B)
Forgetting to adjust γ for the oil’s specific gravity — using water’s γ instead
Forgetting to add the hydrostatic column to the surface pressure (choice C)

problems.statement: A U-tube manometer connects a pressurized air line to the atmosphere. The manometer fluid is mercury ($SG = 13.6$, $\gamma_w = 9{,}810 \text{ N/m}^3$). The mercury column on the air side is $h = 250 \text{ mm}$ higher than on the atmospheric side. What is the gauge pressure in the air line?
problems.eli5: The mercury is higher on the air side, meaning the air pressure pushes the mercury down on the air side and up on the atmospheric side. So P_air = γ_Hg × h. First get γ_Hg = 13.6 × 9,810 = 133,416 N/m³. Convert h = 250 mm = 0.25 m. P = 133,416 × 0.25 = 33,354 Pa = 33.35 kPa. The 2.45 kPa choice uses water’s γ instead of mercury’s. The 333.5 kPa choice forgets to convert mm to m. The 133.4 kPa choice uses h = 1 m.
problems.hint: The pressure difference equals the specific weight of the manometer fluid times the height difference. Don’t forget to use mercury’s specific weight, not water’s.
traps: Using γ_water instead of γ_mercury — gives a result 13.6× too small
Forgetting to convert mm to m — off by a factor of 1,000
Getting the manometer direction wrong — the higher mercury column is on the higher-pressure side

fluid-mechanics/hydrostatic-forces-buoya.name: Hydrostatic Forces & Buoyancy
fluid-mechanics/hydrostatic-forces-buoya.application: Civil engineers calculate hydrostatic forces to design dams, gates, and lock chambers. The resultant force on a submerged surface acts at the center of pressure — not the centroid — which matters for computing overturning moments. Buoyancy governs whether a buried tank floats out of saturated ground, how much a barge settles under load, and the uplift on submerged foundations. On the FE, expect problems requiring the hydrostatic force on a flat surface, locating the center of pressure, or applying Archimedes’ principle.

content.body: When a flat surface is submerged in a static fluid, the pressure distribution creates a resultant force. Finding that force and where it acts is a classic FE problem.
Force on a Submerged Plane Surface
The resultant force equals the pressure at the centroid times the area. Here $h_C$ is the vertical depth from the free surface to the centroid of the submerged surface.
Center of Pressure

The center of pressure is always deeper than the centroid. The offset $I_{xC}/(y_C A)$ gets smaller as the surface goes deeper (because $y_C$ in the denominator grows). For a vertical surface, $y = h$ (slant distance equals vertical depth).
Archimedes’ Principle
The buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced. A floating body displaces its own weight. The center of buoyancy is at the centroid of the displaced fluid volume.
For a rectangular gate: $I_{xC} = bh^3/12$. For a circular gate: $I_{xC} = \pi r^4/4$. These are centroidal moments of inertia — the handbook provides them.
The resultant force acts at the CENTER OF PRESSURE, not the centroid. The force is computed using the pressure at the centroid, but it doesn’t act there — it acts deeper.

problems.statement: A vertical rectangular gate is $2 \text{ m}$ wide and $3 \text{ m}$ tall, with its top edge at the water surface. What is the total hydrostatic force on the gate? Use $\gamma_w = 9{,}810 \text{ N/m}^3$.
problems.eli5: The centroid of a rectangle with its top at the surface is at h_C = 3/2 = 1.5 m. Area = 2 × 3 = 6 m². F = γ × h_C × A = 9,810 × 1.5 × 6 = 88,290 N = 88.3 kN. The 58.9 kN choice uses h_C = 1.0 m (one-third of the height). The 176.6 kN choice uses h_C = 3.0 m (the bottom, not the centroid). The 29.4 kN choice uses h_C = 0.5 m.
problems.hint: For a rectangle with its top at the surface, the centroid is at half the height.
traps: Using the bottom depth (3 m) instead of the centroid depth (1.5 m) — doubles the answer
Forgetting that the centroid of a rectangle is at its center, not at one-third height

problems.statement: For the same gate (vertical, $2 \text{ m}$ wide, $3 \text{ m}$ tall, top edge at the water surface), at what depth below the surface does the resultant force act? The centroidal moment of inertia is $I_{xC} = bh^3/12$.
problems.eli5: The center of pressure is y_CP = y_C + I_xC/(y_C × A). For a vertical surface, y = h. Centroid: y_C = 1.5 m. I_xC = 2(3)^3/12 = 4.5 m^4. A = 6 m². Offset = 4.5/(1.5 × 6) = 0.5 m. So y_CP = 1.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 m. The center of pressure is at 2/3 of the height — that’s a classic result for a rectangle with its top at the surface. The 1.5 m option is the centroid, not the center of pressure. The 1.0 m option is one-third. The 2.5 m option uses the wrong I formula.
problems.hint: The center of pressure is deeper than the centroid. Use the formula y_CP = y_C + I_xC/(y_C × A).
traps: Confusing the centroid with the center of pressure — they’re not the same (choice B)
Using the wrong moment of inertia formula (e.g., bh^3/3 instead of bh^3/12)

problems.statement: A hollow steel tank ($\gamma_{\text{steel}} = 77{,}000 \text{ N/m}^3$) has an outer volume of $2.0 \text{ m}^3$ and a total weight of $15 \text{ kN}$. The tank is fully submerged in water ($\gamma_w = 9{,}810 \text{ N/m}^3$). What is the net upward or downward force on the tank?
problems.eli5: Buoyant force = γ_w × V_displaced = 9,810 × 2.0 = 19,620 N = 19.62 kN. Weight = 15 kN. Since buoyancy > weight, the net force is 19.62 – 15 = 4.62 kN upward — the tank wants to float. The "4.62 kN downward" option gets the right magnitude but wrong direction. The "19.62 kN upward" option gives the buoyant force alone without subtracting weight. The "15.0 kN downward" option ignores buoyancy entirely.
problems.hint: Compare the buoyant force (γ_w × V_outer) to the tank’s weight. The net force determines whether the tank sinks or floats.

steps.text: Since $F_B > W$, the tank tends to float.

traps: Getting the direction wrong — net upward means the tank floats, not sinks
Using the steel’s γ instead of water’s γ for the buoyant force
Forgetting that buoyancy uses the outer (displaced) volume, not the volume of steel

fluid-mechanics/continuity-bernoulli.name: Continuity & Bernoulli’s Equation
fluid-mechanics/continuity-bernoulli.application: The continuity equation and Bernoulli’s equation are the two most-used tools in hydraulic design. Continuity (Q = Av) tells you how velocity changes when a pipe transitions from one diameter to another. Bernoulli connects pressure, velocity, and elevation along a streamline — letting you determine if a hydrant will deliver adequate pressure or compute the velocity of a jet at a spillway. On the FE, these two equations often appear together in a single problem: use continuity to find the velocity, then Bernoulli to find the pressure.

content.body: Two equations form the backbone of every pipe and channel analysis: continuity conserves mass, and Bernoulli conserves energy (for frictionless flow).
Continuity Equation
For a circular pipe, $A = \pi D^2/4$. When the diameter shrinks, velocity increases proportionally to the area ratio.
Bernoulli’s Equation

Each term has units of length (head): $P/\gamma$ is pressure head, $v^2/2g$ is velocity head, and $z$ is elevation head. Bernoulli applies along a streamline for steady, incompressible, inviscid flow.
Energy Equation (with losses)
The energy equation adds a friction head loss term $h_f$ to Bernoulli’s equation. Use this form whenever the problem mentions friction, head loss, or pipe length.

Common setup: a tank discharges through a pipe or nozzle. The surface velocity is negligible ($v_1 \approx 0$), and the surface pressure is atmospheric ($P_1 = 0$ gauge). This simplifies Bernoulli dramatically.
Bernoulli’s equation assumes no friction. If the problem gives you pipe length and roughness, you need the energy equation (Bernoulli + h_f), not pure Bernoulli.

problems.statement: Water flows through a pipe that reduces from $D_1 = 300 \text{ mm}$ to $D_2 = 150 \text{ mm}$. If the velocity in the larger section is $v_1 = 2 \text{ m/s}$, what is the velocity in the smaller section?
problems.eli5: By continuity, A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2. Since A = πD²/4, the π/4 cancels: D_1² v_1 = D_2² v_2. So v_2 = v_1 × (D_1/D_2)² = 2 × (300/150)² = 2 × 4 = 8 m/s. The 4 m/s choice uses the diameter ratio to the first power (2×2=4). The 16 m/s choice squares the diameter ratio twice. The 1 m/s choice reverses the ratio.
problems.hint: Velocity ratio equals the SQUARE of the diameter ratio (since area goes as D²).
traps: Using the diameter ratio to the first power instead of squaring it — gives 4 m/s
Inverting the ratio (D_2/D_1) — gives 0.5 m/s or 1 m/s

problems.statement: Water flows through a horizontal pipe that narrows from $D_1 = 200 \text{ mm}$ to $D_2 = 100 \text{ mm}$. At section 1, the pressure is $P_1 = 250 \text{ kPa}$ and the velocity is $v_1 = 1.5 \text{ m/s}$. Using $\rho = 1{,}000 \text{ kg/m}^3$, what is the pressure at section 2? Assume no friction.
problems.eli5: Two steps: continuity first, then Bernoulli. From continuity, v_2 = 1.5 × (200/100)² = 6.0 m/s. For a horizontal pipe (z_1 = z_2), Bernoulli gives P_2 = P_1 + ρ/2 × (v_1² – v_2²) = 250,000 + 500 × (2.25 – 36) = 250,000 – 16,875 = 233,125 Pa ≈ 233 kPa. Pressure drops because velocity increases — that’s Bernoulli’s principle. The 250 kPa option assumes no pressure change. The 268 kPa option adds instead of subtracting. The 214 kPa option over-estimates the velocity.
problems.hint: Use continuity to find v_2 first, then apply Bernoulli with z_1 = z_2 (horizontal pipe). Pressure drops where velocity increases.
traps: Forgetting to use continuity first — you need v_2 before applying Bernoulli
Adding the velocity term instead of subtracting — pressure should DROP where velocity increases
Forgetting to square the velocities in the kinetic energy terms

problems.statement: A large open tank has a water surface at elevation $z_1 = 10 \text{ m}$. A small nozzle at the bottom discharges to the atmosphere at elevation $z_2 = 0 \text{ m}$. Neglecting friction and the surface velocity, what is the jet velocity at the nozzle? Use $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$.
problems.eli5: This is Torricelli’s theorem — a direct result of Bernoulli. Both pressures are atmospheric (open tank, discharge to atmosphere), so they cancel. Surface velocity is negligible, so v_1 ≈ 0. Bernoulli reduces to z_1 = v_2²/(2g), giving v_2 = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 10) = √196.2 = 14.0 m/s. The 9.9 m/s choice uses √(gh) instead of √(2gh) — forgot the 2. The 19.8 m/s choice uses √(2)·√(2gh) (an extra factor of √2). The 4.43 m/s choice uses √(2g) without h.
problems.hint: When both surfaces are at atmospheric pressure and the tank surface velocity is negligible, Bernoulli simplifies to Torricelli’s theorem: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$.
traps: Forgetting the factor of 2 under the square root — using √(gh) instead of √(2gh)
Not recognizing that both pressures cancel when both sides are open to atmosphere
Including the surface velocity when the tank is large (it’s negligible)

fluid-mechanics/pipe-flow-head-loss.name: Pipe Flow & Head Loss
fluid-mechanics/pipe-flow-head-loss.application: Civil engineers size water mains, sewage force mains, and fire protection systems by computing head loss. The Darcy-Weisbach equation gives friction head loss in any pipe, while the Hazen-Williams equation is the shortcut for water-only systems. The Reynolds number tells you if flow is laminar or turbulent — which determines whether you read the Moody diagram for the friction factor or use the laminar formula directly. On the FE, expect problems that require computing head loss, finding the friction factor from the Moody diagram, or comparing flow regimes.

content.body: Once you have velocity from continuity and pressure from Bernoulli, the next question is: how much energy does friction steal? That’s head loss.
Reynolds Number
Flow regime depends on Reynolds number: $Re < 2{,}100$ is laminar, $Re > 10{,}000$ is fully turbulent, and $2{,}100 < Re < 10{,}000$ is transitional. Most civil engineering pipe flows are turbulent.
Darcy-Weisbach Equation

The friction factor $f$ depends on Reynolds number and relative roughness $\varepsilon/D$. For laminar flow, $f = 64/Re$. For turbulent flow, read $f$ from the Moody diagram (provided in the handbook).
Minor Losses
Fittings, valves, entrances, and expansions cause additional head losses. The loss coefficient $C$ is provided in the problem. Total head loss = major loss (friction) + sum of minor losses.
Hazen-Williams (Water Only)

Where $k_1 = 0.849$ (SI) or $1.318$ (USCS), $C$ is the roughness coefficient, $R_H$ is hydraulic radius, and $S$ is the slope of the energy grade line. This is an empirical formula used specifically for water.
The Moody diagram gives the Darcy friction factor $f$. Some textbooks use the Fanning friction factor $f_F = f/4$. The FE handbook uses Darcy — don’t divide by 4.
For laminar flow, f = 64/Re — no Moody diagram needed. For turbulent flow, you MUST use the Moody diagram or the Colebrook equation. Mixing these up is a common exam mistake.

problems.statement: Water at 20°C ($\nu = 1.003 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2/\text{s}$) flows through a $D = 0.1 \text{ m}$ pipe at $v = 2 \text{ m/s}$. What is the Reynolds number, and is the flow laminar or turbulent?
problems.eli5: Re = vD/ν = 2 × 0.1 / 1.003×10^-6 = 0.2 / 1.003×10^-6 = 199,400. Since 199,400 >> 10,000, the flow is fully turbulent. The Re = 1,994 choice uses D = 0.001 m (didn’t realize D is already in meters). The Re = 19,940 choice uses D = 0.01 m. The Re = 199,400 — laminar choice gets the right Re but misidentifies the flow regime.
problems.hint: Re = vD/ν. Compare your result to the thresholds: < 2,100 is laminar, > 10,000 is turbulent.

steps.text: Since $Re = 199{,}400 > 10{,}000$, the flow is fully turbulent.

traps: Using the wrong diameter units — if given in mm, must convert to meters
Confusing laminar/turbulent thresholds — Re > 4,000 (some refs) vs. Re > 10,000 (fully turbulent)

problems.statement: Water flows at $v = 3 \text{ m/s}$ through a $D = 0.2 \text{ m}$, $L = 100 \text{ m}$ pipe with a Darcy friction factor $f = 0.02$. What is the friction head loss? Use $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$.
problems.eli5: Straight Darcy-Weisbach: h_f = f × L/D × v²/(2g) = 0.02 × 100/0.2 × 3²/(2×9.81) = 0.02 × 500 × 0.4587 = 10 × 0.4587 = 4.587 m ≈ 4.59 m. The 9.17 m choice doubles the answer (maybe using L/D = 1000 by error). The 45.9 m choice uses L/D = 5000 (used D = 0.02). The 0.459 m choice uses L/D = 50 (used D = 2).
problems.hint: Plug directly into Darcy-Weisbach. Watch the units — L and D must be in the same units.
traps: Using the Fanning friction factor (Darcy/4) instead of the Darcy factor — answer would be 4× too small
Miscomputing L/D by using inconsistent units for pipe length and diameter

problems.statement: Water flows at $v = 2.5 \text{ m/s}$ through a pipe system with a Darcy-Weisbach friction head loss of $h_{f} = 3.2 \text{ m}$. The system also includes two $90\degree$ elbows (each with $C = 0.9$) and one globe valve ($C = 10.0$). What is the total head loss? Use $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$.
problems.eli5: Total head loss = major (friction) + minor (fittings). Velocity head = v²/(2g) = 2.5²/19.62 = 0.3184 m. Sum of minor loss coefficients: 2×0.9 + 10.0 = 11.8. Minor losses = 11.8 × 0.3184 = 3.757 m. Total = 3.2 + 3.757 = 6.96 m. The 3.76 m option is the minor loss alone, forgetting to add the 3.2 m friction loss. The 3.20 m option ignores minor losses entirely. The 10.16 m option overcounts the fitting coefficients.
problems.hint: Add up all the minor loss coefficients (ΣC), multiply by v²/(2g), then add the major (friction) head loss.
traps: Forgetting to include minor losses — only reporting the friction head loss
Counting the elbows only once instead of twice
Using the Fanning friction factor when the problem gives the Darcy factor

fluid-mechanics/momentum-equation.name: Momentum Equation
fluid-mechanics/momentum-equation.application: Civil engineers use the momentum equation to compute forces at pipe bends, tees, and reducers — which is how you design thrust blocks and restrained joints for water mains. It also gives the force on a bridge pier from river flow and the reaction force from a fire hose nozzle. On the FE, momentum problems typically involve a pipe bend at some angle, where you solve for the force components using the impulse-momentum principle.

content.body: The momentum equation relates forces to changes in fluid momentum. It’s Newton’s second law applied to a control volume of moving fluid.
General Momentum Equation

The net external force on the control volume equals the rate of change of momentum: (momentum out) minus (momentum in). For steady, incompressible flow with one inlet and one outlet: $\Sigma F = \rho Q (v_2 - v_1)$ in each direction.
Forces on a Pipe Bend

content.latex: P_1 A_1 - P_2 A_2 \cos\alpha - F_x = Q\rho(v_2 \cos\alpha - v_1)
content.label: x-direction (horizontal)

content.body: Here $\alpha$ is the bend angle, $F_x$ and $F_y$ are the force components the bend exerts on the fluid (the force on the bend is equal and opposite), and $W$ is the weight of fluid in the control volume.
Fixed Blade / Deflector
For a jet striking a fixed flat plate ($\alpha = 90\degree$), $F = \rho Q v$ since the deflected velocity has no component in the original direction.

Set up a clear coordinate system FIRST. Sketch the control volume with arrows for inlet velocity, exit velocity, and the forces (pressure and reaction). Then write the momentum equation for each direction.
Don’t forget the pressure forces! A pipe bend has pressure on both the inlet and outlet faces. The momentum equation includes BOTH the pressure forces and the reaction force on the bend.

problems.statement: A horizontal water jet with velocity $v = 15 \text{ m/s}$ and cross-sectional area $A = 0.01 \text{ m}^2$ strikes a fixed, vertical flat plate. What is the force on the plate? Use $\rho = 1{,}000 \text{ kg/m}^3$.
problems.eli5: A jet hitting a flat plate (90° deflection) has its x-momentum completely destroyed. F = ρQv = ρAv² = 1,000 × 0.01 × 15² = 1,000 × 0.01 × 225 = 2,250 N. The 150 N choice forgets to square the velocity (uses ρAv). The 4,500 N choice doubles the force (perhaps thinking about a 180° reversal). The 225 N choice uses A = 0.001.
problems.hint: For a flat plate perpendicular to the jet, the exit velocity has no component in the jet’s original direction, so F = ρAv².

steps.text: Force on the plate (all x-momentum absorbed):

traps: Using F = ρAv instead of ρAv² — forgetting the velocity appears in both Q and the momentum term
Doubling the force — that’s for a 180° reversal, not a 90° flat plate

problems.statement: Water ($\rho = 1{,}000 \text{ kg/m}^3$) flows through a $90\degree$ horizontal pipe bend. The pipe diameter is $D = 0.3 \text{ m}$ throughout, the velocity is $v = 4 \text{ m/s}$, and the pressure is $P = 200 \text{ kPa}$ (assumed constant through the bend). What is the magnitude of the resultant force on the bend?
problems.eli5: For a 90° bend with constant diameter, v_1 = v_2 = v and P_1 = P_2 = P. Set x as the inlet direction, y as the outlet direction. In x: F_x = PA + ρQv (momentum in, nothing goes out in x). In y: F_y = PA + ρQv (momentum out, nothing comes in from y). A = π(0.3)²/4 = 0.0707 m². Q = 0.0707 × 4 = 0.2827 m³/s. PA = 200,000 × 0.0707 = 14,140 N. ρQv = 1,000 × 0.2827 × 4 = 1,131 N. So F_x = F_y = 14,140 + 1,131 = 15,271 N. Resultant = √(F_x² + F_y²) = 15,271√2 = 21,593 N ≈ 21.6 kN. The 14.1 kN choice is just PA = 14,140 N — a single component, forgetting both the momentum term and the √2 resultant factor. The 28.3 kN choice is 2·PA = 28,280 N (uses 2PA instead of the correct PA√2 resultant). The 1.01 kN choice keeps only the momentum term (≈ρQv ~ 1.1 kN), dropping the dominant pressure force PA.
problems.hint: For a 90° bend with the same pipe diameter, both F_x and F_y have the same magnitude. The resultant force is F√2.
problems.handbookFormula: P_1 A_1 - P_2 A_2 \cos\alpha - F_x = Q\rho(v_2 \cos\alpha - v_1)
traps: Forgetting the pressure forces — they’re often larger than the momentum forces
Reporting F_x or F_y instead of the resultant — for a 90° bend you must combine them vectorially
Getting signs wrong in the momentum equation

problems.statement: A fire hose nozzle reduces from $D_1 = 100 \text{ mm}$ to $D_2 = 25 \text{ mm}$. Water ($\rho = 1{,}000 \text{ kg/m}^3$) enters at $v_1 = 2 \text{ m/s}$ and $P_1 = 350 \text{ kPa}$. The jet discharges to the atmosphere ($P_2 = 0$ gauge). What is the axial force required to hold the nozzle? Neglect the weight of water in the nozzle.
problems.eli5: First, continuity: v_2 = v_1(D_1/D_2)² = 2 × (100/25)² = 2 × 16 = 32 m/s. A_1 = π(0.1)²/4 = 0.00785 m². Q = A_1 v_1 = 0.00785 × 2 = 0.01571 m³/s. Momentum equation in x: P_1 A_1 - F = ρQ(v_2 - v_1). So F = P_1 A_1 - ρQ(v_2 - v_1) = 350,000 × 0.00785 - 1,000 × 0.01571 × (32 - 2) = 2,747.5 - 471.3 = 2,278 N. The nozzle holder must push forward (against the flow direction) because the pressure force on the inlet face exceeds the momentum change.
problems.hint: Apply continuity to find v_2, then the momentum equation including the inlet pressure force (the exit is atmospheric).
traps: Forgetting the pressure force on the inlet face — only accounting for momentum change
Not using continuity to find the exit velocity first
Confusing the force direction — the holder pushes forward (toward the nozzle), opposing the hose reaction

fluid-mechanics/flow-measurement.name: Flow Measurement
fluid-mechanics/flow-measurement.application: Civil engineers measure flow to monitor water treatment, calibrate hydraulic models, and verify stormwater controls. Pitot tubes measure point velocity from stagnation pressure. Venturi meters and orifice plates measure flow rate in closed conduits using the Bernoulli principle with a calibration coefficient. On the FE, expect problems using the Pitot tube equation or computing flow through a venturi or orifice meter.

content.body: Flow measurement devices exploit Bernoulli’s equation — they create a measurable pressure difference that correlates with velocity or flow rate.
Pitot Tube

A Pitot tube measures stagnation pressure $P_0$ by pointing directly into the flow. The difference between stagnation and static pressure $P_s$ gives velocity. This is just Bernoulli with one velocity set to zero.
Venturi Meter

content.latex: Q = C_v A_2 \sqrt{\frac{2g\left(\frac{P_1 - P_2}{\gamma} + z_1 - z_2\right)}{1 - \left(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\right)^2}}
content.label: Venturi meter flow rate

content.body: The venturi gradually contracts and then expands, creating a throat with lower pressure. The coefficient $C_v$ accounts for real-fluid effects and is typically 0.95–0.99 for a well-designed venturi.
Orifice Meter

An orifice plate is a sharp-edged restriction. The discharge coefficient $C$ combines the contraction coefficient $C_c$ and velocity coefficient $C_v$. Typical values: sharp-edged orifice $C_c = 0.62$, $C_v = 0.98$.
All three devices use the same underlying principle — Bernoulli. The Pitot measures velocity at a point; the venturi and orifice measure total flow rate through a pipe.
On the FE, you’ll typically be given the coefficient values. Don’t memorize them — just know where they go in the formula.

problems.statement: A Pitot tube in a water stream reads a stagnation pressure of $P_0 = 125 \text{ kPa}$ and a static pressure of $P_s = 100 \text{ kPa}$. What is the flow velocity? Use $\rho = 1{,}000 \text{ kg/m}^3$.
problems.eli5: v = √[2(P_0 – P_s)/ρ] = √[2 × 25,000/1,000] = √50 = 7.07 m/s. The pressure difference is 125 – 100 = 25 kPa = 25,000 Pa. The 5.0 m/s choice forgets the factor of 2 under the root: √(25,000/1,000) = √25 = 5.0. The 0.224 m/s choice fails to convert kPa to Pa, using 25 instead of 25,000: √(2×25/1,000) = √0.05 = 0.224. The 50 m/s choice mis-scales the units (it is not the result of any correct partial step).
problems.hint: Convert kPa to Pa before plugging into the formula. Don’t forget the factor of 2.
traps: Forgetting to convert kPa to Pa — off by a factor of √1000
Dropping the factor of 2 in the numerator — gives v = 5.0 m/s

problems.statement: A horizontal venturi meter has an upstream diameter of $D_1 = 200 \text{ mm}$ and a throat diameter of $D_2 = 100 \text{ mm}$. The pressure difference is $P_1 - P_2 = 40 \text{ kPa}$. If the velocity coefficient is $C_v = 0.98$, what is the flow rate? Use $\gamma = 9{,}810 \text{ N/m}^3$ and $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$.
problems.eli5: A_1 = π(0.2)²/4 = 0.03142 m². A_2 = π(0.1)²/4 = 0.007854 m². Pressure head = ΔP/γ = 40,000/9,810 = 4.077 m. Area ratio term: 1 – (A_2/A_1)² = 1 – (0.007854/0.03142)² = 1 – 0.0625 = 0.9375. Under the root: 2g × 4.077/0.9375 = 19.62 × 4.348 = 85.31. So √85.31 = 9.236. Q = 0.98 × 0.007854 × 9.236 = 0.0711 m³/s. The 0.0721 m³/s choice omits the velocity coefficient (drops C_v). The 0.0180 m³/s choice uses A_2/A_1 to the first power instead of squared in the denominator. The 0.282 m³/s choice mistakenly uses A_1 instead of A_2 as the metering area.
problems.hint: Convert the pressure difference to head (ΔP/γ) and use the throat area A_2 in the formula. Don’t forget the area ratio correction in the denominator.
problems.handbookFormula: Q = C_v A_2 \sqrt{\frac{2g\left(\frac{P_1 - P_2}{\gamma} + z_1 - z_2\right)}{1 - \left(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\right)^2}}
traps: Forgetting to square the area ratio in the denominator
Using the upstream area A_1 instead of the throat area A_2
Forgetting to convert the pressure difference to head (ΔP/γ)

problems.statement: An orifice plate with a $50 \text{ mm}$ opening is installed in a $100 \text{ mm}$ horizontal pipe. The measured pressure drop across the orifice is $\Delta P = 30 \text{ kPa}$. If the orifice coefficient is $C = 0.62$ and the area ratio correction $1 - (A_0/A_1)^2 \approx 0.9375$, what is the flow rate? Use $\gamma = 9{,}810 \text{ N/m}^3$.
problems.eli5: A_0 = π(0.05)²/4 = 0.001963 m². ΔP/γ = 30,000/9,810 = 3.058 m. Under the root: 2g × 3.058 / 0.9375 = 19.62 × 3.262 = 64.02. √64.02 = 8.00. Q = 0.62 × 0.001963 × 8.00 = 0.00974 m³/s. The 0.01539 m³/s distractor uses C = 1.0. The 0.0382 m³/s distractor uses the pipe area instead of the orifice area. The 0.00591 m³/s distractor uses C = 0.62 but drops the area ratio correction.
problems.hint: Same formula structure as the venturi, but with the orifice area A_0 and the orifice coefficient C. The area ratio correction will be given.
traps: Using the pipe diameter instead of the orifice diameter for the area — gives 4× too large
Forgetting the discharge coefficient C — gives the ideal flow rate, not the actual
Not accounting for the area ratio in the denominator

fluid-mechanics/dimensional-analysis-sim.name: Dimensional Analysis & Similitude
fluid-mechanics/dimensional-analysis-sim.application: Civil engineers use dimensional analysis when building physical models — a scale model of a spillway in a hydraulics lab or a wind tunnel model of a bridge deck. The Buckingham Pi theorem tells you how many dimensionless groups exist. Similitude rules (Reynolds, Froude) tell you which parameters to match so model results predict full-scale behavior. On the FE, expect problems using the Pi theorem to count dimensionless groups or applying Froude similitude to scale model results.

content.body: Dimensional analysis reduces the number of variables in a problem by grouping them into dimensionless parameters. Similitude then uses those parameters to relate model behavior to prototype behavior.
Buckingham Pi Theorem
Where $n$ is the number of variables and $r$ is the number of basic dimensions (typically M, L, T for mechanical problems). The result $k$ is how many independent dimensionless π-groups you can form.
Key Dimensionless Numbers

Reynolds number governs problems where viscous forces dominate (pipe flow, drag on submerged objects). Froude number governs problems where gravity forces dominate (open-channel flow, spillways, ship hulls).
Similitude Rules

For dynamic similarity, the model and prototype must have the same relevant dimensionless numbers. In civil engineering, this usually means matching either Reynolds or Froude — rarely both at the same scale.
For open-channel models (spillways, weirs, rivers), match the Froude number. For closed-conduit models (pipe fittings, valve testing), match the Reynolds number.
The Buckingham Pi theorem is quick points on the FE: count variables, count dimensions, subtract. Don’t overthink it — it’s just arithmetic.

problems.statement: A fluid flow problem involves 7 variables expressed in terms of 3 basic dimensions (M, L, T). How many independent dimensionless groups can be formed?
problems.eli5: Buckingham Pi: k = n – r = 7 – 3 = 4 dimensionless groups. That’s it. The choice "3" subtracts one too many. The choice "7" uses n alone. The choice "21" multiplies 7 × 3.
problems.hint: Apply the Buckingham Pi theorem: number of π-groups = number of variables minus number of basic dimensions.

steps.latex: n = 7 \text{ variables}, \quad r = 3 \text{ dimensions (M, L, T)}

traps: Confusing variables with dimensions — n is the number of physical variables, r is the number of base dimensions
Including duplicate or dependent variables in the count

problems.statement: A 1:25 scale model of a spillway is built in a laboratory. Using Froude similitude (same fluid in model and prototype), if the prototype flow velocity is $v_p = 10 \text{ m/s}$, what velocity should the model operate at?
problems.eli5: Froude similitude: Fr_m = Fr_p, so v_m/√(g l_m) = v_p/√(g l_p). Since g is the same and the fluids are the same, v_m = v_p × √(l_m/l_p) = 10 × √(1/25) = 10 × 1/5 = 2.0 m/s. The 0.4 m/s option divides by 25 (uses the length ratio directly, not the square root). The 50 m/s option multiplies by 5. The 10 m/s option uses the same velocity (no scaling).
problems.hint: For Froude similitude, velocity scales as the square root of the length ratio: $v_m/v_p = \sqrt{L_m/L_p}$.
traps: Dividing by the scale factor directly (25) instead of by the square root of the scale factor (5)
Using Reynolds similitude instead of Froude — open-channel flows require Froude matching

problems.statement: A 1:10 scale model of a submerged pipeline is tested in the same fluid as the prototype. Using Reynolds similitude, if the prototype velocity is $v_p = 3 \text{ m/s}$, what model velocity is required?
problems.eli5: Reynolds similitude: Re_m = Re_p. With the same fluid (ν_m = ν_p), we get v_m l_m = v_p l_p, so v_m = v_p × (l_p/l_m) = 3 × 10 = 30 m/s. The model must move FASTER because it’s smaller — to maintain the same Reynolds number, velocity must increase inversely with length. This is why Reynolds similitude is often impractical at small scales. The 0.3 m/s option divides by 10 (confuses the ratio direction). The 3 m/s option uses the same velocity. The 0.949 m/s option divides by the square root of the ratio (confusing with Froude).
problems.hint: Reynolds similitude with the same fluid: v_m = v_p × (L_p/L_m). Smaller model means higher velocity.
traps: Inverting the length ratio — smaller model needs HIGHER velocity, not lower
Confusing Reynolds similitude with Froude similitude — Reynolds uses the linear ratio, Froude uses the square root
Applying Froude scaling (v_m = v_p√(1/10) = 0.949) instead of Reynolds scaling

surveying/angles-distances-bearings.name: Angles, Distances & Bearings
surveying/angles-distances-bearings.application: Every civil engineering project starts with a survey — measuring angles and distances to establish property boundaries, construction staking, and control points. You need to convert between bearings (N 45° E) and azimuths (045°), and understand how angles are measured in the field. On the FE, expect problems converting bearings to azimuths, computing horizontal distances from slope measurements, and interpreting survey data.

content.body: Surveying is all about precisely locating points. Two fundamental measurements — angles and distances — define every point on a job site.
Bearings vs. Azimuths
A bearing is measured from North or South, toward East or West, and is always between 0° and 90°. An azimuth is measured clockwise from North, ranging from 0° to 360°.
Conversion rules: NE quadrant — azimuth = bearing angle. SE quadrant — azimuth = 180° – bearing angle. SW quadrant — azimuth = 180° + bearing angle. NW quadrant — azimuth = 360° – bearing angle.
Horizontal Distance from Slope
Where $SD$ is the slope distance (measured along the ground) and $\alpha$ is the vertical angle from horizontal. EDM (electronic distance measurement) instruments measure slope distance directly.
Interior Angles
For a closed polygon with $n$ sides, the interior angles must sum to $(n-2) \times 180\degree$. This is a quick check for survey closures.
Think of bearings as compass directions — N 30° E means "face north, rotate 30° toward east." Azimuths always start at north and go clockwise, like a clock with north at 12.
When converting S 45° W to an azimuth, don’t subtract from 360°. It’s in the SW quadrant: azimuth = 180° + 45° = 225°.

problems.statement: Convert the bearing N $52\degree$ E to an azimuth.
problems.eli5: In the NE quadrant, the azimuth equals the bearing angle directly. N 52° E = azimuth 52°. The 128° option subtracts from 180° (SE conversion applied incorrectly). The 308° option subtracts from 360° (NW conversion). The 232° option adds 180° (SW conversion).
problems.hint: In the NE quadrant, azimuths and bearing angles are the same value.

steps.text: For bearings in the NE quadrant:

traps: Applying the wrong quadrant conversion formula
Confusing which quadrants add vs. subtract from 180° or 360°

problems.statement: A total station measures a slope distance of $SD = 250.00 \text{ m}$ at a vertical angle of $\alpha = 8\degree$ above horizontal. What is the horizontal distance?
problems.eli5: HD = SD × cos α = 250 × cos 8° = 250 × 0.9903 = 247.56 m. The horizontal distance is always less than or equal to the slope distance. The 250.00 m choice assumes no correction needed. The 34.79 m choice is the vertical distance (SD × sin 8°). The 252.46 m choice divides by cos instead of multiplying.
problems.hint: Horizontal distance = slope distance times cosine of the vertical angle. The result should be slightly less than the slope distance.
traps: Using sine instead of cosine — gives the vertical distance, not horizontal
Dividing by cosine instead of multiplying — gives a value larger than SD

problems.statement: A closed traverse has 5 sides. The measured interior angles are $108\degree$, $120\degree$, $95\degree$, $132\degree$, and $84\degree$. What is the angular misclosure?
problems.eli5: For a 5-sided polygon, the angles should sum to (5 – 2) × 180° = 540°. Actual sum = 108 + 120 + 95 + 132 + 84 = 539°. Misclosure = measured – theoretical = 539 – 540 = –1°. The survey is 1° short. The −5° distractor reflects a formula error (using n instead of n − 2). The +1° distractor gets the sign wrong (it computes theoretical − measured). The 0° distractor assumes the traverse closes perfectly.
problems.hint: Sum the measured angles and compare to the theoretical sum: (n – 2) × 180°.
traps: Using n × 180° instead of (n – 2) × 180° for the theoretical sum
Getting the sign of the misclosure backwards
Arithmetic errors when summing five angles — double-check the addition

surveying/leveling.name: Differential Leveling
surveying/leveling.application: Civil engineers use differential leveling to establish elevations for drainage design, building pad grades, road profiles, and sewer inverts. A level run gives you the elevation difference between benchmarks, and closing the loop back to a known point tells you the accuracy of your survey. On the FE, expect problems computing elevations using the Height of Instrument (HI) method, identifying BS and FS readings, and checking level loop closures.

content.body: Differential leveling determines elevation differences by reading a graduated rod through a level instrument. The key is the Height of Instrument (HI) method.
Height of Instrument Method
Backsight (BS) is the rod reading on a point of known elevation — it’s always added. Foresight (FS) is the rod reading on the point whose elevation you want — it’s always subtracted from HI.
Level Loop Closure

content.label: Allowable closure (M in miles or km)

content.body: Where $C$ is a constant that depends on the survey order (e.g., 0.024 ft for second-order leveling) and $M$ is the total distance in miles (or km, depending on the standard). If the misclosure exceeds the allowable error, the level run must be repeated.
Memory trick: BS is on a KNOWN point (you’re looking BACK at what you know). FS is on the UNKNOWN point (you’re looking FORWARD to where you’re going). BS is added, FS is subtracted.
A turning point (TP) is both a foresight AND a backsight — you read FS from the old setup, move the level, then read BS from the new setup. Don’t confuse the two readings.

problems.statement: A benchmark (BM) has an elevation of $100.00 \text{ m}$. The backsight reading on BM is $1.52 \text{ m}$ and the foresight reading on point A is $2.35 \text{ m}$. What is the elevation of point A?
problems.eli5: HI = 100.00 + 1.52 = 101.52 m. Elev_A = HI – FS = 101.52 – 2.35 = 99.17 m. Point A is lower because the foresight rod reading is larger (the rod sits lower). The 100.83 m choice swaps BS and FS (100.00 – 1.52 + 2.35). The 103.87 m choice adds both BS and FS (100 + 1.52 + 2.35). The 96.13 m choice subtracts both (100 – 1.52 – 2.35).
problems.hint: HI = known elevation + backsight. New elevation = HI – foresight.
traps: Swapping backsight and foresight — BS is added, FS is subtracted, never the reverse
Adding both readings instead of adding BS and subtracting FS

problems.statement: Starting at BM-1 (elevation $250.00 \text{ ft}$), a surveyor records: BS = $4.62$ on BM-1, FS = $3.18$ on TP-1, BS = $5.21$ on TP-1, FS = $1.95$ on point B. What is the elevation of point B?
problems.eli5: Work through it step by step. HI_1 = 250.00 + 4.62 = 254.62. Elev_TP1 = 254.62 – 3.18 = 251.44. HI_2 = 251.44 + 5.21 = 256.65. Elev_B = 256.65 – 1.95 = 254.70 ft. The 251.44 ft choice gives the TP-1 elevation (stopped too early). The 245.30 ft choice reverses all operations. The 248.56 ft choice uses the wrong HI.
problems.hint: Process each instrument setup separately. At each setup: HI = elev + BS, then new elev = HI – FS.
traps: Using the original HI for the second setup instead of recalculating from the turning point
Stopping at the turning point elevation and reporting it as the answer

problems.statement: A level loop starts and ends at BM-A (known elevation $500.00 \text{ ft}$). After running the loop, the computed elevation of BM-A is $499.97 \text{ ft}$. The total loop distance is $4 \text{ miles}$. If the allowable error is $C\sqrt{M}$ with $C = 0.05 \text{ ft}$, does the survey meet the tolerance?
problems.eli5: Misclosure = |499.97 – 500.00| = 0.03 ft. Allowable = 0.05√4 = 0.05 × 2.0 = 0.10 ft. Since 0.03 < 0.10, the survey meets the tolerance. The "allowable (0.01 ft)" option uses C = 0.05/√4 = 0.025 and then rounds incorrectly. The "allowable (0.20 ft)" option uses M² instead of √M. The "misclosure (0.30 ft)" option reads the misclosure as 0.30.
problems.hint: Compute misclosure = |computed – known|. Compare to the allowable error = C√M.
traps: Using M directly instead of √M — gives an allowable of 0.20 ft
Forgetting the absolute value of the misclosure
Confusing the constant C with the total allowable error

surveying/traverse-computations.name: Traverse Computations
surveying/traverse-computations.application: Civil engineers run traverses to establish control points on job sites and verify property boundary closures. You compute latitudes (north-south) and departures (east-west) for each course, check that the traverse closes, and distribute any error using the compass rule. A traverse that doesn’t close within tolerance means the survey data can’t be trusted for design or legal purposes. On the FE, expect problems computing latitudes and departures, finding closure error, and applying the compass rule adjustment.

content.body: A traverse is a series of connected survey lines (courses). Each course has a length and direction. Computing latitudes and departures converts these into a coordinate system.
Latitudes & Departures
Where $L$ is the course length and $\theta$ is the azimuth. Latitudes are positive northward, negative southward. Departures are positive eastward, negative westward.
Closure Error
For a closed traverse, the sum of all latitudes and the sum of all departures should each be zero. The precision ratio is typically expressed as 1:N (e.g., 1:10,000).
Compass Rule Adjustment
The compass rule distributes the closure error proportionally to each course length. Apply the same formula to departures using $E_D$.
Quick check: if the sum of latitudes is positive, the traverse drifted north. If the sum of departures is positive, it drifted east. The corrections push back in the opposite direction.
The precision ratio is expressed as a fraction with 1 in the numerator: if linear error = 0.05 ft and total length = 500 ft, the precision is 1:10,000.

problems.statement: A traverse course has a length of $L = 200 \text{ m}$ and an azimuth of $\theta = 60\degree$. What are the latitude and departure?
problems.eli5: Lat = L cos θ = 200 cos 60° = 200 × 0.5 = 100.0 m. Dep = L sin θ = 200 sin 60° = 200 × 0.866 = 173.2 m. Both are positive because azimuth 60° is in the NE quadrant. The Lat = 173.2 m, Dep = 100.0 m option swaps cosine and sine. The Lat = 141.4 m, Dep = 141.4 m option uses 45° values. The Lat = 100.0 m, Dep = -173.2 m option gets the departure sign wrong.
problems.hint: Latitude = L cos(azimuth), Departure = L sin(azimuth). Check the quadrant for signs.
traps: Swapping sine and cosine — latitude uses cosine (N-S), departure uses sine (E-W)
Getting the sign wrong for the quadrant — NE quadrant has both positive

problems.statement: A closed traverse has the following sums: $\Sigma\text{Lat} = +0.08 \text{ m}$, $\Sigma\text{Dep} = -0.06 \text{ m}$. The total traverse length is $1{,}000 \text{ m}$. What is the precision ratio?
problems.eli5: Linear error = √(0.08² + 0.06²) = √(0.0064 + 0.0036) = √0.01 = 0.10 m. Precision = 0.10/1,000 = 1/10,000 = 1:10,000. The 1:12,500 option uses only the latitude error. The 1:7,143 option uses 0.14 as linear error (0.08 + 0.06). The 1:100,000 option squares the precision ratio.
problems.hint: Find the linear closure error using the Pythagorean theorem, then divide by the total traverse length.
traps: Adding the errors instead of using the Pythagorean theorem (0.08 + 0.06 = 0.14, not 0.10)
Using only one error component instead of both

problems.statement: In the same traverse ($\Sigma L = 1{,}000 \text{ m}$, $E_L = +0.08 \text{ m}$), one course has a length of $250 \text{ m}$. What is the compass rule latitude correction for this course?
problems.eli5: Compass rule: correction = –E_L × (L_i / ΣL) = –0.08 × (250/1000) = –0.08 × 0.25 = –0.020 m. The correction is negative because the traverse drifted north (positive E_L), so we correct southward. The -0.002 m option divides by 10,000 instead of 1,000. The +0.020 m option gets the sign wrong. The -0.080 m option applies the full error to this one course.
problems.hint: The compass rule distributes error proportionally to course length. The sign of the correction is opposite to the error.
traps: Forgetting the negative sign — the correction opposes the error direction
Applying the full error to one course instead of distributing proportionally
Using the course count instead of the course length ratio for distribution

surveying/area-computations.name: Area Computations
surveying/area-computations.application: Civil engineers compute areas for property plats, right-of-way acquisitions, impervious surface calculations in stormwater reports, and wetland delineation boundaries. The coordinate method (also called the shoelace formula) gives exact areas from survey coordinates. The trapezoidal rule and Simpson’s 1/3 rule approximate areas from equally spaced measurements. On the FE, expect problems using the coordinate method to compute the area of a polygon from its vertex coordinates.

content.body: Three methods appear on the FE for computing irregular areas. The coordinate method is exact for polygons; the trapezoidal and Simpson’s rules are approximations for curved boundaries.
Area by Coordinates (Shoelace Method)
List the coordinates in order around the polygon, then cross-multiply adjacent pairs. Sum the products and take half the absolute value. This works for any polygon, regardless of shape.
Trapezoidal Rule

content.latex: A = w\left(\frac{h_1 + h_n}{2} + h_2 + h_3 + \cdots + h_{n-1}\right)
content.label: Trapezoidal rule

content.body: Where $w$ is the common interval between measurements and $h_i$ are the offset distances. The first and last offsets are averaged; all others are added at full value.
Simpson’s 1/3 Rule
Simpson’s rule requires an odd number of measurements (even number of intervals). It’s more accurate than the trapezoidal rule for curved boundaries because it fits parabolic arcs.
For the coordinate method, set up a table: list each vertex’s (x, y), then compute the cross products. Don’t forget to close the polygon by pairing the last point with the first.
Simpson’s 1/3 rule only works when you have an ODD number of measurements (even number of intervals). If you have an even count, use the trapezoidal rule.

problems.statement: A triangle has vertices at A$(0, 0)$, B$(6, 0)$, and C$(3, 4)$. What is the area using the coordinate method?
problems.eli5: Cross products: (0×0 – 6×0) + (6×4 – 3×0) + (3×0 – 0×4) = 0 + 24 + 0 = 24... wait, let me redo: (x_A × y_B – x_B × y_A) + (x_B × y_C – x_C × y_B) + (x_C × y_A – x_A × y_C) = (0×0 – 6×0) + (6×4 – 3×0) + (3×0 – 0×4) = 0 + 24 + 0 = 24. Area = |24|/2 = 12. You can verify with base × height / 2 = 6 × 4 / 2 = 12. 24 sq units forgets to divide by 2. 6 sq units divides by 4 instead. 18 sq units uses 1.5 × sum.
problems.hint: Set up the cross products for each adjacent vertex pair, sum them, take the absolute value, and divide by 2.

steps.text: List vertices in order and compute cross products:

traps: Forgetting to divide by 2 — gives double the area
Getting the cross-product order wrong (x_i × y_{i+1} – x_{i+1} × y_i, not the reverse)

problems.statement: A quadrilateral has vertices at A$(0, 0)$, B$(10, 0)$, C$(8, 6)$, and D$(2, 5)$. What is the area by the coordinate method?
problems.eli5: Cross products: AB: (0)(0) – (10)(0) = 0. BC: (10)(6) – (8)(0) = 60. CD: (8)(5) – (2)(6) = 40 – 12 = 28. DA: (2)(0) – (0)(5) = 0. Sum = 0 + 60 + 28 + 0 = 88. Area = |88|/2 = 44. The 50 sq units option uses a rough rectangle approximation. The 88 sq units option forgets to divide by 2. The 22 sq units option divides by 4.
problems.hint: Four vertices means four cross-product pairs. Don’t forget to pair the last vertex back with the first to close the polygon.
traps: Forgetting to close the polygon — must pair last vertex with first vertex
Forgetting to divide by 2
Getting the subtraction order wrong in the cross products

problems.statement: A surveyor measures offsets from a baseline at $20 \text{ m}$ intervals. The offsets are: $0$, $8$, $12$, $10$, $0 \text{ m}$. What is the area using the trapezoidal rule?
problems.eli5: Trapezoidal rule: A = w[(h_1 + h_n)/2 + h_2 + h_3 + ... + h_{n-1}] = 20[(0 + 0)/2 + 8 + 12 + 10] = 20[0 + 30] = 600 m². The first and last offsets are 0, so their average is 0. The 480 m² choice mis-applies w/2 to all terms. The 800 m² choice uses Simpson’s coefficients incorrectly. The 300 m² choice divides the correct area by 2 again.
problems.hint: Average the first and last offsets, add all the middle offsets at full value, then multiply by the interval width.

steps.latex: A = w\left(\frac{h_1 + h_n}{2} + h_2 + h_3 + h_4\right)

traps: Averaging ALL offsets instead of just the first and last
Forgetting to multiply by the interval width w
Using Simpson’s coefficients (1, 4, 2, 4, 1) when the trapezoidal rule was specified

surveying/earthwork-volumes.name: Earthwork & Volume Computations
surveying/earthwork-volumes.application: Civil engineers compute earthwork volumes to estimate project costs, balance cut and fill quantities, and verify contractor pay quantities. The average end area method is the workhorse for road and site grading projects — you compute cross-section areas at each station, then multiply by the distance between stations to get volume. On the FE, expect problems computing volumes using the average end area or prismoidal formula.

content.body: Earthwork volumes answer the question: how much dirt needs to move? You slice the project into cross-sections and compute volumes between them.
Average End Area Method
Where $A_1$ and $A_2$ are the cross-sectional areas at adjacent stations and $L$ is the distance between them. This slightly overestimates volume for tapered sections.
Prismoidal Formula
Where $A_m$ is the area of the mid-section (at $L/2$). This is more accurate than average end area because it accounts for the taper. Think of it as Simpson’s rule applied to volumes.
Pyramid or Cone
Used when a cross-section tapers to a point — like a stockpile, borrow pit, or the end of a fill embankment.
The average end area method is more common in practice (and on the FE) because you rarely have mid-section data. The prismoidal formula gives a more accurate answer when you do.
Unit trap: if areas are in ft² and distance in ft, the volume is in ft³. Divide by 27 to convert to cubic yards for pay quantities.

problems.statement: Two adjacent cross-sections have areas of $A_1 = 120 \text{ ft}^2$ and $A_2 = 180 \text{ ft}^2$. The distance between stations is $L = 100 \text{ ft}$. What is the volume by the average end area method?
problems.eli5: V = L/2 × (A_1 + A_2) = 100/2 × (120 + 180) = 50 × 300 = 15,000 ft³. The 556 yd³ option converts to cubic yards (15,000/27 = 556) — right number but wrong unit for what was asked. The 30,000 ft³ option uses L instead of L/2. The 7,500 ft³ option divides by 4 instead of 2.
problems.hint: Average the two areas, then multiply by the distance between stations.
traps: Forgetting to divide L by 2 — doubles the volume
Confusing ft³ with yd³ — divide by 27 to convert

problems.statement: Three cross-sections are taken at stations 0, 50 ft, and 100 ft. The areas are $A_1 = 200 \text{ ft}^2$, $A_m = 350 \text{ ft}^2$, and $A_2 = 400 \text{ ft}^2$. What is the volume using the prismoidal formula?
problems.eli5: V = L/6 × (A_1 + 4A_m + A_2) = 100/6 × (200 + 4×350 + 400) = 16.667 × (200 + 1400 + 400) = 16.667 × 2000 = 33,333 ft³. The 31,667 ft³ choice is the simple average of all three areas times L: (200+350+400)/3 × 100 = 31,667. The 30,000 ft³ choice uses the average end area method (L/2 × (A_1+A_2) = 50 × 600 = 30,000). The 35,000 ft³ choice incorrectly multiplies the middle area by L (350 × 100 = 35,000).
problems.hint: The prismoidal formula weights the middle section by 4: V = L/6(A_1 + 4A_m + A_2). The total distance L is 100 ft, not 50.
traps: Using the average end area formula instead of the prismoidal formula
Forgetting the 4× coefficient on the mid-section area
Using L = 50 (half the distance) instead of the full distance between end sections

problems.statement:
A road project has the following station data. What is the total earthwork volume between stations 0+00 and 2+00? Use the average end area method.

Station 0+00: $A = 0 \text{ ft}^2$
Station 1+00: $A = 400 \text{ ft}^2$
Station 2+00: $A = 0 \text{ ft}^2$
problems.eli5: Two segments: 0+00 to 1+00 and 1+00 to 2+00. V_1 = 100/2 × (0 + 400) = 50 × 400 = 20,000 ft³. V_2 = 100/2 × (400 + 0) = 20,000 ft³. Total = 40,000 ft³. The 20,000 ft³ choice only computes one segment. The 80,000 ft³ choice uses L instead of L/2. The 13,333 ft³ choice uses the prismoidal formula by mistake.
problems.hint: Apply the average end area formula to each pair of adjacent stations, then sum the segment volumes.
traps: Only computing one segment and forgetting the other
Forgetting that station 1+00 means 100 ft, not 1 ft
Using the average end area across the entire span instead of segment by segment

surveying/coordinate-geometry.name: Coordinate Geometry & Systems
surveying/coordinate-geometry.application: Modern surveying stores points as coordinates (easting, northing). As a civil engineer you compute a new point's coordinates from a known point and a measured course (forward computation), and recover the distance and direction between two known points (inverse computation). On the FE, expect to apply these and to understand plane coordinate systems like State Plane.

content.body: Coordinate geometry (COGO) connects field measurements to a coordinate grid. Two computations dominate: forward (coordinates from a course) and inverse (distance and direction from coordinates).
Forward Computation

content.label: Departure (ΔE) and latitude (ΔN) of a course

content.body: From a known point, a course of length $L$ at azimuth $Az$ gives a departure $\Delta E$ and latitude $\Delta N$. The new coordinates are $E_2 = E_1 + \Delta E$ and $N_2 = N_1 + \Delta N$.
Inverse Computation

content.latex: L = \sqrt{\Delta E^2 + \Delta N^2}, \quad Az = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\Delta E}{\Delta N}\right)
content.label: Distance and azimuth between two known points

content.body: Given two points, the distance between them is the hypotenuse of the coordinate differences, and the azimuth comes from $\tan^{-1}(\Delta E/\Delta N)$ — with the correct quadrant determined by the algebraic SIGNS of $\Delta E$ and $\Delta N$.
Plane Coordinate Systems

State Plane Coordinate Systems project the curved earth onto a flat grid for a region, so surveyors can work in simple rectangular (E, N) coordinates. A scale factor relates grid distances to ground distances; over small sites the difference is negligible.
Remember departure = E-W = L·sin(Az) and latitude = N-S = L·cos(Az). Sine goes with easting, cosine with northing — the same convention used in traverse latitudes and departures.
The arctangent alone cannot fix the azimuth's quadrant. Always check the signs of ΔE and ΔN to place the line in the correct one of the four quadrants.

problems.statement: Point A is at $(E, N) = (1{,}000, 1{,}000)$ and point B is at $(1{,}300, 1{,}400)$ (units: ft). What is the straight-line distance from A to B?
problems.eli5: ΔE = 1,300 − 1,000 = 300; ΔN = 1,400 − 1,000 = 400. Distance = √(300² + 400²) = √(90,000 + 160,000) = √250,000 = 500 ft (a 3-4-5 triangle). The 700 ft choice just adds ΔE + ΔN. The 350 ft choice averages them. The 250 ft choice halves ΔE.
problems.hint: Distance = √(ΔE² + ΔN²).
traps: Adding ΔE and ΔN instead of using the Pythagorean distance
Mismatching which coordinate is easting vs northing

problems.statement: From point A at $(E, N) = (5{,}000, 5{,}000)$, a course of length $200\text{ ft}$ is run at an azimuth of $30\degree$. What is the NORTHING of the new point?
problems.eli5: Latitude ΔN = L·cos(Az) = 200·cos(30°) = 200(0.8660) = 173.2. New northing = 5,000 + 173.2 = 5,173.2. The 5,100.0 choice mistakenly uses the departure (200·sin30° = 100). The 5,183.0 choice uses a slightly off trig value. The 5,200.0 choice just adds the full length.
problems.hint: Northing change = L·cos(azimuth); add it to the starting northing.
traps: Using sine (departure) for the northing instead of cosine
Adding the full course length instead of its north component

problems.statement: When computing a line's azimuth from coordinate differences as $\tan^{-1}(\Delta E/\Delta N)$, what determines the correct quadrant of the azimuth?

choices.text: The algebraic signs of ΔE and ΔN
The magnitude of the distance only
The order in which the points were surveyed
The units used for the coordinates

problems.eli5: The arctangent returns an angle between −90° and 90°, so it cannot by itself tell which of the four quadrants the line points to. The signs of ΔE (east + / west −) and ΔN (north + / south −) place the line in the correct quadrant. The distance magnitude and the coordinate units do not affect direction; the surveying order confuses bookkeeping with geometry.
problems.hint: Arctangent gives only one of two possible directions — what extra information fixes the quadrant?

steps.text: ΔE sign gives east/west; ΔN sign gives north/south.
Together those signs fix the azimuth's quadrant.

traps: Reporting the raw arctangent without checking the quadrant
Assuming distance or units affect the direction

surveying/horizontal-curves.name: Horizontal Curves
surveying/horizontal-curves.application: Civil engineers design horizontal curves for road alignments that connect tangent sections. The curve geometry — radius, tangent distance, curve length, and external distance — determines lane widths, superelevation, and sight distance. On the FE, expect problems computing curve elements (R, T, L, E, M) from the degree of curve or intersection angle, and checking superelevation requirements.

content.body: Horizontal curves are circular arcs that connect two tangent road segments. The intersection angle $I$ (also called $\Delta$) and the radius $R$ define everything else.
Degree of Curve (Arc Definition)
The degree of curve $D$ is the central angle subtended by a 100-ft arc. A smaller $D$ means a larger radius (gentler curve).
Curve Elements
Superelevation
Where $e$ is superelevation (%), $f$ is side friction factor, $V$ is design speed (mph), and $R$ is radius (ft).
