The tangent distance T is measured from the PC (or PT) to the PI. The curve length L is the arc from PC to PT. These are different measurements even though they relate to the same curve.
Know the relationship D = 5,729.58/R by heart. If given D, find R first, then compute T, L, E, and M from R and I.

problems.statement: A horizontal curve has a degree of curve $D = 6\degree$. What is the radius?
problems.eli5: R = 5,729.58 / D = 5,729.58 / 6 = 954.93 ≈ 955 ft. The 5,730 ft choice is the numerator (D = 1°). The 573 ft choice divides by 10 instead of 6. The 1,667 ft choice uses 10,000/D.
traps: Multiplying instead of dividing — D × R = 5,729.58, so R = 5,729.58/D
Using the chord definition instead of the arc definition of degree of curve

problems.statement: A horizontal curve has $R = 1{,}000 \text{ ft}$ and an intersection angle $I = 40\degree$. What is the tangent distance $T$?
problems.eli5: T = R tan(I/2) = 1,000 × tan(20°) = 1,000 × 0.3640 = 364 ft. The 839 ft choice uses tan(I) = tan(40°) instead of tan(I/2). The 342 ft choice uses sin(I/2) instead of tan(I/2) (1,000 × sin(20°) = 342). The 698 ft choice doubles the correct result.
problems.hint: The tangent distance uses HALF the intersection angle: T = R tan(I/2).
traps: Using the full intersection angle I instead of I/2
Using sine instead of tangent

problems.statement: A horizontal curve has $R = 800 \text{ ft}$, $I = 50\degree$. The PC is at station $25+00$. What is the station of the PT?
problems.eli5: L = πRI/180 = π(800)(50)/180 = 125,663.7/180 = 698.13 ft. Station of PT = station of PC + L = 2500 + 698.13 = 3198.13 = station 31+98.13. The 25+00 choice is the PC itself. The 28+49.07 choice uses L/2 (goes to the midpoint). The 38+96.26 choice uses 2L.
problems.hint: Find the curve length L = πRI/180, then add it to the PC station to get the PT station.
traps: Using degrees in the formula without converting properly — the π/180 does the conversion
Confusing curve length L with tangent distance T
Adding the tangent distance instead of the curve length to get PT station

surveying/vertical-curves.name: Vertical Curves
surveying/vertical-curves.application: Civil engineers design vertical curves — parabolic profiles that transition between road grades. Crest curves must provide adequate stopping sight distance over the top, and sag curves must allow headlight illumination. You compute elevations at any point on the curve using the PVC elevation, the grades, and the curve length. On the FE, expect problems finding the elevation at a specific station on a vertical curve, locating the high or low point, and selecting the minimum curve length for sight distance.

content.body: Vertical curves are parabolas that smoothly transition between two grades. The curve is defined by its length $L$, the incoming grade $g_1$, and the outgoing grade $g_2$.
Vertical Curve Elevation
Where $x$ is the horizontal distance from the PVC, $g_1$ and $g_2$ are grades as decimals (e.g., +3% = 0.03), and $L$ is the curve length in the same units as $x$.
High/Low Point Location

content.label: Distance from PVC to high/low point

content.body: The high point occurs on a crest curve (grade goes from + to –) and the low point on a sag curve (grade goes from – to +). This point matters for drainage design.
Key Stations

PVC (Point of Vertical Curvature) = beginning of curve. PVI (Point of Vertical Intersection) = where the tangent lines meet, at station PVC + L/2. PVT (Point of Vertical Tangency) = end of curve, at station PVC + L.
K-Value and Sight Distance

Where $A = |g_1 - g_2|$ (algebraic difference in grades, in %). Higher $K$ means a gentler curve. Design tables give minimum $K$ values for crest and sag curves based on design speed and sight distance.

Remember: grades $g_1$ and $g_2$ must be in consistent units. If the problem gives percentages, divide by 100 before plugging into the elevation formula, or keep them as percentages and adjust the formula accordingly.
The high/low point is NOT at the PVI. It’s at $x_m = -g_1 L / (g_2 - g_1)$, measured from the PVC. On a symmetric crest, the high point is at the midpoint only if $|g_1| = |g_2|$.

problems.statement: A vertical curve has $g_1 = +4\%$, $g_2 = -2\%$, $L = 600 \text{ ft}$, and $Y_{PVC} = 100 \text{ ft}$. What is the elevation at the PVI?
problems.eli5: The PVI is at x = L/2 = 300 ft from the PVC. But the PVI elevation is on the TANGENT line, not the curve: Y_tangent = Y_PVC + g_1 × (L/2) = 100 + 0.04 × 300 = 100 + 12 = 112 ft. The curve elevation at the PVI would be different (lower for a crest), but the PVI itself is on the tangent. The 106.0 ft choice uses g_1 = 2% instead of 4%. The 100.0 ft choice is just the PVC elevation. The 109.0 ft choice averages the PVC tangent and the 2%-grade results incorrectly.
problems.hint: The PVI is at the intersection of the two tangent lines. Its elevation is Y_PVC + g_1 × (L/2), using the back tangent grade.

steps.text: PVI is at $x = L/2$ from PVC:

traps: Computing the curve elevation at PVI instead of the tangent elevation — the PVI is on the tangent by definition
Forgetting to convert percent grade to decimal (4% = 0.04)

problems.statement: Using the same curve ($g_1 = +4\%$, $g_2 = -2\%$, $L = 600 \text{ ft}$, $Y_{PVC} = 100 \text{ ft}$), what is the curve elevation at $x = 300 \text{ ft}$ (the midpoint)?
problems.eli5: Y = Y_PVC + g_1×x + [(g_2–g_1)/(2L)]×x². Parabola constant a = (–0.02 – 0.04)/(2×600) = –0.00005. Y = 100 + 0.04(300) + (–0.00005)(90,000) = 100 + 12 – 4.5 = 107.5 ft. The tangent elevation at this point is 112 ft, but the curve sits 4.5 ft below the tangent (because it’s a crest curve). The 106.0 ft choice uses the wrong parabola constant. The 112 ft choice is the tangent elevation, not the curve elevation. The 100.0 ft choice is the PVC elevation.
problems.hint: Use the curve elevation formula: $Y = Y_{PVC} + g_1 x + [(g_2 - g_1)/(2L)]x^2$. Convert grades from percent to decimal.

steps.text: The tangent offset at PVI: $E = 112 - 107.5 = 4.5$ ft below the tangent.

problems.handbookFormula: Y = Y_{PVC} + g_1 x + \frac{g_2 - g_1}{2L} x^2
traps: Using the tangent elevation (112 ft) instead of the curve elevation (107.5 ft)
Forgetting to convert percent grades to decimals before using the formula
Getting the sign of the parabola constant wrong

problems.statement: A crest vertical curve has $g_1 = +3\%$ and $g_2 = -1\%$, with $L = 400 \text{ ft}$. How far from the PVC is the high point of the curve?
problems.eli5: x_m = –g_1 × L / (g_2 – g_1) = –(0.03)(400) / (–0.01 – 0.03) = –12 / –0.04 = 300 ft. The high point is 300 ft from the PVC, which is 3/4 of the way along the curve. It’s not at the midpoint because |g_1| ≠ |g_2|. The 400 ft choice puts it at the PVT (x = L). The 200 ft choice assumes the high point is at the midpoint (L/2). The 100 ft choice uses g_1 alone.
problems.hint: The high point is where the slope equals zero: x_m = –g_1 × L / (g_2 – g_1). Use decimal grades.
traps: Assuming the high point is at the midpoint (L/2) — only true when |g_1| = |g_2|
Forgetting to convert grades from percent to decimal
Getting the sign wrong in the denominator (g_2 – g_1, not g_1 – g_2)

water-resources/open-channel-flow.name: Open-Channel Flow & Manning's Equation
water-resources/open-channel-flow.application: Civil engineers size every ditch, swale, culvert, and storm sewer using Manning's equation. You select the roughness coefficient based on channel lining, compute the hydraulic radius from the cross-section geometry, and solve for discharge or normal depth. On the FE, expect problems computing flow in rectangular or circular channels, selecting Manning's $n$, and applying the 1.486 conversion factor for US Customary units.

content.body: Open-channel flow has a free surface exposed to the atmosphere. Manning's equation relates discharge to channel geometry, roughness, and slope.
Manning's Equation

Where $K = 1.486$ for USCS units and $K = 1.0$ for SI units. $n$ is the roughness coefficient, $A$ is the flow area, $R_H = A/P$ is the hydraulic radius, $P$ is the wetted perimeter, and $S$ is the channel slope.
Hydraulic Radius

For a full circular pipe of diameter $D$: $R_H = D/4$. For a rectangular channel of width $b$ and depth $y$: $R_H = by/(b + 2y)$. For a trapezoidal channel, add the sloped sides to the wetted perimeter.
Common Manning's n Values
Concrete: $n \approx 0.013$. Corrugated metal: $n \approx 0.024$. Earth channel (clean): $n \approx 0.022$. Natural stream (clean): $n \approx 0.030$. Natural stream (weedy): $n \approx 0.035$.
The 1.486 factor applies ONLY to US Customary units. In SI, K = 1.0. This is the single most common trap on Manning's problems — forgetting the conversion factor changes your answer by almost 50%.
Hydraulic radius is NOT the physical radius. For a full circular pipe, R_H = D/4, not D/2. Only for very wide, shallow channels does R_H approach the depth y.

problems.statement: A rectangular concrete channel ($n = 0.013$) is $4 \text{ ft}$ wide and carries water $2 \text{ ft}$ deep on a slope of $S = 0.001$. What is the discharge?
problems.eli5: A = 4 × 2 = 8 ft². P = 4 + 2(2) = 8 ft. R_H = 8/8 = 1.0 ft. Q = (1.486/0.013)(8)(1.0)^(2/3)(0.001)^(1/2) = 114.3 × 8 × 1.0 × 0.0316 = 28.9 cfs. The 42.3 cfs choice uses width alone for the wetted perimeter (P = 4 instead of 8), inflating R_H. The 19.5 cfs choice forgets the 1.486 factor. The 14.5 cfs choice halves the correct answer by miscalculating R_H.
problems.hint: Find A, P, and R_H first. Remember K = 1.486 for US Customary units.
traps: Forgetting the 1.486 factor for USCS units — using K = 1.0 gives about 19.5 cfs instead of 28.9 cfs
Using the channel width as the wetted perimeter instead of b + 2y

problems.statement: A concrete circular storm sewer ($n = 0.015$) has a diameter of $D = 3 \text{ ft}$ and flows full on a slope of $S = 0.002$. What is the full-pipe discharge?
problems.eli5: Full circular pipe: A = π(3)²/4 = 7.069 ft². R_H = D/4 = 0.75 ft. (0.75)^(2/3) = 0.826. (0.002)^(1/2) = 0.04472. Q = (1.486/0.015)(7.069)(0.826)(0.04472) = 99.07 × 7.069 × 0.0369 = 25.9 cfs. The 17.4 cfs distractor forgets the 1.486 unit factor (uses K=1). The 40.6 cfs distractor uses R_H = D/2 = 1.5 instead of D/4 = 0.75. The 10.3 cfs distractor applies an incorrect (too-small) hydraulic radius.
problems.hint: For a full circular pipe, R_H = D/4 (not D/2). Don't forget K = 1.486 for USCS.
traps: Using R_H = D/2 (physical radius) instead of R_H = D/4 (hydraulic radius for full pipe)
Forgetting the 1.486 USCS conversion factor

problems.statement: Two channels carry the same discharge on the same slope. Channel A is lined with concrete ($n = 0.013$) and Channel B is an unlined earth channel ($n = 0.025$). If both have the same cross-section, how does the velocity in Channel A compare to Channel B?

choices.text: Channel A is about 1.5 times faster
Channel B is about 1.9 times faster
Channel A is about 1.9 times faster

problems.eli5: Since v = (K/n) R_H^(2/3) S^(1/2), and everything except n is the same, the velocity ratio is v_A/v_B = n_B/n_A = 0.025/0.013 = 1.92 ≈ 1.9. The smoother channel (lower n) has higher velocity. The "same velocity" choice ignores the effect of roughness. The "1.5 times faster" choice uses the wrong ratio. The "Channel B is 1.9 times faster" choice inverts the relationship (it applies n_A/n_B and assigns the gain to the rougher channel).
problems.hint: With the same geometry and slope, velocity is inversely proportional to Manning's n.

steps.text: Since both channels have the same $R_H$, $S$, and $K$:
Channel A is about 1.9 times faster than Channel B.

traps: Thinking higher n means faster flow — higher n means rougher surface and slower flow
Computing n_A/n_B instead of n_B/n_A — velocity is inversely proportional to n

water-resources/energy-critical-flow.name: Specific Energy & Critical Flow
water-resources/energy-critical-flow.application: Civil engineers use specific energy to classify flow as subcritical or supercritical, design channel transitions, and analyze hydraulic jumps. Knowing the critical depth tells you whether your channel is operating safely above or below the energy minimum. On the FE, expect problems computing critical depth in rectangular channels, classifying flow with the Froude number, and finding conjugate depths across a hydraulic jump.

content.body: Specific energy is the total energy at a cross-section measured relative to the channel bottom. It determines whether flow is subcritical (deep and slow) or supercritical (shallow and fast).
Specific Energy
Where $y$ is the flow depth, $v$ is velocity, $Q$ is discharge, $A$ is the flow area, and $\alpha$ is the kinetic energy correction factor (usually 1.0).
Critical Depth
Critical depth occurs at minimum specific energy. The general condition is:
For a rectangular channel of width $B$, the critical depth simplifies to:
Where $q = Q/B$ is the unit discharge (flow per unit width).
Froude Number
Where $y_h = A/T$ is the hydraulic depth. $Fr < 1$ is subcritical flow, $Fr = 1$ is critical, $Fr > 1$ is supercritical.
Hydraulic Jump
A hydraulic jump converts supercritical flow to subcritical flow with significant energy loss. $y_1$ is the upstream supercritical depth and $y_2$ is the downstream subcritical depth.
For rectangular channels, critical depth depends ONLY on discharge and width — not on slope, roughness, or channel length. If the problem gives Q and B, you can find y_c directly.

The Froude number tells you the flow regime instantly: Fr < 1 = subcritical (tranquil), Fr > 1 = supercritical (rapid). Most natural rivers are subcritical; spillways and steep chutes are supercritical.

problems.statement: Water flows at $Q = 27 \text{ m}^3\text{/s}$ in a rectangular channel that is $B = 3 \text{ m}$ wide. What is the critical depth?
problems.eli5: Unit discharge q = Q/B = 27/3 = 9 m²/s. Critical depth y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3) = (81/9.81)^(1/3) = (8.257)^(1/3) = 2.02 m. The 3.00 m choice uses Q instead of q. The 0.97 m choice uses q²/g without the cube root. The 1.44 m choice takes the square root instead of the cube root.
problems.hint: First find the unit discharge q = Q/B, then apply the rectangular critical depth formula.
traps: Using total Q instead of unit discharge q = Q/B in the formula
Taking the square root instead of the cube root

problems.statement: Water flows at a velocity of $v = 4 \text{ m/s}$ at a depth of $y = 0.5 \text{ m}$ in a rectangular channel. What is the Froude number, and is the flow subcritical or supercritical?
problems.eli5: Fr = v / √(gy) = 4 / √(9.81 × 0.5) = 4 / √(4.905) = 4 / 2.215 = 1.81. Since Fr > 1, the flow is supercritical. The Fr = 0.81 (subcritical) choice uses g = 10 and then takes v/gy instead of v/√(gy). The Fr = 0.55 (subcritical) choice inverts the formula (denominator over numerator). The Fr = 1.81 (subcritical) choice gets the number right but classifies it wrong — Fr > 1 is supercritical, not subcritical.
problems.hint: For a rectangular channel, hydraulic depth equals flow depth. Compute Fr = v/√(gy) and compare to 1.
traps: Classifying Fr > 1 as subcritical — supercritical means fast and shallow, subcritical means slow and deep
Forgetting the square root — computing v/(gy) instead of v/√(gy)

problems.statement: A hydraulic jump occurs in a rectangular channel. The upstream depth is $y_1 = 0.4 \text{ m}$ and the upstream Froude number is $Fr_1 = 3.0$. What is the downstream (conjugate) depth $y_2$?
problems.eli5: y_2 = (y_1/2)(−1 + √(1 + 8Fr_1²)) = (0.4/2)(−1 + √(1 + 8×9)) = 0.2 × (−1 + √73) = 0.2 × (−1 + 8.544) = 0.2 × 7.544 = 1.49 m. The downstream depth is about 3.7 times the upstream depth. The 0.80 m choice just doubles y_1. The 1.20 m choice uses Fr_1 = 2 instead of 3. The 3.60 m choice multiplies y_1 by Fr_1² without using the correct formula.
problems.hint: Use the conjugate depth formula: y_2 = (y_1/2)(−1 + √(1 + 8Fr²)). Plug in y_1 and Fr_1 directly.
traps: Forgetting the −1 inside the parentheses — it is part of the formula, not a sign error
Using Fr² without the factor of 8 inside the radical
Confusing y_1 and y_2 — the upstream supercritical depth is always smaller

water-resources/pipe-systems-weirs.name: Hazen-Williams & Weir Formulas
water-resources/pipe-systems-weirs.application: Civil engineers use the Hazen-Williams equation to size water distribution mains and compute head loss in pipe networks. Weir formulas measure flow at treatment plants, streams, and detention pond outlets. On the FE, expect problems computing pipe velocity with Hazen-Williams, selecting the C coefficient for different pipe materials, and calculating discharge over rectangular or V-notch weirs.

content.body: The Hazen-Williams equation is the workhorse of water distribution design. Unlike Darcy-Weisbach (which uses a friction factor), Hazen-Williams uses a single roughness coefficient $C$ that depends only on the pipe material.
Hazen-Williams Equation
Where $k_1 = 0.849$ for SI and $k_1 = 1.318$ for USCS. $C$ is the roughness coefficient (higher = smoother), $R_H$ is the hydraulic radius, and $S_v$ is the slope of the energy grade line ($h_f/L$).
Common C Values
PVC/plastic: $C = 150$. Ductile iron: $C = 140$. Asbestos-cement: $C = 140$. New cast iron: $C = 130$. Concrete: $C = 130$. 20-year-old cast iron: $C = 100$.
Weir Formulas
Weirs are overflow structures used to measure or control flow. The discharge depends on the head $H$ above the weir crest.
Weir coefficients: Rectangular $C = 3.33$ (USCS) or $1.84$ (SI). 90° V-notch $C = 2.54$ (USCS) or $1.40$ (SI).
Higher Hazen-Williams C means a SMOOTHER pipe (less friction). This is the opposite of Manning's n, where higher n means rougher. Don't mix them up.
The contracted weir formula subtracts 0.2H from L to account for end contractions. If the problem says "suppressed" or "full-width," use Q = CLH^(3/2) without the correction.

problems.statement: A suppressed rectangular weir is $L = 5 \text{ ft}$ long. The head over the weir is $H = 1.5 \text{ ft}$. What is the discharge?
problems.eli5: Q = CLH^(3/2) = 3.33 × 5 × (1.5)^(3/2). (1.5)^(3/2) = 1.5 × √1.5 = 1.5 × 1.225 = 1.837. Q = 3.33 × 5 × 1.837 = 30.6 cfs. The 25.0 cfs choice uses H^1 instead of H^(3/2). The 16.9 cfs choice uses the SI coefficient (1.84). The 37.5 cfs choice multiplies by H² instead of H^(3/2).
problems.hint: For a suppressed rectangular weir in USCS: Q = CLH^(3/2) with C = 3.33.
traps: Using the SI coefficient (C = 1.84) instead of the USCS coefficient (C = 3.33)
Confusing H^(3/2) for rectangular with H^(5/2) for V-notch weirs

problems.statement: A 90° V-notch weir measures flow in a stream. The head above the notch is $H = 2.0 \text{ ft}$. What is the discharge?
problems.eli5: V-notch weir: Q = CH^(5/2) = 2.54 × (2.0)^(5/2). (2.0)^(5/2) = 2^2 × √2 = 4 × 1.414 = 5.657. Q = 2.54 × 5.657 = 14.4 cfs. The 10.2 cfs option uses H^2 = 4.0. The 7.2 cfs option uses H^(3/2) instead of H^(5/2) — that's the rectangular weir exponent. The 20.3 cfs option uses H^3 = 8.0.
problems.hint: V-notch weirs use H^(5/2), not H^(3/2). The USCS coefficient for a 90° notch is C = 2.54.
traps: Using H^(3/2) — that's for rectangular weirs. V-notch uses H^(5/2)
Using the rectangular weir coefficient (C = 3.33) instead of the V-notch coefficient (C = 2.54)

problems.statement: Two pipes have the same diameter, length, and hydraulic gradient. Pipe A is new PVC ($C = 150$) and Pipe B is 20-year-old cast iron ($C = 100$). What is the ratio of flow in Pipe A to Pipe B?
problems.eli5: Since Q = k₁ C A R_H^0.63 S^0.54, and everything except C is the same, Q_A/Q_B = C_A/C_B = 150/100 = 1.50. The newer, smoother pipe carries 50% more flow. The $2.25$ option squares the ratio (1.5² = 2.25). The $1.22$ option takes the 0.63 power of the ratio. The $0.67$ option inverts it.
problems.hint: With identical pipe geometry and gradient, flow is directly proportional to C.

steps.text: Since all parameters except $C$ are identical:
Pipe A carries 50% more flow than Pipe B.

traps: Thinking lower C means more flow — higher C means smoother pipe, less friction, more flow
Raising the ratio to a power (0.63 or 0.54) — C enters the equation linearly

water-resources/pumps-water-distribution.name: Pumps & Water Distribution
water-resources/pumps-water-distribution.application: Civil engineers size the pumps that move water through supply, distribution, and wastewater systems. On the FE, expect to compute the power a pump draws (accounting for efficiency), find the net positive suction head available to guard against cavitation, and relate pump head to the static lift plus friction losses of the system.

content.body: A pump adds energy (head) to a fluid. The useful power delivered to the water is the fluid (hydraulic) power; the shaft power the motor must supply is larger because the pump is not 100% efficient.
Pump Power

content.latex: \dot W_{fluid} = \rho g Q H = \gamma Q H
content.label: Fluid (hydraulic) power

content.body: Here $Q$ is the volumetric flow, $H$ is the head added, and $\eta_{pump}$ is the pump efficiency. The motor input (purchased) power divides again by the motor efficiency.
Total Dynamic Head & the System Curve

content.label: Total dynamic head = static lift + friction/minor losses

content.body: The head a pump must provide equals the static lift (elevation difference) plus the friction and minor losses, which grow with $Q^2$. Plotting required head versus flow gives the system curve; its intersection with the pump curve is the operating point.
NPSH & Cavitation

NPSH available is the atmospheric pressure head ($H_{pa}$) plus the static suction head ($H_s$, negative for a suction lift), minus suction-line friction ($\sum h_L$) and the vapor pressure head ($H_{vp}$). To avoid cavitation, $NPSH_A$ must exceed the pump's required $NPSH_R$.
Fluid power uses γQH directly. Because a pump is less than 100% efficient, the brake power the motor delivers is always LARGER — divide by efficiency, never multiply.
In NPSH_A, the static suction term is negative when the pump sits ABOVE the water surface (a suction lift). Sign errors here are the most common NPSH mistake.

problems.statement: A pump delivers $Q = 0.05\text{ m}^3\text{/s}$ against a total head of $H = 30\text{ m}$ at a pump efficiency of $\eta = 0.75$. What brake (shaft) power is required? (Use $\rho g = 9{,}810\text{ N/m}^3$.)
problems.eli5: Fluid power = γQH = 9,810 × 0.05 × 30 = 14,715 W ≈ 14.7 kW. Brake power divides by efficiency: 14.7/0.75 = 19.6 kW. The 14.7 kW option is the fluid power, forgetting efficiency. The 11.0 kW option multiplies by 0.75 instead of dividing. The 26.2 kW option divides by 0.75² (≈ 0.5625) or a similar slip.
problems.hint: Fluid power = γQH. Brake power = fluid power / η_pump (always larger).

steps.text: Divide by efficiency for brake power:

traps: Reporting fluid power and forgetting to divide by efficiency
Multiplying by η instead of dividing — brake power must be larger than fluid power

problems.statement: A pump sits $3.0\text{ m}$ above the water surface it draws from (a suction lift). The atmospheric pressure head is $H_{pa} = 10.3\text{ m}$, the vapor pressure head is $H_{vp} = 0.24\text{ m}$, and the suction-line friction loss is $\sum h_L = 1.0\text{ m}$. What is the net positive suction head available ($NPSH_A$)?
problems.eli5: For a suction lift the static suction head is negative: H_s = −3.0 m. NPSH_A = H_pa + H_s − Σh_L − H_vp = 10.3 − 3.0 − 1.0 − 0.24 = 6.06 ≈ 6.1 m. The 12.1 m choice adds the 3.0 m instead of subtracting (wrong sign for a lift). The 7.3 m choice forgets the friction and vapor terms. The 3.1 m choice mishandles the atmospheric term.
problems.hint: NPSH_A = H_pa + H_s − Σh_L − H_vp, with H_s negative for a suction lift.

steps.text: Suction lift makes the static suction head negative:

traps: Treating a suction lift as a positive static head (wrong sign)
Omitting the vapor pressure or friction terms

problems.statement: A pump moves $Q = 1.1\text{ ft}^3\text{/s}$ of water against a head of $H = 100\text{ ft}$. Using $\gamma = 62.4\text{ lb/ft}^3$ and $1\text{ hp} = 550\text{ ft·lb/s}$, what is the water (hydraulic) horsepower?
problems.eli5: Fluid power = γQH = 62.4 × 1.1 × 100 = 6,864 ft·lb/s. Convert to horsepower: 6,864/550 = 12.48 ≈ 12.5 hp. The 9.2 hp option divides by 746 (the SI watts-per-hp) instead of 550 ft·lb/s. The 6.2 hp option over-divides. The 18.7 hp option adds an efficiency factor that the question did not ask for.
problems.hint: Water horsepower = γQH / 550 when Q is in ft³/s, H in ft, and γ in lb/ft³.
traps: Dividing by 746 W/hp instead of 550 ft·lb/s/hp (mixing unit systems)
Forgetting the conversion entirely and leaving power in ft·lb/s

water-resources/rainfall-runoff.name: Rainfall-Runoff Methods
water-resources/rainfall-runoff.application: Civil engineers use the Rational Method to size storm drains for small catchments and the SCS/NRCS Curve Number method for larger watersheds and detention pond design. You pull rainfall data from intensity-duration-frequency curves, estimate the runoff coefficient or curve number from land cover and soil type, and compute the peak flow your drainage system must handle. On the FE, expect problems applying Q = CIA for the Rational Method and computing runoff depth from the SCS equation.

content.body: Two methods dominate stormwater design: the Rational Method for small sites (under 200 acres) and the SCS/NRCS method for larger watersheds.
Rational Method

Where $Q$ is peak discharge (cfs), $C$ is the runoff coefficient (dimensionless, 0 to 1), $I$ is rainfall intensity (in./hr), and $A$ is watershed area (acres). The units work out because 1 acre-in./hr $\approx$ 1 cfs.
SCS/NRCS Curve Number Method

Where $P$ is precipitation (inches), $Q$ is runoff depth (inches), $S$ is maximum basin retention (inches), and $CN$ is the curve number (0–100). Higher CN means more runoff (impervious surfaces have CN near 98).
Hydrologic Mass Balance

content.latex: P + Q_{in} - Q_{out} + Q_g - E_s - T_s - I = \Delta S_s
content.label: Surface water budget

content.body: The mass balance accounts for all water entering and leaving a system: precipitation, surface inflow/outflow, groundwater contribution, evaporation, transpiration, infiltration, and change in storage.

The Rational Method only works for small watersheds (< 200 acres). The units are sneaky: Q comes out in cfs directly because 1 acre × 1 in./hr ≈ 1.008 cfs ≈ 1 cfs. Don't try to convert units — it's built into the formula.
For the SCS equation, Q is in inches (depth of runoff), NOT cfs. The formula requires P > 0.2S for runoff to occur. If P < 0.2S (the initial abstraction), runoff Q = 0.

problems.statement: A 50-acre commercial site has a runoff coefficient of $C = 0.85$. The design rainfall intensity for the 10-year storm is $I = 4.0 \text{ in./hr}$. What is the peak runoff using the Rational Method?
problems.eli5: Q = CIA = 0.85 × 4.0 × 50 = 170 cfs. That's it — straight plug-and-chug. The 212 cfs option uses C = 1.06 (a common wrong reading from tables). The 42.5 cfs option divides by 4 for some reason. The 340 cfs option doubles the area (uses A = 100 acres instead of 50).
problems.hint: Q = CIA. The units work out directly — no conversion needed.
traps: Trying to convert units — the formula is set up so 1 acre-in./hr ≈ 1 cfs
Using the wrong runoff coefficient for the land use type

problems.statement: A watershed has a curve number of $CN = 80$. If the total rainfall is $P = 5.0 \text{ in.}$, what is the runoff depth using the SCS method?
problems.eli5: First find S: S = 1000/CN – 10 = 1000/80 – 10 = 12.5 – 10 = 2.5 in. Initial abstraction = 0.2S = 0.5 in. Since P = 5.0 > 0.5, runoff occurs. Q = (P – 0.2S)²/(P + 0.8S) = (5.0 – 0.5)²/(5.0 + 2.0) = (4.5)²/7.0 = 20.25/7.0 = 2.89 in. The 5.00 in. choice uses the full precipitation without subtracting initial abstraction. The 4.50 in. choice uses P – 0.2S in the numerator without squaring (4.5/1.0 = 4.5). The 1.50 in. choice uses (P – S) instead of (P – 0.2S).
problems.hint: First compute S = 1000/CN – 10, then plug into Q = (P – 0.2S)²/(P + 0.8S). Check that P > 0.2S.
traps: Forgetting to compute S from CN first — S is NOT the curve number
Using P instead of (P – 0.2S) in the numerator — the initial abstraction must be subtracted
Reporting Q in cfs — the SCS equation gives runoff DEPTH in inches, not discharge

problems.statement: Two adjacent sub-catchments drain to the same inlet. Sub-A has $C_A = 0.90$, $A_A = 30 \text{ acres}$. Sub-B has $C_B = 0.40$, $A_B = 20 \text{ acres}$. The rainfall intensity for the combined time of concentration is $I = 3.5 \text{ in./hr}$. What is the total peak discharge?
problems.eli5: For composite catchments, apply the Rational Method to each and add: Q = I(C_A × A_A + C_B × A_B) = 3.5 × (0.90 × 30 + 0.40 × 20) = 3.5 × (27 + 8) = 3.5 × 35 = 122.5 cfs. The 65.0 cfs option only computes sub-A. The 113.8 cfs option uses C_avg = (0.90 + 0.40)/2 = 0.65 (simple average, not area-weighted) → Q = 0.65 × 3.5 × 50 = 113.8. The 175 cfs option ignores C (Q = I × A_total = 3.5 × 50 = 175).
problems.hint: For composite catchments, Q = I × Σ(C_i × A_i). You can add the CIA products or use a weighted average C.

steps.latex: Q = I \sum(C_i A_i) = I(C_A A_A + C_B A_B)

traps: Averaging the C values without weighting by area — (0.90 + 0.40)/2 = 0.65 is wrong; the area-weighted average is (27 + 8)/50 = 0.70
Forgetting to apply different C values to different sub-catchments
Applying different rainfall intensities to sub-catchments — use the intensity for the combined time of concentration

water-resources/hydrograph-watershed.name: Hydrographs & Watershed Analysis
water-resources/hydrograph-watershed.application: Civil engineers use hydrographs to predict the shape and timing of runoff — not just the peak flow, but how long the storm takes to arrive, peak, and recede. You need the full hydrograph to size detention ponds, route flows through a reservoir, and design outlet structures. Watershed characteristics like time of concentration and drainage area control how fast runoff reaches the outlet. On the FE, expect problems scaling unit hydrographs, computing time of concentration, and applying the hydrologic mass balance.

content.body: A hydrograph plots discharge vs. time at a watershed outlet. The unit hydrograph is the fundamental building block for predicting runoff from any storm.
Unit Hydrograph
A unit hydrograph (UH) is the direct runoff hydrograph resulting from 1 inch (or 1 cm) of excess rainfall applied uniformly over the watershed during a specified duration. Key properties:

The volume under the UH equals 1 inch of runoff over the watershed area. To get the hydrograph for $P$ inches of excess rainfall, multiply all UH ordinates by $P$. For a different storm duration, you need a different UH.
Hydrograph Components

Total streamflow = direct runoff + baseflow. Direct runoff is the storm-generated component. The rising limb reflects rainfall intensity; the falling limb (recession) reflects drainage of stored water. The peak occurs after the centroid of rainfall, delayed by the basin lag time.
Time of Concentration

Time of concentration ($t_c$) is the time for water to travel from the most hydraulically distant point in the watershed to the outlet. For the Rational Method, the design storm duration equals $t_c$ — this produces the maximum peak discharge.
Watershed Storage Routing
Where $I$ is inflow, $O$ is outflow, and $\Delta S/\Delta t$ is the rate of change in storage. This is the basis for reservoir routing (Modified Puls method) used to design detention ponds.
To scale a unit hydrograph: multiply every ordinate by the excess rainfall depth. 3 inches of excess rain → multiply all UH values by 3. The time axis stays the same.
The Rational Method assumes storm duration = time of concentration. If the storm is shorter than t_c, not all of the watershed contributes. If longer, intensity drops (from IDF curves), reducing Q.

problems.statement: A 1-hour unit hydrograph for a watershed has a peak discharge of $500 \text{ cfs}$. If a storm produces $3 \text{ in.}$ of excess rainfall in 1 hour, what is the peak discharge of the direct runoff hydrograph?
problems.eli5: The unit hydrograph is for 1 inch of excess rainfall. For 3 inches, multiply every ordinate by 3. Peak = 500 × 3 = 1,500 cfs. The 500 cfs option doesn't scale (uses 1 inch). The 167 cfs option divides instead of multiplying (500/3 = 167). The 1,000 cfs option doubles instead of tripling.
problems.hint: The unit hydrograph gives the response to 1 inch of excess rainfall. Scale linearly for other amounts.

steps.text: The UH peak is for 1 inch of excess rainfall:

problems.handbookFormula: \text{Unit hydrograph: 1 unit of rainfall over specified duration}
traps: Forgetting to scale the UH by the actual excess rainfall depth
Dividing by the rainfall instead of multiplying

problems.statement: A 100-acre watershed has a time of concentration of $t_c = 30 \text{ min}$. Using the Rational Method with $C = 0.60$, the 30-minute rainfall intensity for the 25-year storm is $I = 4.8 \text{ in./hr}$. What is the peak runoff?
problems.eli5: Q = CIA = 0.60 × 4.8 × 100 = 288 cfs. The key insight is that the storm duration should equal the time of concentration to produce the maximum peak. Since the problem already gives I for the 30-min duration (which equals t_c), just plug in. The 480 cfs choice ignores C (just I×A). The 144 cfs choice uses a halved intensity (perhaps thinking 30 min = half hour needs adjustment). The 576 cfs choice uses C = 1.2 (doubled).
problems.hint: The design storm duration equals the time of concentration. Use Q = CIA with the given intensity.
traps: Converting minutes to hours and dividing the intensity — the intensity is already in in./hr for the correct duration
Using an intensity for a different duration than t_c — Q = CIA requires the intensity for storm duration = t_c

problems.statement: A reservoir receives an inflow of $I = 800 \text{ cfs}$ and releases an outflow of $O = 500 \text{ cfs}$. What is the rate of change in storage?
problems.eli5: I – O = ΔS/Δt. So ΔS/Δt = 800 – 500 = 300 cfs. Since it's positive, storage is INCREASING — more water is coming in than going out. This is the fundamental principle behind detention pond design: during a storm, the pond fills (I > O), storing water to reduce the downstream peak. The "storage is not changing" choice assumes steady state. The "decreasing at 300 cfs" choice reverses the sign. The "increasing at 1,300 cfs" choice adds instead of subtracting.
problems.hint: Apply I – O = ΔS/Δt. A positive result means storage is increasing.

steps.text: Since $\Delta S/\Delta t > 0$, storage is increasing at 300 cfs.

problems.handbookFormula: P + Q_{in} - Q_{out} + Q_g - E_s - T_s - I = \Delta S_s
traps: Subtracting inflow from outflow instead of outflow from inflow (O – I gives the wrong sign)
Confusing "storage increasing" with "water level decreasing"

water-resources/groundwater-wells.name: Groundwater & Wells
water-resources/groundwater-wells.application: Civil engineers use Darcy's law to estimate seepage under dams, flow to dewatering systems, and contaminant transport through aquifers. Well hydraulics (Dupuit and Thiem equations) let you compute drawdown at a pumping well and determine whether pumping will affect neighboring properties. On the FE, expect problems computing Darcy velocity vs. seepage velocity, finding well discharge from drawdown data, and distinguishing confined from unconfined aquifer behavior.

content.body: Groundwater flow through soil follows Darcy's law. Well hydraulics extends this to radial flow toward a pumping well.
Darcy's Law
Where $K$ is hydraulic conductivity (ft/s or m/s), $A$ is the cross-sectional area of flow, $dh/dx$ is the hydraulic gradient, and $q$ is the specific discharge (Darcy velocity).
Seepage Velocity
The actual water velocity through the pores ($v$) is faster than the Darcy velocity ($q$) because water only flows through the void spaces. Divide by the effective porosity $n$.
Well Drawdown — Unconfined Aquifer (Dupuit)

Where $h_1$ and $h_2$ are water surface heights above the aquifer bottom at radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ from the well center. Note the squared heads — the water table in an unconfined aquifer is a curved surface.
Well Drawdown — Confined Aquifer (Thiem)
Where $T = Kb$ is transmissivity, $b$ is the aquifer thickness, and $h_1$, $h_2$ are piezometric heights. Note the linear heads (not squared) — the confined aquifer has constant thickness.

Darcy velocity is NOT the actual water velocity. The real seepage velocity is v = q/n. Darcy velocity treats the entire cross-section as if water flows through all of it, but water only flows through the pores.
Dupuit (unconfined) uses h² differences. Thiem (confined) uses h differences. The memory trick: unconfined has a free surface that curves, so you need the quadratic (h²) form.

problems.statement: Groundwater flows through a sandy aquifer with $K = 5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m/s}$ under a hydraulic gradient of $i = 0.02$. The aquifer cross-section is $A = 200 \text{ m}^2$. If the effective porosity is $n = 0.30$, what is the seepage velocity?
problems.eli5: Darcy velocity: q = Ki = 5×10⁻⁴ × 0.02 = 1.0×10⁻⁵ m/s. Seepage velocity: v = q/n = 1.0×10⁻⁵/0.30 = 3.33×10⁻⁵ m/s. The 1.0×10⁻⁵ m/s option gives the Darcy velocity, not the seepage velocity. The 2.0×10⁻³ m/s option is the volumetric flow Q = q×A = Ki×A, not a velocity. The 1.0×10⁻³ m/s option halves that flow figure — another units mix-up.
problems.hint: Find the Darcy velocity first (q = Ki), then divide by porosity to get seepage velocity.
traps: Reporting the Darcy velocity as the answer — seepage velocity is always larger (divide by porosity)
Multiplying by porosity instead of dividing — water moves faster through pores, not slower

problems.statement: A well pumps from an unconfined aquifer with $K = 5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ ft/s}$. At the well ($r_1 = 0.5 \text{ ft}$), the water level is $h_1 = 40 \text{ ft}$ above the aquifer bottom. At an observation well ($r_2 = 200 \text{ ft}$), the water level is $h_2 = 60 \text{ ft}$. What is the well discharge?
problems.eli5: Dupuit (unconfined): Q = πK(h₂² – h₁²)/ln(r₂/r₁) = π(5×10⁻⁴)(60² – 40²)/ln(200/0.5) = π(0.0005)(2000)/ln(400) = 3.142/5.991 = 0.52 cfs. The 1.05 cfs option uses K = 0.001 (doubled). The 0.011 cfs option uses h differences instead of h² differences (h₂ – h₁ = 20 instead of 2000). The 0.33 cfs option uses log₁₀ instead of ln.
problems.hint: For an unconfined aquifer, use Dupuit's formula with h² differences. Don't forget the natural log in the denominator.
traps: Using h differences instead of h² differences — Dupuit (unconfined) requires squaring the heads
Using log₁₀ instead of ln — the formula uses the natural logarithm
Swapping r_1 and r_2 in the logarithm — r_1 is at the well, r_2 is farther away

problems.statement: A confined aquifer has thickness $b = 20 \text{ m}$ and hydraulic conductivity $K = 3 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m/s}$. A pumping well shows piezometric heads of $h_1 = 25 \text{ m}$ at $r_1 = 10 \text{ m}$ and $h_2 = 30 \text{ m}$ at $r_2 = 100 \text{ m}$. What is the pumping rate?
problems.eli5: For a confined aquifer, use the Thiem equation. T = Kb = 3×10⁻⁵ × 20 = 6×10⁻⁴ m²/s. Q = 2πT(h₂ – h₁)/ln(r₂/r₁) = 2π(6×10⁻⁴)(30 – 25)/ln(100/10) = 2π(6×10⁻⁴)(5)/2.303 = 0.01885/2.303 = 0.0082 m³/s. The 0.082 m³/s choice uses K = 3×10⁻⁴ (ten times too high). The 0.041 m³/s choice is 5× too large (e.g. mistakenly using aquifer thickness b = 100 m instead of 20 m). The 0.0016 m³/s choice comes from a low-by-roughly-5× slip.
problems.hint: For a confined aquifer, use Thiem: Q = 2πT(h₂ – h₁)/ln(r₂/r₁) where T = Kb. Use linear h, not h².
traps: Using Dupuit's formula (h²) for a confined aquifer — Thiem uses linear h differences
Forgetting to compute transmissivity T = Kb before plugging in
Using log₁₀ instead of ln — ln(10) = 2.303, not log₁₀(10) = 1.0

water-resources/water-quality.name: Water Quality & BOD
water-resources/water-quality.application: Civil engineers monitor BOD, dissolved oxygen, and other water quality parameters to evaluate treatment plant performance and assess the impact of discharges on receiving streams. The Streeter-Phelps model predicts how dissolved oxygen changes downstream of a wastewater outfall. On the FE, expect problems computing BOD at a given time, finding the critical oxygen deficit, and applying temperature corrections to rate constants.

content.body: Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) measures the amount of oxygen consumed by microorganisms decomposing organic matter. It is the primary metric for organic pollution in water.
BOD Exertion

Where $L_0$ is the ultimate BOD (mg/L), $k$ is the BOD decay rate constant (base $e$, days$^{-1}$), and $t$ is time (days). $BOD_5$ is the standard 5-day BOD — the oxygen consumed after 5 days at 20°C.
Dissolved Oxygen & Streeter-Phelps
Where $D$ is the oxygen deficit (the difference between saturation and actual DO). The Streeter-Phelps equation models how the deficit changes downstream:

Deoxygenation (BOD consuming oxygen) increases the deficit, while reaeration (atmospheric oxygen dissolving) decreases it. The critical point occurs where these two rates are equal — this is where DO is lowest.
Temperature Corrections
For BOD: $\theta = 1.135$ (4–20°C) or $1.056$ (21–30°C). For reaeration: $\theta = 1.024$. Higher temperatures increase reaction rates.
BOD₅ is NOT the ultimate BOD. The 5-day test only captures about 68% of the ultimate BOD (at k = 0.23/day). Always check whether the problem gives BOD₅ or L₀ — they are different values.
The BOD remaining at time t is L_0 – BOD_t = L_0 × e^(–kt). If you see "BOD remaining" vs. "BOD exerted," they add up to L_0.

problems.statement: A wastewater sample has an ultimate BOD of $L_0 = 300 \text{ mg/L}$ and a decay rate of $k = 0.23 \text{ day}^{-1}$ (base $e$). What is the $BOD_5$?
problems.eli5: BOD₅ = L₀(1 – e^(–kt)) = 300(1 – e^(–0.23×5)) = 300(1 – e^(–1.15)) = 300(1 – 0.317) = 300 × 0.683 = 205 ≈ 204 mg/L. The 300 mg/L choice gives the ultimate BOD, not the 5-day BOD. The 96 mg/L choice gives the BOD remaining (L₀ – BOD₅ = 96), not the BOD exerted. The 150 mg/L choice assumes BOD₅ = L₀/2.
problems.hint: Use BOD_t = L₀(1 – e^(–kt)) with t = 5 days.
traps: Reporting the ultimate BOD (300 mg/L) as the BOD₅ — the 5-day value is always less than ultimate
Computing the BOD remaining (L₀ e^(–kt) = 96) instead of the BOD exerted

problems.statement: A lab measures $BOD_5 = 180 \text{ mg/L}$ for a sample with $k = 0.20 \text{ day}^{-1}$ (base $e$). What is the ultimate BOD ($L_0$)?
problems.eli5: Rearrange: L₀ = BOD₅/(1 – e^(–kt)) = 180/(1 – e^(–0.20 × 5)) = 180/(1 – e^(–1.0)) = 180/(1 – 0.368) = 180/0.632 = 285 mg/L. The ultimate BOD is always larger than the 5-day BOD because the test only captures partial decomposition. The 360 mg/L choice simply doubles BOD₅. The 180 mg/L choice assumes BOD₅ = L₀ (it's not). The 900 mg/L choice multiplies by 5.
problems.hint: Rearrange BOD_t = L₀(1 – e^(–kt)) to solve for L₀ = BOD₅/(1 – e^(–k×5)).
traps: Assuming BOD₅ = L₀ — the 5-day test captures only about 63% of the ultimate BOD (at this k value)
Using the wrong base for k — make sure k is base e (natural), not base 10

problems.statement: A BOD rate constant at 20°C is $k_{20} = 0.23 \text{ day}^{-1}$. Using the temperature correction with $\theta = 1.056$, what is the rate constant at $T = 28\degree\text{C}$?
problems.eli5: k_T = k₂₀ × θ^(T – 20) = 0.23 × 1.056^(28 – 20) = 0.23 × 1.056^8. 1.056^8: 1.056² = 1.1151, 1.056⁴ = 1.2434, 1.056⁸ = 1.5462. k₂₈ = 0.23 × 1.546 = 0.356 ≈ 0.35 day⁻¹. Higher temperature speeds up biodegradation. The 0.46 day⁻¹ option simply doubles k. The 0.15 day⁻¹ option inverts the formula (θ^(20–T)). The 0.23 day⁻¹ option assumes temperature has no effect.
problems.hint: Use k_T = k₂₀θ^(T−20). For T > 20°C, the rate constant increases.
traps: Using (20 – T) instead of (T – 20) in the exponent — gives a smaller k for higher T, which is backwards
Mixing up θ values for different processes — BOD uses 1.056 (21–30°C), reaeration uses 1.024

water-resources/water-treatment.name: Water & Wastewater Treatment
water-resources/water-treatment.application: Civil engineers design and evaluate treatment processes for drinking water and wastewater. You size clarifiers based on overflow rate, compute the food-to-microorganism ratio for activated sludge, and determine solids residence time. On the FE, expect problems computing overflow rate for a settling basin, determining treatment efficiency, and applying activated sludge design parameters.

content.body: Water and wastewater treatment involves physical, chemical, and biological processes to remove contaminants. Clarifier design and activated sludge parameters appear most frequently on the FE.
Clarifier Design

The overflow rate ($v_o$) is the critical settling velocity — particles with a settling velocity greater than $v_o$ will be removed. Typical values: primary clarifier 800–1,200 gpd/ft²; secondary clarifier 400–800 gpd/ft².
Where $V$ is the tank volume and $Q$ is the flow rate. Typical primary clarifier detention time: 2 hours.
Activated Sludge
Where $S_0$ is influent BOD concentration, $V$ is aeration basin volume, and $X_A$ is mixed liquor suspended solids (MLSS). Typical F:M = 0.2–0.4 for conventional activated sludge.

content.label: Solids residence time (SRT or mean cell residence time)

content.body: Where $Q_w$ is waste sludge flow, $X_w$ is waste sludge solids concentration, $Q_e$ is effluent flow, and $X_e$ is effluent solids concentration. SRT typically ranges from 4–15 days for conventional systems.
Settling Velocity
A particle settles if its settling velocity exceeds the overflow rate ($v_s > v_o$). For discrete particles, Stokes’ Law applies in the laminar range.
Overflow rate = Q/A has units of velocity (gpd/ft² or m/d). Think of it as the upward velocity of water in the tank — any particle that settles faster than this will be captured.

Don't confuse SRT (θ_c) with HRT (θ). SRT is the average time solids spend in the system (days to weeks). HRT is the average time water spends in the tank (hours). They are completely different parameters.

problems.statement: A primary clarifier treats a flow of $Q = 2.0 \text{ MGD}$. The tank is circular with a diameter of $60 \text{ ft}$. What is the overflow rate?
problems.eli5: Overflow rate = Q/A. A = π(60)²/4 = 2,827 ft². Q = 2.0 MGD = 2,000,000 gpd. v_o = 2,000,000/2,827 = 708 gpd/ft². This is within the typical range for primary clarifiers (800–1,200), a bit low. The $1{,}415 \text{ gpd/ft}^2$ distractor comes from doubling the correct rate (treating the area as half its true value). The $354 \text{ gpd/ft}^2$ distractor divides the answer by 2 for no reason. The $10{,}610 \text{ gpd/ft}^2$ distractor uses the circumference instead of the area.
problems.hint: Overflow rate = Q/A_surface. Convert MGD to gpd. Area = πD²/4.
traps: Forgetting to convert MGD to gpd (multiply by 1,000,000)
Using the diameter in the area formula without squaring or dividing by 4

problems.statement: An aeration basin treats $Q = 4{,}000 \text{ m}^3\text{/day}$ of wastewater with influent BOD $S_0 = 200 \text{ mg/L}$. The basin volume is $V = 2{,}000 \text{ m}^3$ and MLSS is $X_A = 3{,}000 \text{ mg/L}$. What is the food-to-microorganism (F:M) ratio?
problems.eli5: F:M = QS₀/(VX_A) = (4,000 × 200)/(2,000 × 3,000) = 800,000/6,000,000 = 0.133 ≈ 0.13 day⁻¹. Note that mg/L cancel, leaving m³/day / m³ = day⁻¹. This F:M is on the low end of conventional range (0.2–0.4), closer to extended aeration. The $1.33 \text{ day}^{-1}$ option uses V·X_A with the MLSS scaled down by a factor of ten (a misplaced decimal). The $0.40 \text{ day}^{-1}$ option drops the MLSS term, dividing only by V at the wrong scale. The $0.027 \text{ day}^{-1}$ option mistakenly squares V in the denominator.
problems.hint: F:M = (Q × S₀)/(V × X_A). Make sure units are consistent.
traps: Forgetting to include MLSS (X_A) in the denominator — gives the volumetric loading rate instead of F:M
Getting confused by units — mg/L cancels between S₀ and X_A, leaving 1/time

problems.statement: An activated sludge system has: aeration volume $V = 1{,}500 \text{ m}^3$, MLSS $X_A = 3{,}500 \text{ mg/L}$, waste sludge flow $Q_w = 50 \text{ m}^3\text{/day}$ at concentration $X_w = 10{,}000 \text{ mg/L}$, and effluent flow $Q_e = 5{,}000 \text{ m}^3\text{/day}$ with $X_e = 20 \text{ mg/L}$. What is the solids residence time (SRT)?
problems.eli5: θ_c = VX_A / (Q_wX_w + Q_eX_e) = (1,500 × 3,500) / (50 × 10,000 + 5,000 × 20) = 5,250,000 / (500,000 + 100,000) = 5,250,000 / 600,000 = 8.75 ≈ 8.8 days. This is within the typical range for conventional activated sludge (4–15 days). The 0.3 days choice computes V/Q (HRT = 0.3 days = 7.2 hours) instead of SRT. The 10.5 days choice ignores the effluent solids term (5,250,000 / 500,000 = 10.5 days). The 30.0 days choice uses an incorrect denominator.
problems.hint: SRT = (total solids in system)/(total solids leaving per day). Include both waste sludge and effluent.
traps: Confusing SRT (θ_c, days) with HRT (θ, hours) — SRT divides solids, not volume, by flow
Ignoring the effluent solids term (Q_eX_e) — even low concentrations at high flow rates contribute significantly
Using concentrations without multiplying by flow rates in the denominator

water-resources/drinking-water-treatment.name: Drinking Water Treatment & Disinfection
water-resources/drinking-water-treatment.application: Civil engineers design the conventional surface-water treatment train — coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, and disinfection — to turn raw water into safe drinking water. On the FE, expect to compute a filter loading rate, set a chlorine dose from demand plus required residual, and apply the CT concept for disinfection credit.

content.body: A conventional surface-water plant treats water in sequence: rapid mix (coagulation), flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, and disinfection. Each step targets a different contaminant class, and the FE tends to test one unit at a time.
Coagulation & Flocculation

A coagulant (commonly alum) is added in a rapid-mix basin to neutralize the charge on suspended colloids so they can stick together. Gentle stirring in the flocculation basin then grows small particles into settleable floc, which is removed in the sedimentation (clarifier) step that follows.
Filtration

After settling, water passes through a granular (rapid sand or dual-media) filter. The filtration rate is the flow divided by the plan area of the filter, with typical rapid-sand values of 2--10 gpm/ft². Media are described by effective size ($d_{10}$) and uniformity coefficient ($UC = d_{60}/d_{10}$).
Disinfection
Disinfection (usually chlorination) inactivates pathogens. The applied dose must satisfy the chlorine demand of the water and still leave a target residual:

content.label: C = residual concentration (mg/L), t₁₀ = 10th-percentile contact time (min)

content.body: Disinfection credit is measured by CT — the product of residual concentration and contact time. Higher CT means more inactivation. The Surface Water Treatment Rule requires, for example, 3-log (99.9%) removal/inactivation of Giardia and 4-log (99.99%) of viruses.
CT uses t₁₀ — the time for the fastest 10% of water to pass through the contact basin — not the theoretical detention time V/Q. Baffling raises t₁₀ toward the ideal plug-flow value.

Chlorine DOSE is not the same as RESIDUAL. The dose you feed equals the demand consumed by the water plus the residual you want to keep. If a problem gives demand and a target residual, add them to get the dose.

problems.statement: A rapid sand filter bed is $20\text{ ft}$ long by $15\text{ ft}$ wide and treats a flow of $Q = 1{,}350\text{ gpm}$. What is the filtration (loading) rate?
problems.eli5: Filtration rate = Q/A_plan. The plan area is 20 × 15 = 300 ft². So v_s = 1,350/300 = 4.5 gpm/ft², comfortably inside the typical rapid-sand range of 2--10 gpm/ft². The 9.0 gpm/ft² option uses only half the area (15 ft × 10 ft = 150 ft²). The 0.22 gpm/ft² option inverts the ratio (A/Q). The 45 gpm/ft² option drops a zero in the area (uses 30 ft² instead of 300 ft²).
problems.hint: Filtration rate is the flow divided by the filter plan area (length × width).
traps: Using the bed volume or depth instead of the plan (surface) area
Inverting the ratio to get A/Q instead of Q/A

problems.statement: Raw water exerts a chlorine demand of $2.4\text{ mg/L}$, and the plant must maintain a free residual of $0.6\text{ mg/L}$. For a flow of $Q = 4{,}000\text{ m}^3\text{/day}$, what mass of chlorine must be fed per day?
problems.eli5: First the dose: Dose = Demand + Residual = 2.4 + 0.6 = 3.0 mg/L. Then the mass feed: since 1 mg/L = 1 g/m³, mass = 3.0 g/m³ × 4,000 m³/day = 12,000 g/day = 12.0 kg/day. The 9.6 kg/day option uses only the demand (2.4) and forgets the residual. The 2.4 kg/day option just echoes the demand value with a wrong conversion. The 120 kg/day option slips a factor of 10 in the unit conversion.
problems.hint: Dose = demand + residual. Then mass/day = dose (mg/L = g/m³) × flow (m³/day), converted to kg.
traps: Feeding only the residual or only the demand instead of their sum
Botching the mg/L → g/m³ → kg/day conversion

problems.statement: A chlorine contact basin maintains a free residual of $C = 1.5\text{ mg/L}$. The disinfection guideline requires $CT = 90\text{ mg·min/L}$. What contact time $t_{10}$ is needed to achieve this CT?
problems.eli5: CT = C × t₁₀, so t₁₀ = CT/C = 90/1.5 = 60 min. The 135 min choice multiplies (90 × 1.5) instead of dividing. The 6 min choice divides by 15 (decimal slip). The 0.017 min choice inverts the whole thing (C/CT).
problems.hint: Rearrange CT = C × t₁₀ to t₁₀ = CT/C.
traps: Multiplying C by CT instead of dividing
Using the theoretical detention time V/Q in place of t₁₀

water-resources/water-quality-standards.name: Drinking Water Standards & Hardness
water-resources/water-quality-standards.application: Civil engineers design treatment to meet federal water-quality regulations and to deliver water of acceptable hardness. On the FE, expect to distinguish enforceable health-based standards from aesthetic ones, compute total hardness expressed as CaCO₃, and determine the removal efficiency a process must achieve to meet a discharge limit.

content.body: Under the Safe Drinking Water Act, the EPA sets two tiers of standards. PRIMARY standards are health-based, enforceable Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs). SECONDARY standards are non-enforceable guidelines for aesthetic qualities like taste, color, and odor.
Primary vs. Secondary Standards

Primary (enforceable, health) examples: arsenic 0.010 mg/L, nitrate (as N) 10 mg/L, lead action level 0.015 mg/L, and a turbidity treatment technique (≤ 0.3 NTU in 95% of samples). Secondary (aesthetic) examples: iron 0.3 mg/L, manganese 0.05 mg/L, total dissolved solids 500 mg/L, chloride 250 mg/L, and pH 6.5--8.5.

On the wastewater side, the Clean Water Act regulates discharges through NPDES permits. Conventional secondary treatment must achieve roughly 30 mg/L BOD₅ and 30 mg/L total suspended solids in the effluent (about 85% removal).
Hardness as CaCO₃
Hardness is caused mainly by divalent cations — calcium (Ca²⁺) and magnesium (Mg²⁺). To add them on a common basis, each is converted to an equivalent concentration of calcium carbonate.
Classification (mg/L as CaCO₃): soft < 60, moderately hard 60--120, hard 120--180, very hard > 180.
For calcium, 50/20 = 2.5, so multiply Ca²⁺ (mg/L) by 2.5. For magnesium, 50/12.15 ≈ 4.12. Convert each ion separately, then add.
Primary standards are legally enforceable and protect health; secondary standards are advisory and address aesthetics. A bad taste or rusty color violates only a secondary guideline — not the law.

problems.statement: A water sample contains $\text{Ca}^{2+} = 40\text{ mg/L}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+} = 24.3\text{ mg/L}$. Using equivalent weights of $20$ for Ca²⁺ and $12.15$ for Mg²⁺, what is the total hardness expressed as CaCO₃?
problems.eli5: Convert each ion to CaCO₃ by multiplying by 50/EW. Ca: 40 × (50/20) = 40 × 2.5 = 100. Mg: 24.3 × (50/12.15) = 24.3 × 4.12 = 100. Total = 100 + 100 = 200 mg/L as CaCO₃ (very hard). The 64.3 mg/L option just adds the raw ion concentrations (40 + 24.3) without converting. The 100 mg/L option counts only the calcium. The 150 mg/L option is a partial conversion.
problems.hint: Multiply each ion by 50/EW, then add. Ca uses 50/20 = 2.5; Mg uses 50/12.15 ≈ 4.12.
traps: Adding raw ion concentrations without converting to CaCO₃
Using the same multiplier for Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ — their equivalent weights differ

problems.statement: A wastewater treatment plant receives influent with $BOD_5 = 240\text{ mg/L}$ and must meet a secondary-treatment effluent limit of $30\text{ mg/L}$. What overall BOD removal efficiency is required?
problems.eli5: Removal efficiency = (in − out)/in = (240 − 30)/240 = 210/240 = 0.875 = 87.5%. The 12.5% option is the fraction REMAINING (30/240 = 12.5%), not the fraction removed. The 8.0% option mis-scales the ratio. The 30% option just reports the effluent number (30 mg/L) as a percent.
problems.hint: Efficiency = (influent − effluent)/influent, expressed as a percent.
traps: Computing the fraction remaining (effluent/influent) instead of the fraction removed
Forgetting to divide by the influent concentration

problems.statement: Which of the following is an enforceable, health-based PRIMARY drinking water standard under the Safe Drinking Water Act?
problems.eli5: Arsenic is a toxic contaminant with a legally enforceable, health-based MCL (0.010 mg/L) — a primary standard. Iron, total dissolved solids, and color are all SECONDARY standards: they affect taste, staining, and appearance, not health, and are advisory rather than enforceable.
problems.hint: Primary standards protect health and are enforceable; secondary standards are aesthetic (taste, color, staining) and advisory.

steps.text: Primary standards are enforceable MCLs that protect human health.
Iron, TDS, and color affect aesthetics (staining, taste, appearance) → secondary, advisory.
Arsenic has a health-based MCL → it is the primary standard.

traps: Assuming any numeric limit is enforceable — secondary standards are advisory
Confusing aesthetic parameters (iron, color, TDS) with health-based contaminants

structural/determinacy-stability.name: Determinacy & Stability
structural/determinacy-stability.application: Before analyzing any structure, a civil engineer must determine whether it is stable and whether it is statically determinate or indeterminate. Counting members, reactions, and joints tells you if the structure has enough constraints or too many. If the count fails, the structure is a mechanism and will collapse. On the FE, expect problems classifying trusses and frames using the standard equations.

content.body: The first step in structural analysis is classification: is the structure stable, and is it determinate or indeterminate? Two equations handle the two most common structure types.
Plane Truss

Where $m$ = number of members, $r$ = number of independent reaction components, and $j$ = number of joints. If $m + r < 2j$, the truss is unstable. If $m + r = 2j$, it is stable and statically determinate. If $m + r > 2j$, it is stable and statically indeterminate.
Plane Frame
Where $c$ = number of condition equations (e.g., internal hinges where moment = 0). The same logic applies: less than means unstable, equal means determinate, greater means indeterminate.
Degree of Indeterminacy
For trusses, the degree of indeterminacy = $(m + r) - 2j$. For frames, it is $(3m + r) - (3j + c)$. This tells you how many extra unknowns exist beyond what equilibrium can solve.

A structure can satisfy the numerical count and still be unstable if reactions are concurrent (all pass through one point) or parallel (all act in the same direction). Always check the arrangement, not just the numbers.
Count reactions carefully: a pin support gives 2 components (horizontal + vertical), a roller gives 1, and a fixed support gives 3 (horizontal + vertical + moment).

problems.statement: A planar truss has $m = 11$ members, $r = 3$ reaction components, and $j = 7$ joints. How is the structure classified?
problems.eli5: For a plane truss: m + r = 11 + 3 = 14, and 2j = 2(7) = 14. Since m + r = 2j, the truss is stable and statically determinate. This means you can find all member forces and reactions using equilibrium equations alone. If m + r were greater than 2j, you would need compatibility equations (indeterminate). If less, the structure would be a mechanism.
problems.hint: Use the plane truss equation: compare m + r to 2j.

steps.text: Since $m + r = 2j = 14$, the truss is stable and statically determinate.

traps: Confusing the truss formula (m + r vs 2j) with the frame formula (3m + r vs 3j + c)
Forgetting to count all reaction components — a pin gives 2, a roller gives 1

problems.statement: A portal frame consists of $m = 3$ members and $j = 4$ joints. The left base has a pin support and the right base has a fixed support. There are no internal hinges ($c = 0$). What is the degree of static indeterminacy?
problems.eli5: For a plane frame: compare 3m + r to 3j + c. Reactions: pin = 2 components, fixed = 3 components, so r = 2 + 3 = 5. Then 3m + r = 3(3) + 5 = 14, and 3j + c = 3(4) + 0 = 12. Since 14 > 12, the frame is indeterminate, and the degree = 14 – 12 = 2. That means you need two compatibility equations beyond equilibrium to solve for all unknowns. The "0 (determinate)" choice would require 3m + r = 3j + c exactly. The "3 degrees" choice would happen if both supports were fixed (r = 6, giving 3(3)+6 = 15 vs 12 = 3 degrees).
problems.hint: Count reactions: pin gives 2, fixed gives 3. Then use the frame formula 3m + r vs 3j + c.
traps: Forgetting that a fixed support provides 3 reaction components (not 2)
Using the truss formula (m + r vs 2j) instead of the frame formula (3m + r vs 3j + c)

problems.statement: A planar truss has $m = 9$ members, $r = 3$ reaction components, and $j = 6$ joints. All three reaction components are vertical (parallel). Is the truss stable?
problems.eli5: Numerically: m + r = 9 + 3 = 12, and 2j = 2(6) = 12. The equation says determinate. But the equation is a necessary condition, not sufficient. If all three reaction components are parallel (all vertical), the structure cannot resist any horizontal force — it slides sideways. This is called geometric instability. The truss is unstable even though the count checks out. Always verify that reactions are not all parallel or concurrent. The "stable and determinate" choice assumes the count alone guarantees stability — it does not.
problems.hint: The determinacy equation is necessary but not sufficient. What happens if you apply a horizontal force?

steps.text: The numerical check passes — suggests determinate.
No horizontal reaction exists, so $\Sigma F_x = 0$ cannot be satisfied for any horizontal load. The structure is geometrically unstable.

problems.handbookFormula: m + r = 2j \text{ (necessary but not sufficient for stability)}
traps: Assuming the numerical count alone guarantees stability — arrangement matters
Forgetting that parallel reactions cannot resist loads perpendicular to their direction
Confusing this with the indeterminate case (m + r > 2j) — even indeterminate structures can be unstable if reactions are improperly arranged

structural/truss-analysis-methods.name: Truss Analysis: Joints & Sections
structural/truss-analysis-methods.application: Finding member forces in a determinate truss is a bread-and-butter FE structural-analysis skill. The method of joints gets you forces at a connection; the method of sections cuts straight to one member without solving the whole truss. Knowing when to use each — and spotting zero-force members instantly — saves real time on the exam.

content.body: A truss carries load through axial forces only — every member is in pure tension or compression. Sign convention: treat unknown forces as TENSION (arrow pulling away from the joint). A negative answer then means the member is in compression.
Method of Joints

Isolate one joint and apply the two equilibrium equations $\sum F_x = 0$ and $\sum F_y = 0$. Because a joint gives only two equations, start at a joint with at most two unknown members. Resolve each inclined member into components using its geometry (rise/run).
Method of Sections

To find one specific member force without marching through every joint, cut an imaginary section through the truss (through at most three members whose forces are unknown) and treat one side as a rigid body. Take moments about the point where the other two cut members intersect — that isolates the force you want in a single equation.

content.label: Pick the moment center to eliminate the other two cut members

content.body: Zero-Force Members

Two quick rules: (1) at an unloaded joint with only two non-collinear members, both are zero-force; (2) at an unloaded joint with three members where two are collinear, the third (non-collinear) member is zero-force. Identifying these first removes members from the problem.

Use the method of sections when the problem asks for ONE member force (especially a chord member mid-truss). Use the method of joints when you need several forces or you're near a support. Always find the support reactions first.
A negative member force is not an error — it means your tension assumption was wrong and the member is in compression. Report the magnitude with the correct sense (T or C).

problems.statement: At joint A, a $500\text{ lb}$ vertical (downward) load is carried by two members: a horizontal member AB and a diagonal member AC oriented at $45^\circ$ above the horizontal. Using the method of joints, what is the force in diagonal AC?
problems.eli5: Only the diagonal can resist the vertical load — the horizontal member has no vertical component. So $\sum F_y = 0$ gives $F_{AC}\sin 45^\circ = 500$, hence $F_{AC} = 500/0.707 = 707$ lb. The 500 lb choice forgets to divide by $\sin 45^\circ$. The 354 lb choice multiplies by $\sin 45^\circ$ instead of dividing.
problems.hint: Only the diagonal has a vertical component — use $\sum F_y = 0$ at joint A.

steps.text: Horizontal member AB carries no vertical force, so the diagonal must balance the load.

traps: Forgetting to divide by sin 45° and reporting 500 lb
Multiplying by sin 45° (354) instead of dividing

problems.statement: A parallel-chord truss has panel length $4\text{ m}$ and height $3\text{ m}$. The left support reaction is $30\text{ kN}$ (upward) and there are no loads within the first panel. Taking a vertical section through the first panel and summing moments about the top-chord joint at the far end of the panel, what is the force in the bottom chord?
problems.eli5: Summing moments about the top joint kills the diagonal and the top chord (they pass through or are arms about that point), leaving only the bottom chord. The reaction acts $4\text{ m}$ horizontally from the moment center; the bottom chord acts at the $3\text{ m}$ height. So $30(4) = F_{BC}(3)$, giving $F_{BC} = 120/3 = 40\text{ kN}$ tension. The 120 kN option forgets to divide by the 3 m height.
problems.hint: Take moments about the top joint so only the bottom chord remains: reaction × panel length = force × height.

steps.text: Moment center at the top joint eliminates the top chord and diagonal.
$\sum M = 0$: reaction times its horizontal arm equals bottom-chord force times the height.

traps: Forgetting to divide by the truss height (reporting 120 kN)
Using the height as the reaction's moment arm instead of the panel length

problems.statement: At an unloaded joint, three members meet: two are collinear (in a straight line through the joint) and the third comes in at an angle. No external load or reaction acts at this joint. What is the force in the angled (third) member?

choices.text: Equal to the force in the collinear members

problems.eli5: Set up equilibrium perpendicular to the two collinear members. The two collinear members have no component in that perpendicular direction, and there's no external load — so the only force with a component there is the angled member, which must therefore be zero. This is the classic zero-force-member rule.
problems.hint: Sum forces perpendicular to the two collinear members.

steps.text: The two collinear members act along one line; resolve forces perpendicular to that line.
Only the angled member has a perpendicular component, and there is no external load to balance it.
Therefore the angled member carries zero force (zero-force member).

problems.handbookPage: p. 97, Plane Truss: Method of Joints
traps: Assuming every member carries load — zero-force members are common at unloaded joints
Confusing this with the two-member unloaded-joint rule

structural/deflection-virtual-work.name: Deflection of Determinate Structures
structural/deflection-virtual-work.application: The FE asks you to find how far a determinate beam, truss, or frame moves under load — for serviceability checks and to set up indeterminate analysis. The unit-load (virtual work) method is the general tool, and for common beams you simply look up a deflection formula. Both show up on the exam.

content.body: To find the deflection (or rotation) at a point, apply a VIRTUAL unit load there in the direction you want, then integrate the product of the real and virtual internal forces. This 'unit-load method' works for any determinate structure.
Trusses — Unit-Load Method

content.label: N = real member force, n = force from a unit load at the point

content.body: For each member, multiply the real axial force $N$ by the force $n$ produced by a unit load at the joint of interest, times $L/AE$, and sum over all members.
Beams & Frames — Unit-Load Method

content.label: M = real moment diagram, m = moment from the virtual unit load

content.body: Standard Beam Deflections (lookups)

On the exam, first check whether the beam/loading matches a standard case in the handbook deflection table — if so, just plug into the formula. Reserve the full unit-load integral for non-standard cases or truss/frame deflections.
Watch the powers of L: a point load gives $L^3$, a distributed load gives $L^4$. And keep units consistent — mixing kN·m² with N·mm² is the #1 numerical error.

problems.statement: Using the unit-load method for a truss, $\delta = \sum nNL/AE$. For one member, the real force is $N = 50\text{ kN}$, the virtual (unit-load) force is $n = 0.5$, the length is $L = 4\text{ m}$, and $AE = 200{,}000\text{ kN}$. What is this member's contribution to the joint deflection?
problems.eli5: Plug into $nNL/AE = (0.5)(50)(4)/200{,}000 = 100/200{,}000 = 0.0005\text{ m} = 0.5\text{ mm}$. The trap is units: $0.0005\text{ m}$ is $0.5\text{ mm}$, not $5\text{ mm}$ (the $5.0\text{ mm}$ choice) or $0.05\text{ mm}$ (the $0.05\text{ mm}$ choice).
problems.hint: Compute nNL then divide by AE; convert meters to millimeters carefully.
traps: Unit slip: writing 5 mm or 0.05 mm instead of 0.5 mm
Forgetting to multiply by the virtual force n

problems.statement: A simply supported beam of length $L = 6\text{ m}$ carries a central point load $P = 20\text{ kN}$. The flexural rigidity is $EI = 40{,}000\text{ kN·m}^2$. What is the maximum deflection?
problems.eli5: Central point load on a simple span uses $\delta = PL^3/48EI = 20(6^3)/(48 \times 40{,}000) = 4320/1{,}920{,}000 = 0.00225\text{ m} = 2.25\text{ mm}$. The 9 mm choice uses $PL^3/12EI$ by mistake; the 1.13 mm choice halves the answer.
problems.hint: Central point load, simple span → $PL^3/48EI$.

steps.text: Identify the standard case: simple span, central P.

traps: Using the wrong constant (e.g. 12EI) in the denominator
Mixing the point-load (L³) and UDL (L⁴) formulas

problems.statement: A cantilever beam of length $L = 3\text{ m}$ carries a point load $P = 10\text{ kN}$ at its free end. With $EI = 20{,}000\text{ kN·m}^2$, what is the tip deflection?
problems.eli5: End-loaded cantilever: $\delta = PL^3/3EI = 10(27)/(3 \times 20{,}000) = 270/60{,}000 = 0.0045\text{ m} = 4.5\text{ mm}$. The 2.25 mm distractor wrongly uses $PL^3/6EI$ (an erroneous denominator constant of 6 instead of 3); the 13.5 mm distractor drops the factor entirely and uses $PL^3/EI$.
problems.hint: End-loaded cantilever → $PL^3/3EI$.

steps.text: Standard case: cantilever, end point load.

traps: Using a simple-span constant (48EI) for a cantilever
Dropping the factor of 3 in the denominator

structural/indeterminate-structures.name: Elementary Indeterminate Structures
structural/indeterminate-structures.application: Real structures are usually statically indeterminate — continuous beams, fixed-end members, propped cantilevers. The FE keeps this elementary: count the degree of indeterminacy, then handle a single redundant with the force method (consistent deformations) or recall standard results like the propped-cantilever reaction and fixed-end moments.

content.body: A structure is statically indeterminate when it has more reaction/internal unknowns than equilibrium equations. The degree of static indeterminacy (DSI) is how many extra unknowns there are — the number of redundants you must release to make it determinate.
Degree of Indeterminacy

content.label: m = members, r = reactions, n = joints (frames), c = condition eqns, j = joints (truss)

content.body: Quick beam check: a beam with $r$ reaction components and no internal hinges is indeterminate to degree $r - 3$. A propped cantilever (fixed + roller) has $3 + 1 = 4$ reactions, so $DSI = 4 - 3 = 1$.
Force Method (Consistent Deformations)

For one redundant: remove it to get a determinate 'primary' structure. Find the deflection at the released point due to the loads ($\delta_{10}$) and due to a unit value of the redundant ($\delta_{11}$). Compatibility requires the real deflection there to be zero, so the redundant is $R = -\delta_{10}/\delta_{11}$.
Standard Results Worth Memorizing

On the FE, recognizing the standard case usually beats setting up the full force method. Memorize the propped-cantilever prop reaction (3wL/8) and the fixed-end moments (wL²/12 for UDL, PL/8 for a central point load).
Don't confuse fixed-end moment wL²/12 with the simple-span maximum moment wL²/8 — the fixed ends pull the moment down at midspan and create end moments instead.

problems.statement: A propped cantilever beam is fixed at one end and supported on a roller at the other. What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
problems.eli5: Count reactions: the fixed end provides 3 (horizontal, vertical, moment) and the roller provides 1 (vertical), giving 4. A planar beam has 3 equilibrium equations, so $DSI = 4 - 3 = 1$ — indeterminate to the first degree. The "0" option would be a determinate beam (e.g., simply supported).
problems.hint: Count reaction components, subtract the 3 equilibrium equations.

steps.text: Fixed end = 3 reactions; roller = 1 reaction; total $r = 4$.

traps: Counting the fixed end as 2 reactions (it provides 3, including the moment)
Treating the propped cantilever as determinate (DSI = 0)

problems.statement: A propped cantilever (fixed at one end, roller at the other) of length $L = 8\text{ m}$ carries a uniformly distributed load $w = 12\text{ kN/m}$. What is the reaction at the propped (roller) end?
problems.eli5: The standard propped-cantilever result for a UDL gives the prop (roller) reaction $R = 3wL/8 = 3(12)(8)/8 = 36\text{ kN}$. The 48 kN choice is the simple-span half-load $wL/2$, ignoring that the fixed end takes more (it carries 60 kN). The 24 kN choice uses $wL/4$.
problems.hint: Propped cantilever under UDL: prop reaction = 3wL/8.
traps: Using wL/2 = 48 kN (the simple-span reaction) instead of 3wL/8
Splitting the load evenly between supports

problems.statement: A beam fixed at both ends spans $L = 6\text{ m}$ and carries a uniformly distributed load $w = 10\text{ kN/m}$. What is the magnitude of the fixed-end moment at each support?
problems.eli5: Fixed-fixed beam under UDL: the fixed-end moment is $wL^2/12 = 10(6^2)/12 = 360/12 = 30\text{ kN·m}$. The 45 kN·m choice uses the simple-span midspan moment $wL^2/8$ by mistake — that's the wrong formula for a fixed end.
problems.hint: Fixed-fixed beam, UDL → fixed-end moment = wL²/12.

steps.text: Standard result for a fixed-fixed beam under UDL.

traps: Using wL²/8 = 45 kN·m (the simple-span moment) for the fixed end
Confusing the end moment with the reduced midspan moment (wL²/24)

structural/load-combinations.name: Loads & Load Combinations
structural/load-combinations.application: Every structural design begins with load combinations from ASCE 7. You factor dead, live, wind, snow, and seismic loads using prescribed multipliers to ensure adequate safety. LRFD (strength design) factors loads up and compares to nominal strength; ASD (allowable stress) uses unfactored loads against reduced allowable capacity. On the FE, expect problems computing the controlling factored load and applying live load reduction.

content.body: ASCE 7-16 defines two parallel sets of load combinations: LRFD (Load and Resistance Factor Design) and ASD (Allowable Stress Design). Both produce safe designs but use different philosophies.
LRFD Load Combinations
The key LRFD combinations are:
Where $D$ = dead load, $L$ = floor live load, $L_r$ = roof live load, $S$ = snow, $R$ = rain, $W$ = wind, $E$ = earthquake. The controlling combination produces the largest total factored load.
ASD Load Combinations

ASD combinations use unfactored (service) loads. The basic ones are $D$, $D + L$, and $D + 0.75L + 0.75(L_r \text{ or } S \text{ or } R)$. ASD compares service loads to allowable capacity = nominal strength / safety factor $\Omega$.
Live Load Reduction

Where $L_o$ is the unreduced live load, $K_{LL}$ is the live load element factor (4 for columns, 2 for beams), and $A_T$ is the tributary area in ft$^2$. The reduced load $L$ cannot be less than $0.50 L_o$ for one floor or $0.40 L_o$ for two or more floors.
LRFD Combination 2 usually controls for gravity-only loading (no wind or seismic). But when snow is large relative to floor live load, Combination 3 can control. Always check multiple combinations.
Quick check: if the problem says "LRFD" or "strength design," use factored loads. If it says "ASD" or "allowable stress," use service loads. Read the stem carefully before computing.

problems.statement: A beam supports a dead load of $D = 20 \text{ kips}$ and a floor live load of $L = 40 \text{ kips}$. What is the factored load using LRFD Combination 2 ($1.2D + 1.6L$)?
problems.eli5: 1.2D + 1.6L = 1.2(20) + 1.6(40) = 24 + 64 = 88 kips. This is the most common LRFD combination for gravity loading. The 60 kips option is the unfactored sum D + L. The 96 kips option applies 1.6 to both D and L, which is wrong — dead load gets a lower factor (1.2) because it is more predictable. The 84 kips option might come from using wrong factors like 1.4D + L.
problems.hint: Multiply D by 1.2 and L by 1.6, then add.
traps: Using unfactored loads (D + L = 60) instead of applying LRFD factors
Applying the 1.6 factor to dead load instead of 1.2 — dead load has a lower factor because it is more predictable

problems.statement: A column supports $D = 30 \text{ kips}$, $L = 50 \text{ kips}$ (floor live), and $S = 20 \text{ kips}$ (snow). No wind or seismic loads act. Which LRFD combination produces the largest factored axial load?
problems.eli5: Check each relevant combination. Combo 1: 1.4D = 1.4(30) = 42. Combo 2: 1.2D + 1.6L + 0.5S = 1.2(30) + 1.6(50) + 0.5(20) = 36 + 80 + 10 = 126. Combo 3: 1.2D + 1.6S + L = 1.2(30) + 1.6(20) + 1.0(50) = 36 + 32 + 50 = 118. The controlling case is Combo 2 at 126 kips.
