When floor live load is larger than snow, Combo 2 usually controls because L gets the 1.6 factor. When snow dominates, Combo 3 can control.
problems.hint: Evaluate at least Combos 1, 2, and 3. In Combo 2, L gets 1.6 and S gets 0.5. In Combo 3, S gets 1.6 and L gets 1.0.
traps: Only checking one combination instead of all relevant ones
Mixing up which load gets the 1.6 factor in Combo 2 vs. Combo 3 — Combo 2 puts 1.6 on L, Combo 3 puts 1.6 on S

problems.statement: An interior column ($K_{LL} = 4$) supports one floor with a tributary area of $A_T = 600 \text{ ft}^2$. The unreduced floor live load is $L_o = 50 \text{ psf}$. What is the reduced live load?
problems.eli5: L = L_o(0.25 + 15/√(K_LL × A_T)) = 50(0.25 + 15/√(4 × 600)) = 50(0.25 + 15/√2400) = 50(0.25 + 15/49.0) = 50(0.25 + 0.306) = 50(0.556) = 27.8 ≈ 28 psf. Check the minimum: for one floor, L ≥ 0.50 L_o = 25 psf. Since 28 > 25, the reduction is valid. The 50 psf option is the unreduced load. The 25 psf option is the minimum allowed — it would apply only if the formula gave a value below 25. The 13 psf option uses 0.25 × L_o, which misapplies the formula.
problems.hint: Use $L = L_o(0.25 + 15/\sqrt{K_{LL} A_T})$ and check against the minimum of $0.50 L_o$.

steps.text: Check minimum: $L \geq 0.50 L_o = 25$ psf. Since $28 > 25$, OK.

traps: Forgetting to check the minimum reduced live load (0.50 L_o for one floor, 0.40 L_o for two or more)
Using K_LL = 2 (for beams) instead of K_LL = 4 (for columns)
Forgetting that A_T must be in ft² to match the formula constants

structural/influence-lines.name: Influence Lines
structural/influence-lines.application: Influence lines tell you where to place a moving load to produce the maximum structural response — maximum reaction, shear, or moment at a specific point. This is critical for bridge design where truck loads travel across a span. On the FE, expect problems using influence line ordinates to compute maximum effects from one or more concentrated loads.

content.body: An influence line (IL) shows how a single response quantity (reaction, shear, or moment at a fixed point) varies as a unit load moves across the structure.
Influence Line for Reactions
For a simply supported beam of span $L$, the IL for the left reaction $R_A$ is a straight line from 1.0 at A to 0 at B. The IL ordinate at any position $x$ from A is $(L - x)/L$.
Influence Line for Shear

The IL for shear at a section located at distance $a$ from the left support has two key ordinates: just to the right of the section, the ordinate is $1 - a/L$; just to the left, it is $-a/L$. The IL jumps by exactly 1.0 at the section.
Influence Line for Moment

The IL for bending moment at a section at distance $a$ from the left support is triangular, with a peak ordinate of $a(L - a)/L$ at the section itself. At midspan ($a = L/2$), the peak ordinate is $L/4$.
Using Influence Lines

To find the effect of concentrated loads, multiply each load by the IL ordinate at its position and sum: $R = \Sigma P_i \times \eta_i$, where $\eta_i$ is the ordinate under load $P_i$. For a distributed load, multiply the load intensity by the area under the IL over the loaded region.
For maximum moment at midspan, place the largest load directly at midspan (where the IL ordinate is highest). For maximum shear, place the largest load just to the right of the section.
On the FE, influence line problems are almost always about simply supported beams. The IL shapes are straight lines — no curves. Just remember the key ordinates and interpolate linearly.

problems.statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 24 \text{ ft}$. A single concentrated load $P = 12 \text{ kips}$ can be placed anywhere on the beam. Using the influence line for shear at a section 6 ft from the left support, what is the maximum positive shear at that section?
problems.eli5: The IL for positive shear at a section has its maximum ordinate just to the right of the section. At a = 6 ft from the left support of a span L = 24 ft, the IL ordinate just to the right = 1 – a/L = 1 – 6/24 = 0.75. Maximum positive shear = P × 0.75 = 12 × 0.75 = 9.0 kips. The 12 kips choice assumes the full load becomes shear. The 3 kips choice uses the negative ordinate a/L = 0.25. The 6 kips choice is half the load.
problems.hint: The IL for shear at distance a from the left support has a maximum positive ordinate of 1 – a/L, just to the right of the section.

steps.text: IL ordinate for positive shear just to the right:

problems.handbookFormula: \text{IL for shear at section } a: \eta^+ = 1 - a/L
traps: Using a/L (the negative ordinate) instead of 1 – a/L (the positive ordinate)
Assuming the entire load becomes shear at the section — the load must be multiplied by the IL ordinate

problems.statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 30 \text{ ft}$. A concentrated load of $P = 20 \text{ kips}$ moves across the beam. What is the maximum bending moment at midspan?
problems.eli5: The IL for moment at midspan is a triangle with peak ordinate = L/4 at midspan. Peak ordinate = 30/4 = 7.5 ft. Maximum moment = P × (L/4) = 20 × 7.5 = 150 kip-ft. This occurs when the load is placed directly at midspan. The 300 kip-ft option might come from PL/2, confusing moment with the reaction formula. The 75 kip-ft option halves the correct answer. The 600 kip-ft option uses P × L = 20 × 30.
problems.hint: The IL for moment at midspan has a peak ordinate of L/4. Maximum M = P × L/4.
problems.handbookFormula: \text{IL for moment at midspan: peak ordinate} = L/4
traps: Confusing L/4 (IL ordinate for moment) with L/2 (the location of midspan)
Computing PL/4 instead of P × (L/4) — they are the same thing, but watch the units (the IL ordinate has units of length)

problems.statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 40 \text{ ft}$. Two concentrated loads, $P_1 = 20 \text{ kips}$ and $P_2 = 10 \text{ kips}$, are spaced 8 ft apart and move across the beam together. What is the maximum bending moment at midspan?
problems.eli5: The IL for moment at midspan (x = 20 ft) is triangular with peak = L/4 = 10 ft. The IL ordinate at any position x is x/2 for x ≤ 20 and (40 – x)/2 for x ≥ 20. To maximize the total moment, place the heavier load (20 kips) at midspan where the ordinate is highest (10 ft). The lighter load (10 kips) lands at x = 28 ft (or x = 12 ft), with ordinate (40–28)/2 = 6 ft. Total M = 20(10) + 10(6) = 200 + 60 = 260 kip-ft. The 240 kip-ft choice places both loads equidistant from midspan: at x=16 and x=24, both ordinates = 8, giving 20(8)+10(8) = 240. But putting the heavier load at the peak gives a larger total.
problems.hint: Place the heaviest load at the IL peak. Then compute the IL ordinate at the position of the other load. Sum P_i × η_i.

steps.text: IL for midspan moment (peak at x = 20 ft):

traps: Placing both loads symmetrically about midspan instead of placing the heavier load at the peak — the heavier load should go where the IL ordinate is highest
Only computing the effect of the larger load and ignoring the smaller one
Forgetting that both load positions are possible (loads can approach from either side)

structural/rc-flexure-shear.name: RC Beams: Flexure & Shear
structural/rc-flexure-shear.application: Reinforced concrete beam design is the most heavily tested structural design topic on the FE. You compute the Whitney stress block depth to find moment capacity, then check whether the concrete alone can carry the shear or if stirrups are needed. On the FE, expect problems computing nominal moment capacity from given reinforcement, checking shear adequacy, and finding required stirrup spacing.

content.body: ACI 318-14 uses the Whitney rectangular stress block to simplify the nonlinear concrete compression zone into an equivalent rectangle of depth $a$.
Flexure — Singly Reinforced Beams

Where $A_s$ is the steel area, $f_y$ is yield strength, $f_c'$ is concrete compressive strength, $b$ is beam width, and $d$ is effective depth (to centroid of tension steel). The design check is $\phi M_n \geq M_u$ with $\phi = 0.90$ for tension-controlled sections.
Shear

Where $\lambda = 1.0$ for normal weight concrete and $0.75$ for lightweight. The shear check is $\phi V_n \geq V_u$ with $\phi = 0.75$. Total shear strength $V_n = V_c + V_s$, where $V_s$ is the stirrup contribution.
If $V_u \leq \phi V_c / 2$, no stirrups are required. If $\phi V_c / 2 < V_u \leq \phi V_c$, provide minimum stirrups. If $V_u > \phi V_c$, compute $V_s$ and the required spacing $s$.

The effective depth d is NOT the total beam height h. It is measured from the top of the beam to the centroid of the tension steel: d = h – cover – stirrup diameter – bar radius. Getting d wrong changes everything.
For shear: V_c uses √f'c in PSI (not ksi). If f'c = 4,000 psi, then √f'c = 63.2 psi. A common mistake is using √4 = 2 (from ksi) and getting V_c off by a factor of 1,000.

problems.statement: A singly reinforced concrete beam has $b = 12 \text{ in.}$, $d = 18 \text{ in.}$, $A_s = 3.00 \text{ in}^2$, $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$, and $f_c' = 4 \text{ ksi}$. What is the nominal moment capacity $M_n$?
problems.eli5: First find a = A_s f_y / (0.85 f'c b) = 3.00 × 60 / (0.85 × 4 × 12) = 180/40.8 = 4.41 in. Then M_n = A_s f_y (d – a/2) = 3.00 × 60 × (18 – 4.41/2) = 180 × 15.80 = 2,843 kip-in = 237 kip-ft. The 270 kip-ft choice uses d instead of (d – a/2), which overestimates the lever arm. The 213 kip-ft choice is φM_n = 0.90 × 237 — the problem asks for nominal, not design. The 180 kip-ft choice computes A_s × f_y and divides by 12 without the lever arm.
problems.hint: Find a first, then compute M_n = A_s f_y (d – a/2). Convert kip-in to kip-ft by dividing by 12.
traps: Using d instead of (d – a/2) for the moment arm — you must subtract half the stress block depth
Reporting φM_n instead of M_n — read the question carefully to see if it asks for nominal or design capacity

problems.statement: A concrete beam has $b_w = 12 \text{ in.}$, $d = 20 \text{ in.}$, and $f_c' = 3{,}000 \text{ psi}$ (normal weight). The factored shear at the critical section is $V_u = 22 \text{ kips}$. What is the shear status?

choices.text: Only minimum stirrups — $\phi V_c / 2 < V_u \leq \phi V_c$

problems.eli5: V_c = 2λ√f'c × b_w × d = 2(1.0)√3000 × 12 × 20 = 2(54.77)(240) = 26,290 lb = 26.3 kips. φV_c = 0.75 × 26.3 = 19.7 kips. φV_c/2 = 9.9 kips. Since V_u = 22 > φV_c = 19.7, the concrete alone cannot carry the shear. Stirrups must be designed to carry V_s = V_u/φ – V_c = 22/0.75 – 26.3 = 29.3 – 26.3 = 3.0 kips. The "no stirrups needed" choice would apply if V_u ≤ 9.9. The "only minimum stirrups" choice would apply if 9.9 < V_u ≤ 19.7.
problems.hint: Compute V_c = 2√f'c × b_w × d (in lb), then compare V_u to φV_c and φV_c/2.

steps.latex: V_u = 22 > \phi V_c = 19.7 \implies \text{stirrups required with computed } V_s

traps: Using f'c in ksi instead of psi — √4 ≠ √4000; the formula uses psi units
Comparing V_u to V_c instead of φV_c — always include the φ = 0.75 factor on the capacity side

problems.statement: A concrete beam has $b_w = 14 \text{ in.}$, $d = 24 \text{ in.}$, $f_c' = 4{,}000 \text{ psi}$, and $V_u = 70 \text{ kips}$. Using #3 U-stirrups ($A_v = 0.22 \text{ in}^2$ for two legs) with $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$, what is the required stirrup spacing?
problems.eli5: First find V_c = 2(1.0)√4000 × 14 × 24 = 2(63.25)(336) = 42,504 lb = 42.5 kips. Then V_s = V_u/φ – V_c = 70/0.75 – 42.5 = 93.3 – 42.5 = 50.8 kips. Required spacing: s = A_v f_y d / V_s = 0.22 × 60 × 24 / 50.8 = 316.8/50.8 = 6.24 in. → use 6 in. Check max spacing: V_s = 50.8 < 4b_w d√f'c = 85.2 kips, so max spacing = d/2 = 12 in. Since 6 < 12, the required spacing of 6 in. controls. The 12 in. choice is the maximum spacing d/2, but the required V_s demands closer spacing. The 24 in. choice is a code maximum that only applies when V_s is very small.
problems.hint: Find V_s = V_u/φ – V_c, then s = A_v f_y d / V_s. Check against maximum spacing.

steps.text: Check max spacing: $V_s = 50.8 < 4 b_w d \sqrt{f_c'}  = 85.2$ kips, so max $s = d/2 = 12$ in. Since $6 < 12$, use $s = 6$ in.

traps: Using d/2 as the spacing without checking if V_s demands closer spacing — d/2 is a maximum, not the design spacing
Forgetting to divide V_u by φ before subtracting V_c — the equation is V_s = V_u/φ – V_c, not V_u – V_c
Using total stirrup bar area instead of A_v for two legs — for a U-stirrup, A_v = 2 × (one leg area)

structural/rc-columns.name: RC Columns
structural/rc-columns.application: Reinforced concrete columns carry axial load and moment simultaneously. On the FE, the most common problem type is computing the maximum axial load capacity of a short tied column using the ACI formula. You also need to know the reinforcement ratio limits and the difference between tension-controlled and compression-controlled sections. Interaction diagrams appear in the handbook but are rarely tested numerically.

content.body: ACI 318 limits the longitudinal reinforcement ratio and provides a simplified formula for the maximum axial capacity of short columns (no slenderness effects).
Reinforcement Ratio Limits

Where $A_{st}$ is the total area of longitudinal steel and $A_g$ is the gross cross-sectional area. Below 1% risks a brittle failure under bending; above 8% creates congestion and construction issues.
Short Tied Column Capacity

The 0.80 factor accounts for accidental eccentricity (columns never see truly concentric load). For tied columns under compression control, $\phi = 0.65$. For spiral columns, use 0.85 instead of 0.80 and $\phi = 0.75$.
Strain Classification
The resistance factor $\phi$ depends on the net tensile strain $\varepsilon_t$ in the extreme tension reinforcement:
$\varepsilon_t \geq 0.005$: tension-controlled, $\phi = 0.90$. $\varepsilon_t \leq 0.002$: compression-controlled, $\phi = 0.65$ (tied). Between: transition zone, $\phi = 0.48 + 83\varepsilon_t$.
The 0.80 factor is ONLY for columns. Beams use φM_n directly without the 0.80 reduction. If you see this factor in a problem, it is a column.
For pure axial capacity problems (no moment), just use the φP_n formula directly. The 0.85f'c term handles the concrete contribution and A_st f_y handles the steel.

problems.statement: A short tied column is $16 \text{ in.} \times 16 \text{ in.}$ with 8 #9 bars ($A_{st} = 8.00 \text{ in}^2$), $f_c' = 4 \text{ ksi}$, and $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$. What is the maximum design axial load $\phi P_n$?
problems.eli5: A_g = 16 × 16 = 256 in². φP_n = 0.80 × 0.65 × [0.85 × 4 × (256 – 8) + 8 × 60] = 0.52 × [3.4 × 248 + 480] = 0.52 × [843.2 + 480] = 0.52 × 1323.2 = 688 kips. The 1,323 kips option omits both the 0.80 factor and φ. The 860 kips option applies only φ = 0.65 without the 0.80 accidental eccentricity factor. The 1,058 kips option applies only 0.80 without φ. You need BOTH factors for tied columns.
problems.hint: Use φP_n = 0.80φ[0.85f'c(A_g – A_st) + A_st f_y] with φ = 0.65 for tied columns.
traps: Forgetting the 0.80 accidental eccentricity factor — this is unique to columns and does not apply to beams
Using φ = 0.90 (beam value) instead of φ = 0.65 (tied column under compression control)

problems.statement: A concrete column is $18 \text{ in.} \times 18 \text{ in.}$ with 4 #8 bars (each $A_b = 0.79 \text{ in}^2$). Is the reinforcement ratio within ACI limits?
problems.eli5: A_st = 4 × 0.79 = 3.16 in². A_g = 18 × 18 = 324 in². ρ_g = 3.16/324 = 0.00975 = 0.975%. ACI requires 0.01 ≤ ρ_g ≤ 0.08 (1% to 8%). Since 0.975% < 1%, the reinforcement is below the minimum. This means the column has insufficient steel to prevent a sudden brittle failure under combined axial load and bending. The fix is to add more bars or use larger bars. The "Yes — within the 1% to 8% range" choice would require ρ_g ≥ 0.01. The "At the exact minimum of 1%" choice would require exactly 0.01.
problems.hint: Compute ρ_g = A_st / A_g and compare to the ACI limits of 0.01 ≤ ρ_g ≤ 0.08.

steps.text: ACI limits: $0.01 \leq \rho_g \leq 0.08$. Since $0.00975 < 0.01$, the ratio is below minimum.

traps: Rounding 0.975% up to 1% and calling it adequate — ACI requires strictly ≥ 1%
Confusing bar area with bar diameter — #8 has diameter 1.000 in. but area 0.79 in²

problems.statement: A short tied column ($14 \text{ in.} \times 20 \text{ in.}$) has $A_{st} = 6.00 \text{ in}^2$, $f_c' = 5 \text{ ksi}$, and $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$. The factored axial load is $P_u = 550 \text{ kips}$. Is the column adequate?

choices.text: Cannot determine without an interaction diagram

problems.eli5: A_g = 14 × 20 = 280 in². Check ρ_g = 6.0/280 = 0.0214 (within 1–8% ✔). φP_n = 0.80(0.65)[0.85(5)(280 – 6) + 6(60)] = 0.52[4.25(274) + 360] = 0.52[1164.5 + 360] = 0.52 × 1524.5 = 793 kips. Since P_u = 550 < 793, the column is adequate. The 524 kips option might come from using φ = 0.65 but replacing 0.80 with some other factor. The 1,525 kips option is the value inside the brackets without applying 0.80φ. For pure axial load (no significant moment), this formula check is sufficient; an interaction diagram is needed only when significant moment acts simultaneously.
problems.hint: Compute φP_n using the tied column formula and compare to P_u.

steps.text: Compare: $P_u = 550 < \phi P_n = 793$ kips. The column is adequate.

traps: Forgetting to subtract A_st from A_g in the concrete term — the formula uses (A_g – A_st) because steel displaces concrete
Using φ = 0.90 (tension-controlled) instead of φ = 0.65 (compression-controlled tied column)
Omitting the 0.80 factor that accounts for accidental eccentricity

structural/steel-beams.name: Steel Beams
structural/steel-beams.application: Steel beam design per AISC 360-16 centers on checking flexural strength and lateral-torsional buckling (LTB). If the beam is fully braced, it reaches its full plastic moment. If the unbraced length exceeds a threshold, the capacity drops. On the FE, expect problems computing the plastic moment capacity, selecting beam sizes from AISC tables, and checking whether LTB reduces the available strength.

content.body: For doubly symmetric compact I-shapes (most W-shapes), the flexural design check is $\phi_b M_n \geq M_u$ (LRFD) or $M_n/\Omega_b \geq M_a$ (ASD).
Yielding (Full Bracing)

Where $F_y$ = yield stress and $Z_x$ = plastic section modulus. LRFD uses $\phi_b = 0.90$; ASD uses $\Omega_b = 1.67$. This is the maximum possible moment — it applies when the compression flange is fully braced ($L_b \leq L_p$).
Lateral-Torsional Buckling (LTB)
When the unbraced length $L_b$ exceeds $L_p$, the compression flange can buckle sideways, reducing capacity. For $L_p < L_b \leq L_r$:

content.latex: M_n = C_b \left[M_p - (M_p - 0.7 F_y S_x)\frac{L_b - L_p}{L_r - L_p}\right] \leq M_p
content.label: Inelastic LTB

content.body: Where $C_b$ is the moment gradient factor ($C_b = 1.0$ for uniform moment, often > 1.0 for non-uniform moment), $S_x$ is the elastic section modulus, and $L_p$, $L_r$ are tabulated for each shape.
Shear
Where $A_w = d \times t_w$ (web area) and $C_{v1} = 1.0$ for most rolled W-shapes. Use $\phi_v = 1.00$ (LRFD).
Z_x (plastic modulus) is for LRFD. S_x (elastic modulus) is for ASD or for the LTB formula. Using S_x instead of Z_x for the plastic moment underestimates capacity by 10–15%.
If the problem says "fully braced" or "continuous lateral support," L_b ≤ L_p and M_n = F_y Z_x. Skip the LTB check entirely.

problems.statement: A W-shape steel beam has $Z_x = 120 \text{ in}^3$ and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. The beam has full lateral bracing. What is the LRFD design flexural strength $\phi_b M_n$?
problems.eli5: With full bracing, $M_n = M_p = F_y Z_x = 50 \times 120 = 6{,}000$ kip-in $= 500$ kip-ft. Then $\phi_b M_n = 0.90 \times 500 = 450$ kip-ft. The 500 kip-ft choice is the nominal capacity without the $\phi$ factor. The 299 kip-ft choice is the ASD allowable: $M_p/\Omega_b = 500/1.67 = 299$ — a common trap if you mix up LRFD and ASD. The 333 kip-ft choice comes from using $\phi = 2/3$ incorrectly.
problems.hint: $M_p = F_y Z_x$ (convert to kip-ft), then multiply by $\phi_b = 0.90$.
traps: Reporting the nominal capacity (500) instead of the design capacity (450) — always include $\phi_b$ for LRFD
Using $M_p/\Omega_b$ (ASD) when the problem asks for $\phi_b M_n$ (LRFD)

problems.statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 20 \text{ ft}$ and has full lateral bracing. The beam has $Z_x = 80 \text{ in}^3$ and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. What is the maximum factored uniform load $w_u$ the beam can carry?
problems.eli5: $M_p = F_y Z_x = 50 \times 80 = 4{,}000$ kip-in $= 333.3$ kip-ft. $\phi_b M_p = 0.90 \times 333.3 = 300$ kip-ft. For a simply supported beam with uniform load: $M_u = w_u L^2/8$. Set $M_u = \phi_b M_p$: $w_u = 8 \times 300 / (20^2) = 2{,}400/400 = 6.0$ kip/ft. The 6.67 kip/ft choice uses the nominal $M_p = 333$ without the $\phi$ factor: $8 \times 333/400 = 6.67$. The 4.0 kip/ft choice uses the ASD value: $M_p/\Omega_b = 333/1.67 = 200$, then $8 \times 200/400 = 4.0$.
problems.hint: Compute $\phi_b M_p$ first, then set $M_u = w_u L^2/8$ and solve for $w_u$.
traps: Forgetting the $\phi$ factor and using $M_p$ directly — the factored load capacity is based on $\phi M_p$, not $M_p$
Using the ASD safety factor instead of the LRFD $\phi$ — read whether the problem says LRFD or ASD

problems.statement: A W-shape beam has $M_p = 500 \text{ kip-ft}$ and $0.7 F_y S_x = 300 \text{ kip-ft}$. The unbraced length is $L_b = 15 \text{ ft}$, with $L_p = 8 \text{ ft}$ and $L_r = 25 \text{ ft}$. Using $C_b = 1.0$, what is the nominal flexural strength $M_n$?
problems.eli5: Since $L_p = 8 < L_b = 15 \leq L_r = 25$, we are in the inelastic LTB zone. $M_n = C_b[M_p - (M_p - 0.7F_yS_x)(L_b - L_p)/(L_r - L_p)] = 1.0[500 - (500 - 300)(15 - 8)/(25 - 8)] = 500 - 200(7/17) = 500 - 82.4 = 417.6 \approx 418$ kip-ft. Also check $M_n \leq M_p = 500$ ✓. The 500 kip-ft choice ignores LTB entirely and uses $M_p$. The 300 kip-ft choice uses the lower bound $0.7F_yS_x$. The 376 kip-ft choice is $\phi_b \times 418 = 0.90 \times 418$ — the problem asks for $M_n$ (nominal), not $\phi M_n$ (design).
problems.hint: Since $L_p < L_b \leq L_r$, use the inelastic LTB formula. Linear interpolation between $M_p$ and $0.7F_yS_x$.

steps.text: Check range: $L_p = 8 < L_b = 15 \leq L_r = 25$ → inelastic LTB.

traps: Ignoring LTB when $L_b > L_p$ — even if the beam is compact, the unbraced length can reduce capacity
Confusing nominal $M_n$ with design $\phi M_n$ — read whether the problem asks for nominal or design strength
Using $C_b = 1.0$ when the actual loading would give $C_b > 1.0$ — $C_b = 1.0$ is conservative (uniform moment)

structural/steel-columns.name: Steel Columns
structural/steel-columns.application: Steel column design revolves around buckling. The critical stress depends on the slenderness ratio KL/r and whether the column buckles inelastically or elastically. The AISC Table 4-14 in the FE Handbook gives available critical stress directly from KL/r, making the design process a table lookup. On the FE, expect problems computing the slenderness ratio and the design compressive strength.

content.body: Column strength is governed by buckling. The LRFD design compressive strength is $\phi_c P_n$ with $\phi_c = 0.90$.
Slenderness Ratio

Where $K$ is the effective length factor, $L$ is the unbraced length, and $r$ is the radius of gyration (use the smallest $r$ for the controlling axis). Buckling occurs about the axis with the largest KL/r.
Critical Stress
The critical stress $F_{cr}$ depends on KL/r:
If $KL/r \leq 4.71\sqrt{E/F_y}$: inelastic buckling, $F_{cr} = 0.658^{F_y/F_e} \cdot F_y$.
If $KL/r > 4.71\sqrt{E/F_y}$: elastic buckling, $F_{cr} = 0.877 F_e$.
Effective Length Factor K

AISC Table C-A-7.1 gives recommended K values: fixed-fixed $K = 0.65$, fixed-pin $K = 0.80$, pin-pin $K = 1.0$, fixed-free (cantilever) $K = 2.10$. These are design values (slightly conservative vs. theoretical).
On the FE, you can skip the F_cr formulas entirely. AISC Table 4-14 gives φF_cr directly for any KL/r value. Just compute KL/r, look up φF_cr, and multiply by A_g.
Always use the LARGER KL/r (weaker axis) to govern design. For W-shapes, r_y < r_x, so buckling about the weak axis usually controls unless the column is braced differently about each axis.

problems.statement: A steel column has an effective length $KL = 15 \text{ ft}$ and a weak-axis radius of gyration $r_y = 1.91 \text{ in.}$ What is the slenderness ratio $KL/r_y$?
problems.eli5: First convert $KL$ to inches: $15 \times 12 = 180$ in. Then $KL/r_y = 180/1.91 = 94.2 \approx 94$. The choice 180 is $KL$ in inches without dividing by $r$. The choice 31 uses the strong-axis $r_x$ (if $r_x = 5.85$ in., then $180/5.85 = 30.8 \approx 31$). The choice 7.9 reverses the fraction ($r/KL \times 1000$). Always convert feet to inches before dividing by $r$.
problems.hint: Convert $KL$ from feet to inches first, then divide by $r_y$.
traps: Forgetting to convert $KL$ from feet to inches before dividing by $r$ (which is in inches)
Using $r_x$ (strong axis) instead of $r_y$ (weak axis) — the larger $KL/r$ controls

problems.statement: A steel column has $KL/r = 60$ and a cross-sectional area $A_g = 15.0 \text{ in}^2$. Using $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$ and AISC Table 4-14 (which gives $\phi_c F_{cr} = 34.6 \text{ ksi}$ at $KL/r = 60$), what is the LRFD design compressive strength?
problems.eli5: $\phi_c P_n = \phi_c F_{cr} \times A_g = 34.6 \times 15.0 = 519$ kips. That is the total design compressive strength after buckling reduction and safety factor. The 750 kips choice is $F_y \times A_g = 50 \times 15 = 750$, which ignores buckling entirely — this would only be correct for a zero-length column. The 345 kips choice might come from an incorrect table lookup. The 675 kips choice applies $\phi_c = 0.90$ to the gross yield: $0.90 \times 750 = 675$, still ignoring buckling.
problems.hint: Design strength $= \phi_c F_{cr} \times A_g$. The $\phi_c F_{cr}$ value is read directly from the AISC table.
traps: Using $F_y$ directly instead of $F_{cr}$ — buckling reduces the effective stress below yield for slender columns
Applying $\phi_c$ again on top of $\phi_c F_{cr}$ — the table value already includes $\phi_c = 0.90$

problems.statement: Two columns use the same W-shape ($r_y = 2.0 \text{ in.}$). Column A has an unbraced length of $12 \text{ ft}$ with pin-pin supports ($K = 1.0$). Column B has an unbraced length of $18 \text{ ft}$ with fixed-pin supports ($K = 0.80$). Which column has the higher slenderness ratio?
problems.eli5: Column A: $KL/r = (1.0 \times 12 \times 12)/2.0 = 144/2.0 = 72$. Column B: $KL/r = (0.80 \times 18 \times 12)/2.0 = 172.8/2.0 = 86.4 \approx 86$. Column B has the higher $KL/r$ despite having a lower $K$ factor, because its physical length is much longer. Higher $KL/r$ means lower $\phi_c F_{cr}$ and therefore lower design strength. The choice "Column A because $K = 1.0 > 0.80$" is the trap — a lower $K$ factor helps, but it does not always compensate for a much longer column. You must compute the actual $KL/r$ to compare.
problems.hint: Compute $KL/r$ for each column. Remember: $K$ reduces the effective length, but a much longer column can still have a higher $KL/r$.

steps.text: Column B has the higher slenderness ratio ($86 > 72$), so it has lower design strength.

traps: Assuming a lower $K$ automatically means better performance — the physical length matters too
Forgetting to convert feet to inches when computing $KL/r$
Using $r_x$ instead of $r_y$ — weak-axis buckling typically governs for W-shapes

structural/steel-tension.name: Steel Tension Members
structural/steel-tension.application: Steel tension members (braces, truss chords, hangers) must be checked for two failure modes: yielding on the gross section and rupture on the net section through bolt holes. The controlling limit state — whichever gives the smaller design strength — governs. On the FE, expect problems computing net area with bolt holes, effective net area with the shear lag factor U, and determining which limit state controls.

content.body: AISC 360-16 defines two limit states for tension members. Both must be checked, and the smaller design strength controls.
Yielding on Gross Section
This limit state checks whether the entire cross-section yields. It uses the gross area $A_g$ (no bolt hole deductions) and the yield stress $F_y$.
Rupture on Net Section

This checks whether the member fractures at the weakest cross-section (through bolt holes). The effective net area $A_e = U \times A_n$, where $U$ is the shear lag factor (1.0 for flat bars connected through all elements).
Net Area with Bolt Holes
For each bolt hole, subtract $(d_b + 1/8\text{"})$ from the gross width. The $1/8\text{"} = 1/16\text{"} \text{(clearance)} + 1/16\text{"} \text{(damage)}$.

Yielding uses φ = 0.90 but rupture uses φ = 0.75. The lower φ for rupture reflects the more sudden, less ductile failure mode. Because of these different φ values, rupture often controls even when F_u A_n > F_y A_g.
For a flat bar connected by bolts through the full width: U = 1.0. For angles or channels connected through only one leg/flange: U = 1 – x̄/L (shear lag reduction). The FE usually tests flat bars.

problems.statement: A flat bar ($1/2 \text{ in.} \times 6 \text{ in.}$) is used as a tension member with $F_y = 36 \text{ ksi}$ and $F_u = 58 \text{ ksi}$. There are no bolt holes. What is the LRFD design tensile strength for yielding?
problems.eli5: $A_g = 0.5 \times 6 = 3.0$ in$^2$. For yielding: $\phi_y P_n = 0.90 \times F_y \times A_g = 0.90 \times 36 \times 3.0 = 97.2 \approx 97$ kips. The 108 kips choice is $F_y \times A_g = 108$ without the $\phi$ factor. The 174 kips choice uses $F_u$ instead of $F_y$ with no $\phi$ factor: $174 = F_u \times A_g = 58 \times 3.0$. The 131 kips choice uses $\phi = 0.75$ with $F_u$: $0.75 \times 58 \times 3.0 = 130.5 \approx 131$ — that is the rupture check, not yielding.
problems.hint: For yielding: $\phi_y P_n = 0.90 \times F_y \times A_g$. No bolt hole deductions.
traps: Using $F_u$ instead of $F_y$ for yielding — yielding uses $F_y$ (yield stress), rupture uses $F_u$ (ultimate stress)
Forgetting the $\phi_y = 0.90$ factor

problems.statement: A plate tension member is $1/2 \text{ in.}$ thick and $10 \text{ in.}$ wide. Two $7/8 \text{-in.}$ diameter bolts are placed at the same cross-section (side by side). What is the net area $A_n$?
problems.eli5: For each bolt hole, subtract $(d_b + 1/8")$ from the gross width: $7/8 + 1/8 = 1.0$ in. per hole. With 2 holes: $A_n = [10 - 2(1.0)] \times 0.5 = 8.0 \times 0.5 = 4.00$ in$^2$. The $1/8"$ comes from $1/16"$ hole clearance $+ 1/16"$ drilling damage. The $4.13 \text{ in}^2$ option subtracts only $d_b = 0.875$ per hole without the extra $1/8"$: $[10 - 2(0.875)] \times 0.5 = 4.125$. The $5.00 \text{ in}^2$ option is the gross area with no deductions. The $4.06 \text{ in}^2$ option adds only $1/16"$ instead of $1/8"$ to each bolt diameter.
problems.hint: Net width $=$ gross width $- \Sigma(d_b + 1/8")$ for each hole. Then multiply by thickness.
traps: Subtracting only the bolt diameter without adding the 1/8" for clearance and damage
Adding only 1/16" (clearance) instead of 1/8" (clearance + damage)
Forgetting to deduct holes at all and using the gross area

problems.statement: A plate member ($1/2 \text{ in.} \times 8 \text{ in.}$) has $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$ and $F_u = 65 \text{ ksi}$. Two $3/4 \text{-in.}$ bolts attach it at one cross-section. For a flat bar, $U = 1.0$. Which limit state controls, and what is the design tension capacity?
problems.eli5: Gross area: $A_g = 8 \times 0.5 = 4.0$ in$^2$. Net area: $A_n = [8 - 2(3/4 + 1/8)] \times 0.5 = [8 - 2(0.875)] \times 0.5 = [8 - 1.75] \times 0.5 = 6.25 \times 0.5 = 3.125$ in$^2$. With $U = 1.0$: $A_e = 3.125$ in$^2$. Yielding: $\phi_y P_n = 0.90 \times 50 \times 4.0 = 180$ kips. Rupture: $\phi_t P_n = 0.75 \times 65 \times 3.125 = 152.3 \approx 152$ kips. Controlling $= \min(180, 152) = 152$ kips (rupture). Even though rupture uses a higher material strength ($F_u > F_y$), the smaller net area and lower $\phi$ factor make it control. The 180-kips yielding choice picks the larger value, but the smaller capacity governs.
problems.hint: Compute both $\phi_y F_y A_g$ (yielding) and $\phi_t F_u A_e$ (rupture). The smaller one controls.
problems.handbookFormula: \text{Yielding: } \phi_y P_n = 0.90 F_y A_g; \quad \text{Rupture: } \phi_t P_n = 0.75 F_u A_e
traps: Picking the larger value as the capacity — the smaller design strength controls because it represents the weaker failure mode
Using the same $\phi$ factor for both limit states — yielding uses 0.90, rupture uses 0.75
Forgetting to deduct bolt holes for the rupture check or deducting holes for the yielding check (yielding uses $A_g$)

geotechnical/phase-relations.name: Phase Relations
geotechnical/phase-relations.application: Every soil sample is a mixture of solids, water, and air. Phase relations convert between the properties you measure in the lab (water content, unit weight) and the properties you need for design (void ratio, degree of saturation). On the FE, expect 2–3 problems that give you some soil properties and ask you to compute the others using the phase diagram relationships.

content.body: The phase diagram divides soil into three phases: solids, water, and air. All soil index properties relate the weights and volumes of these phases.
Weight-Volume Definitions

content.label: Total, dry, and saturated unit weight

content.body: Index Properties
Useful Relationships
The master relationship linking w, $G_s$, $S$, and $e$ is $Se = \omega G_s$. At full saturation ($S = 1$), this simplifies to $e = \omega G_s$.

content.label: Dry unit weight from total unit weight

content.body: When a problem says "fully saturated," set S = 1 and use e = wGs. This one substitution unlocks void ratio from just water content and specific gravity.
Keep w as a decimal in formulas (0.20, not 20%). The formula Se = wGs uses the decimal form. Only multiply by 100 when reporting the percentage.

problems.statement: A fully saturated soil has a water content $\omega = 20\%$ and specific gravity $G_s = 2.70$. What is the void ratio $e$?
problems.eli5: When soil is fully saturated, S = 1. The master relationship Se = wGs becomes e = wGs = 0.20 × 2.70 = 0.54. The 0.74 choice might come from using w = 0.274 or a different Gs. The 2.70 choice is just the specific gravity. The 0.20 choice confuses the water content with the void ratio.
problems.hint: At full saturation, S = 1. Use Se = wGs to solve directly for e.
traps: Using w = 20 instead of 0.20 in the formula — water content must be a decimal in Se = wGs
Confusing void ratio (e) with porosity (n) — n = e/(1+e)

problems.statement: A soil has total unit weight $\gamma = 120 \text{ pcf}$, water content $\omega = 15\%$, and $G_s = 2.65$. What is the degree of saturation $S$?
problems.eli5: First get the dry unit weight: γd = γ/(1+w) = 120/1.15 = 104.3 pcf. Then find e from γd = Gsγw/(1+e): e = Gsγw/γd – 1 = 2.65 × 62.4/104.3 – 1 = 0.586. Finally S = wGs/e = 0.15 × 2.65/0.586 = 0.678 ≈ 68%. The 85% choice might come from skipping the e calculation and guessing. The 100% choice assumes full saturation, which the problem does not state.
problems.hint: Find γd first, then compute e, then use S = wGs/e.
traps: Using total unit weight instead of dry unit weight to compute void ratio
Forgetting to subtract 1 when solving for e from γd = Gsγw/(1+e)

problems.statement: A saturated soil has $\gamma_{sat} = 125 \text{ pcf}$ and $G_s = 2.72$. What is the water content $\omega$?
problems.eli5: Start with γsat = (Gs + e)γw/(1+e). Plug in: 125(1+e) = 62.4(2.72+e). Expand: 125 + 125e = 169.73 + 62.4e. Solve: 62.6e = 44.73, so e = 0.714. Since the soil is saturated (S = 1): w = Se/Gs = e/Gs = 0.714/2.72 = 0.263 = 26%. The 71% choice confuses e with w — the void ratio is 0.714 but the water content is e/Gs. The 17% choice might come from using the wrong unit weight formula.
problems.hint: Solve the γsat formula for e first. Then use w = e/Gs (since S = 1 for saturated soil).
traps: Reporting the void ratio (0.714) as the water content — w = e/Gs, not e itself
Using γw = 9.81 kN/m³ when the problem is in US customary units (γw = 62.4 pcf)
Forgetting that saturated means S = 1, which simplifies Se = wGs to e = wGs

geotechnical/soil-classification.name: Soil Classification
geotechnical/soil-classification.application: Soil classification communicates subsurface conditions in a standard language. The Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) assigns a two-letter symbol based on grain size and plasticity. The AASHTO system rates soils for highway subgrade suitability. On the FE, expect problems that give sieve data and Atterberg limits and ask you to classify the soil or compute the coefficient of uniformity.

content.body: Two classification systems appear on the FE: USCS (ASTM D2487) for general geotechnical work and AASHTO for transportation subgrades.
USCS — First Split

If more than 50% is retained on the No. 200 sieve (0.075 mm), the soil is coarse-grained. Otherwise, it is fine-grained. Coarse-grained soils are further split at the No. 4 sieve: gravels (G) vs. sands (S).
Gradation Coefficients
Well-graded sands (SW) need $C_u \geq 6$ AND $1 \leq C_c \leq 3$. Well-graded gravels (GW) need $C_u \geq 4$ AND $1 \leq C_c \leq 3$. If either criterion fails, the soil is poorly graded (SP or GP).
Plasticity Chart (Fine-Grained Soils)

Fine-grained soils plot on the plasticity chart using LL (x-axis) and PI (y-axis). The A-line separates clays (above) from silts (below): $\text{PI} = 0.73(\text{LL} - 20)$. The LL = 50 boundary separates low plasticity (L) from high plasticity (H).
Plasticity Index
USCS decision tree: (1) Coarse or fine? (% passing #200). (2) If coarse: gravel or sand? Then check Cu and Cc. (3) If fine: plot on plasticity chart (above/below A-line, LL < or > 50).
Both Cu AND Cc must be satisfied for well-graded. A sand with Cu = 15 but Cc = 0.5 is still SP (poorly graded) because Cc is outside the 1–3 range.

problems.statement: A soil has 80% passing the No. 200 sieve, $LL = 45$, and $PI = 22$. What is its USCS classification?
problems.eli5: More than 50% passes #200, so it is fine-grained. LL = 45 < 50, so it is low-plasticity (L). On the A-line at LL = 45: PI = 0.73(45 – 20) = 18.25. Since the actual PI = 22 > 18.25, the soil plots above the A-line → clay (C). Combine: CL (lean clay). ML would be below the A-line. CH requires LL ≥ 50. SC is a coarse-grained soil with clay fines.
problems.hint: Check: fine or coarse? Then: LL < or > 50? Then: above or below the A-line?
traps: Confusing CL with ML — CL is above the A-line (clay), ML is below (silt)
Using LL = 50 as the clay/silt boundary instead of the A-line — LL = 50 separates L from H, not clay from silt

problems.statement: A sand has $D_{10} = 0.15 \text{ mm}$, $D_{30} = 0.50 \text{ mm}$, $D_{60} = 2.0 \text{ mm}$. Less than 5% passes the No. 200 sieve. What is its USCS classification?
problems.eli5: Less than 50% passes #200 → coarse. It is identified as a sand (more than 50% of the coarse fraction passes the No. 4 sieve). With < 5% fines, classify based on gradation. Cu = D60/D10 = 2.0/0.15 = 13.3 (need ≥ 6 ✔). Cc = (D30)²/(D10 × D60) = 0.25/0.30 = 0.83 (need 1–3 ✘). Since Cc fails the range, it is poorly graded: SP. The SW option requires BOTH the Cu and Cc criteria to be met. The SM option would need > 12% fines.
problems.hint: Compute both Cu and Cc. Both must pass for well-graded (W); if either fails, it is poorly graded (P).

steps.text: $C_c = 0.83 < 1$ → outside the 1–3 range ✘. Classification: **SP** (poorly graded sand).

traps: Assuming the sand is well-graded because Cu ≥ 6 — BOTH Cu and Cc must pass
Using the gravel criteria (Cu ≥ 4) instead of the sand criteria (Cu ≥ 6)

problems.statement: A soil has $LL = 55$, $PI = 28$, and 60% passing the No. 200 sieve. What is the USCS classification?
problems.eli5: 60% passes #200 → fine-grained. LL = 55 > 50 → high plasticity (H). A-line at LL = 55: PI = 0.73(55 – 20) = 25.6. Actual PI = 28 > 25.6 → above A-line → clay (C). Classification: CH (fat clay). The MH choice is below the A-line (silt). The CL choice requires LL < 50. The OH choice is an organic soil which requires lab testing (oven-dried LL) — not determinable from the given data alone, so assume inorganic.
problems.hint: Fine or coarse? LL < or > 50? Above or below the A-line? Each step narrows to one symbol.
traps: Confusing CH with MH — above the A-line is always clay (C), below is silt (M)
Using LL = 50 as the clay/silt boundary instead of the A-line
Choosing OH without evidence of organic content — organic classification requires comparing oven-dried LL to natural LL

geotechnical/effective-stress.name: Effective Stress
geotechnical/effective-stress.application: Effective stress is the single most important concept in geotechnical engineering. It is the stress carried by the soil skeleton, and it controls strength, compressibility, and volume change. When a water table is present, you subtract the pore water pressure from the total stress to get the effective stress. On the FE, expect problems drawing stress profiles through layered soils with and without a water table.

content.body: Total stress at a point equals the weight of everything above it. Effective stress is what the soil skeleton actually feels.
Fundamental Equation
Where $\sigma$ is total vertical stress, $u = h_w \gamma_w$ is pore water pressure, and $h_w$ is the height of water above the point.
Stress Profile Construction

Above the water table: $\sigma = \gamma H$ and $u = 0$, so $\sigma' = \sigma$. Below the water table: $\sigma = \gamma_1 H_1 + \gamma_{sat} H_2$ and $u = \gamma_w H_2$, so $\sigma' = \gamma_1 H_1 + (\gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w) H_2 = \gamma_1 H_1 + \gamma' H_2$.
With Surcharge
A uniform surcharge $q$ at the surface adds $q$ to total stress at every depth but does not change pore water pressure: $\sigma' = q + \gamma_1 H_1 + \gamma' H_2$.
Shortcut: below the water table, use the buoyant unit weight γ' = γsat – γw to compute effective stress directly. This avoids computing total stress and pore pressure separately.
The water table position is critical. Pore pressure only exists below the WT. Above the WT, u = 0 (ignoring capillary effects). Never subtract γw from a layer that is above the water table.

problems.statement: A 10-ft-thick saturated soil layer has $\gamma_{sat} = 115 \text{ pcf}$. The water table is at the ground surface. What is the effective stress at the bottom of the layer?
problems.eli5: σ = γsat × H = 115 × 10 = 1,150 psf. u = γw × H = 62.4 × 10 = 624 psf. σ' = 1,150 – 624 = 526 psf. Or use the shortcut: σ' = γ' × H = (115 – 62.4) × 10 = 52.6 × 10 = 526 psf. The 1,150 psf option is the total stress — forgetting to subtract pore pressure. The 624 psf option is the pore pressure itself.
problems.hint: σ' = σ – u. Compute total stress and pore water pressure separately, then subtract.
traps: Reporting total stress instead of effective stress — always subtract pore pressure below the WT
Using γw = 64 pcf or some other value instead of 62.4 pcf

problems.statement: A site has 5 ft of dry sand ($\gamma = 110 \text{ pcf}$) over 8 ft of saturated clay ($\gamma_{sat} = 120 \text{ pcf}$). The water table is at the sand-clay interface. What is the effective vertical stress at the bottom of the clay?
problems.eli5: Total stress at the bottom: σ = 110(5) + 120(8) = 550 + 960 = 1,510 psf. Pore pressure: u = 62.4(8) = 499 psf (water is 8 ft deep below the WT). Effective: σ' = 1,510 – 499 = 1,011 psf. The 1,510 psf option is the total stress. The 960 psf option is only the clay layer contribution without the sand above. The 526 psf option uses only the buoyant weight of clay without the sand overburden.
problems.hint: Total stress includes both layers. Pore pressure only exists in the saturated zone (below the WT).

steps.text: Total stress at bottom of clay:
Pore water pressure (8 ft below WT):

traps: Subtracting pore pressure through the sand layer too — the sand is above the WT so u = 0 there
Using buoyant unit weight for the sand above the WT — only subtract γw below the water table

problems.statement: A site has a $100 \text{ psf}$ uniform surcharge on the surface. Below: 6 ft of sand ($\gamma = 105 \text{ pcf}$, above WT) over 10 ft of saturated clay ($\gamma_{sat} = 118 \text{ pcf}$). The WT is at the sand-clay interface. What is the effective vertical stress at the bottom of the clay?
problems.eli5: Total stress: σ = 100 + 105(6) + 118(10) = 100 + 630 + 1,180 = 1,910 psf. Pore pressure: u = 62.4(10) = 624 psf. Effective: σ' = 1,910 – 624 = 1,286 psf. The surcharge adds to total stress but NOT to pore pressure. The 1,910 psf option forgets to subtract u. The 1,186 psf option forgot the surcharge. The 1,810 psf option subtracted the surcharge from total stress instead of subtracting pore pressure.
problems.hint: Surcharge adds to total stress at all depths but does not change pore water pressure.

steps.text: Pore water pressure (10 ft below WT):

traps: Adding the surcharge to pore pressure — surcharge increases total stress only, not u
Forgetting to include the surcharge in the total stress calculation
Subtracting γw through the dry sand layer above the water table

geotechnical/consolidation.name: Consolidation & Settlement
geotechnical/consolidation.application: When load is applied to saturated clay, water slowly squeezes out and the soil compresses over time — this is consolidation. You compute total settlement using the compression index and the e-log p curve, then predict how long it takes using the time factor. On the FE, expect problems computing settlement with the three consolidation cases and using the time factor table.

content.body: Consolidation settlement depends on whether the current stress exceeds the preconsolidation pressure $p_c$ (the maximum past stress the soil has experienced).
Three Settlement Cases
Case 1 — Entirely in recompression ($p_0 + \Delta p < p_c$):

content.label: OC clay, stress stays below pc

content.body: Case 2 — Normally consolidated ($p_0 \geq p_c$):
Case 3 — Crosses preconsolidation ($p_0 < p_c < p_0 + \Delta p$):
Index Correlations
Time Rate of Consolidation

content.label: Time factor and settlement at time t

content.body: Where $H_{dr}$ is the drainage path length: $H/2$ for two-way drainage (permeable boundaries top and bottom), $H$ for one-way drainage. Use the $T_v$ vs. $U$ table in the handbook to convert between time factor and degree of consolidation.
For U ≤ 60%: Tv ≈ (π/4)(U/100)². For U > 60%: Tv ≈ −0.933 log(1 – U/100) – 0.085. But on the FE, just use the table — it is faster and error-free.
Hdr is half the layer thickness only for two-way drainage. If the clay sits on rock (impermeable), Hdr = full thickness. This doubles the time for the same degree of consolidation.

problems.statement: A normally consolidated clay layer is $10 \text{ ft}$ thick with $e_0 = 0.90$ and $C_c = 0.30$. The current effective stress is $\sigma_0' = 1{,}000 \text{ psf}$ and the stress increase is $\Delta\sigma = 500 \text{ psf}$. What is the consolidation settlement?
problems.eli5: NC clay → Case 2: ΔH = H/(1+e0) × Cc × log(σ0’+Δσ)/σ0’ = 10/(1.90) × 0.30 × log(1500/1000) = 5.263 × 0.30 × 0.1761 = 0.278 ft = 3.3 in. The 6.3 in. option might come from using H = 10 without dividing by (1+e0). The 1.6 in. option uses Cr instead of Cc. The 10 in. option ignores the log term and just multiplies H × Cc.
problems.hint: NC clay uses Case 2 with Cc (not Cr). Remember to divide H by (1 + e0).
traps: Using Cr instead of Cc for normally consolidated clay — Cr is only for overconsolidated clay below pc
Forgetting to divide H by (1 + e0)

problems.statement: For the clay in Problem 1, $c_v = 0.50 \text{ ft}^2\text{/day}$ with two-way drainage ($H_{dr} = 5 \text{ ft}$). How long does it take for 50% consolidation? Use $T_v = 0.197$ at $U = 50\%$.
problems.eli5: Tv = cv·t/Hdr² → t = Tv·Hdr²/cv = 0.197 × 25/0.50 = 9.85 ≈ 10 days. Two-way drainage means Hdr = H/2 = 5 ft. The 20 days choice uses Hdr = 10 ft (one-way drainage). The 5 days choice might divide by 2 again. The 39 days choice uses Tv = 0.785 (for U = 90%).
problems.hint: Rearrange Tv = cv·t/Hdr² to solve for t. Two-way drainage means Hdr = H/2.
traps: Using the full layer thickness (H = 10) instead of Hdr = H/2 for two-way drainage — this quadruples the time
Confusing Tv with U — Tv is the time factor, U is the degree of consolidation (%)

problems.statement: An overconsolidated clay has $e_0 = 1.10$, $C_c = 0.40$, $C_r = 0.06$, $H = 12 \text{ ft}$. Current stress $\sigma_0' = 800 \text{ psf}$, preconsolidation $p_c = 1{,}200 \text{ psf}$, added stress $\Delta\sigma = 600 \text{ psf}$ (so $\sigma_0' + \Delta\sigma = 1{,}400 > p_c$). What is the settlement?
problems.eli5: Since p0 = 800 < pc = 1,200 < p0+Δp = 1,400 → Case 3 (crosses preconsolidation). ΔH = H/(1+e0) × [Cr × log(pc/p0) + Cc × log((p0+Δp)/pc)] = 12/2.10 × [0.06 × log(1200/800) + 0.40 × log(1400/1200)] = 5.714 × [0.06 × 0.1761 + 0.40 × 0.0669] = 5.714 × [0.01057 + 0.02678] = 5.714 × 0.03735 = 0.213 ft = 2.6 in. The 4.8 in. choice uses Cc for both terms. The 0.9 in. choice uses Cr for both terms. The key is recognizing which case applies.
problems.hint: Check: does the final stress exceed pc? If so, use Case 3 — Cr below pc and Cc above pc.
traps: Using Cc for the entire stress range — use Cr from p0 to pc and Cc from pc to p0+Δp
Using Case 1 (Cr only) when the final stress actually exceeds pc
Forgetting to divide by (1 + e0)

geotechnical/shear-strength.name: Shear Strength of Soils
geotechnical/shear-strength.application: Soil shear strength controls whether foundations, slopes, and retaining structures are stable. The Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion defines the maximum shear stress a soil can resist on any plane. On the FE, expect problems computing shear strength from given parameters, or extracting the friction angle from triaxial test results using the Mohr circle.

content.body: The Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion gives the shear strength on a failure plane as a function of the normal effective stress on that plane.
Mohr-Coulomb Criterion
Where $c'$ is the effective cohesion, $\sigma_N'$ is the effective normal stress on the failure plane, and $\phi'$ is the effective friction angle. For granular soils (sands), $c' = 0$.
Undrained Analysis (φ = 0)

For saturated clays under rapid loading (undrained), use total stress parameters: $\tau_f = c_u$ where $c_u$ is the undrained shear strength and $\phi_u = 0$. The undrained strength equals half the deviator stress at failure: $c_u = (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2$.
Mohr Circle Relationships

content.label: Center and radius of Mohr circle

content.body: For a cohesionless soil ($c = 0$), the failure envelope passes through the origin and $\sin \phi = t/s$.
Quick check: for c = 0, sin φ = (σ1 – σ3)/(σ1 + σ3). This is the fastest way to get φ from a triaxial test without drawing the Mohr circle.
Drained (c’, φ’) parameters use effective stresses. Undrained (cu, φu = 0) parameters use total stresses. Mixing these is a common exam trap — check which drainage condition the problem specifies.

problems.statement: A soil has $c' = 200 \text{ psf}$ and $\phi' = 30\degree$. What is the shear strength on a plane where the effective normal stress is $\sigma_N' = 1{,}000 \text{ psf}$?
problems.eli5: τf = c’ + σN’ tan φ’ = 200 + 1,000 × tan 30° = 200 + 1,000 × 0.5774 = 200 + 577 = 777 psf. The 577 psf option forgot the cohesion term. The 1,000 psf option is just the normal stress. The 200 psf option is just the cohesion — ignoring the frictional component entirely.
problems.hint: Plug directly into the Mohr-Coulomb equation: τf = c + σ’ tan φ.
traps: Forgetting the cohesion term c — the shear strength has two components
Using sin φ instead of tan φ in the Mohr-Coulomb equation

problems.statement: A triaxial test on a cohesionless soil ($c = 0$) gives $\sigma_1 = 6{,}000 \text{ psf}$ and $\sigma_3 = 2{,}000 \text{ psf}$ at failure. What is the friction angle $\phi$?
problems.eli5: For c = 0: sin φ = (σ1 – σ3)/(σ1 + σ3) = (6,000 – 2,000)/(6,000 + 2,000) = 4,000/8,000 = 0.50. φ = arcsin(0.50) = 30°. The 45° choice might come from using tan⁻¹(σ1/σ3) incorrectly. The 26.6° choice is arctan(0.50) — a common mistake from using tan instead of sin.
problems.hint: For c = 0: sin φ = (σ1 – σ3)/(σ1 + σ3). No need to draw the Mohr circle.
traps: Using arctan(0.50) instead of arcsin(0.50) — the Mohr circle gives sin φ = t/s, not tan φ
Computing σ1/σ3 = 3.0 and using it as φ or tan φ

problems.statement: An unconsolidated-undrained (UU) triaxial test on a saturated clay gives $\sigma_3 = 1{,}500 \text{ psf}$ and $(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3) = 2{,}400 \text{ psf}$ at failure. What is the undrained cohesion $c_u$?
problems.eli5: In a UU test on saturated clay, φu = 0. The Mohr circle has its center at s = (σ1+σ3)/2 and radius t = (σ1–σ3)/2. For φ = 0, the failure envelope is a horizontal line at τ = cu, and cu = the radius = (σ1–σ3)/2 = 2,400/2 = 1,200 psf. The 2,400 psf choice is the deviator stress itself, not halved. The 2,700 psf choice is (σ1+σ3)/2 = (3,900+1,500)/2 — that is the center of the Mohr circle, not the radius. The 1,500 psf choice is just σ3.
problems.hint: For φ = 0 (undrained clay): cu = (σ1 – σ3)/2 = radius of the Mohr circle.

steps.text: For $\phi_u = 0$, undrained cohesion = radius of Mohr circle:

traps: Using the full deviator stress (2,400) as cu instead of half of it
Computing (σ1+σ3)/2 (center of circle) instead of (σ1–σ3)/2 (radius)
Trying to use the drained formula sin φ = t/s when the problem specifies undrained (UU) conditions

geotechnical/permeability-seepage.name: Permeability & Seepage
geotechnical/permeability-seepage.application: Water moving through soil controls dewatering, drainage, and the stability of dams, levees, and excavations. As a civil engineer you use Darcy's law to estimate flow, flow nets to quantify seepage under structures, and the critical hydraulic gradient to guard against quick (boiling) conditions. On the FE, expect to compute discharge, seepage quantity from a flow net, and the critical gradient.

content.body: Permeability (hydraulic conductivity, k) measures how easily water flows through soil. Darcy's law relates the flow rate to the hydraulic gradient and the cross-sectional area.
Darcy's Law

content.label: Flow rate; i = dh/dL (hydraulic gradient), A = total cross-sectional area

content.body: The discharge velocity is $v = ki$, based on the total area. The actual SEEPAGE velocity through the pores is faster: $v_s = v/n = ki/n$, where $n$ is the porosity.
Flow Nets

content.label: Seepage per unit width; Nf = flow channels, Nd = equipotential drops, H = total head

content.body: A flow net is a graphical grid of flow lines and equipotential lines. Counting the number of flow channels ($N_f$) and head drops ($N_d$) gives the seepage quantity beneath a dam or sheet pile per unit width.
Critical Hydraulic Gradient

content.label: Gradient at which upward seepage causes a quick condition

content.body: When upward seepage reduces the effective stress to zero, the soil "boils" (quick condition). This happens at the critical gradient $i_c$. The factor of safety against piping is $FS = i_c / i_{exit}$.
The critical gradient is almost always near 1.0 for typical sands, because γ′ ≈ γ_w. A quick condition is therefore a real risk wherever the upward exit gradient approaches unity.
Discharge velocity (v = ki) is NOT the real particle speed. Divide by porosity to get the seepage velocity — water travels faster through the smaller pore area than the total-area velocity implies.

problems.statement: Water flows through a soil sample with hydraulic conductivity $k = 0.01\text{ cm/s}$ under a hydraulic gradient $i = 0.5$. The cross-sectional area is $A = 100\text{ cm}^2$. What is the flow rate?
problems.eli5: Darcy: q = kiA = 0.01 × 0.5 × 100 = 0.5 cm³/s. The 5.0 cm^3/s option inflates the result tenfold. The 0.05 cm^3/s option multiplies in an extra factor of 0.1. The 50 cm^3/s option drops the gradient and shifts a decimal.
problems.hint: q = k × i × A. Keep units consistent (cm/s, cm²).
traps: Forgetting to multiply by the hydraulic gradient
Mixing length units between k and A

problems.statement: A saturated sand has specific gravity $G_s = 2.70$ and void ratio $e = 0.85$. What is the critical hydraulic gradient at which a quick condition occurs?
problems.eli5: i_c = (Gs − 1)/(1 + e) = (2.70 − 1)/(1 + 0.85) = 1.70/1.85 = 0.92. The 1.00 choice wrongly assumes i_c is always exactly 1.0. The 1.85 choice just reports the denominator (1 + e) = 1.85 instead of the full ratio. The 0.54 choice inverts the fraction, using (1 + e)/(Gs − 1) instead of (Gs − 1)/(1 + e).
problems.hint: Critical gradient i_c = (Gs − 1)/(1 + e).
traps: Assuming the critical gradient is always exactly 1.0
Forgetting to divide by (1 + e)

problems.statement: Seepage beneath a dam is analyzed with a flow net having $N_f = 4$ flow channels and $N_d = 12$ equipotential drops. The hydraulic conductivity is $k = 2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m/s}$ and the total head loss is $H = 6\text{ m}$. What is the seepage rate per unit width?
problems.eli5: q = kH(Nf/Nd) = (2×10⁻⁵)(6)(4/12) = (2×10⁻⁵)(6)(0.333) = 4.0×10⁻⁵ m³/s per m. The 3.6×10⁻⁴ choice inverts the ratio (Nd/Nf = 12/4 = 3). The 1.0×10⁻⁵ choice mishandles the head. The 2.4×10⁻⁴ choice uses an incorrect ratio value.
problems.hint: q = k × H × (Nf/Nd) per unit width.
traps: Inverting the ratio to Nd/Nf
Forgetting to multiply by the total head H

geotechnical/slope-stability.name: Slope Stability
geotechnical/slope-stability.application: Embankments, cut slopes, levees, and natural hillsides can fail by sliding along a slip surface. As a civil engineer you compute a factor of safety comparing the soil's shearing resistance to the driving force of gravity. On the FE, expect the infinite-slope factor of safety for cohesionless soil, the effect of seepage, and the planar slip-surface factor of safety.

content.body: Slope stability is expressed as a factor of safety — the ratio of forces (or moments) resisting failure to those driving it. FS > 1 means stable; FS = 1 is incipient failure.
Infinite Slope (Cohesionless, Dry)

content.label: Dry cohesionless infinite slope; β = slope angle

content.body: For a dry sand slope, stability depends only on the friction angle versus the slope angle — independent of depth. The slope is stable as long as $\beta < \phi$.
Effect of Seepage

content.label: Seepage parallel to a cohesionless slope

content.body: Steady seepage parallel to the slope roughly halves the factor of safety (since $\gamma'/\gamma_{sat} \approx 0.5$). This is why slopes that stand when dry can fail after prolonged rainfall.
Planar Slip Surface

content.label: Wedge on a planar slip surface; α = slip angle, Ls = slip length

content.body: For cohesionless soil (c = 0), the infinite-slope FS reduces to tan φ / tan β — the depth and unit weight cancel out entirely when the slope is dry.
Always check whether seepage is present. Forgetting the γ′/γ_sat reduction can overstate the factor of safety by roughly a factor of two.

problems.statement: A dry cohesionless sand slope is inclined at $\beta = 20\degree$. The soil's friction angle is $\phi = 34\degree$. What is the factor of safety against sliding?
problems.eli5: For a dry cohesionless infinite slope, FS = tan φ / tan β = tan 34° / tan 20° = 0.6745/0.3640 = 1.85. The 0.54 choice inverts the ratio (tan β / tan φ). The 1.70 choice subtracts angles incorrectly. The 0.93 choice applies a seepage reduction that is not present here.
problems.hint: Dry cohesionless slope: FS = tan φ / tan β.
traps: Inverting to tan β / tan φ
Applying a seepage reduction when the slope is dry

problems.statement: The same cohesionless slope ($\phi = 34\degree$, $\beta = 20\degree$) becomes fully saturated with seepage parallel to the slope. With $\gamma_{sat} = 19.62\text{ kN/m}^3$ and $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$, what is the new factor of safety?
problems.eli5: With seepage, FS = (γ′/γ_sat)(tan φ/tan β). Here γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w = 19.62 − 9.81 = 9.81, so γ′/γ_sat = 9.81/19.62 = 0.5. The dry FS was 1.85, so FS = 0.5 × 1.85 = 0.93 — now UNSTABLE. The 1.85 option ignores seepage (it is the dry FS). The 3.70 option multiplies by tan φ/tan β twice instead of reducing. The 0.50 option reports only the reduction factor.
problems.hint: Multiply the dry FS by γ′/γ_sat, where γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w.
traps: Ignoring the seepage reduction and reporting the dry value
Using γ_sat instead of γ′ in the numerator

problems.statement: A soil wedge is analyzed on a planar slip surface. The cohesion contributes $cL_s = 120\text{ kN/m}$, the wedge weight is $W = 400\text{ kN/m}$, the slip angle is $\alpha = 25\degree$, and the friction angle is $\phi = 20\degree$. What is the factor of safety?
problems.eli5: FS = (cLs + W cos α tan φ)/(W sin α). Numerator = 120 + 400(cos 25°)(tan 20°) = 120 + 400(0.9063)(0.3640) = 120 + 132 = 252. Denominator = W sin α = 400(0.4226) = 169. FS = 252/169 = 1.49. The 0.78 choice drops the cohesion term. The 2.10 choice adds cohesion twice. The 1.00 choice ignores the friction term.
problems.hint: FS = (cLs + W cos α tan φ) / (W sin α).
traps: Omitting the cohesion term cLs from the resisting force
Swapping sin and cos for the driving and resisting components

geotechnical/bearing-capacity.name: Bearing Capacity
geotechnical/bearing-capacity.application: Bearing capacity is the maximum pressure a foundation can apply to the soil before a shear failure occurs. Terzaghi’s equation uses bearing capacity factors that depend on the friction angle, plus contributions from cohesion, overburden, and footing width. On the FE, expect problems computing ultimate or allowable bearing capacity for strip footings with given Nc, Nq, and Nγ values.

content.body: Terzaghi’s bearing capacity equation gives the ultimate load per unit area that causes shear failure under a strip footing.
Ultimate Bearing Capacity

content.latex: q_{ult} = c N_c + \gamma' D_f N_q + \frac{1}{2} \gamma' B N_\gamma
content.label: Terzaghi's bearing capacity

content.body: Where $c$ = cohesion, $D_f$ = depth of footing, $B$ = footing width, $\gamma'$ = effective unit weight of soil, and $N_c$, $N_q$, $N_\gamma$ are bearing capacity factors that depend on $\phi$.
Allowable Bearing Capacity
Typical FS = 3 for bearing capacity. The allowable pressure is what you compare to the actual foundation pressure from structural loads.
Special Case: φ = 0 (Undrained Clay)
For purely cohesive soil: $N_c \approx 5.14$, $N_q = 1$, $N_\gamma = 0$. The equation simplifies to $q_{ult} = c_u \times 5.14 + \gamma D_f$.
On the FE, the bearing capacity factors will be given in the problem. You do not need to memorize Nc, Nq, Nγ values for different φ angles — just plug into the formula.
FS divides the ultimate bearing capacity, not the applied load. qallow = qult/FS. Also, use the effective unit weight (γ’ if below WT, γ if above) for the γ terms.

problems.statement: A strip footing rests on clay with undrained shear strength $c_u = 1{,}500 \text{ psf}$. Using $\phi = 0$ factors ($N_c = 5.14$, $N_q = 1$, $N_\gamma = 0$) and footing depth $D_f = 0$, what is the ultimate bearing capacity?
problems.eli5: qult = cNc + γ’(0)Nq + 0 = 1,500 × 5.14 + 0 + 0 = 7,710 psf. With Df = 0, the overburden term vanishes. The 1,500 psf option is just the cohesion. The 5,140 psf option uses c = 1,000 or confuses Nc with the answer. The 3,855 psf option divides by FS = 2 prematurely — the problem asks for ultimate, not allowable.
problems.hint: For φ = 0: Nγ = 0 and Nq contributes only if there is overburden (Df > 0).
problems.handbookFormula: q_{ult} = c N_c + \gamma' D_f N_q + \frac{1}{2} \gamma' B N_\gamma
traps: Dividing by FS when the problem asks for ultimate (not allowable) bearing capacity
Forgetting that for φ = 0, the Nγ term is zero

problems.statement: A strip footing ($B = 4 \text{ ft}$) is at depth $D_f = 3 \text{ ft}$ in a soil with $c = 0$, $\phi = 30\degree$, $\gamma = 120 \text{ pcf}$. Given $N_c = 30.14$, $N_q = 18.40$, $N_\gamma = 15.07$. What is the ultimate bearing capacity?
problems.eli5: qult = cNc + γDfNq + 0.5γBNγ = 0(30.14) + 120(3)(18.40) + 0.5(120)(4)(15.07) = 0 + 6,624 + 3,617 = 10,241 ≈ 10,240 psf. Since c = 0, the cohesion term drops out. The 6,624 psf option is only the overburden (Nq) term. The 3,617 psf option is only the width (Nγ) term. You need all three terms (even though one is zero here).
problems.hint: With c = 0, only the Nq and Nγ terms contribute. Compute each separately, then add.
problems.handbookFormula: q_{ult} = c N_c + \gamma' D_f N_q + \frac{1}{2} \gamma' B N_\gamma
traps: Forgetting the 1/2 factor on the Nγ term — it is 0.5γBNγ, not γBNγ
Only computing one of the three terms instead of summing all contributions

problems.statement: A 5-ft-wide strip footing at $D_f = 3 \text{ ft}$ sits on soil with $c = 500 \text{ psf}$, $\phi = 20\degree$, $\gamma = 115 \text{ pcf}$. Given $N_c = 14.83$, $N_q = 6.40$, $N_\gamma = 3.54$. What is the allowable bearing pressure with $FS = 3$?
problems.eli5: qult = cNc + γDfNq + 0.5γBNγ = 500(14.83) + 115(3)(6.40) + 0.5(115)(5)(3.54) = 7,415 + 2,208 + 1,018 = 10,641 psf. qallow = 10,641/3 = 3,547 ≈ 3,550 psf. The 10,640 psf option is the ultimate capacity without dividing by FS. The 7,415 psf option is only the cohesion term. The 2,210 psf option divides the overburden term alone by FS.
problems.hint: Compute all three terms of qult first. Then divide the total by FS = 3.
problems.handbookFormula: q_{ult} = c N_c + \gamma' D_f N_q + \frac{1}{2} \gamma' B N_\gamma
traps: Reporting qult as the answer when the problem asks for qallow — always check whether FS is needed
Applying FS to each term separately instead of dividing the total qult by FS
Forgetting the 1/2 factor on the Nγ term

geotechnical/lateral-earth-pressure.name: Lateral Earth Pressure
geotechnical/lateral-earth-pressure.application: Lateral earth pressure is the horizontal force that soil exerts on retaining walls, basement walls, and braced excavations. The pressure depends on wall movement: active (wall moves away), passive (wall pushes into soil), or at-rest (rigid wall, no movement). On the FE, expect problems computing the Rankine coefficients Ka, Kp, or K0 and the resulting force on a wall.

content.body: Rankine earth pressure theory assumes a smooth wall and level backfill with no cohesion ($c = 0$). The pressure increases linearly with depth.
Rankine Coefficients
At-Rest Coefficient
For overconsolidated soils: $K_0 = (1 - \sin \phi)\,\text{OCR}^{\sin \phi}$.
Active Force on a Wall

content.label: Total active force per unit wall length

content.body: The resultant acts at $H/3$ from the base of the wall. For a uniform surcharge $q$ on the surface, add a rectangular pressure of $K_a \cdot q$ over the full wall height.
Quick check: Ka × Kp = 1. If Ka = 1/3, then Kp = 3. This is a good sanity check on your calculation.
Active is always LESS than at-rest, which is LESS than passive: Ka < K0 < Kp. If your Ka comes out larger than 1 or your Kp comes out less than 1, you swapped the angle formula.

problems.statement: A soil has $\phi' = 30\degree$. What is the Rankine active earth pressure coefficient $K_a$?
problems.eli5: Ka = tan²(45° – 30°/2) = tan²(30°) = (0.5774)² = 0.333 = 1/3. The 3.0 option is Kp, the passive coefficient (or 1/Ka). The 0.577 option is tan 30°, not tan² 30°. The 0.50 option is sin 30°.
problems.hint: Ka = tan²(45° – φ/2). First compute the angle, then take tan².
traps: Using tan instead of tan² — the coefficient is the square of the tangent
Swapping the sign: using (45 + φ/2) gives Kp, not Ka

problems.statement: A 15-ft-tall retaining wall has backfill with $\phi' = 30\degree$, $\gamma = 120 \text{ pcf}$, $c = 0$. What is the total active force per foot of wall?
problems.eli5: Ka = 1/3 (from φ = 30°). Pa = 0.5 × Ka × γ × H² = 0.5 × (1/3) × 120 × 15² = 0.5 × 0.333 × 120 × 225 = 4,500 lb/ft. The 9,000 lb/ft choice forgets the 1/2 factor (uses KaγH² instead of 0.5KaγH²). The 13,500 lb/ft choice omits Ka entirely (uses Ka = 1: 0.5 x 1 x 120 x 225 = 13,500). The 2,250 lb/ft choice divides by 2 an extra time.
problems.hint: Active force on a wall: Pa = 0.5 × Ka × γ × H². The pressure diagram is a triangle.
traps: Forgetting the 1/2 factor — the pressure diagram is triangular, so the resultant is half the rectangle
Using Kp instead of Ka — active pressure is when the wall moves AWAY from the soil

problems.statement: A 12-ft retaining wall retains soil with $\gamma = 120 \text{ pcf}$, $\phi' = 30\degree$, $c = 0$. A uniform surcharge of $200 \text{ psf}$ is on the surface. What is the total active force on the wall (soil + surcharge)?
problems.eli5: Ka = 1/3. Soil: Pa(soil) = 0.5 × (1/3) × 120 × 12² = 0.5 × 40 × 144 = 2,880 lb/ft (triangular). Surcharge: Pa(surcharge) = Ka × q × H = (1/3) × 200 × 12 = 800 lb/ft (rectangular). Total = 2,880 + 800 = 3,680 lb/ft. The 2,880 lb/ft option ignores the surcharge. The 4,800 lb/ft option adds the surcharge force incorrectly or uses a higher Ka. The 800 lb/ft option is only the surcharge contribution.
problems.hint: The surcharge creates a uniform (rectangular) pressure of Ka × q over the full height, added to the triangular soil pressure.
traps: Forgetting to multiply the surcharge by Ka — the surcharge is not applied directly as a horizontal force; it is reduced by Ka
Adding the surcharge to the soil pressure without applying Ka first
Treating the surcharge pressure as triangular instead of rectangular

geotechnical/retaining-walls.name: Retaining Wall Stability
geotechnical/retaining-walls.application: Retaining wall design requires checking three failure modes: overturning about the toe, sliding along the base, and bearing capacity failure beneath the footing. Each check produces a factor of safety. On the FE, expect problems computing the FS against overturning or sliding, or finding the eccentricity and maximum base pressure under the wall.

content.body: A gravity retaining wall must satisfy three stability checks. Each computes a factor of safety (FS) that must exceed a minimum value (typically 1.5–2.0 for overturning, 1.5 for sliding, 3.0 for bearing).
Factor of Safety Against Overturning
Where $\Sigma M_R$ = sum of resisting moments about the toe and $M_O$ = overturning moment from the active earth pressure resultant.
Factor of Safety Against Sliding
Base Pressure (Eccentricity Method)
For the resultant to stay within the middle third of the base, $e \leq B/6$. If $e > B/6$, tension develops at the heel (undesirable for soil).
The eccentricity formula computes where the resultant vertical force hits the base, measured from the center. A small e means the load is well-centered; a large e means it is close to the toe.

Moments about the TOE: the weight of the wall and soil above the footing create resisting moments (clockwise), while the active pressure creates the overturning moment (counter-clockwise). Be consistent about the sign convention.

problems.statement: A retaining wall has total resisting moment $\Sigma M_R = 15{,}000 \text{ lb-ft/ft}$ and overturning moment $M_O = 5{,}000 \text{ lb-ft/ft}$ about the toe. What is the factor of safety against overturning?
problems.eli5: FS = ΣMR / MO = 15,000/5,000 = 3.0. This is a direct formula application. The 2.0 option might come from dividing something else. The 5.0 option reversed a number. The 0.33 option inverted the ratio (MO/MR).
problems.hint: FS(overturning) = resisting moments / overturning moment. Just divide.
traps: Inverting the ratio — FS = resisting/driving, not driving/resisting
Subtracting MO from MR instead of dividing

problems.statement: A retaining wall has total vertical force $\Sigma V = 5{,}000 \text{ lb/ft}$, base width $B = 6 \text{ ft}$, $\Sigma M_R = 18{,}000 \text{ lb-ft/ft}$, and $M_O = 6{,}000 \text{ lb-ft/ft}$. What is the eccentricity $e$ of the resultant on the base?
problems.eli5: First find where the resultant hits the base (measured from the toe): x̄ = (ΣMR – MO)/ΣV = (18,000 – 6,000)/5,000 = 12,000/5,000 = 2.40 ft. Eccentricity from the center: e = B/2 – x̄ = 3.0 – 2.4 = 0.60 ft. Check: B/6 = 1.0 ft, and e = 0.60 < 1.0, so the resultant is in the middle third ✔. The 2.40 ft option is x̄, the distance from the toe, not the eccentricity from the center. The 3.00 ft option is B/2. The 1.20 ft option doubles e by mistake.
problems.hint: Find x̄ (distance from toe), then e = B/2 – x̄.
traps: Reporting x̄ (distance from toe) as the eccentricity — eccentricity is measured from the center of the base
Forgetting to subtract MO from MR before dividing by ΣV

problems.statement: A gravity retaining wall has base width $B = 8 \text{ ft}$. The resultant vertical force $\Sigma V = 8{,}000 \text{ lb/ft}$ acts $3.0 \text{ ft}$ from the toe. What is the maximum pressure at the toe?
problems.eli5: Eccentricity: e = B/2 – x̄ = 4.0 – 3.0 = 1.0 ft. Check: B/6 = 8/6 = 1.33 ft, and e = 1.0 < 1.33 ✔ (in middle third). Toe pressure: qtoe = (ΣV/B)(1 + 6e/B) = (8,000/8)(1 + 6(1.0)/8) = 1,000(1 + 0.75) = 1,000 × 1.75 = 1,750 psf. The 1,000 psf option is the uniform pressure (ΣV/B) without the eccentricity effect. The 2,000 psf option uses e = B/6 = 1.33. The 1,333 psf option might come from a different eccentricity.
problems.hint: Find e = B/2 – x̄. Then qtoe = (ΣV/B)(1 + 6e/B).
traps: Using ΣV/B as the answer without accounting for eccentricity — this only works when e = 0 (resultant at the center)
Forgetting the factor of 6 in 6e/B — the formula is derived from the trapezoidal stress distribution
Using e in the wrong formula — the (1 + 6e/B) formula only applies when e ≤ B/6

geotechnical/deep-foundations.name: Deep Foundations
geotechnical/deep-foundations.application: When near-surface soils are too weak or compressible to carry a structure on shallow footings, civil engineers use deep foundations — driven piles or drilled shafts — to transfer load to deeper, stronger soil or rock. On the FE, expect to combine end bearing and skin friction into a total pile capacity and to reason about when deep foundations are needed and how pile groups behave.

content.body: A deep foundation carries load far below the surface. It is chosen when shallow footings would settle excessively or lack bearing capacity — for example, soft clay or loose fill over a firm stratum at depth.
Load Transfer

content.label: Total capacity = end bearing + skin (shaft) friction
qp = unit end bearing, Ap = tip area, fs = unit skin friction, As = shaft surface area

content.body: A pile resists load two ways: END BEARING at the tip (like a tiny footing) and SKIN FRICTION along the shaft. End-bearing piles reach a firm layer; friction piles develop most of their capacity along the shaft in deep uniform soil.
Pile Groups

Piles are usually installed in groups capped together. The group capacity may be less than the sum of individual piles (group efficiency < 1 in clays), and a group settles more and influences soil deeper than a single pile because the stressed zone overlaps.
Negative Skin Friction

If soil around a pile settles MORE than the pile (e.g., fill placed over compressible clay), it drags down on the shaft. This downward "negative skin friction" (downdrag) adds load to the pile rather than supporting it.
Total pile capacity is simply end bearing plus skin friction. Identify which dominates: a pile bearing on rock is mostly end bearing; a long pile in uniform clay is mostly skin friction.
Negative skin friction adds to the load on a pile — it does NOT help support it. Settling fill or consolidating clay around the shaft is a downdrag force to design for, not a resistance.

problems.statement: A pile has a unit end-bearing resistance $q_p = 2{,}000\text{ kPa}$ over a tip area $A_p = 0.20\text{ m}^2$, and a unit skin friction $f_s = 50\text{ kPa}$ over a shaft surface area $A_s = 12\text{ m}^2$. What is the ultimate pile capacity?
problems.eli5: Q_ult = Qp + Qs = qp·Ap + fs·As = (2,000)(0.20) + (50)(12) = 400 + 600 = 1,000 kN. The 400 kN option is only the end bearing. The 600 kN option is only the skin friction. The 2,600 kN option mistakenly uses the tip area as 1.0 m² (2,000 + 600).
problems.hint: Q_ult = qp·Ap + fs·As — add end bearing and skin friction.
traps: Reporting only end bearing or only skin friction
Using the shaft area for end bearing or vice versa

problems.statement: A site has 8 m of soft compressible clay overlying dense gravel. Why would a deep foundation be preferred over a shallow footing for a heavily loaded column?

choices.text: To transfer the load through the weak clay to the firm gravel, limiting settlement
Because deep foundations are always cheaper than footings
To increase the bearing pressure on the soft clay
Because shallow footings cannot be used under any column

problems.eli5: The soft clay would settle excessively under a shallow footing. A deep foundation bypasses the weak clay and transfers the load to the dense gravel below, controlling settlement and providing adequate capacity. The claim that deep foundations are always cheaper is false (piles are usually more expensive). The option about increasing bearing pressure on the soft clay is backwards — you want to relieve, not increase, load on the clay. The claim that shallow footings can never be used overstates the case.
problems.hint: What problem does the soft clay create, and how does reaching the gravel solve it?

steps.text: Soft clay under a footing would settle excessively and lacks capacity.
A deep foundation carries load through the clay to the dense gravel.
This limits settlement and provides adequate bearing.

traps: Assuming deep foundations are chosen for cost rather than performance
Thinking the goal is to load the weak layer more

problems.statement: Fill is placed over a soft clay layer through which a pile passes. As the clay consolidates and settles relative to the pile, what force develops on the pile shaft?

choices.text: Negative skin friction (downdrag), which adds load to the pile
Positive skin friction that increases the pile capacity
An upward buoyant force that relieves the pile
No force, because the clay and pile move together

problems.eli5: When surrounding soil settles MORE than the pile, it drags down on the shaft — negative skin friction (downdrag). This acts as an additional downward load the pile must carry, not as support. The "positive skin friction increases capacity" choice reverses the direction. The "upward buoyant force" choice invents a relief that does not exist here. The "no force, clay and pile move together" choice ignores the relative settlement that causes downdrag.
problems.hint: Which way does the friction act when the soil settles faster than the pile?

steps.text: Consolidating clay settles more than the pile.
The relative downward movement drags on the shaft.
This is negative skin friction (downdrag), adding load to the pile.

traps: Assuming the friction always helps support the pile
Ignoring relative settlement between soil and pile

geotechnical/compaction-stabilization.name: Compaction & Soil Improvement
geotechnical/compaction-stabilization.application: Before building on or with soil, civil engineers densify and improve it. Compaction increases strength and reduces settlement, and is verified in the field against a laboratory maximum dry density. As a civil engineer you run Proctor tests, specify relative compaction, evaluate relative density of granular fills, and select stabilization methods. On the FE, expect relative compaction, relative density, and stabilization questions.
