content.body: Compaction expels air to pack soil particles closer, raising dry density. A Proctor test (standard or modified) compacts soil at several moisture contents to find the maximum dry density and the optimum moisture content (OMC).
Relative Compaction

content.label: Field dry density as a % of the lab maximum

content.body: Specifications typically require relative compaction of at least 90--95% of the Proctor maximum. Field dry density is checked with a sand-cone or nuclear-gauge test.
Relative Density (Granular Soils)

content.label: Density state of sands and gravels

content.body: For clean sands and gravels, relative density (how the in-place void ratio compares to the loosest and densest states) describes the compaction state better than relative compaction.
Soil Improvement & Stabilization

When compaction alone is insufficient, soils are stabilized: mechanically (blending gradations, densification), chemically (LIME is effective in plastic clays — it reduces plasticity and swelling; CEMENT works well in granular soils), or with geosynthetics for reinforcement, separation, and drainage. Proper drainage removes water that would otherwise weaken the soil.
Match the chemical stabilizer to the soil: lime for high-plasticity clays (it reduces the plasticity index), cement for granular and low-plasticity soils.
Relative compaction (vs. a Proctor maximum) and relative density (vs. loosest/densest void ratios) are different measures. Relative density applies to cohesionless soils; do not mix the two formulas.

problems.statement: A field dry unit weight of $118\text{ pcf}$ is measured on a fill whose laboratory maximum dry unit weight (modified Proctor) is $124\text{ pcf}$. What is the relative compaction?
problems.eli5: RC = (γd,field/γd,max) × 100 = (118/124) × 100 = 95.2%, which would satisfy a typical 95% specification. The 105% choice inverts the ratio (124/118). The 5.1% choice computes the percent difference (6/118). The 90.0% choice is a guess at the spec value.
problems.hint: Relative compaction = (field dry density / lab maximum dry density) × 100.
traps: Inverting the ratio (lab over field)
Confusing relative compaction with relative density

problems.statement: A sand has maximum void ratio $e_{max} = 0.90$, minimum void ratio $e_{min} = 0.40$, and an in-place void ratio $e = 0.60$. What is its relative density?
problems.eli5: Dr = (emax − e)/(emax − emin) × 100 = (0.90 − 0.60)/(0.90 − 0.40) × 100 = 0.30/0.50 × 100 = 60% — a medium-dense sand. The 40% choice uses (e − emin) in the numerator. The 67% choice uses (e − emin)/(emax − e). The 33% choice inverts the numerator difference.
problems.hint: Dr = (emax − e)/(emax − emin) × 100.
traps: Using (e − emin) in the numerator instead of (emax − e)
Forgetting to multiply by 100

problems.statement: A high-plasticity clay subgrade is too soft and swells when wet. Which chemical stabilizer is most appropriate?

choices.text: Portland cement (alone, in the plastic clay)
Fly ash used purely as a filler

problems.eli5: Lime is the classic stabilizer for high-plasticity clays: it reduces the plasticity index, controls swelling, and improves workability and strength. Cement is more effective in granular and low-plasticity soils. Adding water would worsen a swelling clay, and fly ash as a mere filler does not chemically stabilize it.
problems.hint: Which additive specifically reduces the plasticity and swelling of clay?

steps.text: High-plasticity clay needs its plasticity and swelling reduced.
Lime reacts with clay minerals to lower the plasticity index.
Therefore lime is the appropriate stabilizer (cement suits granular soils).

traps: Defaulting to cement for every soil — it suits granular, not plastic clay
Assuming added water improves a swelling clay

transportation/stopping-sight-distance.name: Stopping Sight Distance & PHF
transportation/stopping-sight-distance.application: Stopping sight distance (SSD) is the minimum distance a driver needs to see ahead to stop safely for an unexpected obstacle. It controls everything from vertical curve design to horizontal clearance requirements. The FE Handbook provides the SSD formula with a deceleration rate and grade adjustment, plus intersection sight distance (ISD) for stop-controlled approaches. Expect problems plugging into the SSD formula with or without grade, and computing the Peak Hour Factor from 15-minute traffic counts.

content.body: SSD has two components: the distance traveled during perception-reaction time and the braking distance. The formula combines both into a single expression using design speed in mph.
Stopping Sight Distance

Where $V$ = design speed (mph), $t$ = perception-reaction time (sec, typically 2.5 s), $a$ = deceleration (ft/sec\u00B2, typically 11.2), $G$ = percent grade $\div$ 100 (positive for uphill). The factor 1.47 converts mph to ft/sec.
Grade Sign Convention

Uphill grades are positive ($+G$). Going uphill, gravity helps the driver stop, so the denominator is larger and SSD is shorter. Going downhill ($-G$), gravity fights braking, so SSD is longer. A common exam trap is reversing this sign.
Intersection Sight Distance
Where $V_{\text{major}}$ = design speed of the major road (mph) and $t_g$ = time gap for the entering vehicle (sec). This is the sight triangle distance for a vehicle waiting at a stop sign.
Peak Hour Factor

Where $V$ = hourly volume (veh/hr) and $V_{15}$ = peak 15-minute volume within that hour. PHF ranges from 0.25 (all traffic in one 15-min period) to 1.00 (perfectly uniform flow). The peak flow rate equals $4 \times V_{15}$, which is always $\geq V$.

The 1.47 in the SSD formula is just 5,280/3,600 (miles to feet, hours to seconds). If the problem gives speed in ft/sec, skip the 1.47 and use v directly for the reaction distance: SSD = vt + v²/(2a).
Uphill = positive G = SHORTER SSD (easier to stop). Downhill = negative G = LONGER SSD (harder to stop). If a problem says "4% downgrade," use G = −0.04.

problems.statement: A roadway has a design speed of $60 \text{ mph}$ on a level grade. Using $t = 2.5 \text{ s}$ and $a = 11.2 \text{ ft/sec}^2$, what is the stopping sight distance?
problems.eli5: Plug straight into the formula. Reaction distance = 1.47 × 60 × 2.5 = 220.5 ft. Braking distance = 60² / [30 × (11.2/32.2)] = 3,600/10.43 = 345.1 ft. Total SSD = 220.5 + 345.1 = 565.6 ≈ 566 ft. The 345 ft choice is the braking distance alone — forgot the reaction component. The 221 ft choice is the reaction distance alone — forgot braking. The 750 ft choice uses a wrong deceleration value.
problems.hint: Two components: reaction distance (1.47Vt) plus braking distance (V² over the 30-term).
traps: Reporting only the braking distance (345 ft) and forgetting the reaction distance
Reporting only the reaction distance (221 ft) and forgetting braking

problems.statement: A road has a design speed of $60 \text{ mph}$ on a $4\%$ downgrade. Using $t = 2.5 \text{ s}$ and $a = 11.2 \text{ ft/sec}^2$, what is the SSD?
problems.eli5: Downgrade means G = −0.04. The denominator becomes 30 × (0.348 − 0.04) = 30 × 0.308 = 9.23. Braking distance = 3,600/9.23 = 390 ft. Add reaction = 220.5 ft. SSD = 610 ft. The 566 ft option used G = 0 (level). The 530 ft option used G = +0.04 (uphill — wrong direction). The 390 ft option is braking only. The key trap: downhill makes stopping HARDER, so SSD is LONGER.
problems.hint: Downgrade = negative G in the denominator. The denominator gets smaller, so braking distance gets longer.
traps: Using +G for a downgrade — uphill is positive, downhill is negative
Using G = 0 and ignoring the grade entirely
Forgetting to add the reaction distance to the braking distance

problems.statement: A road carries $1{,}200 \text{ veh/hr}$. The peak 15-minute volume within that hour is $400 \text{ veh}$. What is the peak 15-minute flow rate?
problems.eli5: The peak flow rate extrapolates the worst 15 minutes to an hourly rate: 4 × V₁₅ = 4 × 400 = 1,600 veh/hr. Equivalently, PHF = V/(4×V₁₅) = 1,200/1,600 = 0.75, and flow rate = V/PHF = 1,200/0.75 = 1,600. The tricky part: the flow rate is HIGHER than the hourly volume because it represents the peak surge. The 1,200 veh/hr choice is the hourly volume itself — that is the demand, not the peak rate. The 400 veh/hr choice is V₁₅ without multiplying by 4. The 900 veh/hr choice multiplied V × PHF instead of dividing.
problems.hint: The flow rate is 4 × V₁₅ — it converts a 15-minute count into an equivalent hourly rate.
traps: Confusing the hourly volume (1,200) with the peak flow rate (1,600) — the flow rate is always ≥ the hourly volume
Multiplying V × PHF instead of dividing — that gives 900, which is less than the hourly volume (impossible for a peak rate)

transportation/vertical-curves.name: Vertical Curve Design
transportation/vertical-curves.application: Vertical curves are parabolas that transition between two road grades. Crest curves must provide adequate sight distance over the hill; sag curves must illuminate the road with headlights at night. The FE Handbook gives separate formulas for crest and sag curves, each with S ≤ L and S > L cases. Expect problems computing minimum curve length from sight distance, finding the tangent offset at the PVI, or using the K-value to compare designs.

content.body: A vertical curve is a second-degree parabola connecting two tangent grades $g_1$ (entering) and $g_2$ (exiting). Grades are expressed as decimals (e.g., +3% = 0.03). The algebraic difference is $A = |g_2 - g_1| \times 100$.
Parabolic Curve Equations

content.label: Tangent offset at distance x from PVC
Rate of vertical curvature (ft per % change)

content.body: Minimum Curve Length — Crest (Stopping Sight Distance)

content.label: Standard criteria: h₁ = 3.50 ft, h₂ = 2.0 ft
Crest when sight distance exceeds curve length

content.body: Minimum Curve Length — Sag (Headlight Criteria)

content.label: Sag when sight distance exceeds curve length

content.body: Always assume S ≤ L first (the most common case on the FE). Compute L, then verify that S ≤ L. If not, switch to the S > L formula.
Crest and sag formulas are DIFFERENT. The crest formula denominator (2,158) is a constant. The sag formula denominator (400 + 3.5S) depends on S. Mixing them up is a common exam mistake.

problems.statement: A crest vertical curve has $A = 8$ and required stopping sight distance $S = 500 \text{ ft}$. Assuming $S \leq L$, what is the minimum curve length?
problems.eli5: Direct plug-in: L = AS²/2,158 = 8 × 500²/2,158 = 8 × 250,000/2,158 = 2,000,000/2,158 = 927 ft. Check: S = 500 < L = 927, so S ≤ L is satisfied. The 500 ft choice confused L with S. The 730 ft choice used the S > L formula (2×500 − 2,158/8 = 1,000 − 270 = 730). The 464 ft choice used A/2 = 4 instead of 8.
problems.hint: Crest, S ≤ L: L = AS²/2,158. Just plug in A and S.
traps: Using the S > L formula when the problem specifies S ≤ L
Using the sag formula denominator (400 + 3.5S) instead of the crest constant (2,158)

problems.statement: A crest vertical curve connects a $+3\%$ grade to a $-5\%$ grade with curve length $L = 800 \text{ ft}$. What is the tangent offset $E$ at the PVI?
problems.eli5: E = (g₂ − g₁) × L/8. Convert grades to decimals: g₁ = +0.03, g₂ = −0.05. E = (−0.05 − 0.03) × 800/8 = −0.08 × 100 = −8.0 ft. The magnitude is 8.0 ft. The negative sign means the curve dips below the tangent line (crest). The 16 ft choice used L/4 instead of L/8. The 4 ft choice used L/16. The 32 ft choice used L/2.
problems.hint: The shortcut: E = (g₂ − g₁) × L / 8. The PVI is at the midpoint of the curve.

steps.text: Magnitude: $|E| = 8.0$ ft (curve is 8 ft below the tangent at midpoint)

traps: Forgetting to convert percentage grades to decimals before subtracting
Using L/4 instead of L/8 in the shortcut formula — the derivation is E = a(L/2)² where a = (g₂−g₁)/(2L)

problems.statement: A sag vertical curve connects a $-4\%$ grade to a $+4\%$ grade. The required SSD is $300 \text{ ft}$. Using the headlight criteria with $S \leq L$, what is the minimum curve length?
problems.eli5: A = |g₂ − g₁| × 100 = |0.04 − (−0.04)| × 100 = 0.08 × 100 = 8. Sag headlight formula (S ≤ L): L = AS²/(400 + 3.5S) = 8 × 90,000/(400 + 1,050) = 720,000/1,450 = 497 ft. Verify: S = 300 < L = 497 ✔. The 334 ft option used the crest formula AS²/2,158 = 720,000/2,158 = 334. The 419 ft option used the S > L sag formula. The 600 ft option used 2S.
problems.hint: This is a SAG curve — use L = AS²/(400 + 3.5S), not the crest formula with 2,158.
traps: Using the crest formula (2,158) instead of the sag formula (400 + 3.5S) — gives 334 ft, much too short
Computing A incorrectly — remember A = |g₂ − g₁| × 100, and the grades must be in decimal
Using the S > L formula without checking that S ≤ L is satisfied

transportation/horizontal-curves.name: Horizontal Curve Design
transportation/horizontal-curves.application: Horizontal curves guide vehicles through direction changes on a roadway. The curve geometry is defined by the radius (R), degree of curve (D), and intersection angle (I). Engineers compute tangent length, curve length, and middle ordinate to lay out the curve in the field, then set the superelevation rate to counteract centrifugal force at the design speed. On the FE, expect problems converting between R and D, computing T and L, or finding the required superelevation.

content.body: A simple circular curve is defined by its radius $R$ and the intersection angle $I$ (also called $\Delta$). The degree of curve $D$ is the central angle subtended by a 100-ft arc.
Radius and Degree of Curve

content.label: Arc definition of degree of curve

content.body: Tangent and Curve Length

content.label: Tangent distance (PI to PC or PT)
Curve length (arc from PC to PT)

content.body: Middle Ordinate and External Distance
Superelevation
Where $e$ = superelevation rate (%), $f$ = side friction factor, $V$ = design speed (mph), and $R$ = curve radius (ft). The 0.01 converts $e$ from percent to decimal.
The formula R = 5,729.58/D is for the arc definition (100-ft arc). This is the standard used on highway design. Don't confuse it with the chord definition used in railroad work.
T uses tan(I/2), not tan(I). Forgetting to halve the intersection angle is one of the most common mistakes on horizontal curve problems.

problems.statement: A horizontal curve has a degree of curve $D = 6\degree$. What is the curve radius?
problems.eli5: R = 5,729.58/D = 5,729.58/6 = 954.9 ≈ 955 ft. Direct division. The 5,730 ft option forgot to divide by D (used D = 1). The 34,377 ft option multiplied instead of dividing: 5,729.58 × 6 = 34,377. The 478 ft option divided by 12 instead of 6.
problems.hint: R = 5,729.58 / D. Just divide.
traps: Multiplying 5,729.58 by D instead of dividing — the relationship is inverse
Confusing arc definition with chord definition

problems.statement: A horizontal curve has $R = 1{,}200 \text{ ft}$ and intersection angle $I = 30\degree$. What is the tangent distance $T$?
problems.eli5: T = R tan(I/2) = 1,200 × tan(15°) = 1,200 × 0.2679 = 321.5 ≈ 322 ft. The 693 ft choice used tan(I) = tan(30°) = 0.5774 instead of tan(I/2) — forgot to halve the angle: 1,200 × 0.5774 = 693. The 628 ft choice is the curve length L = RI(π/180) = 1,200 × 30 × π/180 = 628 — confused T with L. The 161 ft choice divided by 2 one too many times.
problems.hint: T = R tan(I/2). Make sure to halve the intersection angle before taking the tangent.
traps: Using tan(I) instead of tan(I/2) — the intersection angle must be halved
Confusing tangent distance T with curve length L

problems.statement: A curve has design speed $V = 45 \text{ mph}$, radius $R = 600 \text{ ft}$, and side friction factor $f = 0.15$. What is the required superelevation rate $e$?
problems.eli5: 0.01e + f = V²/(15R) = 45²/(15 × 600) = 2,025/9,000 = 0.225. Solve: 0.01e = 0.225 − 0.15 = 0.075. e = 7.5%. The 22.5% option forgot to subtract f — set 0.01e = 0.225, so e = 22.5. The 0.075% option solved for 0.01e and reported that as e without dividing by 0.01. The 15.0% option confused e with f × 100.
problems.hint: Solve 0.01e + f = V²/(15R) for e. Remember e is in percent, so 0.01e converts it to decimal.
traps: Forgetting to subtract the friction factor f before solving for e
Reporting 0.01e (= 0.075) as e — the factor of 0.01 must be divided out
Confusing the formula with e + f = V²/(gR) from physics — the handbook uses the highway version with 15R

transportation/signal-timing.name: Traffic Signal Timing
transportation/signal-timing.application: Traffic signal timing balances safety and efficiency at intersections. The yellow interval gives drivers time to stop or clear the intersection; the all-red clearance protects crossing traffic; and the pedestrian green ensures walkers can cross safely. The FE Handbook provides formulas for all three. Expect problems computing the yellow interval from approach speed and deceleration, the red clearance from intersection width, or the minimum pedestrian green time.

content.body: The change interval (yellow + all-red) is the critical safety element of signal timing. It must be long enough for a vehicle at the decision point to either stop or clear the intersection.
Yellow Interval

Where $t$ = driver reaction time (sec), $v$ = approach speed (ft/sec), $a$ = deceleration (ft/sec\u00B2), $G$ = grade (decimal, $+$ uphill). The $64.4 = 2g$ accounts for the effect of grade on deceleration.
Red Clearance Interval
Where $W$ = intersection width curb-to-curb (ft) and $l$ = vehicle length (ft). This is the time for a vehicle entering on yellow to clear the far side of the intersection.
Pedestrian Green Time
Where $L$ = crosswalk length (ft), $S_p$ = pedestrian speed (default 3.5 ft/sec), and $N_{\text{ped}}$ = number of pedestrians per interval. The 3.2-second start-up is built in.
The yellow interval formula uses v in ft/sec, not mph. If given speed in mph, multiply by 1.467 to convert: 50 mph × 1.467 = 73.3 ft/sec. Forgetting this conversion is a very common exam error.

For the red clearance, both the intersection width W AND the vehicle length l go in the numerator. The vehicle must travel W + l to fully clear the intersection. Forgetting l underestimates the red time.

problems.statement: An intersection approach has a speed of $50 \text{ mph}$. Using driver reaction time $t = 1.0 \text{ s}$ and deceleration $a = 10 \text{ ft/sec}^2$ on a level grade, what is the yellow interval?
problems.eli5: First convert 50 mph to ft/sec: 50 × 1.467 = 73.3 ft/sec. Then y = t + v/(2a) = 1.0 + 73.3/(2 × 10) = 1.0 + 73.3/20 = 1.0 + 3.67 = 4.67 ≈ 4.7 sec. The 3.5 sec option used mph directly: 1.0 + 50/20 = 3.5 — forgot to convert to ft/sec. The 3.7 sec option forgot the reaction time: 73.3/20 = 3.67. The 8.3 sec option used v/a instead of v/(2a): 1.0 + 73.3/10 = 8.3.
problems.hint: Convert mph to ft/sec first (multiply by 1.467), then plug into y = t + v/(2a).
traps: Using mph instead of ft/sec — the formula requires v in ft/sec
Forgetting the factor of 2 in the denominator — v/(2a), not v/a

problems.statement: An intersection is $60 \text{ ft}$ wide (curb to curb). A design vehicle is $20 \text{ ft}$ long and approaches at $50 \text{ mph}$. What is the all-red clearance interval?
problems.eli5: Convert speed: 50 × 1.467 = 73.3 ft/sec. r = (W + l)/v = (60 + 20)/73.3 = 80/73.3 = 1.09 ≈ 1.1 sec. The 1.6 sec choice used mph instead of ft/sec: 80/50 = 1.6. The 0.8 sec choice forgot the vehicle length: 60/73.3 = 0.82. The 0.9 sec choice inverted and divided v by (W+l).
problems.hint: r = (W + l)/v. Don't forget to include the vehicle length AND convert speed to ft/sec.
traps: Using mph instead of ft/sec — gives 1.6 sec instead of 1.1 sec
Forgetting to add the vehicle length l — the vehicle must fully clear the intersection

problems.statement: A crosswalk is $56 \text{ ft}$ long with a default pedestrian speed of $3.5 \text{ ft/sec}$. During the peak signal cycle, $15$ pedestrians are expected. What is the minimum pedestrian green time $G_p$?
problems.eli5: Gp = 3.2 + L/Sp + 0.27Nped = 3.2 + 56/3.5 + 0.27 × 15 = 3.2 + 16.0 + 4.05 = 23.25 ≈ 23.3 sec. Three components: start-up (3.2), walking time (16.0), and pedestrian volume adjustment (4.05). The 19.2 sec option forgot the Nped term: 3.2 + 16.0. The 21.3 sec option used Sp = 4.0 instead of 3.5: 3.2 + 14.0 + 4.05. The 7.3 sec option forgot the walking time entirely: 3.2 + 4.05.
problems.hint: Three terms: 3.2 start-up + L/Sp walking + 0.27Nped volume adjustment.
traps: Forgetting the 0.27Nped term — the pedestrian count affects the required green time
Using a pedestrian speed other than the default 3.5 ft/sec when none is specified
Forgetting the 3.2-second start-up constant

transportation/traffic-flow.name: Traffic Flow & Crash Rates
transportation/traffic-flow.application: Traffic flow theory describes the relationship between speed, density, and flow on a roadway. The Greenshields model assumes a linear speed-density relationship, which produces a parabolic flow-density curve with a single peak (maximum flow). Crash rate formulas let engineers compare the safety performance of intersections and road segments using a per-million-vehicle exposure rate. On the FE, expect problems finding maximum flow or speed from Greenshields, or computing RMEV/RMVM from crash and traffic data.

content.body: The fundamental relationship is $V = S \times D$: flow equals speed times density. The Greenshields model adds a linear constraint between speed and density, producing closed-form expressions for maximum flow and optimum density.
Greenshields Speed-Density Model

content.label: Speed as a function of density

content.body: Where $S_f$ = free-flow speed (mph) at zero density, $D_j$ = jam density (veh/mi/ln) at zero speed, and $D$ = current density.
Maximum Flow and Optimum Density

content.label: Optimum density and speed at max flow

content.body: At maximum flow, both speed and density are exactly half their extreme values. This is a useful quick-check.
Crash Rate — Intersections (RMEV)
Where $A$ = number of crashes per year and $V = ADT \times 365$ = total entering vehicles per year.
Crash Rate — Road Segments (RMVM)
Where $VMT = ADT \times (\text{days}) \times (\text{length in miles})$.
At maximum flow: speed = Sf/2, density = Dj/2, flow = DjSf/4. These three relationships are all you need for most Greenshields problems on the FE.
For RMEV, V = ADT × 365. Don't forget to annualize the daily traffic. A common mistake is dividing crashes by ADT directly without multiplying by 365.

problems.statement: A freeway has free-flow speed $S_f = 70 \text{ mph}$ and jam density $D_j = 180 \text{ veh/mi/ln}$. Using the Greenshields model, what is the maximum flow?
problems.eli5: Vm = DjSf/4 = 180 × 70/4 = 12,600/4 = 3,150 veh/hr/ln. Direct formula application. The 12,600 option forgot to divide by 4: Dj × Sf = 12,600. The 6,300 option divided by 2 instead of 4. The 1,575 option divided by 8 instead of 4.
problems.hint: Maximum flow = DjSf/4. One formula, two inputs.
traps: Forgetting to divide by 4 — the product DjSf is NOT the maximum flow
Dividing by 2 instead of 4 — the factor comes from the parabolic flow-density curve

problems.statement: A road has $S_f = 60 \text{ mph}$ and $D_j = 120 \text{ veh/mi/ln}$. What is the speed when density is $D = 40 \text{ veh/mi/ln}$?
problems.eli5: S = Sf − (Sf/Dj) × D = 60 − (60/120) × 40 = 60 − 0.5 × 40 = 60 − 20 = 40 mph. The 60 mph choice used Sf directly without the density reduction. The 20 mph choice computed only the reduction term (Sf/Dj × D = 20) and forgot to subtract from Sf. The 30 mph choice is the optimum speed So = Sf/2, which occurs at D = Dj/2 = 60, not at D = 40.
problems.hint: Greenshields: S = Sf − (Sf/Dj) × D. Compute the slope first, then the speed.
traps: Confusing the optimum speed (Sf/2 = 30) with the speed at a given density
Using Sf without subtracting the density term — speed decreases as density increases

problems.statement: An intersection has $12$ crashes in one year. The ADT entering from all approaches is $8{,}000 \text{ veh/day}$. What is the crash rate per million entering vehicles (RMEV)?
problems.eli5: V = ADT × 365 = 8,000 × 365 = 2,920,000 vehicles/year. RMEV = A × 1,000,000/V = 12 × 1,000,000/2,920,000 = 12,000,000/2,920,000 = 4.11 crashes per million entering vehicles. The 1,500 choice forgot to multiply ADT by 365: 12,000,000/8,000 = 1,500 — way too high. The 0.0041 choice forgot the ×1,000,000 factor: 12/2,920,000. The 12 choice is just the raw crash count without normalizing by traffic volume.
problems.hint: Annualize: V = ADT × 365. Then RMEV = A × 1,000,000/V.
traps: Forgetting to multiply ADT by 365 to get annual volume — gives a crash rate 365× too high
Forgetting the ×1,000,000 factor — the rate is per MILLION vehicles, not per vehicle

transportation/capacity-los.name: Freeway Capacity & Level of Service
transportation/capacity-los.application: Freeway capacity analysis converts a raw traffic volume into a per-lane passenger-car flow rate, then compares the resulting density to the LOS table to rate the facility from A (free flow) through F (breakdown). The conversion accounts for the peak hour factor (PHF), number of lanes, and the presence of heavy vehicles using the passenger car equivalent (PCE). On the FE, expect problems computing the heavy-vehicle adjustment factor, the demand flow rate, or determining the LOS from density.

content.body: The analysis converts the measured hourly volume into an equivalent passenger-car flow rate per lane, then finds density and looks up the LOS.
Demand Flow Rate
Where $V$ = hourly volume (veh/hr), $PHF$ = peak hour factor, $N$ = number of lanes in the analysis direction, and $f_{HV}$ = heavy-vehicle adjustment factor.
Heavy-Vehicle Factor
Where $P_T$ = proportion of trucks and $E_T$ = passenger car equivalent (PCE). For level terrain $E_T = 2.0$; for rolling terrain $E_T = 3.0$.
Density and LOS
Where $S$ = mean speed (mph). Compare $D$ to the LOS table: A ($\leq 11$), B ($> 11$–18), C ($> 18$–26), D ($> 26$–35), E ($> 35$–45), F ($> 45$, demand exceeds capacity).
The LOS table is based on DENSITY, not volume or speed. Compute vp first, then D = vp/S, then look up D in the table.
PCE values differ by terrain: ET = 2.0 (level) vs. 3.0 (rolling). Using the wrong terrain doubles the truck impact. Always check what terrain the problem specifies.

problems.statement: A freeway has $10\%$ trucks ($P_T = 0.10$) on level terrain ($E_T = 2.0$). What is the heavy-vehicle adjustment factor $f_{HV}$?
problems.eli5: fHV = 1/(1 + PT(ET − 1)) = 1/(1 + 0.10(2.0 − 1)) = 1/(1 + 0.10) = 1/1.10 = 0.909. The 0.833 option used rolling terrain ET = 3.0: 1/(1 + 0.10 × 2) = 1/1.20. The 1.100 option inverted the formula and got the denominator itself. The 0.800 option used PT × ET = 0.20, then 1 − 0.20 = 0.80.
problems.hint: fHV = 1/(1 + PT(ET − 1)). Subtract 1 from ET first, then multiply by PT.
traps: Using rolling terrain PCE (3.0) when the problem specifies level terrain (2.0)
Using PT × ET directly instead of PT × (ET − 1) — the −1 accounts for replacing a truck with a passenger car

problems.statement: A 3-lane directional freeway carries $V = 4{,}500 \text{ veh/hr}$ with $PHF = 0.92$ and $f_{HV} = 0.909$. What is the demand flow rate $v_p$?
problems.eli5: vp = V/(PHF × N × fHV) = 4,500/(0.92 × 3 × 0.909) = 4,500/2.509 = 1,793 pc/h/ln. All three adjustments (PHF, lanes, heavy vehicles) must be applied. The 1,630 pc/h/ln choice forgot fHV: 4,500/(0.92 × 3) = 4,500/2.76 = 1,630. The 1,650 pc/h/ln choice forgot PHF: 4,500/(3 × 0.909) = 4,500/2.73 = 1,650. The 4,500 pc/h/ln choice applied no adjustments at all.
problems.hint: vp = V / (PHF × N × fHV). All three factors go in the denominator.
traps: Forgetting one of the three adjustment factors in the denominator
Multiplying by the factors instead of dividing — the flow rate per lane is always higher than V/N

problems.statement: A 2-lane directional freeway has $V = 3{,}600 \text{ veh/hr}$, $PHF = 0.90$, $P_T = 0.10$, $E_T = 2.0$, and mean speed $S = 60 \text{ mph}$. What is the level of service?
problems.eli5: Step 1: fHV = 1/(1 + 0.10 × 1) = 1/1.10 = 0.909. Step 2: vp = 3,600/(0.90 × 2 × 0.909) = 3,600/1.636 = 2,200 pc/h/ln. Step 3: D = vp/S = 2,200/60 = 36.7 pc/mi/ln. Step 4: From the LOS table, D = 36.7 falls in >35–45 → LOS E. The LOS D choice results from forgetting fHV: vp = 3,600/(0.90 × 2) = 2,000, D = 33.3 → >26–35. The LOS C choice might come from using 3 lanes. The LOS F choice would require D > 45.
problems.hint: Compute fHV, then vp, then D = vp/S. Look up D in the LOS table.
traps: Forgetting the fHV adjustment — dropping it moves the answer from LOS E to LOS D
Using volume directly as density — density = flow/speed, not flow alone
Reading the LOS table incorrectly — the boundaries are density-based, not flow-based

transportation/travel-demand.name: Travel Demand & Trip Distribution
transportation/travel-demand.application: Before a road or transit line is designed, planners forecast how many trips will use it and where they will go. As a civil engineer you apply the four-step travel demand model and use the gravity model to distribute trips among destination zones. On the FE, expect to identify the planning steps and to compute trips between zones with the gravity model.

content.body: Regional travel is forecast with the classic FOUR-STEP model, applied in order to a set of traffic analysis zones.
The Four-Step Model

(1) Trip GENERATION — how many trips each zone produces and attracts, from land use. (2) Trip DISTRIBUTION — where the trips go, usually via the gravity model. (3) MODE choice — which travel mode (auto, transit, walk). (4) Traffic ASSIGNMENT — which routes the trips take through the network.
Gravity Model (Trip Distribution)

content.latex: T_{ij} = P_i \left[ \frac{A_j F_{ij} K_{ij}}{\sum_j A_j F_{ij} K_{ij}} \right]
content.label: Trips from zone i to zone j

content.body: Here $P_i$ is the trips produced in zone $i$, $A_j$ the trips attracted to zone $j$, $F_{ij}$ a friction factor that DECREASES as travel time/impedance between $i$ and $j$ increases, and $K_{ij}$ a socioeconomic adjustment. Trips spread to each destination in proportion to its attractions and its friction factor.
Like gravity between masses, trips grow with the "mass" of attractions (Aj) and shrink with distance/impedance (through the friction factor Fij). Closer, more attractive zones get more trips.
The denominator sums over ALL destination zones j. Forgetting to normalize by that sum is the most common gravity-model error — the fractions to all zones must add to 1.

problems.statement: Zone $i$ produces $P_i = 1{,}000$ trips. They can go to Zone 1 ($A_1 = 200$, $F_{i1} = 0.5$) or Zone 2 ($A_2 = 300$, $F_{i2} = 0.2$), with $K = 1$ for both. How many trips go from Zone $i$ to Zone 1?
problems.eli5: Compute each zone’s weight A·F: Zone 1 = 200(0.5) = 100; Zone 2 = 300(0.2) = 60; sum = 160. Fraction to Zone 1 = 100/160 = 0.625, so T = 1,000 × 0.625 = 625 trips. The 375-trips option is the trips to Zone 2 (60/160 × 1,000 = 375). The 400-trips option uses attractions only (200/500). The 500-trips option splits the trips evenly.
problems.hint: Weight each destination by A×F, normalize by the sum, then multiply by Pi.
problems.handbookFormula: T_{ij} = P_i [A_j F_{ij} K_{ij} / \sum A_j F_{ij} K_{ij}]
traps: Distributing by attractions alone and ignoring the friction factor
Forgetting to normalize by the sum over all destination zones

problems.statement: In the four-step travel demand model, which step uses the gravity model?
problems.eli5: The gravity model distributes the trips produced by each zone among destination zones — that is trip DISTRIBUTION (step 2). Trip generation (step 1) just counts productions and attractions; mode choice (step 3) splits trips among modes; traffic assignment (step 4) loads trips onto routes.
problems.hint: Which step decides WHERE the generated trips go?

steps.text: Generation counts trips; distribution sends them to destinations.
The gravity model allocates trips among zones.
So it belongs to the trip distribution step.

traps: Confusing trip generation (counts) with trip distribution (allocation)
Associating the gravity model with route assignment

problems.statement: In the gravity model, as the travel time (impedance) between two zones increases, the number of trips distributed between them generally:

choices.text: Decreases, because the friction factor decreases
Increases, because the friction factor increases
Stays the same — only attractions matter
Depends only on the number of productions

problems.eli5: The friction factor F decreases as travel time or distance grows, so more-distant zones receive fewer trips — just as gravitational attraction weakens with distance. The "increases because the friction factor increases" choice reverses this. The "only attractions matter" and "depends only on productions" choices ignore the impedance term entirely.
problems.hint: The friction factor models resistance to travel — what happens to it as distance grows?

steps.text: Friction factor F falls as impedance (time/distance) rises.
Lower F means a smaller share of trips to that zone.
So trips between the zones decrease.

traps: Thinking longer travel times attract more trips
Ignoring impedance and using attractions alone

transportation/traffic-control-devices.name: Traffic Control Devices & Warrants
transportation/traffic-control-devices.application: Signs, signals, and markings are how engineers communicate with drivers. As a civil engineer you apply the MUTCD to select and place these devices, recognize sign categories by shape and color, and understand that a traffic signal is installed only when a warrant is met. On the FE, expect conceptual questions on device categories and signal warrants.

content.body: The Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) is the national standard governing all traffic control devices. To be effective, a device must fulfill a need, command attention, convey a clear and simple meaning, command road-user respect, and give adequate time for response.
Categories of Signs

REGULATORY signs tell drivers what they must or must not do (e.g., STOP, YIELD, speed limit) — typically white rectangles, with the red octagon reserved for STOP. WARNING signs alert drivers to conditions ahead and are yellow diamonds. GUIDE signs give directions and distances and are green.
Signal Warrants

A traffic signal is installed only when a MUTCD WARRANT is satisfied — for example, the eight-hour vehicular volume, peak-hour volume, pedestrian volume, school crossing, or crash-experience warrants. Meeting a warrant shows a signal is justified, but engineering judgment still governs the final decision.
Read signs by shape and color: red octagon = STOP, yellow diamond = warning, green = guide/direction, white rectangle = regulatory. The shape alone often tells you the category.

A signal is NOT automatically an improvement. Unwarranted signals can increase rear-end crashes and cause excessive delay — which is exactly why the MUTCD requires a warrant analysis before one is installed.

problems.statement: A yellow, diamond-shaped sign warning of a curve ahead belongs to which category of traffic control device?
problems.eli5: Yellow diamond-shaped signs are WARNING signs — they alert drivers to conditions ahead such as curves, intersections, or merges. Regulatory signs state laws (STOP, speed limit). Guide signs are green and give directions. A construction barricade is a temporary-traffic-control device, not this sign.
problems.hint: Yellow + diamond shape signals which category in the MUTCD?

steps.text: Shape and color identify the category.
Yellow diamond = warning of a condition ahead.
So it is a warning sign.

traps: Confusing warning (yellow diamond) with regulatory (white rectangle/red octagon)
Assuming all signs that mention hazards are regulatory

problems.statement: Why does the MUTCD require a warrant analysis before a traffic signal is installed at an intersection?

choices.text: Because an unwarranted signal can increase rear-end crashes and delay; a signal must be justified
Because signals always reduce all types of crashes
Because warrants set the signal’s cycle length
Because federal law bans all signals without a permit fee

problems.eli5: Signals are not automatically beneficial — installing one where it is not warranted can raise rear-end crashes and create unnecessary delay. Warrants test whether conditions (volumes, pedestrians, crashes) justify a signal. The claim that signals always reduce all types of crashes is false (signals can increase some crash types, like rear-end). The option about cycle length confuses warrants with timing design. The federal permit-fee option is fabricated.
problems.hint: Is a signal always an improvement? What can go wrong if one is installed unnecessarily?

steps.text: Signals can worsen rear-end crashes and add delay.
Warrants check whether conditions justify a signal.
So a warrant analysis prevents installing unjustified signals.

traps: Assuming a signal always improves safety
Confusing signal warrants with cycle-length/timing design

problems.statement: A STOP sign is an example of which category of traffic control device?
problems.eli5: A STOP sign imposes a legal requirement — drivers must stop — so it is a REGULATORY sign (the distinctive red octagon is reserved for STOP). Warning signs (yellow diamonds) alert to conditions; guide signs (green) give directions; recreational signs mark parks and points of interest.
problems.hint: Does a STOP sign state a law (regulatory) or merely warn of a condition?

steps.text: A STOP sign legally requires drivers to stop.
Devices that impose legal requirements are regulatory.
So a STOP sign is a regulatory sign.

traps: Calling STOP a warning sign because it concerns safety
Associating the red octagon with anything other than regulatory control

transportation/pavement-design.name: Pavement Design (AASHTO)
transportation/pavement-design.application: The AASHTO method designs flexible (asphalt) pavements by computing the required Structural Number (SN) from traffic loading and soil support, then selecting layer thicknesses that provide that SN. Each layer contributes based on its structural coefficient and drainage condition. Load equivalency factors convert mixed axle loads to 18-kip equivalent single-axle loads (ESALs). On the FE, expect problems computing SN from given layers, solving for a missing layer thickness, or applying load equivalency factors.

content.body: The Structural Number (SN) is a single index that represents the total pavement strength. Each layer contributes to SN based on its thickness, structural coefficient, and drainage factor.
AASHTO Structural Number Equation

content.latex: SN = a_1 D_1 + a_2 D_2 m_2 + a_3 D_3 m_3 + \ldots
content.label: Structural number

content.body: Where $a_i$ = layer coefficient, $D_i$ = layer thickness (inches), and $m_i$ = drainage coefficient. The surface layer (layer 1) has $m_1 = 1.0$ by convention; $m$ for base and subbase layers accounts for drainage quality (assume $m = 1.0$ unless stated otherwise).
Typical Layer Coefficients
Hot-mix asphalt surface: $a_1 \approx 0.44$. Crushed-stone base: $a_2 \approx 0.14$. Granular subbase: $a_3 \approx 0.11$. These are given in FE problems; you do not need to memorize them.
Load Equivalency Factors

Different axle loads cause different amounts of damage. The load equivalency factor (LEF) converts any axle load to the number of equivalent 18-kip single-axle loads (ESALs). The FE Handbook provides a table of LEFs for single and tandem axles at various weights.
To find a missing layer thickness, rearrange the SN equation: D2 = (SN − a1D1 − a3D3m3)/(a2 × m2). Solve for the one unknown.
Don't forget the drainage coefficients (m values) for base and subbase layers. Assuming m = 1.0 when the problem gives a lower value will undersize the pavement.

problems.statement: A flexible pavement has: surface $a_1 = 0.44$, $D_1 = 3 \text{ in}$; base $a_2 = 0.14$, $D_2 = 8 \text{ in}$, $m_2 = 1.0$; subbase $a_3 = 0.11$, $D_3 = 10 \text{ in}$, $m_3 = 1.0$. What is the structural number?
problems.eli5: SN = a1D1 + a2D2m2 + a3D3m3 = 0.44(3) + 0.14(8)(1.0) + 0.11(10)(1.0) = 1.32 + 1.12 + 1.10 = 3.54. Just multiply each layer and sum. The 2.44 option forgot the subbase: 1.32 + 1.12. The 1.32 option computed only the surface layer. The 0.69 option summed the coefficients without multiplying by thicknesses: 0.44 + 0.14 + 0.11.
problems.hint: Multiply each layer's coefficient × thickness × drainage factor, then add them up.
traps: Forgetting to include all three layers in the sum
Summing coefficients without multiplying by layer thickness

problems.statement: A pavement requires $SN = 4.0$. The surface has $a_1 = 0.44$, $D_1 = 4 \text{ in}$. The subbase has $a_3 = 0.11$, $D_3 = 12 \text{ in}$, $m_3 = 0.80$. The base has $a_2 = 0.14$ and $m_2 = 1.0$. What minimum base thickness $D_2$ is required?
problems.eli5: Surface: 0.44 × 4 = 1.76. Subbase: 0.11 × 12 × 0.80 = 1.056. Remaining SN: 4.0 − 1.76 − 1.056 = 1.184. D2 = 1.184/(0.14 × 1.0) = 8.46 ≈ 8.5 in. The 6.6 in option ignored the drainage coefficient m3 = 0.80, using m3 = 1.0: subbase = 1.32, remaining = 0.92, D2 = 6.57. The 28.6 in option solved for D2 without accounting for other layers: 4.0/0.14 = 28.6. The 12.6 in option mixed up layer coefficients.
problems.hint: Rearrange: D2 = (SN − a1D1 − a3D3m3) / (a2 × m2).
traps: Ignoring the drainage coefficient m3 = 0.80 — using m = 1.0 underestimates the required base thickness
Solving D2 = SN/a2 without subtracting other layers' contributions

problems.statement: A road receives $1{,}000$ passes of a $24{,}000 \text{ lb}$ single-axle load per year. The load equivalency factor for a $24{,}000 \text{ lb}$ single axle is $3.03$. How many ESALs does this produce annually?
problems.eli5: ESALs = passes × LEF = 1,000 × 3.03 = 3,030. Each pass of a 24-kip single axle does 3.03 times the damage of a standard 18-kip axle. The 260 choice used the tandem-axle LEF (0.260) instead of the single-axle LEF (3.03) — always check single vs. tandem in the table. The 1,000 choice assumed LEF = 1.0 (only true for an 18-kip axle). The 24,000 choice multiplied by the axle weight instead of the LEF.
problems.hint: ESALs = number of passes × load equivalency factor. Read the correct column (single vs. tandem) from the table.

steps.text: Look up LEF for 24,000 lb single axle: $3.03$

problems.handbookFormula: SN = a_1 D_1 + a_2 D_2 m_2 + \ldots
traps: Reading the tandem-axle column (0.260) instead of the single-axle column (3.03) — off by a factor of ~12
Assuming LEF = 1.0 for all axle loads — LEF = 1.0 only for the reference 18-kip single axle

transportation/earthwork.name: Earthwork Volumes
transportation/earthwork.application: Earthwork calculations determine how much soil must be excavated (cut) or placed (fill) along a highway corridor. Engineers compute volumes between cross sections using the average end area method or the more accurate prismoidal formula. These volumes drive project cost estimates and the mass haul diagram that optimizes where cut material is moved to fill areas. On the FE, expect problems applying both volume formulas and converting cubic feet to cubic yards.

content.body: Given cross-sectional areas at two stations separated by distance $L$, two formulas estimate the volume of earthwork between them.
Average End Area Formula
This method averages the two end areas and multiplies by the distance. It always overestimates the true volume (unless the two areas are equal).
Prismoidal Formula
Where $A_m$ = cross-sectional area at the midpoint between the two stations. This is more accurate because it accounts for the shape change through the middle of the section.
Unit Conversion
Earthwork quantities are reported in cubic yards ($\text{yd}^3$). If the formula gives $\text{ft}^3$ (when $L$ and $A$ are in feet), divide by 27 to convert.

The average end area method always overestimates (or equals) the prismoidal result. The difference grows as the two end areas become more unequal. If the problem asks for the "more accurate" method, use the prismoidal formula.
Don't forget to divide by 27 when converting ft³ to yd³. A common mistake is reporting the answer in ft³ when the problem asks for yd³ — the answer will be 27× too large.

problems.statement: Two cross sections are $100 \text{ ft}$ apart with areas $A_1 = 200 \text{ ft}^2$ and $A_2 = 300 \text{ ft}^2$. What is the earthwork volume using the average end area method?
problems.eli5: V = L(A1 + A2)/2 = 100(200 + 300)/2 = 100 × 250 = 25,000 ft³. Convert: 25,000/27 = 926 yd³. The 1,852 yd³ option forgot to divide by 2 in the average: 100 × 500/27 = 1,852. The 25,000 option is the answer in ft³, not yd³ — forgot to divide by 27. The 741 yd³ option used only A1: 100 × 200/27 = 741.
problems.hint: Average the two areas, multiply by L, then divide by 27 to convert ft³ to yd³.
traps: Forgetting to divide by 2 — the formula averages the two end areas, not sums them
Reporting the answer in ft³ instead of yd³ — always check units

problems.statement: Two cross sections $100 \text{ ft}$ apart have areas $A_1 = 200 \text{ ft}^2$ and $A_2 = 300 \text{ ft}^2$. The mid-section area is $A_m = 240 \text{ ft}^2$. What is the volume using the prismoidal formula?
problems.eli5: V = L(A1 + 4Am + A2)/6 = 100(200 + 4×240 + 300)/6 = 100(200 + 960 + 300)/6 = 100 × 1,460/6 = 146,000/6 = 24,333 ft³. Convert: 24,333/27 = 901 yd³. The 926 yd³ option used the average end area method (ignoring Am). The 5,407 yd³ option forgot to divide by 6: 146,000/27 = 5,407. The 913 yd³ option used a simple average (A1+Am+A2)/3 instead of the weighted prismoidal formula.
problems.hint: Prismoidal: L(A1 + 4Am + A2)/6. The mid-section gets weighted 4×.
traps: Using the average end area formula instead of the prismoidal — gives 926 yd³ (overestimate)
Forgetting to divide by 6 in the prismoidal formula

problems.statement: A cut section has $A_1 = 150 \text{ ft}^2$, $A_2 = 350 \text{ ft}^2$, and mid-section $A_m = 230 \text{ ft}^2$. Stations are $200 \text{ ft}$ apart. What is the earthwork volume using the prismoidal formula?
problems.eli5: V = L(A1 + 4Am + A2)/6 = 200(150 + 4×230 + 350)/6 = 200(150 + 920 + 350)/6 = 200 × 1,420/6 = 284,000/6 = 47,333 ft³ = 47,333/27 = 1,753 yd³. The 1,852 yd³ option used average end area: 200(150+350)/2 = 50,000 ft³ = 1,852 yd³ — notice the overestimate vs. prismoidal. The 10,519 yd³ option forgot to divide by 6: 284,000/27 = 10,519. The 876 yd³ option divided the volume by 2 for no reason.
problems.hint: Apply L(A1 + 4Am + A2)/6, then divide by 27 for yd³. The prismoidal formula gives a smaller volume than average end area when A1 ≠ A2.

steps.text: Compare: average end area gives $200(150+350)/2 = 50{,}000 \text{ ft}^3 = 1{,}852 \text{ yd}^3$ (overestimates by 99 yd\u00B3)

traps: Using average end area instead of prismoidal — gives 1,852 yd³ (a 5.6% overestimate here)
Forgetting to divide by 6 — the prismoidal formula has a denominator of 6, not 2
Forgetting the ft³ to yd³ conversion (divide by 27)

transportation/rigid-pavement.name: Rigid Pavement Design
transportation/rigid-pavement.application: Highways and airfields use rigid (Portland cement concrete) pavement where heavy loads and long service life justify it. As a civil engineer you should understand how a rigid slab carries load differently from flexible asphalt, what the modulus of subgrade reaction represents, and why joints and dowels are used. On the FE, expect conceptual questions comparing rigid and flexible pavement and on joint function.

content.body: Rigid pavement is a Portland cement concrete (PCC) slab. Unlike flexible (asphalt) pavement, which flexes and spreads load downward through granular layers, a rigid slab is stiff and carries load by BEAM (slab) action — bending and distributing the wheel load over a wide area of subgrade.
Rigid vs. Flexible

Flexible pavement relies on the strength of each layer and is designed with the AASHTO structural number (SN). Rigid pavement relies on the slab’s flexural strength (concrete modulus of rupture) and spreads load so widely that it depends much less on subgrade strength. Because of this, rigid pavement tolerates weak subgrades better but costs more initially.
Modulus of Subgrade Reaction

The support a subgrade provides to a rigid slab is characterized by the modulus of subgrade reaction $k$ — the pressure required to produce a unit deflection (units of force per length cubed, e.g., pci). A higher $k$ means a stiffer foundation.
Joints

Concrete slabs crack from temperature and shrinkage stresses, so joints are built in: CONTRACTION joints control where cracks form, EXPANSION joints allow thermal growth, and CONSTRUCTION joints occur where paving stops. DOWEL bars across transverse joints transfer wheel load from one slab to the next while still allowing the slabs to move.

Think "beam vs. blanket": a rigid slab acts like a beam bridging weak spots, while flexible pavement acts like a blanket transmitting load down through its layers. That is why rigid pavement is less sensitive to subgrade strength.

Dowel bars TRANSFER load across a joint while permitting movement — they are not there to tie slabs rigidly together. Confusing dowels (load transfer) with tie bars (holding joints closed) is a common mistake.

problems.statement: How does a rigid (PCC) pavement primarily distribute wheel loads to the subgrade, compared with a flexible (asphalt) pavement?

choices.text: By beam/slab action, spreading the load over a wide subgrade area
By flexing and transmitting load downward through granular layers
By concentrating the load directly beneath the wheel
It does not transmit load to the subgrade at all

problems.eli5: A rigid slab is stiff and bends like a beam, spreading each wheel load over a wide area of subgrade — so it depends less on subgrade strength. The "flexing and transmitting load through granular layers" option describes flexible (asphalt) pavement. The "concentrating the load directly beneath the wheel" option is the opposite of what a slab does. The "does not transmit load to the subgrade at all" option is incorrect — load still reaches the subgrade, just spread out.
problems.hint: A stiff slab behaves like a beam; flexible pavement behaves like layered granular material.

steps.text: Flexible pavement spreads load down through its layers.
A rigid slab bends as a beam, distributing load over a wide area.
So rigid pavement uses slab/beam action.

traps: Swapping the rigid and flexible load-distribution mechanisms
Assuming a slab concentrates load beneath the wheel

problems.statement: What is the primary purpose of dowel bars placed across transverse joints in a rigid pavement?

choices.text: To transfer wheel load between adjacent slabs while allowing movement
To bond the slabs together so they cannot move
To increase the concrete’s compressive strength

problems.eli5: Dowel bars span a transverse joint and transfer wheel load from one slab to the next, reducing faulting, while still letting the slabs expand and contract. "Bond the slabs together so they cannot move" describes tie bars (which hold longitudinal joints closed). "Increase the concrete's compressive strength" confuses dowels with reinforcement. "Waterproof the joint" is the job of joint sealant, not dowels.
problems.hint: Dowels handle load transfer across a joint — do they lock the slabs or let them move?

steps.text: Slabs must be free to expand and contract at joints.
Dowel bars carry load across the joint without locking the slabs.
So their purpose is load transfer with movement.

traps: Confusing dowel bars (load transfer) with tie bars (hold joints closed)
Treating dowels as structural reinforcement for strength

problems.statement: The modulus of subgrade reaction ($k$) used in rigid pavement design represents:

choices.text: The pressure required to produce a unit deflection of the subgrade
The flexural strength of the concrete slab
The total thickness of the pavement structure
The number of equivalent single-axle loads

problems.eli5: The modulus of subgrade reaction k is the foundation stiffness — pressure per unit deflection (e.g., pci) — describing how firmly the subgrade supports the slab. The flexural-strength option is the concrete’s modulus of rupture. The total-thickness option is a thickness, not a stiffness. The equivalent-single-axle-loads option is the ESAL traffic measure.
problems.hint: k describes how stiff the foundation is: how much pressure for how much deflection?

steps.text: k relates subgrade pressure to deflection.
It is the pressure to cause a unit deflection (force/length³).
Higher k means a stiffer foundation under the slab.

traps: Confusing subgrade stiffness (k) with concrete flexural strength
Mistaking k for a thickness or traffic parameter

construction/cpm-fundamentals.name: CPM Scheduling Basics
construction/cpm-fundamentals.application: The Critical Path Method (CPM) is how civil engineers plan and control construction projects. Every activity has a duration and dependencies on other activities. The network diagram shows the sequence, and the critical path identifies which activities control the project completion date. On the FE, expect problems involving precedence relationships, reading network diagrams, and understanding the difference between activity-on-node and activity-on-arrow notation.

content.body: CPM uses a network of activities connected by logical relationships. Each activity has a duration and may depend on one or more predecessor activities.
Precedence Relationships

Finish-to-Start (FS): the most common type — activity B cannot start until activity A finishes. Start-to-Start (SS): B cannot start until A starts. Finish-to-Finish (FF): B cannot finish until A finishes.
Activity-on-Node (AON) Notation

In AON (the modern standard), each box represents an activity. The box shows: Early Start (ES), Early Finish (EF), Late Start (LS), Late Finish (LF), Duration (D), and Float. Arrows between boxes show dependencies.
Key Definitions
The critical path is the longest path through the network. Activities on the critical path have zero total float — any delay pushes the project end date.
Finish-to-Start is assumed unless stated otherwise. If a problem just says "B follows A" or "B depends on A," it means FS.
Don't confuse AON (boxes = activities) with AOA (arrows = activities). The FE can use either notation. Read the diagram carefully to identify which convention is being used.

problems.statement: Activity A has a duration of 5 days. Activity B depends on A (finish-to-start) and has a duration of 3 days. If A starts on day 0, what is the early finish of B?
problems.eli5: A starts day 0, finishes day 5 ($ES = 0$, $EF = 0 + 5 = 5$). B starts when A finishes (FS), so $ES_B = 5$. $EF_B = 5 + 3 = 8$. Day 5 is EF of A, not B. Day 3 is just B's duration. Day 15 multiplied $5 \times 3$ instead of adding.
problems.hint: EF = ES + Duration. B's ES equals A's EF in a finish-to-start relationship.
traps: Reporting A's early finish (5) instead of B's early finish (8)
Multiplying durations instead of adding them sequentially

problems.statement: In a CPM network, activity C has two predecessors: A (EF = 6) and B (EF = 9). Both relationships are finish-to-start. What is the early start of C?
problems.eli5: When an activity has multiple predecessors (all FS), its $ES$ = the MAXIMUM of all predecessor EFs. C cannot start until BOTH A and B are done. $\max(6, 9) = 9$. The "Day 6" choice took the minimum — C can't start at day 6 because B isn't done yet. The "Day 15" choice added both EFs. The "Day 7.5" choice averaged them.
problems.hint: ES of an activity = MAX of all predecessor EFs. The activity waits for the LAST predecessor to finish.
traps: Using MIN instead of MAX — the activity must wait for ALL predecessors, not just the first one
Adding or averaging predecessor EFs instead of taking the maximum

problems.statement: A project has 4 activities. A (duration = 4, no predecessors), B (duration = 6, predecessor A), C (duration = 3, predecessor A), D (duration = 2, predecessors B and C). What is the project duration?
problems.eli5: Forward pass: A(0,4). B starts at 4, finishes at 10. C starts at 4, finishes at 7. D starts at max(10,7) = 10, finishes at 12. Project duration = 12 days (the EF of the last activity). Two paths exist: A→B→D = 4+6+2 = 12, and A→C→D = 4+3+2 = 9. The longest path (12) controls. The 9 days option used the shorter path A→C→D. The 15 days option added all durations. The 10 days option forgot activity D.
problems.hint: Run the forward pass for all activities. The project duration = EF of the last activity.

steps.text: Project duration = $EF_D = 12$ days. Critical path: A \u2192 B \u2192 D.

traps: Using the shorter path (A→C→D = 9) instead of the critical (longest) path
Summing ALL durations (4+6+3+2 = 15) instead of finding the longest path

construction/forward-backward-pass.name: Forward & Backward Pass
construction/forward-backward-pass.application: The forward pass computes the earliest each activity can start and finish; the backward pass computes the latest each can start and finish without delaying the project. Together they reveal total float and identify the critical path. On the FE, expect problems that give a small network and ask you to compute ES, EF, LS, or LF for specific activities using these two passes.

content.body: The forward pass works left-to-right through the network, computing ES and EF. The backward pass works right-to-left, computing LF and LS.
Forward Pass Rules
Start with $ES = 0$ for the first activity (or activities with no predecessors). Work left to right.
Backward Pass Rules
Start with $LF =$ project duration for the last activity (or activities with no successors). Work right to left.
Forward pass uses MAX (wait for the slowest predecessor). Backward pass uses MIN (can't be later than the tightest successor). Think: "MAX forward, MIN backward."
A common error is using MIN on the forward pass or MAX on the backward pass. The logic is opposite: forward = MAX of predecessors, backward = MIN of successors.

problems.statement: Network: A (duration 3, no predecessors), B (duration 4, predecessor A), C (duration 2, predecessor A), D (duration 6, predecessor B), E (duration 3, predecessors B and C). What is the early start and early finish of activity E?
problems.eli5: Forward pass: A(0,3). B(3,7). C(3,5). E depends on B and C, so $ES_E = \max(EF_B, EF_C) = \max(7, 5) = 7$. $EF_E = 7 + 3 = 10$. The ES=5,EF=8 option used $EF_C = 5$ as ES (took min instead of max). The ES=3,EF=6 option used $ES = EF_A = 3$ (skipped B and C). The ES=9,EF=12 option used a wrong, larger predecessor finish.
problems.hint: E depends on B AND C. Use MAX of their EFs to find ES of E.

steps.text: E has predecessors B and C:

traps: Using MIN instead of MAX for the forward pass — E can't start until BOTH predecessors finish

problems.statement: Using the same network (A:3, B:4, C:2, D:6, E:3; D predecessor B, E predecessors B\&C), the project duration is $13$ days. What is the late start of activity C?
problems.eli5: Backward pass: D(7,13), E(10,13). C feeds only E, so $LF_C = LS_E = 10$. $LS_C = LF_C - D_C = 10 - 2 = 8$. Choice "Day 3" is $LS_B$ from the backward pass — the question asked for $LS$, not $ES$. Choice "Day 5" is a distractor that does not correspond to a real CPM value for C ($EF_C = 2$). Choice "Day 10" is $LF_C$, not $LS_C$ — forgot to subtract the duration.
problems.hint: Run the backward pass: LF of C = LS of its successor (E). Then LS = LF − duration.

steps.text: B feeds D and E: $LF_B = \min(LS_D, LS_E) = \min(7, 10) = 7$, $LS_B = 3$

problems.handbookFormula: LS = LF - D,\quad LF = \text{Earliest } LS \text{ of successors}
traps: Confusing ES (forward pass) with LS (backward pass) — read the question carefully
Reporting LF instead of LS — don't forget to subtract the duration

problems.statement: In the same network, what is the late finish of activity B?
problems.eli5: B feeds two successors: D ($LS_D = 7$) and E ($LS_E = 10$). The backward pass uses MIN: $LF_B = \min(7, 10) = 7$. B must finish by day 7 so that D can start on time. The Day 10 option used $LS_E$ only, ignoring D. The Day 13 option used the project end date. The Day 4 option is $LS_B + 1$ or confused with duration.
problems.hint: When an activity feeds multiple successors, its LF = MIN of all successor LSs. The backward pass uses MIN.
traps: Using MAX instead of MIN on the backward pass — B must finish before its tightest successor
Only considering one successor and ignoring the other

construction/float-critical-path.name: Float & Critical Path
construction/float-critical-path.application: Total float tells you how much an activity can slip without delaying the project. Free float tells you how much it can slip without affecting any successor. Activities with zero total float form the critical path — the longest chain through the network that controls the project duration. On the FE, expect problems computing total float, identifying critical activities, and distinguishing total float from free float.

content.body: After the forward and backward passes, float reveals how much scheduling flexibility each activity has.
Total Float
Total float is the maximum delay an activity can experience without pushing the project end date. Both formulas give the same result.
Free Float
Free float is the maximum delay without affecting any immediate successor's early start. Free float $\leq$ total float, always.
Critical Path
The critical path is the sequence of activities with $TF = 0$. It is also the longest path through the network. Any delay on the critical path delays the entire project.
Shortcut: to find the critical path, trace the longest duration path through the network. You don't always need the full backward pass — just compare path lengths.

Free float ≤ total float. If your free float exceeds total float, something is wrong. Also, an activity can have TF > 0 but FF = 0 — delaying it won't affect the project end, but it will affect a successor.

problems.statement: Activity C has $ES = 3$, $EF = 5$, $LS = 8$, $LF = 10$. What is the total float?
problems.eli5: $TF = LS - ES = 8 - 3 = 5$ days. Or equivalently, $TF = LF - EF = 10 - 5 = 5$ days. Both give the same answer. The 2-day choice is the duration ($EF - ES = 5 - 3 = 2$). The 0-day choice would mean it is critical — it is not. The 7-day choice subtracted wrong values ($LF - ES = 10 - 3 = 7$, but that is not the formula).
problems.hint: Total float = LS − ES (or LF − EF). Both formulas give the same result.
traps: Confusing duration (EF − ES) with float (LS − ES)
Computing LF − ES (= 7) — that is not a valid float formula

problems.statement: A project has paths: A\u2192B\u2192D (4+6+5 = 15 days), A\u2192C\u2192E (4+3+3 = 10 days), A\u2192C\u2192D (4+3+5 = 12 days). Which is the critical path and what is the project duration?
problems.eli5: The critical path is the LONGEST path through the network: A→B→D = 15 days. This is the minimum time to complete the project. A→C→E (10) is the shortest path — not critical. A→C→D (12) is an intermediate path. The "all paths, 37 days" option summed every path, which makes no sense since activities run concurrently.
problems.hint: The critical path = the longest path = the path that takes the most time. Compare total durations.
traps: Choosing the shortest path as critical — the critical path is the LONGEST
Summing all paths instead of comparing them — parallel paths overlap

problems.statement: In the network from earlier lessons (A:3, B:4, C:2, D:6, E:3; D predecessor B, E predecessors B\&C), activity C has $ES = 3$, $EF = 5$. The earliest successor start is $ES_E = 7$. What is the free float of C?
problems.eli5: Free float $= \min(ES_{\text{successors}}) - EF_i = 7 - 5 = 2$ days. C can slip 2 days without pushing E's early start. But C's total float is 5 ($LS - ES = 8 - 3 = 5$). So C has 2 days of free float and 5 days of total float. The extra 3 days of total float would delay E's start (but not the project end). The 5-days choice is total float, not free float. The 0-days choice would mean no free slack. The 3-days choice is $TF - FF$, which is not a standard metric.
problems.hint: Free float = (earliest successor ES) − (your EF). It's always ≤ total float.

steps.text: C feeds E. Earliest successor start: $ES_E = 7$
Compare: total float of C = $LS_C - ES_C = 8 - 3 = 5$ days. $FF \leq TF$ \checkmark

traps: Confusing free float (2) with total float (5) — free float only considers the immediate successor
Free float is always ≤ total float — if you get a larger free float, recheck

construction/earned-value-analysis.name: Earned Value Analysis
construction/earned-value-analysis.application: Earned value analysis (EVA) tracks project performance by comparing three cost curves: what you planned to spend (BCWS), what the work is actually worth (BCWP), and what you actually spent (ACWP). The cost variance tells you if you are over or under budget; the schedule variance tells you if you are ahead or behind schedule. On the FE, expect problems computing CV and SV from given values, or interpreting what the signs mean.

content.body: Earned value uses three measurements at a reporting date to assess cost and schedule performance simultaneously.
Three Key Values

$BCWS$ (Budgeted Cost of Work Scheduled) = what you planned to spend by now. $ACWP$ (Actual Cost of Work Performed) = what you actually spent. $BCWP$ (Budgeted Cost of Work Performed) = the budgeted value of the work you actually completed.
Cost Variance
$CV > 0$: under budget (spent less than the work is worth). $CV < 0$: over budget (spent more than the work is worth).
Schedule Variance
$SV > 0$: ahead of schedule (completed more work than planned). $SV < 0$: behind schedule (completed less than planned).
Memory trick: BCWP (Earned Value) is the common term in both formulas. CV = BCWP − ACWP (compare earned to actual cost). SV = BCWP − BCWS (compare earned to planned schedule).

Schedule variance is measured in DOLLARS, not days. A negative SV means you earned less value than planned, which implies you are behind schedule. But it doesn't directly tell you how many days behind.

problems.statement: At month 6 of a project: $BCWP = 400{,}000$, $ACWP = 450{,}000$. What is the cost variance, and is the project over or under budget?
problems.eli5: $CV = BCWP - ACWP = 400{,}000 - 450{,}000 = -50{,}000$. Negative CV means the project spent more than the work is worth — over budget. The +50,000 (under budget) choice flipped the subtraction order. The -50,000 (under budget) choice got the sign right but misinterpreted it. The +50,000 (over budget) choice got both wrong.
problems.hint: CV = Earned − Actual. Negative = over budget (you spent more than you earned).
traps: Subtracting in the wrong order (ACWP − BCWP) — the formula is BCWP − ACWP
Misinterpreting the sign: negative CV = over budget, positive = under budget

problems.statement: At week 10: $BCWS = 500{,}000$, $BCWP = 420{,}000$, $ACWP = 480{,}000$. What is the schedule variance?
problems.eli5: $SV = BCWP - BCWS = 420{,}000 - 500{,}000 = -80{,}000$. Negative SV means the project earned less value than planned — behind schedule. The $-60{,}000$ choice confused SV with CV: $BCWP - ACWP = 420{,}000 - 480{,}000 = -60{,}000$. That is the cost variance, not the schedule variance. The $+80{,}000$ choice flipped the sign. The $+20{,}000$ choice used $BCWS - ACWP = 500{,}000 - 480{,}000 = 20{,}000$, which is not a standard formula.
problems.hint: SV = BCWP − BCWS. Don't confuse it with CV = BCWP − ACWP.

steps.text: Interpretation: $SV < 0$ \u2192 behind schedule (earned less than planned)
For comparison: $CV = BCWP - ACWP = 420{,}000 - 480{,}000 = -60{,}000$ (also over budget)

traps: Computing CV instead of SV — SV uses BCWS, CV uses ACWP
Mixing up the three values: BCWS (planned), ACWP (actual cost), BCWP (earned value)

problems.statement: A project reports: planned value (BCWS) = 300,000, earned value (BCWP) = 270,000, actual cost (ACWP) = 250,000. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Ahead of schedule and over budget
Ahead of schedule and under budget

problems.eli5: $SV = BCWP - BCWS = 270{,}000 - 300{,}000 = -30{,}000 < 0$ — behind schedule. $CV = BCWP - ACWP = 270{,}000 - 250{,}000 = +20{,}000 > 0$ — under budget. So the project did less work than planned (behind schedule) but spent less than the work is worth (under budget). This combination is common — the crew is efficient but slow. "Ahead of schedule and under budget" has schedule wrong. "Behind schedule and over budget" has cost wrong. "Ahead of schedule and over budget" has both wrong.
problems.hint: Compute both CV and SV. CV tells you cost performance, SV tells you schedule performance.

steps.text: Result: behind schedule AND under budget

problems.handbookFormula: CV = BCWP - ACWP,\quad SV = BCWP - BCWS
traps: Assuming over budget and behind schedule always go together — they are independent measures
Mixing up the sign interpretation: positive = good (under budget or ahead of schedule)

construction/project-forecasting.name: Performance Indices & Forecasting
construction/project-forecasting.application: Performance indices (CPI and SPI) normalize the cost and schedule variances into ratios, making it easy to compare projects of different sizes. Forecasting formulas use the CPI to predict the total cost at completion (EAC) and the remaining cost (ETC). On the FE, expect problems computing CPI/SPI and using them to forecast the estimate at completion.

content.body: The Cost Performance Index and Schedule Performance Index express efficiency as ratios rather than dollar amounts.
Performance Indices
$CPI > 1.0$: under budget. $CPI < 1.0$: over budget. Same logic for SPI and schedule.
Forecasting to Completion
Where $BAC$ = budget at completion (the original total budget). ETC estimates how much more money is needed. EAC is the forecasted total project cost.

CPI < 1.0 means every dollar you spend only earns CPI dollars of value. ETC divides remaining work by CPI, which inflates the cost proportionally. If CPI = 0.80, remaining work costs 25% more than budgeted.
ETC uses remaining work (BAC − BCWP), not remaining budget (BAC − ACWP). It divides by CPI to account for the cost inefficiency trend. Don't confuse the numerator.

problems.statement: A project has $BCWP = 600{,}000$ and $ACWP = 750{,}000$. What is the CPI?
problems.eli5: CPI = BCWP/ACWP = 600,000/750,000 = 0.80. For every dollar spent, only 0.80 of value is earned — the project is over budget. The 1.25 choice inverted the ratio: ACWP/BCWP. The 0.75 choice might come from a different calculation. The 150,000 choice is the cost variance CV, not the index.
problems.hint: CPI = Earned / Actual = BCWP / ACWP. Less than 1.0 = over budget.
traps: Inverting the ratio (ACWP/BCWP = 1.25) — CPI = Earned/Actual, not Actual/Earned
Confusing the index (ratio) with the variance (dollar amount)

problems.statement: A project has $BAC = 2{,}000{,}000$, $BCWP = 600{,}000$, and $CPI = 0.80$. What is the estimate to complete (ETC)?
problems.eli5: ETC = (BAC − BCWP)/CPI = (2,000,000 − 600,000)/0.80 = 1,400,000/0.80 = 1,750,000. The remaining work (1.4M budgeted) will cost more because CPI < 1.0. The 1,400,000 option forgot to divide by CPI — it assumed the remaining work will cost exactly as budgeted. The 1,000,000 option used BAC/2. The 2,500,000 option is the EAC (BAC/CPI), not ETC.
problems.hint: ETC = (BAC − BCWP) / CPI. The remaining work is inflated by the cost performance.
traps: Using BAC − BCWP as ETC without dividing by CPI — this ignores the cost overrun trend
Using BAC − ACWP in the numerator instead of BAC − BCWP

problems.statement: Continuing: $ACWP = 750{,}000$ and $ETC = 1{,}750{,}000$. The original budget was $BAC = 2{,}000{,}000$. What is the estimate at completion (EAC)?
problems.eli5: EAC = ACWP + ETC = 750,000 + 1,750,000 = 2,500,000. The project originally budgeted 2,000,000 but is now forecast to cost 2,500,000 — a 25% overrun. The 2,000,000 option is BAC (the original budget), ignoring the overrun trend. The 1,750,000 option is ETC alone, not EAC. The 2,150,000 option might come from using CPI = 1.0 for ETC: ETC = 1,400,000, EAC = 750,000 + 1,400,000 = 2,150,000.
problems.hint: EAC = money already spent (ACWP) + money still needed (ETC).
traps: Reporting ETC (1,750,000) as EAC — EAC includes the money already spent
Using BAC as EAC — BAC is the original budget, EAC is the revised forecast
Using CPI = 1.0 when computing ETC — this assumes the overrun trend stops, giving a falsely optimistic forecast

construction/delivery-methods.name: Project Delivery Methods
construction/delivery-methods.application: Project delivery methods define how design and construction responsibilities are allocated between the owner, designer, and contractor. The choice affects cost risk, schedule control, and change-order authority. Design-bid-build is the traditional method; design-build combines responsibilities under one entity; CM-at-risk brings the contractor in early for cost input. On the FE, expect scenario-based questions asking you to identify which delivery method fits a given situation.

content.body: The three main delivery methods differ in who holds design responsibility, who holds construction risk, and how early the contractor is involved.
Design-Bid-Build (DBB)

The traditional method. The owner hires a designer to complete plans and specifications, then solicits competitive bids from contractors. The lowest responsible bidder wins. The owner holds separate contracts for design and construction. Best when the scope is well-defined and cost certainty is a priority.
Design-Build (DB)

A single entity is responsible for both design and construction. The owner has one contract and one point of accountability. Faster delivery because design and construction can overlap. Best when the owner wants speed and single-point responsibility but can accept less control over design details.
CM-at-Risk (CMAR)

The construction manager joins the team during design and provides a Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP). The CM acts as a general contractor during construction. Best when the owner wants contractor input during design without giving up separate design control.
Key differentiator: in DBB, the contractor has NO input on design. In DB, the same team designs and builds. In CMAR, the contractor advises during design but the designer is a separate entity.
DBB does NOT mean the lowest price overall — it means the lowest responsible bid for the defined scope. Change orders in DBB can be costly because the contractor had no design input.

problems.statement: A public agency requires competitive bidding by law and has complete plans and specifications. Which delivery method is most appropriate?
problems.eli5: DBB is the standard for public projects that require competitive bidding on complete plans. The agency already has full plans and specs — they just need to advertise for bids. DB and CMAR involve contractor involvement before plans are complete. IPD is a collaborative method rarely mandated by law.
problems.hint: Complete plans + competitive bidding = the traditional method.

steps.text: Plans are complete → no need for contractor design input
Competitive bidding required by law → DBB is the standard public procurement method

traps: Choosing DB when the plans are already complete — DB combines design and construction, which is not needed here

problems.statement: An owner wants to fast-track a project and have a single entity responsible for both design and construction. Which delivery method should they use?
problems.eli5: DB is the answer when the owner wants speed (overlapping design and construction) and single-point responsibility. In DB, one entity handles everything. DBB cannot fast-track because design must be complete before bidding. CMAR provides early contractor input but keeps design and construction under separate contracts. Force account means the owner does the work with their own forces.
problems.hint: Single entity + fast-track = design-build.

steps.text: Single entity for design + construction → Design-Build

traps: Confusing CMAR with DB — in CMAR, the designer and CM are separate entities even though the CM is involved early

problems.statement: An owner wants contractor input during the design phase to improve constructability, but wants to retain a separate design professional. The contractor will provide a Guaranteed Maximum Price. Which delivery method fits?
problems.eli5: The key clues are: (1) contractor input during design → rules out DBB. (2) SEPARATE design professional → rules out DB (where one entity does both). (3) GMP → characteristic of CMAR. In CMAR, the CM joins early, advises on constructability, and later provides a GMP before construction starts. Design-Build puts design and construction under one contract. Design-Bid-Build has no contractor involvement during design. Job Order Contracting is for small, repetitive maintenance work.
problems.hint: Contractor input + separate designer + GMP = the hallmarks of CM-at-Risk.

steps.text: Contractor input during design → not DBB

traps: Confusing CMAR with DB — the key difference is whether the designer is a separate entity
Choosing DBB when the problem explicitly mentions contractor involvement during design

construction/construction-safety.name: Construction Safety (OSHA)
construction/construction-safety.application: OSHA regulations set minimum safety standards for construction sites. Civil engineers must understand these requirements because they affect design decisions (specifying trench protection, designing for erection sequences) and construction administration (reviewing safety plans, conducting site inspections). On the FE, expect scenario-based questions about excavation safety thresholds, fall protection requirements, and the engineer's responsibility during construction.

content.body: OSHA standards for construction (29 CFR 1926) cover excavations, fall protection, scaffolding, crane operations, and personal protective equipment. The FE tests the most common rules.
Excavation Safety

Trenches deeper than 5 ft require a protective system: sloping/benching the sides, shoring (hydraulic or timber), or shielding (trench box). Trenches deeper than 20 ft require a system designed by a registered professional engineer.
Fall Protection

Fall protection is required at heights of 6 ft or more in general construction. Options include guardrails, safety nets, and personal fall arrest systems (harness + lanyard). Steel erection has a trigger height of 15 ft for connectors.
Confined Spaces

A confined space has limited entry/exit, is not designed for continuous occupancy, and may have hazardous atmospheres. A permit-required confined space needs atmospheric testing, ventilation, a rescue plan, and an attendant at the entry.
Engineer's Role

The engineer of record designs for constructability and may specify required safety measures in the plans (e.g., shoring for deep excavations). During construction, the engineer reviews submittals, observes work, and verifies compliance with the contract documents.
The two magic numbers: 5 ft for excavation protection and 6 ft for fall protection. If a question mentions a trench deeper than 5 ft without protection, that is an OSHA violation.
Sloping, shoring, and shielding are all acceptable excavation protection methods. The choice depends on soil type, space, and cost. Type C soil (the weakest) requires the flattest slope (1.5H:1V).
