problems.statement: A contractor is excavating a trench that is $7 \text{ ft}$ deep for a sewer line. No protective system is installed. Is this an OSHA violation?

choices.text: No — protection is only required for permanent excavations
No — protection is only required above 10 ft
Yes — trenches deeper than 5 ft require protection
Yes — but only if the soil is Type C

problems.eli5: OSHA requires a protective system (sloping, shoring, or shielding) for all trenches deeper than 5 ft, regardless of soil type. At 7 ft with no protection, this is a clear violation. The "protection only above 10 ft" choice uses the wrong threshold (there is no 10 ft rule). The "only for permanent excavations" choice is wrong — temporary excavations still need protection. The "only if Type C soil" choice is wrong — the 5 ft rule applies to all soil types, not just Type C.
problems.hint: The OSHA threshold for excavation protection is 5 ft depth.

steps.text: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.652: trenches > 5 ft deep require protective systems
Trench is 7 ft > 5 ft \u2192 protection required but not installed \u2192 OSHA violation

traps: Thinking 10 ft is the threshold — it is 5 ft for excavations
Thinking soil type determines whether protection is needed — soil type affects the METHOD, not the requirement

problems.statement: A worker is operating on a scaffold platform $8 \text{ ft}$ above the ground without guardrails, safety nets, or a harness. Is fall protection required?

choices.text: Yes — fall protection is required at 6 ft in construction
No — fall protection is only required above 10 ft
No — scaffolds are exempt from fall protection
Yes — but only for steel erection work

problems.eli5: OSHA requires fall protection at 6 ft for general construction. At 8 ft without any protection, this is a violation. The "10 ft" choice uses the general industry threshold — construction is 6 ft. The "scaffolds are exempt" choice is wrong — scaffolds require guardrails at the platform edge. The "only for steel erection" choice is wrong — steel erection has a HIGHER trigger (15 ft for connectors), but general construction is 6 ft.
problems.hint: Construction fall protection trigger = 6 ft. General industry = different.

steps.text: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.501: fall protection required at 6 ft in construction
8 ft > 6 ft, no protection in place \u2192 violation

traps: Using the 10 ft general industry threshold instead of the 6 ft construction threshold
Thinking scaffolds are exempt — they are not; guardrails are required

problems.statement: An excavation is $22 \text{ ft}$ deep. What level of engineering involvement is required for the protective system?

choices.text: Standard OSHA tables can be used without engineering
The contractor's competent person can design it
Must be designed by a registered professional engineer
No protective system is needed at this depth

problems.eli5: OSHA requires that excavations deeper than 20 ft have a protective system designed by a registered professional engineer. At 22 ft, a PE must design the shoring, sloping, or shielding system. For excavations 5–20 ft, the contractor's competent person can use OSHA’s standard tables (Appendix A/B). The contractor's-competent-person option is correct for shallower trenches (5–20 ft). The standard OSHA tables option is also only for 5–20 ft. The "no protective system needed" option is flat wrong — 5 ft is the threshold above which a protective system is required.
problems.hint: Two thresholds: 5 ft (protection required) and 20 ft (PE-designed system required).

steps.text: OSHA: > 20 ft \u2192 system must be designed by a registered PE

traps: Not knowing the 20 ft PE-design threshold — this is a less-known but testable OSHA rule
Confusing the 5 ft (protection needed) and 20 ft (PE design needed) thresholds

math-slq-q1.statement: A surveyor records two elevation points along a proposed road centerline: Point A at station $0{+}00$ with elevation $120.0\,\text{ft}$ and Point B at station $3{+}00$ with elevation $126.0\,\text{ft}$. What is the grade (slope) of the road between the two points?
math-slq-q1.eli5: Station notation is just a way of writing distance in hundreds of feet — station 3+00 means 300 ft. Once you see that, it's just rise over run: 6 ft of rise over 300 ft of run = 0.02 = 2%. The trap is forgetting to convert stations to feet and using "3" instead of "300," which gives you 200% — obviously wrong but easy to do under pressure.
math-slq-q1.hint: Convert the station numbers to feet before dividing.

steps.text: Convert stations to feet: Station $0{+}00 = 0\,\text{ft}$, Station $3{+}00 = 300\,\text{ft}$.

traps: Forgetting to convert station notation to feet
Confusing rise/run with run/rise

math-slq-q2.statement: A property boundary runs from point $P(2, 3)$ to point $Q(8, 7)$. A utility easement must be laid perpendicular to this boundary through point $Q$. What is the slope of the easement line?
math-slq-q2.eli5: First find the slope of the boundary line — rise over run gives you 2/3. Then flip it and negate it for the perpendicular slope: 2/3 becomes -3/2. The most common mistake is only flipping without negating (getting 3/2) or only negating without flipping (getting -2/3). You have to do both — flip AND negate.
math-slq-q2.hint: Perpendicular means negative reciprocal — flip the fraction and change the sign.

steps.text: Find the slope of boundary PQ:

traps: Only negating without taking the reciprocal
Only taking the reciprocal without negating

math-slq-q3.statement: A projectile is launched from a $5\,\text{m}$ high embankment with an initial vertical velocity of $12\,\text{m/s}$. Its height is modeled by $h(t) = -4.9t^2 + 12t + 5$. At what time does the projectile hit the ground?
math-slq-q3.eli5: Set the height equation equal to zero and use the quadratic formula. You'll get two roots — one negative and one positive. Negative time doesn't make physical sense, so throw it away. The sneaky part: the negative root (-0.36) shows up as the 0.36 s choice without the minus sign. If you forget to check which root is physically valid, you might pick it. Always ask yourself: does my answer make sense in the real world?
math-slq-q3.hint: Set $h(t) = 0$ and apply the quadratic formula. One of the two roots won't make physical sense.

steps.text: Discard the negative root (time can't be negative):

traps: Selecting the negative root (appears as choice A without the minus sign)
Sign errors with the negative leading coefficient (a = -4.9)
Forgetting the embankment adds 5 m to initial height

math-log-q1.eli5: The power rule says you can pull the exponent out front: $\log(10^x) = x\log(10)$. And $\log_{10}(10) = 1$ because '10 to the what power gives 10? The answer is 1.' So the whole thing simplifies to just $x = 3.5$. The trap is overthinking it — some students try to compute $10^{3.5}$ and get confused. The log and the exponent with the same base just cancel.
math-log-q1.hint: What happens when the base of the log matches the base of the exponent?
traps: Computing 10^3.5 instead of recognizing the identity
Multiplying 10 by 3.5

math-log-q2.statement: A contaminant in a groundwater well decays according to $C = C_0 \cdot e^{-0.03t}$, where $t$ is in days. How many days until the concentration drops to 25% of its initial value?
math-log-q2.eli5: You need to 'undo' the exponential, and the natural log does exactly that — $\ln(e^{\text{something}}) = \text{something}$. So take $\ln$ of both sides to bring the exponent down. The main trap is forgetting to divide out $C_0$ first, or getting confused by the negatives. Both $\ln(0.25)$ and $-0.03$ are negative, so they cancel and $t$ comes out positive — which makes sense because time cannot be negative.
math-log-q2.hint: Divide both sides by $C_0$ first, then take the natural log to isolate $t$.

steps.text: Set $C = 0.25 C_0$ and divide both sides by $C_0$:
Take the natural log of both sides:

traps: Forgetting to divide by $C_0$ before taking the log
Sign error with the two negatives giving a negative time

math-log-q3.eli5: Three terms with the same base — combine them. Subtraction means divide, addition means multiply: $\log_2(32/4 \times 8) = \log_2(64)$. Then ask: 2 to the what power gives 64? Count the doublings: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 — that is 6. The trap is trying to evaluate each log separately and then doing regular arithmetic on the results without being careful. You can do it that way too ($5 - 2 + 3 = 6$), but combining first is faster and less error-prone. The sneaky distractor is 36 — which is what you get if you multiply the separate values ($5 \times 2 \times 3$) instead of adding them.
math-log-q3.hint: Combine the logs into a single log using the product and quotient rules before evaluating.

steps.text: Combine using log rules — quotient and product:

traps: Multiplying the individual log values instead of adding them
Misapplying the quotient rule order

math-rtt-q1.statement: A surveyor measures the angle of elevation to the top of a building as $35°$ from a point $50\,\text{m}$ away on level ground. What is the height of the building?
math-rtt-q1.eli5: You are standing 50 m from a building and looking up at $35°$. You know the ground distance (adjacent) and want the height (opposite) — that is tangent. Multiply 50 by $\tan(35°)$ and you are done. The trap is using sin or cos instead.
math-rtt-q1.hint: You know the adjacent side and want the opposite — which trig ratio connects those two?

steps.text: Identify the triangle: building height is opposite the 35° angle, the 50 m ground distance is adjacent.
Pick the ratio that connects opposite and adjacent:

traps: Using sin or cos instead of tan
Calculator in radian mode

math-rtt-q2.statement: A cable exerts a force of $12\,\text{kN}$ at $40°$ above the horizontal on a bridge anchor. What is the horizontal component of the force?
math-rtt-q2.eli5: "40 degrees above horizontal" means the angle is measured FROM the horizontal axis. The horizontal component is the side touching the angle — that's adjacent — so you use cosine. The classic trap is using sin for horizontal because it "feels" right. Remember: cos is cozy with the adjacent side.
math-rtt-q2.hint: The angle is measured from the horizontal axis — which side of the triangle is the horizontal component relative to that angle?

steps.text: The angle is measured from horizontal, so the horizontal component is adjacent to the angle.
Use cosine to find the adjacent (horizontal) component:

traps: Using sin instead of cos for the horizontal component
Dividing by cos instead of multiplying

math-rtt-q3.statement: An engineer stands at point A and measures the angle of elevation to the top of a tower as $25°$. She walks $30\,\text{m}$ closer to the tower to point B and measures the angle of elevation as $42°$. What is the height of the tower?
math-rtt-q3.eli5: This is a two-triangle problem. You set up tan equations from both positions — each has the same unknown height h but different distances. Write both equations, substitute one into the other, and solve for h. It looks nasty but it's just algebra after the two tan equations are set up. Don't try to shortcut — set up both equations first, then eliminate d.
math-rtt-q3.hint: Set up a separate tan equation from each observation point. Both share the same unknown height — eliminate the distance variable.

steps.text: Let h = tower height, d = horizontal distance from B to the base.

traps: Forgetting to add 30 m to the distance from A
Rounding intermediate values too early

math-lsc-q1.statement: In triangle ABC, angle $A = 40°$, angle $B = 75°$, and side $a = 18\,\text{m}$. What is the length of side $b$?
math-lsc-q1.eli5: You have a side and its opposite angle (a and A), plus another angle (B). That's a textbook Law of Sines setup. Cross-multiply to isolate b: multiply 18 by sin(75°)/sin(40°). The most common mistake is flipping the fraction and getting a smaller number instead of a bigger one.
math-lsc-q1.hint: You have a complete side-angle pair (a and A) — which law lets you use that directly?

steps.text: Identify the known pair: side a = 18 m is opposite angle A = 40°. We want side b opposite angle B = 75°.

traps: Flipping the sin ratio and getting a smaller answer
Using cos instead of sin

math-lsc-q2.statement: A surveyor measures two sides of a triangular lot as $85\,\text{m}$ and $110\,\text{m}$ with an included angle of $62°$. What is the length of the third side?
math-lsc-q2.eli5: When you see two sides and the angle between them, that is SAS — go straight to Law of Cosines. It is basically the Pythagorean theorem with a correction term ($-2ab\cos C$) for non-right triangles. The trap is forgetting to subtract that term, or accidentally using sine instead of cosine.
math-lsc-q2.hint: You know two sides and the included angle — which formula generalizes the Pythagorean theorem for non-right triangles?

steps.text: Two sides and included angle (SAS) → Law of Cosines.

traps: Adding the cosine term instead of subtracting
Using sin instead of cos in the formula

math-lsc-q3.statement: A triangular truss has sides $a = 6.0\,\text{m}$, $b = 8.0\,\text{m}$, and $c = 11.0\,\text{m}$. What is the measure of angle $C$ (the angle opposite the longest side)?
math-lsc-q3.eli5: When you have all three sides but no angles, rearrange the Law of Cosines to solve for cosine of the angle. The key insight: if the numerator comes out negative, the cosine is negative, which means the angle is obtuse (bigger than 90°). Don't panic when you see a negative — just hit inverse cosine on your calculator and it handles it. The trap is second-guessing the negative and subtracting from 180°.
math-lsc-q3.hint: Rearrange the Law of Cosines to isolate $\cos C$. What does a negative value of cosine tell you about the angle?

steps.text: All three sides known (SSS) → rearrange Law of Cosines to solve for the angle.

traps: Sign error using +c² in the numerator
Subtracting from 180° when cosine is negative

math-uci-q1.statement: What is the exact value of $\cos 60°$?
math-uci-q1.eli5: The unit circle point at $60°$ is $(1/2,\, \sqrt{3}/2)$. Cosine is always the x-coordinate, sine is the y-coordinate. The trap is mixing them up — $\sqrt{3}/2$ (the √3/2 choice) is the sine of $60°$, not the cosine. If you remember that $\cos 60° = 1/2$ and $\sin 60° = \sqrt{3}/2$, you have the most commonly tested pair down.
math-uci-q1.hint: On the unit circle, cosine is the x-coordinate and sine is the y-coordinate at any angle.

steps.text: Recall the unit circle: at 60°, the coordinates are (1/2, √3/2).

traps: Confusing sin and cos (picking $\sqrt{3}/2$)
Mixing up 45° and 60° values

math-uci-q2.statement: If $\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}$ and $\theta$ is in the second quadrant, what is $\cos\theta$?
math-uci-q2.eli5: Plug $\sin\theta$ into the Pythagorean identity and solve for $\cos\theta$. You get $\pm 4/5$. Now the quadrant matters — in Q2, $x$ is negative, so cosine is negative. The trap is forgetting the quadrant and picking the positive root. Always check which quadrant you are in after solving.
math-uci-q2.hint: Use $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ to find $|\cos\theta|$, then decide the sign based on the quadrant.
traps: Forgetting the sign from the quadrant
Confusing sin and cos values

math-uci-q3.statement: If $\sin\theta = \frac{5}{13}$ and $\theta$ is in the first quadrant, what is the value of $\sin 2\theta$?
math-uci-q3.eli5: This is a two-step problem. Step 1: use the Pythagorean identity to find $\cos\theta = 12/13$. Step 2: plug both into the double-angle formula $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$. The most common mistake is thinking "double angle" means "just double the sine" — it does not. You need both $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$. The second trap is forgetting the 2 out front.
math-uci-q3.hint: The double-angle formula needs both $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ — find the missing one first with the Pythagorean identity.

steps.text: Find cos θ using the Pythagorean identity:

traps: Just doubling $\sin\theta$ without multiplying by $\cos\theta$
Forgetting the factor of 2

math-cc-q1.statement: A circular retention pond is modeled by the equation $(x - 5)^2 + (y + 3)^2 = 64$. What are the center and radius of the pond?
math-cc-q1.eli5: Read the center straight from the equation: $(x - 5)$ means $h = 5$, and $(y + 3)$ means $k = -3$ because $y + 3 = y - (-3)$. The number on the right is $r^2$, not $r$ — so take the square root. The two traps are getting the sign of $k$ wrong and forgetting to square-root the radius.
math-cc-q1.hint: The sign inside the parentheses is opposite to the coordinate — $(y + 3)$ means $k = -3$. And 64 is $r^2$, not $r$.
traps: Flipping the sign of $k$
Giving $r^2$ instead of $r$

math-cc-q2.statement: A tunnel cross-section is described by $x^2 + y^2 - 10x + 6y + 18 = 0$. What is the radius of the circular cross-section?
math-cc-q2.eli5: Move the constant to the right side, then complete the square for both $x$ and $y$. For $x^2 - 10x$, half of 10 is 5, squared is 25 — add 25 to both sides. For $y^2 + 6y$, half of 6 is 3, squared is 9 — add 9 to both sides. Now you have standard form and can read off the radius. The trap is forgetting to add the completing-the-square values to both sides, or giving $r^2$ as the answer.
math-cc-q2.hint: Group the x and y terms, then complete the square for each — remember to add the same values to both sides.

steps.text: Complete the square for both variables:

traps: Forgetting to add completing-the-square values to both sides
Giving $r^2$ instead of $r$

math-cc-q3.statement: A vertical highway curve is modeled by $y = -0.004x^2 + 2.4x - 200$. At what horizontal distance $x$ does the curve reach its maximum elevation, and what is that elevation?
math-cc-q3.eli5: For a parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$, the vertex is at $x = -b/(2a)$. Plug in $a = -0.004$ and $b = 2.4$ to get $x = 300$. Then substitute $x = 300$ back into the equation to get $y = 160$. The big trap is forgetting the 2 in the denominator and using $-b/a = 600$ instead. Always double-check by plugging the $x$ value back in.
math-cc-q3.hint: The vertex of $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ is at $x = -b/(2a)$ — do not forget the 2 in the denominator.

steps.text: Since a = -0.004 < 0, the parabola opens downward — the vertex is the maximum.
Plug x = 300 back in to find y:

traps: Forgetting the 2 in the denominator and using -b/a
Reading the constant term as the max y value

math-dr-q1.eli5: The power rule says bring the exponent down and subtract one from the power. But the argument isn't just x — it's 3x + 5 — so you have to chain rule it. That means you also multiply by the derivative of the inside, which is 3. The most common mistake is forgetting that extra factor of 3. The choice $4(3x + 5)^3$ is exactly what you get if you skip the chain rule.
math-dr-q1.hint: The argument isn't plain x — what extra factor does the chain rule add?

steps.text: Recognize this as a chain rule problem: the outer function is $u^4$ and the inner function is $u = 3x + 5$.
Multiply by the derivative of the inner function:

traps: Forgetting the chain rule and omitting the factor of 3
Leaving the exponent as 4 instead of reducing to 3

math-dr-q2.statement: Find the derivative of $f(x) = x^2 e^{3x}$.
math-dr-q2.eli5: Two functions multiplied together means product rule. The tricky part is that e^(3x) also needs the chain rule — its derivative is 3e^(3x), not just e^(3x). The choice e^{3x}(2x + x^2) is what you get if you forget that chain rule factor of 3 on the exponential. The choice 2xe^{3x} only differentiates the x² part and ignores the product rule entirely. Always ask: am I using BOTH terms of the product rule?
math-dr-q2.hint: Two functions multiplied means product rule. And $e^{3x}$ needs the chain rule for its own derivative.

steps.text: Identify $u = x^2$ and $v = e^{3x}$. This needs the product rule.
Find each derivative: $du/dx = 2x$ and $dv/dx = 3e^{3x}$ (chain rule on the exponential).

traps: Forgetting the chain rule on e^(3x) (missing the factor of 3)
Only differentiating one factor and ignoring the product rule

math-dr-q3.eli5: Quotient rule: 'lo d-hi minus hi d-lo over lo-lo.' The denominator function ($x^2 + 1$) goes first in the numerator — it multiplies the derivative of the top ($\cos x$). Then subtract the top ($\sin x$) times the derivative of the bottom ($2x$). The classic trap is flipping the subtraction order. The choice with a plus where there should be a minus (cos x term plus 2x sin x) is wrong. The choice with the terms in the wrong order entirely (2x sin x minus the cos x term) is also wrong. The mnemonic saves you: lo d-hi MINUS hi d-lo.
math-dr-q3.hint: 'Lo d-hi minus hi d-lo over lo-lo' — the bottom function goes first in the numerator.

steps.text: Identify $u = \sin x$ and $v = x^2 + 1$. This needs the quotient rule.

traps: Flipping the subtraction order in the quotient rule numerator
Forgetting to square the denominator
Simplifying the denominator instead of leaving it as (x² + 1)²

math-ad-q1.statement: Find the value of $x$ at which $f(x) = -2x^2 + 16x - 5$ reaches its maximum.
math-ad-q1.eli5: Take the derivative, set it to zero, solve for $x$. That is it. The second derivative is $-4$, which is negative — concave down — so it is a max, not a min. Since the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward, so of course it is a max. The choice $x = 8$ is what you get if you forget the factor of 2 when differentiating $-2x^2$. Always double-check your power rule on the leading term.
math-ad-q1.hint: Set $f'(x) = 0$ and solve. Is the parabola opening up or down?
traps: Forgetting the coefficient when differentiating $-2x^2$ (getting $-2x$ instead of $-4x$)
Reporting the max value of $f(x)$ instead of the $x$-location

math-ad-q2.statement: A civil engineer models the cost per meter of a retaining wall as $C(h) = 3h^2 - 36h + 150$, where $h$ is the wall height in meters. What wall height minimizes the cost, and what is the minimum cost?
math-ad-q2.eli5: Same process — derivative, set to zero, solve. You get $h = 6$. The second derivative is positive ($6 > 0$), so it is concave up — a minimum. The extra step is plugging $h = 6$ back into the original function to get the cost. The choice giving C = 150/m is the trap for students who find the right $h$ but give the constant term (150) as the cost instead of actually evaluating $C(6)$. Always plug back in.
math-ad-q2.hint: After finding where $C'(h) = 0$, plug that value back into the original $C(h)$ to find the minimum cost.
traps: Giving the constant term as the min cost instead of evaluating C(6)
Arithmetic error in evaluating the quadratic at h = 6

math-ad-q3.statement: A beam deflection curve is modeled by $y(x) = x^3 - 12x^2 + 36x$, where $x$ is in meters along the beam and $y$ is deflection. At what point does the curvature of the beam change direction (inflection point)?
math-ad-q3.eli5: An inflection point is where the curve changes from bending one way to bending the other — concave up to concave down or vice versa. Set the SECOND derivative to zero, not the first. That is the most common mistake: students set y' = 0 and find critical points instead. The choices x = 2 m and x = 6 m are the critical points where y' = 0 — those are max/min locations, not inflection points. The inflection point is where y'' = 0 and actually changes sign.
math-ad-q3.hint: Inflection points come from the second derivative, not the first. Set $y''(x) = 0$.

steps.text: Set the second derivative to zero:
Verify sign change: $y''(3) = -6 < 0$ and $y''(5) = 6 > 0$ — sign changes, confirming inflection point.

math-ad-q3.handbookFormula: f''(a) = 0 \text{ and } f''(x) \text{ changes sign} \implies \text{inflection point}
traps: Setting y'(x) = 0 instead of y''(x) = 0 (finding critical points instead of inflection points)
Not verifying that y'' actually changes sign at the candidate point

math-ic-q1.statement: A retaining wall footing exerts a parabolically varying pressure on the soil given by $q(x) = 3x^2$ kPa, where $x$ is in meters from the toe. Find the total force per unit width over the first 2 m of the footing.
math-ic-q1.eli5: Total force from a varying pressure is just the integral of the pressure function over the loaded length. Power rule: bring the exponent up by 1 and divide. The 3 and the 1/3 cancel perfectly here — clean answer, no tricks.
math-ic-q1.hint: Integrate the pressure function from 0 to 2 using the power rule.

steps.text: Total force = area under the pressure curve:

traps: Forgetting to evaluate at both limits (plugging in only the upper bound)
Confusing pressure (kPa) with force (kN/m) — the integral of pressure over length gives force per unit width

math-ic-q2.eli5: You've got $x$ times $e^{2x}$ — two different types multiplied together, so it's integration by parts. LIATE says pick $u = x$ (algebraic) since it comes before exponential. Then $dv = e^{2x}\,dx$ and you integrate that to get $v$. Watch the factor of 1/2 from integrating $e^{2x}$ — that's where most errors happen.
math-ic-q2.hint: LIATE: $x$ is algebraic (A), $e^{2x}$ is exponential (E). Algebraic comes first — let $u = x$.
traps: Forgetting the 1/2 factor when integrating $e^{2x}$ (the antiderivative is $\frac{e^{2x}}{2}$, not $e^{2x}$)
Picking $u$ and $dv$ backwards — if you let $u = e^{2x}$, the integral gets harder, not easier

math-ic-q3.eli5: Whenever you see $\sin^n x \cdot \cos x$ (or $\cos^n x \cdot \sin x$), it's screaming for u-sub. The $\cos x$ is the derivative of $\sin x$ — that's the $g'(x)$ that makes substitution work. After substituting, you're left with a basic power rule integral. Don't forget to change the limits when it's a definite integral.
math-ic-q3.hint: Notice that $\cos x$ is the derivative of $\sin x$. Let $u = \sin x$.

steps.text: Recognize the pattern: $\sin^3 x \cdot \cos x = f(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)$ where $g(x) = \sin x$.

traps: Forgetting to change the integration limits when substituting (going back to $x$ limits with a $u$ antiderivative)
Mixing up which function is $u$ and which is $du$ — the one with the higher power ($\sin^3 x$) stays, its derivative ($\cos x\,dx$) becomes $du$

math-lh-q1.eli5: Plug in $x = 0$ and you get $0/0$ — that is the signal to use L'Hopital's. Derivative of $\sin x$ is $\cos x$, derivative of $x$ is 1. Now plug in 0 again: $\cos(0) = 1$. Done in one round. This is probably the most classic L'Hopital's example you will ever see.
math-lh-q1.hint: Direct substitution gives 0/0. Differentiate the numerator and denominator separately.

steps.text: Apply L'Hopital's — differentiate top and bottom:

traps: Trying to simplify sin x / x algebraically instead of just applying the rule
Applying the quotient rule instead of differentiating top and bottom independently

math-lh-q2.eli5: First try gives 0/0, so you differentiate top and bottom. But the second try also gives 0/0 — apply the rule again. Third try: e^x / 2 evaluated at 0 gives 1/2. Two rounds is the most the FE will usually ask for. If you're on round 3+, you probably made a derivative error earlier.
math-lh-q2.hint: After the first application you still get 0/0. Apply L'Hopital's a second time.

steps.text: First round — differentiate top and bottom:

traps: Stopping after the first round when the result is still indeterminate
Forgetting to differentiate the constant -1 in e^x - 1 (its derivative is 0, which simplifies things)

math-lh-q3.eli5: This is a trap problem. You see a fraction with $x \to 0$ and want to reach for L'Hopital's — but check the form first! $e^0 / 0 = 1/0$, which is NOT indeterminate. It is a 'blow up' form. The numerator is a finite nonzero number and the denominator goes to zero, so the function goes to $\pm\infty$. Since it goes to $+\infty$ from the right and $-\infty$ from the left, the limit DNE.
math-lh-q3.hint: Before applying L'Hopital's, check: does direct substitution actually give 0/0 or ∞/∞?

steps.text: L'Hopital's Rule does NOT apply here.
Since left and right limits disagree, the two-sided limit does not exist.

math-lh-q3.handbookPage: p. 48, L'Hopital's Rule (applies only to 0/0 or ∞/∞ forms)
traps: Blindly applying L'Hopital's without checking the indeterminate form — applying it here gives lim e^x/1 = 1, which is WRONG
Choosing ∞ instead of DNE — the one-sided limits must agree for the two-sided limit to exist

math-vbu-q1.statement: A surveyor measures a displacement of $\vec{d} = 30\hat{i} + 40\hat{j}$ meters from a benchmark. What is the total distance from the benchmark?
math-vbu-q1.eli5: Distance is the magnitude of the displacement vector. Square each component, add them, take the square root. This is a 3-4-5 right triangle scaled by 10 — if you recognize the Pythagorean triple you can skip the calculator entirely.
math-vbu-q1.hint: The total distance is the magnitude of the vector, not the sum of components.
traps: Adding components directly (30 + 40 = 70) instead of using the magnitude formula
Forgetting to square root — 900 + 1600 = 2500 is not the answer, √2500 = 50 is

math-vbu-q2.statement: A force acts along the direction from point $A(1, 2, 2)$ to point $B(4, 6, 2)$. What is the unit vector from $A$ to $B$?
math-vbu-q2.eli5: Two steps: first get the direction vector by subtracting coordinates (B − A), then divide every component by the magnitude. The choice 3î + 4ĵ + 0k̂ is the direction vector before normalizing — that's the most common mistake. Always check that your unit vector's magnitude equals 1: √(0.6² + 0.8²) = √(0.36 + 0.64) = 1. ✓
math-vbu-q2.hint: Subtract A from B to get the direction vector, then divide by its magnitude.
traps: Forgetting to divide by the magnitude — choice B is the raw direction vector, not the unit vector
Subtracting in the wrong order (A − B instead of B − A) — this reverses the direction

math-vbu-q3.statement: Three forces act on a gusset plate: $\vec{F}_1 = 500\hat{i} + 0\hat{j}$ N, $\vec{F}_2 = -200\hat{i} + 300\hat{j}$ N, and $\vec{F}_3 = 0\hat{i} - 400\hat{j}$ N. What is the magnitude of the resultant force?
math-vbu-q3.eli5: Vector addition is component-by-component — add all the x's together, add all the y's together. Then the resultant magnitude is √(Rx² + Ry²). The trap is adding magnitudes directly (500 + 360.6 + 400 ≈ 1261) — that only works if all forces point the same direction, which they never do in real problems. Here √100000 = 100√10 ≈ 316 N.
math-vbu-q3.hint: Add the x-components and y-components separately, then find the magnitude of the resultant vector.
traps: Adding magnitudes directly instead of adding components — forces in opposite directions partially cancel
Forgetting the negative signs on components — F₂ₓ = -200 and F₃ᵧ = -400 are critical

math-dpa-q1.eli5: Multiply matching components and add: x with x, y with y. That's it. The negative sign on B_x = -2 is critical — (3)(-2) = -6, not +6. Then add (4)(5) = 20. Total: 14. The choice -6 is just the first term without adding the second.
math-dpa-q1.hint: Multiply x-components together, multiply y-components together, then add.
traps: Dropping the negative sign: (3)(-2) = -6, not +6
Cross-multiplying components (A_x B_y) instead of matching (A_x B_x) — that's the cross product pattern

math-dpa-q2.eli5: This is the standard three-step workflow: (1) compute the dot product with components, (2) compute both magnitudes, (3) divide and take inverse cosine. Vector A points along the x-axis, vector B points at 45° in the xy-plane — so the answer makes geometric sense. Always sanity-check your angle.
traps: Forgetting to compute magnitudes and dividing dot product by component sums instead
Getting $\cos\theta = 1/\sqrt{2}$ but reporting $\theta = 1/\sqrt{2}$ without taking $\cos^{-1}$

math-dpa-q3.statement: A force $\vec{F} = 300\hat{i} + 600\hat{j} - 300\hat{k}$ N acts at a joint. A structural member runs from the joint in the direction $\vec{d} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 1\hat{k}$. What is the component of the force along the member?
math-dpa-q3.eli5: The scalar projection tells you how much of the force acts along the member's axis. Compute the dot product (which mixes all three components), then divide by the magnitude of the direction vector — not the force vector. The 1500 N option is the raw dot product without dividing — the most common mistake. The 900 N option is the sum of force component magnitudes, which ignores direction entirely.
math-dpa-q3.hint: The component of F along d is (F · d) / |d| — divide by the magnitude of the direction, not the force.
traps: Using the raw dot product (1500) without dividing by |d| — the projection requires normalization
Dividing by |F| instead of |d| — you project onto the direction vector, not the force

math-cpa-q1.eli5: i × j = k — this is the right-hand rule in action. Point your fingers along x, curl them toward y, and your thumb points along z. This is one of those "just know it" results that saves time. The -1k̂ choice has the wrong sign — that would be j × i, the reversed order.
math-cpa-q1.hint: Use the determinant formula, or recall that i × j = k.
math-cpa-q1.handbookFormula: \vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ A_x & A_y & A_z \\ B_x & B_y & B_z \end{vmatrix}
traps: Reversing the order: B × A = -k, not +k
Thinking the cross product of perpendicular unit vectors is zero — that's the dot product (i · j = 0)

math-cpa-q2.statement: A force $\vec{F} = 0\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} - 50\hat{k}$ N (downward) is applied at point $P$. The position vector from the pivot $O$ to $P$ is $\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$ m. What is the moment $\vec{M}_O = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$?
math-cpa-q2.eli5: Moment = r × F. Set up the 3×3 determinant and expand carefully. The j component has the MINUS sign in front of the cofactor — so you get -(3·(-50) - 0) = -(-150) = +150. That negative-of-a-negative is where most people mess up. The distractor $200\hat{i} - 150\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$ flips all the signs — that is F × r (wrong order).
math-cpa-q2.hint: Set up the determinant with r in the second row and F in the third row. Watch the sign on the j cofactor.
traps: Forgetting the negative sign on the j cofactor — the pattern is +, −, + across the three components
Reversing r and F — moment is r × F, not F × r

math-cpa-q3.statement: Two edges of a triangular plot are defined by $\vec{u} = 4\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$ m and $\vec{v} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$ m. What is the area of the triangle?
math-cpa-q3.eli5: The cross product magnitude gives the parallelogram area. A triangle is half the parallelogram. So: compute the cross product, take the magnitude, divide by 2. The 12 m² choice is the parallelogram area without halving — the most common mistake. Since both vectors lie in the xy-plane, the cross product points purely in the k direction, which makes the magnitude easy.
math-cpa-q3.hint: Triangle area = ½|u × v|. Compute the cross product first, then take half its magnitude.
traps: Forgetting to divide by 2 — the cross product magnitude gives the parallelogram area, not the triangle area
Using the dot product instead of the cross product — the dot product gives a scalar related to $\cos\theta$, not an area

math-spr-q1.statement: A spreadsheet cell contains the formula =A1+A2*A3. The cells hold A1 = 2, A2 = 3, and A3 = 4. What value does the cell display?
math-spr-q1.eli5: Spreadsheets follow PEMDAS, so multiplication happens before addition. Compute A2*A3 = 3*4 = 12 first, then add A1: 2 + 12 = 14. The 20 option is the classic mistake of working strictly left to right as (2+3)*4. The 9 option just adds all three. The 24 option multiplies all three.
math-spr-q1.hint: Spreadsheets obey order of operations — do the multiplication before the addition.

steps.text: Apply precedence: multiplication before addition. Evaluate A2*A3 first.

traps: Evaluating left-to-right as (2+3)*4 = 20 instead of obeying precedence
Adding all three values (9) and ignoring the operators

math-spr-q2.statement: Cell C1 contains the formula =A1*$B$1, where A1 = 5 and B1 = 10, so C1 displays 50. The formula in C1 is copied down into C2, and cell A2 = 8. What value does C2 display?
math-spr-q2.eli5: When you copy down one row, the RELATIVE reference A1 shifts to A2, but the ABSOLUTE reference $B$1 stays locked. So C2 becomes =A2*$B$1 = 8 × 10 = 80. The 50 option assumes the A reference didn't move (it isn't locked, so it does). The 18 option adds instead of multiplies. The 800 option shifts or multiplies the locked reference by mistake.
math-spr-q2.hint: A1 is relative (it shifts when copied); $B$1 is absolute (it stays put).

steps.text: Copying down one row shifts relative references down one row: A1 → A2.
The absolute reference $B$1 does not change.

traps: Thinking A1 stays fixed — it is relative and shifts to A2
Accidentally shifting the locked $B$1 reference

math-spr-q3.statement: A cell contains =IF(A1>=10, A1*2, A1+5). Cell A1 holds the value 12. What does the cell display?
math-spr-q3.eli5: IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false) checks the test first. Here A1>=10 asks 'is 12 at least 10?' — yes, so the function returns the TRUE result, A1*2 = 12 × 2 = 24. The choice 17 is the FALSE branch A1+5, which only applies if the test fails. The choice 1 is the mistake of treating TRUE as the literal number 1.
math-spr-q3.hint: Evaluate the test (is A1 ≥ 10?) and return the matching branch.

steps.text: Because the test is TRUE, return the second argument: A1*2.

traps: Returning the FALSE branch (A1+5 = 17) even though the test passes
Treating the logical result TRUE as the number 1

math-prg-q1.statement: Trace this pseudocode: total = 0; FOR i = 1 TO 4: total = total + i. What is the value of total after the loop finishes?
math-prg-q1.eli5: The loop runs for i = 1, 2, 3, 4 (inclusive endpoints), adding i to a running total each pass: 0+1+2+3+4 = 10. The 6 option stops at i = 3, the off-by-one error. The 15 option runs one extra pass to i = 5. The 4 option is just the number of iterations, not the sum.
math-prg-q1.hint: FOR i = 1 TO 4 runs four times (1,2,3,4). Add each i to the running total.

steps.text: i = 4: total = 6 + 4 = 10. Loop ends (i would be 5, past 4).

traps: Stopping at i = 3 (off-by-one) for a total of 6
Reporting the iteration count (4) instead of the accumulated sum

math-prg-q2.statement: Given the logic: IF x > 10 THEN y = 1; ELSE IF x > 5 THEN y = 2; ELSE y = 3. If x = 7, what is the value of y?
math-prg-q2.eli5: Conditions are checked top to bottom and the first true one wins. x = 7 is not greater than 10 (first test fails), but 7 > 5 is true (second test), so y = 2 and the final ELSE is skipped. The value 1 would require x > 10. The value 3 would require both tests to fail (x ≤ 5).
math-prg-q2.hint: Check conditions in order; the first TRUE branch runs and the rest are skipped.

steps.text: First test: x > 10 → 7 > 10 → FALSE. Skip y = 1.
Second test: x > 5 → 7 > 5 → TRUE. Set y = 2.
The remaining ELSE branch is skipped. y = 2.

traps: Falling through to the final ELSE (y = 3) instead of stopping at the first true test
Confusing the strict inequality (7 is not > 10)

math-prg-q3.statement: Trace this WHILE loop: x = 1; WHILE x < 100: x = x * 2. What is the value of x when the loop stops?
math-prg-q3.eli5: A WHILE loop keeps doubling as long as x < 100, and it stops the moment the condition fails. The sequence is 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32 → 64 → 128. When x = 64 the condition (64 < 100) is still true, so it doubles once more to 128. Now 128 < 100 is false, so the loop stops with x = 128. The choice 64 stops one pass too early. The choice 100 assumes the loop caps at the limit, which it does not.
math-prg-q3.hint: Keep doubling while x < 100; the value that breaks the condition is the final value.

steps.text: At x = 64 the condition 64 < 100 is still true, so double once more: x = 128.
Now 128 < 100 is FALSE, so the loop exits with x = 128.

traps: Stopping at 64 because it is the last value below 100, forgetting the loop doubles it again
Assuming the result is capped at the limit value (100)

math-num-q1.statement: Use one iteration of Newton's method to improve the estimate of a root of $f(x) = x^2 - 2$, starting from $x_0 = 1.5$. (Here $f'(x) = 2x$.) What is $x_1$?
math-num-q1.eli5: x₁ = x₀ − f(x₀)/f′(x₀). f(1.5) = 1.5² − 2 = 0.25; f′(1.5) = 2(1.5) = 3. So x₁ = 1.5 − 0.25/3 = 1.5 − 0.0833 = 1.417 (approaching √2 ≈ 1.4142). The 1.333 choice forgets to square (uses x-2 over 2). The 1.500 choice is just the starting value. The 1.250 choice over-corrects.
math-num-q1.hint: x₁ = x₀ − f(x₀)/f′(x₀); compute f and f′ at 1.5.

steps.text: Evaluate f and f′ at x₀ = 1.5:

traps: Forgetting to divide by the derivative
Adding instead of subtracting the correction

math-num-q2.statement: The bisection method can find a root in an interval $[a, b]$ only if which condition holds?

choices.text: The function changes sign over the interval: $f(a)\cdot f(b) < 0$
The function is positive at both ends
The derivative is zero somewhere in the interval
The interval is shorter than 1 unit

math-num-q2.eli5: Bisection relies on the Intermediate Value Theorem: if a continuous function has opposite signs at the two endpoints (f(a)·f(b) < 0), a root must lie between them. The "positive at both ends" option gives no guarantee of a root. The "derivative is zero" and "interval shorter than 1 unit" options are irrelevant to the bracketing requirement.
math-num-q2.hint: What must be true about the function's sign at the two ends of the interval?

steps.text: Bisection brackets a root between sign changes.
A sign change means f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs.

traps: Thinking same-sign endpoints can bracket a root
Confusing the bisection requirement with a derivative condition

math-num-q3.statement: Under what condition is Newton's method most likely to FAIL to converge?

choices.text: When the initial estimate is far from the root or the derivative is near zero
When the initial estimate is very close to the root
When the function is a straight line

math-num-q3.eli5: Newton's method follows the tangent slope. A poor (far) starting guess or a near-zero derivative (a nearly flat tangent) throws the next estimate far away, so the method may diverge or oscillate. A close starting guess and a straight line (where it converges in one step) are ideal, not failures. A large derivative gives small, well-behaved steps.
math-num-q3.hint: The method uses the slope — what makes a tangent line send you far from the root?

steps.text: Newton's step is f(x)/f′(x); a near-zero f′ makes the step huge.
A far initial guess can also send iterations away from the root.
So poor guesses or near-zero derivatives cause failure.

traps: Assuming a close initial guess causes failure
Overlooking the near-zero-derivative problem

math-slq-ex1.statement: A tunnel centerline runs from coordinates $(100, 200)$ to $(400, 500)$. What is the length of the tunnel in meters?
math-slq-ex1.eli5: Use the distance formula. The horizontal run is 300, the vertical rise is 300. Plug into $d = \sqrt{300^2 + 300^2} = \sqrt{180{,}000} = 424.3$ m. Common mistake is adding the components ($300 + 300 = 600$) instead of using the distance formula.
math-slq-ex1.hint: Use the distance formula between two points.
traps: Adding components instead of using the distance formula
Forgetting to take the square root

math-slq-ex2.statement: Two lines have slopes $m_1 = 3$ and $m_2 = -\frac{1}{3}$. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: The lines intersect but are neither parallel nor perpendicular

math-slq-ex2.eli5: Two lines are perpendicular when their slopes are negative reciprocals. Check: $3 \times (-1/3) = -1$. That confirms they are perpendicular. Parallel lines have equal slopes, and coincident means they are the same line.
math-slq-ex2.hint: Check if the product of the slopes equals $-1$.

steps.text: Since the product is $-1$, the lines are perpendicular.

traps: Confusing perpendicular (product = -1) with parallel (equal slopes)

math-slq-ex3.statement: A retaining wall base runs from point $A(1, 4)$ to point $B(7, 12)$. A drainage line must pass through the midpoint of $AB$ with slope $m = -2$. What is the equation of the drainage line in slope-intercept form?
math-slq-ex3.eli5: Two steps here: first find the midpoint of $AB$, then use point-slope form with the given slope. Midpoint is just the average of the coordinates: $((1+7)/2,\,(4+12)/2) = (4, 8)$. Then plug into $y - 8 = -2(x - 4)$ and simplify to $y = -2x + 16$. The trap is using point A or B instead of the midpoint, which gives you one of the wrong answers.
math-slq-ex3.hint: Find the midpoint of AB first, then apply the point-slope formula with the given slope.
traps: Using an endpoint instead of the midpoint
Distributing the slope incorrectly when expanding point-slope form

math-slq-ex4.statement: A quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ has a discriminant of $b^2 - 4ac = -16$. Which statement about the roots is correct?

choices.text: There are two distinct real roots
There is exactly one repeated real root

math-slq-ex4.eli5: The discriminant tells you everything about the nature of the roots. Positive means two distinct real roots, zero means one repeated root, negative means no real roots (complex conjugate pair). A negative discriminant means $\sqrt{\Delta}$ involves the square root of a negative number in the quadratic formula, which has no real solution. The equation can still be solved with complex numbers, so the choice claiming the equation cannot be solved is wrong — it is solvable, just not over the reals.
math-slq-ex4.hint: Recall what the sign of the discriminant tells you about the number and type of roots.

steps.text: A negative discriminant means $\sqrt{\Delta}$ is imaginary:
The quadratic formula produces complex conjugate roots — no real solutions exist.

traps: Confusing "no real roots" with "no solution at all" — complex roots still exist
Thinking a negative discriminant means one root

math-log-ex1.eli5: Rewrite the equation in log form: $x = \log_3(81)$. You're asking '3 to what power gives 81?' Count: $3^1 = 3$, $3^2 = 9$, $3^3 = 27$, $3^4 = 81$. So $x = 4$. Alternatively, take $\log$ of both sides and use the power rule to bring $x$ down. Either way, the answer is 4. The trap is confusing 81 with $3^3 = 27$.
math-log-ex1.hint: Rewrite the equation as a logarithm: $x = \log_3(81)$.
traps: Confusing powers of 3 — 3^3 = 27, not 81
Dividing 81 by 3 repeatedly but losing count

math-log-ex2.eli5: Use the identity $\ln(e^n) = n$ on each term. The first term gives 4, the second gives $-1$. Add them: $4 + (-1) = 3$. You could also combine first using the product rule: $\ln(e^4 \cdot e^{-1}) = \ln(e^3) = 3$. Either path works. The trap is multiplying the exponents instead of adding them ($4 \times -1 = -4$), which is the choice $-4$.
math-log-ex2.hint: Apply $\ln(e^n) = n$ to each term, then add the results.

steps.text: Apply the identity to each term:

traps: Multiplying the exponents (4 times -1) instead of adding
Dropping the negative sign on the second term

math-log-ex3.statement: An investment doubles in value according to $2 = e^{0.06t}$, where $t$ is in years. How many years does it take to double?
math-log-ex3.eli5: Take the natural log of both sides to bring the exponent down: $\ln(2) = 0.06t$. Then divide: $t = \ln(2) / 0.06 = 0.6931 / 0.06 = 11.6$ years. The main mistake is using $\log_{10}(2)$ instead of $\ln(2)$ — those are different numbers. Since the base of the exponent is $e$, you need the natural log to cancel it.
math-log-ex3.hint: Take $\ln$ of both sides to undo the exponential, then isolate $t$.

steps.text: Take natural log of both sides:

traps: Using log base 10 instead of natural log
Dividing 0.06 by ln(2) instead of the other way around

math-log-ex4.statement: Which of the following is a valid logarithmic identity?
math-log-ex4.eli5: The power rule says you can pull an exponent out as a coefficient: $\log(x^c) = c \cdot \log x$. The other three choices are the most common log mistakes students make. There is NO log rule for sums ($x + y$) or differences ($x - y$) inside a log. And the product rule says $\log(xy) = \log x + \log y$ (addition), not multiplication. If you remember only one thing: logs turn multiplication into addition and powers into multiplication — never sums into anything.
math-log-ex4.hint: Only products, quotients, and powers have log identities. Sums and differences inside a log cannot be split.

steps.text: The sum choice is wrong: $\log(x + y) \neq \log x + \log y$ — no identity for sums.
The difference choice is wrong: $\log(x - y) \neq \log x - \log y$ — no identity for differences.
The product choice is wrong: the product rule gives addition, not multiplication: $\log(xy) = \log x + \log y$.

traps: Confusing the product rule — log(xy) = log x + log y, not log x times log y
Thinking log(x + y) can be split — there is no identity for sums inside a log

math-rtt-ex1.statement: A ladder leans against a wall at an angle of $65°$ with the ground. If the foot of the ladder is $3.0\,\text{m}$ from the wall, how long is the ladder?
math-rtt-ex1.eli5: You know the adjacent side (3.0 m from the wall) and the angle with the ground ($65°$), and you want the hypotenuse (the ladder). Adjacent over hypotenuse is cosine: $\cos 65° = 3/L$, so $L = 3/\cos 65° = 3/0.4226 = 7.1$ m. The trap is using sine instead of cosine, which would give you the wall height, not the ladder length.
math-rtt-ex1.hint: You know the side adjacent to the angle and need the hypotenuse. Which trig ratio connects those?

steps.text: The ground distance (3.0 m) is adjacent to the 65 degree angle. The ladder is the hypotenuse.

traps: Using sine instead of cosine
Multiplying by cos instead of dividing

math-rtt-ex2.statement: A guy wire attached to the top of a $20\,\text{m}$ antenna makes a $55°$ angle with the ground. What is the length of the guy wire?
math-rtt-ex2.eli5: The antenna height (20 m) is opposite the $55°$ angle. The wire is the hypotenuse. Opposite over hypotenuse is sine: $\sin 55° = 20/W$, so $W = 20/\sin 55° = 20/0.8192 = 24.4$ m. The classic trap is using tangent, which connects opposite and adjacent, not opposite and hypotenuse.
math-rtt-ex2.hint: You know the opposite side and need the hypotenuse. SOH-CAH-TOA tells you which ratio to use.

steps.text: The antenna (20 m) is opposite the 55 degree angle at ground level. The wire is the hypotenuse.

traps: Using tangent instead of sine
Using cos instead of sin — that gives the ground distance, not the wire length

math-rtt-ex3.statement: A ramp rises $1.5\,\text{m}$ over a horizontal distance of $12\,\text{m}$. What is the angle of incline of the ramp?
math-rtt-ex3.eli5: You know the opposite (rise = 1.5 m) and the adjacent (run = 12 m). That is tangent. Take the inverse tangent of $1.5/12 = 0.125$ to get $7.1°$. The $0.125°$ choice is the ratio itself without taking the inverse trig function. The $82.9°$ choice is $90°$ minus the correct answer — that would be the angle from the vertical, not the horizontal.
math-rtt-ex3.hint: You have the rise and the run. Which trig function relates opposite to adjacent?
traps: Reporting the ratio as the angle instead of taking inverse tangent
Giving the complement (90 minus the angle) instead of the angle from horizontal

math-rtt-ex4.statement: A force $F$ acts at angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. An engineer writes $F_x = F\sin\theta$ and $F_y = F\cos\theta$. What error did the engineer make?

choices.text: The formulas are correct as written
The sin and cos are swapped — $F_x$ should use cos and $F_y$ should use sin
The force should be divided by the trig functions, not multiplied

math-rtt-ex4.eli5: When the angle is measured from the horizontal, the horizontal component is adjacent to the angle, so it uses cosine. The vertical component is opposite the angle, so it uses sine. The engineer swapped them. This is the single most common trig error on the FE exam. Remember: cosine is "cozy" with the adjacent side, and the adjacent side is the one the angle is measured from. The correct formulas are $F_x = F\cos\theta$ and $F_y = F\sin\theta$.
math-rtt-ex4.hint: When the angle is measured FROM the horizontal, which component (horizontal or vertical) is adjacent to that angle?

steps.text: The angle $\theta$ is measured from the horizontal axis.
The horizontal component is adjacent to $\theta$, so it uses cosine:
The vertical component is opposite $\theta$, so it uses sine:
The engineer swapped sin and cos.

traps: Assuming the formulas look correct because the components have some trig function
Forgetting that the reference direction of the angle determines which function to use

math-lsc-ex1.statement: In triangle $PQR$, angle $P = 50°$, angle $Q = 65°$, and side $p = 24\,\text{m}$ (opposite angle $P$). What is the length of side $q$ (opposite angle $Q$)?
math-lsc-ex1.eli5: You have a complete side-angle pair ($p$ and $P$) plus another angle ($Q$), so Law of Sines is your move. Set up the proportion and cross-multiply to solve for $q$. The bigger angle ($65°$ vs $50°$) should give a bigger side, so $q > 24$ is a quick sanity check. If your answer came out smaller, you probably flipped the fraction.
math-lsc-ex1.hint: You have a side-angle pair — which law works directly with that setup?
traps: Flipping the sine ratio and dividing instead of multiplying
Using cosine instead of sine in the Law of Sines

math-lsc-ex2.statement: Two sides of a triangular parcel measure $a = 120\,\text{m}$ and $b = 95\,\text{m}$, with an included angle $C = 48°$. What is the length of the third side $c$?
math-lsc-ex2.eli5: Two sides and the angle between them (SAS) means Law of Cosines. Plug in, compute each piece, then take the square root. The included angle is less than $90°$, so $\cos 48°$ is positive and the correction term subtracts from $a^2 + b^2$. If the angle were obtuse, $\cos C$ would be negative and you would actually add — that is a subtlety to watch for.
math-lsc-ex2.hint: Two sides with their included angle — which formula generalizes the Pythagorean theorem?
traps: Adding the cosine correction instead of subtracting it
Forgetting to take the square root at the end

math-lsc-ex3.statement: A triangular truss has sides $a = 7.5\,\text{m}$, $b = 9.0\,\text{m}$, and $c = 5.0\,\text{m}$. What is angle $A$ (opposite side $a$)?
math-lsc-ex3.eli5: All three sides, no angles — SSS situation. Rearrange the Law of Cosines to isolate $\cos A$. Plug in the sides, do the arithmetic, and take inverse cosine. The numerator here comes out positive, so the angle is acute (less than $90°$). If it had come out negative, the angle would be obtuse. Always let the sign of the cosine tell you the story.
math-lsc-ex3.hint: Rearrange the Law of Cosines to solve for the angle: $\cos A = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}$.
traps: Mixing up which side to subtract in the numerator — always subtract the side opposite the angle you want
Squaring side lengths incorrectly (7.5² = 56.25, not 52.5)

math-lsc-ex4.statement: A surveyor knows two angles and the side between them (ASA). Which is the most efficient approach to solve the triangle?

choices.text: Apply the Law of Cosines directly
Find the third angle, then use the Law of Sines
Convert to an SAS case and apply the Law of Cosines

math-lsc-ex4.eli5: With ASA you know two angles — and since the angles in a triangle sum to 180°, the third angle is free. Now you have a complete side-angle pair, which is exactly what the Law of Sines needs. The Law of Cosines requires SAS or SSS, and the Pythagorean theorem only works for right triangles. The decision tree is simple: if you can form a side-angle pair, use Sines; if you have SAS or SSS, use Cosines.
math-lsc-ex4.hint: The three angles of a triangle sum to 180°. Once you know all three angles, which law uses a side-angle pair?

steps.text: Two known angles means you can find the third: $C = 180° - A - B$.
Now you have a complete side-angle pair (the given side and its opposite angle).
Apply the Law of Sines to find the remaining sides.

traps: Trying to use the Law of Cosines without having two sides
Forgetting to compute the third angle first

math-ucti-ex1.statement: What is the exact value of $\sin 150°$?
math-ucti-ex1.eli5: 150° is in the second quadrant. Its reference angle is $180° - 150° = 30°$. Sine of 30° is $1/2$. In Q2, sine is positive (y-coordinates are positive above the x-axis), so $\sin 150° = +1/2$. The trap is picking the negative version — sine is only negative in Q3 and Q4. Also don't confuse $\sin 30°$ with $\cos 30°$ which is $\sqrt{3}/2$.
math-ucti-ex1.hint: Find the reference angle for 150°, then determine the sign from the quadrant.
traps: Applying a negative sign — sine is positive in Q2
Using $\cos 30° = \sqrt{3}/2$ instead of $\sin 30° = 1/2$

math-ucti-ex2.statement: If $\cos\theta = \frac{7}{25}$ and $\theta$ is in the fourth quadrant, what is $\sin\theta$?
math-ucti-ex2.eli5: Start with the Pythagorean identity: $\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta = 1 - 49/625 = 576/625$. Square root gives $\pm 24/25$. Now check the quadrant: Q4 means y is negative, so sine is negative. The answer is $-24/25$ (the $-\frac{24}{25}$ choice). The $\frac{24}{25}$ choice is the positive root — that's Q1, not Q4. Always let the quadrant tell you the sign.
math-ucti-ex2.hint: Use $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$, then pick the sign from the quadrant.
traps: Choosing the positive root and ignoring the quadrant
Arithmetic error: 625 - 49 = 576, not 576/25

math-ucti-ex3.statement: If $\cos\theta = \frac{3}{5}$ and $\theta$ is in the first quadrant, what is the value of $\cos 2\theta$?
math-ucti-ex3.eli5: Use the double-angle formula $\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1$. Plug in: $2(9/25) - 1 = 18/25 - 25/25 = -7/25$. The choice $\frac{6}{5}$ is wrong because it just doubles cos — that's not how double-angle works. The choice $\frac{9}{25}$ uses $\cos^2\theta$ without the doubling and subtraction. The negative result is totally fine — it means $2\theta$ lands in Q2 or Q3 where cosine is negative.
traps: Just doubling the cosine value (2 times 3/5 = 6/5) instead of using the double-angle formula
Using the wrong form of the double-angle identity

math-ucti-ex4.statement: In which quadrants is the tangent function positive?
math-ucti-ex4.eli5: Tangent is sine divided by cosine. It's positive when both have the same sign. In Q1, both sin and cos are positive — positive/positive = positive. In Q3, both are negative — negative/negative = positive. In Q2 and Q4, they have opposite signs, so tangent is negative. The mnemonic 'All Students Take Calculus' tells you which trig functions are positive in each quadrant: All (Q1), Sine (Q2), Tangent (Q3), Cosine (Q4).
math-ucti-ex4.hint: Tangent = sin/cos. In which quadrants do sine and cosine share the same sign?

steps.text: Recall $\tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$. It's positive when sin and cos have the same sign.
Q2 and Q4 have opposite signs for sin and cos, so tan < 0.

traps: Confusing tangent sign rules with sine or cosine sign rules
Thinking tangent is positive wherever sine is positive

math-cc-ex1.statement: A circular water tank has an equation $(x + 2)^2 + (y - 7)^2 = 36$. What is the diameter of the tank?
math-cc-ex1.eli5: Read the standard form: the right side is $r^2$, so $r = \sqrt{36} = 6$. The diameter is twice the radius, so 12. The choice 6 is the radius, not the diameter. The choice 36 is $r^2$. Always check whether the question asks for radius or diameter.
math-cc-ex1.hint: The right side of the circle equation is $r^2$, not $r$. And diameter is twice the radius.
traps: Giving the radius instead of the diameter
Giving $r^2$ as the answer

math-cc-ex2.statement: Convert the equation $x^2 + y^2 + 8x - 6y = 0$ to standard form and find the center of the circle.
math-cc-ex2.eli5: Complete the square for both $x$ and $y$. For $x$: half of 8 is 4, squared is 16. For $y$: half of $-6$ is $-3$, squared is 9. Add both to each side. You get $(x+4)^2 + (y-3)^2 = 25$. The center is $(-4, 3)$ because $x + 4 = x - (-4)$. The choice with center $(4, -3)$ flips the signs — that is the most common error with completing the square.
math-cc-ex2.hint: Complete the square for x and y separately. Remember the sign convention: $(x - h)$ means center coordinate $h$.
traps: Flipping the sign of h and k when reading from the standard form
Forgetting to add the completing-the-square constants to both sides

math-cc-ex3.statement: An elliptical culvert has the equation $\frac{x^2}{16} + \frac{y^2}{9} = 1$. What is the length of the major axis?
math-cc-ex3.eli5: The larger denominator tells you which axis is major. Here $16 > 9$, so the major axis is along $x$. The semi-major axis is $a = \sqrt{16} = 4$, but the FULL major axis is $2a = 8$. The choice "4" is the semi-major axis — the question asks for the full length. The choice "6" is the minor axis length ($2 \times 3 = 6$).
math-cc-ex3.hint: The semi-axis is the square root of the denominator. The full axis length is twice that.
traps: Giving the semi-axis instead of the full axis length
Confusing major and minor axes

math-cc-ex4.statement: A conic section has the general equation $Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0$. If $A = C$ and $B = 0$, what type of conic is it?
math-cc-ex4.eli5: When $A = C$ and $B = 0$, the $x^2$ and $y^2$ terms have the same coefficient and there is no $xy$ term. That is the definition of a circle — both axes are scaled the same, so the curve has equal "width" in every direction. An ellipse would have $A \neq C$. A parabola has only one squared term (either $A$ or $C$ is zero). A hyperbola has opposite signs for $A$ and $C$.
math-cc-ex4.hint: Think about what makes a circle different from an ellipse — it is the relationship between the coefficients of $x^2$ and $y^2$.

steps.text: When $A = C$ and $B = 0$, the equation becomes $A(x^2 + y^2) + Dx + Ey + F = 0$.
Dividing through by $A$ gives $x^2 + y^2 + \ldots = 0$, which is a circle.
Equal coefficients on $x^2$ and $y^2$ with no $xy$ term defines a circle.

traps: Confusing circle (A = C) with ellipse (A ≠ C)
Forgetting that B must be zero for the standard circle form

math-dr-ex1.eli5: The derivative of $\ln(u)$ is $1/u$ times $du/dx$ — chain rule. The outer derivative gives $1/(5x^2 + 1)$, and the inner derivative is $10x$. Multiply them together. The choice $\frac{1}{5x^2+1}$ is what you get if you skip the chain rule entirely. The choice $\frac{5x}{5x^2+1}$ misses the factor of 2 from differentiating $x^2$.
math-dr-ex1.hint: The argument is not plain $x$ — what does the chain rule add?

steps.text: Identify the chain rule: outer function is $\ln(u)$, inner function is $u = 5x^2 + 1$.
Multiply by derivative of the inner:

traps: Forgetting the chain rule and omitting the inner derivative
Getting the inner derivative wrong — $d/dx(5x^2) = 10x$, not $5x$

math-dr-ex2.eli5: Two functions multiplied means product rule. And $\sin(2t)$ needs the chain rule for its derivative — you get $\cos(2t) \cdot 2$, not just $\cos(2t)$. The choice $3t^2 \sin(2t) + t^3 \cos(2t)$ is the classic trap: it applies the product rule correctly but forgets the chain rule factor of 2 on the trig part. The choice $3t^2 \cos(2t)$ only differentiates one factor. Always check: did I use BOTH product rule terms, and did I chain rule the inner function?
math-dr-ex2.hint: Product rule first, then chain rule on $\sin(2t)$.
traps: Forgetting the chain rule factor of 2 when differentiating $\sin(2t)$
Only differentiating one of the two factors

math-dr-ex3.eli5: Quotient rule: lo d-hi minus hi d-lo over lo-lo. The denominator ($x + 3$) times the derivative of the numerator ($e^x$) minus the numerator ($e^x$) times the derivative of the denominator (1), all over $(x + 3)^2$. Factor out $e^x$: you get $e^x(x + 3 - 1)/(x + 3)^2 = e^x(x + 2)/(x + 3)^2$. The choice $\frac{e^x}{x+3} - \frac{e^x}{(x+3)^2}$ is mathematically equivalent but unsimplified; the correct option here is the simplified form $\frac{e^x(x+2)}{(x+3)^2}$. On the FE, always check whether your answer matches a simplified form in the choices.
math-dr-ex3.hint: Apply the quotient rule, then factor $e^x$ from the numerator.
traps: Flipping the subtraction in the quotient rule — it is $v\,du - u\,dv$, not $u\,dv - v\,du$
Forgetting to factor and not matching any answer choice

math-dr-ex4.statement: The derivative of $\sin(3x^2)$ requires which rule(s)?
math-dr-ex4.eli5: There are two layers of composition here. The outermost function is $\sin(\cdot)$, and the inner function is $3x^2$. To differentiate $\sin(u)$ you get $\cos(u) \cdot du/dx$. But $u = 3x^2$, and differentiating that uses the power rule (which is itself a form of chain rule applied to the $x^2$). So the chain rule fires once (for $\sin \to \cos$ on the inner $3x^2$), and the inner derivative $3x^2 \to 6x$ is just the power rule, not a second nested chain rule. There's no product of two separate functions of $x$, so the product rule doesn't apply here.
math-dr-ex4.hint: Count the layers of composition: how many functions are nested inside each other?

steps.text: 3. Differentiate the inner function with the power rule (not a second chain rule, since $3x^2$ is not itself a composition):   [LaTeX: \frac{d}{dx}(3x^2) = 6x]

traps: Thinking a single chain rule application is enough — the inner function $3x^2$ also needs differentiation
Confusing this with a product rule situation — $\sin(3x^2)$ is a composition, not a product

math-ad-ex1.statement: Find the $x$-value at which $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 2$ has a local maximum.
math-ad-ex1.eli5: Take the derivative: $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 3(x-1)(x-3)$. Setting it to zero gives $x = 1$ and $x = 3$. Now use the second derivative test: $f''(x) = 6x - 12$. At $x = 1$: $f''(1) = -6 < 0$ — concave down, so it's a max. At $x = 3$: $f''(3) = 6 > 0$ — concave up, so it's a min. The question asks for the max, so $x = 1$.
math-ad-ex1.hint: Set $f'(x) = 0$ to find critical points, then use $f''(x)$ to classify each one.
traps: Reporting the local minimum (x = 3) instead of the local maximum (x = 1)
Forgetting to factor and making an error solving the quadratic

math-ad-ex2.statement: A civil engineer models the total cost of a drainage pipe as $C(d) = 500d + \frac{20000}{d}$, where $d$ is the diameter in meters. What diameter minimizes the cost?
math-ad-ex2.eli5: Rewrite $20000/d$ as $20000d^{-1}$, then differentiate: $C'(d) = 500 - 20000d^{-2}$. Set to zero: $500 = 20000/d^2$, so $d^2 = 40$ and $d = \sqrt{40} \approx 6.32$. The second derivative is $40000/d^3$, which is positive for any positive $d$, confirming a minimum. The distractor $d = 40\,\text{m}$ comes from dividing 20000 by 500 without taking the square root.
math-ad-ex2.hint: Rewrite $20000/d$ as $20000d^{-1}$ before differentiating, then set $C'(d) = 0$.
traps: Forgetting to apply the power rule to $20{,}000/d$ — it is $-20{,}000/d^2$, not $-20{,}000$
Dividing 20,000 by 500 to get 40 but forgetting to take the square root

math-ad-ex3.eli5: An inflection point is where the second derivative equals zero and changes sign. First derivative: $6x^2 - 18x + 12$. Second derivative: $12x - 18$. Set to zero: $x = 18/12 = 1.5$. Check sign change: $f''(1) = -6 < 0$ and $f''(2) = 6 > 0$ — yes, it changes sign. The choices $x = 1$ and $x = 2$ are the critical points where $f'(x) = 0$ — the classic mistake of using the first derivative instead of the second.
math-ad-ex3.hint: Set the second derivative (not the first) to zero.

steps.text: Verify sign change: $f''(1) = -6$ and $f''(2) = 6$ — sign changes, confirming inflection point.

math-ad-ex3.handbookFormula: f''(a) = 0 \text{ and } f''(x) \text{ changes sign} \implies \text{inflection point}
traps: Using $f'(x) = 0$ instead of $f''(x) = 0$ — that gives critical points, not inflection points
Arithmetic error in solving $12x = 18$

math-ad-ex4.statement: At a critical point where $f'(a) = 0$, the second derivative test is inconclusive when:
math-ad-ex4.eli5: The second derivative test classifies critical points as max ($f'' < 0$), min ($f'' > 0$), or inconclusive ($f'' = 0$). When the second derivative is zero, the test fails — you can't tell if it's a max, min, or neither. Consider $f(x) = x^4$: $f'(0) = 0$ and $f''(0) = 0$, but it's a minimum. Meanwhile $f(x) = x^3$: $f'(0) = 0$ and $f''(0) = 0$, but it's neither a max nor a min. Same second derivative value, different conclusions — that's why it's called inconclusive.
math-ad-ex4.hint: The second derivative test gives three outcomes depending on the sign of $f''(a)$. What if the sign is neither positive nor negative?

steps.text: $f''(a) = 0$ means the test is inconclusive — you need another method (first derivative test or higher-order derivatives).

traps: Thinking $f''(a) = 0$ always means inflection point — it could be a flat max/min like $x^4$
Confusing 'inconclusive' with 'does not exist'

math-ic-ex1.eli5: Integrate term by term: the antiderivative of $2x$ is $x^2$ and the antiderivative of $3$ is $3x$. Evaluate from 1 to 4: $(16 + 12) - (1 + 3) = 28 - 4 = 24$. The trap is forgetting to evaluate at the lower limit — if you only plug in $x = 4$ you get 28, which isn't even a choice, but arithmetic mistakes can land you elsewhere.
math-ic-ex1.hint: Find the antiderivative, then evaluate at the upper and lower limits and subtract.
traps: Forgetting to evaluate at the lower limit
Antiderivative error — the antiderivative of $2x$ is $x^2$, not $2x^2$

math-ic-ex2.eli5: The $x$ out front and the $x^2$ in the exponent are screaming for u-substitution. Let $u = x^2$, so $du = 2x\,dx$. The $4x\,dx$ becomes $2\,du$. The integral simplifies to $2\int e^u\,du = 2e^u$. Change limits: when $x = 0$, $u = 0$; when $x = 2$, $u = 4$. So you get $2(e^4 - e^0) = 2(e^4 - 1)$.
math-ic-ex2.hint: The $x$ in $4x\,dx$ and the $x^2$ in the exponent suggest $u = x^2$.
traps: Forgetting to account for the factor of 2 when converting $4x\,dx$ to $du$
Not changing the limits of integration when substituting

math-ic-ex3.eli5: This is an integration by parts problem. LIATE says $\ln x$ (Log) comes before $x$ (Algebraic), so let $u = \ln x$ and $dv = x\,dx$. Then $du = dx/x$ and $v = x^2/2$. The formula gives $(x^2/2)\ln x - \int x/2\,dx = (x^2/2)\ln x - x^2/4$. Evaluate from 0 to 1: at $x = 1$, $\ln 1 = 0$ so the first term vanishes, leaving $-1/4$. At $x = 0$ both terms go to 0 (given in the hint). So the answer is $-1/4$.
math-ic-ex3.hint: LIATE: $\ln x$ is a log (L), which comes first — let $u = \ln x$.

steps.text: Integration by parts: let $u = \ln x$, $dv = x\,dx$.

traps: Choosing $u$ and $dv$ backwards — if you let $u = x$, you would need to integrate $\ln x$, which is harder
Forgetting the negative sign from the by-parts formula

math-ic-ex4.statement: When evaluating a definite integral, why is the constant of integration $+C$ not needed?

choices.text: The constant is always zero for definite integrals
The constant cancels when you subtract $F(a)$ from $F(b)$
Definite integrals do not involve antiderivatives
The constant is absorbed into the limits of integration

math-ic-ex4.eli5: When you compute $F(b) - F(a)$, any constant $C$ appears in both terms: $(F(b) + C) - (F(a) + C) = F(b) - F(a)$. The $C$'s cancel out perfectly. It's not that $C = 0$ or that it doesn't exist — it's that it subtracts away. This is a subtle but important distinction. The choice claiming definite integrals do not involve antiderivatives is flat wrong — definite integrals absolutely use antiderivatives (that's the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus). The choice claiming the constant is always zero is a common misconception.
math-ic-ex4.hint: Write out $F(b) + C$ and $F(a) + C$ and subtract them — what happens to $C$?

steps.text: The $+C$ terms cancel, so the constant does not affect the result.

traps: Thinking $C = 0$ rather than understanding it cancels
Believing definite integrals don't use antiderivatives

math-lr-ex1.eli5: Plug in $x = 0$: $(1 - 1)/0 = 0/0$ — indeterminate, so L'Hopital's applies. Differentiate top and bottom: $\sin x / 2x$. Plug in again: $0/0$ — still indeterminate! Apply a second time: $\cos x / 2$. Now plug in: $\cos 0 / 2 = 1/2$. Two rounds is typical for the FE. If you stopped after one round, you'd get stuck — don't quit early.
math-lr-ex1.hint: Direct substitution gives 0/0. You may need to apply the rule more than once.
traps: Stopping after one round when the result is still 0/0
Differentiating incorrectly: $d/dx(1 - \cos x) = \sin x$, not $-\sin x$

math-lr-ex2.eli5: As $x \to \infty$, both the top and bottom blow up: $\infty / \infty$. That's an indeterminate form, so L'Hopital's applies. First round: $6x / e^x$ — still $\infty/\infty$. Second round: $6 / e^x$. Now the top is a constant and the bottom goes to infinity, so the limit is 0. The exponential always wins against any polynomial. This is a key fact for the FE.
math-lr-ex2.hint: This is $\infty/\infty$ form. Apply L'Hopital's until the numerator stops growing.
traps: Assuming infinity/infinity always diverges — it can converge to zero
Differentiating $e^x$ incorrectly (it is its own derivative)

math-lr-ex3.eli5: Plug in 0: $(0 - 0)/0 = 0/0$. First round: $(\sec^2 x - 1)/3x^2$. At $x = 0$: $0/0$ again. Second round: use $\sec^2 x - 1 = \tan^2 x$ or just differentiate directly. The derivative of $\sec^2 x - 1$ is $2\sec^2 x \tan x$, and the derivative of $3x^2$ is $6x$. Still $0/0$. Third round: differentiate again. Eventually you get $1/3$. This is a classic three-round L'Hopital's problem.
math-lr-ex3.hint: You'll need to apply L'Hopital's Rule multiple times. Keep differentiating until the form resolves.
traps: Stopping too early — this problem requires three rounds
Differentiating $\sec^2(x)$ incorrectly — its derivative is $2\sec^2(x)\tan(x)$

math-lr-ex4.statement: Which of the following is NOT an indeterminate form where L'Hopital's Rule applies?

choices.text: All of the above are indeterminate forms

math-lr-ex4.eli5: L'Hopital's Rule only applies to two forms: $0/0$ and $\infty/\infty$. The form $1/0$ is NOT indeterminate — it means the function blows up to $\pm\infty$ or the limit doesn't exist. The rule explicitly requires an indeterminate form before you can differentiate. Applying L'Hopital's when the form isn't indeterminate gives a wrong answer. This is the trap in problems like $\lim_{x \to 0} e^x/x$ — students apply the rule without checking and get 1, but the correct answer is DNE.
math-lr-ex4.hint: L'Hopital's Rule has exactly two qualifying forms. Any fraction with a nonzero numerator and zero denominator is not one of them.

steps.text: $1/0$ is NOT indeterminate — it represents a function that blows up. The limit is $\pm\infty$ or DNE.
L'Hopital's must NOT be applied to non-indeterminate forms.

traps: Thinking any fraction with zero in the denominator qualifies as indeterminate
Applying L'Hopital's to 1/0 and getting a wrong finite answer

math-vbu-ex1.statement: A cable exerts a force along the direction $\vec{d} = 6\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$ meters. What is the magnitude of this direction vector?
math-vbu-ex1.eli5: Square each component, add them up, take the square root: $\sqrt{36 + 4 + 9} = \sqrt{49} = 7$. Don't forget to include the negative component — squaring it makes it positive anyway ($(-3)^2 = 9$). The trap is adding the raw components ($6 + 2 - 3 = 5$) instead of using the magnitude formula.
math-vbu-ex1.hint: The magnitude formula uses the square root of the sum of squares — not just the sum of components.
traps: Adding components directly (6 + 2 - 3 = 5) instead of using sum of squares
Forgetting to square the negative component

math-vbu-ex2.statement: Find the unit vector in the direction of $\vec{v} = 2\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$.
math-vbu-ex2.eli5: First find the magnitude: $\sqrt{4 + 36 + 9} = \sqrt{49} = 7$. Then divide each component by 7. The choice that just repeats 2i - 6j + 3k is the original vector — that's what you get if you skip the normalization. The choice dividing by 11 divides by the sum of components instead of the magnitude (7). Always verify: the unit vector's magnitude should equal 1.
math-vbu-ex2.hint: Compute the magnitude first, then divide every component by it.
traps: Dividing by the sum of absolute values of components instead of the magnitude
Forgetting to normalize — reporting the raw vector as the unit vector

math-vbu-ex3.statement: A 350 N force acts along the direction from point $A(1, -1, 2)$ to point $B(3, 3, -1)$. Express the force as a vector $\vec{F}$.
math-vbu-ex3.eli5: Three steps: (1) direction vector $B - A = (2, 4, -3)$, (2) magnitude $= \sqrt{4 + 16 + 9} = \sqrt{29}$, (3) unit vector times 350. Each component of the unit vector gets multiplied by 350. The unit-vector-only choice ($\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}}\hat{i} + \frac{4}{\sqrt{29}}\hat{j} - \frac{3}{\sqrt{29}}\hat{k}$) leaves off the 350 multiplier. The $700\hat{i} + 1400\hat{j} - 1050\hat{k}$ choice multiplied 350 by the direction vector without normalizing first.
math-vbu-ex3.hint: Find the unit vector from A to B, then multiply by the force magnitude.
traps: Multiplying the force magnitude by the raw direction vector instead of the unit vector
Subtracting A from B in the wrong order

math-vbu-ex4.statement: A vector $\vec{A}$ has components $A_x = -5$ and $A_y = 0$. Which statement is true?

choices.text: The vector is a zero vector
The vector points in the negative $x$-direction with magnitude 5
The vector points in the positive $x$-direction with magnitude 5

math-vbu-ex4.eli5: Magnitude is always positive: $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{(-5)^2 + 0^2} = 5$, not $-5$. The negative sign on the component tells you direction, not magnitude. The "magnitude is -5" choice is the most common mistake — magnitudes can never be negative. The "positive x-direction with magnitude 5" choice gets the magnitude right but the direction wrong. A negative $x$-component means the vector points in the negative $x$-direction. Separating magnitude from direction is fundamental to vector analysis.
math-vbu-ex4.hint: Magnitude is always non-negative — the sign of a component indicates direction, not size.

steps.text: Since $A_x < 0$ and $A_y = 0$, the vector points along the negative $x$-axis.

traps: Reporting a negative magnitude — magnitudes are always non-negative
Confusing the sign of a component with the sign of the magnitude

math-dpa-ex1.eli5: Multiply matching components and add: $(5)(-1) + (-3)(4) + (2)(6) = -5 - 12 + 12 = -5$. Watch the signs carefully — the negative components produce negative products. The $-12$ and $+12$ cancel, leaving just $-5$ from the first pair. A negative dot product means the vectors point in generally opposite directions (the angle between them is obtuse).
math-dpa-ex1.hint: Multiply x with x, y with y, z with z, then add all three products.
traps: Dropping the negative signs during multiplication
Cross-multiplying components (x with y) instead of matching (x with x)

math-dpa-ex2.eli5: Three steps: (1) dot product: $(2)(0) + (2)(3) + (1)(4) = 0 + 6 + 4 = 10$, (2) magnitudes: $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{4 + 4 + 1} = 3$ and $|\vec{B}| = \sqrt{0 + 9 + 16} = 5$, (3) $\cos\theta = 10/(3 \times 5) = 10/15 = 0.6667$, so $\theta = \cos^{-1}(0.6667) \approx 48.2°$. The trap is forgetting to compute both magnitudes and dividing by just one of them. Always do all three steps in order.
math-dpa-ex2.hint: Compute the dot product, both magnitudes, then use the angle formula.
traps: Forgetting to divide by both magnitudes
Arithmetic error in the dot product — every component pair matters

math-dpa-ex3.statement: A load $\vec{F} = 200\hat{i} + 400\hat{j} + 100\hat{k}$ N acts at a joint. A beam runs in the direction $\vec{d} = 4\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$. What is the scalar projection of the force onto the beam?
