Getting the cross-product order wrong (x_i × y_{i+1} – x_{i+1} × y_i, not the reverse)

surv-ac-q2.statement: A quadrilateral has vertices at A$(0, 0)$, B$(10, 0)$, C$(8, 6)$, and D$(2, 5)$. What is the area by the coordinate method?
surv-ac-q2.eli5: Cross products: AB: (0)(0) – (10)(0) = 0. BC: (10)(6) – (8)(0) = 60. CD: (8)(5) – (2)(6) = 40 – 12 = 28. DA: (2)(0) – (0)(5) = 0. Sum = 0 + 60 + 28 + 0 = 88. Area = |88|/2 = 44. The 50 sq units option uses a rough rectangle approximation. The 88 sq units option forgets to divide by 2. The 22 sq units option divides by 4.
surv-ac-q2.hint: Four vertices means four cross-product pairs. Don’t forget to pair the last vertex back with the first to close the polygon.
traps: Forgetting to close the polygon — must pair last vertex with first vertex
Forgetting to divide by 2
Getting the subtraction order wrong in the cross products

surv-ac-q3.statement: A surveyor measures offsets from a baseline at $20 \text{ m}$ intervals. The offsets are: $0$, $8$, $12$, $10$, $0 \text{ m}$. What is the area using the trapezoidal rule?
surv-ac-q3.eli5: Trapezoidal rule: A = w[(h_1 + h_n)/2 + h_2 + h_3 + ... + h_{n-1}] = 20[(0 + 0)/2 + 8 + 12 + 10] = 20[0 + 30] = 600 m². The first and last offsets are 0, so their average is 0. The 480 m² choice mis-applies w/2 to all terms. The 800 m² choice uses Simpson’s coefficients incorrectly. The 300 m² choice divides the correct area by 2 again.
surv-ac-q3.hint: Average the first and last offsets, add all the middle offsets at full value, then multiply by the interval width.

steps.latex: A = w\left(\frac{h_1 + h_n}{2} + h_2 + h_3 + h_4\right)

traps: Averaging ALL offsets instead of just the first and last
Forgetting to multiply by the interval width w
Using Simpson’s coefficients (1, 4, 2, 4, 1) when the trapezoidal rule was specified

surv-ev-q1.statement: Two adjacent cross-sections have areas of $A_1 = 120 \text{ ft}^2$ and $A_2 = 180 \text{ ft}^2$. The distance between stations is $L = 100 \text{ ft}$. What is the volume by the average end area method?
surv-ev-q1.eli5: V = L/2 × (A_1 + A_2) = 100/2 × (120 + 180) = 50 × 300 = 15,000 ft³. The 556 yd³ option converts to cubic yards (15,000/27 = 556) — right number but wrong unit for what was asked. The 30,000 ft³ option uses L instead of L/2. The 7,500 ft³ option divides by 4 instead of 2.
surv-ev-q1.hint: Average the two areas, then multiply by the distance between stations.
traps: Forgetting to divide L by 2 — doubles the volume
Confusing ft³ with yd³ — divide by 27 to convert

surv-ev-q2.statement: Three cross-sections are taken at stations 0, 50 ft, and 100 ft. The areas are $A_1 = 200 \text{ ft}^2$, $A_m = 350 \text{ ft}^2$, and $A_2 = 400 \text{ ft}^2$. What is the volume using the prismoidal formula?
surv-ev-q2.eli5: V = L/6 × (A_1 + 4A_m + A_2) = 100/6 × (200 + 4×350 + 400) = 16.667 × (200 + 1400 + 400) = 16.667 × 2000 = 33,333 ft³. The 31,667 ft³ choice is the simple average of all three areas times L: (200+350+400)/3 × 100 = 31,667. The 30,000 ft³ choice uses the average end area method (L/2 × (A_1+A_2) = 50 × 600 = 30,000). The 35,000 ft³ choice incorrectly multiplies the middle area by L (350 × 100 = 35,000).
surv-ev-q2.hint: The prismoidal formula weights the middle section by 4: V = L/6(A_1 + 4A_m + A_2). The total distance L is 100 ft, not 50.
traps: Using the average end area formula instead of the prismoidal formula
Forgetting the 4× coefficient on the mid-section area
Using L = 50 (half the distance) instead of the full distance between end sections

surv-ev-q3.statement:
A road project has the following station data. What is the total earthwork volume between stations 0+00 and 2+00? Use the average end area method.

Station 0+00: $A = 0 \text{ ft}^2$
Station 1+00: $A = 400 \text{ ft}^2$
Station 2+00: $A = 0 \text{ ft}^2$
surv-ev-q3.eli5: Two segments: 0+00 to 1+00 and 1+00 to 2+00. V_1 = 100/2 × (0 + 400) = 50 × 400 = 20,000 ft³. V_2 = 100/2 × (400 + 0) = 20,000 ft³. Total = 40,000 ft³. The 20,000 ft³ choice only computes one segment. The 80,000 ft³ choice uses L instead of L/2. The 13,333 ft³ choice uses the prismoidal formula by mistake.
surv-ev-q3.hint: Apply the average end area formula to each pair of adjacent stations, then sum the segment volumes.
traps: Only computing one segment and forgetting the other
Forgetting that station 1+00 means 100 ft, not 1 ft
Using the average end area across the entire span instead of segment by segment

surv-cg-q1.statement: Point A is at $(E, N) = (1{,}000, 1{,}000)$ and point B is at $(1{,}300, 1{,}400)$ (units: ft). What is the straight-line distance from A to B?
surv-cg-q1.eli5: ΔE = 1,300 − 1,000 = 300; ΔN = 1,400 − 1,000 = 400. Distance = √(300² + 400²) = √(90,000 + 160,000) = √250,000 = 500 ft (a 3-4-5 triangle). The 700 ft choice just adds ΔE + ΔN. The 350 ft choice averages them. The 250 ft choice halves ΔE.
traps: Adding ΔE and ΔN instead of using the Pythagorean distance
Mismatching which coordinate is easting vs northing

surv-cg-q2.statement: From point A at $(E, N) = (5{,}000, 5{,}000)$, a course of length $200\text{ ft}$ is run at an azimuth of $30\degree$. What is the NORTHING of the new point?
surv-cg-q2.eli5: Latitude ΔN = L·cos(Az) = 200·cos(30°) = 200(0.8660) = 173.2. New northing = 5,000 + 173.2 = 5,173.2. The 5,100.0 choice mistakenly uses the departure (200·sin30° = 100). The 5,183.0 choice uses a slightly off trig value. The 5,200.0 choice just adds the full length.
surv-cg-q2.hint: Northing change = L·cos(azimuth); add it to the starting northing.
traps: Using sine (departure) for the northing instead of cosine
Adding the full course length instead of its north component

surv-cg-q3.statement: When computing a line's azimuth from coordinate differences as $\tan^{-1}(\Delta E/\Delta N)$, what determines the correct quadrant of the azimuth?

choices.text: The algebraic signs of ΔE and ΔN
The magnitude of the distance only
The order in which the points were surveyed
The units used for the coordinates

surv-cg-q3.eli5: The arctangent returns an angle between −90° and 90°, so it cannot by itself tell which of the four quadrants the line points to. The signs of ΔE (east + / west −) and ΔN (north + / south −) place the line in the correct quadrant. The distance magnitude and the coordinate units do not affect direction; the surveying order confuses bookkeeping with geometry.
surv-cg-q3.hint: Arctangent gives only one of two possible directions — what extra information fixes the quadrant?

steps.text: ΔE sign gives east/west; ΔN sign gives north/south.
Together those signs fix the azimuth's quadrant.

traps: Reporting the raw arctangent without checking the quadrant
Assuming distance or units affect the direction

surv-hc-q1.statement: A horizontal curve has a degree of curve $D = 6\degree$. What is the radius?
surv-hc-q1.eli5: R = 5,729.58 / D = 5,729.58 / 6 = 954.93 ≈ 955 ft. The 5,730 ft choice is the numerator (D = 1°). The 573 ft choice divides by 10 instead of 6. The 1,667 ft choice uses 10,000/D.
traps: Multiplying instead of dividing — D × R = 5,729.58, so R = 5,729.58/D
Using the chord definition instead of the arc definition of degree of curve

surv-hc-q2.statement: A horizontal curve has $R = 1{,}000 \text{ ft}$ and an intersection angle $I = 40\degree$. What is the tangent distance $T$?
surv-hc-q2.eli5: T = R tan(I/2) = 1,000 × tan(20°) = 1,000 × 0.3640 = 364 ft. The 839 ft choice uses tan(I) = tan(40°) instead of tan(I/2). The 342 ft choice uses sin(I/2) instead of tan(I/2) (1,000 × sin(20°) = 342). The 698 ft choice doubles the correct result.
surv-hc-q2.hint: The tangent distance uses HALF the intersection angle: T = R tan(I/2).
traps: Using the full intersection angle I instead of I/2
Using sine instead of tangent

surv-hc-q3.statement: A horizontal curve has $R = 800 \text{ ft}$, $I = 50\degree$. The PC is at station $25+00$. What is the station of the PT?
surv-hc-q3.eli5: L = πRI/180 = π(800)(50)/180 = 125,663.7/180 = 698.13 ft. Station of PT = station of PC + L = 2500 + 698.13 = 3198.13 = station 31+98.13. The 25+00 choice is the PC itself. The 28+49.07 choice uses L/2 (goes to the midpoint). The 38+96.26 choice uses 2L.
surv-hc-q3.hint: Find the curve length L = πRI/180, then add it to the PC station to get the PT station.
traps: Using degrees in the formula without converting properly — the π/180 does the conversion
Confusing curve length L with tangent distance T
Adding the tangent distance instead of the curve length to get PT station

surv-vc-q1.statement: A vertical curve has $g_1 = +4\%$, $g_2 = -2\%$, $L = 600 \text{ ft}$, and $Y_{PVC} = 100 \text{ ft}$. What is the elevation at the PVI?
surv-vc-q1.eli5: The PVI is at x = L/2 = 300 ft from the PVC. But the PVI elevation is on the TANGENT line, not the curve: Y_tangent = Y_PVC + g_1 × (L/2) = 100 + 0.04 × 300 = 100 + 12 = 112 ft. The curve elevation at the PVI would be different (lower for a crest), but the PVI itself is on the tangent. The 106.0 ft choice uses g_1 = 2% instead of 4%. The 100.0 ft choice is just the PVC elevation. The 109.0 ft choice averages the PVC tangent and the 2%-grade results incorrectly.
surv-vc-q1.hint: The PVI is at the intersection of the two tangent lines. Its elevation is Y_PVC + g_1 × (L/2), using the back tangent grade.

steps.text: PVI is at $x = L/2$ from PVC:

traps: Computing the curve elevation at PVI instead of the tangent elevation — the PVI is on the tangent by definition
Forgetting to convert percent grade to decimal (4% = 0.04)

surv-vc-q2.statement: Using the same curve ($g_1 = +4\%$, $g_2 = -2\%$, $L = 600 \text{ ft}$, $Y_{PVC} = 100 \text{ ft}$), what is the curve elevation at $x = 300 \text{ ft}$ (the midpoint)?
surv-vc-q2.eli5: Y = Y_PVC + g_1×x + [(g_2–g_1)/(2L)]×x². Parabola constant a = (–0.02 – 0.04)/(2×600) = –0.00005. Y = 100 + 0.04(300) + (–0.00005)(90,000) = 100 + 12 – 4.5 = 107.5 ft. The tangent elevation at this point is 112 ft, but the curve sits 4.5 ft below the tangent (because it’s a crest curve). The 106.0 ft choice uses the wrong parabola constant. The 112 ft choice is the tangent elevation, not the curve elevation. The 100.0 ft choice is the PVC elevation.
surv-vc-q2.hint: Use the curve elevation formula: $Y = Y_{PVC} + g_1 x + [(g_2 - g_1)/(2L)]x^2$. Convert grades from percent to decimal.

steps.text: The tangent offset at PVI: $E = 112 - 107.5 = 4.5$ ft below the tangent.

surv-vc-q2.handbookFormula: Y = Y_{PVC} + g_1 x + \frac{g_2 - g_1}{2L} x^2
traps: Using the tangent elevation (112 ft) instead of the curve elevation (107.5 ft)
Forgetting to convert percent grades to decimals before using the formula
Getting the sign of the parabola constant wrong

surv-vc-q3.statement: A crest vertical curve has $g_1 = +3\%$ and $g_2 = -1\%$, with $L = 400 \text{ ft}$. How far from the PVC is the high point of the curve?
surv-vc-q3.eli5: x_m = –g_1 × L / (g_2 – g_1) = –(0.03)(400) / (–0.01 – 0.03) = –12 / –0.04 = 300 ft. The high point is 300 ft from the PVC, which is 3/4 of the way along the curve. It’s not at the midpoint because |g_1| ≠ |g_2|. The 400 ft choice puts it at the PVT (x = L). The 200 ft choice assumes the high point is at the midpoint (L/2). The 100 ft choice uses g_1 alone.
surv-vc-q3.hint: The high point is where the slope equals zero: x_m = –g_1 × L / (g_2 – g_1). Use decimal grades.
traps: Assuming the high point is at the midpoint (L/2) — only true when |g_1| = |g_2|
Forgetting to convert grades from percent to decimal
Getting the sign wrong in the denominator (g_2 – g_1, not g_1 – g_2)

surv-adb-ex1.statement: A surveyor measures a bearing of N 45° E from point A to point B, a distance of 200 m. What is the northing (latitude) of point B relative to A?
surv-adb-ex1.eli5: The latitude (northing) is the north-south component: distance times cosine of the bearing angle. $\text{Lat} = 200 \cos 45° = 200 \times 0.7071 = 141.4$ m. The departure (easting) would be $200 \sin 45° = 141.4$ m too, since it is a 45-degree bearing. Common trap is mixing up which trig function gives latitude vs departure.
surv-adb-ex1.hint: Latitude = distance times cosine of the bearing angle.

steps.text: For a bearing of N 45\degree E:

traps: Using sine instead of cosine for latitude
Confusing bearing angle with azimuth

surv-adb-ex2.statement: The bearing S 30° W is equivalent to which azimuth?
surv-adb-ex2.eli5: S 30° W means 30 degrees west of due south. Due south is 180° azimuth. Going 30 degrees toward west (clockwise from north) gives $180 + 30 = 210°$. The key is remembering that azimuth is measured clockwise from north (0°/360°).
surv-adb-ex2.hint: Due south is azimuth 180°. Which direction from south is "west"?

steps.text: S 30\degree W means 30\degree west of south.
West of south adds to the azimuth:

traps: Subtracting instead of adding for the SW quadrant
Confusing the quadrant directions

surv-adb-ex3.statement: A slope distance of $SD = 185.00 \text{ ft}$ is measured at a vertical angle of $\alpha = 12\degree$ below horizontal. What is the vertical distance (elevation difference)?
surv-adb-ex3.eli5: $VD = SD \sin\alpha = 185 \times \sin 12° = 185 \times 0.2079 = 38.44$ ft. But the angle is below horizontal, so the elevation difference is negative (you are going downhill). $VD = -38.44$ ft. The +38.44 ft choice has the right magnitude but wrong sign. The 180.91 ft choice is the horizontal distance, not the vertical. The -180.91 ft choice applies the negative to the horizontal distance by mistake.
surv-adb-ex3.hint: Use $VD = SD \sin\alpha$ and watch the sign. Below horizontal means the target point is lower.

steps.text: The angle is below horizontal, so the target is lower:

traps: Ignoring the sign convention — below horizontal means negative elevation change
Using cosine instead of sine for vertical distance

surv-adb-ex4.statement: A closed traverse has 6 sides. Five of the interior angles have been measured: $115\degree$, $128\degree$, $97\degree$, $142\degree$, and $108\degree$. What must the sixth angle be for the traverse to close geometrically?
surv-adb-ex4.eli5: For a 6-sided polygon, the interior angles must sum to $(6 - 2) \times 180 = 720°$. The five known angles sum to $115 + 128 + 97 + 142 + 108 = 590°$. The sixth angle $= 720 - 590 = 130°$. The $120°$ choice is close but arithmetically wrong. The $90°$ choice is a guess. The $150°$ choice overshoots, the kind of error you get from using $n \times 180 = 1080°$ instead of $(n - 2) \times 180 = 720°$.
surv-adb-ex4.hint: Find the theoretical sum of interior angles for a 6-sided polygon, then subtract the five known angles.
traps: Using $n \times 180$ instead of $(n - 2) \times 180$ for the theoretical sum
Arithmetic errors when summing five angles quickly

surv-lev-ex1.statement: A benchmark has an elevation of $320.00 \text{ ft}$. A surveyor sets up a level and reads a backsight of $6.38 \text{ ft}$ on the benchmark. The foresight on a new point X is $4.17 \text{ ft}$. What is the elevation of point X?
surv-lev-ex1.eli5: First find the Height of Instrument: $HI = 320.00 + 6.38 = 326.38$ ft. Then subtract the foresight to get the new elevation: $\text{Elev}_X = 326.38 - 4.17 = 322.21$ ft. Point X is higher than the benchmark because the FS reading is smaller than the BS reading. The 309.45 ft choice subtracts both readings. The 317.79 ft choice subtracts the BS instead of adding it. The 330.55 ft choice adds both readings.
surv-lev-ex1.hint: $HI$ = known elevation + BS, then new elevation = $HI$ - FS.
traps: Subtracting the backsight instead of adding it to the known elevation

surv-lev-ex2.statement: Starting from BM-A (elevation $450.00 \text{ ft}$), a level run records: BS = $3.82$ on BM-A, FS = $7.14$ on TP-1, BS = $6.55$ on TP-1, FS = $2.41$ on TP-2, BS = $4.90$ on TP-2, FS = $5.63$ on point C. What is the elevation of point C?
surv-lev-ex2.eli5: Work through each setup. $HI_1 = 450.00 + 3.82 = 453.82$. $\text{Elev}_{TP1} = 453.82 - 7.14 = 446.68$. $HI_2 = 446.68 + 6.55 = 453.23$. $\text{Elev}_{TP2} = 453.23 - 2.41 = 450.82$. $HI_3 = 450.82 + 4.90 = 455.72$. $\text{Elev}_C = 455.72 - 5.63 = 450.09$ ft. A shortcut is sum of BS minus sum of FS plus starting elevation: $(3.82 + 6.55 + 4.90) - (7.14 + 2.41 + 5.63) + 450 = 15.27 - 15.18 + 450 = 450.09$. The 446.68 ft choice is the TP-1 elevation. The 450.82 ft choice is the TP-2 elevation. The 453.32 ft choice comes from mishandling the BS/FS signs.
surv-lev-ex2.hint: Process each setup: HI = elev + BS, new elev = HI - FS. Or use the shortcut: final elev = start elev + (sum BS - sum FS).
traps: Stopping at an intermediate turning point and reporting it as the final answer
Carrying forward the wrong HI after a turning point

surv-lev-ex3.statement: A level loop has a total distance of $9 \text{ miles}$. The loop starts and closes on BM-7 (known elevation $812.45 \text{ ft}$). The computed closing elevation is $812.57 \text{ ft}$. If the allowable error is $C\sqrt{M}$ with $C = 0.035 \text{ ft}$, does the survey meet the tolerance?

choices.text: Yes -- misclosure ($0.12 \text{ ft}$) is greater than allowable ($0.105 \text{ ft}$), so it fails
No -- misclosure ($0.12 \text{ ft}$) exceeds allowable ($0.105 \text{ ft}$)
Yes -- misclosure ($0.12 \text{ ft}$) is less than allowable ($0.315 \text{ ft}$)
No -- misclosure ($1.20 \text{ ft}$) exceeds allowable ($0.105 \text{ ft}$)

surv-lev-ex3.eli5: Misclosure $= |812.57 - 812.45| = 0.12$ ft. Allowable $= 0.035 \times \sqrt{9} = 0.035 \times 3.0 = 0.105$ ft. Since $0.12 > 0.105$, the survey does NOT meet the tolerance and must be rerun. The "Yes -- fails" choice states the correct numbers but draws the wrong conclusion (it says Yes yet describes a failure). The "less than allowable (0.315 ft)" choice uses $C \times M$ instead of $C \times \sqrt{M}$. The "misclosure (1.20 ft)" choice misreads the misclosure as 1.20 ft.
surv-lev-ex3.hint: Misclosure = |computed - known|. Allowable $= C\sqrt{M}$. Compare the two values.

steps.text: Compare: $0.12 > 0.105$ -- survey fails tolerance and must be rerun.

traps: Multiplying $C$ by $M$ instead of $\sqrt{M}$
Drawing the wrong pass/fail conclusion after computing correct values

surv-lev-ex4.statement: During a differential leveling run, a surveyor moves the instrument to a new position. At the new setup, which rod reading is taken FIRST on the turning point?

choices.text: A backsight, because the turning point is now a point of known elevation
A foresight, because the turning point is ahead of the instrument
Either reading can be taken first -- the order does not matter
An intermediate sight, because the turning point is between setups

surv-lev-ex4.eli5: A turning point has TWO roles: it receives a foresight from the old instrument setup (which determines its elevation), then it receives a backsight from the new instrument setup (which establishes the new HI). After moving the instrument, the TP already has a known elevation from the previous foresight, so the first reading from the new position is a backsight on the TP. The "foresight" choice confuses the physical direction with the surveying definition. The "either order" choice is wrong because order matters -- the FS must come before the instrument moves. The "intermediate sight" choice confuses intermediate sights with turning points.
surv-lev-ex4.hint: Think about what "backsight" means: a reading on a point whose elevation is already known.

steps.text: From the old setup, the surveyor takes a foresight (FS) on the turning point, determining its elevation.
The instrument moves to a new position. The turning point now has a known elevation.
From the new setup, the surveyor reads a backsight (BS) on the turning point to establish the new HI:

traps: Confusing the physical direction of the sight with the surveying definition of BS and FS

surv-tc-ex1.statement: A traverse course has a length of $350 \text{ m}$ and a bearing of S $55\degree$ E. What is the departure?
surv-tc-ex1.eli5: Departure $= L \sin\theta = 350 \times \sin 55° = 350 \times 0.8192 = 286.7$ m. The bearing is SE, so the departure is positive (eastward). The latitude would be negative (southward), but we only need the departure here. The -286.7 m option gets the sign wrong. The 200.8 m option uses cosine (that gives the latitude magnitude). The -200.8 m option uses cosine with a wrong sign.
surv-tc-ex1.hint: Departure = L sin(bearing angle). Check the quadrant to determine the sign: east is positive.

steps.text: S 55\degree E is in the SE quadrant — departure is eastward (positive).

traps: Confusing sine and cosine — departure uses sine, latitude uses cosine
Getting the sign wrong for the SE quadrant

surv-tc-ex2.statement: A 4-sided closed traverse has courses with lengths $200$, $300$, $250$, and $150 \text{ m}$. The sum of latitudes is $+0.12 \text{ m}$ and the sum of departures is $-0.09 \text{ m}$. What is the linear closure error?
surv-tc-ex2.eli5: Linear error $= \sqrt{E_L^2 + E_D^2} = \sqrt{0.12^2 + 0.09^2} = \sqrt{0.0144 + 0.0081} = \sqrt{0.0225} = 0.15$ m. This is a classic 3-4-5 right triangle relationship (0.09, 0.12, 0.15). The 0.03 m choice subtracts the errors. The 0.21 m choice adds the errors ($0.12 + 0.09 = 0.21$). The 0.105 m choice averages them.
surv-tc-ex2.hint: The linear closure error combines both error components using the Pythagorean theorem.

steps.text: Combine the latitude and departure errors:

traps: Adding the error components instead of using Pythagorean theorem
Forgetting to square each error before adding

surv-tc-ex3.statement: A closed traverse has a precision ratio of $1:5{,}000$. Which of the following best describes what this means?

choices.text: For every 5,000 units of traverse length, the position error is 1 unit
The angular error is 1/5,000 of a degree
The survey was completed in 1/5,000 of the expected time

surv-tc-ex3.eli5: The precision ratio is the linear closure error divided by the total traverse length, expressed as 1:N. A ratio of 1:5,000 means that for every 5,000 feet (or meters) of traverse, the position closes to within 1 foot (or meter). Higher N means better precision. This is a standard way surveyors communicate how accurate a traverse closure is.
surv-tc-ex3.hint: Precision ratio = linear error / total length. Think about what the numerator and denominator represent.

steps.text: For 1:5,000, the error is 1 unit per 5,000 units of traverse length.

traps: Confusing precision ratio with angular error
Thinking a larger denominator means worse precision (it means better)

surv-tc-ex4.statement: A closed traverse has $\Sigma L = 1{,}500 \text{ m}$, $E_L = +0.09 \text{ m}$, and $E_D = -0.12 \text{ m}$. A course with length $375 \text{ m}$ has a raw departure of $+210.50 \text{ m}$. What is the adjusted departure after applying the compass rule?
surv-tc-ex4.eli5: Compass rule departure correction $= -E_D \times (L_i / \Sigma L) = -(-0.12) \times (375/1500) = +0.12 \times 0.25 = +0.03$ m. Adjusted departure $= 210.50 + 0.03 = 210.53$ m. The negative departure error means the traverse drifted west, so we correct eastward (add). The +210.47 m choice subtracts the correction instead of adding it. The +210.80 m choice overcorrects with the full error. The +210.20 m choice applies the latitude error to the departure.
surv-tc-ex4.hint: Compass rule correction for departure = -E_D * (course length / total length). The sign of the correction opposes the error.
traps: Getting the sign of the correction wrong — correction opposes the error
Applying the latitude error to the departure correction

surv-ac-ex1.statement: A triangle has vertices at $(0, 0)$, $(8, 0)$, and $(4, 6)$. What is the area using the coordinate method?
surv-ac-ex1.eli5: Cross products: $(0 \times 0 - 8 \times 0) + (8 \times 6 - 4 \times 0) + (4 \times 0 - 0 \times 6) = 0 + 48 + 0 = 48$. Area $= |48|/2 = 24$ sq units. You can double-check: base = 8, height = 6, so $A = 8 \times 6 / 2 = 24$. The 16 sq units choice uses base times height / 3. The 48 sq units choice forgets the 1/2. The 32 sq units choice uses base times height / 1.5.
surv-ac-ex1.hint: Set up cross products for adjacent vertex pairs: sum of $(x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i)$, then take half the absolute value.

steps.text: List vertices and compute cross products:

traps: Forgetting to divide by 2 — gives double the actual area
Reversing the cross product order

surv-ac-ex2.statement: Offsets from a baseline are measured at $25 \text{ m}$ intervals: $0$, $10$, $14$, $11$, $6$, $0 \text{ m}$. What is the area using the trapezoidal rule?
surv-ac-ex2.eli5: Trapezoidal rule: $A = w[(h_1 + h_n)/2 + h_2 + h_3 + \cdots + h_{n-1}]$. $A = 25[(0+0)/2 + 10 + 14 + 11 + 6] = 25 \times 41 = 1025$ m². The first and last offsets are 0 so their average is 0, and the interior offsets are summed at full value. The 1,281 m² choice applies Simpson coefficients by mistake. The 512.5 m² choice divides the whole thing by 2. The 850 m² choice drops one of the interior offsets.
surv-ac-ex2.hint: Average the first and last offsets, then add all interior offsets. Multiply by the common interval.

steps.latex: A = w\left(\frac{h_1 + h_n}{2} + h_2 + h_3 + h_4 + h_5\right)

surv-ac-ex2.handbookFormula: A = w\left(\frac{h_1 + h_n}{2} + h_2 + h_3 + \cdots + h_{n-1}\right)
traps: Averaging all offsets instead of only the first and last
Forgetting to multiply by the interval width

surv-ac-ex3.statement: Offsets from a baseline are measured at $10 \text{ m}$ intervals: $0$, $5$, $8$, $6$, $0 \text{ m}$. What is the area using Simpson’s 1/3 rule?
surv-ac-ex3.eli5: Simpson's 1/3 rule: $A = (w/3)(h_1 + 4h_2 + 2h_3 + 4h_4 + h_5)$. We have 5 measurements (odd), so we have 4 intervals (even) — Simpson's applies. $A = (10/3)(0 + 4 \times 5 + 2 \times 8 + 4 \times 6 + 0) = (10/3)(0 + 20 + 16 + 24 + 0) = (10/3)(60) = 200$ m². The 126.7 m² choice uses $w/3$ but misses the coefficients. The 190.0 m² choice uses the trapezoidal rule. The 280.0 m² choice uses $w$ instead of $w/3$.
surv-ac-ex3.hint: Simpson’s 1/3 rule requires an odd number of offsets. The pattern of coefficients is 1, 4, 2, 4, 1.

steps.text: Verify: 5 offsets (odd count), so Simpson’s 1/3 rule applies.

traps: Mixing up the 4-2-4 coefficient pattern
Using Simpson’s rule with an even number of offsets (it requires odd)

surv-ac-ex4.statement: A surveyor has 6 equally-spaced offset measurements along an irregular boundary. Which area computation method can NOT be directly applied?

choices.text: Both Simpson’s 1/3 rule and trapezoidal rule

surv-ac-ex4.eli5: Simpson’s 1/3 rule requires an odd number of offset measurements (even number of intervals). With 6 measurements, you have an even number of offsets and 5 intervals (odd), so Simpson’s 1/3 rule cannot be applied directly. The trapezoidal rule works with any number of offsets. The average end area method is for volumes, not plan areas, but it has no even/odd restriction. The key constraint to remember is: Simpson’s 1/3 needs an ODD count of offsets.
surv-ac-ex4.hint: Think about which method has a restriction on the number of offsets being odd or even.

steps.text: Simpson’s 1/3 rule requires an odd number of offset measurements (even number of intervals).
6 offsets = even count, so Simpson’s 1/3 rule cannot be applied directly.
The trapezoidal rule has no such restriction — it works with any number of offsets.

traps: Confusing the requirement — Simpson’s needs odd offsets (even intervals), not the other way around

surv-ev-ex1.statement: Two adjacent cross-sections have areas $A_1 = 225 \text{ ft}^2$ and $A_2 = 375 \text{ ft}^2$, separated by $100 \text{ ft}$. What is the volume by the average end area method, in cubic yards?
surv-ev-ex1.eli5: $V = (L/2)(A_1 + A_2) = (100/2)(225 + 375) = 50 \times 600 = 30000$ ft³. Convert to cubic yards: $30000 / 27 = 1111$ yd³. The 556 yd³ choice divides by 54 instead of 27. The 30,000 yd³ choice gives the volume in ft³, not yd³. The 2,222 yd³ choice forgets to divide $L$ by 2 (gets 60,000 ft³ / 27).
surv-ev-ex1.hint: Average end area: $V = (L/2)(A_1 + A_2)$, then divide by 27 to convert ft³ to yd³.
traps: Forgetting to convert from ft^3 to yd^3 by dividing by 27

surv-ev-ex2.statement: Three cross-sections are taken at stations 0, 40 ft, and 80 ft with areas $A_1 = 150 \text{ ft}^2$, $A_m = 280 \text{ ft}^2$, and $A_2 = 350 \text{ ft}^2$. What is the volume using the prismoidal formula?
surv-ev-ex2.eli5: $V = (L/6)(A_1 + 4A_m + A_2) = (80/6)(150 + 4 \times 280 + 350) = 13.333 \times 1620 = 21600$ ft³. The total distance $L$ between the end sections is 80 ft, not 40. The 20,000 ft³ option uses the average end area method: $(80/2)(150 + 350) = 20000$. The 10,400 ft³ option uses too small an L. The 26,133 ft³ option uses a different (incorrect) weighting.
surv-ev-ex2.hint: Prismoidal: $V = (L/6)(A_1 + 4A_m + A_2)$. The total length $L$ is 80 ft (from station 0 to station 80).
traps: Using the average end area formula instead of the prismoidal formula
Using half the distance (40 ft) instead of the full distance (80 ft) between end sections

surv-ev-ex3.statement:
A road project has cross-section areas at four stations spaced 100 ft apart:

Station 0+00: $A = 0 \text{ ft}^2$
Station 1+00: $A = 300 \text{ ft}^2$
Station 2+00: $A = 500 \text{ ft}^2$
Station 3+00: $A = 200 \text{ ft}^2$

Using the average end area method, what is the total volume in cubic yards?
surv-ev-ex3.eli5: Apply average end area to each segment. $V_1 = (100/2)(0 + 300) = 15000$ ft³. $V_2 = (100/2)(300 + 500) = 40000$ ft³. $V_3 = (100/2)(500 + 200) = 35000$ ft³. Total $= 15000 + 40000 + 35000 = 90000$ ft³. Convert to cubic yards: $90000 / 27 = 3333$ yd³. The 3,704 yd³ option includes an extra segment from a miscount. The 1,852 yd³ option only computes two of the three segments. The 6,667 yd³ option forgets to divide $L$ by 2 in each segment.
surv-ev-ex3.hint: Apply the average end area formula to each pair of adjacent stations, sum all segment volumes, then convert to cubic yards (divide by 27).
traps: Computing only one or two segments instead of all three
Forgetting to divide by 27 to convert ft^3 to yd^3

surv-ev-ex4.statement: A stockpile has a roughly conical shape with a base area of $2{,}000 \text{ ft}^2$ and a height of $15 \text{ ft}$. What is the estimated volume?
surv-ev-ex4.eli5: A cone (or pyramid) volume is $V = h \times A_{base} / 3 = 15 \times 2000 / 3 = 10000$ ft³. The 1/3 factor distinguishes a cone from a cylinder. The 30,000 ft³ choice uses $V = h \times A$ (no 1/3 factor — that is a cylinder). The 15,000 ft³ choice uses $V = h \times A / 2$ (average end area with $A_2 = 0$, which overcounts). The 5,000 ft³ choice divides by 6 instead of 3.
surv-ev-ex4.hint: A cone tapers to a point, so V = (h x A_base) / 3, not h x A.
traps: Using $V = hA$ (cylinder formula) instead of the cone/pyramid formula with the 1/3 factor
Using the average end area with $A_2 = 0$, which gives $hA/2$ instead of $hA/3$

surv-hc-ex1.statement: A horizontal curve has a radius $R = 1{,}200 \text{ ft}$ and an intersection angle $I = 30\degree$. What is the curve length $L$?
surv-hc-ex1.eli5: $L = \pi R I / 180 = \pi \times 1200 \times 30 / 180 = 200\pi = 628$ ft. The 322 ft choice is the tangent distance $T = R\tan(I/2) = 1200\tan 15\degree \approx 322$ ft, not the curve length. The 436 ft choice is a wrong value that does not correspond to $L$. The 1{,}257 ft choice uses $I = 60\degree$ (doubles the angle), giving $400\pi$.
traps: Using I/2 instead of the full intersection angle I in the curve length formula

surv-hc-ex2.statement: A horizontal curve has $R = 600 \text{ ft}$ and $I = 90\degree$. What is the middle ordinate $M$?
surv-hc-ex2.eli5: $M = R(1 - \cos(I/2)) = 600(1 - \cos 45°) = 600(1 - 0.7071) = 600 \times 0.2929 = 175.7$ ft. The middle ordinate is the distance from the curve midpoint to the long chord. The 248.5 ft choice uses $R(\sec(I/2) - 1)$, which is the external distance $E$, not $M$. The 300.0 ft choice is simply $R/2$. The 424.3 ft choice uses $R \cos 45°$ instead of $R(1 - \cos 45°)$.
surv-hc-ex2.hint: $M = R(1 - \cos(I/2))$. Use half the intersection angle inside the cosine.
traps: Using the full angle I instead of I/2 in the cosine
Confusing middle ordinate M with external distance E

surv-hc-ex3.statement: A horizontal curve has $D = 5\degree$ and $I = 30\degree$. The PI is at station $50+00$. What is the station of the PC?
surv-hc-ex3.eli5: First find $R$: $R = 5729.58 / 5 = 1145.92$ ft. Then the tangent distance: $T = R \tan(I/2) = 1145.92 \times \tan 15° = 1145.92 \times 0.2680 = 307.05$ ft. Station of PC $= PI - T = 5000 - 307.05 = 4692.95$ = station 46+92.95. The $47+00.00$ choice rounds $T$ to 300 ft. The $53+07.05$ choice adds $T$ to the PI instead of subtracting (that gives the PT via the tangent, not the PC). The $44+00.00$ choice subtracts $L$ instead of $T$.
surv-hc-ex3.hint: Find $R$ from $D$, then $T = R \tan(I/2)$. Station of PC = Station of PI $- T$.
traps: Adding T to the PI station instead of subtracting it to find the PC
Using the full angle I in the tangent formula instead of I/2

surv-hc-ex4.statement: A horizontal curve has PI at station $30+00$ and a tangent distance $T = 400 \text{ ft}$. The curve length is $L = 750 \text{ ft}$. A surveyor needs to lay out the curve. Which of the following correctly identifies the PC, PT, and the relationship between them?

choices.text: PC at $26+00$, PT at $33+50$; the PT station is found by adding $L$ to the PC station, not by adding $T$ to the PI
PC at $26+00$, PT at $34+00$; the PT station is found by adding $T$ to the PI
PC at $26+00$, PT at $30+00$; the PT is always at the PI station
PC at $30+00$, PT at $37+50$; the PC is at the PI and the PT is at PC + $L$

surv-hc-ex4.eli5: $PC = PI - T = 3000 - 400 = 2600$ = station 26+00. $PT = PC + L = 2600 + 750 = 3350$ = station 33+50. The key insight is that PT is found by adding the arc length $L$ to the PC station, NOT by adding $T$ to the PI. The tangent distance $T$ goes from the PI back to the PC (or forward to the PT along the tangent), but the actual curve station at the PT uses the arc distance $L$. The choice with PT at 34+00 adds $T$ to the PI for the PT (that gives a point on the tangent, not the curve). The choice with PT at 30+00 confuses the PT with the PI. The choice with PC at 30+00 places the PC at the PI.
surv-hc-ex4.hint: PC = PI - T. PT = PC + L (arc length along the curve). Do NOT compute PT as PI + T.

steps.text: Note: PT is NOT at PI + T = 30+00 + 4+00 = 34+00. The curve arc L and tangent T are different distances.

traps: Computing PT as PI + T instead of PC + L -- T and L are different distances
Confusing the PI with the PC or PT

surv-vc-ex1.statement: A vertical curve has $g_1 = +2\%$, $g_2 = -2\%$, $L = 400 \text{ ft}$, and $Y_{PVC} = 150.0 \text{ ft}$. What is the curve elevation at $x = 100 \text{ ft}$ from the PVC?
surv-vc-ex1.eli5: Plug into the curve formula: $Y = Y_{PVC} + g_1 x + [(g_2 - g_1)/(2L)]x^2$. The parabola constant $a = (-0.02 - 0.02)/(2 \times 400) = -0.04/800 = -0.00005$. $Y = 150 + 0.02(100) + (-0.00005)(100^2) = 150 + 2.0 - 0.5 = 151.5$ ft. The 152.0 ft choice is the tangent elevation, ignoring the parabolic correction. The 150.0 ft choice is the PVC elevation. The 148.0 ft choice subtracts the grade instead of adding it.
surv-vc-ex1.hint: Use the curve formula Y = Y_PVC + g_1 x + [(g_2 - g_1)/(2L)]x^2. Convert percent grades to decimals.
surv-vc-ex1.handbookFormula: Y = Y_{PVC} + g_1 x + \frac{g_2 - g_1}{2L} x^2
traps: Forgetting to convert percent grade to decimal (2% = 0.02, not 2)

surv-vc-ex2.statement: A sag vertical curve has $g_1 = -2\%$, $g_2 = +4\%$, $L = 600 \text{ ft}$, and $Y_{PVC} = 340.00 \text{ ft}$. How far from the PVC is the low point, and what is the elevation there?
surv-vc-ex2.eli5: The low point is at $x_m = -g_1 L/(g_2 - g_1) = -(-0.02)(600)/(0.04 - (-0.02)) = 12/0.06 = 200$ ft from the PVC. Elevation: $Y = 340 + (-0.02)(200) + [(0.04 - (-0.02))/(2 \times 600)](200^2) = 340 - 4.0 + 2.0 = 338.00$ ft. The 400 ft option uses $x_m = -g_2 L/(g_1 - g_2)$. The 300 ft / 337.50 ft option puts the low point at $L/2$ (only true when $|g_1| = |g_2|$). The 200 ft / 336.00 ft option gets the location right but computes the elevation using only the tangent.
surv-vc-ex2.hint: Low point is at $x_m = -g_1 L/(g_2 - g_1)$. Then plug $x_m$ into the curve elevation formula.
traps: Assuming the low point is at L/2 -- only true when the absolute values of the grades are equal
Getting the sign wrong in the denominator (g_2 - g_1, not g_1 - g_2)

surv-vc-ex3.statement: A crest vertical curve has $g_1 = +3\%$ and $g_2 = -5\%$. The required stopping sight distance is $S = 500 \text{ ft}$. Using the standard criteria ($h_1 = 3.50 \text{ ft}$, $h_2 = 2.0 \text{ ft}$) and assuming $S \le L$, what is the minimum curve length?
surv-vc-ex3.eli5: $A = |g_1 - g_2| = |3 - (-5)| = 8\%$. For a crest curve with $S \le L$ and standard criteria, $L = AS^2 / 2158 = 8 \times 500^2 / 2158 = 2000000 / 2158 = 927$ ft. Since $L = 927 > S = 500$, the assumption $S \le L$ is valid. The 1,855 ft choice uses the general/headlight denominator (1,079) instead of the standard-criteria denominator (2,158). The 556 ft choice mis-divides (it is not what $A=5$ would give; $A=5$ yields 579 ft). The 463 ft choice divides $L$ by 2.
surv-vc-ex3.hint: For a crest curve with $S \le L$ and standard criteria, $L = AS^2 / 2158$. First find $A = |g_1 - g_2|$ in percent.

steps.text: Check assumption: $L = 927 > S = 500$, so S <= L is valid.

traps: Using the wrong denominator -- 2,158 is for standard criteria with h_1 = 3.5 and h_2 = 2.0
Computing A incorrectly by not taking the absolute difference

surv-vc-ex4.statement: A crest vertical curve has $g_1 = +4\%$ and $g_2 = -2\%$. A designer needs a minimum rate of vertical curvature $K = 120$. What is the minimum curve length $L$?
surv-vc-ex4.eli5: $K = L/A$, so $L = K \times A$. First find $A = |g_1 - g_2| = |4 - (-2)| = 6\%$. Then $L = 120 \times 6 = 720$ ft. The $K$-value represents feet of curve per percent change in grade — a higher $K$ means a longer, gentler curve with better sight distance. The 480 ft option uses $A = 4$ (only one grade, not the difference). The 240 ft option uses $A = 2$. The 20 ft option uses $K/A$ instead of $K \times A$.
surv-vc-ex4.hint: K = L/A, so L = K x A. Remember that A = |g_1 - g_2| is in percent.
traps: Using only one grade instead of the algebraic difference A = |g_1 - g_2|
Dividing K by A instead of multiplying

surv-cg-ex1.statement: Point A is at $(E, N) = (2{,}000, 3{,}000)$ and point B at $(2{,}600, 3{,}800)$ (ft). What is the straight-line distance from A to B?
surv-cg-ex1.eli5: ΔE = 600, ΔN = 800; distance = √(600² + 800²) = √(360,000 + 640,000) = √1,000,000 = 1,000 ft (a 6-8-10 triangle). The 1,400 ft option adds the differences (600 + 800). The 700 ft option averages them. The 500 ft option halves the correct distance (1,000/2).
traps: Adding ΔE and ΔN instead of using the Pythagorean distance
Swapping easting and northing

surv-adb-cp1.statement: A line has an azimuth of $247\degree$. What is the equivalent bearing?
surv-adb-cp1.eli5: An azimuth of $247\degree$ falls between $180\degree$ and $270\degree$, which is the SW quadrant. In the SW quadrant the bearing angle is azimuth minus $180\degree$: $247 - 180 = 67\degree$, giving S $67\degree$ W. The N $67\degree$ W option treats it as the NW quadrant. The S $23\degree$ W option subtracts from $270\degree$ ($270 - 247 = 23$) instead of from $180\degree$. The S $67\degree$ E option keeps the magnitude but puts it in the wrong (SE) quadrant.
surv-adb-cp1.hint: Find which quadrant the azimuth lies in first, then convert. For $180\degree$ to $270\degree$ (SW), bearing angle = azimuth minus $180\degree$.

For the SW quadrant, the bearing angle equals the azimuth minus $180\degree$:
Write the bearing in the SW quadrant:

Assigning the wrong quadrant letters (NW or SE instead of SW)

surv-adb-cp2.statement: A survey line has a forward azimuth of $138\degree$. At the next station, an angle to the right (clockwise, measured from the back line to the next line) of $95\degree$ is turned. What is the forward azimuth of the next line?
surv-adb-cp2.eli5: At the occupied station, first find the back azimuth of the incoming line: $138 + 180 = 318\degree$. The angle to the right is measured clockwise from that back line to the next line, so add it: $318 + 95 = 413\degree$. That exceeds a full circle, so subtract $360\degree$: $413 - 360 = 53\degree$, the forward azimuth of the next line. The $233\degree$ choice mistakenly adds another $180\degree$ (reports the back azimuth of the next line). The $413\degree$ choice forgets to subtract $360\degree$. The $43\degree$ choice subtracts the angle from the forward azimuth instead of adding it (treats it as an angle to the left).
surv-adb-cp2.hint: Next forward azimuth = back azimuth of the current line ($+180\degree$) $+$ angle to the right; reduce to the $0\degree$ to $360\degree$ range.

Reporting the back azimuth instead of the forward azimuth of the next line

surv-lev-cp1.statement: A differential level run from BM-5 (elevation $612.40 \text{ ft}$) to point P records four backsights totaling $\Sigma BS = 18.62 \text{ ft}$ and four foresights totaling $\Sigma FS = 22.07 \text{ ft}$. What is the elevation of point P?
surv-lev-cp1.eli5: For a full level run the final elevation equals the starting elevation plus the sum of all backsights minus the sum of all foresights: $\text{Elev}_P = 612.40 + 18.62 - 22.07 = 608.95$ ft. Since the foresights total more than the backsights, the point ends up lower than BM-5. The 615.85 ft choice reverses the sign of the net difference (adds $3.45$ instead of subtracting). The 653.09 ft choice adds both sums to the elevation. The 571.71 ft choice subtracts both sums.
surv-lev-cp1.hint: For an entire run: final elevation = start elevation + (sum of BS) - (sum of FS).

Adding both sums instead of taking BS minus FS

surv-lev-cp2.statement: In differential leveling, the systematic errors from Earth curvature and atmospheric refraction are most effectively eliminated by which field procedure?

choices.text: Taking all readings to the nearest $0.001 \text{ ft}$ with a precise level
Balancing the backsight and foresight distances at each setup
Using a longer level loop so the errors average out
Always reading the backsight before the foresight

surv-lev-cp2.eli5: Curvature and refraction both depend on the sighting distance, and they affect a backsight and a foresight in the same direction. If the backsight distance equals the foresight distance at each setup, the two errors are equal and cancel when you compute the elevation difference (HI uses BS, then subtracts FS). Reading to the nearest 0.001 ft improves precision but does nothing about a systematic distance-dependent error. Using a longer loop is wrong because a systematic error accumulates rather than averaging out. Always reading the backsight first only fixes reading order, not the curvature-refraction effect.
surv-lev-cp2.hint: These errors grow with sighting distance and affect BS and FS the same way. What makes them cancel in the BS minus FS difference?

steps.text: Curvature and refraction error grows with the square of the sighting distance and is the same sign for an equal-length backsight and foresight.
The elevation difference uses backsight minus foresight, so equal distances make the errors cancel:
Therefore balancing BS and FS distances at each setup removes the systematic effect.

traps: Confusing precision (reading resolution) with the elimination of a systematic error
Believing systematic errors average out over a long run like random errors do

surv-tc-cp1.statement: A traverse course has a latitude of $-150.0 \text{ m}$ and a departure of $-150.0 \text{ m}$. What is the length of the course?
surv-tc-cp1.eli5: The course length is the hypotenuse of the latitude and departure components: $L = \sqrt{\text{Lat}^2 + \text{Dep}^2} = \sqrt{(-150)^2 + (-150)^2} = \sqrt{45{,}000} = 212.1$ m. The signs do not matter once squared. The $150.0$ m choice reports just one component. The $300.0$ m choice adds the magnitudes ($150 + 150$). The $106.1$ m choice divides one component by $\sqrt{2}$ instead of multiplying.
surv-tc-cp1.hint: The course length is the resultant of the latitude and departure: $L = \sqrt{\text{Lat}^2 + \text{Dep}^2}$.

steps.text: Combine the components with the Pythagorean theorem:

traps: Adding the two components instead of using the Pythagorean theorem
Reporting a single component as the length

surv-tc-cp2.statement: A traverse course has a latitude of $+86.6 \text{ m}$ (north) and a departure of $-50.0 \text{ m}$ (west). What is the azimuth of the course?
surv-tc-cp2.eli5: A positive latitude (north) and negative departure (west) place the course in the NW quadrant. The reference (bearing) angle is $\arctan(|\text{Dep}| / |\text{Lat}|) = \arctan(50/86.6) = \arctan(0.5774) = 30\degree$, giving N $30\degree$ W. Converting an NW bearing to azimuth: $360 - 30 = 330\degree$. The $30\degree$ choice gives the NE azimuth (ignores the west sign). The $150\degree$ choice treats it as SE ($180 - 30$). The $300\degree$ choice uses $\arctan(\text{Lat}/\text{Dep})$ and lands on the wrong reference angle in the wrong quadrant.
surv-tc-cp2.hint: Use the signs to find the quadrant, then $\tan(\text{bearing}) = |\text{Dep}| / |\text{Lat}|$. Convert the NW bearing to azimuth with $360\degree - \theta$.

Convert the NW bearing N $30\degree$ W to an azimuth:

Taking arctan of latitude over departure instead of departure over latitude

surv-ac-cp1.statement: A parcel has vertices, in order, at $(0, 0)$, $(12, 0)$, $(16, 8)$, $(6, 12)$, and $(0, 8)$. What is the area by the coordinate (shoelace) method?
surv-ac-cp1.eli5: Apply the shoelace sum $\sum(x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i)$ around the polygon, closing the last vertex back to the first. The five edge cross products are $0$, $96$, $144$, $48$, and $0$, summing to $288$. The area is half the absolute value: $|288|/2 = 144$ sq units. The 288 sq units choice forgets to divide by 2 and reports the raw sum. The 72 sq units choice divides by 4. The 120 sq units choice drops the $48$ edge term ($240/2 = 120$).
surv-ac-cp1.hint: Sum $(x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i)$ for all five edges (pairing the last vertex with the first), then halve the absolute value.

Failing to close the polygon by pairing the last vertex with the first

surv-ac-cp2.statement: A rectangular construction easement measures $200 \text{ ft}$ by $435.6 \text{ ft}$. What is its area in acres? (1 acre $= 43{,}560 \text{ ft}^2$.)
surv-ac-cp2.eli5: First the area in square feet: $200 \times 435.6 = 87{,}120 \text{ ft}^2$. Convert to acres by dividing by $43{,}560$: $87{,}120 / 43{,}560 = 2.00$ acres. The 1.00-acre choice divides by twice the conversion factor (or halves a side). The 4.00-acre choice divides by half the conversion factor. The 0.50-acre choice over-divides by applying the conversion twice.
surv-ac-cp2.hint: Compute the area in square feet, then divide by 43,560 to get acres.
traps: Dividing a side length by the conversion factor instead of the total area
Forgetting the acre conversion and leaving the answer in square feet

surv-ev-cp1.statement: A borrow pit yields $5{,}400 \text{ yd}^3$ of bank (in-place) material. The soil has a shrinkage of $15\%$ when compacted in the fill. How many cubic yards of compacted fill does this produce?
surv-ev-cp1.eli5: Shrinkage means compacted fill occupies less volume than the bank material it came from. Compacted volume = bank volume $\times (1 - \text{shrinkage}) = 5{,}400 \times (1 - 0.15) = 5{,}400 \times 0.85 = 4{,}590$ yd³. The 6,210 yd³ choice adds 15 percent instead of subtracting it. The 810 yd³ choice reports only the lost volume ($5{,}400 \times 0.15$). The 6,353 yd³ choice divides by $0.85$ (that direction is for finding required bank volume from a known fill).
surv-ev-cp1.hint: Compacted fill volume = bank volume times (1 minus the shrinkage fraction).

steps.text: Apply the shrinkage factor to the bank volume:

Dividing by (1 - S) instead of multiplying, which solves the reverse problem

surv-ev-cp2.statement: Two adjacent cross-sections are separated by $150 \text{ ft}$. The cut area at the first is $A_1 = 240 \text{ ft}^2$ and at the second is $A_2 = 168 \text{ ft}^2$. Using the average end area method, what is the cut volume in cubic yards?
surv-ev-cp2.eli5: Average end area volume: $V = (L/2)(A_1 + A_2) = (150/2)(240 + 168) = 75 \times 408 = 30{,}600 \text{ ft}^3$. Convert to cubic yards by dividing by 27: $30{,}600 / 27 = 1{,}133$ yd³. The $30{,}600 \text{ yd}^3$ choice leaves the answer in cubic feet. The $2{,}267 \text{ yd}^3$ choice forgets to divide $L$ by 2 ($61{,}200/27$). The $1{,}700 \text{ yd}^3$ choice divides by 18 instead of 27.
surv-ev-cp2.hint: Use $V = (L/2)(A_1 + A_2)$ in cubic feet, then divide by 27 to get cubic yards.
