traps: Leaving the volume in cubic feet instead of converting to cubic yards
Forgetting to divide the distance by 2 in the average end area formula

surv-hc-cp1.statement: A horizontal curve has a radius $R = 500 \text{ ft}$ and an intersection angle $I = 60\degree$. What is the external distance $E$?
surv-hc-cp1.eli5: External distance $E = R(\sec(I/2) - 1) = 500(\sec 30\degree - 1) = 500(1.1547 - 1) = 500 \times 0.1547 = 77.4$ ft. The external distance is the gap from the PI to the midpoint of the curve. The 67.0 ft choice uses the middle ordinate formula $R(1 - \cos(I/2)) = 500(1 - 0.866) = 67.0$ ft. The 288.7 ft choice is the tangent distance $T = R\tan(I/2)$. The 250.0 ft choice is $R/2$.
surv-hc-cp1.hint: External distance $E = R(\sec(I/2) - 1)$. Recall $\sec\theta = 1/\cos\theta$ and use half the intersection angle.

steps.text: External distance formula with half the intersection angle:

traps: Confusing the external distance E with the middle ordinate M
Using the full intersection angle I instead of I/2 inside the secant

surv-hc-cp2.statement: A horizontal curve has a radius $R = 700 \text{ ft}$ and an intersection angle $I = 80\degree$. What is the length of the long chord $LC$?
surv-hc-cp2.eli5: Long chord $LC = 2R\sin(I/2) = 2 \times 700 \times \sin 40\degree = 1{,}400 \times 0.6428 = 899.9$ ft. The long chord connects the PC directly to the PT. The 1,377.4 ft option uses the full angle, $2R\sin I = 1{,}400 \times 0.9848$. The 449.9 ft option drops the factor of 2 ($R\sin(I/2)$). The 587.4 ft option uses $2R\tan(I/2)$ and a wrong reduction.
surv-hc-cp2.hint: Long chord $LC = 2R\sin(I/2)$. Use half the intersection angle inside the sine.
traps: Using the full angle I instead of I/2 inside the sine
Dropping the factor of 2 and computing only half the chord

surv-vc-cp1.statement: A vertical curve has $g_1 = -3\%$, $g_2 = +1\%$, $L = 500 \text{ ft}$, and $Y_{PVC} = 240.00 \text{ ft}$. What is the curve elevation $200 \text{ ft}$ from the PVC?
surv-vc-cp1.eli5: Use $Y = Y_{PVC} + g_1 x + [(g_2 - g_1)/(2L)]x^2$. The parabola constant is $(0.01 - (-0.03))/(2 \times 500) = 0.04/1000 = +0.00004$. Then $Y = 240 + (-0.03)(200) + (0.00004)(200^2) = 240 - 6 + 1.6 = 235.60$ ft. The 234.00 ft option is the tangent-only elevation ($240 - 6$), ignoring the parabolic term. The 246.00 ft option uses the wrong sign on $g_1$. The 237.20 ft option doubles the parabolic correction.
surv-vc-cp1.hint: Apply $Y = Y_{PVC} + g_1 x + [(g_2 - g_1)/(2L)]x^2$ with grades as decimals.
surv-vc-cp1.handbookFormula: Y = Y_{PVC} + g_1 x + \frac{g_2 - g_1}{2L} x^2
traps: Dropping the parabolic term and reporting the tangent elevation
Forgetting to convert percent grades to decimals

surv-vc-cp2.statement: A symmetric vertical curve has $g_1 = +2\%$, $g_2 = -4\%$, and length $L = 600 \text{ ft}$. What is the vertical offset (tangent offset) from the back tangent to the curve at the PVI?
surv-vc-cp2.eli5: The midpoint (PVI) tangent offset of a symmetric parabola is $e = AL/8$ when $A$ is expressed as a decimal grade difference. Here $A = |g_1 - g_2| = |0.02 - (-0.04)| = 0.06$, so $e = (0.06)(600)/8 = 36/8 = 4.50$ ft. Equivalently, the parabola constant $a = (g_2 - g_1)/(2L) = -0.00005$ gives an offset magnitude of $|a|(L/2)^2 = 0.00005 \times 300^2 = 4.50$ ft. The 9.00 ft choice uses $AL/4$. The 2.25 ft choice uses $AL/16$. The 1.50 ft choice uses only $g_1$ in $g_1 L/8$.
surv-vc-cp2.hint: For a symmetric curve the midpoint tangent offset is $e = AL/8$, with $A = |g_1 - g_2|$ as a decimal.

steps.text: Algebraic grade difference as a decimal:

traps: Using AL/4 (the full vertical distance between tangents) instead of AL/8 for the midpoint offset
Using a single grade instead of the algebraic difference A = |g_1 - g_2|

surv-cg-cp1.statement: A course of length $150\text{ ft}$ is run at an azimuth of $60\degree$. What is its departure (east-west component)?
surv-cg-cp1.eli5: Departure = L·sin(Az) = 150·sin(60°) = 150(0.8660) = 129.9 ft. The 75.0 ft choice uses cos with a slip (150·cos60° = 75 is actually the latitude). The 150.0 ft choice is the full length. The 86.6 ft choice applies sin to the wrong angle.
traps: Using cosine (latitude) for the departure
Reporting the full course length

wr-ocf-q1.statement: A rectangular concrete channel ($n = 0.013$) is $4 \text{ ft}$ wide and carries water $2 \text{ ft}$ deep on a slope of $S = 0.001$. What is the discharge?
wr-ocf-q1.eli5: A = 4 × 2 = 8 ft². P = 4 + 2(2) = 8 ft. R_H = 8/8 = 1.0 ft. Q = (1.486/0.013)(8)(1.0)^(2/3)(0.001)^(1/2) = 114.3 × 8 × 1.0 × 0.0316 = 28.9 cfs. The 42.3 cfs choice uses width alone for the wetted perimeter (P = 4 instead of 8), inflating R_H. The 19.5 cfs choice forgets the 1.486 factor. The 14.5 cfs choice halves the correct answer by miscalculating R_H.
wr-ocf-q1.hint: Find A, P, and R_H first. Remember K = 1.486 for US Customary units.
traps: Forgetting the 1.486 factor for USCS units — using K = 1.0 gives about 19.5 cfs instead of 28.9 cfs
Using the channel width as the wetted perimeter instead of b + 2y

wr-ocf-q2.statement: A concrete circular storm sewer ($n = 0.015$) has a diameter of $D = 3 \text{ ft}$ and flows full on a slope of $S = 0.002$. What is the full-pipe discharge?
wr-ocf-q2.eli5: Full circular pipe: A = π(3)²/4 = 7.069 ft². R_H = D/4 = 0.75 ft. (0.75)^(2/3) = 0.826. (0.002)^(1/2) = 0.04472. Q = (1.486/0.015)(7.069)(0.826)(0.04472) = 99.07 × 7.069 × 0.0369 = 25.9 cfs. The 17.4 cfs distractor forgets the 1.486 unit factor (uses K=1). The 40.6 cfs distractor uses R_H = D/2 = 1.5 instead of D/4 = 0.75. The 10.3 cfs distractor applies an incorrect (too-small) hydraulic radius.
wr-ocf-q2.hint: For a full circular pipe, R_H = D/4 (not D/2). Don't forget K = 1.486 for USCS.
traps: Using R_H = D/2 (physical radius) instead of R_H = D/4 (hydraulic radius for full pipe)
Forgetting the 1.486 USCS conversion factor

wr-ocf-q3.statement: Two channels carry the same discharge on the same slope. Channel A is lined with concrete ($n = 0.013$) and Channel B is an unlined earth channel ($n = 0.025$). If both have the same cross-section, how does the velocity in Channel A compare to Channel B?

choices.text: Channel A is about 1.5 times faster
Channel B is about 1.9 times faster
Channel A is about 1.9 times faster

wr-ocf-q3.eli5: Since v = (K/n) R_H^(2/3) S^(1/2), and everything except n is the same, the velocity ratio is v_A/v_B = n_B/n_A = 0.025/0.013 = 1.92 ≈ 1.9. The smoother channel (lower n) has higher velocity. The "same velocity" choice ignores the effect of roughness. The "1.5 times faster" choice uses the wrong ratio. The "Channel B is 1.9 times faster" choice inverts the relationship (it applies n_A/n_B and assigns the gain to the rougher channel).
wr-ocf-q3.hint: With the same geometry and slope, velocity is inversely proportional to Manning's n.

steps.text: Since both channels have the same $R_H$, $S$, and $K$:
Channel A is about 1.9 times faster than Channel B.

traps: Thinking higher n means faster flow — higher n means rougher surface and slower flow
Computing n_A/n_B instead of n_B/n_A — velocity is inversely proportional to n

wr-ecf-q1.statement: Water flows at $Q = 27 \text{ m}^3\text{/s}$ in a rectangular channel that is $B = 3 \text{ m}$ wide. What is the critical depth?
wr-ecf-q1.eli5: Unit discharge q = Q/B = 27/3 = 9 m²/s. Critical depth y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3) = (81/9.81)^(1/3) = (8.257)^(1/3) = 2.02 m. The 3.00 m choice uses Q instead of q. The 0.97 m choice uses q²/g without the cube root. The 1.44 m choice takes the square root instead of the cube root.
wr-ecf-q1.hint: First find the unit discharge q = Q/B, then apply the rectangular critical depth formula.
traps: Using total Q instead of unit discharge q = Q/B in the formula
Taking the square root instead of the cube root

wr-ecf-q2.statement: Water flows at a velocity of $v = 4 \text{ m/s}$ at a depth of $y = 0.5 \text{ m}$ in a rectangular channel. What is the Froude number, and is the flow subcritical or supercritical?
wr-ecf-q2.eli5: Fr = v / √(gy) = 4 / √(9.81 × 0.5) = 4 / √(4.905) = 4 / 2.215 = 1.81. Since Fr > 1, the flow is supercritical. The Fr = 0.81 (subcritical) choice uses g = 10 and then takes v/gy instead of v/√(gy). The Fr = 0.55 (subcritical) choice inverts the formula (denominator over numerator). The Fr = 1.81 (subcritical) choice gets the number right but classifies it wrong — Fr > 1 is supercritical, not subcritical.
wr-ecf-q2.hint: For a rectangular channel, hydraulic depth equals flow depth. Compute Fr = v/√(gy) and compare to 1.
traps: Classifying Fr > 1 as subcritical — supercritical means fast and shallow, subcritical means slow and deep
Forgetting the square root — computing v/(gy) instead of v/√(gy)

wr-ecf-q3.statement: A hydraulic jump occurs in a rectangular channel. The upstream depth is $y_1 = 0.4 \text{ m}$ and the upstream Froude number is $Fr_1 = 3.0$. What is the downstream (conjugate) depth $y_2$?
wr-ecf-q3.eli5: y_2 = (y_1/2)(−1 + √(1 + 8Fr_1²)) = (0.4/2)(−1 + √(1 + 8×9)) = 0.2 × (−1 + √73) = 0.2 × (−1 + 8.544) = 0.2 × 7.544 = 1.49 m. The downstream depth is about 3.7 times the upstream depth. The 0.80 m choice just doubles y_1. The 1.20 m choice uses Fr_1 = 2 instead of 3. The 3.60 m choice multiplies y_1 by Fr_1² without using the correct formula.
wr-ecf-q3.hint: Use the conjugate depth formula: y_2 = (y_1/2)(−1 + √(1 + 8Fr²)). Plug in y_1 and Fr_1 directly.
traps: Forgetting the −1 inside the parentheses — it is part of the formula, not a sign error
Using Fr² without the factor of 8 inside the radical
Confusing y_1 and y_2 — the upstream supercritical depth is always smaller

wr-psw-q1.statement: A suppressed rectangular weir is $L = 5 \text{ ft}$ long. The head over the weir is $H = 1.5 \text{ ft}$. What is the discharge?
wr-psw-q1.eli5: Q = CLH^(3/2) = 3.33 × 5 × (1.5)^(3/2). (1.5)^(3/2) = 1.5 × √1.5 = 1.5 × 1.225 = 1.837. Q = 3.33 × 5 × 1.837 = 30.6 cfs. The 25.0 cfs choice uses H^1 instead of H^(3/2). The 16.9 cfs choice uses the SI coefficient (1.84). The 37.5 cfs choice multiplies by H² instead of H^(3/2).
wr-psw-q1.hint: For a suppressed rectangular weir in USCS: Q = CLH^(3/2) with C = 3.33.
traps: Using the SI coefficient (C = 1.84) instead of the USCS coefficient (C = 3.33)
Confusing H^(3/2) for rectangular with H^(5/2) for V-notch weirs

wr-psw-q2.statement: A 90° V-notch weir measures flow in a stream. The head above the notch is $H = 2.0 \text{ ft}$. What is the discharge?
wr-psw-q2.eli5: V-notch weir: Q = CH^(5/2) = 2.54 × (2.0)^(5/2). (2.0)^(5/2) = 2^2 × √2 = 4 × 1.414 = 5.657. Q = 2.54 × 5.657 = 14.4 cfs. The 10.2 cfs option uses H^2 = 4.0. The 7.2 cfs option uses H^(3/2) instead of H^(5/2) — that's the rectangular weir exponent. The 20.3 cfs option uses H^3 = 8.0.
wr-psw-q2.hint: V-notch weirs use H^(5/2), not H^(3/2). The USCS coefficient for a 90° notch is C = 2.54.
traps: Using H^(3/2) — that's for rectangular weirs. V-notch uses H^(5/2)
Using the rectangular weir coefficient (C = 3.33) instead of the V-notch coefficient (C = 2.54)

wr-psw-q3.statement: Two pipes have the same diameter, length, and hydraulic gradient. Pipe A is new PVC ($C = 150$) and Pipe B is 20-year-old cast iron ($C = 100$). What is the ratio of flow in Pipe A to Pipe B?
wr-psw-q3.eli5: Since Q = k₁ C A R_H^0.63 S^0.54, and everything except C is the same, Q_A/Q_B = C_A/C_B = 150/100 = 1.50. The newer, smoother pipe carries 50% more flow. The $2.25$ option squares the ratio (1.5² = 2.25). The $1.22$ option takes the 0.63 power of the ratio. The $0.67$ option inverts it.
wr-psw-q3.hint: With identical pipe geometry and gradient, flow is directly proportional to C.

steps.text: Since all parameters except $C$ are identical:
Pipe A carries 50% more flow than Pipe B.

traps: Thinking lower C means more flow — higher C means smoother pipe, less friction, more flow
Raising the ratio to a power (0.63 or 0.54) — C enters the equation linearly

wr-pwd-q1.statement: A pump delivers $Q = 0.05\text{ m}^3\text{/s}$ against a total head of $H = 30\text{ m}$ at a pump efficiency of $\eta = 0.75$. What brake (shaft) power is required? (Use $\rho g = 9{,}810\text{ N/m}^3$.)
wr-pwd-q1.eli5: Fluid power = γQH = 9,810 × 0.05 × 30 = 14,715 W ≈ 14.7 kW. Brake power divides by efficiency: 14.7/0.75 = 19.6 kW. The 14.7 kW option is the fluid power, forgetting efficiency. The 11.0 kW option multiplies by 0.75 instead of dividing. The 26.2 kW option divides by 0.75² (≈ 0.5625) or a similar slip.
wr-pwd-q1.hint: Fluid power = γQH. Brake power = fluid power / η_pump (always larger).

steps.text: Divide by efficiency for brake power:

traps: Reporting fluid power and forgetting to divide by efficiency
Multiplying by η instead of dividing — brake power must be larger than fluid power

wr-pwd-q2.statement: A pump sits $3.0\text{ m}$ above the water surface it draws from (a suction lift). The atmospheric pressure head is $H_{pa} = 10.3\text{ m}$, the vapor pressure head is $H_{vp} = 0.24\text{ m}$, and the suction-line friction loss is $\sum h_L = 1.0\text{ m}$. What is the net positive suction head available ($NPSH_A$)?
wr-pwd-q2.eli5: For a suction lift the static suction head is negative: H_s = −3.0 m. NPSH_A = H_pa + H_s − Σh_L − H_vp = 10.3 − 3.0 − 1.0 − 0.24 = 6.06 ≈ 6.1 m. The 12.1 m choice adds the 3.0 m instead of subtracting (wrong sign for a lift). The 7.3 m choice forgets the friction and vapor terms. The 3.1 m choice mishandles the atmospheric term.
wr-pwd-q2.hint: NPSH_A = H_pa + H_s − Σh_L − H_vp, with H_s negative for a suction lift.

steps.text: Suction lift makes the static suction head negative:

traps: Treating a suction lift as a positive static head (wrong sign)
Omitting the vapor pressure or friction terms

wr-pwd-q3.statement: A pump moves $Q = 1.1\text{ ft}^3\text{/s}$ of water against a head of $H = 100\text{ ft}$. Using $\gamma = 62.4\text{ lb/ft}^3$ and $1\text{ hp} = 550\text{ ft·lb/s}$, what is the water (hydraulic) horsepower?
wr-pwd-q3.eli5: Fluid power = γQH = 62.4 × 1.1 × 100 = 6,864 ft·lb/s. Convert to horsepower: 6,864/550 = 12.48 ≈ 12.5 hp. The 9.2 hp option divides by 746 (the SI watts-per-hp) instead of 550 ft·lb/s. The 6.2 hp option over-divides. The 18.7 hp option adds an efficiency factor that the question did not ask for.
wr-pwd-q3.hint: Water horsepower = γQH / 550 when Q is in ft³/s, H in ft, and γ in lb/ft³.
traps: Dividing by 746 W/hp instead of 550 ft·lb/s/hp (mixing unit systems)
Forgetting the conversion entirely and leaving power in ft·lb/s

wr-rr-q1.statement: A 50-acre commercial site has a runoff coefficient of $C = 0.85$. The design rainfall intensity for the 10-year storm is $I = 4.0 \text{ in./hr}$. What is the peak runoff using the Rational Method?
wr-rr-q1.eli5: Q = CIA = 0.85 × 4.0 × 50 = 170 cfs. That's it — straight plug-and-chug. The 212 cfs option uses C = 1.06 (a common wrong reading from tables). The 42.5 cfs option divides by 4 for some reason. The 340 cfs option doubles the area (uses A = 100 acres instead of 50).
wr-rr-q1.hint: Q = CIA. The units work out directly — no conversion needed.
traps: Trying to convert units — the formula is set up so 1 acre-in./hr ≈ 1 cfs
Using the wrong runoff coefficient for the land use type

wr-rr-q2.statement: A watershed has a curve number of $CN = 80$. If the total rainfall is $P = 5.0 \text{ in.}$, what is the runoff depth using the SCS method?
wr-rr-q2.eli5: First find S: S = 1000/CN – 10 = 1000/80 – 10 = 12.5 – 10 = 2.5 in. Initial abstraction = 0.2S = 0.5 in. Since P = 5.0 > 0.5, runoff occurs. Q = (P – 0.2S)²/(P + 0.8S) = (5.0 – 0.5)²/(5.0 + 2.0) = (4.5)²/7.0 = 20.25/7.0 = 2.89 in. The 5.00 in. choice uses the full precipitation without subtracting initial abstraction. The 4.50 in. choice uses P – 0.2S in the numerator without squaring (4.5/1.0 = 4.5). The 1.50 in. choice uses (P – S) instead of (P – 0.2S).
wr-rr-q2.hint: First compute S = 1000/CN – 10, then plug into Q = (P – 0.2S)²/(P + 0.8S). Check that P > 0.2S.
traps: Forgetting to compute S from CN first — S is NOT the curve number
Using P instead of (P – 0.2S) in the numerator — the initial abstraction must be subtracted
Reporting Q in cfs — the SCS equation gives runoff DEPTH in inches, not discharge

wr-rr-q3.statement: Two adjacent sub-catchments drain to the same inlet. Sub-A has $C_A = 0.90$, $A_A = 30 \text{ acres}$. Sub-B has $C_B = 0.40$, $A_B = 20 \text{ acres}$. The rainfall intensity for the combined time of concentration is $I = 3.5 \text{ in./hr}$. What is the total peak discharge?
wr-rr-q3.eli5: For composite catchments, apply the Rational Method to each and add: Q = I(C_A × A_A + C_B × A_B) = 3.5 × (0.90 × 30 + 0.40 × 20) = 3.5 × (27 + 8) = 3.5 × 35 = 122.5 cfs. The 65.0 cfs option only computes sub-A. The 113.8 cfs option uses C_avg = (0.90 + 0.40)/2 = 0.65 (simple average, not area-weighted) → Q = 0.65 × 3.5 × 50 = 113.8. The 175 cfs option ignores C (Q = I × A_total = 3.5 × 50 = 175).
wr-rr-q3.hint: For composite catchments, Q = I × Σ(C_i × A_i). You can add the CIA products or use a weighted average C.

steps.latex: Q = I \sum(C_i A_i) = I(C_A A_A + C_B A_B)

traps: Averaging the C values without weighting by area — (0.90 + 0.40)/2 = 0.65 is wrong; the area-weighted average is (27 + 8)/50 = 0.70
Forgetting to apply different C values to different sub-catchments
Applying different rainfall intensities to sub-catchments — use the intensity for the combined time of concentration

wr-hw-q1.statement: A 1-hour unit hydrograph for a watershed has a peak discharge of $500 \text{ cfs}$. If a storm produces $3 \text{ in.}$ of excess rainfall in 1 hour, what is the peak discharge of the direct runoff hydrograph?
wr-hw-q1.eli5: The unit hydrograph is for 1 inch of excess rainfall. For 3 inches, multiply every ordinate by 3. Peak = 500 × 3 = 1,500 cfs. The 500 cfs option doesn't scale (uses 1 inch). The 167 cfs option divides instead of multiplying (500/3 = 167). The 1,000 cfs option doubles instead of tripling.
wr-hw-q1.hint: The unit hydrograph gives the response to 1 inch of excess rainfall. Scale linearly for other amounts.

steps.text: The UH peak is for 1 inch of excess rainfall:

wr-hw-q1.handbookFormula: \text{Unit hydrograph: 1 unit of rainfall over specified duration}
traps: Forgetting to scale the UH by the actual excess rainfall depth
Dividing by the rainfall instead of multiplying

wr-hw-q2.statement: A 100-acre watershed has a time of concentration of $t_c = 30 \text{ min}$. Using the Rational Method with $C = 0.60$, the 30-minute rainfall intensity for the 25-year storm is $I = 4.8 \text{ in./hr}$. What is the peak runoff?
wr-hw-q2.eli5: Q = CIA = 0.60 × 4.8 × 100 = 288 cfs. The key insight is that the storm duration should equal the time of concentration to produce the maximum peak. Since the problem already gives I for the 30-min duration (which equals t_c), just plug in. The 480 cfs choice ignores C (just I×A). The 144 cfs choice uses a halved intensity (perhaps thinking 30 min = half hour needs adjustment). The 576 cfs choice uses C = 1.2 (doubled).
wr-hw-q2.hint: The design storm duration equals the time of concentration. Use Q = CIA with the given intensity.
traps: Converting minutes to hours and dividing the intensity — the intensity is already in in./hr for the correct duration
Using an intensity for a different duration than t_c — Q = CIA requires the intensity for storm duration = t_c

wr-hw-q3.statement: A reservoir receives an inflow of $I = 800 \text{ cfs}$ and releases an outflow of $O = 500 \text{ cfs}$. What is the rate of change in storage?
wr-hw-q3.eli5: I – O = ΔS/Δt. So ΔS/Δt = 800 – 500 = 300 cfs. Since it's positive, storage is INCREASING — more water is coming in than going out. This is the fundamental principle behind detention pond design: during a storm, the pond fills (I > O), storing water to reduce the downstream peak. The "storage is not changing" choice assumes steady state. The "decreasing at 300 cfs" choice reverses the sign. The "increasing at 1,300 cfs" choice adds instead of subtracting.
wr-hw-q3.hint: Apply I – O = ΔS/Δt. A positive result means storage is increasing.

steps.text: Since $\Delta S/\Delta t > 0$, storage is increasing at 300 cfs.

wr-hw-q3.handbookFormula: P + Q_{in} - Q_{out} + Q_g - E_s - T_s - I = \Delta S_s
traps: Subtracting inflow from outflow instead of outflow from inflow (O – I gives the wrong sign)
Confusing "storage increasing" with "water level decreasing"

wr-gw-q1.statement: Groundwater flows through a sandy aquifer with $K = 5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m/s}$ under a hydraulic gradient of $i = 0.02$. The aquifer cross-section is $A = 200 \text{ m}^2$. If the effective porosity is $n = 0.30$, what is the seepage velocity?
wr-gw-q1.eli5: Darcy velocity: q = Ki = 5×10⁻⁴ × 0.02 = 1.0×10⁻⁵ m/s. Seepage velocity: v = q/n = 1.0×10⁻⁵/0.30 = 3.33×10⁻⁵ m/s. The 1.0×10⁻⁵ m/s option gives the Darcy velocity, not the seepage velocity. The 2.0×10⁻³ m/s option is the volumetric flow Q = q×A = Ki×A, not a velocity. The 1.0×10⁻³ m/s option halves that flow figure — another units mix-up.
wr-gw-q1.hint: Find the Darcy velocity first (q = Ki), then divide by porosity to get seepage velocity.
traps: Reporting the Darcy velocity as the answer — seepage velocity is always larger (divide by porosity)
Multiplying by porosity instead of dividing — water moves faster through pores, not slower

wr-gw-q2.statement: A well pumps from an unconfined aquifer with $K = 5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ ft/s}$. At the well ($r_1 = 0.5 \text{ ft}$), the water level is $h_1 = 40 \text{ ft}$ above the aquifer bottom. At an observation well ($r_2 = 200 \text{ ft}$), the water level is $h_2 = 60 \text{ ft}$. What is the well discharge?
wr-gw-q2.eli5: Dupuit (unconfined): Q = πK(h₂² – h₁²)/ln(r₂/r₁) = π(5×10⁻⁴)(60² – 40²)/ln(200/0.5) = π(0.0005)(2000)/ln(400) = 3.142/5.991 = 0.52 cfs. The 1.05 cfs option uses K = 0.001 (doubled). The 0.011 cfs option uses h differences instead of h² differences (h₂ – h₁ = 20 instead of 2000). The 0.33 cfs option uses log₁₀ instead of ln.
wr-gw-q2.hint: For an unconfined aquifer, use Dupuit's formula with h² differences. Don't forget the natural log in the denominator.
traps: Using h differences instead of h² differences — Dupuit (unconfined) requires squaring the heads
Using log₁₀ instead of ln — the formula uses the natural logarithm
Swapping r_1 and r_2 in the logarithm — r_1 is at the well, r_2 is farther away

wr-gw-q3.statement: A confined aquifer has thickness $b = 20 \text{ m}$ and hydraulic conductivity $K = 3 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m/s}$. A pumping well shows piezometric heads of $h_1 = 25 \text{ m}$ at $r_1 = 10 \text{ m}$ and $h_2 = 30 \text{ m}$ at $r_2 = 100 \text{ m}$. What is the pumping rate?
wr-gw-q3.eli5: For a confined aquifer, use the Thiem equation. T = Kb = 3×10⁻⁵ × 20 = 6×10⁻⁴ m²/s. Q = 2πT(h₂ – h₁)/ln(r₂/r₁) = 2π(6×10⁻⁴)(30 – 25)/ln(100/10) = 2π(6×10⁻⁴)(5)/2.303 = 0.01885/2.303 = 0.0082 m³/s. The 0.082 m³/s choice uses K = 3×10⁻⁴ (ten times too high). The 0.041 m³/s choice is 5× too large (e.g. mistakenly using aquifer thickness b = 100 m instead of 20 m). The 0.0016 m³/s choice comes from a low-by-roughly-5× slip.
wr-gw-q3.hint: For a confined aquifer, use Thiem: Q = 2πT(h₂ – h₁)/ln(r₂/r₁) where T = Kb. Use linear h, not h².
traps: Using Dupuit's formula (h²) for a confined aquifer — Thiem uses linear h differences
Forgetting to compute transmissivity T = Kb before plugging in
Using log₁₀ instead of ln — ln(10) = 2.303, not log₁₀(10) = 1.0

wr-wq-q1.statement: A wastewater sample has an ultimate BOD of $L_0 = 300 \text{ mg/L}$ and a decay rate of $k = 0.23 \text{ day}^{-1}$ (base $e$). What is the $BOD_5$?
wr-wq-q1.eli5: BOD₅ = L₀(1 – e^(–kt)) = 300(1 – e^(–0.23×5)) = 300(1 – e^(–1.15)) = 300(1 – 0.317) = 300 × 0.683 = 205 ≈ 204 mg/L. The 300 mg/L choice gives the ultimate BOD, not the 5-day BOD. The 96 mg/L choice gives the BOD remaining (L₀ – BOD₅ = 96), not the BOD exerted. The 150 mg/L choice assumes BOD₅ = L₀/2.
wr-wq-q1.hint: Use BOD_t = L₀(1 – e^(–kt)) with t = 5 days.
traps: Reporting the ultimate BOD (300 mg/L) as the BOD₅ — the 5-day value is always less than ultimate
Computing the BOD remaining (L₀ e^(–kt) = 96) instead of the BOD exerted

wr-wq-q2.statement: A lab measures $BOD_5 = 180 \text{ mg/L}$ for a sample with $k = 0.20 \text{ day}^{-1}$ (base $e$). What is the ultimate BOD ($L_0$)?
wr-wq-q2.eli5: Rearrange: L₀ = BOD₅/(1 – e^(–kt)) = 180/(1 – e^(–0.20 × 5)) = 180/(1 – e^(–1.0)) = 180/(1 – 0.368) = 180/0.632 = 285 mg/L. The ultimate BOD is always larger than the 5-day BOD because the test only captures partial decomposition. The 360 mg/L choice simply doubles BOD₅. The 180 mg/L choice assumes BOD₅ = L₀ (it's not). The 900 mg/L choice multiplies by 5.
wr-wq-q2.hint: Rearrange BOD_t = L₀(1 – e^(–kt)) to solve for L₀ = BOD₅/(1 – e^(–k×5)).
traps: Assuming BOD₅ = L₀ — the 5-day test captures only about 63% of the ultimate BOD (at this k value)
Using the wrong base for k — make sure k is base e (natural), not base 10

wr-wq-q3.statement: A BOD rate constant at 20°C is $k_{20} = 0.23 \text{ day}^{-1}$. Using the temperature correction with $\theta = 1.056$, what is the rate constant at $T = 28\degree\text{C}$?
wr-wq-q3.eli5: k_T = k₂₀ × θ^(T – 20) = 0.23 × 1.056^(28 – 20) = 0.23 × 1.056^8. 1.056^8: 1.056² = 1.1151, 1.056⁴ = 1.2434, 1.056⁸ = 1.5462. k₂₈ = 0.23 × 1.546 = 0.356 ≈ 0.35 day⁻¹. Higher temperature speeds up biodegradation. The 0.46 day⁻¹ option simply doubles k. The 0.15 day⁻¹ option inverts the formula (θ^(20–T)). The 0.23 day⁻¹ option assumes temperature has no effect.
wr-wq-q3.hint: Use k_T = k₂₀θ^(T−20). For T > 20°C, the rate constant increases.
traps: Using (20 – T) instead of (T – 20) in the exponent — gives a smaller k for higher T, which is backwards
Mixing up θ values for different processes — BOD uses 1.056 (21–30°C), reaeration uses 1.024

wr-wt-q1.statement: A primary clarifier treats a flow of $Q = 2.0 \text{ MGD}$. The tank is circular with a diameter of $60 \text{ ft}$. What is the overflow rate?
wr-wt-q1.eli5: Overflow rate = Q/A. A = π(60)²/4 = 2,827 ft². Q = 2.0 MGD = 2,000,000 gpd. v_o = 2,000,000/2,827 = 708 gpd/ft². This is within the typical range for primary clarifiers (800–1,200), a bit low. The $1{,}415 \text{ gpd/ft}^2$ distractor comes from doubling the correct rate (treating the area as half its true value). The $354 \text{ gpd/ft}^2$ distractor divides the answer by 2 for no reason. The $10{,}610 \text{ gpd/ft}^2$ distractor uses the circumference instead of the area.
wr-wt-q1.hint: Overflow rate = Q/A_surface. Convert MGD to gpd. Area = πD²/4.
traps: Forgetting to convert MGD to gpd (multiply by 1,000,000)
Using the diameter in the area formula without squaring or dividing by 4

wr-wt-q2.statement: An aeration basin treats $Q = 4{,}000 \text{ m}^3\text{/day}$ of wastewater with influent BOD $S_0 = 200 \text{ mg/L}$. The basin volume is $V = 2{,}000 \text{ m}^3$ and MLSS is $X_A = 3{,}000 \text{ mg/L}$. What is the food-to-microorganism (F:M) ratio?
wr-wt-q2.eli5: F:M = QS₀/(VX_A) = (4,000 × 200)/(2,000 × 3,000) = 800,000/6,000,000 = 0.133 ≈ 0.13 day⁻¹. Note that mg/L cancel, leaving m³/day / m³ = day⁻¹. This F:M is on the low end of conventional range (0.2–0.4), closer to extended aeration. The $1.33 \text{ day}^{-1}$ option uses V·X_A with the MLSS scaled down by a factor of ten (a misplaced decimal). The $0.40 \text{ day}^{-1}$ option drops the MLSS term, dividing only by V at the wrong scale. The $0.027 \text{ day}^{-1}$ option mistakenly squares V in the denominator.
wr-wt-q2.hint: F:M = (Q × S₀)/(V × X_A). Make sure units are consistent.
traps: Forgetting to include MLSS (X_A) in the denominator — gives the volumetric loading rate instead of F:M
Getting confused by units — mg/L cancels between S₀ and X_A, leaving 1/time

wr-wt-q3.statement: An activated sludge system has: aeration volume $V = 1{,}500 \text{ m}^3$, MLSS $X_A = 3{,}500 \text{ mg/L}$, waste sludge flow $Q_w = 50 \text{ m}^3\text{/day}$ at concentration $X_w = 10{,}000 \text{ mg/L}$, and effluent flow $Q_e = 5{,}000 \text{ m}^3\text{/day}$ with $X_e = 20 \text{ mg/L}$. What is the solids residence time (SRT)?
wr-wt-q3.eli5: θ_c = VX_A / (Q_wX_w + Q_eX_e) = (1,500 × 3,500) / (50 × 10,000 + 5,000 × 20) = 5,250,000 / (500,000 + 100,000) = 5,250,000 / 600,000 = 8.75 ≈ 8.8 days. This is within the typical range for conventional activated sludge (4–15 days). The 0.3 days choice computes V/Q (HRT = 0.3 days = 7.2 hours) instead of SRT. The 10.5 days choice ignores the effluent solids term (5,250,000 / 500,000 = 10.5 days). The 30.0 days choice uses an incorrect denominator.
wr-wt-q3.hint: SRT = (total solids in system)/(total solids leaving per day). Include both waste sludge and effluent.
traps: Confusing SRT (θ_c, days) with HRT (θ, hours) — SRT divides solids, not volume, by flow
Ignoring the effluent solids term (Q_eX_e) — even low concentrations at high flow rates contribute significantly
Using concentrations without multiplying by flow rates in the denominator

wr-dwt-q1.statement: A rapid sand filter bed is $20\text{ ft}$ long by $15\text{ ft}$ wide and treats a flow of $Q = 1{,}350\text{ gpm}$. What is the filtration (loading) rate?
wr-dwt-q1.eli5: Filtration rate = Q/A_plan. The plan area is 20 × 15 = 300 ft². So v_s = 1,350/300 = 4.5 gpm/ft², comfortably inside the typical rapid-sand range of 2--10 gpm/ft². The 9.0 gpm/ft² option uses only half the area (15 ft × 10 ft = 150 ft²). The 0.22 gpm/ft² option inverts the ratio (A/Q). The 45 gpm/ft² option drops a zero in the area (uses 30 ft² instead of 300 ft²).
wr-dwt-q1.hint: Filtration rate is the flow divided by the filter plan area (length × width).
traps: Using the bed volume or depth instead of the plan (surface) area
Inverting the ratio to get A/Q instead of Q/A

wr-dwt-q2.statement: Raw water exerts a chlorine demand of $2.4\text{ mg/L}$, and the plant must maintain a free residual of $0.6\text{ mg/L}$. For a flow of $Q = 4{,}000\text{ m}^3\text{/day}$, what mass of chlorine must be fed per day?
wr-dwt-q2.eli5: First the dose: Dose = Demand + Residual = 2.4 + 0.6 = 3.0 mg/L. Then the mass feed: since 1 mg/L = 1 g/m³, mass = 3.0 g/m³ × 4,000 m³/day = 12,000 g/day = 12.0 kg/day. The 9.6 kg/day option uses only the demand (2.4) and forgets the residual. The 2.4 kg/day option just echoes the demand value with a wrong conversion. The 120 kg/day option slips a factor of 10 in the unit conversion.
wr-dwt-q2.hint: Dose = demand + residual. Then mass/day = dose (mg/L = g/m³) × flow (m³/day), converted to kg.
traps: Feeding only the residual or only the demand instead of their sum
Botching the mg/L → g/m³ → kg/day conversion

wr-dwt-q3.statement: A chlorine contact basin maintains a free residual of $C = 1.5\text{ mg/L}$. The disinfection guideline requires $CT = 90\text{ mg·min/L}$. What contact time $t_{10}$ is needed to achieve this CT?
wr-dwt-q3.eli5: CT = C × t₁₀, so t₁₀ = CT/C = 90/1.5 = 60 min. The 135 min choice multiplies (90 × 1.5) instead of dividing. The 6 min choice divides by 15 (decimal slip). The 0.017 min choice inverts the whole thing (C/CT).
wr-dwt-q3.hint: Rearrange CT = C × t₁₀ to t₁₀ = CT/C.
traps: Multiplying C by CT instead of dividing
Using the theoretical detention time V/Q in place of t₁₀

wr-wqs-q1.statement: A water sample contains $\text{Ca}^{2+} = 40\text{ mg/L}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+} = 24.3\text{ mg/L}$. Using equivalent weights of $20$ for Ca²⁺ and $12.15$ for Mg²⁺, what is the total hardness expressed as CaCO₃?
wr-wqs-q1.eli5: Convert each ion to CaCO₃ by multiplying by 50/EW. Ca: 40 × (50/20) = 40 × 2.5 = 100. Mg: 24.3 × (50/12.15) = 24.3 × 4.12 = 100. Total = 100 + 100 = 200 mg/L as CaCO₃ (very hard). The 64.3 mg/L option just adds the raw ion concentrations (40 + 24.3) without converting. The 100 mg/L option counts only the calcium. The 150 mg/L option is a partial conversion.
wr-wqs-q1.hint: Multiply each ion by 50/EW, then add. Ca uses 50/20 = 2.5; Mg uses 50/12.15 ≈ 4.12.
traps: Adding raw ion concentrations without converting to CaCO₃
Using the same multiplier for Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ — their equivalent weights differ

wr-wqs-q2.statement: A wastewater treatment plant receives influent with $BOD_5 = 240\text{ mg/L}$ and must meet a secondary-treatment effluent limit of $30\text{ mg/L}$. What overall BOD removal efficiency is required?
wr-wqs-q2.eli5: Removal efficiency = (in − out)/in = (240 − 30)/240 = 210/240 = 0.875 = 87.5%. The 12.5% option is the fraction REMAINING (30/240 = 12.5%), not the fraction removed. The 8.0% option mis-scales the ratio. The 30% option just reports the effluent number (30 mg/L) as a percent.
wr-wqs-q2.hint: Efficiency = (influent − effluent)/influent, expressed as a percent.
traps: Computing the fraction remaining (effluent/influent) instead of the fraction removed
Forgetting to divide by the influent concentration

wr-wqs-q3.statement: Which of the following is an enforceable, health-based PRIMARY drinking water standard under the Safe Drinking Water Act?
wr-wqs-q3.eli5: Arsenic is a toxic contaminant with a legally enforceable, health-based MCL (0.010 mg/L) — a primary standard. Iron, total dissolved solids, and color are all SECONDARY standards: they affect taste, staining, and appearance, not health, and are advisory rather than enforceable.
wr-wqs-q3.hint: Primary standards protect health and are enforceable; secondary standards are aesthetic (taste, color, staining) and advisory.

steps.text: Primary standards are enforceable MCLs that protect human health.
Iron, TDS, and color affect aesthetics (staining, taste, appearance) → secondary, advisory.
Arsenic has a health-based MCL → it is the primary standard.

traps: Assuming any numeric limit is enforceable — secondary standards are advisory
Confusing aesthetic parameters (iron, color, TDS) with health-based contaminants

wr-ocf-ex1.statement: Manning's equation uses the factor $K = 1.486$ in US Customary units and $K = 1.0$ in SI units. What happens to the computed discharge if an engineer accidentally uses $K = 1.0$ with US Customary inputs?

choices.text: The discharge is overestimated by about 49%
The discharge is underestimated by about 33%
The discharge is unaffected because units cancel
The discharge is underestimated by about 50%

wr-ocf-ex1.eli5: If you use $K = 1.0$ instead of 1.486, you get $Q_{wrong} = Q_{correct}/1.486$, which means your answer is about 67% of the correct value. That is an underestimate of about 33%. This is a classic FE trap because forgetting the conversion factor does not produce an obviously wrong answer. The "overestimated by about 49%" choice reverses the direction of the error (1.486/1.0 = 1.486, a 49% overestimate). The "unaffected because units cancel" choice ignores the factor entirely. The "underestimated by about 50%" choice confuses the percentage.
wr-ocf-ex1.hint: Compare $Q$ with $K = 1.0$ to $Q$ with $K = 1.486$. The ratio tells you how far off you are.
traps: Thinking the units cancel out automatically
Confusing underestimate with overestimate

wr-ocf-ex2.statement: A trapezoidal earth channel ($n = 0.022$) has a bottom width of $b = 3\,\text{m}$, side slopes of 2H:1V, and a flow depth of $y = 1.5\,\text{m}$ on a slope of $S = 0.0004$. What is the discharge?
wr-ocf-ex2.eli5: For a trapezoid with 2:1 side slopes: $A = (b + zy)y = (3 + 2 \times 1.5)(1.5) = 6 \times 1.5 = 9.0$ m$^2$. $P = b + 2y\sqrt{1 + z^2} = 3 + 2(1.5)\sqrt{1 + 4} = 3 + 3\sqrt{5} = 3 + 6.708 = 9.708$ m. $R_H = 9.0/9.708 = 0.927$ m. SI units so $K = 1.0$. $Q = (1/0.022)(9.0)(0.927)^{2/3}(0.0004)^{1/2} = 45.45 \times 9.0 \times 0.951 \times 0.02 = 7.8$ m$^3$/s. The 3.2 m³/s choice omits the side slopes from the area. The 7.1 m³/s choice uses $K = 1.486$ (wrong for SI). The 9.5 m³/s choice uses the bottom width alone for the wetted perimeter.
wr-ocf-ex2.hint: For a trapezoid: $A = (b + zy)y$ and $P = b + 2y\sqrt{1+z^2}$. Use $K = 1.0$ for SI.
traps: Forgetting to include the side slopes when computing area and wetted perimeter
Using K = 1.486 with SI units

wr-ocf-ex3.statement: For a circular storm sewer flowing completely full, the hydraulic radius $R_H$ equals:
wr-ocf-ex3.eli5: $R_H = A/P$. For a full circle: $A = \pi D^2/4$ and $P = \pi D$. So $R_H = (\pi D^2/4)/(\pi D) = D/4$. Many students pick $D/2$ because they confuse hydraulic radius with the geometric radius. The hydraulic radius is area divided by wetted perimeter, not the pipe radius. The $D/2$ option is the geometric radius. The $D$ option is the diameter itself. The $\pi D/4$ option is the area divided by $D$, not by $\pi D$.
wr-ocf-ex3.hint: Hydraulic radius = $A/P$. For a full pipe, $A = \pi D^2/4$ and $P = \pi D$.
traps: Confusing hydraulic radius (D/4) with geometric radius (D/2)

wr-ocf-ex4.statement: A rectangular concrete channel ($n = 0.013$) must carry $Q = 50\,\text{ft}^3/\text{s}$ on a slope of $S = 0.0009$. If the channel is $6\,\text{ft}$ wide, what is the approximate normal depth?
wr-ocf-ex4.eli5: This requires trial and error. Manning's: $Q = (1.486/n)\,A\,R_H^{2/3}\,S^{1/2}$. Try $y = 2.1$ ft: $A = 6 \times 2.1 = 12.6$ ft$^2$, $P = 6 + 2(2.1) = 10.2$ ft, $R_H = 12.6/10.2 = 1.235$ ft. $Q = (1.486/0.013)(12.6)(1.235)^{2/3}(0.0009)^{1/2} = 114.3 \times 12.6 \times 1.151 \times 0.03 = 49.8$ cfs. That is essentially 50 cfs, so the normal depth is approximately 2.1 ft. The 1.6 ft choice underestimates by using $K = 1.0$ instead of 1.486. The 3.1 ft choice overestimates area. The 4.0 ft choice assumes $R_H = y$.
wr-ocf-ex4.hint: Set up Manning's equation and solve for depth by trial. Remember $K = 1.486$ for USCS.
traps: Forgetting the USCS factor $K = 1.486$ shifts the answer significantly
Assuming $R_H$ equals the depth $y$ instead of computing $A/P$

wr-ecf-ex1.statement: A rectangular channel is 3 m wide with a flow rate of $12\,\text{m}^3/\text{s}$. What is the critical depth?
wr-ecf-ex1.eli5: For a rectangular channel, critical depth is $y_c = (q^2/g)^{1/3}$ where $q = Q/b$ is the unit discharge. $q = 12/3 = 4$ m$^2$/s. $y_c = (16/9.81)^{1/3} = (1.631)^{1/3} = 1.18$ m. The trap is using $Q$ instead of $q$ (forgetting to divide by width).
traps: Using total discharge $Q$ instead of unit discharge $q$
Forgetting to take the cube root

wr-ecf-ex2.statement: At critical flow conditions in an open channel, the Froude number equals:
wr-ecf-ex2.eli5: The Froude number is the ratio of flow velocity to wave speed. At critical flow, $Fr = 1$ exactly. $Fr < 1$ is subcritical (tranquil) flow. $Fr > 1$ is supercritical (rapid) flow. This is one of those definitions you just need to know -- it shows up frequently on the FE.
wr-ecf-ex2.hint: Recall the definition of the Froude number and what critical flow means.

steps.text: This means the flow velocity equals the wave propagation speed.

traps: Confusing Froude number with Reynolds number

wr-ecf-ex3.statement: A hydraulic jump forms in a rectangular channel. The upstream supercritical depth is $y_1 = 0.3\,\text{m}$ and the upstream Froude number is $Fr_1 = 4.0$. What is the conjugate (downstream) depth $y_2$?
wr-ecf-ex3.eli5: Use the conjugate depth formula: $y_2 = (y_1/2)(-1 + \sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2}) = (0.3/2)(-1 + \sqrt{1 + 8 \times 16}) = 0.15 \times (-1 + \sqrt{129}) = 0.15 \times (-1 + 11.36) = 0.15 \times 10.36 = 1.55$ m. The downstream subcritical depth is about 5 times the upstream depth. The 1.20 m option corresponds to using $Fr_1 = 3$ instead of 4. The 3.60 m option comes from multiplying $y_1$ by $Fr_1^2$ directly. The 0.85 m option drops the factor of 8 inside the radical.
traps: Omitting the factor of 8 multiplying $Fr^2$ inside the radical
Forgetting the $-1$ term inside the parentheses

wr-ecf-ex4.statement: In a rectangular open channel, flow transitions from subcritical to supercritical. Which of the following best describes what happens to the specific energy and depth?

choices.text: Specific energy decreases to a minimum at critical depth, then increases as depth continues to decrease
Specific energy increases continuously as depth decreases
Specific energy stays constant while the Froude number increases past 1
Depth increases past critical depth while velocity decreases

wr-ecf-ex4.eli5: The specific energy diagram is a curve with two branches. As you move from subcritical (deep, slow) toward critical depth, the specific energy drops to a minimum. If the flow continues to supercritical (shallow, fast), the kinetic energy term grows rapidly and E increases again. So there is a minimum at the critical point. The "specific energy increases continuously as depth decreases" choice ignores the minimum and says it only goes up. The "specific energy stays constant while the Froude number increases past 1" choice describes a transition at constant energy, which would mean the channel changes between two alternate depths, not a smooth transition. The "depth increases past critical depth while velocity decreases" choice describes the wrong direction of change.
wr-ecf-ex4.hint: Think about the specific energy diagram: it has an upper limb (subcritical), a lower limb (supercritical), and a minimum at critical depth.

steps.text: At critical depth, $E$ is at its minimum value $E_{min}$.
On the subcritical limb (above $y_c$), decreasing $y$ decreases $E$ toward $E_{min}$.
On the supercritical limb (below $y_c$), decreasing $y$ further increases $E$ because the velocity head dominates.

traps: Assuming specific energy is always monotonically related to depth
Confusing the specific energy diagram with the depth-discharge relationship

wr-psw-ex1.statement: In the Hazen-Williams equation, the roughness coefficient $C$ for a new PVC pipe is 150, while a 20-year-old cast iron pipe has $C = 100$. Which statement correctly describes how $C$ relates to pipe performance?

choices.text: $C$ only affects velocity, not discharge, because area is independent of roughness
Higher $C$ means a rougher pipe interior and greater head loss for the same flow
Higher $C$ has the same meaning as higher Manning's $n$ — both indicate smoother surfaces
Higher $C$ means a smoother pipe interior and greater flow capacity for the same head loss

wr-psw-ex1.eli5: In Hazen-Williams, $C$ appears directly in the numerator: $v = k\,C\,R_H^{0.63}\,S^{0.54}$. A larger $C$ means higher velocity and more flow for the same pipe and gradient. This is the opposite of Manning's $n$, where higher $n$ means rougher and slower. The choice claiming $C$ only affects velocity forgets that $Q = vA$, so anything that increases $v$ also increases $Q$. The choice that higher $C$ means a rougher pipe reverses the meaning. The choice equating $C$ with Manning's $n$ confuses Hazen-Williams $C$ with Manning's $n$ — they work in opposite directions.
wr-psw-ex1.hint: Look at where $C$ appears in the Hazen-Williams equation — is it in the numerator or denominator?

steps.text: $C$ is in the numerator, so larger $C$ gives larger $v$ and therefore larger $Q = vA$.
Higher $C$ = smoother pipe = less friction = more flow.

traps: Confusing Hazen-Williams C (higher = smoother) with Manning's n (higher = rougher)

wr-psw-ex2.statement: A contracted rectangular weir has a crest length of $L = 4.0\text{ ft}$ and a head of $H = 1.2\text{ ft}$ above the crest. Using the contracted weir formula with $C = 3.33$, what is the discharge?
wr-psw-ex2.eli5: For a contracted rectangular weir: $Q = C(L - 0.2H)H^{3/2}$. Effective length $= L - 0.2H = 4.0 - 0.24 = 3.76$ ft. $H^{3/2} = (1.2)^{3/2} = 1.2 \times \sqrt{1.2} = 1.2 \times 1.095 = 1.315$. $Q = 3.33 \times 3.76 \times 1.315 = 16.5$ cfs. The 17.5 cfs choice uses the suppressed formula $Q = CLH^{3/2} = 3.33 \times 4.0 \times 1.315 = 17.5$ without the contraction correction. The 21.9 cfs choice uses $H^{5/2}$ instead of $H^{3/2}$. The 9.1 cfs choice uses the SI coefficient $C = 1.84$.
wr-psw-ex2.hint: For a contracted weir: $Q = C(L - 0.2H)H^{3/2}$. Subtract the contraction correction from the crest length before multiplying.
traps: Using the suppressed weir formula (no contraction correction) when the problem says contracted
Using H^(5/2) — that exponent is for V-notch weirs, not rectangular

wr-psw-ex3.statement: A 90-degree V-notch weir and a suppressed rectangular weir are both measuring discharge with the same head $H$ above their respective crests. If $H$ doubles, which statement is correct about the increase in discharge?

choices.text: The rectangular weir discharge increases more because it has a wider opening
Both discharges increase by the same factor because weir equations are linear in $H$
The V-notch discharge increases by a factor of $2^{5/2} \approx 5.66$, while the rectangular increases by $2^{3/2} \approx 2.83$
The V-notch discharge increases by a factor of $2^{3/2}$ and the rectangular by $2^{5/2}$

wr-psw-ex3.eli5: V-notch: $Q = CH^{5/2}$, so doubling $H$ multiplies $Q$ by $2^{5/2} = 4\sqrt{2} = 5.66$. Rectangular: $Q = CLH^{3/2}$, so doubling $H$ multiplies $Q$ by $2^{3/2} = 2\sqrt{2} = 2.83$. The V-notch is more sensitive to head changes because it has a higher exponent. This is why V-notch weirs are preferred for measuring low flows — small changes in head produce larger, more measurable changes in discharge. The "wider opening" choice confuses geometry with the exponent sensitivity. The "same factor / linear in H" choice ignores the nonlinear exponents. The choice giving the V-notch 2^{3/2} and the rectangular 2^{5/2} swaps the exponents.
wr-psw-ex3.hint: Compare the exponents on $H$ in each weir formula. How does $Q$ scale when $H$ doubles?

steps.text: The V-notch weir is more sensitive to changes in head.

traps: Swapping the exponents between rectangular (3/2) and V-notch (5/2)
Thinking weir discharge is linearly proportional to head

wr-psw-ex4.statement: A 10-inch diameter new cast iron pipe ($C = 130$) is $800\text{ ft}$ long with a head loss of $h_f = 4.0\text{ ft}$. Using $Q = k_1 C A R_H^{0.63} S_v^{0.54}$ with $k_1 = 1.318$ and $R_H = D/4$ for a full pipe, what is the discharge?
wr-psw-ex4.eli5: $D = 10$ in. $= 0.833$ ft. $A = \pi(0.833)^2/4 = 0.545$ ft$^2$. $R_H = D/4 = 0.208$ ft. $S = h_f/L = 4.0/800 = 0.005$. $v = 1.318 \times 130 \times (0.208)^{0.63} \times (0.005)^{0.54}$. $(0.208)^{0.63} = 0.372$. $(0.005)^{0.54} = 0.0572$. $v = 171.3 \times 0.372 \times 0.0572 = 3.65$ fps. $Q = v \times A = 3.65 \times 0.545 = 2.0$ cfs. The 3.1 cfs distractor uses $R_H = D/2$ instead of $D/4$, which inflates the hydraulic radius and gives a higher $Q$. The 1.3 cfs distractor accidentally uses the SI factor $k_1 = 0.849$ instead of 1.318. The 0.73 cfs distractor results from a low-flow error such as misreading the hydraulic-radius or area term.
wr-psw-ex4.hint: Convert the diameter to feet first. Then find $R_H = D/4$, $A = \pi D^2/4$, and $S_v = h_f/L$.
traps: Using $R_H = D/2$ (geometric radius) instead of $R_H = D/4$ (hydraulic radius)
Forgetting to convert the diameter from inches to feet before computing $A$ and $R_H$

wr-rr-ex1.statement: A 30-acre parking lot has a runoff coefficient of $C = 0.70$. The 10-year design rainfall intensity for the site's time of concentration is $I = 5.5\text{ in./hr}$. What is the peak runoff using the Rational Method?
wr-rr-ex1.eli5: $Q = CIA = 0.70 \times 5.5 \times 30 = 115.5$ cfs. Straight plug-and-chug with no unit conversion needed since 1 acre-in./hr is approximately 1 cfs. The 165.0 cfs choice ignores $C$ and computes $Q = IA = 5.5 \times 30 = 165$. The 57.8 cfs choice divides by 2 for no valid reason. The 11.6 cfs choice converts acres to hectares unnecessarily.
wr-rr-ex1.hint: Q = CIA. The units work out directly — no conversion factor needed.
traps: Trying to convert units — the Rational Method is set up so 1 acre-in./hr is approximately 1 cfs

wr-rr-ex2.statement: A watershed has a curve number of $CN = 75$. A storm produces $P = 6.0\text{ in.}$ of total rainfall. What is the runoff depth using the SCS/NRCS method?
wr-rr-ex2.eli5: First find $S$: $S = 1000/CN - 10 = 1000/75 - 10 = 13.33 - 10 = 3.33$ in. Initial abstraction $= 0.2S = 0.667$ in. Since $P = 6.0 > 0.667$, runoff occurs. $Q = (P - 0.2S)^2/(P + 0.8S) = (6.0 - 0.667)^2/(6.0 + 2.667) = (5.333)^2/8.667 = 28.44/8.667 = 3.28$ in. The 2.67 in. choice uses $(P - S)$ instead of $(P - 0.2S)$ in the numerator. The 6.00 in. choice assumes all rainfall becomes runoff. The 4.50 in. choice uses $P \times CN/100$ which is not the SCS formula.
wr-rr-ex2.hint: First compute $S = 1000/CN - 10$, then check that $P > 0.2S$, then plug into $Q = (P - 0.2S)^2/(P + 0.8S)$.
traps: Using P instead of (P - 0.2S) in the numerator — you must subtract the initial abstraction
Reporting Q in cfs — the SCS equation gives runoff depth in inches, not discharge

wr-rr-ex3.statement: A watershed has a curve number of $CN = 98$ (impervious). Another has $CN = 55$ (forest on sandy soil). Which statement is correct about the SCS retention parameter $S$?

choices.text: Higher CN gives higher $S$, meaning the watershed retains more rainfall and produces less runoff
Higher CN gives lower $S$, meaning the watershed retains less rainfall and produces more runoff
$S$ is independent of CN — it depends only on soil type
Both watersheds have the same $S$ because $S$ only varies with storm duration

wr-rr-ex3.eli5: $S = 1000/CN - 10$. For $CN = 98$: $S = 1000/98 - 10 = 0.20$ in. (almost no retention). For $CN = 55$: $S = 1000/55 - 10 = 8.18$ in. (lots of retention). Higher $CN$ means a more impervious surface, so less water is retained in the soil and more becomes runoff. The choice claiming higher CN gives higher S reverses the relationship. The choice claiming S depends only on soil type ignores that $S$ is computed directly from $CN$. The choice claiming both have the same S because S varies only with storm duration confuses $S$ with storm parameters.
wr-rr-ex3.hint: Look at the formula $S = 1000/CN - 10$. What happens to $S$ when CN increases toward 100?

steps.text: Higher CN means lower S — less water retained, more runoff.

traps: Thinking higher CN means more retention — it is the opposite: higher CN = more impervious = more runoff

wr-rr-ex4.statement: In the hydrologic mass balance equation $P + Q_{in} - Q_{out} + Q_g - E_s - T_s - I = \Delta S_s$, a detention pond receives stormwater inflow but has no groundwater contribution, no evaporation, no transpiration, and no infiltration. During a storm, the inflow exceeds the outflow. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Storage is increasing because $Q_{in} > Q_{out}$ and all other terms are zero, so $\Delta S_s > 0$
Storage is decreasing because the pond is releasing water through the outlet
Storage is unchanged because the mass balance always equals zero
Storage depends on precipitation, not inflow and outflow

wr-rr-ex4.eli5: With $P = 0$ (rain falls on the watershed, not directly counted here), $Q_g = 0$, $E_s = 0$, $T_s = 0$, and $I = 0$, the balance simplifies to $Q_{in} - Q_{out} = \Delta S$. Since $Q_{in} > Q_{out}$, $\Delta S > 0$, meaning storage is increasing. The pond is filling up, which is exactly the purpose of detention — temporarily store peak flows to reduce downstream flooding. The "storage is decreasing" choice is wrong because although water is leaving, more is entering. The "storage is unchanged" choice confuses mass balance with zero change. The "storage depends on precipitation" choice ignores that inflow/outflow are the dominant terms for a pond.
wr-rr-ex4.hint: Simplify the mass balance by setting all zero terms to zero. What sign does $\Delta S_s$ have when $Q_{in} > Q_{out}$?

steps.text: Simplify with all zero terms removed:
Positive $\Delta S_s$ means storage is increasing — the pond is filling.

wr-rr-ex4.handbookFormula: P + Q_{in} - Q_{out} + Q_g - E_s - T_s - I = \Delta S_s
traps: Confusing "outflow exists" with "storage decreasing" — storage increases whenever inflow exceeds outflow
Assuming the mass balance equation always equals zero — it equals the change in storage, not zero

wr-hw-ex1.statement: A 1-hour unit hydrograph has a peak of $400\text{ cfs}$ and a time base of $6\text{ hours}$. If the storm duration changes to 2 hours (but the same watershed), what happens to the unit hydrograph?

choices.text: The peak doubles to 800 cfs because the storm is twice as long
A different unit hydrograph must be derived — the 1-hour UH cannot be used directly for a 2-hour storm
The peak stays at 400 cfs because the unit hydrograph is independent of storm duration
The time base halves to 3 hours because the storm is shorter relative to the watershed

wr-hw-ex1.eli5: A unit hydrograph is defined for a specific storm duration. A 1-hour UH gives the response to 1 inch of excess rainfall applied over 1 hour. For a 2-hour storm, you need a 2-hour UH, which has a different shape (typically a lower peak and longer time base). You can derive the 2-hour UH from the 1-hour UH using S-curve or superposition methods, but you cannot just reuse the 1-hour UH. The "peak doubles to 800 cfs" choice confuses scaling by rainfall depth with changing duration. The "peak stays at 400 cfs" choice ignores the duration dependency. The "time base halves to 3 hours" choice inverts the relationship.
wr-hw-ex1.hint: A unit hydrograph is defined for a specific rainfall duration. Changing the duration requires a new UH.

steps.text: A unit hydrograph is tied to a specific storm duration.
The 1-hour UH gives the response to 1 inch of excess rain over 1 hour.
For a 2-hour storm, a 2-hour UH must be derived (via S-curve or superposition).

wr-hw-ex1.handbookFormula: \text{Unit hydrograph: 1 unit of rainfall over specified duration}
traps: Confusing scaling by rainfall depth (multiply ordinates) with changing the storm duration (requires a new UH)

wr-hw-ex2.statement: A 1-hour unit hydrograph for a watershed has a peak discharge of $300\text{ cfs}$. A storm produces $2.5\text{ in.}$ of excess rainfall in 1 hour. What is the peak discharge of the direct runoff hydrograph?
wr-hw-ex2.eli5: The unit hydrograph represents the response to 1 inch of excess rainfall. To get the hydrograph for 2.5 inches, multiply every ordinate by 2.5. Peak $= 300 \times 2.5 = 750$ cfs. The time axis does not change — only the magnitudes scale. The 120 cfs choice divides instead of multiplying ($300/2.5 = 120$). The 300 cfs choice does not scale at all (assumes 1 inch). The 600 cfs choice multiplies by 2 instead of 2.5.
wr-hw-ex2.hint: The unit hydrograph gives the response to 1 inch of excess rainfall. Scale linearly for other amounts.

steps.text: UH peak for 1 inch of excess rainfall:

wr-hw-ex2.handbookFormula: \text{Unit hydrograph: 1 unit of rainfall over specified duration}
traps: Dividing by the rainfall depth instead of multiplying
Trying to adjust the time axis — only ordinates scale, not the time base

wr-hw-ex3.statement: For the Rational Method, the design storm duration is set equal to the time of concentration ($t_c$). What happens to the peak discharge $Q$ if a storm duration shorter than $t_c$ is used?

choices.text: $Q$ increases because shorter storms have higher rainfall intensities from the IDF curve
$Q$ decreases because not all of the watershed area contributes flow to the outlet simultaneously
$Q$ stays the same because the runoff coefficient and area do not change
$Q$ doubles for every halving of storm duration

wr-hw-ex3.eli5: At duration = t_c, the entire watershed contributes flow to the outlet simultaneously, which maximizes Q. If the storm is shorter than t_c, parts of the watershed that are farther away have not had time to contribute their runoff to the outlet. Even though a shorter storm has higher intensity (from the IDF curve), the reduced contributing area more than offsets it. The Rational Method specifically uses duration = t_c to capture the maximum peak. The choice that Q increases is partially true (shorter storms are more intense) but misses that not all area contributes. The choice that Q stays the same ignores the time dimension. The choice that Q doubles for every halving of duration has no physical basis.
wr-hw-ex3.hint: Think about what $t_c$ represents — the travel time from the farthest point. What happens if the storm ends before that water arrives?

steps.text: At $t_c$, the entire watershed contributes flow simultaneously.
If storm $< t_c$, distant areas have not contributed yet, reducing $Q$.
This is why the Rational Method sets storm duration $= t_c$ for maximum $Q$.

traps: Thinking shorter storms always produce higher Q because of higher intensity — the reduced contributing area matters more

wr-hw-ex4.statement: A detention pond receives a constant inflow of $I = 120\text{ cfs}$ during the peak of a storm. The pond outlet discharges $O = 45\text{ cfs}$. After $2\text{ hours}$, how much water has accumulated in the pond?
wr-hw-ex4.eli5: $I - O = \Delta S/\Delta t$, so $\Delta S/\Delta t = 120 - 45 = 75$ cfs $= 75$ ft$^3$/s. Over 2 hours: $\Delta S = 75 \times (2 \times 3600) = 75 \times 7200 = 540{,}000$ ft$^3$. You must convert hours to seconds because the flow rates are in cfs (ft$^3$ per second). The 75 cfs choice gives the storage rate but not the accumulated volume. The 864,000 ft$^3$ choice uses $I \times t$ without subtracting outflow ($120 \times 7200 = 864{,}000$). The 324,000 ft$^3$ choice uses $O \times t$ ($45 \times 7200 = 324{,}000$).
wr-hw-ex4.hint: Use $I - O = \Delta S/\Delta t$. Find the net storage rate first, then multiply by time (convert hours to seconds).
traps: Forgetting to convert hours to seconds when flow rates are in cfs
Reporting the storage rate (75 cfs) instead of the accumulated volume

wr-gw-ex1.statement: An aquifer has a hydraulic conductivity of $K = 2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s}$, a hydraulic gradient of $i = 0.01$, and an effective porosity of $n = 0.25$. A technician reports the groundwater velocity as $2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m/s}$. What error did the technician make?

choices.text: The technician multiplied by porosity instead of dividing, making the answer too small
The technician reported the Darcy velocity ($q = Ki$) instead of the seepage velocity ($v = q/n$), which is 4 times larger
The technician used the correct formula but forgot to square the gradient
There is no error — this is the correct seepage velocity

wr-gw-ex1.eli5: Darcy velocity: $q = Ki = 2 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.01 = 2 \times 10^{-6}$ m/s. That is what the technician reported. But the actual seepage velocity is $v = q/n = 2 \times 10^{-6}/0.25 = 8 \times 10^{-6}$ m/s, which is 4 times larger. The Darcy velocity treats the entire cross-section as if water flows through all of it, but water only moves through the pore spaces. Dividing by porosity corrects for this. The "multiplied by porosity" choice describes multiplying by $n$, which would give an even smaller value ($5 \times 10^{-7}$). The "forgot to square the gradient" choice has no basis. The "no error" choice is wrong because $2 \times 10^{-6}$ is the Darcy velocity, not the seepage velocity.
wr-gw-ex1.hint: Compute both $q = Ki$ and $v = q/n$. Which one matches the reported value?

steps.text: The reported value matches $q$, not $v$. The seepage velocity is 4 times larger.

traps: Confusing Darcy velocity with seepage velocity — seepage velocity is always larger because water only flows through pores

wr-gw-ex2.statement: A confined aquifer has transmissivity $T = 0.002\text{ m}^2\text{/s}$. A pumping well shows piezometric heads of $h_1 = 42\text{ m}$ at $r_1 = 0.3\text{ m}$ and $h_2 = 50\text{ m}$ at $r_2 = 150\text{ m}$. What is the pumping rate using the Thiem equation?
wr-gw-ex2.eli5: Thiem equation for a confined aquifer: $Q = 2\pi T(h_2 - h_1)/\ln(r_2/r_1)$. $Q = 2\pi(0.002)(50 - 42)/\ln(150/0.3) = 2\pi(0.002)(8)/\ln(500) = 0.1005/6.215 = 0.016$ m$^3$/s. The 0.032 m$^3$/s choice uses $h^2$ differences (Dupuit formula for unconfined) instead of linear $h$. The 0.008 m$^3$/s choice uses $\pi$ instead of $2\pi$ (missing the factor of 2). The 0.0036 m$^3$/s choice uses log base 10 instead of natural log.
wr-gw-ex2.hint: For a confined aquifer, use Thiem: $Q = 2\pi T(h_2 - h_1)/\ln(r_2/r_1)$. Use linear heads (not squared).
traps: Using Dupuit ($h^2$ differences) for a confined aquifer — Thiem uses linear $h$
Using log base 10 instead of natural log — $\ln(500) = 6.215$, not $\log(500) = 2.699$

wr-gw-ex3.statement: A well pumps from an unconfined aquifer using Dupuit's formula: $Q = \pi K(h_2^2 - h_1^2)/\ln(r_2/r_1)$. A student mistakenly applies the Thiem equation (linear $h$) instead. Compared to the correct answer, the student's computed $Q$ will be:

choices.text: Too high, because using linear heads overestimates the driving force
Too low, because $(h_2 - h_1) < (h_2^2 - h_1^2)/h_{avg}$ when the drawdown is large relative to the saturated thickness
The same, because both formulas give identical results
It depends only on whether $r_1 < r_2$ or $r_1 > r_2$

wr-gw-ex3.eli5: Dupuit uses $h^2$ differences: $h_2^2 - h_1^2 = (h_2 + h_1)(h_2 - h_1)$. The Thiem equation uses $h_2 - h_1$. The Dupuit formula effectively multiplies the head difference by the sum of the heads $(h_2 + h_1)$ (twice the average saturated thickness), which accounts for the fact that the flow area decreases as the water table drops near the well. Using linear $h$ underestimates this effect, giving a lower $Q$. The two formulas only agree when drawdown is very small compared to the total saturated thickness. The "too high" choice reverses the direction. The "both formulas give identical results" choice is wrong for unconfined aquifers. The "depends only on whether $r_1 < r_2$" choice has no physical basis.
wr-gw-ex3.hint: Factor $h_2^2 - h_1^2 = (h_2 + h_1)(h_2 - h_1)$. Compare this to just $(h_2 - h_1)$.

steps.text: Dupuit has the extra factor $(h_2 + h_1)$, so using Thiem underestimates $Q$.

traps: Thinking linear and quadratic head formulas give the same result — they only agree for very small drawdowns

wr-gw-ex4.statement: Groundwater flows through a sand layer with $K = 8 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m/s}$. The hydraulic gradient is $i = 0.015$ and the effective porosity is $n = 0.35$. A contamination source is $630\text{ m}$ upgradient. How long will it take the contamination front to reach the monitoring well? (Assume advection only.)
wr-gw-ex4.eli5: First find the Darcy velocity: $q = Ki = 8 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.015 = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ m/s. Then the seepage velocity: $v = q/n = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}/0.35 = 3.43 \times 10^{-5}$ m/s. Travel time $= \text{distance}/\text{velocity} = 630/3.43 \times 10^{-5} = 1.837 \times 10^7$ seconds. Convert to hours: $1.837 \times 10^7/3600 = 5{,}100$ hours (about 213 days). Contaminants travel at the seepage velocity, not the Darcy velocity. The 14,600 hours option uses the Darcy velocity (not dividing by porosity) — about 3 times too long. The 1,460 hours option divides by 10 instead of converting properly (likely a decimal error). The 18,400 hours option reports the raw seconds value (1.837e7) with the thousands dropped, never converting to hours.
wr-gw-ex4.hint: Find the seepage velocity ($v = Ki/n$), then compute $t = \text{distance}/v$. Convert seconds to hours.
traps: Using Darcy velocity instead of seepage velocity — contamination moves at the actual pore velocity, which is faster
Forgetting to convert seconds to hours in the final answer

wr-wq-ex1.statement: A wastewater sample has an ultimate BOD of $L_0 = 250\text{ mg/L}$ and a decay rate of $k = 0.23\text{ day}^{-1}$ (base $e$). What is the BOD exerted at day 3 ($BOD_3$)?
wr-wq-ex1.eli5: $BOD_3 = L_0(1 - e^{-kt}) = 250(1 - e^{-0.23 \times 3}) = 250(1 - e^{-0.69}) = 250(1 - 0.502) = 250 \times 0.498 = 125$ mg/L. About half the ultimate BOD has been exerted by day 3. The 250 mg/L choice gives the ultimate BOD, not the 3-day value. The 63 mg/L choice is roughly $BOD_1$ (one-day exertion). The 188 mg/L choice is closer to the $BOD_5$ range, not $BOD_3$.
traps: Confusing BOD exerted with BOD remaining — the remaining is L0 x e^(-kt) = 125, which happens to equal the exerted value at this point

wr-wq-ex2.statement: In the Streeter-Phelps dissolved oxygen sag model, the critical point (minimum DO) occurs where:

choices.text: The BOD has been completely consumed
The rate of deoxygenation (BOD consumption) equals the rate of reaeration from the atmosphere
The stream velocity reaches its minimum value

wr-wq-ex2.eli5: The DO sag curve has two competing processes: deoxygenation (organisms consuming oxygen as they decompose BOD) and reaeration (atmospheric oxygen dissolving into the water). Upstream of the critical point, deoxygenation dominates and DO drops. At the critical point, the two rates are exactly equal — DO stops dropping. Downstream of it, reaeration dominates and DO recovers. The "BOD completely consumed" choice is wrong because significant BOD may remain at the critical point. The "DO reaches zero" choice is wrong because DO rarely reaches zero in practice. The "minimum stream velocity" choice confuses velocity with the oxygen balance.
wr-wq-ex2.hint: The oxygen deficit is increasing when deoxygenation exceeds reaeration, and decreasing when reaeration exceeds deoxygenation. The minimum DO is where they balance.

steps.text: At the critical point: $k_d L = k_r D$, so $dD/dt = 0$ and the deficit stops growing.

traps: Thinking DO must reach zero at the critical point — it is simply the minimum, which may still be well above zero

wr-wq-ex3.statement: A lab measures $BOD_5 = 150\text{ mg/L}$ with a rate constant of $k = 0.15\text{ day}^{-1}$ (base $e$). What is the ultimate BOD ($L_0$)?
wr-wq-ex3.eli5: Rearrange: $L_0 = BOD_5/(1 - e^{-kt}) = 150/(1 - e^{-0.15 \times 5}) = 150/(1 - e^{-0.75}) = 150/(1 - 0.472) = 150/0.528 = 284$ mg/L. At this slower decay rate, the 5-day test captures only about 53% of the ultimate BOD, so $L_0$ is nearly double the $BOD_5$. The 150 mg/L choice assumes $BOD_5 = L_0$. The 225 mg/L choice uses $L_0 = 1.5 \times BOD_5$ (a rough approximation, but not correct here). The 750 mg/L choice multiplies by 5.
wr-wq-ex3.hint: Rearrange $BOD_t = L_0(1 - e^{-kt})$ to solve for $L_0$.
traps: Assuming BOD5 equals the ultimate BOD — the 5-day test only captures a fraction of the total
Using the wrong base for k — make sure k is base e, not base 10

wr-wq-ex4.statement: A BOD rate constant at 20\degree\text{C} is $k_{20} = 0.20\text{ day}^{-1}$. Using $k_T = k_{20}\theta^{(T-20)}$ with $\theta = 1.056$ for temperatures above 20\degree\text{C}, what is the effect on $k$ at $T = 30\degree\text{C}$?

choices.text: $k$ increases to about $0.34\text{ day}^{-1}$ because higher temperature accelerates biological decomposition
$k$ decreases to about $0.12\text{ day}^{-1}$ because warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen
$k$ stays at $0.20\text{ day}^{-1}$ because the rate constant is independent of temperature
$k$ increases to about $0.40\text{ day}^{-1}$ because the exponent is $(T - 20) = 10$

wr-wq-ex4.eli5: $k_{30} = k_{20} \times \theta^{(T-20)} = 0.20 \times 1.056^{10} = 0.20 \times 1.724 = 0.345$, approximately $0.34$ day$^{-1}$. Higher temperature speeds up microbial metabolism, so organic matter decomposes faster and the BOD rate constant increases. While it is true that warmer water holds less DO (which affects the oxygen balance), the rate constant itself increases with temperature. The "decreases to about 0.12" choice confuses the effect on DO saturation with the effect on $k$. The "stays at 0.20" choice ignores temperature dependence entirely. The "increases to about 0.40" choice overestimates by using a larger $\theta$ value or miscalculating the power.
wr-wq-ex4.hint: Plug in $T = 30$ to get the exponent $(30 - 20) = 10$. Then compute $1.056^{10}$.
traps: Confusing the effect on k (increases) with the effect on DO saturation (decreases) at higher temperatures
Using (20 - T) instead of (T - 20) in the exponent, which gives a smaller k for higher T

wr-wt-ex1.statement: A secondary clarifier treats a flow of $Q = 1.5\text{ MGD}$. The tank is circular with a diameter of $50\text{ ft}$. What is the overflow rate?
wr-wt-ex1.eli5: Overflow rate $= Q/A$. $A = \pi(50)^2/4 = 1{,}963$ ft$^2$. $Q = 1.5$ MGD $= 1{,}500{,}000$ gpd. $v_o = 1{,}500{,}000/1{,}963 = 764$ gpd/ft$^2$. This falls within the typical range for secondary clarifiers (400--800 gpd/ft$^2$). The 1{,}528 distractor divides $Q$ by half the surface area. The 382 distractor halves the correct overflow rate. The 30{,}000 distractor forgets to square the diameter in the area formula (uses $A \propto D$ instead of $D^2$).
wr-wt-ex1.hint: Overflow rate = $Q/A_{surface}$. Convert MGD to gpd and compute the circular area.
traps: Forgetting to convert MGD to gpd — 1 MGD = 1,000,000 gpd
Using the diameter without squaring it in the area formula

wr-wt-ex2.statement: A settling basin has an overflow rate of $v_o = 600\text{ gpd/ft}^2$. Particle A has a settling velocity of $800\text{ gpd/ft}^2$ and Particle B has a settling velocity of $400\text{ gpd/ft}^2$. Which particles are removed?

choices.text: Both particles are completely removed because both are heavier than water
Particle A is completely removed; Particle B is only partially removed
Neither particle is removed because the overflow rate is positive
Particle B is completely removed; Particle A is only partially removed

wr-wt-ex2.eli5: The overflow rate acts as a threshold: any particle with $v_s > v_o$ will settle to the bottom before being carried out, so it is completely removed. Particle A: $v_s = 800 > 600$, so it settles faster than the upward flow velocity and is fully captured. Particle B: $v_s = 400 < 600$, so some of these particles will be carried over the weir. The fraction removed is roughly $v_s/v_o = 400/600 = 67\%$. The "both completely removed" choice ignores the overflow rate criterion. The "neither removed" choice misunderstands what overflow rate means. The "B removed, A partial" choice reverses the comparison.
wr-wt-ex2.hint: A particle is completely removed if its settling velocity exceeds the overflow rate ($v_s > v_o$).

steps.text: Particle A: $v_s = 800 > v_o = 600$, so it is completely removed.
Particle B: $v_s = 400 < v_o = 600$, so it is only partially removed.

traps: Reversing the comparison — particles with v_s > v_o are removed, not the other way around

wr-wt-ex3.statement: An aeration basin treats $Q = 5{,}000\text{ m}^3\text{/day}$ of wastewater with influent BOD $S_0 = 180\text{ mg/L}$. The basin volume is $V = 3{,}000\text{ m}^3$ and MLSS is $X_A = 2{,}500\text{ mg/L}$. What is the food-to-microorganism (F:M) ratio?
wr-wt-ex3.eli5: $F{:}M = Q \times S_0/(V \times X_A) = (5{,}000 \times 180)/(3{,}000 \times 2{,}500) = 900{,}000/7{,}500{,}000 = 0.12$ day$^{-1}$. The mg/L units cancel between $S_0$ and $X_A$, leaving m$^3$/day divided by m$^3$, which gives day$^{-1}$. This F:M is below the conventional range (0.2--0.4), suggesting extended aeration. The $1.20\text{ day}^{-1}$ choice inverts some terms. The $0.30\text{ day}^{-1}$ choice divides only by $V$ (ignores $X_A$). The $0.036\text{ day}^{-1}$ choice squares the volume in the denominator.
wr-wt-ex3.hint: F:M = $(Q \times S_0)/(V \times X_A)$. Make sure all units are consistent.
traps: Forgetting to include MLSS (X_A) in the denominator
Getting confused by units — mg/L cancels between S_0 and X_A, leaving 1/time

wr-wt-ex4.statement: An activated sludge plant operator reports an SRT ($\theta_c$) of $8\text{ hours}$ and an HRT ($\theta$) of $10\text{ days}$. Is this plausible?

choices.text: No — SRT is always much longer than HRT. The values are likely swapped.
Yes — SRT can be shorter than HRT if the sludge is wasted rapidly
Yes — SRT and HRT are independent parameters that can take any values
No — SRT and HRT must always be equal in a properly designed system

wr-wt-ex4.eli5: SRT (solids residence time) measures how long bacteria stay in the system — typically 4--15 days for conventional activated sludge. HRT (hydraulic residence time) measures how long water stays in the aeration basin — typically 4--8 hours. SRT is always much longer than HRT because we recycle the sludge (solids) back to the aeration basin, keeping the bacteria in the system far longer than the water. The reported values ($\theta_c = 8$ hr, $\theta = 10$ days) are clearly swapped. The "Yes — SRT can be shorter than HRT if the sludge is wasted rapidly" choice is wrong because rapid wasting still gives SRT of at least a few days. The "SRT and HRT are independent parameters" choice ignores the physical constraint that sludge recycle makes SRT $>$ HRT. The "SRT and HRT must always be equal" choice is wrong because they are never equal in practice.
wr-wt-ex4.hint: Think about typical values: SRT is in days (4-15), HRT is in hours (4-8). Which parameter should be larger?

steps.text: Typical SRT: 4–15 days (solids are recycled in the system).
Typical HRT: 4–8 hours (water passes through relatively quickly).
SRT should always be much longer than HRT. The reported values are swapped.

traps: Confusing SRT (days) with HRT (hours) — they differ by orders of magnitude
Thinking SRT and HRT should be equal — sludge recycle makes SRT much longer

wr-dwt-ex1.statement: A rapid sand filter bed measures $24\text{ ft}$ by $12\text{ ft}$ and treats a flow of $Q = 1{,}728\text{ gpm}$. What is the filtration (loading) rate?
wr-dwt-ex1.eli5: Filtration rate = Q/A_plan. Area = 24 × 12 = 288 ft². v_s = 1,728/288 = 6.0 gpm/ft², within the typical rapid-sand range of 2--10 gpm/ft². The 3.0 gpm/ft² choice doubles the area (1,728/576). The 0.17 gpm/ft² choice inverts the ratio (288/1,728). The 60 gpm/ft² choice drops a zero.
wr-dwt-ex1.hint: Filtration rate = flow / plan area (length × width).
traps: Using bed depth or volume instead of plan area
Inverting to A/Q

wr-dwt-ex2.statement: Water with a chlorine demand of $1.8\text{ mg/L}$ must be dosed to leave a free residual of $0.5\text{ mg/L}$. For a flow of $Q = 2.0\text{ MGD}$, what is the chlorine feed rate? (Use $\text{lb/day} = \text{mg/L} \times \text{MGD} \times 8.34$.)
wr-dwt-ex2.eli5: Dose = demand + residual = 1.8 + 0.5 = 2.3 mg/L. Feed rate = 2.3 × 2.0 × 8.34 = 38.4 lb/day. The 30.0 lb/day choice mis-scales the product without the proper 8.34 factor. The 15.0 lb/day choice roughly halves it. The 21.7 lb/day choice uses only the demand (1.8) × flow × 8.34, forgetting the 0.5 residual.
wr-dwt-ex2.hint: Dose = demand + residual, then lb/day = dose × MGD × 8.34.
traps: Feeding only the demand and omitting the target residual
Forgetting the 8.34 lb/(mg/L·MG) conversion

wr-wqs-ex1.statement: A groundwater sample contains $\text{Ca}^{2+} = 70\text{ mg/L}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+} = 20\text{ mg/L}$. Using equivalent weights of $20$ (Ca²⁺) and $12.15$ (Mg²⁺), what is the total hardness as CaCO₃?
wr-wqs-ex1.eli5: Convert each ion by 50/EW. Ca: 70 × 2.5 = 175. Mg: 20 × (50/12.15) = 20 × 4.12 = 82. Total = 175 + 82 = 257 mg/L as CaCO₃ (very hard). The 90 mg/L option adds raw ion values (70 + 20). The 175 mg/L option counts only calcium. The 200 mg/L option is a partial conversion.
wr-wqs-ex1.hint: Multiply each ion by 50/EW (Ca → 2.5, Mg → 4.12), then add.
traps: Adding raw ion concentrations without converting to CaCO₃
Using the calcium multiplier (2.5) for magnesium

wr-pwd-ex1.statement: A pump delivers $Q = 0.08\text{ m}^3\text{/s}$ against a head of $H = 25\text{ m}$ at an efficiency of $\eta = 0.80$. What brake power is required? (Use $\rho g = 9{,}810\text{ N/m}^3$.)
wr-pwd-ex1.eli5: Fluid power = γQH = 9,810 × 0.08 × 25 = 19,620 W ≈ 19.6 kW. Brake power = 19.6/0.80 = 24.5 kW. The 19.6 kW option is fluid power (no efficiency applied). The 15.7 kW option multiplies by 0.80 instead of dividing. The 30.7 kW option applies the efficiency twice.
wr-pwd-ex1.hint: Fluid power = γQH; brake power = fluid power / η.
traps: Forgetting to divide by efficiency
Multiplying by η instead of dividing

wr-ocf-cp1.statement: A triangular (V-shaped) roadside swale lined with grass ($n = 0.018$) has symmetric side slopes of 1.5H:1V and carries flow at a depth of $y = 1.2\,\text{m}$ on a slope of $S = 0.0016$. What is the discharge?
wr-ocf-cp1.eli5: A triangular channel has no bottom width, so $A = zy^2 = 1.5(1.2)^2 = 2.16$ m$^2$ and the wetted perimeter is both sloped sides: $P = 2y\sqrt{1+z^2} = 2(1.2)\sqrt{1+2.25} = 4.327$ m. $R_H = 2.16/4.327 = 0.499$ m. SI units so $K = 1.0$: $Q = (1/0.018)(2.16)(0.499)^{2/3}(0.0016)^{1/2} = 3.02$ m$^3$/s. The 4.47 m³/s distractor uses $P = 2y$ (vertical depth only) instead of the sloped sides, inflating $R_H$. The 0.95 m³/s distractor mistakes the triangular area for $A = zy^2/2 = 1.08$ m$^2$ (treating it as half base times height with the wrong base), which (together with the smaller $R_H$) drops $Q$ to about $0.95$ m$^3$/s. The 4.49 m³/s distractor uses $K = 1.486$ (USCS) with SI inputs.
wr-ocf-cp1.hint: For a triangular channel: $A = zy^2$ and $P = 2y\sqrt{1+z^2}$. Use $K = 1.0$ for SI.
traps: Using $P = 2y$ instead of the sloped-side length $2y\sqrt{1+z^2}$
Computing the triangular area as $zy^2/2$ instead of $zy^2$
Using $K = 1.486$ with SI inputs instead of $K = 1.0$

wr-ocf-cp2.statement: A corrugated metal culvert ($n = 0.024$) with a diameter of $D = 4\,\text{ft}$ flows exactly half full on a slope of $S = 0.005$. What is the discharge?
wr-ocf-cp2.eli5: For a pipe flowing half full: $A = \pi D^2/8 = \pi(4)^2/8 = 6.283$ ft$^2$ and $P = \pi D/2 = 2\pi = 6.283$ ft, so $R_H = A/P = 1.0$ ft. The neat result is that a half-full pipe has the SAME hydraulic radius as a full pipe ($D/4 = 1.0$ ft), but only half the flow area. $Q = (1.486/0.024)(6.283)(1.0)^{2/3}(0.005)^{1/2} = 27.5$ cfs. The 55.0 cfs choice uses the full-pipe area ($\pi D^2/4$), doubling the answer. The 43.7 cfs choice uses $R_H = D/2$ instead of $D/4$. The 18.5 cfs choice forgets the $K = 1.486$ factor for USCS units.
wr-ocf-cp2.hint: Half-full pipe: $A = \pi D^2/8$, $P = \pi D/2$. Note $R_H$ still equals $D/4$.
traps: Using the full-pipe area $\pi D^2/4$ instead of the half-full area $\pi D^2/8$
Using $R_H = D/2$ instead of $R_H = D/4$ for the half-full pipe

wr-ecf-cp1.statement: Water flows at $Q = 20\,\text{m}^3\text{/s}$ in a rectangular channel $B = 4\,\text{m}$ wide at a depth of $y = 2.5\,\text{m}$. What is the specific energy of the flow?
wr-ecf-cp1.eli5: Specific energy is depth plus velocity head: $E = y + v^2/(2g)$. First the velocity: $v = Q/A = 20/(4 \times 2.5) = 2.0$ m/s. Then $v^2/(2g) = 4/(2 \times 9.81) = 0.204$ m. $E = 2.5 + 0.204 = 2.70$ m. The 2.50 m choice reports only the depth, forgetting the velocity head entirely. The 2.91 m choice uses $v^2/g$ (omitting the factor of 2 in the velocity head). The 0.20 m choice reports only the velocity head, forgetting to add the depth.
wr-ecf-cp1.hint: Use $E = y + v^2/(2g)$ where $v = Q/(By)$. Do not forget the factor of 2.
traps: Forgetting the velocity head and reporting only the depth
Omitting the factor of 2 in the velocity head ($v^2/g$ instead of $v^2/2g$)

wr-ecf-cp2.statement: A hydraulic jump in a wide rectangular channel has an upstream (supercritical) depth of $y_1 = 0.5\,\text{m}$ and a downstream (subcritical) conjugate depth of $y_2 = 2.5\,\text{m}$. What is the energy lost across the jump?
wr-ecf-cp2.eli5: When both conjugate depths are known, the energy loss has a closed form: $\Delta E = (y_2 - y_1)^3/(4 y_1 y_2)$. $\Delta E = (2.5 - 0.5)^3/(4 \times 0.5 \times 2.5) = (2.0)^3/5.0 = 8/5 = 1.60$ m. The 6.40 m option omits the factor of 4 in the denominator: $(2.0)^3/(0.5 \times 2.5) = 6.40$. The 2.00 m option just reports the depth difference $y_2 - y_1 = 2.0$. The 4.00 m option drops $y_2$ from the denominator: $(2.0)^3/(4 \times 0.5) = 4.00$.
wr-ecf-cp2.hint: Use the conjugate-depth energy loss formula: $\Delta E = \dfrac{(y_2 - y_1)^3}{4 y_1 y_2}$.

traps: Omitting the factor of 4 in the denominator
Dropping one of the depths from the product $y_1 y_2$ in the denominator
