wr-psw-cp1.statement: An 8-inch ductile iron main ($C = 140$) is $1{,}200\,\text{ft}$ long and carries $Q = 1.8\,\text{ft}^3\text{/s}$ flowing full. Using $Q = k_1 C A R_H^{0.63} S_v^{0.54}$ with $k_1 = 1.318$ and $R_H = D/4$, what is the head loss over the full length?
wr-psw-cp1.eli5: Convert $D = 8\text{ in.} = 0.667$ ft, so $A = \pi(0.667)^2/4 = 0.349$ ft$^2$ and $R_H = D/4 = 0.167$ ft. Rearrange Hazen-Williams for the slope: $S_v = [Q/(k_1 C A R_H^{0.63})]^{1/0.54}$. Plugging in: $S_v = [1.8/(1.318 \times 140 \times 0.349 \times 0.167^{0.63})]^{1/0.54} = 0.01073$. Head loss $= S_v L = 0.01073 \times 1{,}200 = 12.9$ ft. The $5.7$ ft choice uses $R_H = D/2$, overstating $R_H$ and lowering the required slope. The $24.0$ ft choice uses the rougher 20-year cast iron value $C = 100$. The $29.1$ ft choice uses the SI coefficient $k_1 = 0.849$ instead of the USCS $1.318$.
wr-psw-cp1.hint: Solve Hazen-Williams for $S_v$, then multiply by $L$. Convert diameter to feet and use $R_H = D/4$.

steps.text: Solve Hazen-Williams for the energy slope:

traps: Using $R_H = D/2$ instead of $R_H = D/4$ for the full pipe
Using the SI coefficient $k_1 = 0.849$ instead of the USCS $k_1 = 1.318$

wr-psw-cp2.statement: A 90-degree V-notch weir at a stream gauging station passes a discharge of $Q = 8.0\,\text{ft}^3\text{/s}$. Using the USCS coefficient $C = 2.54$, what is the head $H$ above the notch?
wr-psw-cp2.eli5: The 90-degree V-notch formula is $Q = CH^{5/2}$, so $H = (Q/C)^{2/5} = (8.0/2.54)^{0.4} = (3.150)^{0.4} = 1.58$ ft. The 2.01 ft choice uses the SI coefficient $C = 1.40$ instead of the USCS $2.54$. The 2.15 ft choice uses the rectangular weir exponent $3/2$, solving $H = (Q/C)^{2/3} = 2.15$. The 3.15 ft choice forgets the exponent entirely, computing $H = Q/C = 3.15$.
wr-psw-cp2.hint: Invert $Q = CH^{5/2}$ to get $H = (Q/C)^{2/5}$. The V-notch exponent is $5/2$, not $3/2$.
traps: Using the rectangular exponent $3/2$ instead of the V-notch exponent $5/2$
Using the SI coefficient $C = 1.40$ instead of the USCS $C = 2.54$

wr-rr-cp1.statement: A watershed is 70 percent residential ($CN = 80$) and 30 percent open space ($CN = 60$) by area. A storm delivers $P = 3.5\,\text{in.}$ of rainfall. Using the area-weighted composite curve number and the SCS method, what is the runoff depth?
wr-rr-cp1.eli5: First find the composite curve number weighted by area: $CN = 0.70(80) + 0.30(60) = 56 + 18 = 74$. Then $S = 1000/CN - 10 = 1000/74 - 10 = 3.51$ in. Check: $0.2S = 0.70$ in. $< P = 3.5$ in., so runoff occurs. $Q = (P - 0.2S)^2/(P + 0.8S) = (3.5 - 0.70)^2/(3.5 + 2.81) = (2.80)^2/6.31 = 7.84/6.31 = 1.24$ in. The 1.94 in. distractor omits the initial-abstraction subtraction in the numerator, using $P^2/(P + 0.8S) = 1.94$. The 2.80 in. distractor reports the un-squared numerator $(P - 0.2S) = 2.80$. The 3.50 in. distractor assumes all rainfall becomes runoff.
wr-rr-cp1.hint: Area-weight the curve numbers first, find $S$, then apply $Q = (P - 0.2S)^2/(P + 0.8S)$.
traps: Forgetting to area-weight the curve numbers before computing $S$
Forgetting to subtract the initial abstraction $0.2S$ in the numerator

wr-rr-cp2.statement: A storm drain inlet must be sized for a peak design flow of $Q = 90\,\text{cfs}$. The contributing area has a runoff coefficient $C = 0.55$ and the design rainfall intensity is $I = 3.0\,\text{in./hr}$. Using the Rational Method, what drainage area does this represent?
wr-rr-cp2.eli5: Rearrange $Q = CIA$ to solve for area: $A = Q/(CI) = 90/(0.55 \times 3.0) = 90/1.65 = 54.5$ acres. The Rational Method units work out directly (1 acre-in./hr $\approx$ 1 cfs), so no conversion is needed. The 16.5-acre choice multiplies by $C$ instead of dividing: $QC/I = 90(0.55)/3.0 = 16.5$. The 30.0-acre choice ignores $C$ entirely: $Q/I = 90/3.0 = 30$. The 163.6-acre choice forgets the intensity: $Q/C = 90/0.55 = 163.6$.
wr-rr-cp2.hint: Rearrange $Q = CIA$ to $A = Q/(CI)$. The runoff coefficient goes in the denominator.
traps: Multiplying by $C$ instead of dividing — the coefficient belongs in the denominator
Dropping the runoff coefficient and computing $Q/I$

wr-hw-cp1.statement: A 1-hour unit hydrograph has ordinates (in cfs) of $0,\;100,\;300,\;150,\;0$ at $t = 0,1,2,3,4$ hours. A storm produces $2\,\text{in.}$ of excess rainfall in the first hour followed by $3\,\text{in.}$ in the second hour. Using superposition, what is the peak of the direct runoff hydrograph?
wr-hw-cp1.eli5: Each rainfall pulse produces its own scaled, lagged unit hydrograph; you add the two. The 3-inch pulse starts one hour later than the 2-inch pulse. Tabulate hour by hour and sum. The maximum occurs at hour 3: from the 2-inch pulse $2 \times 150 = 300$, plus from the lagged 3-inch pulse $3 \times 300 = 900$, totaling $1{,}200$ cfs. The 1,500 cfs choice simply scales the UH peak by the total depth ($5 \times 300 = 1{,}500$), which is wrong because the two pulses do not peak in the same hour. The 900 cfs choice counts only the 3-inch pulse on the UH peak ($3 \times 300$). The 600 cfs choice counts only the 2-inch pulse peak ($2 \times 300$) and ignores the lagged 3-inch pulse.
wr-hw-cp1.hint: Lag the second pulse by one hour, scale each pulse by its depth, then sum the overlapping ordinates.

steps.text: Pulse 1 (2 in.) scaled UH peaks at hour 2:
Pulse 2 (3 in.) is lagged 1 hour; its UH peak lands at hour 3:

traps: Scaling the UH peak by the total depth (5 in.) instead of superposing the lagged pulses
Forgetting to lag the second pulse by one hour before adding ordinates

wr-hw-cp2.statement: A storm produces a direct runoff volume of $1{,}500\,\text{acre-ft}$ from a watershed with a drainage area of $6{,}000\,\text{acres}$. What is the equivalent depth of direct runoff over the watershed?
wr-hw-cp2.eli5: Runoff depth is volume divided by area, then converted to inches. In consistent units, depth $= V/A = 1{,}500/6{,}000 = 0.25$ ft. Convert to inches: $0.25 \times 12 = 3.0$ in. The acre cancels between acre-ft and acres, leaving feet, which you multiply by 12. The 0.25 in. choice stops at 0.25 ft but mislabels it as inches (forgot the factor of 12). The 6.0 in. choice doubles the result by an arithmetic slip. The 36.0 in. choice multiplies by 12 twice (applies 144 instead of 12).
wr-hw-cp2.hint: Depth $= V/A$ gives feet; multiply by 12 to get inches. The acres cancel.
traps: Reporting 0.25 ft as inches — you must multiply by 12
Applying the 12 in./ft conversion twice

wr-gw-cp1.statement: Water seeps horizontally through a confined sand layer beneath a dam. The hydraulic conductivity is $K = 4 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{m/s}$, the flow cross-section is $A = 300\,\text{m}^2$, and the head drops $6\,\text{m}$ over a flow path length of $120\,\text{m}$. What is the seepage discharge in cubic meters per day?
wr-gw-cp1.eli5: Darcy's law gives the volumetric flow: $Q = KAi$, where the gradient is $i = dh/L = 6/120 = 0.05$. So $Q = (4 \times 10^{-5})(300)(0.05) = 6.0 \times 10^{-4}$ m$^3$/s. Convert to per day: $6.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 86{,}400 = 51.8$ m$^3$/day. The $0.17$ m$^3$/day choice forgets the cross-sectional area, using $Ki$ only (times 86,400). The $6{,}221$ m$^3$/day choice forgets to divide the head drop by the path length, using $i = 6$ instead of $0.05$, inflating $Q$ by 120 times. The $2.6$ m$^3$/day choice mishandles the area, dividing by it instead of multiplying.
wr-gw-cp1.hint: Use $Q = KAi$ with $i = dh/L$. Then convert seconds to days (multiply by 86,400).
traps: Using $i = dh$ instead of $i = dh/L$, inflating $Q$ by the path length
Forgetting to convert m$^3$/s to m$^3$/day (factor of 86,400)

wr-gw-cp2.statement: A well in an unconfined aquifer ($K = 6 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{ft/s}$) is pumped at $Q = 0.8\,\text{ft}^3\text{/s}$. At an observation point $r_2 = 300\,\text{ft}$ away the saturated thickness is undisturbed at $h_2 = 80\,\text{ft}$. Using Dupuit's formula, what is the water level $h_1$ at the well face ($r_1 = 1\,\text{ft}$)?
wr-gw-cp2.eli5: Rearrange Dupuit, $Q = \pi K(h_2^2 - h_1^2)/\ln(r_2/r_1)$, to solve for the well-face head: $h_1 = \sqrt{h_2^2 - Q\ln(r_2/r_1)/(\pi K)}$. The log term: $\ln(300/1) = 5.70$. So $h_1 = \sqrt{80^2 - 0.8(5.70)/(\pi \times 6 \times 10^{-4})} = \sqrt{6400 - 2419} = \sqrt{3981} = 63.1$ ft. The drawdown is about 17 ft. The 73.1 ft choice uses $\log_{10}$ instead of the natural log. The 72.0 ft choice uses $2\pi$ (the confined Thiem coefficient) instead of $\pi$. The 80.0 ft choice forgets to apply any drawdown and just reports the undisturbed level.
wr-gw-cp2.hint: Rearrange Dupuit for $h_1 = \sqrt{h_2^2 - Q\ln(r_2/r_1)/(\pi K)}$. Use the natural log and $\pi$ (not $2\pi$).

steps.text: Dupuit's formula solved for the well-face head:

traps: Using $2\pi$ (confined Thiem) instead of $\pi$ (unconfined Dupuit)
Using $\log_{10}$ instead of the natural logarithm

wr-wq-cp1.statement: A wastewater sample has an ultimate BOD of $L_0 = 320\,\text{mg/L}$ and a decay rate of $k = 0.18\,\text{day}^{-1}$ (base $e$). What is the BOD remaining (not yet exerted) after 4 days?
wr-wq-cp1.eli5: BOD remaining is the organic matter not yet decomposed: $L_t = L_0 e^{-kt} = 320\,e^{-0.18 \times 4} = 320\,e^{-0.72} = 320(0.487) = 155.8$ mg/L. Note the BOD exerted ($L_0(1 - e^{-kt}) = 164.2$) plus the remaining ($155.8$) sum to the ultimate $320$. The 164.2 mg/L choice gives the BOD exerted rather than remaining. The 57.6 mg/L choice applies $kt$ as a percentage ($0.18 \times 4 = 0.72$, then $320 \times 0.18 = 57.6$), a formula confusion. The 320 mg/L choice reports the ultimate BOD, as if no decay had occurred.
wr-wq-cp1.hint: BOD remaining is $L_t = L_0 e^{-kt}$ — exponential decay, not the exerted form $L_0(1 - e^{-kt})$.
traps: Computing the BOD exerted $L_0(1 - e^{-kt})$ instead of the remaining $L_0 e^{-kt}$
Reporting the ultimate BOD as if no decomposition had occurred

wr-wq-cp2.statement: Downstream of an outfall, the deoxygenation rate is $k_d = 0.2\,\text{day}^{-1}$, the reaeration rate is $k_r = 0.4\,\text{day}^{-1}$, the ultimate BOD load is $L_a = 20\,\text{mg/L}$, and the initial deficit is $D_0 = 0$. If the saturation dissolved oxygen is $DO_{sat} = 9.0\,\text{mg/L}$, what is the minimum (critical) dissolved oxygen in the stream?
wr-wq-cp2.eli5: Find the critical time, then the critical deficit, then subtract from saturation. With $D_0 = 0$, the critical time is $t_c = \frac{1}{k_r - k_d}\ln(k_r/k_d) = \frac{1}{0.2}\ln(2) = 3.47$ days. The critical deficit is $D_c = \frac{k_d}{k_r}L_a e^{-k_d t_c} = \frac{0.2}{0.4}(20)e^{-0.2(3.47)} = 10(0.5) = 5.0$ mg/L. Minimum DO $= DO_{sat} - D_c = 9.0 - 5.0 = 4.0$ mg/L. The 5.0 mg/L choice reports the critical deficit itself, forgetting to subtract it from saturation. The 9.0 mg/L choice ignores the deficit entirely. The 0.0 mg/L choice wrongly drops the decay factor $e^{-k_d t_c}$, giving $D_c = 10$ and a negative DO clamped to zero.
wr-wq-cp2.hint: Compute $t_c = \frac{1}{k_r-k_d}\ln(k_r/k_d)$, then $D_c = \frac{k_d}{k_r}L_a e^{-k_d t_c}$, then $DO_{min} = DO_{sat} - D_c$.
traps: Reporting the critical deficit instead of subtracting it from $DO_{sat}$
Dropping the $e^{-k_d t_c}$ factor and using $D_c = (k_d/k_r)L_a$

wr-wt-cp1.statement: A rectangular primary sedimentation tank measures $80\,\text{ft}$ long by $20\,\text{ft}$ wide by $12\,\text{ft}$ deep and treats a flow of $Q = 1.5\,\text{MGD}$. What is the hydraulic detention time? (Use $1\,\text{ft}^3 = 7.48\,\text{gal}$.)
wr-wt-cp1.eli5: Detention time is volume over flow: $\theta = V/Q$. The tank volume is $V = 80 \times 20 \times 12 = 19{,}200$ ft$^3$. Convert the flow to ft$^3$/day: $Q = 1{,}500{,}000\,\text{gpd}/7.48 = 200{,}535$ ft$^3$/day. So $\theta = 19{,}200/200{,}535 = 0.0958$ days $= 0.0958 \times 24 = 2.3$ hours, a typical primary clarifier value. The 0.31 hours choice forgets to divide by 7.48 (treats gallons as cubic feet). The 17.2 hours choice inverts the gallon conversion. The 0.096 choice reports the answer in days (0.096) rather than converting to hours.
wr-wt-cp1.hint: $\theta = V/Q$. Convert MGD to ft$^3$/day by dividing gallons by 7.48, then convert days to hours.
traps: Forgetting the 7.48 gal/ft$^3$ conversion when changing MGD to ft$^3$/day
Reporting the detention time in days instead of converting to hours

wr-wt-cp2.statement: A circular secondary clarifier must be sized so the overflow rate does not exceed $v_o = 900\,\text{gpd/ft}^2$ at a design flow of $Q = 2.5\,\text{MGD}$. What minimum tank diameter is required?
wr-wt-cp2.eli5: Overflow rate is $v_o = Q/A$, so the required surface area is $A = Q/v_o = 2{,}500{,}000/900 = 2{,}778$ ft$^2$. For a circular tank $A = \pi D^2/4$, so $D = \sqrt{4A/\pi} = \sqrt{4(2{,}778)/\pi} = \sqrt{3{,}537} = 59.5$ ft. The 29.7 ft choice forgets the factor of 4, computing $D = \sqrt{A/\pi} = 29.7$ ft (this is actually the radius). The 88.4 ft choice uses $A = \pi D^2$ without the $1/4$. The 2,778 ft choice reports the surface area itself rather than solving for the diameter.
wr-wt-cp2.hint: Find $A = Q/v_o$, then invert $A = \pi D^2/4$ to get $D = \sqrt{4A/\pi}$.

steps.text: Solve the circular area for diameter:

traps: Omitting the factor of 4, which yields the radius (29.7 ft) instead of the diameter
Reporting the required area rather than solving for the diameter

wr-dwt-cp1.statement: A chlorine contact basin holds a free residual of $C = 2.0\,\text{mg/L}$, and the $10$th-percentile contact time is $t_{10} = 45\,\text{min}$. What disinfection CT value is achieved?
wr-dwt-cp1.eli5: CT = C × t₁₀ = 2.0 × 45 = 90 mg·min/L. The 22.5 mg·min/L choice divides instead of multiplying (45/2). The 47 mg·min/L choice adds the two values (2 + 45). The 0.044 mg·min/L choice divides C by t₁₀ (2/45) rather than multiplying.
wr-dwt-cp1.hint: CT is simply the residual concentration times the contact time.
traps: Using the theoretical detention time V/Q instead of t₁₀
Adding C and t₁₀ instead of multiplying

wr-dwt-cp2.statement: A filter sand has an effective size $d_{10} = 0.50\,\text{mm}$ and $d_{60} = 0.75\,\text{mm}$. What is the uniformity coefficient of the media?
wr-dwt-cp2.eli5: Uniformity coefficient UC = d₆₀/d₁₀ = 0.75/0.50 = 1.5. A lower UC means more uniform grain sizes. The 0.67 option inverts the ratio (d₁₀/d₆₀). The 1.25 option uses a wrong pairing. The 0.25 option subtracts the sizes.
traps: Inverting the ratio to d₁₀/d₆₀
Confusing effective size (d₁₀) with the median size

wr-wqs-cp1.statement: A wastewater plant receives total suspended solids of $220\,\text{mg/L}$ and must discharge at or below $30\,\text{mg/L}$. What TSS removal efficiency is required?
wr-wqs-cp1.eli5: Efficiency = (in − out)/in = (220 − 30)/220 = 190/220 = 0.864 = 86.4%. The 13.6% choice is the fraction remaining (30/220). The 30% choice reports the effluent number as a percent. The 7.3% choice inverts the ratio.
traps: Computing the fraction remaining instead of removed
Forgetting to divide by the influent concentration

wr-pwd-cp1.statement: A pump must overcome a static lift of $18\,\text{m}$ plus friction and minor losses of $6.5\,\text{m}$ while delivering $Q = 0.030\,\text{m}^3\text{/s}$ at a pump efficiency of $\eta = 0.70$. What brake power is required? (Use $\rho g = 9{,}810\,\text{N/m}^3$.)
wr-pwd-cp1.eli5: Total dynamic head = static + losses = 18 + 6.5 = 24.5 m. Fluid power = γQH = 9,810 × 0.030 × 24.5 = 7,210 W ≈ 7.2 kW. Brake power = 7.2/0.70 = 10.3 kW. The 7.2 kW option is the fluid power (no efficiency). The 5.3 kW option uses only the static lift (9,810 × 0.030 × 18 ≈ 5,300 W). The 5.0 kW option multiplies by 0.70 instead of dividing (7.2 × 0.70 ≈ 5.0).
wr-pwd-cp1.hint: TDH = static lift + losses. Fluid power = γQ·TDH; brake power = fluid power / η.
traps: Forgetting to add friction losses to the static lift
Omitting the efficiency division

str-ds-q1.statement: A planar truss has $m = 11$ members, $r = 3$ reaction components, and $j = 7$ joints. How is the structure classified?
str-ds-q1.eli5: For a plane truss: m + r = 11 + 3 = 14, and 2j = 2(7) = 14. Since m + r = 2j, the truss is stable and statically determinate. This means you can find all member forces and reactions using equilibrium equations alone. If m + r were greater than 2j, you would need compatibility equations (indeterminate). If less, the structure would be a mechanism.
str-ds-q1.hint: Use the plane truss equation: compare m + r to 2j.

steps.text: Since $m + r = 2j = 14$, the truss is stable and statically determinate.

traps: Confusing the truss formula (m + r vs 2j) with the frame formula (3m + r vs 3j + c)
Forgetting to count all reaction components — a pin gives 2, a roller gives 1

str-ds-q2.statement: A portal frame consists of $m = 3$ members and $j = 4$ joints. The left base has a pin support and the right base has a fixed support. There are no internal hinges ($c = 0$). What is the degree of static indeterminacy?
str-ds-q2.eli5: For a plane frame: compare 3m + r to 3j + c. Reactions: pin = 2 components, fixed = 3 components, so r = 2 + 3 = 5. Then 3m + r = 3(3) + 5 = 14, and 3j + c = 3(4) + 0 = 12. Since 14 > 12, the frame is indeterminate, and the degree = 14 – 12 = 2. That means you need two compatibility equations beyond equilibrium to solve for all unknowns. The "0 (determinate)" choice would require 3m + r = 3j + c exactly. The "3 degrees" choice would happen if both supports were fixed (r = 6, giving 3(3)+6 = 15 vs 12 = 3 degrees).
str-ds-q2.hint: Count reactions: pin gives 2, fixed gives 3. Then use the frame formula 3m + r vs 3j + c.
traps: Forgetting that a fixed support provides 3 reaction components (not 2)
Using the truss formula (m + r vs 2j) instead of the frame formula (3m + r vs 3j + c)

str-ds-q3.statement: A planar truss has $m = 9$ members, $r = 3$ reaction components, and $j = 6$ joints. All three reaction components are vertical (parallel). Is the truss stable?
str-ds-q3.eli5: Numerically: m + r = 9 + 3 = 12, and 2j = 2(6) = 12. The equation says determinate. But the equation is a necessary condition, not sufficient. If all three reaction components are parallel (all vertical), the structure cannot resist any horizontal force — it slides sideways. This is called geometric instability. The truss is unstable even though the count checks out. Always verify that reactions are not all parallel or concurrent. The "stable and determinate" choice assumes the count alone guarantees stability — it does not.
str-ds-q3.hint: The determinacy equation is necessary but not sufficient. What happens if you apply a horizontal force?

steps.text: The numerical check passes — suggests determinate.
No horizontal reaction exists, so $\Sigma F_x = 0$ cannot be satisfied for any horizontal load. The structure is geometrically unstable.

str-ds-q3.handbookFormula: m + r = 2j \text{ (necessary but not sufficient for stability)}
traps: Assuming the numerical count alone guarantees stability — arrangement matters
Forgetting that parallel reactions cannot resist loads perpendicular to their direction
Confusing this with the indeterminate case (m + r > 2j) — even indeterminate structures can be unstable if reactions are improperly arranged

str-tam-q1.statement: At joint A, a $500\text{ lb}$ vertical (downward) load is carried by two members: a horizontal member AB and a diagonal member AC oriented at $45^\circ$ above the horizontal. Using the method of joints, what is the force in diagonal AC?
str-tam-q1.eli5: Only the diagonal can resist the vertical load — the horizontal member has no vertical component. So $\sum F_y = 0$ gives $F_{AC}\sin 45^\circ = 500$, hence $F_{AC} = 500/0.707 = 707$ lb. The 500 lb choice forgets to divide by $\sin 45^\circ$. The 354 lb choice multiplies by $\sin 45^\circ$ instead of dividing.
str-tam-q1.hint: Only the diagonal has a vertical component — use $\sum F_y = 0$ at joint A.

steps.text: Horizontal member AB carries no vertical force, so the diagonal must balance the load.

traps: Forgetting to divide by sin 45° and reporting 500 lb
Multiplying by sin 45° (354) instead of dividing

str-tam-q2.statement: A parallel-chord truss has panel length $4\text{ m}$ and height $3\text{ m}$. The left support reaction is $30\text{ kN}$ (upward) and there are no loads within the first panel. Taking a vertical section through the first panel and summing moments about the top-chord joint at the far end of the panel, what is the force in the bottom chord?
str-tam-q2.eli5: Summing moments about the top joint kills the diagonal and the top chord (they pass through or are arms about that point), leaving only the bottom chord. The reaction acts $4\text{ m}$ horizontally from the moment center; the bottom chord acts at the $3\text{ m}$ height. So $30(4) = F_{BC}(3)$, giving $F_{BC} = 120/3 = 40\text{ kN}$ tension. The 120 kN option forgets to divide by the 3 m height.
str-tam-q2.hint: Take moments about the top joint so only the bottom chord remains: reaction × panel length = force × height.

steps.text: Moment center at the top joint eliminates the top chord and diagonal.
$\sum M = 0$: reaction times its horizontal arm equals bottom-chord force times the height.

traps: Forgetting to divide by the truss height (reporting 120 kN)
Using the height as the reaction's moment arm instead of the panel length

str-tam-q3.statement: At an unloaded joint, three members meet: two are collinear (in a straight line through the joint) and the third comes in at an angle. No external load or reaction acts at this joint. What is the force in the angled (third) member?

choices.text: Equal to the force in the collinear members

str-tam-q3.eli5: Set up equilibrium perpendicular to the two collinear members. The two collinear members have no component in that perpendicular direction, and there's no external load — so the only force with a component there is the angled member, which must therefore be zero. This is the classic zero-force-member rule.
str-tam-q3.hint: Sum forces perpendicular to the two collinear members.

steps.text: The two collinear members act along one line; resolve forces perpendicular to that line.
Only the angled member has a perpendicular component, and there is no external load to balance it.
Therefore the angled member carries zero force (zero-force member).

str-tam-q3.handbookPage: p. 97, Plane Truss: Method of Joints
traps: Assuming every member carries load — zero-force members are common at unloaded joints
Confusing this with the two-member unloaded-joint rule

str-dvw-q1.statement: Using the unit-load method for a truss, $\delta = \sum nNL/AE$. For one member, the real force is $N = 50\text{ kN}$, the virtual (unit-load) force is $n = 0.5$, the length is $L = 4\text{ m}$, and $AE = 200{,}000\text{ kN}$. What is this member's contribution to the joint deflection?
str-dvw-q1.eli5: Plug into $nNL/AE = (0.5)(50)(4)/200{,}000 = 100/200{,}000 = 0.0005\text{ m} = 0.5\text{ mm}$. The trap is units: $0.0005\text{ m}$ is $0.5\text{ mm}$, not $5\text{ mm}$ (the $5.0\text{ mm}$ choice) or $0.05\text{ mm}$ (the $0.05\text{ mm}$ choice).
str-dvw-q1.hint: Compute nNL then divide by AE; convert meters to millimeters carefully.
traps: Unit slip: writing 5 mm or 0.05 mm instead of 0.5 mm
Forgetting to multiply by the virtual force n

str-dvw-q2.statement: A simply supported beam of length $L = 6\text{ m}$ carries a central point load $P = 20\text{ kN}$. The flexural rigidity is $EI = 40{,}000\text{ kN·m}^2$. What is the maximum deflection?
str-dvw-q2.eli5: Central point load on a simple span uses $\delta = PL^3/48EI = 20(6^3)/(48 \times 40{,}000) = 4320/1{,}920{,}000 = 0.00225\text{ m} = 2.25\text{ mm}$. The 9 mm choice uses $PL^3/12EI$ by mistake; the 1.13 mm choice halves the answer.

steps.text: Identify the standard case: simple span, central P.

traps: Using the wrong constant (e.g. 12EI) in the denominator
Mixing the point-load (L³) and UDL (L⁴) formulas

str-dvw-q3.statement: A cantilever beam of length $L = 3\text{ m}$ carries a point load $P = 10\text{ kN}$ at its free end. With $EI = 20{,}000\text{ kN·m}^2$, what is the tip deflection?
str-dvw-q3.eli5: End-loaded cantilever: $\delta = PL^3/3EI = 10(27)/(3 \times 20{,}000) = 270/60{,}000 = 0.0045\text{ m} = 4.5\text{ mm}$. The 2.25 mm distractor wrongly uses $PL^3/6EI$ (an erroneous denominator constant of 6 instead of 3); the 13.5 mm distractor drops the factor entirely and uses $PL^3/EI$.

steps.text: Standard case: cantilever, end point load.

traps: Using a simple-span constant (48EI) for a cantilever
Dropping the factor of 3 in the denominator

str-ind-q1.statement: A propped cantilever beam is fixed at one end and supported on a roller at the other. What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
str-ind-q1.eli5: Count reactions: the fixed end provides 3 (horizontal, vertical, moment) and the roller provides 1 (vertical), giving 4. A planar beam has 3 equilibrium equations, so $DSI = 4 - 3 = 1$ — indeterminate to the first degree. The "0" option would be a determinate beam (e.g., simply supported).
str-ind-q1.hint: Count reaction components, subtract the 3 equilibrium equations.

steps.text: Fixed end = 3 reactions; roller = 1 reaction; total $r = 4$.

traps: Counting the fixed end as 2 reactions (it provides 3, including the moment)
Treating the propped cantilever as determinate (DSI = 0)

str-ind-q2.statement: A propped cantilever (fixed at one end, roller at the other) of length $L = 8\text{ m}$ carries a uniformly distributed load $w = 12\text{ kN/m}$. What is the reaction at the propped (roller) end?
str-ind-q2.eli5: The standard propped-cantilever result for a UDL gives the prop (roller) reaction $R = 3wL/8 = 3(12)(8)/8 = 36\text{ kN}$. The 48 kN choice is the simple-span half-load $wL/2$, ignoring that the fixed end takes more (it carries 60 kN). The 24 kN choice uses $wL/4$.
str-ind-q2.hint: Propped cantilever under UDL: prop reaction = 3wL/8.
traps: Using wL/2 = 48 kN (the simple-span reaction) instead of 3wL/8
Splitting the load evenly between supports

str-ind-q3.statement: A beam fixed at both ends spans $L = 6\text{ m}$ and carries a uniformly distributed load $w = 10\text{ kN/m}$. What is the magnitude of the fixed-end moment at each support?
str-ind-q3.eli5: Fixed-fixed beam under UDL: the fixed-end moment is $wL^2/12 = 10(6^2)/12 = 360/12 = 30\text{ kN·m}$. The 45 kN·m choice uses the simple-span midspan moment $wL^2/8$ by mistake — that's the wrong formula for a fixed end.
str-ind-q3.hint: Fixed-fixed beam, UDL → fixed-end moment = wL²/12.

steps.text: Standard result for a fixed-fixed beam under UDL.

traps: Using wL²/8 = 45 kN·m (the simple-span moment) for the fixed end
Confusing the end moment with the reduced midspan moment (wL²/24)

str-lc-q1.statement: A beam supports a dead load of $D = 20 \text{ kips}$ and a floor live load of $L = 40 \text{ kips}$. What is the factored load using LRFD Combination 2 ($1.2D + 1.6L$)?
str-lc-q1.eli5: 1.2D + 1.6L = 1.2(20) + 1.6(40) = 24 + 64 = 88 kips. This is the most common LRFD combination for gravity loading. The 60 kips option is the unfactored sum D + L. The 96 kips option applies 1.6 to both D and L, which is wrong — dead load gets a lower factor (1.2) because it is more predictable. The 84 kips option might come from using wrong factors like 1.4D + L.
str-lc-q1.hint: Multiply D by 1.2 and L by 1.6, then add.
traps: Using unfactored loads (D + L = 60) instead of applying LRFD factors
Applying the 1.6 factor to dead load instead of 1.2 — dead load has a lower factor because it is more predictable

str-lc-q2.statement: A column supports $D = 30 \text{ kips}$, $L = 50 \text{ kips}$ (floor live), and $S = 20 \text{ kips}$ (snow). No wind or seismic loads act. Which LRFD combination produces the largest factored axial load?
str-lc-q2.eli5: Check each relevant combination. Combo 1: 1.4D = 1.4(30) = 42. Combo 2: 1.2D + 1.6L + 0.5S = 1.2(30) + 1.6(50) + 0.5(20) = 36 + 80 + 10 = 126. Combo 3: 1.2D + 1.6S + L = 1.2(30) + 1.6(20) + 1.0(50) = 36 + 32 + 50 = 118. The controlling case is Combo 2 at 126 kips. When floor live load is larger than snow, Combo 2 usually controls because L gets the 1.6 factor. When snow dominates, Combo 3 can control.
str-lc-q2.hint: Evaluate at least Combos 1, 2, and 3. In Combo 2, L gets 1.6 and S gets 0.5. In Combo 3, S gets 1.6 and L gets 1.0.
traps: Only checking one combination instead of all relevant ones
Mixing up which load gets the 1.6 factor in Combo 2 vs. Combo 3 — Combo 2 puts 1.6 on L, Combo 3 puts 1.6 on S

str-lc-q3.statement: An interior column ($K_{LL} = 4$) supports one floor with a tributary area of $A_T = 600 \text{ ft}^2$. The unreduced floor live load is $L_o = 50 \text{ psf}$. What is the reduced live load?
str-lc-q3.eli5: L = L_o(0.25 + 15/√(K_LL × A_T)) = 50(0.25 + 15/√(4 × 600)) = 50(0.25 + 15/√2400) = 50(0.25 + 15/49.0) = 50(0.25 + 0.306) = 50(0.556) = 27.8 ≈ 28 psf. Check the minimum: for one floor, L ≥ 0.50 L_o = 25 psf. Since 28 > 25, the reduction is valid. The 50 psf option is the unreduced load. The 25 psf option is the minimum allowed — it would apply only if the formula gave a value below 25. The 13 psf option uses 0.25 × L_o, which misapplies the formula.
str-lc-q3.hint: Use $L = L_o(0.25 + 15/\sqrt{K_{LL} A_T})$ and check against the minimum of $0.50 L_o$.

steps.text: Check minimum: $L \geq 0.50 L_o = 25$ psf. Since $28 > 25$, OK.

traps: Forgetting to check the minimum reduced live load (0.50 L_o for one floor, 0.40 L_o for two or more)
Using K_LL = 2 (for beams) instead of K_LL = 4 (for columns)
Forgetting that A_T must be in ft² to match the formula constants

str-il-q1.statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 24 \text{ ft}$. A single concentrated load $P = 12 \text{ kips}$ can be placed anywhere on the beam. Using the influence line for shear at a section 6 ft from the left support, what is the maximum positive shear at that section?
str-il-q1.eli5: The IL for positive shear at a section has its maximum ordinate just to the right of the section. At a = 6 ft from the left support of a span L = 24 ft, the IL ordinate just to the right = 1 – a/L = 1 – 6/24 = 0.75. Maximum positive shear = P × 0.75 = 12 × 0.75 = 9.0 kips. The 12 kips choice assumes the full load becomes shear. The 3 kips choice uses the negative ordinate a/L = 0.25. The 6 kips choice is half the load.
str-il-q1.hint: The IL for shear at distance a from the left support has a maximum positive ordinate of 1 – a/L, just to the right of the section.

steps.text: IL ordinate for positive shear just to the right:

str-il-q1.handbookFormula: \text{IL for shear at section } a: \eta^+ = 1 - a/L
traps: Using a/L (the negative ordinate) instead of 1 – a/L (the positive ordinate)
Assuming the entire load becomes shear at the section — the load must be multiplied by the IL ordinate

str-il-q2.statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 30 \text{ ft}$. A concentrated load of $P = 20 \text{ kips}$ moves across the beam. What is the maximum bending moment at midspan?
str-il-q2.eli5: The IL for moment at midspan is a triangle with peak ordinate = L/4 at midspan. Peak ordinate = 30/4 = 7.5 ft. Maximum moment = P × (L/4) = 20 × 7.5 = 150 kip-ft. This occurs when the load is placed directly at midspan. The 300 kip-ft option might come from PL/2, confusing moment with the reaction formula. The 75 kip-ft option halves the correct answer. The 600 kip-ft option uses P × L = 20 × 30.
str-il-q2.hint: The IL for moment at midspan has a peak ordinate of L/4. Maximum M = P × L/4.
str-il-q2.handbookFormula: \text{IL for moment at midspan: peak ordinate} = L/4
traps: Confusing L/4 (IL ordinate for moment) with L/2 (the location of midspan)
Computing PL/4 instead of P × (L/4) — they are the same thing, but watch the units (the IL ordinate has units of length)

str-il-q3.statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 40 \text{ ft}$. Two concentrated loads, $P_1 = 20 \text{ kips}$ and $P_2 = 10 \text{ kips}$, are spaced 8 ft apart and move across the beam together. What is the maximum bending moment at midspan?
str-il-q3.eli5: The IL for moment at midspan (x = 20 ft) is triangular with peak = L/4 = 10 ft. The IL ordinate at any position x is x/2 for x ≤ 20 and (40 – x)/2 for x ≥ 20. To maximize the total moment, place the heavier load (20 kips) at midspan where the ordinate is highest (10 ft). The lighter load (10 kips) lands at x = 28 ft (or x = 12 ft), with ordinate (40–28)/2 = 6 ft. Total M = 20(10) + 10(6) = 200 + 60 = 260 kip-ft. The 240 kip-ft choice places both loads equidistant from midspan: at x=16 and x=24, both ordinates = 8, giving 20(8)+10(8) = 240. But putting the heavier load at the peak gives a larger total.
str-il-q3.hint: Place the heaviest load at the IL peak. Then compute the IL ordinate at the position of the other load. Sum P_i × η_i.

steps.text: IL for midspan moment (peak at x = 20 ft):

traps: Placing both loads symmetrically about midspan instead of placing the heavier load at the peak — the heavier load should go where the IL ordinate is highest
Only computing the effect of the larger load and ignoring the smaller one
Forgetting that both load positions are possible (loads can approach from either side)

str-rfs-q1.statement: A singly reinforced concrete beam has $b = 12 \text{ in.}$, $d = 18 \text{ in.}$, $A_s = 3.00 \text{ in}^2$, $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$, and $f_c' = 4 \text{ ksi}$. What is the nominal moment capacity $M_n$?
str-rfs-q1.eli5: First find a = A_s f_y / (0.85 f'c b) = 3.00 × 60 / (0.85 × 4 × 12) = 180/40.8 = 4.41 in. Then M_n = A_s f_y (d – a/2) = 3.00 × 60 × (18 – 4.41/2) = 180 × 15.80 = 2,843 kip-in = 237 kip-ft. The 270 kip-ft choice uses d instead of (d – a/2), which overestimates the lever arm. The 213 kip-ft choice is φM_n = 0.90 × 237 — the problem asks for nominal, not design. The 180 kip-ft choice computes A_s × f_y and divides by 12 without the lever arm.
str-rfs-q1.hint: Find a first, then compute M_n = A_s f_y (d – a/2). Convert kip-in to kip-ft by dividing by 12.
traps: Using d instead of (d – a/2) for the moment arm — you must subtract half the stress block depth
Reporting φM_n instead of M_n — read the question carefully to see if it asks for nominal or design capacity

str-rfs-q2.statement: A concrete beam has $b_w = 12 \text{ in.}$, $d = 20 \text{ in.}$, and $f_c' = 3{,}000 \text{ psi}$ (normal weight). The factored shear at the critical section is $V_u = 22 \text{ kips}$. What is the shear status?

choices.text: Only minimum stirrups — $\phi V_c / 2 < V_u \leq \phi V_c$

str-rfs-q2.eli5: V_c = 2λ√f'c × b_w × d = 2(1.0)√3000 × 12 × 20 = 2(54.77)(240) = 26,290 lb = 26.3 kips. φV_c = 0.75 × 26.3 = 19.7 kips. φV_c/2 = 9.9 kips. Since V_u = 22 > φV_c = 19.7, the concrete alone cannot carry the shear. Stirrups must be designed to carry V_s = V_u/φ – V_c = 22/0.75 – 26.3 = 29.3 – 26.3 = 3.0 kips. The "no stirrups needed" choice would apply if V_u ≤ 9.9. The "only minimum stirrups" choice would apply if 9.9 < V_u ≤ 19.7.
str-rfs-q2.hint: Compute V_c = 2√f'c × b_w × d (in lb), then compare V_u to φV_c and φV_c/2.

steps.latex: V_u = 22 > \phi V_c = 19.7 \implies \text{stirrups required with computed } V_s

traps: Using f'c in ksi instead of psi — √4 ≠ √4000; the formula uses psi units
Comparing V_u to V_c instead of φV_c — always include the φ = 0.75 factor on the capacity side

str-rfs-q3.statement: A concrete beam has $b_w = 14 \text{ in.}$, $d = 24 \text{ in.}$, $f_c' = 4{,}000 \text{ psi}$, and $V_u = 70 \text{ kips}$. Using #3 U-stirrups ($A_v = 0.22 \text{ in}^2$ for two legs) with $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$, what is the required stirrup spacing?
str-rfs-q3.eli5: First find V_c = 2(1.0)√4000 × 14 × 24 = 2(63.25)(336) = 42,504 lb = 42.5 kips. Then V_s = V_u/φ – V_c = 70/0.75 – 42.5 = 93.3 – 42.5 = 50.8 kips. Required spacing: s = A_v f_y d / V_s = 0.22 × 60 × 24 / 50.8 = 316.8/50.8 = 6.24 in. → use 6 in. Check max spacing: V_s = 50.8 < 4b_w d√f'c = 85.2 kips, so max spacing = d/2 = 12 in. Since 6 < 12, the required spacing of 6 in. controls. The 12 in. choice is the maximum spacing d/2, but the required V_s demands closer spacing. The 24 in. choice is a code maximum that only applies when V_s is very small.
str-rfs-q3.hint: Find V_s = V_u/φ – V_c, then s = A_v f_y d / V_s. Check against maximum spacing.

steps.text: Check max spacing: $V_s = 50.8 < 4 b_w d \sqrt{f_c'}  = 85.2$ kips, so max $s = d/2 = 12$ in. Since $6 < 12$, use $s = 6$ in.

traps: Using d/2 as the spacing without checking if V_s demands closer spacing — d/2 is a maximum, not the design spacing
Forgetting to divide V_u by φ before subtracting V_c — the equation is V_s = V_u/φ – V_c, not V_u – V_c
Using total stirrup bar area instead of A_v for two legs — for a U-stirrup, A_v = 2 × (one leg area)

str-rcc-q1.statement: A short tied column is $16 \text{ in.} \times 16 \text{ in.}$ with 8 #9 bars ($A_{st} = 8.00 \text{ in}^2$), $f_c' = 4 \text{ ksi}$, and $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$. What is the maximum design axial load $\phi P_n$?
str-rcc-q1.eli5: A_g = 16 × 16 = 256 in². φP_n = 0.80 × 0.65 × [0.85 × 4 × (256 – 8) + 8 × 60] = 0.52 × [3.4 × 248 + 480] = 0.52 × [843.2 + 480] = 0.52 × 1323.2 = 688 kips. The 1,323 kips option omits both the 0.80 factor and φ. The 860 kips option applies only φ = 0.65 without the 0.80 accidental eccentricity factor. The 1,058 kips option applies only 0.80 without φ. You need BOTH factors for tied columns.
str-rcc-q1.hint: Use φP_n = 0.80φ[0.85f'c(A_g – A_st) + A_st f_y] with φ = 0.65 for tied columns.
traps: Forgetting the 0.80 accidental eccentricity factor — this is unique to columns and does not apply to beams
Using φ = 0.90 (beam value) instead of φ = 0.65 (tied column under compression control)

str-rcc-q2.statement: A concrete column is $18 \text{ in.} \times 18 \text{ in.}$ with 4 #8 bars (each $A_b = 0.79 \text{ in}^2$). Is the reinforcement ratio within ACI limits?
str-rcc-q2.eli5: A_st = 4 × 0.79 = 3.16 in². A_g = 18 × 18 = 324 in². ρ_g = 3.16/324 = 0.00975 = 0.975%. ACI requires 0.01 ≤ ρ_g ≤ 0.08 (1% to 8%). Since 0.975% < 1%, the reinforcement is below the minimum. This means the column has insufficient steel to prevent a sudden brittle failure under combined axial load and bending. The fix is to add more bars or use larger bars. The "Yes — within the 1% to 8% range" choice would require ρ_g ≥ 0.01. The "At the exact minimum of 1%" choice would require exactly 0.01.
str-rcc-q2.hint: Compute ρ_g = A_st / A_g and compare to the ACI limits of 0.01 ≤ ρ_g ≤ 0.08.

steps.text: ACI limits: $0.01 \leq \rho_g \leq 0.08$. Since $0.00975 < 0.01$, the ratio is below minimum.

traps: Rounding 0.975% up to 1% and calling it adequate — ACI requires strictly ≥ 1%
Confusing bar area with bar diameter — #8 has diameter 1.000 in. but area 0.79 in²

str-rcc-q3.statement: A short tied column ($14 \text{ in.} \times 20 \text{ in.}$) has $A_{st} = 6.00 \text{ in}^2$, $f_c' = 5 \text{ ksi}$, and $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$. The factored axial load is $P_u = 550 \text{ kips}$. Is the column adequate?

choices.text: Cannot determine without an interaction diagram

str-rcc-q3.eli5: A_g = 14 × 20 = 280 in². Check ρ_g = 6.0/280 = 0.0214 (within 1–8% ✔). φP_n = 0.80(0.65)[0.85(5)(280 – 6) + 6(60)] = 0.52[4.25(274) + 360] = 0.52[1164.5 + 360] = 0.52 × 1524.5 = 793 kips. Since P_u = 550 < 793, the column is adequate. The 524 kips option might come from using φ = 0.65 but replacing 0.80 with some other factor. The 1,525 kips option is the value inside the brackets without applying 0.80φ. For pure axial load (no significant moment), this formula check is sufficient; an interaction diagram is needed only when significant moment acts simultaneously.
str-rcc-q3.hint: Compute φP_n using the tied column formula and compare to P_u.

steps.text: Compare: $P_u = 550 < \phi P_n = 793$ kips. The column is adequate.

traps: Forgetting to subtract A_st from A_g in the concrete term — the formula uses (A_g – A_st) because steel displaces concrete
Using φ = 0.90 (tension-controlled) instead of φ = 0.65 (compression-controlled tied column)
Omitting the 0.80 factor that accounts for accidental eccentricity

str-sb-q1.statement: A W-shape steel beam has $Z_x = 120 \text{ in}^3$ and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. The beam has full lateral bracing. What is the LRFD design flexural strength $\phi_b M_n$?
str-sb-q1.eli5: With full bracing, $M_n = M_p = F_y Z_x = 50 \times 120 = 6{,}000$ kip-in $= 500$ kip-ft. Then $\phi_b M_n = 0.90 \times 500 = 450$ kip-ft. The 500 kip-ft choice is the nominal capacity without the $\phi$ factor. The 299 kip-ft choice is the ASD allowable: $M_p/\Omega_b = 500/1.67 = 299$ — a common trap if you mix up LRFD and ASD. The 333 kip-ft choice comes from using $\phi = 2/3$ incorrectly.
str-sb-q1.hint: $M_p = F_y Z_x$ (convert to kip-ft), then multiply by $\phi_b = 0.90$.
traps: Reporting the nominal capacity (500) instead of the design capacity (450) — always include $\phi_b$ for LRFD
Using $M_p/\Omega_b$ (ASD) when the problem asks for $\phi_b M_n$ (LRFD)

str-sb-q2.statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 20 \text{ ft}$ and has full lateral bracing. The beam has $Z_x = 80 \text{ in}^3$ and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. What is the maximum factored uniform load $w_u$ the beam can carry?
str-sb-q2.eli5: $M_p = F_y Z_x = 50 \times 80 = 4{,}000$ kip-in $= 333.3$ kip-ft. $\phi_b M_p = 0.90 \times 333.3 = 300$ kip-ft. For a simply supported beam with uniform load: $M_u = w_u L^2/8$. Set $M_u = \phi_b M_p$: $w_u = 8 \times 300 / (20^2) = 2{,}400/400 = 6.0$ kip/ft. The 6.67 kip/ft choice uses the nominal $M_p = 333$ without the $\phi$ factor: $8 \times 333/400 = 6.67$. The 4.0 kip/ft choice uses the ASD value: $M_p/\Omega_b = 333/1.67 = 200$, then $8 \times 200/400 = 4.0$.
str-sb-q2.hint: Compute $\phi_b M_p$ first, then set $M_u = w_u L^2/8$ and solve for $w_u$.
traps: Forgetting the $\phi$ factor and using $M_p$ directly — the factored load capacity is based on $\phi M_p$, not $M_p$
Using the ASD safety factor instead of the LRFD $\phi$ — read whether the problem says LRFD or ASD

str-sb-q3.statement: A W-shape beam has $M_p = 500 \text{ kip-ft}$ and $0.7 F_y S_x = 300 \text{ kip-ft}$. The unbraced length is $L_b = 15 \text{ ft}$, with $L_p = 8 \text{ ft}$ and $L_r = 25 \text{ ft}$. Using $C_b = 1.0$, what is the nominal flexural strength $M_n$?
str-sb-q3.eli5: Since $L_p = 8 < L_b = 15 \leq L_r = 25$, we are in the inelastic LTB zone. $M_n = C_b[M_p - (M_p - 0.7F_yS_x)(L_b - L_p)/(L_r - L_p)] = 1.0[500 - (500 - 300)(15 - 8)/(25 - 8)] = 500 - 200(7/17) = 500 - 82.4 = 417.6 \approx 418$ kip-ft. Also check $M_n \leq M_p = 500$ ✓. The 500 kip-ft choice ignores LTB entirely and uses $M_p$. The 300 kip-ft choice uses the lower bound $0.7F_yS_x$. The 376 kip-ft choice is $\phi_b \times 418 = 0.90 \times 418$ — the problem asks for $M_n$ (nominal), not $\phi M_n$ (design).
str-sb-q3.hint: Since $L_p < L_b \leq L_r$, use the inelastic LTB formula. Linear interpolation between $M_p$ and $0.7F_yS_x$.

steps.text: Check range: $L_p = 8 < L_b = 15 \leq L_r = 25$ → inelastic LTB.

traps: Ignoring LTB when $L_b > L_p$ — even if the beam is compact, the unbraced length can reduce capacity
Confusing nominal $M_n$ with design $\phi M_n$ — read whether the problem asks for nominal or design strength
Using $C_b = 1.0$ when the actual loading would give $C_b > 1.0$ — $C_b = 1.0$ is conservative (uniform moment)

str-sc-q1.statement: A steel column has an effective length $KL = 15 \text{ ft}$ and a weak-axis radius of gyration $r_y = 1.91 \text{ in.}$ What is the slenderness ratio $KL/r_y$?
str-sc-q1.eli5: First convert $KL$ to inches: $15 \times 12 = 180$ in. Then $KL/r_y = 180/1.91 = 94.2 \approx 94$. The choice 180 is $KL$ in inches without dividing by $r$. The choice 31 uses the strong-axis $r_x$ (if $r_x = 5.85$ in., then $180/5.85 = 30.8 \approx 31$). The choice 7.9 reverses the fraction ($r/KL \times 1000$). Always convert feet to inches before dividing by $r$.
str-sc-q1.hint: Convert $KL$ from feet to inches first, then divide by $r_y$.
traps: Forgetting to convert $KL$ from feet to inches before dividing by $r$ (which is in inches)
Using $r_x$ (strong axis) instead of $r_y$ (weak axis) — the larger $KL/r$ controls

str-sc-q2.statement: A steel column has $KL/r = 60$ and a cross-sectional area $A_g = 15.0 \text{ in}^2$. Using $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$ and AISC Table 4-14 (which gives $\phi_c F_{cr} = 34.6 \text{ ksi}$ at $KL/r = 60$), what is the LRFD design compressive strength?
str-sc-q2.eli5: $\phi_c P_n = \phi_c F_{cr} \times A_g = 34.6 \times 15.0 = 519$ kips. That is the total design compressive strength after buckling reduction and safety factor. The 750 kips choice is $F_y \times A_g = 50 \times 15 = 750$, which ignores buckling entirely — this would only be correct for a zero-length column. The 345 kips choice might come from an incorrect table lookup. The 675 kips choice applies $\phi_c = 0.90$ to the gross yield: $0.90 \times 750 = 675$, still ignoring buckling.
str-sc-q2.hint: Design strength $= \phi_c F_{cr} \times A_g$. The $\phi_c F_{cr}$ value is read directly from the AISC table.
traps: Using $F_y$ directly instead of $F_{cr}$ — buckling reduces the effective stress below yield for slender columns
Applying $\phi_c$ again on top of $\phi_c F_{cr}$ — the table value already includes $\phi_c = 0.90$

str-sc-q3.statement: Two columns use the same W-shape ($r_y = 2.0 \text{ in.}$). Column A has an unbraced length of $12 \text{ ft}$ with pin-pin supports ($K = 1.0$). Column B has an unbraced length of $18 \text{ ft}$ with fixed-pin supports ($K = 0.80$). Which column has the higher slenderness ratio?
str-sc-q3.eli5: Column A: $KL/r = (1.0 \times 12 \times 12)/2.0 = 144/2.0 = 72$. Column B: $KL/r = (0.80 \times 18 \times 12)/2.0 = 172.8/2.0 = 86.4 \approx 86$. Column B has the higher $KL/r$ despite having a lower $K$ factor, because its physical length is much longer. Higher $KL/r$ means lower $\phi_c F_{cr}$ and therefore lower design strength. The choice "Column A because $K = 1.0 > 0.80$" is the trap — a lower $K$ factor helps, but it does not always compensate for a much longer column. You must compute the actual $KL/r$ to compare.
str-sc-q3.hint: Compute $KL/r$ for each column. Remember: $K$ reduces the effective length, but a much longer column can still have a higher $KL/r$.

steps.text: Column B has the higher slenderness ratio ($86 > 72$), so it has lower design strength.

traps: Assuming a lower $K$ automatically means better performance — the physical length matters too
Forgetting to convert feet to inches when computing $KL/r$
Using $r_x$ instead of $r_y$ — weak-axis buckling typically governs for W-shapes

str-st-q1.statement: A flat bar ($1/2 \text{ in.} \times 6 \text{ in.}$) is used as a tension member with $F_y = 36 \text{ ksi}$ and $F_u = 58 \text{ ksi}$. There are no bolt holes. What is the LRFD design tensile strength for yielding?
str-st-q1.eli5: $A_g = 0.5 \times 6 = 3.0$ in$^2$. For yielding: $\phi_y P_n = 0.90 \times F_y \times A_g = 0.90 \times 36 \times 3.0 = 97.2 \approx 97$ kips. The 108 kips choice is $F_y \times A_g = 108$ without the $\phi$ factor. The 174 kips choice uses $F_u$ instead of $F_y$ with no $\phi$ factor: $174 = F_u \times A_g = 58 \times 3.0$. The 131 kips choice uses $\phi = 0.75$ with $F_u$: $0.75 \times 58 \times 3.0 = 130.5 \approx 131$ — that is the rupture check, not yielding.
str-st-q1.hint: For yielding: $\phi_y P_n = 0.90 \times F_y \times A_g$. No bolt hole deductions.
traps: Using $F_u$ instead of $F_y$ for yielding — yielding uses $F_y$ (yield stress), rupture uses $F_u$ (ultimate stress)
Forgetting the $\phi_y = 0.90$ factor

str-st-q2.statement: A plate tension member is $1/2 \text{ in.}$ thick and $10 \text{ in.}$ wide. Two $7/8 \text{-in.}$ diameter bolts are placed at the same cross-section (side by side). What is the net area $A_n$?
str-st-q2.eli5: For each bolt hole, subtract $(d_b + 1/8")$ from the gross width: $7/8 + 1/8 = 1.0$ in. per hole. With 2 holes: $A_n = [10 - 2(1.0)] \times 0.5 = 8.0 \times 0.5 = 4.00$ in$^2$. The $1/8"$ comes from $1/16"$ hole clearance $+ 1/16"$ drilling damage. The $4.13 \text{ in}^2$ option subtracts only $d_b = 0.875$ per hole without the extra $1/8"$: $[10 - 2(0.875)] \times 0.5 = 4.125$. The $5.00 \text{ in}^2$ option is the gross area with no deductions. The $4.06 \text{ in}^2$ option adds only $1/16"$ instead of $1/8"$ to each bolt diameter.
str-st-q2.hint: Net width $=$ gross width $- \Sigma(d_b + 1/8")$ for each hole. Then multiply by thickness.
traps: Subtracting only the bolt diameter without adding the 1/8" for clearance and damage
Adding only 1/16" (clearance) instead of 1/8" (clearance + damage)
Forgetting to deduct holes at all and using the gross area

str-st-q3.statement: A plate member ($1/2 \text{ in.} \times 8 \text{ in.}$) has $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$ and $F_u = 65 \text{ ksi}$. Two $3/4 \text{-in.}$ bolts attach it at one cross-section. For a flat bar, $U = 1.0$. Which limit state controls, and what is the design tension capacity?
str-st-q3.eli5: Gross area: $A_g = 8 \times 0.5 = 4.0$ in$^2$. Net area: $A_n = [8 - 2(3/4 + 1/8)] \times 0.5 = [8 - 2(0.875)] \times 0.5 = [8 - 1.75] \times 0.5 = 6.25 \times 0.5 = 3.125$ in$^2$. With $U = 1.0$: $A_e = 3.125$ in$^2$. Yielding: $\phi_y P_n = 0.90 \times 50 \times 4.0 = 180$ kips. Rupture: $\phi_t P_n = 0.75 \times 65 \times 3.125 = 152.3 \approx 152$ kips. Controlling $= \min(180, 152) = 152$ kips (rupture). Even though rupture uses a higher material strength ($F_u > F_y$), the smaller net area and lower $\phi$ factor make it control. The 180-kips yielding choice picks the larger value, but the smaller capacity governs.
str-st-q3.hint: Compute both $\phi_y F_y A_g$ (yielding) and $\phi_t F_u A_e$ (rupture). The smaller one controls.
str-st-q3.handbookFormula: \text{Yielding: } \phi_y P_n = 0.90 F_y A_g; \quad \text{Rupture: } \phi_t P_n = 0.75 F_u A_e
traps: Picking the larger value as the capacity — the smaller design strength controls because it represents the weaker failure mode
Using the same $\phi$ factor for both limit states — yielding uses 0.90, rupture uses 0.75
Forgetting to deduct bolt holes for the rupture check or deducting holes for the yielding check (yielding uses $A_g$)

str-ds-ex1.statement: A planar truss has 9 members, 6 joints, and 3 external reactions. Is the truss statically determinate?

choices.text: No, it is statically indeterminate by 2 degrees
No, it is statically indeterminate by 1 degree

str-ds-ex1.eli5: For a truss: $m + r = 2j$ for determinate. Here: $9 + 3 = 12$, and $2(6) = 12$. Since $m + r = 2j$, the truss is statically determinate. If $m + r > 2j$, it is indeterminate. If $m + r < 2j$, it is unstable.
str-ds-ex1.hint: Check if $m + r = 2j$ for a truss.

steps.text: Determinacy condition for a planar truss:
Since $12 = 12$, the truss is statically determinate.

traps: Confusing the truss formula (m+r=2j) with the beam/frame formula (3m+r=3j+c)

str-ds-ex2.statement: A structure is externally stable but has $m + r > 2j$. This means the structure is:
str-ds-ex2.eli5: When $m + r > 2j$, there are more unknowns than equilibrium equations. The structure has redundant members or supports -- it is statically indeterminate. You would need compatibility equations in addition to equilibrium to solve it. The degree of indeterminacy is $(m + r) - 2j$.
str-ds-ex2.hint: What happens when there are more unknowns than equilibrium equations?

steps.text: $m + r > 2j$ means more unknowns than equations of equilibrium.
The structure has redundant members/supports and is statically indeterminate.

traps: Confusing indeterminacy with instability — indeterminate means too many supports, unstable means too few

str-ds-ex3.statement: A plane frame has $m = 5$ members, $j = 6$ joints, and two internal hinges ($c = 2$). The supports consist of two pin supports and one roller. What is the degree of static indeterminacy?
str-ds-ex3.eli5: For frames, compare $3m + r$ to $3j + c$. Reactions: two pins give $2 + 2 = 4$, one roller gives 1, so $r = 5$. Then $3m + r = 3(5) + 5 = 20$, and $3j + c = 3(6) + 2 = 20$. Since $20 = 20$, the frame is statically determinate (degree = 0). Each internal hinge provides one extra condition equation, which reduces the degree of indeterminacy. Without those two hinges, the frame would be indeterminate to the 2nd degree.
str-ds-ex3.hint: Count reactions from all supports, then use the frame formula $3m + r$ vs $3j + c$.
traps: Forgetting to include internal hinges in the condition equations (c) — each hinge adds one equation
Mixing up the truss formula (m + r vs 2j) with the frame formula (3m + r vs 3j + c)

str-ds-ex4.statement: A planar truss satisfies $m + r > 2j$. However, all external reactions pass through a single point. What is the correct classification?

choices.text: Unstable — concurrent reactions cannot maintain equilibrium
Indeterminate unless a moment equation is added

str-ds-ex4.eli5: The numerical count $m + r > 2j$ suggests indeterminacy, but that equation is only a necessary condition for stability, not a sufficient one. If all reaction lines of action pass through a single point (concurrent reactions), the structure cannot resist a moment about that point. Apply the moment equilibrium equation $\Sigma M = 0$ at that point and you get 0 = something nonzero, which is impossible. The structure is geometrically unstable regardless of how many extra members or reactions it has. Always check the arrangement of reactions, not just the count.
str-ds-ex4.hint: The determinacy equation is necessary but not sufficient. What happens if you sum moments about the point where all reactions intersect?

steps.text: But all reactions pass through one point (concurrent).
$\Sigma M$ about that point cannot be satisfied for arbitrary loading — the structure is geometrically unstable.
Geometric instability overrides the numerical count.

traps: Assuming the numerical count alone guarantees stability — arrangement of reactions matters
Confusing concurrent reactions (all through one point) with parallel reactions (all in one direction) — both cause instability

str-lc-ex1.statement: A roof beam supports $D = 15 \text{ kips}$ and a roof live load $L_r = 20 \text{ kips}$. No floor live load, snow, wind, or seismic. What is the factored load using LRFD Combination 3 ($1.2D + 1.6L_r$)?
str-lc-ex1.eli5: Combination 3 with only roof live load active is $1.2D + 1.6L_r = 1.2(15) + 1.6(20) = 18 + 32 = 50$ kips. The 35 kips choice is the unfactored sum $D + L_r = 15 + 20$. The 21 kips choice is Combination 1: $1.4D = 1.4(15) = 21$. The 56 kips choice comes from applying 1.6 to both loads: $1.6(15) + 1.6(20) = 56$, but dead load gets 1.2, not 1.6.
str-lc-ex1.hint: Apply the load factors directly: 1.2 on D and 1.6 on $L_r$.
traps: Applying 1.6 to dead load instead of 1.2 — dead load always gets the lower factor

str-lc-ex2.statement: In LRFD, why does dead load receive a lower load factor (1.2) than live load (1.6)?

choices.text: Dead load is more predictable; live load has greater statistical variability
Dead load is always smaller than live load
ASCE 7 assigns factors based on load duration, not uncertainty
Dead load only acts during construction, so it needs a smaller factor

str-lc-ex2.eli5: Load factors in LRFD reflect the uncertainty in predicting each load magnitude. Dead load (self-weight of structure, permanent fixtures) can be calculated accurately from material densities and dimensions, so its variability is low — hence a 1.2 factor. Live load (people, furniture, stored goods) is much harder to predict and varies widely over a building's life, so it gets the larger 1.6 factor. The "dead load is always smaller than live load" choice is wrong because dead load can easily exceed live load in some structures. The "factors based on load duration" choice confuses duration with uncertainty. The "dead load only acts during construction" choice is incorrect — dead load acts permanently, not just during construction.
str-lc-ex2.hint: Think about which load can be estimated more reliably from engineering calculations.

steps.text: Dead load is computed from known material weights and geometry — low uncertainty.
Live load depends on occupancy and use — high variability over the structure's life.
Higher uncertainty → higher load factor to maintain a consistent safety margin.

traps: Assuming load factors are based on magnitude rather than uncertainty — a small but uncertain load still gets a high factor

str-lc-ex3.statement: An interior beam ($K_{LL} = 2$) supports one floor with a tributary area of $A_T = 1{,}200 \text{ ft}^2$. The unreduced live load is $L_o = 80 \text{ psf}$. What is the reduced live load?
str-lc-ex3.eli5: $L = L_o(0.25 + 15/\sqrt{K_{LL} \cdot A_T}) = 80(0.25 + 15/\sqrt{2 \times 1200}) = 80(0.25 + 15/\sqrt{2400}) = 80(0.25 + 15/49.0) = 80(0.25 + 0.306) = 80(0.556) = 44.5 \approx 44$ psf. Check minimum: for one floor, $L \geq 0.50 L_o = 40$ psf. Since $44 > 40$, the reduction is valid. The 40 psf choice is the minimum allowed — it would only apply if the formula gave a value below 40. The 80 psf choice is the unreduced load. The 20 psf choice misapplies $0.25 \times L_o$.
str-lc-ex3.hint: Use $L = L_o(0.25 + 15/\sqrt{K_{LL} A_T})$ with $K_{LL} = 2$ for beams, then check the one-floor minimum.
traps: Using $K_{LL} = 4$ (column value) instead of $K_{LL} = 2$ (beam value)
Skipping the minimum live load check — the formula can over-reduce if the influence area is very large

str-lc-ex4.statement: A column supports $D = 50 \text{ kips}$, $L = 30 \text{ kips}$, and $S = 60 \text{ kips}$. In LRFD Combination 2, $L$ gets the 1.6 factor. In Combination 3, $S$ gets the 1.6 factor. Which combination controls and why?

choices.text: Combination 1 ($70 \text{ kips}$) — dead load alone is the critical case
Combination 2 ($138 \text{ kips}$) — Combination 2 always controls for gravity loading
Combination 3 ($186 \text{ kips}$) — snow dominates floor live load, so the 1.6 factor on $S$ produces a larger total
They are equal because $D$ has the same factor in both

str-lc-ex4.eli5: Combo 2: $1.2(50) + 1.6(30) + 0.5(60) = 60 + 48 + 30 = 138$ kips. Combo 3: $1.2(50) + 1.6(60) + 1.0(30) = 60 + 96 + 30 = 186$ kips. Combo 3 controls at 186 kips because snow ($S = 60$) is much larger than floor live load ($L = 30$), so putting the 1.6 factor on snow amplifies the dominant transient load. The Combination 2 (138 kips) choice assumes Combo 2 always governs — that is only true when floor live load exceeds snow. You must always evaluate multiple combinations and pick the largest.
str-lc-ex4.hint: Compute both combinations. The 1.6 factor amplifies whichever load it multiplies — when $S > L$, putting 1.6 on $S$ produces more.

steps.text: Combo 3 controls ($186 > 138$) because snow is the dominant transient load.

traps: Assuming Combination 2 always controls — it only does when floor live load exceeds roof/snow loads
Forgetting to include the companion load in Combination 3 ($L$ at factor 1.0)

str-il-ex1.statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 20 \text{ ft}$. Using the influence line for the left reaction $R_A$, what is the IL ordinate when a unit load is placed $5 \text{ ft}$ from the left support?
str-il-ex1.eli5: The influence line ordinate for the left reaction at position $x$ from the left support is $(L - x)/L$. At $x = 5$ ft: $(20 - 5)/20 = 15/20 = 0.75$. This means when a unit load sits 5 ft from A, the left reaction carries 75% of it. The 0.25 choice uses $x/L$ instead of $(L - x)/L$ -- that would be the reaction at B. The 1.0 choice is the ordinate when the load is directly over A ($x = 0$).
str-il-ex1.hint: The IL for $R_A$ is linear from 1.0 at A to 0 at B. The ordinate at position $x$ from A is $(L - x)/L$.
traps: Using x/L instead of (L - x)/L — that gives the right reaction, not the left

str-il-ex2.statement: For a simply supported beam, where does the influence line for bending moment at a section located at distance $a$ from the left support have its maximum ordinate?

choices.text: Directly at the section, with ordinate $a(L - a)/L$
At the left support, with ordinate 1.0
At the right support, with ordinate 1.0

str-il-ex2.eli5: The influence line for bending moment at a section is triangular. It goes from 0 at both supports to a peak at the section itself. The peak ordinate is $a(L - a)/L$. This means to produce the maximum moment at that section, you place the load directly at the section. The midspan-ordinate choice ($L/4$) is only correct when the section happens to be at midspan ($a = L/2$, giving $L/4$). The two support choices (ordinate 1.0 at a support) describe the reaction influence line, not the moment influence line.
str-il-ex2.hint: The IL for moment at a section forms a triangle — think about where the peak of that triangle occurs.

steps.text: The IL for moment at section $a$ is triangular, peaking at the section.

traps: Assuming the peak is always L/4 — that is only true at midspan
Confusing the moment IL (triangular, peaks at the section) with the reaction IL (linear, peaks at the support)

str-il-ex3.statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 30 \text{ ft}$. A uniform distributed load of $w = 2 \text{ kip/ft}$ covers the entire span. Using the influence line for moment at midspan, what is the maximum bending moment at midspan?
str-il-ex3.eli5: For a distributed load, the effect equals the load intensity times the area under the IL over the loaded region. The IL for midspan moment is a triangle with base $L = 30$ ft and peak $L/4 = 7.5$ ft. Area $= (1/2)(30)(7.5) = 112.5$ ft$^2$. Moment $= w \times \text{Area} = 2 \times 112.5 = 225$ kip-ft. You can verify: $M = wL^2/8 = 2(30)^2/8 = 225$ kip-ft -- same answer. The 112.5 kip-ft choice forgets to multiply by $w$. The 450 kip-ft choice doubles the triangle area. The 150 kip-ft choice uses $L/4 = 7.5$ as the area instead of computing the triangle area.
str-il-ex3.hint: For a distributed load, multiply the load intensity by the area under the IL diagram. The IL is a triangle with base L and peak L/4.
traps: Using P times ordinate (for concentrated loads) instead of w times area (for distributed loads)
Computing the area of the triangle incorrectly — remember it is (1/2)(base)(height)

str-il-ex4.statement: A simply supported beam has a section at the quarter point ($a = L/4$). The influence line for shear at that section has a positive ordinate of $+0.75$ just to the right and a negative ordinate of $-0.25$ just to the left. To maximize the positive shear using a single moving concentrated load, where should the load be placed?

choices.text: Just to the left of the section
Just to the right of the section

str-il-ex4.eli5: The IL for shear at a section jumps by 1.0 at the section. On the right side of the section, the ordinate is positive and maximum just to the right of the cut ($+0.75$), decreasing linearly to 0 at the right support. On the left side, ordinates are negative. To maximize the positive shear, place the load where the positive ordinate is largest — that is just to the right of the section. Placing the load at midspan gives a smaller positive ordinate (the IL decreases linearly from the section to the right support). Placing it just to the left gives the maximum negative shear ($-0.25$), not positive. At the right support, the ordinate is 0.
str-il-ex4.hint: The IL for positive shear is largest immediately to the right of the section and decreases linearly toward the right support.

steps.text: IL for shear at section $a = L/4$:
Just right of section: $\eta = 1 - a/L = 1 - 0.25 = +0.75$ (maximum positive)
Maximum positive shear occurs when the load is just to the right of the section.

traps: Placing the load at midspan — the IL ordinate at midspan is less than the ordinate just right of the section unless the section is at midspan
Confusing positive and negative shear — the jump in the IL occurs at the section, and the sign changes there

str-rfs-ex1.statement: A singly reinforced beam has $b = 14 \text{ in.}$, $d = 22 \text{ in.}$, $A_s = 4.00 \text{ in}^2$, $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$, and $f_c' = 3 \text{ ksi}$. What is the stress block depth $a$?
str-rfs-ex1.eli5: $a = A_s f_y / (0.85 f_c' b) = 4.00 \times 60 / (0.85 \times 3 \times 14) = 240/35.7 = 6.72$ in. The 5.71 in. choice could come from $A_s f_y / (f_c' b) = 240/42 = 5.71$ if you forget the 0.85 -- that is the trap. The 7.56 in. choice uses $b = 12$ instead of 14. The 4.00 in. choice is just $A_s$ -- a nonsensical substitution.
str-rfs-ex1.hint: $a = A_s f_y / (0.85 f_c' b)$. Make sure to include the 0.85 factor in the denominator.
traps: Forgetting the 0.85 coefficient in the denominator — this would overestimate $a$ and underestimate the moment arm

str-rfs-ex2.statement: In the ACI flexure formula $M_n = A_s f_y (d - a/2)$, the term $(d - a/2)$ represents the internal moment arm. Why is it measured from the centroid of tension steel to half the stress block depth rather than to the top of the beam?

choices.text: The resultant concrete compression force acts at the centroid of the Whitney stress block, which is at $a/2$ from the top
The concrete is assumed to carry no tension, so only the top half matters
The stress block depth $a$ always equals $d$, making the arm $d/2$
ACI uses $d - a/2$ as a safety reduction, not an actual moment arm

str-rfs-ex2.eli5: The Whitney stress block replaces the actual nonlinear compression zone with a uniform rectangular block of depth $a$. The resultant compressive force $C = 0.85 f_c' b a$ acts at the centroid of this rectangle, which is $a/2$ from the compression face. The tension force $T = A_s f_y$ acts at the centroid of the steel, located at depth $d$. The moment is force times lever arm: $M_n = T \times (d - a/2)$. The "concrete carries no tension" choice is partially true but does not explain the lever arm formula. The choice claiming $a$ always equals $d$ is wrong — $a$ is much smaller than $d$ in typical designs. The choice calling $d - a/2$ a safety reduction is wrong — this is a real mechanics derivation, not an arbitrary reduction.
str-rfs-ex2.hint: Think about where the resultant compression force acts in a uniform rectangular stress block.

steps.text: Whitney stress block: uniform stress $0.85 f_c'$ over depth $a$.
Moment arm = distance between C and T:

traps: Using $d$ instead of $(d - a/2)$ as the moment arm — this overestimates capacity by ignoring the offset of the compression resultant

str-rfs-ex3.statement: A concrete beam has $b_w = 16 \text{ in.}$, $d = 26 \text{ in.}$, and $f_c' = 5{,}000 \text{ psi}$ (normal weight). What is the design concrete shear capacity $\phi V_c$?
str-rfs-ex3.eli5: $V_c = 2\lambda\sqrt{f_c'} \cdot b_w d = 2(1.0)\sqrt{5000} \times 16 \times 26 = 2(70.71)(416) = 58{,}830$ lb $= 58.8$ kips. $\phi V_c = 0.75 \times 58.8 = 44.1 \approx 44.2$ kips. The 58.9 kips choice is $V_c$ without the $\phi$ factor. The 5.9 kips choice uses $\sqrt{f_c'}$ in ksi: $\sqrt{5} = 2.236$, then $2(2.236)(416) = 1{,}860$ lb $= 1.86$ kips — way too low. Actually, 5.9 might come from $2\sqrt{5}(16)(26)/1000 = 5.87$, confirming the ksi vs. psi trap. The 29.5 kips choice halves $V_c$ somehow, perhaps using $\lambda = 0.75$ for lightweight concrete when it should be 1.0 for normal weight.
str-rfs-ex3.hint: Use $V_c = 2\sqrt{f_c'} \cdot b_w d$ with $f_c'$ in psi. Then multiply by $\phi = 0.75$.
traps: Using $f_c'$ in ksi instead of psi — this produces an answer 1,000 times too small
Forgetting $\phi = 0.75$ for shear — always apply the resistance factor

str-rfs-ex4.statement: A concrete beam has $V_u = 20 \text{ kips}$ at the critical section and $\phi V_c = 30 \text{ kips}$. What is the shear reinforcement requirement?

choices.text: Provide minimum stirrups — $\phi V_c/2 < V_u \leq \phi V_c$
Enlarge the section — concrete cannot carry any shear at all

str-rfs-ex4.eli5: $\phi V_c/2 = 30/2 = 15$ kips. Since $\phi V_c/2 = 15 < V_u = 20 \leq \phi V_c = 30$, the code says provide minimum stirrups. The threshold is: $V_u \leq \phi V_c/2$ means no stirrups; $\phi V_c/2 < V_u \leq \phi V_c$ means minimum stirrups; $V_u > \phi V_c$ means design stirrups for $V_s$. With $V_u = 20$ falling between $\phi V_c/2 = 15$ and $\phi V_c = 30$, minimum stirrups are required. The "no stirrups needed" choice would require $V_u \leq 15$. The "design stirrups for computed $V_s$" choice would require $V_u > 30$. The "enlarge the section" choice is wrong — concrete absolutely carries shear through $V_c$.
str-rfs-ex4.hint: Compare $V_u$ to both $\phi V_c/2$ and $\phi V_c$ to determine which shear reinforcement zone applies.

steps.text: $V_u = 20$ kips, and $\phi V_c/2 = 15 < 20 \leq 30 = \phi V_c$, so provide minimum stirrups.
If $V_u > \phi V_c = 30$, then stirrups with computed $V_s$ would be required.

str-rfs-ex4.handbookFormula: V_u \leq \phi V_c/2 \text{ (no stirrups)}, \quad V_u > \phi V_c \text{ (computed } V_s\text{)}
traps: Confusing the three shear zones — there are three distinct requirements depending on the $V_u$/$\phi V_c$ ratio
Comparing $V_u$ to $V_c$ instead of $\phi V_c$ — always use the factored capacity for comparison

str-rcc-ex1.statement: A short tied column is $14 \text{ in.} \times 14 \text{ in.}$ with 4 #8 bars ($A_{st} = 3.16 \text{ in}^2$), $f_c' = 4 \text{ ksi}$, and $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$. What is the maximum design axial load $\phi P_n$?
str-rcc-ex1.eli5: $A_g = 14 \times 14 = 196$ in$^2$. $\phi P_n = 0.80(0.65)[0.85(4)(196 - 3.16) + 3.16(60)] = 0.52[3.4(192.84) + 189.6] = 0.52[655.7 + 189.6] = 0.52(845.3) = 440$ kips. The 845 kips choice is the value inside the brackets without applying the 0.80 or $\phi$ factors. The 549 kips choice applies only $\phi = 0.65$: $0.65 \times 845.3 = 549$. The 676 kips choice applies only $0.80$: $0.80 \times 845.3 = 676$. You need BOTH factors for tied columns.
str-rcc-ex1.hint: Use $\phi P_n = 0.80\phi[0.85 f_c'(A_g - A_{st}) + A_{st} f_y]$ with $\phi = 0.65$ for tied columns.
traps: Forgetting the 0.80 accidental eccentricity factor — it only applies to columns, not beams

str-rcc-ex2.statement: The ACI column capacity formula includes a 0.80 factor for tied columns (0.85 for spiral columns). What does this factor account for?

choices.text: A material safety factor equivalent to the resistance factor $\phi$
The difference in concrete strength between cylinders and the actual column
The weight of the column itself, which reduces its load-carrying capacity
Accidental eccentricity — columns never truly carry pure concentric axial load

str-rcc-ex2.eli5: In practice, no column carries a perfectly centered axial load. Construction tolerances, member crookedness, and load eccentricities introduce bending even when the design intent is pure compression. The 0.80 factor (0.85 for spiral columns) reduces the theoretical capacity to account for this inevitable moment. Spiral columns get a slightly more favorable factor because spirals provide better confinement and ductility, allowing the column to maintain capacity under eccentric loading. The cylinder-vs-actual-strength choice describes the 0.85 $f_c'$ coefficient in the stress block, not the 0.80 column factor. The self-weight choice is wrong — self-weight is handled through loads, not capacity reduction. The choice equating it with $\phi$ confuses it with the resistance factor, which is a separate reliability factor.
str-rcc-ex2.hint: Think about whether a column in a real building ever carries load at the exact center of its cross-section.

steps.text: Real columns always have some eccentricity from construction tolerances and load path imperfections.
Tied columns: 0.80 factor. Spiral columns: 0.85 (better confinement).
This factor is separate from $\phi$ — both are applied: $\phi P_n = 0.80\phi[\ldots]$

traps: Confusing the 0.80 factor with the 0.85 in $0.85 f_c'$ — the 0.85 on $f_c'$ accounts for concrete strength differences between test cylinders and the actual structure

str-rcc-ex3.statement: A short spiral column is $20 \text{ in.}$ in diameter with 6 #9 bars ($A_{st} = 6.00 \text{ in}^2$), $f_c' = 5 \text{ ksi}$, and $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$. What is $\phi P_n$? (Use $\phi = 0.75$ and the 0.85 factor for spiral columns.)
str-rcc-ex3.eli5: $A_g = \pi(10)^2 = 314.2$ in$^2$. Inner bracket: $0.85(5)(314.2 - 6.0) + 6.0(60) = 4.25(308.2) + 360 = 1{,}310 + 360 = 1{,}670$ kips. $\phi P_n = 0.85(0.75)(1{,}670) = 0.6375 \times 1{,}670 = 1{,}065$ kips. The 1,670 kips choice is the value inside the brackets without the 0.85 and $\phi$ factors. The 869 kips choice uses $0.52$ (tied column factors: $0.80 \times 0.65$) instead of $0.6375$ (spiral factors: $0.85 \times 0.75$). The 1,253 kips choice applies only $\phi = 0.75$ without the 0.85 accidental eccentricity factor.
str-rcc-ex3.hint: For circular columns, $A_g = \pi r^2$. Use the spiral column formula: $0.85\phi[0.85 f_c'(A_g - A_{st}) + A_{st} f_y]$ with $\phi = 0.75$.
traps: Using 0.80 (tied column factor) instead of 0.85 (spiral column factor)
Using $\phi = 0.65$ (tied) instead of $\phi = 0.75$ (spiral)

str-rcc-ex4.statement: A concrete column has $\varepsilon_t = 0.0015$ (net tensile strain in the extreme tension steel). What is the section classification and the correct $\phi$ factor for a tied column?

choices.text: Cannot be determined without knowing $f_c'$ and $f_y$

str-rcc-ex4.eli5: ACI classifies sections by the net tensile strain $\varepsilon_t$ in the extreme tension reinforcement at nominal strength. If $\varepsilon_t \leq 0.002$, the section is compression-controlled -- the concrete crushes before the steel yields significantly. For tied columns, $\phi = 0.65$. If $\varepsilon_t \geq 0.005$, the section is tension-controlled with $\phi = 0.90$. Between 0.002 and 0.005 is the transition zone, where $\phi$ is interpolated. Here, $\varepsilon_t = 0.0015 < 0.002$, so the section is compression-controlled. The tension-controlled choice requires $\varepsilon_t \geq 0.005$. The transition-zone choice requires $\varepsilon_t$ between 0.002 and 0.005. The "cannot be determined" choice is wrong -- the classification depends only on strain, not material properties.
str-rcc-ex4.hint: Compare $\varepsilon_t$ to the ACI thresholds: 0.002 (compression-controlled boundary) and 0.005 (tension-controlled boundary).

steps.text: For spiral columns: $\phi = 0.75$ (but the problem specifies tied).

traps: Confusing the strain thresholds — 0.002 is the compression-controlled limit, 0.005 is the tension-controlled limit
Using $\phi = 0.90$ for all column sections — this only applies to tension-controlled sections like beams

str-sb-ex1.statement: A fully braced W-shape has $Z_x = 96 \text{ in}^3$ and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. What is the LRFD design flexural strength $\phi_b M_n$?
str-sb-ex1.eli5: With full bracing, $M_n = M_p = F_y Z_x = 50 \times 96 = 4{,}800$ kip-in $= 400$ kip-ft. Then $\phi_b M_n = 0.90 \times 400 = 360$ kip-ft. The 400 kip-ft choice is the nominal capacity without $\phi_b$. The 240 kip-ft choice is the ASD allowable: $M_p / \Omega_b = 400/1.67 = 240$. The 288 kip-ft choice comes from using $S_x$ instead of $Z_x$ (a typical $S_x/Z_x$ ratio of about 0.89 would give roughly this).
str-sb-ex1.hint: $M_p = F_y Z_x$, then multiply by $\phi_b = 0.90$. Convert kip-in to kip-ft by dividing by 12.
traps: Reporting nominal $M_p$ instead of design $\phi_b M_p$ — always include the resistance factor for LRFD

str-sb-ex2.statement: A W-shape beam has full lateral bracing and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. The elastic section modulus is $S_x = 100 \text{ in}^3$ and the plastic section modulus is $Z_x = 112 \text{ in}^3$. Which modulus should be used for the LRFD plastic moment capacity?

choices.text: $Z_x = 112 \text{ in}^3$ — the plastic modulus is used for LRFD strength design
$S_x = 100 \text{ in}^3$ — the elastic modulus is always more conservative
Either one — they give the same design strength after applying $\phi$
$S_x$ for compact sections, $Z_x$ for non-compact sections

str-sb-ex2.eli5: For LRFD, the plastic moment capacity is $M_p = F_y Z_x$, using the plastic section modulus. The plastic modulus accounts for the full cross-section reaching yield stress, which is the actual failure mode for compact sections with full bracing. $S_x$ (elastic modulus) is used in the lateral-torsional buckling formula as the lower-bound term ($0.7 F_y S_x$) and in ASD. Using $S_x$ for the plastic moment underestimates capacity by about 10–15% for typical W-shapes. The $S_x$ choice is more conservative but incorrect for LRFD — LRFD is calibrated to use $Z_x$. The choice that swaps moduli by compactness has it backwards.
str-sb-ex2.hint: LRFD uses plastic moment capacity, which requires the section modulus that corresponds to full yielding of the cross-section.

steps.text: $Z_x$ = plastic section modulus: assumes entire cross-section yields.
$S_x$ = elastic section modulus: assumes linear stress distribution up to first yield.

traps: Using $S_x$ instead of $Z_x$ for the plastic moment — $S_x$ is for elastic/ASD calculations and the LTB formula
Assuming more conservative always means correct — LRFD is calibrated to use $Z_x$

str-sb-ex3.statement: A W-shape has $d = 14 \text{ in.}$, $t_w = 0.415 \text{ in.}$, and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. With $C_{v1} = 1.0$ and $\phi_v = 1.00$, what is the LRFD design shear strength $\phi_v V_n$?
str-sb-ex3.eli5: $A_w = d \times t_w = 14 \times 0.415 = 5.81$ in$^2$. $V_n = 0.6 F_y A_w C_{v1} = 0.6(50)(5.81)(1.0) = 174.3 \approx 174$ kips. With $\phi_v = 1.00$: $\phi_v V_n = 174$ kips. The 291 kips option uses $F_y A_w = 50 \times 5.81 = 291$ without the $0.6$ factor. The 350 kips option uses the full section area instead of web area. The 145 kips option incorrectly uses $\phi_v = 0.90$ or applies $0.5 F_y$ instead of $0.6 F_y$.
str-sb-ex3.hint: Shear capacity uses the web area $A_w = d \times t_w$ and $V_n = 0.6 F_y A_w C_{v1}$.
traps: Using the full cross-sectional area instead of web area $A_w = d \times t_w$
Forgetting the 0.6 coefficient — shear yield stress is $0.6 F_y$, not $F_y$

str-sb-ex4.statement: A W-shape beam has $M_p = 600 \text{ kip-ft}$, $L_p = 10 \text{ ft}$, and $L_r = 30 \text{ ft}$. The unbraced length is $L_b = 10 \text{ ft}$. A second identical beam has $L_b = 20 \text{ ft}$ with $C_b = 1.0$. How do their nominal flexural strengths compare?

choices.text: The second beam has elastic LTB since $L_b > L_r$
Both beams reach $M_p = 600$ because they use the same section
Both are reduced by LTB because neither is continuously braced
The first beam reaches $M_p = 600$; the second is reduced below $M_p$ by inelastic LTB

str-sb-ex4.eli5: The first beam has $L_b = 10 = L_p$, so it is fully braced and reaches $M_n = M_p = 600$ kip-ft. The second beam has $L_p = 10 < L_b = 20 \leq L_r = 30$, so it falls in the inelastic LTB zone. Its capacity is reduced by the linear interpolation formula: $M_n = M_p - (M_p - 0.7 F_y S_x)(L_b - L_p)/(L_r - L_p) < M_p$. The "both reach $M_p$" choice ignores the effect of unbraced length — same section does not mean same capacity if bracing conditions differ. The "both are reduced by LTB" choice is wrong because the first beam meets $L_b \leq L_p$. The "elastic LTB" choice is wrong because $L_b = 20 < L_r = 30$, so the second beam is in inelastic LTB, not elastic.
str-sb-ex4.hint: Compare $L_b$ to $L_p$ and $L_r$ for each beam. If $L_b \leq L_p$, full $M_p$. If $L_p < L_b \leq L_r$, inelastic LTB reduces capacity.

steps.text: Beam 1: $L_b = 10 \leq L_p = 10$ — no LTB, $M_n = M_p = 600$ kip-ft.
Beam 2: $L_p = 10 < L_b = 20 \leq L_r = 30$ — inelastic LTB zone.

traps: Assuming the same section always gives the same capacity — bracing conditions can reduce flexural strength significantly
Confusing $L_b = L_p$ (full capacity) with $L_b > L_p$ (LTB reduction)

str-sc-ex1.statement: A steel column has pin-pin supports ($K = 1.0$), an unbraced length of $10 \text{ ft}$, and $r_y = 1.50 \text{ in.}$ What is the slenderness ratio $KL/r_y$?
