str-sc-ex1.eli5: Convert $KL$ to inches: $1.0 \times 10 \times 12 = 120$ in. Then $KL/r_y = 120/1.50 = 80$. The 120 distractor is $KL$ in inches without dividing by $r$. The 6.7 distractor forgets to convert feet to inches: $10/1.50 \approx 6.7$. The 40 distractor uses half the length or otherwise miscounts the unit conversion.
str-sc-ex1.hint: Convert the unbraced length from feet to inches before dividing by $r_y$.
traps: Forgetting to convert feet to inches — $r$ is always given in inches on the FE

str-sc-ex2.statement: A cantilever column has a recommended effective length factor $K = 2.10$. A pin-pin column has $K = 1.0$. If both have the same physical length and cross-section, which has the lower design compressive strength?

choices.text: Both have the same strength because they have the same cross-section
The pin-pin column — its lower $K$ means less restraint and lower capacity
The cantilever — its larger $K$ produces a higher $KL/r$, reducing $\phi_c F_{cr}$
The cantilever — but only because it has a different $\phi_c$ factor

str-sc-ex2.eli5: The effective length factor $K$ converts the physical length into an equivalent pin-pin length for buckling. A cantilever ($K = 2.10$) has an effective length more than twice the physical length because one end is free to translate. This dramatically increases $KL/r$, which reduces the critical buckling stress $F_{cr}$. The pin-pin column ($K = 1.0$) buckles over exactly its physical length. Higher $KL/r$ always means lower strength. The choice claiming the pin-pin column is weaker confuses $K$ with restraint — lower $K$ actually means MORE restraint (better support conditions). The choice saying both have the same strength ignores the role of end conditions. The choice blaming a different $\phi_c$ factor is wrong because $\phi_c = 0.90$ for both.
str-sc-ex2.hint: Higher $K$ means a longer effective length for buckling. Longer effective length means higher $KL/r$ and lower critical stress.

steps.text: Since $2.10 L/r > 1.0 L/r$, the cantilever has higher slenderness and lower $F_{cr}$.

traps: Thinking lower $K$ means less stability — it is the opposite; lower $K$ means better end restraint and more stability

str-sc-ex3.statement: A W10x49 column ($A_g = 14.4 \text{ in}^2$, $r_y = 2.54 \text{ in.}$) has fixed-pin supports ($K = 0.80$) and an unbraced length of $16 \text{ ft}$. Using $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$ and AISC Table 4-14 ($\phi_c F_{cr} = 38.3 \text{ ksi}$ at $KL/r = 60$), what is the LRFD design compressive strength?
str-sc-ex3.eli5: $KL = 0.80 \times 16 \times 12 = 153.6$ in. $KL/r_y = 153.6/2.54 = 60.5 \approx 60$. From the table at $KL/r = 60$: $\phi_c F_{cr} = 38.3$ ksi. $\phi_c P_n = 38.3 \times 14.4 = 551.5 \approx 552$ kips. The 720 kips choice is $F_y \times A_g = 50 \times 14.4 = 720$, ignoring buckling. The 648 kips choice is $0.90 \times 720 = 648$, applying only $\phi$ without buckling reduction. The 383 kips choice might use the wrong area or an incorrect table value.
str-sc-ex3.hint: Compute $KL/r_y$, look up $\phi_c F_{cr}$ from the table, then multiply by $A_g$.
traps: Using $F_y$ directly instead of the table value $\phi_c F_{cr}$ — buckling reduces the effective stress
Applying $\phi_c = 0.90$ again on top of $\phi_c F_{cr}$ — the table value already includes $\phi_c$

str-sc-ex4.statement: A W-shape column has $r_x = 6.0 \text{ in.}$ and $r_y = 2.0 \text{ in.}$ The column is braced at every $12 \text{ ft}$ in the strong axis and at every $6 \text{ ft}$ in the weak axis (both pin-pin, $K = 1.0$). Which axis controls buckling?

choices.text: Neither controls — check only the axis with the larger $r$ value
Strong axis controls because it has the longer unbraced length
Weak axis controls because $r_y < r_x$, regardless of bracing
Strong axis ($KL/r_x = 24$) and weak axis ($KL/r_y = 36$) — weak axis controls with the larger ratio

str-sc-ex4.eli5: Strong axis: $KL/r_x = (1.0 \times 12 \times 12)/6.0 = 144/6.0 = 24$. Weak axis: $KL/r_y = (1.0 \times 6 \times 12)/2.0 = 72/2.0 = 36$. The weak axis has the larger slenderness ratio ($36 > 24$), so it controls. Even though the weak axis has a shorter unbraced length (6 ft vs. 12 ft), $r_y$ is so much smaller than $r_x$ that it still produces the larger $KL/r$. The "strong axis controls because it has the longer unbraced length" choice only considers length, not the radius of gyration. The "weak axis controls because $r_y < r_x$, regardless of bracing" choice states the conclusion correctly but for the wrong reason — you must compute both ratios, not assume. The "check only the axis with the larger $r$ value" choice is backwards — check the axis with the LARGER $KL/r$, not the larger $r$.
str-sc-ex4.hint: Compute $KL/r$ for both axes using their respective unbraced lengths. The larger ratio governs.

steps.text: Weak axis controls ($36 > 24$) despite having the shorter unbraced length.

traps: Assuming the longer unbraced length always controls — the radius of gyration matters just as much
Checking only one axis — you must compute $KL/r$ for both axes and use the larger value

str-st-ex1.statement: A flat bar ($3/8 \text{ in.} \times 8 \text{ in.}$) has two $3/4 \text{-in.}$ diameter bolts at the same cross-section. What is the net area $A_n$?
str-st-ex1.eli5: Each bolt hole subtracts $d_b + 1/8\text{"} = 3/4 + 1/8 = 7/8 = 0.875$ in. from the gross width. With two holes: net width $= 8 - 2(0.875) = 8 - 1.75 = 6.25$ in. Then $A_n = 6.25 \times 3/8 = 6.25 \times 0.375 = 2.34$ in$^2$. The 2.44 choice subtracts only $d_b = 0.75$ per hole without the 1/8" addition: $(8 - 1.50)(0.375) = 2.44$. The 3.00 choice is the gross area with no deductions. The 2.63 choice subtracts only one hole instead of two.
str-st-ex1.hint: Subtract $(d_b + 1/8\text{"})$ for each hole from the gross width, then multiply by thickness.
traps: Forgetting the 1/8" addition for clearance and damage — the hole is larger than the bolt

str-st-ex2.statement: Why does AISC use a lower resistance factor ($\phi = 0.75$) for tensile rupture than for tensile yielding ($\phi = 0.90$)?

choices.text: Rupture is a sudden, brittle failure with no warning, so a larger safety margin is needed
Rupture uses a higher material strength ($F_u$), so the factor must compensate
Rupture only occurs in low-grade steels that need extra conservatism
The lower factor accounts for bolt hole drilling inaccuracy

str-st-ex2.eli5: Yielding spreads across the gross section gradually — the member elongates and gives visible warning before failure. Rupture, on the other hand, happens suddenly at the weakest net section with little plastic deformation. Because rupture is a more dangerous failure mode (no warning, no redistribution), AISC applies a lower resistance factor to build in a larger safety margin. The "higher material strength (Fu)" choice confuses material strength with reliability philosophy. The "low-grade steels only" choice is wrong — rupture can occur in any grade of steel. The "bolt hole drilling inaccuracy" choice is partially related (hole deductions matter) but the fundamental reason is the brittle failure mode.
str-st-ex2.hint: Think about which failure mode gives more warning and allows load redistribution.

steps.text: Yielding: gradual, ductile — the member stretches visibly before failure.
Rupture: sudden, brittle — fracture at the net section with little warning.
More dangerous failure modes get lower $\phi$ factors to increase the safety margin.

traps: Thinking the lower factor is just to offset the higher $F_u$ value — the reason is fundamentally about failure mode ductility

str-st-ex3.statement: A flat bar ($5/8 \text{ in.} \times 10 \text{ in.}$) has three $7/8 \text{-in.}$ bolts at one cross-section. $F_y = 36 \text{ ksi}$, $F_u = 58 \text{ ksi}$, $U = 1.0$. What is the LRFD design tensile capacity?
str-st-ex3.eli5: $A_g = 10 \times 0.625 = 6.25$ in$^2$. Each hole: $7/8 + 1/8 = 1.0$ in. $A_n = [10 - 3(1.0)] \times 0.625 = 7.0 \times 0.625 = 4.375$ in$^2$. With $U = 1.0$: $A_e = 4.375$ in$^2$. Yielding: $\phi P_n = 0.90 \times 36 \times 6.25 = 202.5$ kips. Rupture: $\phi P_n = 0.75 \times 58 \times 4.375 = 190$ kips. Controlling = min(202.5, 190) = 190 kips (rupture governs). The 203 kips choice is the yielding value, but that is the larger capacity — the smaller one controls. The 225 kips choice uses $F_y \times A_g$ without the $\phi$ factor. The 254 kips choice is $F_u \times A_n$ without $\phi$.
str-st-ex3.hint: Check both yielding ($\phi_y F_y A_g$) and rupture ($\phi_t F_u A_e$). The smaller value controls.

steps.text: Net area (3 holes at 1.0 in. each):

str-st-ex3.handbookFormula: \text{Yielding: } \phi_y P_n = 0.90 F_y A_g; \quad \text{Rupture: } \phi_t P_n = 0.75 F_u A_e
traps: Picking the larger capacity instead of the smaller — the weaker limit state controls
Forgetting to add 1/8" to each bolt diameter for hole size

str-st-ex4.statement: An angle connected by bolts through only one leg is used as a tension brace. Compared to a flat bar connected through its full width (both with the same $A_n$), how does the angle's effective net area $A_e$ differ?

choices.text: $A_e$ is the same — $U = 1.0$ for all tension members
$A_e$ is larger because the unconnected leg adds extra capacity
$A_e$ is smaller because the shear lag factor $U < 1.0$ reduces the effective area for the unconnected leg
$A_e$ is smaller because angles use a different $\phi$ factor

str-st-ex4.eli5: When a tension member is connected through only part of its cross-section (like an angle bolted through one leg), the stress does not distribute uniformly across the full section. The unconnected leg experiences "shear lag" — it cannot fully develop its tensile capacity before the connection ends. AISC accounts for this with the shear lag factor $U = 1 - \bar{x}/L$, where $\bar{x}$ is the distance from the connection plane to the centroid of the member and $L$ is the connection length. For a flat bar bolted through its full width, all elements are connected so $U = 1.0$. For an angle connected through one leg, $U < 1.0$, reducing $A_e = U \cdot A_n$. The "larger because the unconnected leg adds extra capacity" option is backwards. The "same, U = 1.0 for all tension members" option is only true for fully connected members. The "different phi factor" option confuses shear lag with resistance factors.
str-st-ex4.hint: Shear lag means not all of the cross-section can develop full stress when only part of it is connected.

steps.text: For a flat bar connected through its full width: $U = 1.0$.
For an angle connected through one leg:

steps.latex: A_e = U \cdot A_n \quad (\text{reduced by shear lag})

traps: Assuming $U = 1.0$ for all shapes — it equals 1.0 only when all cross-sectional elements are connected
Confusing shear lag reduction with resistance factor reduction — they are separate concepts

str-tam-ex1.statement: At a truss joint, an $8\text{ kN}$ vertical (downward) load is resisted by a horizontal member and a diagonal member inclined at $60^\circ$ above the horizontal. What is the force in the diagonal?
str-tam-ex1.eli5: Only the diagonal resists the vertical load. $\sum F_y = 0$: $F\sin 60^\circ = 8$, so $F = 8/0.866 = 9.24\text{ kN}$. The 6.93 kN option multiplies by sin 60° instead of dividing. The 8.0 kN option forgets the angle entirely.
str-tam-ex1.hint: Only the diagonal has a vertical component: F·sin60° = 8.

steps.text: $\sum F_y = 0$ at the joint: the diagonal carries the vertical load.

traps: Multiplying by sin 60° instead of dividing (6.93 kN)
Ignoring the inclination and reporting 8 kN

str-tam-ex2.statement: A vertical section through a parallel-chord truss cuts a diagonal inclined at $45^\circ$. The net vertical shear carried across that section is $20\text{ kN}$. What is the force in the diagonal?
str-tam-ex2.eli5: Only the diagonal has a vertical component, so it carries the section shear: $F\sin 45^\circ = 20$, giving $F = 20/0.707 = 28.3\text{ kN}$. The 14.1 kN option multiplies by sin 45° instead of dividing.
str-tam-ex2.hint: The diagonal’s vertical component equals the section shear.

steps.text: Method of sections, vertical equilibrium: only the diagonal resists shear.

traps: Multiplying by sin 45° (14.1) instead of dividing
Reporting the shear (20) as the member force

str-dvw-ex1.statement: A simply supported beam of length $L = 5\text{ m}$ carries a uniformly distributed load $w = 8\text{ kN/m}$. With $EI = 25{,}000\text{ kN·m}^2$, what is the maximum deflection?
str-dvw-ex1.eli5: Simple span under UDL: $\delta = 5wL^4/384EI = 5(8)(5^4)/(384 \times 25{,}000) = 25{,}000/9{,}600{,}000 = 0.0026\text{ m} = 2.6\text{ mm}$. The 4.2 mm option uses the point-load deflection formula; the 10.4 mm option drops the 384 constant.
traps: Using the point-load formula (PL³/48EI) for a distributed load
Using L³ instead of L⁴ for a distributed load

str-ind-ex1.statement: A beam is fixed (built in) at both ends with no internal hinges. What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
str-ind-ex1.eli5: Each fixed end gives 3 reactions (H, V, M), so $r = 6$. A planar beam has 3 equilibrium equations, so $DSI = 6 - 3 = 3$. The choice giving 1 is a propped cantilever, not fixed-fixed. The choice giving 6 forgets to subtract the equilibrium equations.
str-ind-ex1.hint: Two fixed ends = 6 reactions; subtract 3 equilibrium equations.
traps: Confusing a fixed-fixed beam (DSI 3) with a propped cantilever (DSI 1)
Forgetting to subtract the 3 equilibrium equations

str-ds-cp1.statement: A rigid plane frame has $m = 6$ members and $j = 6$ joints. Both bases are fixed supports and there are no internal hinges ($c = 0$). What is the degree of static indeterminacy?
str-ds-cp1.eli5: For a plane frame, compare $3m + r$ to $3j + c$. Two fixed supports give $r = 3 + 3 = 6$ reaction components. Then $3m + r = 3(6) + 6 = 24$, and $3j + c = 3(6) + 0 = 18$. The degree of indeterminacy is $24 - 18 = 6$. The value 3 results from counting only one fixed support ($r = 3$): $21 - 18 = 3$. The value 4 results from treating each base as a pin ($r = 4$): $22 - 18 = 4$. The value 0 wrongly applies the truss formula $m + r$ vs $2j$.
str-ds-cp1.hint: Count reactions (each fixed support gives 3), then use $3m + r$ vs $3j + c$.
traps: Counting a fixed support as 2 reactions instead of 3 — a fixed base resists horizontal force, vertical force, and moment
Applying the truss formula (m + r vs 2j) to a rigid frame

str-ds-cp2.statement: A single straight beam (one rigid member) is supported by a pin at one end and a pin at the other end, with no internal hinges. Treating it as a planar beam with 3 equilibrium equations, how is it classified externally?

choices.text: Stable and externally indeterminate to the 1st degree
Stable and externally indeterminate to the 3rd degree

str-ds-cp2.eli5: Each pin provides 2 reaction components, so $r = 2 + 2 = 4$. A planar beam has 3 independent equilibrium equations ($\Sigma F_x = 0$, $\Sigma F_y = 0$, $\Sigma M = 0$). The external degree of indeterminacy is $r - 3 = 4 - 3 = 1$. Two pins introduce one redundant horizontal restraint that equilibrium alone cannot resolve. The "stable and statically determinate" choice would require exactly $r = 3$, which is the familiar pin-plus-roller case. The "unstable — mechanism" choice would require $r < 3$. The "indeterminate to the 3rd degree" choice overcounts the redundancy — only one extra reaction component exists beyond the three equilibrium equations.
str-ds-cp2.hint: Count the reaction components, then compare to the 3 equilibrium equations of a planar beam.

steps.text: Equilibrium equations for a planar beam:

traps: Treating a pin as 1 reaction component instead of 2
Assuming any beam with two supports is automatically determinate — a pin-pin beam has a redundant horizontal restraint

str-lc-cp1.statement: A beam carries $D = 40 \text{ kips}$, floor live load $L = 30 \text{ kips}$, and snow $S = 24 \text{ kips}$. Using the ASD combination $D + 0.75L + 0.75(L_r \text{ or } S \text{ or } R)$, what is the design (service-level) load?
str-lc-cp1.eli5: ASD uses unfactored loads with the 0.75 companion factor: $D + 0.75L + 0.75S = 40 + 0.75(30) + 0.75(24) = 40 + 22.5 + 18 = 80.5$ kips. The 94 kips option is the plain sum $D + L + S = 40 + 30 + 24$, forgetting the 0.75 factors. The 84 kips option is the LRFD combination $1.2D + 1.6L = 48 + 48$ — wrong because the problem specifies ASD. The 62.5 kips option drops the snow term and uses only $D + 0.75L = 40 + 22.5$.
str-lc-cp1.hint: ASD uses service loads. Apply the 0.75 companion factor to both $L$ and $S$.
traps: Applying LRFD load factors (1.2, 1.6) to an ASD combination
Forgetting the 0.75 companion factor on the live and snow loads

str-lc-cp2.statement: A heavily loaded transfer girder supports $D = 100 \text{ kips}$ and a small floor live load $L = 10 \text{ kips}$ (no snow, wind, or seismic). Which LRFD combination controls and what is the controlling factored load?
str-lc-cp2.eli5: Combination 1 is $1.4D = 1.4(100) = 140$ kips. Combination 2 is $1.2D + 1.6L = 1.2(100) + 1.6(10) = 120 + 16 = 136$ kips. Because dead load dominates and live load is small, Combination 1 (140) produces the larger factored load and controls. This is the case the $1.4D$ combination exists for. The 136 kips option is Combination 2, which is smaller here. The 120 kips option keeps only the $1.2D$ term and drops live load. The 110 kips option is the unfactored service load $D + L$.
str-lc-cp2.hint: When dead load dominates, check Combination 1 ($1.4D$) against Combination 2 ($1.2D + 1.6L$).

steps.text: Controlling: Combination 1 at 140 kips (dead load dominates).

traps: Assuming Combination 2 always controls — when live load is small relative to dead load, $1.4D$ governs
Reporting the unfactored service load instead of the factored LRFD load

str-il-cp1.statement: A simply supported beam spans $L = 20 \text{ ft}$. A uniform load $w = 3 \text{ kip/ft}$ covers only the left half (from the left support to midspan). Using the influence line for the left reaction $R_A$, what is $R_A$?
str-il-cp1.eli5: The IL for $R_A$ is a straight line from $1.0$ at A to $0$ at B, so the ordinate at distance $x$ is $(L - x)/L$. Over the loaded region (0 to 10 ft) the ordinate runs from $1.0$ down to $0.5$. The area under the IL there is the trapezoid $\tfrac{1.0 + 0.5}{2}(10) = 7.5$. For a distributed load, $R_A = w \times \text{area} = 3 \times 7.5 = 22.5$ kips. Check by statics: the half-span load is $3(10) = 30$ kips acting at $5$ ft from A, so $R_A = 30(20 - 5)/20 = 22.5$ kips. The 30 kips option is the total applied load, not the reaction. The 15 kips option is the right reaction $R_B$. The 7.5 option is the IL area without multiplying by $w$.
str-il-cp1.hint: For a distributed load, multiply $w$ by the area under the reaction IL over the loaded region (a trapezoid here).

steps.text: IL ordinate at A and at midspan:
Area under IL over the loaded half:

traps: Multiplying $w$ by the full span instead of only the loaded region
Using the IL ordinate at a single point instead of the area under the loaded length

str-il-cp2.statement: A simply supported beam carries a uniform load over its entire span. Using the influence line for shear at midspan (which is positive to the right of the cut and negative to the left, with equal triangular areas), what is the shear at midspan?

choices.text: Zero — the equal positive and negative IL areas cancel
Equal to the midspan moment divided by $L$

str-il-cp2.eli5: The IL for shear at midspan is antisymmetric: a positive triangle on the right half and an equal negative triangle on the left half. For a uniform load over the whole span, the shear equals $w$ times the net area under the IL. Because the positive and negative areas are equal in magnitude, they cancel and the net shear at midspan is zero. This matches the familiar result that shear is zero at the point of maximum moment in a symmetric beam. The "maximum positive" and "maximum negative" choices assume the load sits on only one half of the span. The choice equating shear to the midspan moment divided by L confuses the shear-moment relationship.
str-il-cp2.hint: For a full-span uniform load, the shear equals $w$ times the net (signed) area under the shear IL.

steps.text: Midspan shear IL: positive triangle (right half) and negative triangle (left half) of equal area.
Net area for a full-span uniform load:

str-il-cp2.handbookFormula: V = w \times \text{(net signed area under IL)}
traps: Forgetting that the shear IL has both positive and negative regions that cancel under full loading
To maximize shear at a section, load only the region of one sign — full-span loading gives the net effect, not the maximum

str-rfs-cp1.statement: A singly reinforced concrete beam has $b_w = 12 \text{ in.}$, $d = 20 \text{ in.}$, $f_c' = 4{,}000 \text{ psi}$, and $f_y = 60{,}000 \text{ psi}$. What is the ACI minimum flexural steel area $A_{s,\min}$?
str-rfs-cp1.eli5: ACI requires $A_{s,\min}$ to be the larger of $\frac{3\sqrt{f_c'}}{f_y} b_w d$ and $\frac{200}{f_y} b_w d$, with stresses in psi. First term: $\frac{3\sqrt{4000}}{60000}(12)(20) = \frac{189.7}{60000}(240) = 0.759$ in$^2$. Second term: $\frac{200}{60000}(12)(20) = \frac{200}{60000}(240) = 0.80$ in$^2$. The larger value governs, so $A_{s,\min} = 0.80$ in$^2$. The 0.76 in$^2$ choice is the first term alone — but the $200/f_y$ term controls for $f_c' \leq 4{,}444$ psi. The 0.40 in$^2$ choice drops $b_w$. The 1.60 in$^2$ choice doubles the area by a unit slip.
str-rfs-cp1.hint: Compute both $\frac{3\sqrt{f_c'}}{f_y} b_w d$ and $\frac{200}{f_y} b_w d$ (psi units) and take the larger.
traps: Computing only one of the two expressions — ACI requires the larger
Using $f_c'$ and $f_y$ in ksi instead of psi, which scales the result incorrectly

str-rfs-cp2.statement: A reinforced concrete beam ($d = 22 \text{ in.}$) uses #4 U-stirrups ($A_v = 0.40 \text{ in}^2$ for two legs) with $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$ spaced at $s = 8 \text{ in.}$ What is the shear strength contributed by the stirrups, $V_s$?
str-rfs-cp2.eli5: $V_s = \frac{A_v f_y d}{s} = \frac{0.40 \times 60 \times 22}{8} = \frac{528}{8} = 66$ kips. The 33 kips option uses only one stirrup leg ($A_v = 0.20$) instead of the two-leg area. The 132 kips option halves the spacing to $s = 4$ in. by mistake. The 30 kips option drops $d$ and uses an incorrect lever term.
str-rfs-cp2.hint: Use $V_s = A_v f_y d / s$ with the two-leg stirrup area.
traps: Using a single stirrup leg area instead of $A_v$ for both legs
Substituting the wrong spacing — $s$ is the center-to-center stirrup spacing

str-rcc-cp1.statement: A short tied column is $12 \text{ in.} \times 18 \text{ in.}$ with $A_{st} = 4.00 \text{ in}^2$, $f_c' = 4 \text{ ksi}$, and $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$. What is the maximum design axial load $\phi P_n$?
str-rcc-cp1.eli5: $A_g = 12 \times 18 = 216$ in$^2$. Inside the brackets: $0.85(4)(216 - 4.0) + 4.0(60) = 3.4(212) + 240 = 720.8 + 240 = 960.8$ kips. For a tied column apply both factors: $\phi P_n = 0.80(0.65)(960.8) = 0.52 \times 960.8 = 500$ kips. The 961 kips choice omits both the 0.80 and $\phi$ factors. The 625 kips choice applies only $\phi = 0.65$. The 769 kips choice applies only the 0.80 factor.
str-rcc-cp1.hint: Use $\phi P_n = 0.80\phi[0.85 f_c'(A_g - A_{st}) + A_{st} f_y]$ with $\phi = 0.65$ for tied columns.
traps: Forgetting the 0.80 accidental eccentricity factor for tied columns
Forgetting to subtract $A_{st}$ from $A_g$ in the concrete term

str-rcc-cp2.statement: A designer proposes a tied column with a longitudinal reinforcement ratio of $\rho_g = 0.10$ (10 percent). Per ACI 318, what is the issue?

choices.text: It is acceptable — there is no upper limit on $\rho_g$
It is below the 1 percent minimum, risking brittle failure
It exceeds the 8 percent maximum, causing bar congestion and poor concrete placement
It is only a problem for spiral columns, not tied columns

str-rcc-cp2.eli5: ACI limits the longitudinal steel ratio to $0.01 \leq \rho_g \leq 0.08$ (1 to 8 percent). A 10 percent ratio exceeds the 8 percent maximum. The upper limit prevents reinforcement congestion that makes it impossible to place and consolidate concrete around the bars and at lap splices. The "acceptable — no upper limit" choice is wrong because an upper limit exists. The "below the 1 percent minimum" choice has the direction backwards — 10 percent is far above, not below, the minimum. The "only a problem for spiral columns" choice is wrong because the limits apply to both tied and spiral columns.
str-rcc-cp2.hint: Recall the ACI reinforcement ratio limits for columns and which bound 10 percent violates.

steps.text: Exceeds the 8 percent maximum — causes bar congestion and placement problems.

traps: Forgetting that ACI imposes an 8 percent upper limit, not just a 1 percent lower limit
Confusing the upper-limit violation (congestion) with the lower-limit violation (brittle failure)

str-sb-cp1.statement: A fully braced W-shape has $Z_x = 100 \text{ in}^3$ and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. What is the ASD allowable flexural strength $M_n/\Omega_b$?
str-sb-cp1.eli5: With full bracing, $M_n = M_p = F_y Z_x = 50 \times 100 = 5{,}000$ kip-in $= 416.7$ kip-ft. For ASD, divide by $\Omega_b = 1.67$: $M_n/\Omega_b = 416.7/1.67 = 249.5 \approx 250$ kip-ft. The 417 kip-ft choice is the nominal $M_n$ without applying $\Omega_b$. The 375 kip-ft choice is the LRFD design strength $\phi_b M_n = 0.90 \times 416.7$ — the problem asks for ASD. The 278 kip-ft choice uses an incorrect $\Omega_b = 1.50$.
str-sb-cp1.hint: ASD allowable moment $= M_n/\Omega_b$ with $\Omega_b = 1.67$. Convert kip-in to kip-ft.
traps: Using the LRFD factor $\phi_b = 0.90$ when the problem asks for ASD
Reporting nominal $M_n$ without dividing by $\Omega_b$

str-sb-cp2.statement: A W-shape has $d = 18 \text{ in.}$, $t_w = 0.30 \text{ in.}$, and $F_y = 36 \text{ ksi}$. With $C_{v1} = 1.0$ and $\phi_v = 1.00$, what is the LRFD design shear strength $\phi_v V_n$?
str-sb-cp2.eli5: Web area $A_w = d \times t_w = 18 \times 0.30 = 5.40$ in$^2$. Nominal shear $V_n = 0.6 F_y A_w C_{v1} = 0.6(36)(5.40)(1.0) = 116.6$ kips. With $\phi_v = 1.00$: $\phi_v V_n = 117$ kips. The 194 kips choice omits the 0.6 coefficient ($36 \times 5.40 = 194$). The 162 kips choice uses $0.5 F_y$ instead of $0.6 F_y$ on a larger web area. The 105 kips choice applies $\phi_v = 0.90$ instead of $1.00$ ($0.9 \times 116.6 = 105$).
str-sb-cp2.hint: Shear uses the web area $A_w = d \times t_w$ and $V_n = 0.6 F_y A_w C_{v1}$.
traps: Forgetting the 0.6 shear-yield coefficient
Using the full cross-sectional area instead of the web area

str-sc-cp1.statement: A steel column has $KL/r = 140$, $E = 29{,}000 \text{ ksi}$, and $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$. Since $KL/r > 4.71\sqrt{E/F_y}$, elastic buckling governs. What is the critical stress $F_{cr}$?
str-sc-cp1.eli5: Euler stress: $F_e = \frac{\pi^2 E}{(KL/r)^2} = \frac{\pi^2 (29{,}000)}{140^2} = \frac{286{,}218}{19{,}600} = 14.6$ ksi. For elastic buckling, $F_{cr} = 0.877 F_e = 0.877(14.6) = 12.8$ ksi. The 14.6 ksi choice is $F_e$ itself — it forgets the 0.877 elastic-buckling reduction. The 25.9 ksi choice misapplies the inelastic formula $0.658^{F_y/F_e} F_y$. The 9.6 ksi choice applies the 0.658 base directly.
str-sc-cp1.hint: First find $F_e = \pi^2 E/(KL/r)^2$, then apply $F_{cr} = 0.877 F_e$ for elastic buckling.
traps: Reporting $F_e$ instead of $F_{cr}$ — elastic buckling reduces $F_e$ by the 0.877 factor
Applying the inelastic formula $0.658^{F_y/F_e} F_y$ when $KL/r$ exceeds the elastic threshold

str-sc-cp2.statement: A steel column has $KL/r = 90$, $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$, and $E = 29{,}000 \text{ ksi}$. Which buckling regime governs, and how do you know?

choices.text: Elastic buckling, because $KL/r > 50$ always means elastic
Cannot be determined without the cross-sectional area

str-sc-cp2.eli5: The dividing line between inelastic and elastic column buckling is $4.71\sqrt{E/F_y} = 4.71\sqrt{29{,}000/50} = 4.71\sqrt{580} = 4.71(24.08) = 113.4$. Since the column slenderness $KL/r = 90$ is less than 113.4, the column buckles inelastically and uses $F_{cr} = 0.658^{F_y/F_e} F_y$. The "elastic buckling, because $KL/r = 90 > 113$" choice has the inequality backwards. The "$KL/r > 50$ always means elastic" choice uses an arbitrary cutoff of 50, which is not the AISC threshold. The "cannot be determined without the cross-sectional area" choice is wrong — the regime depends only on $KL/r$, $E$, and $F_y$, not on area.
str-sc-cp2.hint: Compute $4.71\sqrt{E/F_y}$ and compare it to $KL/r$. Below the threshold is inelastic.

steps.text: Since $KL/r$ is below the threshold, inelastic buckling governs.

traps: Reversing the inequality — slenderness below the threshold is inelastic, above is elastic
Using a memorized round-number cutoff instead of computing $4.71\sqrt{E/F_y}$

str-st-cp1.statement: A plate ($3/8 \text{ in.} \times 10 \text{ in.}$) carries three $7/8 \text{-in.}$ bolts arranged in a zig-zag chain. The diagonal failure path runs through all three holes with two staggered segments, each having longitudinal stagger $s = 1.5 \text{ in.}$ and transverse gage $g = 2.5 \text{ in.}$ For this staggered path through all three holes, what is the net area $A_n$?
str-st-cp1.eli5: For a staggered (zig-zag) failure path, the net width is $b_g - \Sigma d_h + \Sigma \frac{s^2}{4g}$. Each hole diameter is $d_h = d_b + 1/8 = 7/8 + 1/8 = 1.0$ in. The three-hole path crosses 3 holes and has 2 diagonal segments, so add $\frac{s^2}{4g}$ twice: net width $= 10 - 3(1.0) + 2\left(\frac{1.5^2}{4(2.5)}\right) = 10 - 3 + 2(0.225) = 10 - 3 + 0.45 = 7.45$ in. Net area $= 7.45 \times 0.375 = 2.79$ in$^2$. The 3.00 in^2 choice takes the straight transverse cut through only the two in-line holes, $(10 - 2.0)(0.375)$, ignoring the third hole and the stagger. The 2.93 in^2 choice adds the two $s^2/4g$ terms but forgets the $1/8$ in. hole allowance, using $d_h = 0.875$: $(10 - 3(0.875) + 0.45)(0.375)$. The 2.63 in^2 choice deducts all three holes but omits the $s^2/4g$ correction: $(10 - 3.0)(0.375)$.
str-st-cp1.hint: For a staggered path, add $s^2/(4g)$ back for each diagonal segment: $b_n = b_g - \Sigma d_h + \Sigma \frac{s^2}{4g}$. A path through 3 holes has 2 diagonal segments.

steps.text: Net width along the staggered path (3 holes, 2 diagonals):

traps: Omitting the $s^2/4g$ correction for each diagonal (staggered) segment
Forgetting to add $1/8$ in. to the bolt diameter for the hole allowance
Counting only the in-line holes on a straight cut instead of all holes on the zig-zag path

str-st-cp2.statement: A single angle is bolted through one leg as a tension member. Its net area is $A_n = 4.00 \text{ in}^2$, the distance from the connection plane to the member centroid is $\bar{x} = 1.20 \text{ in.}$, and the connection length is $L = 9.0 \text{ in.}$ What is the effective net area $A_e$?
str-st-cp2.eli5: The shear lag factor is $U = 1 - \bar{x}/L = 1 - 1.20/9.0 = 1 - 0.1333 = 0.867$. The effective net area is $A_e = U A_n = 0.867 \times 4.00 = 3.47$ in$^2$. The 4.00 in$^2$ choice assumes $U = 1.0$, which only applies when all cross-sectional elements are connected. The 0.87 in$^2$ choice reports $U$ itself, not $A_e$. The 3.20 in$^2$ choice subtracts $\bar{x} \times A_n / L$ incorrectly or uses $U = 0.80$.
str-st-cp2.hint: Find the shear lag factor $U = 1 - \bar{x}/L$, then $A_e = U A_n$.
traps: Assuming $U = 1.0$ for an angle connected through only one leg
Reporting the shear lag factor $U$ instead of multiplying it by $A_n$

str-dvw-cp1.statement: A cantilever beam of length $L = 4\text{ m}$ carries a uniformly distributed load $w = 6\text{ kN/m}$ over its full length. With $EI = 30{,}000\text{ kN·m}^2$, what is the tip deflection?
str-dvw-cp1.eli5: Cantilever under UDL: $\delta = wL^4/8EI = 6(4^4)/(8 \times 30{,}000) = 1536/240{,}000 = 0.0064\text{ m} = 6.4\text{ mm}$. The 25.6 mm choice uses the wrong denominator (2EI instead of 8EI); the 1.6 mm choice divides the correct answer by 4 (e.g. using L² instead of L⁴ scaling).
traps: Dropping the factor of 8 in the denominator
Using a point-load formula for a distributed load

str-ind-cp1.statement: A beam fixed at both ends spans $L = 6\text{ m}$ and carries a central point load $P = 24\text{ kN}$. What is the magnitude of the fixed-end moment at each support?
str-ind-cp1.eli5: Fixed-fixed beam, central point load: the fixed-end moment is $PL/8 = 24(6)/8 = 18\text{ kN·m}$. The 36 kN·m choice uses $PL/4$ (the simple-span midspan moment). The 144 kN·m choice forgets to divide entirely.
str-ind-cp1.hint: Fixed-fixed, central P → fixed-end moment = PL/8.

steps.text: Standard result for a fixed-fixed beam under a central point load.

traps: Using PL/4 = 36 (the simple-span midspan moment) for the fixed end
Forgetting the division by 8

geo-pr-q1.statement: A fully saturated soil has a water content $\omega = 20\%$ and specific gravity $G_s = 2.70$. What is the void ratio $e$?
geo-pr-q1.eli5: When soil is fully saturated, S = 1. The master relationship Se = wGs becomes e = wGs = 0.20 × 2.70 = 0.54. The 0.74 choice might come from using w = 0.274 or a different Gs. The 2.70 choice is just the specific gravity. The 0.20 choice confuses the water content with the void ratio.
geo-pr-q1.hint: At full saturation, S = 1. Use Se = wGs to solve directly for e.
traps: Using w = 20 instead of 0.20 in the formula — water content must be a decimal in Se = wGs
Confusing void ratio (e) with porosity (n) — n = e/(1+e)

geo-pr-q2.statement: A soil has total unit weight $\gamma = 120 \text{ pcf}$, water content $\omega = 15\%$, and $G_s = 2.65$. What is the degree of saturation $S$?
geo-pr-q2.eli5: First get the dry unit weight: γd = γ/(1+w) = 120/1.15 = 104.3 pcf. Then find e from γd = Gsγw/(1+e): e = Gsγw/γd – 1 = 2.65 × 62.4/104.3 – 1 = 0.586. Finally S = wGs/e = 0.15 × 2.65/0.586 = 0.678 ≈ 68%. The 85% choice might come from skipping the e calculation and guessing. The 100% choice assumes full saturation, which the problem does not state.
geo-pr-q2.hint: Find γd first, then compute e, then use S = wGs/e.
traps: Using total unit weight instead of dry unit weight to compute void ratio
Forgetting to subtract 1 when solving for e from γd = Gsγw/(1+e)

geo-pr-q3.statement: A saturated soil has $\gamma_{sat} = 125 \text{ pcf}$ and $G_s = 2.72$. What is the water content $\omega$?
geo-pr-q3.eli5: Start with γsat = (Gs + e)γw/(1+e). Plug in: 125(1+e) = 62.4(2.72+e). Expand: 125 + 125e = 169.73 + 62.4e. Solve: 62.6e = 44.73, so e = 0.714. Since the soil is saturated (S = 1): w = Se/Gs = e/Gs = 0.714/2.72 = 0.263 = 26%. The 71% choice confuses e with w — the void ratio is 0.714 but the water content is e/Gs. The 17% choice might come from using the wrong unit weight formula.
geo-pr-q3.hint: Solve the γsat formula for e first. Then use w = e/Gs (since S = 1 for saturated soil).
traps: Reporting the void ratio (0.714) as the water content — w = e/Gs, not e itself
Using γw = 9.81 kN/m³ when the problem is in US customary units (γw = 62.4 pcf)
Forgetting that saturated means S = 1, which simplifies Se = wGs to e = wGs

geo-sc-q1.statement: A soil has 80% passing the No. 200 sieve, $LL = 45$, and $PI = 22$. What is its USCS classification?
geo-sc-q1.eli5: More than 50% passes #200, so it is fine-grained. LL = 45 < 50, so it is low-plasticity (L). On the A-line at LL = 45: PI = 0.73(45 – 20) = 18.25. Since the actual PI = 22 > 18.25, the soil plots above the A-line → clay (C). Combine: CL (lean clay). ML would be below the A-line. CH requires LL ≥ 50. SC is a coarse-grained soil with clay fines.
geo-sc-q1.hint: Check: fine or coarse? Then: LL < or > 50? Then: above or below the A-line?
traps: Confusing CL with ML — CL is above the A-line (clay), ML is below (silt)
Using LL = 50 as the clay/silt boundary instead of the A-line — LL = 50 separates L from H, not clay from silt

geo-sc-q2.statement: A sand has $D_{10} = 0.15 \text{ mm}$, $D_{30} = 0.50 \text{ mm}$, $D_{60} = 2.0 \text{ mm}$. Less than 5% passes the No. 200 sieve. What is its USCS classification?
geo-sc-q2.eli5: Less than 50% passes #200 → coarse. It is identified as a sand (more than 50% of the coarse fraction passes the No. 4 sieve). With < 5% fines, classify based on gradation. Cu = D60/D10 = 2.0/0.15 = 13.3 (need ≥ 6 ✔). Cc = (D30)²/(D10 × D60) = 0.25/0.30 = 0.83 (need 1–3 ✘). Since Cc fails the range, it is poorly graded: SP. The SW option requires BOTH the Cu and Cc criteria to be met. The SM option would need > 12% fines.
geo-sc-q2.hint: Compute both Cu and Cc. Both must pass for well-graded (W); if either fails, it is poorly graded (P).

steps.text: $C_c = 0.83 < 1$ → outside the 1–3 range ✘. Classification: **SP** (poorly graded sand).

traps: Assuming the sand is well-graded because Cu ≥ 6 — BOTH Cu and Cc must pass
Using the gravel criteria (Cu ≥ 4) instead of the sand criteria (Cu ≥ 6)

geo-sc-q3.statement: A soil has $LL = 55$, $PI = 28$, and 60% passing the No. 200 sieve. What is the USCS classification?
geo-sc-q3.eli5: 60% passes #200 → fine-grained. LL = 55 > 50 → high plasticity (H). A-line at LL = 55: PI = 0.73(55 – 20) = 25.6. Actual PI = 28 > 25.6 → above A-line → clay (C). Classification: CH (fat clay). The MH choice is below the A-line (silt). The CL choice requires LL < 50. The OH choice is an organic soil which requires lab testing (oven-dried LL) — not determinable from the given data alone, so assume inorganic.
geo-sc-q3.hint: Fine or coarse? LL < or > 50? Above or below the A-line? Each step narrows to one symbol.
traps: Confusing CH with MH — above the A-line is always clay (C), below is silt (M)
Using LL = 50 as the clay/silt boundary instead of the A-line
Choosing OH without evidence of organic content — organic classification requires comparing oven-dried LL to natural LL

geo-es-q1.statement: A 10-ft-thick saturated soil layer has $\gamma_{sat} = 115 \text{ pcf}$. The water table is at the ground surface. What is the effective stress at the bottom of the layer?
geo-es-q1.eli5: σ = γsat × H = 115 × 10 = 1,150 psf. u = γw × H = 62.4 × 10 = 624 psf. σ' = 1,150 – 624 = 526 psf. Or use the shortcut: σ' = γ' × H = (115 – 62.4) × 10 = 52.6 × 10 = 526 psf. The 1,150 psf option is the total stress — forgetting to subtract pore pressure. The 624 psf option is the pore pressure itself.
geo-es-q1.hint: σ' = σ – u. Compute total stress and pore water pressure separately, then subtract.
traps: Reporting total stress instead of effective stress — always subtract pore pressure below the WT
Using γw = 64 pcf or some other value instead of 62.4 pcf

geo-es-q2.statement: A site has 5 ft of dry sand ($\gamma = 110 \text{ pcf}$) over 8 ft of saturated clay ($\gamma_{sat} = 120 \text{ pcf}$). The water table is at the sand-clay interface. What is the effective vertical stress at the bottom of the clay?
geo-es-q2.eli5: Total stress at the bottom: σ = 110(5) + 120(8) = 550 + 960 = 1,510 psf. Pore pressure: u = 62.4(8) = 499 psf (water is 8 ft deep below the WT). Effective: σ' = 1,510 – 499 = 1,011 psf. The 1,510 psf option is the total stress. The 960 psf option is only the clay layer contribution without the sand above. The 526 psf option uses only the buoyant weight of clay without the sand overburden.
geo-es-q2.hint: Total stress includes both layers. Pore pressure only exists in the saturated zone (below the WT).

steps.text: Total stress at bottom of clay:
Pore water pressure (8 ft below WT):

traps: Subtracting pore pressure through the sand layer too — the sand is above the WT so u = 0 there
Using buoyant unit weight for the sand above the WT — only subtract γw below the water table

geo-es-q3.statement: A site has a $100 \text{ psf}$ uniform surcharge on the surface. Below: 6 ft of sand ($\gamma = 105 \text{ pcf}$, above WT) over 10 ft of saturated clay ($\gamma_{sat} = 118 \text{ pcf}$). The WT is at the sand-clay interface. What is the effective vertical stress at the bottom of the clay?
geo-es-q3.eli5: Total stress: σ = 100 + 105(6) + 118(10) = 100 + 630 + 1,180 = 1,910 psf. Pore pressure: u = 62.4(10) = 624 psf. Effective: σ' = 1,910 – 624 = 1,286 psf. The surcharge adds to total stress but NOT to pore pressure. The 1,910 psf option forgets to subtract u. The 1,186 psf option forgot the surcharge. The 1,810 psf option subtracted the surcharge from total stress instead of subtracting pore pressure.
geo-es-q3.hint: Surcharge adds to total stress at all depths but does not change pore water pressure.

steps.text: Pore water pressure (10 ft below WT):

traps: Adding the surcharge to pore pressure — surcharge increases total stress only, not u
Forgetting to include the surcharge in the total stress calculation
Subtracting γw through the dry sand layer above the water table

geo-co-q1.statement: A normally consolidated clay layer is $10 \text{ ft}$ thick with $e_0 = 0.90$ and $C_c = 0.30$. The current effective stress is $\sigma_0' = 1{,}000 \text{ psf}$ and the stress increase is $\Delta\sigma = 500 \text{ psf}$. What is the consolidation settlement?
geo-co-q1.eli5: NC clay → Case 2: ΔH = H/(1+e0) × Cc × log(σ0’+Δσ)/σ0’ = 10/(1.90) × 0.30 × log(1500/1000) = 5.263 × 0.30 × 0.1761 = 0.278 ft = 3.3 in. The 6.3 in. option might come from using H = 10 without dividing by (1+e0). The 1.6 in. option uses Cr instead of Cc. The 10 in. option ignores the log term and just multiplies H × Cc.
geo-co-q1.hint: NC clay uses Case 2 with Cc (not Cr). Remember to divide H by (1 + e0).
traps: Using Cr instead of Cc for normally consolidated clay — Cr is only for overconsolidated clay below pc
Forgetting to divide H by (1 + e0)

geo-co-q2.statement: For the clay in Problem 1, $c_v = 0.50 \text{ ft}^2\text{/day}$ with two-way drainage ($H_{dr} = 5 \text{ ft}$). How long does it take for 50% consolidation? Use $T_v = 0.197$ at $U = 50\%$.
geo-co-q2.eli5: Tv = cv·t/Hdr² → t = Tv·Hdr²/cv = 0.197 × 25/0.50 = 9.85 ≈ 10 days. Two-way drainage means Hdr = H/2 = 5 ft. The 20 days choice uses Hdr = 10 ft (one-way drainage). The 5 days choice might divide by 2 again. The 39 days choice uses Tv = 0.785 (for U = 90%).
geo-co-q2.hint: Rearrange Tv = cv·t/Hdr² to solve for t. Two-way drainage means Hdr = H/2.
traps: Using the full layer thickness (H = 10) instead of Hdr = H/2 for two-way drainage — this quadruples the time
Confusing Tv with U — Tv is the time factor, U is the degree of consolidation (%)

geo-co-q3.statement: An overconsolidated clay has $e_0 = 1.10$, $C_c = 0.40$, $C_r = 0.06$, $H = 12 \text{ ft}$. Current stress $\sigma_0' = 800 \text{ psf}$, preconsolidation $p_c = 1{,}200 \text{ psf}$, added stress $\Delta\sigma = 600 \text{ psf}$ (so $\sigma_0' + \Delta\sigma = 1{,}400 > p_c$). What is the settlement?
geo-co-q3.eli5: Since p0 = 800 < pc = 1,200 < p0+Δp = 1,400 → Case 3 (crosses preconsolidation). ΔH = H/(1+e0) × [Cr × log(pc/p0) + Cc × log((p0+Δp)/pc)] = 12/2.10 × [0.06 × log(1200/800) + 0.40 × log(1400/1200)] = 5.714 × [0.06 × 0.1761 + 0.40 × 0.0669] = 5.714 × [0.01057 + 0.02678] = 5.714 × 0.03735 = 0.213 ft = 2.6 in. The 4.8 in. choice uses Cc for both terms. The 0.9 in. choice uses Cr for both terms. The key is recognizing which case applies.
geo-co-q3.hint: Check: does the final stress exceed pc? If so, use Case 3 — Cr below pc and Cc above pc.
traps: Using Cc for the entire stress range — use Cr from p0 to pc and Cc from pc to p0+Δp
Using Case 1 (Cr only) when the final stress actually exceeds pc
Forgetting to divide by (1 + e0)

geo-ss-q1.statement: A soil has $c' = 200 \text{ psf}$ and $\phi' = 30\degree$. What is the shear strength on a plane where the effective normal stress is $\sigma_N' = 1{,}000 \text{ psf}$?
geo-ss-q1.eli5: τf = c’ + σN’ tan φ’ = 200 + 1,000 × tan 30° = 200 + 1,000 × 0.5774 = 200 + 577 = 777 psf. The 577 psf option forgot the cohesion term. The 1,000 psf option is just the normal stress. The 200 psf option is just the cohesion — ignoring the frictional component entirely.
geo-ss-q1.hint: Plug directly into the Mohr-Coulomb equation: τf = c + σ’ tan φ.
traps: Forgetting the cohesion term c — the shear strength has two components
Using sin φ instead of tan φ in the Mohr-Coulomb equation

geo-ss-q2.statement: A triaxial test on a cohesionless soil ($c = 0$) gives $\sigma_1 = 6{,}000 \text{ psf}$ and $\sigma_3 = 2{,}000 \text{ psf}$ at failure. What is the friction angle $\phi$?
geo-ss-q2.eli5: For c = 0: sin φ = (σ1 – σ3)/(σ1 + σ3) = (6,000 – 2,000)/(6,000 + 2,000) = 4,000/8,000 = 0.50. φ = arcsin(0.50) = 30°. The 45° choice might come from using tan⁻¹(σ1/σ3) incorrectly. The 26.6° choice is arctan(0.50) — a common mistake from using tan instead of sin.
geo-ss-q2.hint: For c = 0: sin φ = (σ1 – σ3)/(σ1 + σ3). No need to draw the Mohr circle.
traps: Using arctan(0.50) instead of arcsin(0.50) — the Mohr circle gives sin φ = t/s, not tan φ
Computing σ1/σ3 = 3.0 and using it as φ or tan φ

geo-ss-q3.statement: An unconsolidated-undrained (UU) triaxial test on a saturated clay gives $\sigma_3 = 1{,}500 \text{ psf}$ and $(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3) = 2{,}400 \text{ psf}$ at failure. What is the undrained cohesion $c_u$?
geo-ss-q3.eli5: In a UU test on saturated clay, φu = 0. The Mohr circle has its center at s = (σ1+σ3)/2 and radius t = (σ1–σ3)/2. For φ = 0, the failure envelope is a horizontal line at τ = cu, and cu = the radius = (σ1–σ3)/2 = 2,400/2 = 1,200 psf. The 2,400 psf choice is the deviator stress itself, not halved. The 2,700 psf choice is (σ1+σ3)/2 = (3,900+1,500)/2 — that is the center of the Mohr circle, not the radius. The 1,500 psf choice is just σ3.
geo-ss-q3.hint: For φ = 0 (undrained clay): cu = (σ1 – σ3)/2 = radius of the Mohr circle.

steps.text: For $\phi_u = 0$, undrained cohesion = radius of Mohr circle:

traps: Using the full deviator stress (2,400) as cu instead of half of it
Computing (σ1+σ3)/2 (center of circle) instead of (σ1–σ3)/2 (radius)
Trying to use the drained formula sin φ = t/s when the problem specifies undrained (UU) conditions

geo-seep-q1.statement: Water flows through a soil sample with hydraulic conductivity $k = 0.01\text{ cm/s}$ under a hydraulic gradient $i = 0.5$. The cross-sectional area is $A = 100\text{ cm}^2$. What is the flow rate?
geo-seep-q1.eli5: Darcy: q = kiA = 0.01 × 0.5 × 100 = 0.5 cm³/s. The 5.0 cm^3/s option inflates the result tenfold. The 0.05 cm^3/s option multiplies in an extra factor of 0.1. The 50 cm^3/s option drops the gradient and shifts a decimal.
geo-seep-q1.hint: q = k × i × A. Keep units consistent (cm/s, cm²).
traps: Forgetting to multiply by the hydraulic gradient
Mixing length units between k and A

geo-seep-q2.statement: A saturated sand has specific gravity $G_s = 2.70$ and void ratio $e = 0.85$. What is the critical hydraulic gradient at which a quick condition occurs?
geo-seep-q2.eli5: i_c = (Gs − 1)/(1 + e) = (2.70 − 1)/(1 + 0.85) = 1.70/1.85 = 0.92. The 1.00 choice wrongly assumes i_c is always exactly 1.0. The 1.85 choice just reports the denominator (1 + e) = 1.85 instead of the full ratio. The 0.54 choice inverts the fraction, using (1 + e)/(Gs − 1) instead of (Gs − 1)/(1 + e).
traps: Assuming the critical gradient is always exactly 1.0
Forgetting to divide by (1 + e)

geo-seep-q3.statement: Seepage beneath a dam is analyzed with a flow net having $N_f = 4$ flow channels and $N_d = 12$ equipotential drops. The hydraulic conductivity is $k = 2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m/s}$ and the total head loss is $H = 6\text{ m}$. What is the seepage rate per unit width?
geo-seep-q3.eli5: q = kH(Nf/Nd) = (2×10⁻⁵)(6)(4/12) = (2×10⁻⁵)(6)(0.333) = 4.0×10⁻⁵ m³/s per m. The 3.6×10⁻⁴ choice inverts the ratio (Nd/Nf = 12/4 = 3). The 1.0×10⁻⁵ choice mishandles the head. The 2.4×10⁻⁴ choice uses an incorrect ratio value.
geo-seep-q3.hint: q = k × H × (Nf/Nd) per unit width.
traps: Inverting the ratio to Nd/Nf
Forgetting to multiply by the total head H

geo-slp-q1.statement: A dry cohesionless sand slope is inclined at $\beta = 20\degree$. The soil's friction angle is $\phi = 34\degree$. What is the factor of safety against sliding?
geo-slp-q1.eli5: For a dry cohesionless infinite slope, FS = tan φ / tan β = tan 34° / tan 20° = 0.6745/0.3640 = 1.85. The 0.54 choice inverts the ratio (tan β / tan φ). The 1.70 choice subtracts angles incorrectly. The 0.93 choice applies a seepage reduction that is not present here.
geo-slp-q1.hint: Dry cohesionless slope: FS = tan φ / tan β.
traps: Inverting to tan β / tan φ
Applying a seepage reduction when the slope is dry

geo-slp-q2.statement: The same cohesionless slope ($\phi = 34\degree$, $\beta = 20\degree$) becomes fully saturated with seepage parallel to the slope. With $\gamma_{sat} = 19.62\text{ kN/m}^3$ and $\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3$, what is the new factor of safety?
geo-slp-q2.eli5: With seepage, FS = (γ′/γ_sat)(tan φ/tan β). Here γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w = 19.62 − 9.81 = 9.81, so γ′/γ_sat = 9.81/19.62 = 0.5. The dry FS was 1.85, so FS = 0.5 × 1.85 = 0.93 — now UNSTABLE. The 1.85 option ignores seepage (it is the dry FS). The 3.70 option multiplies by tan φ/tan β twice instead of reducing. The 0.50 option reports only the reduction factor.
geo-slp-q2.hint: Multiply the dry FS by γ′/γ_sat, where γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w.
traps: Ignoring the seepage reduction and reporting the dry value
Using γ_sat instead of γ′ in the numerator

geo-slp-q3.statement: A soil wedge is analyzed on a planar slip surface. The cohesion contributes $cL_s = 120\text{ kN/m}$, the wedge weight is $W = 400\text{ kN/m}$, the slip angle is $\alpha = 25\degree$, and the friction angle is $\phi = 20\degree$. What is the factor of safety?
geo-slp-q3.eli5: FS = (cLs + W cos α tan φ)/(W sin α). Numerator = 120 + 400(cos 25°)(tan 20°) = 120 + 400(0.9063)(0.3640) = 120 + 132 = 252. Denominator = W sin α = 400(0.4226) = 169. FS = 252/169 = 1.49. The 0.78 choice drops the cohesion term. The 2.10 choice adds cohesion twice. The 1.00 choice ignores the friction term.
geo-slp-q3.hint: FS = (cLs + W cos α tan φ) / (W sin α).
traps: Omitting the cohesion term cLs from the resisting force
Swapping sin and cos for the driving and resisting components

geo-bc-q1.statement: A strip footing rests on clay with undrained shear strength $c_u = 1{,}500 \text{ psf}$. Using $\phi = 0$ factors ($N_c = 5.14$, $N_q = 1$, $N_\gamma = 0$) and footing depth $D_f = 0$, what is the ultimate bearing capacity?
geo-bc-q1.eli5: qult = cNc + γ’(0)Nq + 0 = 1,500 × 5.14 + 0 + 0 = 7,710 psf. With Df = 0, the overburden term vanishes. The 1,500 psf option is just the cohesion. The 5,140 psf option uses c = 1,000 or confuses Nc with the answer. The 3,855 psf option divides by FS = 2 prematurely — the problem asks for ultimate, not allowable.
geo-bc-q1.hint: For φ = 0: Nγ = 0 and Nq contributes only if there is overburden (Df > 0).
geo-bc-q1.handbookFormula: q_{ult} = c N_c + \gamma' D_f N_q + \frac{1}{2} \gamma' B N_\gamma
traps: Dividing by FS when the problem asks for ultimate (not allowable) bearing capacity
Forgetting that for φ = 0, the Nγ term is zero

geo-bc-q2.statement: A strip footing ($B = 4 \text{ ft}$) is at depth $D_f = 3 \text{ ft}$ in a soil with $c = 0$, $\phi = 30\degree$, $\gamma = 120 \text{ pcf}$. Given $N_c = 30.14$, $N_q = 18.40$, $N_\gamma = 15.07$. What is the ultimate bearing capacity?
geo-bc-q2.eli5: qult = cNc + γDfNq + 0.5γBNγ = 0(30.14) + 120(3)(18.40) + 0.5(120)(4)(15.07) = 0 + 6,624 + 3,617 = 10,241 ≈ 10,240 psf. Since c = 0, the cohesion term drops out. The 6,624 psf option is only the overburden (Nq) term. The 3,617 psf option is only the width (Nγ) term. You need all three terms (even though one is zero here).
geo-bc-q2.hint: With c = 0, only the Nq and Nγ terms contribute. Compute each separately, then add.
geo-bc-q2.handbookFormula: q_{ult} = c N_c + \gamma' D_f N_q + \frac{1}{2} \gamma' B N_\gamma
traps: Forgetting the 1/2 factor on the Nγ term — it is 0.5γBNγ, not γBNγ
Only computing one of the three terms instead of summing all contributions

geo-bc-q3.statement: A 5-ft-wide strip footing at $D_f = 3 \text{ ft}$ sits on soil with $c = 500 \text{ psf}$, $\phi = 20\degree$, $\gamma = 115 \text{ pcf}$. Given $N_c = 14.83$, $N_q = 6.40$, $N_\gamma = 3.54$. What is the allowable bearing pressure with $FS = 3$?
geo-bc-q3.eli5: qult = cNc + γDfNq + 0.5γBNγ = 500(14.83) + 115(3)(6.40) + 0.5(115)(5)(3.54) = 7,415 + 2,208 + 1,018 = 10,641 psf. qallow = 10,641/3 = 3,547 ≈ 3,550 psf. The 10,640 psf option is the ultimate capacity without dividing by FS. The 7,415 psf option is only the cohesion term. The 2,210 psf option divides the overburden term alone by FS.
geo-bc-q3.hint: Compute all three terms of qult first. Then divide the total by FS = 3.
geo-bc-q3.handbookFormula: q_{ult} = c N_c + \gamma' D_f N_q + \frac{1}{2} \gamma' B N_\gamma
traps: Reporting qult as the answer when the problem asks for qallow — always check whether FS is needed
Applying FS to each term separately instead of dividing the total qult by FS
Forgetting the 1/2 factor on the Nγ term

geo-le-q1.statement: A soil has $\phi' = 30\degree$. What is the Rankine active earth pressure coefficient $K_a$?
geo-le-q1.eli5: Ka = tan²(45° – 30°/2) = tan²(30°) = (0.5774)² = 0.333 = 1/3. The 3.0 option is Kp, the passive coefficient (or 1/Ka). The 0.577 option is tan 30°, not tan² 30°. The 0.50 option is sin 30°.
geo-le-q1.hint: Ka = tan²(45° – φ/2). First compute the angle, then take tan².
traps: Using tan instead of tan² — the coefficient is the square of the tangent
Swapping the sign: using (45 + φ/2) gives Kp, not Ka

geo-le-q2.statement: A 15-ft-tall retaining wall has backfill with $\phi' = 30\degree$, $\gamma = 120 \text{ pcf}$, $c = 0$. What is the total active force per foot of wall?
geo-le-q2.eli5: Ka = 1/3 (from φ = 30°). Pa = 0.5 × Ka × γ × H² = 0.5 × (1/3) × 120 × 15² = 0.5 × 0.333 × 120 × 225 = 4,500 lb/ft. The 9,000 lb/ft choice forgets the 1/2 factor (uses KaγH² instead of 0.5KaγH²). The 13,500 lb/ft choice omits Ka entirely (uses Ka = 1: 0.5 x 1 x 120 x 225 = 13,500). The 2,250 lb/ft choice divides by 2 an extra time.
geo-le-q2.hint: Active force on a wall: Pa = 0.5 × Ka × γ × H². The pressure diagram is a triangle.
traps: Forgetting the 1/2 factor — the pressure diagram is triangular, so the resultant is half the rectangle
Using Kp instead of Ka — active pressure is when the wall moves AWAY from the soil

geo-le-q3.statement: A 12-ft retaining wall retains soil with $\gamma = 120 \text{ pcf}$, $\phi' = 30\degree$, $c = 0$. A uniform surcharge of $200 \text{ psf}$ is on the surface. What is the total active force on the wall (soil + surcharge)?
geo-le-q3.eli5: Ka = 1/3. Soil: Pa(soil) = 0.5 × (1/3) × 120 × 12² = 0.5 × 40 × 144 = 2,880 lb/ft (triangular). Surcharge: Pa(surcharge) = Ka × q × H = (1/3) × 200 × 12 = 800 lb/ft (rectangular). Total = 2,880 + 800 = 3,680 lb/ft. The 2,880 lb/ft option ignores the surcharge. The 4,800 lb/ft option adds the surcharge force incorrectly or uses a higher Ka. The 800 lb/ft option is only the surcharge contribution.
geo-le-q3.hint: The surcharge creates a uniform (rectangular) pressure of Ka × q over the full height, added to the triangular soil pressure.
traps: Forgetting to multiply the surcharge by Ka — the surcharge is not applied directly as a horizontal force; it is reduced by Ka
Adding the surcharge to the soil pressure without applying Ka first
Treating the surcharge pressure as triangular instead of rectangular

geo-rw-q1.statement: A retaining wall has total resisting moment $\Sigma M_R = 15{,}000 \text{ lb-ft/ft}$ and overturning moment $M_O = 5{,}000 \text{ lb-ft/ft}$ about the toe. What is the factor of safety against overturning?
geo-rw-q1.eli5: FS = ΣMR / MO = 15,000/5,000 = 3.0. This is a direct formula application. The 2.0 option might come from dividing something else. The 5.0 option reversed a number. The 0.33 option inverted the ratio (MO/MR).
geo-rw-q1.hint: FS(overturning) = resisting moments / overturning moment. Just divide.
traps: Inverting the ratio — FS = resisting/driving, not driving/resisting
Subtracting MO from MR instead of dividing

geo-rw-q2.statement: A retaining wall has total vertical force $\Sigma V = 5{,}000 \text{ lb/ft}$, base width $B = 6 \text{ ft}$, $\Sigma M_R = 18{,}000 \text{ lb-ft/ft}$, and $M_O = 6{,}000 \text{ lb-ft/ft}$. What is the eccentricity $e$ of the resultant on the base?
geo-rw-q2.eli5: First find where the resultant hits the base (measured from the toe): x̄ = (ΣMR – MO)/ΣV = (18,000 – 6,000)/5,000 = 12,000/5,000 = 2.40 ft. Eccentricity from the center: e = B/2 – x̄ = 3.0 – 2.4 = 0.60 ft. Check: B/6 = 1.0 ft, and e = 0.60 < 1.0, so the resultant is in the middle third ✔. The 2.40 ft option is x̄, the distance from the toe, not the eccentricity from the center. The 3.00 ft option is B/2. The 1.20 ft option doubles e by mistake.
geo-rw-q2.hint: Find x̄ (distance from toe), then e = B/2 – x̄.
traps: Reporting x̄ (distance from toe) as the eccentricity — eccentricity is measured from the center of the base
Forgetting to subtract MO from MR before dividing by ΣV

geo-rw-q3.statement: A gravity retaining wall has base width $B = 8 \text{ ft}$. The resultant vertical force $\Sigma V = 8{,}000 \text{ lb/ft}$ acts $3.0 \text{ ft}$ from the toe. What is the maximum pressure at the toe?
geo-rw-q3.eli5: Eccentricity: e = B/2 – x̄ = 4.0 – 3.0 = 1.0 ft. Check: B/6 = 8/6 = 1.33 ft, and e = 1.0 < 1.33 ✔ (in middle third). Toe pressure: qtoe = (ΣV/B)(1 + 6e/B) = (8,000/8)(1 + 6(1.0)/8) = 1,000(1 + 0.75) = 1,000 × 1.75 = 1,750 psf. The 1,000 psf option is the uniform pressure (ΣV/B) without the eccentricity effect. The 2,000 psf option uses e = B/6 = 1.33. The 1,333 psf option might come from a different eccentricity.
geo-rw-q3.hint: Find e = B/2 – x̄. Then qtoe = (ΣV/B)(1 + 6e/B).
traps: Using ΣV/B as the answer without accounting for eccentricity — this only works when e = 0 (resultant at the center)
Forgetting the factor of 6 in 6e/B — the formula is derived from the trapezoidal stress distribution
Using e in the wrong formula — the (1 + 6e/B) formula only applies when e ≤ B/6

geo-dfn-q1.statement: A pile has a unit end-bearing resistance $q_p = 2{,}000\text{ kPa}$ over a tip area $A_p = 0.20\text{ m}^2$, and a unit skin friction $f_s = 50\text{ kPa}$ over a shaft surface area $A_s = 12\text{ m}^2$. What is the ultimate pile capacity?
geo-dfn-q1.eli5: Q_ult = Qp + Qs = qp·Ap + fs·As = (2,000)(0.20) + (50)(12) = 400 + 600 = 1,000 kN. The 400 kN option is only the end bearing. The 600 kN option is only the skin friction. The 2,600 kN option mistakenly uses the tip area as 1.0 m² (2,000 + 600).
geo-dfn-q1.hint: Q_ult = qp·Ap + fs·As — add end bearing and skin friction.
traps: Reporting only end bearing or only skin friction
Using the shaft area for end bearing or vice versa

geo-dfn-q2.statement: A site has 8 m of soft compressible clay overlying dense gravel. Why would a deep foundation be preferred over a shallow footing for a heavily loaded column?

choices.text: To transfer the load through the weak clay to the firm gravel, limiting settlement
Because deep foundations are always cheaper than footings
To increase the bearing pressure on the soft clay
Because shallow footings cannot be used under any column

geo-dfn-q2.eli5: The soft clay would settle excessively under a shallow footing. A deep foundation bypasses the weak clay and transfers the load to the dense gravel below, controlling settlement and providing adequate capacity. The claim that deep foundations are always cheaper is false (piles are usually more expensive). The option about increasing bearing pressure on the soft clay is backwards — you want to relieve, not increase, load on the clay. The claim that shallow footings can never be used overstates the case.
geo-dfn-q2.hint: What problem does the soft clay create, and how does reaching the gravel solve it?

steps.text: Soft clay under a footing would settle excessively and lacks capacity.
A deep foundation carries load through the clay to the dense gravel.
This limits settlement and provides adequate bearing.

traps: Assuming deep foundations are chosen for cost rather than performance
Thinking the goal is to load the weak layer more

geo-dfn-q3.statement: Fill is placed over a soft clay layer through which a pile passes. As the clay consolidates and settles relative to the pile, what force develops on the pile shaft?

choices.text: Negative skin friction (downdrag), which adds load to the pile
Positive skin friction that increases the pile capacity
An upward buoyant force that relieves the pile
No force, because the clay and pile move together

geo-dfn-q3.eli5: When surrounding soil settles MORE than the pile, it drags down on the shaft — negative skin friction (downdrag). This acts as an additional downward load the pile must carry, not as support. The "positive skin friction increases capacity" choice reverses the direction. The "upward buoyant force" choice invents a relief that does not exist here. The "no force, clay and pile move together" choice ignores the relative settlement that causes downdrag.
geo-dfn-q3.hint: Which way does the friction act when the soil settles faster than the pile?

steps.text: Consolidating clay settles more than the pile.
The relative downward movement drags on the shaft.
This is negative skin friction (downdrag), adding load to the pile.

traps: Assuming the friction always helps support the pile
Ignoring relative settlement between soil and pile

geo-cmp-q1.statement: A field dry unit weight of $118\text{ pcf}$ is measured on a fill whose laboratory maximum dry unit weight (modified Proctor) is $124\text{ pcf}$. What is the relative compaction?
geo-cmp-q1.eli5: RC = (γd,field/γd,max) × 100 = (118/124) × 100 = 95.2%, which would satisfy a typical 95% specification. The 105% choice inverts the ratio (124/118). The 5.1% choice computes the percent difference (6/118). The 90.0% choice is a guess at the spec value.
geo-cmp-q1.hint: Relative compaction = (field dry density / lab maximum dry density) × 100.
traps: Inverting the ratio (lab over field)
Confusing relative compaction with relative density

geo-cmp-q2.statement: A sand has maximum void ratio $e_{max} = 0.90$, minimum void ratio $e_{min} = 0.40$, and an in-place void ratio $e = 0.60$. What is its relative density?
geo-cmp-q2.eli5: Dr = (emax − e)/(emax − emin) × 100 = (0.90 − 0.60)/(0.90 − 0.40) × 100 = 0.30/0.50 × 100 = 60% — a medium-dense sand. The 40% choice uses (e − emin) in the numerator. The 67% choice uses (e − emin)/(emax − e). The 33% choice inverts the numerator difference.
traps: Using (e − emin) in the numerator instead of (emax − e)
Forgetting to multiply by 100

geo-cmp-q3.statement: A high-plasticity clay subgrade is too soft and swells when wet. Which chemical stabilizer is most appropriate?

choices.text: Portland cement (alone, in the plastic clay)
Fly ash used purely as a filler

geo-cmp-q3.eli5: Lime is the classic stabilizer for high-plasticity clays: it reduces the plasticity index, controls swelling, and improves workability and strength. Cement is more effective in granular and low-plasticity soils. Adding water would worsen a swelling clay, and fly ash as a mere filler does not chemically stabilize it.
geo-cmp-q3.hint: Which additive specifically reduces the plasticity and swelling of clay?

steps.text: High-plasticity clay needs its plasticity and swelling reduced.
Lime reacts with clay minerals to lower the plasticity index.
Therefore lime is the appropriate stabilizer (cement suits granular soils).

traps: Defaulting to cement for every soil — it suits granular, not plastic clay
Assuming added water improves a swelling clay

geo-pr-ex1.statement: A soil sample has a void ratio $e = 0.65$ and specific gravity $G_s = 2.70$. What is the porosity $n$?
geo-pr-ex1.eli5: Porosity relates to void ratio by $n = e/(1+e) = 0.65/(1+0.65) = 0.65/1.65 = 0.394$. The 0.650 option is the void ratio itself, not the porosity. The 0.241 option might come from $e/(1+G_s)$. The 0.606 option might come from $1/(1+e)$, which is the reciprocal relationship.
geo-pr-ex1.hint: Porosity $n = e/(1+e)$. This is one of the core phase-relation identities.
traps: Confusing void ratio (e) with porosity (n) and reporting e as the answer

geo-pr-ex2.statement: A soil sample is tested and found to have a degree of saturation $S = 100\%$. Which of the following statements is correct?

choices.text: The soil contains no air and no water
All void space is filled with water, and $e = \omega G_s$

geo-pr-ex2.eli5: When $S = 100\%$, the voids are completely filled with water (no air phase). The master relationship $Se = \omega G_s$ simplifies to $e = \omega G_s$. The "no air and no water" choice is backwards -- full saturation means all voids have water, not that the soil is completely dry. The "void ratio must equal 1.0" choice is wrong because $e$ depends on the soil structure, not saturation alone. The "water content equals $G_s$" choice mixes up the formula -- $\omega = e/G_s$ at full saturation, not $\omega = G_s$.
geo-pr-ex2.hint: At $S = 1$, the master relationship $Se = \omega G_s$ simplifies. Think about what $S = 100\%$ means physically for the void space.

steps.text: When $S = 100\%$, all voids are water-filled (no air).

traps: Assuming full saturation forces a specific void ratio -- e depends on soil fabric, not saturation

geo-pr-ex3.statement: A soil has total unit weight $\gamma = 125 \text{ pcf}$ and water content $\omega = 22\%$. What is the dry unit weight $\gamma_d$?
geo-pr-ex3.eli5: Dry unit weight strips out the water: $\gamma_d = \gamma/(1+\omega) = 125/(1+0.22) = 125/1.22 = 102.5$ pcf. The 97.5 pcf option might come from subtracting $\gamma \times \omega = 125 \times 0.22 = 27.5$, giving $125 - 27.5 = 97.5$ -- that is wrong because the water content is based on the weight of solids, not total weight. The 125 pcf option is the total unit weight, not dry. The 27.5 pcf option is just $\gamma \times \omega$, which has no physical meaning here.
geo-pr-ex3.hint: The formula $\gamma_d = \gamma/(1+\omega)$ converts total unit weight to dry unit weight. Keep $\omega$ as a decimal.
traps: Subtracting $\gamma \times \omega$ from $\gamma$ instead of dividing -- water content is defined relative to solids weight, not total weight

geo-pr-ex4.statement: A contractor measures the water content $\omega$ and total unit weight $\gamma$ of a compacted fill. Which sequence correctly determines the degree of saturation?

choices.text: Compute $\gamma_d = \gamma/(1+\omega)$, then find $e$ from $\gamma_d = G_s \gamma_w/(1+e)$, then $S = \omega G_s / e$

geo-pr-ex4.eli5: To get $S$ you need $e$, and to get $e$ you need $\gamma_d$. Step 1: $\gamma_d = \gamma/(1+\omega)$ strips out the water weight. Step 2: rearranging $\gamma_d = G_s \gamma_w/(1+e)$ gives $e$. Step 3: $Se = \omega G_s$ gives $S = \omega G_s/e$. The $e = \omega G_s$ choice is wrong because $e = \omega G_s$ only works at full saturation ($S = 1$), and then computing $S = e/(1+e)$ is not the degree of saturation. The $\gamma_d = \gamma \times \omega$ choice makes up a formula -- $\gamma_d$ is not $\gamma \times \omega$. The $n = \omega/G_s$ choice also fabricates a relationship.
geo-pr-ex4.hint: You need three steps: total to dry unit weight, dry unit weight to void ratio, then void ratio to saturation.
traps: Assuming $e = \omega G_s$ without checking that $S = 1$ first -- that identity only holds for fully saturated soil

geo-sc-ex1.statement: A sand has $D_{10} = 0.25 \text{ mm}$, $D_{30} = 1.5 \text{ mm}$, and $D_{60} = 10 \text{ mm}$ with less than 5% fines. What is the coefficient of uniformity $C_u$?
geo-sc-ex1.eli5: $C_u = D_{60}/D_{10} = 10/0.25 = 40$. This is a direct formula plug-in. The value 6 is the minimum $C_u$ threshold for well-graded sand, not the calculated value. The value 0.90 is the coefficient of curvature $C_c = (D_{30})^2/(D_{10} \times D_{60})$. The value 4 is the minimum $C_u$ for well-graded gravel.
geo-sc-ex1.hint: $C_u = D_{60}/D_{10}$. It measures how spread out the grain sizes are.
traps: Confusing $C_u$ with $C_c$ -- $C_u$ uses only $D_{60}$ and $D_{10}$, while $C_c$ also uses $D_{30}$

geo-sc-ex2.statement: A soil has 70% passing the No. 200 sieve, $LL = 40$, and $PI = 12$. On the USCS plasticity chart, the A-line value at $LL = 40$ is $PI_A = 0.73(40-20) = 14.6$. Since $PI = 12 < 14.6$, the soil plots below the A-line. What is the USCS classification?
geo-sc-ex2.eli5: 70% passing #200 means fine-grained. $LL = 40 < 50$ means low plasticity (L). The problem already tells you the soil plots below the A-line, which means silt (M). So the classification is ML (low-plasticity silt). CL would be above the A-line. SM is a coarse-grained soil with silty fines. MH requires $LL \geq 50$.
geo-sc-ex2.hint: Follow the USCS decision tree: fine or coarse, then LL < or > 50, then above or below the A-line.
traps: Confusing above/below the A-line -- above is clay (C), below is silt (M)

geo-sc-ex3.statement: A coarse-grained soil has 40% retained on the No. 4 sieve, 55% passing the No. 4 sieve and retained on the No. 200 sieve, and 5% passing the No. 200 sieve. The gradation coefficients are $C_u = 8$ and $C_c = 2.1$. What is the USCS classification?
geo-sc-ex3.eli5: Only 5% passes #200, so the soil is coarse-grained. Of the coarse fraction (95%), 55% passes the No. 4 sieve -- that is more than half, so it is a sand (S), not gravel (G). With < 5% fines, classify by gradation. For sand: $C_u \geq 6$ ($8 \geq 6$, passes) AND $1 \leq C_c \leq 3$ (2.1 is in range, passes). Both criteria met, so it is well-graded sand: SW. The GW option would require more than half the coarse fraction retained on the No. 4 sieve. The SP option would have one of the gradation criteria fail. The SM option requires > 12% fines.
geo-sc-ex3.hint: First decide sand vs. gravel (based on the No. 4 sieve split of the coarse fraction), then check both Cu and Cc.

steps.text: Of the coarse fraction: more than half passes No. 4 -> sand (S).

traps: Classifying as gravel because 40% is retained on No. 4 -- the split is based on the coarse fraction, not total

geo-sc-ex4.statement: A fine-grained soil has $LL = 62$ and $PL = 25$. Compute the plasticity index and determine whether the soil plots above or below the A-line. What is the USCS classification?
geo-sc-ex4.eli5: $PI = LL - PL = 62 - 25 = 37$. The soil is fine-grained with $LL = 62 > 50$, so it is high plasticity (H). A-line at $LL = 62$: $PI_A = 0.73(62 - 20) = 0.73(42) = 30.7$. Actual $PI = 37 > 30.7$, so it plots above the A-line -- clay (C). Classification: CH (fat clay). MH would be below the A-line. CL requires $LL < 50$. OH is organic soil, which requires comparing oven-dried LL to natural LL -- not determinable from this data alone.
geo-sc-ex4.hint: Compute PI = LL - PL, then compare it to the A-line value at the given LL.
traps: Choosing MH because LL > 50 -- the LL = 50 line separates L from H, but you still need the A-line to decide clay vs. silt
Selecting OH without evidence of organic content

geo-es-ex1.statement: A uniform surcharge $q$ is placed on the ground surface above a saturated clay layer. Which statement correctly describes the effect on effective stress at a point within the clay?

choices.text: Effective stress increases by $2q$ because both total stress and pore pressure increase by $q$
Both total stress and pore pressure increase by $q$, so effective stress is unchanged
The surcharge has no effect below the water table
Total stress increases by $q$ at all depths, but pore pressure is unchanged, so effective stress increases by $q$

geo-es-ex1.eli5: A surface surcharge adds $q$ to the total vertical stress at every depth. However, it does not change the hydrostatic pore water pressure ($u = \gamma_w \times h_w$ is unchanged). Since $\sigma' = \sigma - u$, the effective stress increases by $q$. The "unchanged effective stress" option describes an undrained loading response in the short term, but the question is about the static equilibrium condition. The "no effect below the water table" option is wrong because surcharge absolutely affects stress below the WT. The "increases by $2q$" option invents a $2q$ increase that has no basis.
geo-es-ex1.hint: Apply $\sigma' = \sigma - u$. The surcharge adds to $\sigma$ but not to hydrostatic $u$.

steps.text: A surcharge $q$ adds to total stress at all depths:
Hydrostatic pore pressure depends only on water depth:

traps: Thinking the surcharge increases pore pressure under static (drained) conditions -- it does not affect hydrostatic $u$

geo-es-ex2.statement: A 12-ft-thick saturated clay layer has $\gamma_{sat} = 118 \text{ pcf}$ with the water table at the ground surface. What is the effective vertical stress at a depth of 8 ft?
geo-es-ex2.eli5: $\sigma = \gamma_{sat} \times h = 118 \times 8 = 944$ psf. $u = \gamma_w \times h = 62.4 \times 8 = 499.2$ psf. $\sigma' = 944 - 499 = 445$ psf. Or use the shortcut: $\sigma' = \gamma' \times h = (118 - 62.4) \times 8 = 55.6 \times 8 = 444.8 \approx 445$ psf. The 944 psf choice is the total stress. The 499 psf choice is the pore water pressure. The 1,416 psf choice would come from using the full 12 ft instead of 8 ft.
geo-es-ex2.hint: $\sigma' = \sigma - u$. Compute total stress and pore pressure at 8 ft depth, then subtract.
traps: Computing stress at 12 ft (bottom of layer) instead of 8 ft as asked
Reporting total stress as the answer without subtracting pore pressure

geo-es-ex3.statement: At a site, the water table drops by 5 ft due to pumping. The soil above the new water table was previously saturated and is now moist with $\gamma_{moist} = 110 \text{ pcf}$. What happens to the effective stress at a point 20 ft below the original water table?

choices.text: Effective stress decreases because the water table dropped
Effective stress stays the same because sigma and u both decrease equally
Effective stress increases because pore pressure decreases more than total stress decreases
Effective stress is unaffected because the point is still below the water table

geo-es-ex3.eli5: When the WT drops 5 ft, pore pressure at our point decreases by $\gamma_w \times 5 = 62.4 \times 5 = 312$ psf. Total stress changes because the 5-ft zone above went from saturated (~120 pcf) to moist (110 pcf), so total stress decreases by about $(120 - 110) \times 5 = 50$ psf. Since $\sigma' = \sigma - u$, and $u$ decreased by 312 while $\sigma$ decreased by only 50, the net change in effective stress is +262 psf -- it increases. The "stays the same" choice is wrong because $\sigma$ and $u$ do not decrease equally. The "effective stress decreases" choice confuses direction. The "unaffected because still below the water table" choice ignores that the WT position affects pore pressure at all depths below it.
geo-es-ex3.hint: Compare the change in total stress vs. the change in pore pressure. Whichever changes more controls the direction of effective stress change.
traps: Assuming total stress and pore pressure decrease equally -- $\gamma_w$ is much larger than the difference between saturated and moist unit weights

geo-es-ex4.statement: A profile has 4 ft of dry sand ($\gamma = 105 \text{ pcf}$), then 6 ft of saturated sand ($\gamma_{sat} = 120 \text{ pcf}$), then 10 ft of saturated clay ($\gamma_{sat} = 115 \text{ pcf}$). The water table is at the top of the saturated sand. A $150 \text{ psf}$ surcharge sits on the surface. What is the effective stress at the bottom of the clay?
geo-es-ex4.eli5: Total stress: $\sigma = 150 + 105(4) + 120(6) + 115(10) = 150 + 420 + 720 + 1{,}150 = 2{,}440$ psf. Pore pressure: $u = 62.4(6 + 10) = 62.4(16) = 998$ psf. Effective: $\sigma' = 2{,}440 - 998 = 1{,}442$ psf. The 2,440 psf choice is the total stress without subtracting pore pressure. The 1,292 psf choice forgot to include the surcharge ($2{,}290 - 998 = 1{,}292$). The 998 psf choice is just the pore water pressure.
geo-es-ex4.hint: Total stress = surcharge + weight of all three layers. Pore pressure = $\gamma_w$ times total water depth below WT.

steps.text: Pore water pressure (16 ft below WT):

traps: Forgetting to include the surcharge in total stress
Computing pore pressure using only the clay thickness (10 ft) instead of the full depth below the WT (16 ft)

geo-con-ex1.statement: A normally consolidated clay has $C_c = 0.35$, $e_0 = 0.80$, and $H_0 = 8 \text{ ft}$. The effective stress increases from $\sigma_0' = 2{,}000 \text{ psf}$ to $\sigma_0' + \Delta\sigma = 4{,}000 \text{ psf}$. What is the consolidation settlement?
geo-con-ex1.eli5: NC clay uses Case 2: $\Delta H = H_0/(1+e_0) \times C_c \times \log((p_0+\Delta p)/p_0) = 8/(1.80) \times 0.35 \times \log(4000/2000) = 4.444 \times 0.35 \times \log(2) = 4.444 \times 0.35 \times 0.3010 = 0.468$ ft $= 5.6$ in. The 11.2 in. distractor forgets to divide by $(1+e_0)$. The 2.8 in. distractor might use $C_r$ instead of $C_c$. The 18.7 in. distractor uses $\ln$ instead of $\log_{10}$.
geo-con-ex1.hint: NC clay means Case 2 with $C_c$. Remember $\log$ is base-10 (common logarithm).
traps: Using $\ln$ (natural log) instead of $\log_{10}$ -- the consolidation formula uses common logarithm

geo-con-ex2.statement: A clay layer is drained on top (sand) and sits on impermeable rock at the bottom. The layer is 20 ft thick. What is the drainage path length $H_{dr}$ for computing the time factor $T_v$?
geo-con-ex2.eli5: With sand on top (permeable) and rock on bottom (impermeable), water can only drain upward -- this is one-way drainage. For one-way drainage, $H_{dr}$ equals the full layer thickness: $H_{dr} = H = 20$ ft. The 10 ft choice would be correct for two-way drainage ($H_{dr} = H/2$), but that requires permeable boundaries on both sides. The 40 ft choice doubles the thickness for no reason. The 5 ft choice divides by 4, which is not a valid drainage path.
geo-con-ex2.hint: Count the number of drainage faces. One-way: $H_{dr} = H$. Two-way: $H_{dr} = H/2$.
traps: Automatically halving the thickness -- $H_{dr} = H/2$ only applies for two-way drainage with permeable boundaries on both sides

geo-con-ex3.statement: A clay layer has $c_v = 0.40 \text{ ft}^2\text{/day}$ and two-way drainage with $H_{dr} = 8 \text{ ft}$. Using $T_v = 0.848$ for $U = 90\%$, how many days for 90% consolidation?
geo-con-ex3.eli5: $t = T_v \times H_{dr}^2 / c_v = 0.848 \times 64 / 0.40 = 54.27 / 0.40 = 135.7 \approx 136$ days. The 542-day choice uses the full layer thickness $H = 16$ ft instead of $H_{dr} = 8$ ft (quadruples the time). The 17-day choice might divide by $H_{dr}$ instead of $H_{dr}^2$. The 68-day choice divides the correct answer by 2 for no reason.
geo-con-ex3.hint: Rearrange $T_v = c_v t / H_{dr}^2$ to solve for $t$. Make sure you use $H_{dr}$, not the full thickness.
traps: Using the full layer thickness $H$ instead of $H_{dr}$ -- for two-way drainage, $H_{dr} = H/2$
Confusing $T_v$ values -- $T_v = 0.197$ is for $U = 50\%$, not 90%

geo-con-ex4.statement: An overconsolidated clay has $p_0' = 1{,}500 \text{ psf}$ and $p_c = 3{,}000 \text{ psf}$. A new fill increases stress by $\Delta\sigma = 1{,}000 \text{ psf}$. Which consolidation case applies, and which compression index controls the settlement?

choices.text: Case 1 with $C_c$, because all consolidation uses the compression index
Case 2 (normally consolidated) with $C_c$, because the soil is being loaded
Case 1 (entirely in recompression) with $C_r$, because $p_0' + \Delta\sigma = 2{,}500 < p_c = 3{,}000$

geo-con-ex4.eli5: The final stress is $p_0 + \Delta p = 1{,}500 + 1{,}000 = 2{,}500$ psf. Since $2{,}500 < p_c = 3{,}000$, the entire stress increase stays below the preconsolidation pressure. This is Case 1 -- entirely in the recompression range. The applicable index is $C_r$ (recompression), not $C_c$ (virgin compression). Case 2 applies only to NC clay ($p_0 \geq p_c$). Case 3 applies when the final stress crosses $p_c$ ($p_0 < p_c < p_0 + \Delta p$). The choice claiming Case 1 with $C_c$ is wrong because Case 1 uses $C_r$, not $C_c$.
