choices.text: The computed T will be too small, leading to an underestimate of the tangent length
The computed T will be too large, leading to an overestimate of the tangent length
No effect because $\tan(I) = 2\tan(I/2)$ for all angles
The effect depends on whether $I$ is greater or less than $90\degree$

trans-hc-ex2.eli5: For any angle $I$ between 0 and 180 degrees (realistic for curves), $\tan(I) > \tan(I/2)$ since the tangent function is increasing on $(0\degree, 90\degree)$ and $I/2 < I$. So using $\tan(I)$ gives a larger number, making $T$ too large. The "too small / underestimate" choice gets the direction wrong. The "no effect because $\tan(I) = 2\tan(I/2)$" choice states a false identity -- $\tan(I)$ is NOT equal to $2\tan(I/2)$ in general. The "depends on whether $I$ is greater or less than $90\degree$" choice is wrong because for typical highway intersection angles (well under $90\degree$), the effect is always an overestimate.
trans-hc-ex2.hint: For angles between 0 and 90 degrees, how does tan(I) compare to tan(I/2)?

steps.text: For typical curve intersection angles ($0 < I < 90\degree$), $\tan(I/2)$ uses a smaller argument than $\tan(I)$, and both arguments stay in the range where tangent is increasing and positive.
Since tangent is increasing on $(0\degree, 90\degree)$, $\tan(I) > \tan(I/2)$ for typical intersection angles.
Therefore $R\tan(I) > R\tan(I/2)$, and the computed T is too large.

traps: Assuming tan(I) = 2 tan(I/2), which is not a valid trigonometric identity

trans-hc-ex3.statement: A horizontal curve has $R = 800 \text{ ft}$ and intersection angle $I = 50\degree$. What is the curve length $L$?
trans-hc-ex3.eli5: $L = R \times I \times (\pi/180) = 800 \times 50 \times (\pi/180) = 800 \times 0.8727 = 698$ ft. The 373 ft choice is the tangent distance $T = R\tan(I/2) = 800 \times \tan(25\degree) = 373$, not the curve length. The 466 ft choice incorrectly used a modified radian conversion. The 1,396 ft choice doubled the curve length for no reason: $2 \times 698$.
trans-hc-ex3.hint: L = R x I x (pi/180). Make sure I is in degrees and you convert to radians.
traps: Confusing curve length L with tangent distance T
Forgetting to convert the intersection angle from degrees to radians

trans-hc-ex4.statement: A curve with design speed $V = 55 \text{ mph}$, radius $R = 900 \text{ ft}$, and superelevation $e = 6\%$ is analyzed. If the side friction demand exceeds the available friction factor $f$, what does this indicate about the design?

choices.text: The curve radius is too tight for the design speed and superelevation -- vehicles may slide outward
The curve is overdesigned and the radius should be reduced
The superelevation is too high and should be lowered
The design is acceptable because friction demand varies with weather

trans-hc-ex4.eli5: From $0.01e + f = V^2/(15R)$, the required side friction is $f = V^2/(15R) - 0.01e = 55^2/(15 \times 900) - 0.06 = 3{,}025/13{,}500 - 0.06 = 0.224 - 0.06 = 0.164$. Typical max $f$ values for 55 mph are around 0.13--0.14. If the demand (0.164) exceeds the supply, vehicles cannot maintain the curve at that speed without skidding outward. The fix is a larger radius, lower speed, or higher superelevation. The choice to reduce the radius makes the problem worse (smaller R raises V^2/15R). The choice to reduce superelevation also worsens friction demand. The choice claiming the design is acceptable dismisses a real safety concern.
trans-hc-ex4.hint: When friction demand exceeds supply, the centripetal force requirement exceeds what the tires and road can provide.

steps.text: Required friction: $f = V^2/(15R) - 0.01e$. If this exceeds available $f$, the vehicle cannot hold the curve.
A larger radius R reduces $V^2/(15R)$, reducing friction demand.
If friction demand > supply, vehicles tend to slide outward (understeer), which is a safety hazard.

traps: Thinking a smaller radius fixes the problem -- it makes friction demand worse
Assuming friction surplus means overdesign when in fact it means adequate design margin

trans-st-ex1.statement: An approach has a speed of $40 \text{ mph}$ on a level grade. Using $t = 1.0 \text{ s}$ and $a = 10 \text{ ft/sec}^2$, what is the yellow interval?
trans-st-ex1.eli5: Convert 40 mph to ft/sec: $40 \times 1.467 = 58.7$ ft/sec. Then $y = t + v/(2a) = 1.0 + 58.7/(2 \times 10) = 1.0 + 58.7/20 = 1.0 + 2.93 = 3.93$, which rounds to 3.9 sec. The 3.0 sec choice used mph directly: $1.0 + 40/20 = 3.0$. The 6.9 sec choice used $v/a$ instead of $v/(2a)$: $1.0 + 58.7/10 = 6.87$. The 2.9 sec choice forgot the reaction time: $58.7/20 = 2.93$.
trans-st-ex1.hint: Convert to ft/sec first, then y = t + v/(2a). Do not forget the factor of 2.
traps: Using mph instead of ft/sec in the formula

trans-st-ex2.statement: The all-red clearance interval formula is $r = (W + l)/v$. Why is the vehicle length $l$ included in the numerator?

choices.text: The vehicle length accounts for the acceleration distance needed to enter the intersection
The vehicle must travel the full intersection width plus its own length to completely clear the far side before conflicting traffic enters
The vehicle length is a safety buffer added to account for driver hesitation
The vehicle length adjusts for the distance between the stop bar and the curb line

trans-st-ex2.eli5: When the signal turns red, a vehicle that just entered must cross the entire intersection width $W$ before the conflicting phase starts. But the vehicle is not a point -- the rear bumper must also clear the far side. So the total clearance distance is $W$ (intersection width) plus $l$ (vehicle length). If you only used $W$, the tail end of the vehicle would still be in the intersection when cross traffic gets the green. The acceleration-distance choice confuses clearance with acceleration. The driver-hesitation safety-buffer choice has no basis in the formula derivation. The stop-bar-to-curb choice misidentifies what $l$ represents.
trans-st-ex2.hint: Think about what it means for a vehicle to "completely clear" the intersection -- where does its rear bumper need to be?

steps.text: The vehicle enters at the near curb and must exit past the far curb.
The front bumper travels $W$, but the rear bumper is still $l$ feet behind.
Total distance to fully clear: $W + l$, giving $r = (W + l)/v$.

traps: Thinking the vehicle length is a safety factor rather than a geometric requirement

trans-st-ex3.statement: An intersection approach has speed $45 \text{ mph}$ on a $3\%$ downgrade. Using $t = 1.0 \text{ s}$ and $a = 10 \text{ ft/sec}^2$, what is the yellow interval?
trans-st-ex3.eli5: Convert 45 mph: $v = 45 \times 1.467 = 66.0$ ft/sec. On a 3% downgrade, gravity opposes braking, reducing effective deceleration. The denominator becomes $2a - 64.4(0.03) = 20 - 1.932 = 18.07$. $y = 1.0 + 66.0/18.07 = 1.0 + 3.65 = 4.65$, approximately 4.7 sec. The 4.3 sec option used a level grade ($G = 0$): $1.0 + 66.0/20 = 4.3$. The 3.5 sec option used mph instead of ft/sec: $1.0 + 45/18.07 = 3.5$. The 3.3 sec option used both mph and level grade: $1.0 + 45/20 = 3.25$.
trans-st-ex3.hint: Downgrade reduces effective deceleration. The denominator becomes 2a - 64.4G where G = 0.03 for a 3% downgrade.
traps: Ignoring the grade adjustment and using a level-grade denominator
Reversing the grade sign -- downhill reduces effective deceleration, making yellow longer

trans-st-ex4.statement: A traffic engineer designs a signal with a yellow interval of $3.0 \text{ sec}$ for an approach with design speed $50 \text{ mph}$. Using $t = 1.0 \text{ s}$ and $a = 10 \text{ ft/sec}^2$, is this yellow time adequate?

choices.text: No -- the required yellow is 4.7 sec; using 3.0 sec creates a dilemma zone where drivers can neither stop nor clear the intersection
Yes -- 3.0 sec is the standard minimum yellow for all approach speeds
Yes -- the 3.0 sec yellow is adequate because drivers will slow down on approach
No -- but the shortfall can be made up by extending the all-red interval

trans-st-ex4.eli5: Compute the required yellow: v = 50 x 1.467 = 73.3 ft/sec. y = 1.0 + 73.3/(2 x 10) = 1.0 + 3.67 = 4.67, approximately 4.7 sec. The actual yellow of 3.0 sec is 1.7 sec too short. This creates a "dilemma zone" -- a region where a driver is too close to stop safely but too far to clear the intersection during the yellow. This is a serious safety problem. The "3.0 sec is the standard minimum for all speeds" option is wrong because yellow time is speed-dependent. The "adequate because drivers will slow down" option assumes drivers slow down, but the design must accommodate the design speed. The "make up the shortfall with the all-red interval" option is wrong because the all-red serves a different purpose (clearance of vehicles already in the intersection, not stopping decisions).
trans-st-ex4.hint: Compute the required yellow and compare. What happens when yellow is shorter than needed?

steps.text: A deficit creates a dilemma zone where drivers at certain distances can neither stop nor clear safely.

traps: Assuming a fixed minimum yellow works for all speeds
Thinking the all-red interval can compensate for an inadequate yellow

trans-tf-ex1.statement: A freeway has free-flow speed $S_f = 60 \text{ mph}$ and jam density $D_j = 200 \text{ veh/mi/ln}$. What is the optimum density at maximum flow?
trans-tf-ex1.eli5: At maximum flow, the optimum density is exactly half the jam density: $D_o = D_j/2 = 200/2 = 100$ veh/mi/ln. This comes straight from the Greenshields model. The choice 200 is the jam density itself, not the optimum. The choice 50 divides the jam density by 4 instead of 2. The choice 150 is three-quarters of the jam density, which has no significance in the model.
trans-tf-ex1.hint: At maximum flow, both speed and density are half their extreme values.
traps: Using $D_j$ directly as the optimum density instead of dividing by 2

trans-tf-ex2.statement: In the Greenshields model, what happens to flow as density increases from zero toward jam density?

choices.text: Flow increases linearly until it reaches jam density
Flow increases to a maximum at half the jam density, then decreases back to zero
Flow remains constant regardless of density
Flow decreases monotonically from free-flow conditions to jam density

trans-tf-ex2.eli5: The Greenshields model produces a parabolic flow-density curve. At zero density, flow is zero (no cars). As density increases, flow rises to a peak at $D = D_j/2$, then falls back to zero at jam density (cars are bumper-to-bumper, speed = 0). The "increases linearly until jam density" option incorrectly assumes a linear relationship. The "flow remains constant" option ignores the speed-density tradeoff. The "decreases monotonically from free-flow to jam density" option describes a monotonically decreasing function, but flow actually starts at zero when there are no vehicles.
trans-tf-ex2.hint: The flow-density curve from the Greenshields model is a parabola. Where is its peak?

steps.text: At $D = D_j/2$: flow reaches its maximum $V_m = D_j S_f / 4$.

traps: Assuming flow increases linearly with density instead of following a parabolic curve

trans-tf-ex3.statement: A 2-mile road segment has an ADT of $12{,}000 \text{ veh/day}$ and recorded $8$ crashes over a 3-year period. What is the crash rate per million vehicle-miles traveled (RMVM)?
trans-tf-ex3.eli5: $VMT = ADT \times \text{days} \times \text{length} = 12{,}000 \times (365 \times 3) \times 2 = 12{,}000 \times 1{,}095 \times 2 = 26{,}280{,}000$ vehicle-miles. $RMVM = A \times 1{,}000{,}000 / VMT = 8 \times 1{,}000{,}000 / 26{,}280{,}000 = 0.304$ which rounds to 0.30. The 0.91 distractor used only 1 year instead of 3: $VMT = 8{,}760{,}000$, $RMVM = 8{,}000{,}000/8{,}760{,}000 = 0.91$. The 109.6 distractor mis-scales the result (omits the segment length and misapplies the million factor). The 1.10 distractor underestimates VMT by using a reduced length and/or period.
trans-tf-ex3.hint: $VMT = ADT \times \text{total days} \times \text{segment length}$. Use the full study period, not just one year.
traps: Using only one year of data when the study covers multiple years
Forgetting to include the segment length in VMT

trans-tf-ex4.statement: An engineer computes the RMEV for two intersections. Intersection A has RMEV $= 3.5$ and Intersection B has RMEV $= 1.8$. The ADT at Intersection A is twice the ADT at Intersection B. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Intersection A has a higher crash rate per vehicle exposure, so it may warrant safety improvements first
Intersection A is safer because it carries more traffic
The two intersections cannot be compared because they have different ADTs
Intersection B is more dangerous because a lower RMEV means more severe crashes

trans-tf-ex4.eli5: RMEV already normalizes crashes by exposure (per million entering vehicles), so different ADTs are already accounted for. A higher RMEV means more crashes per million vehicles, regardless of total volume. Intersection A at 3.5 has nearly double the crash rate of B at 1.8, making it the stronger candidate for safety review. The "safer because it carries more traffic" choice confuses volume with safety. The "cannot be compared" choice is wrong because RMEV exists precisely to enable such comparisons. The "lower RMEV means more severe crashes" choice reverses the meaning of RMEV.
trans-tf-ex4.hint: RMEV already accounts for traffic volume differences. Higher RMEV = higher crash rate per vehicle.

steps.text: RMEV = crashes per million entering vehicles. It normalizes by exposure, so different ADTs are already handled.
Intersection A: 3.5 crashes/MEV > Intersection B: 1.8 crashes/MEV.
Higher RMEV means worse crash performance per vehicle, so A may need safety attention first.

traps: Thinking higher volume means more dangerous regardless of the rate
Believing different ADTs make RMEV comparisons invalid

trans-cl-ex1.statement: A freeway segment has a free-flow speed of $110\,\text{km/h}$, 3 lanes per direction, and a peak-hour volume of 5400 vehicles. If the peak-hour factor (PHF) is 0.90, what is the peak 15-minute flow rate per lane?
trans-cl-ex1.eli5: The peak 15-min flow rate adjusts the hourly volume for the peaking within the hour: $V_p = V/(PHF \times N) = 5400/(0.90 \times 3) = 5400/2.7 = 2000$ veh/h/ln. The PHF accounts for the fact that traffic does not flow uniformly throughout the hour. Common trap is forgetting to divide by the number of lanes.
trans-cl-ex1.hint: Use $V_p = V/(PHF \times N)$ where $N$ is the number of lanes.
traps: Forgetting to divide by the number of lanes
Using PHF as a multiplier instead of dividing by it

trans-cl-ex2.statement: On a freeway operating at Level of Service (LOS) F, which condition is most likely occurring?

choices.text: Stable flow with some speed reductions
Forced or breakdown flow with stop-and-go conditions

trans-cl-ex2.eli5: LOS grades go from A (best, free flow) to F (worst, breakdown). LOS F means demand exceeds capacity — you get queuing, stop-and-go traffic, and long delays. LOS A-C is good, D is approaching unstable, E is at capacity, F is breakdown. This is one of those definitions the FE loves to test.
trans-cl-ex2.hint: LOS uses a grading scale A through F — what does F represent?

steps.text: LOS A: Free flow, high speeds, low density.
LOS E: At capacity, unstable flow.
LOS F: Forced/breakdown flow — demand exceeds capacity, stop-and-go conditions.

traps: Confusing LOS E (at capacity) with LOS F (breakdown)

trans-cl-ex3.statement: A 3-lane directional freeway carries $V = 3{,}500\,\text{veh/hr}$ with $PHF = 0.92$, $15\%$ trucks ($P_T = 0.15$), and rolling terrain ($E_T = 3.0$). The mean speed is $55\,\text{mph}$. What is the density?
trans-cl-ex3.eli5: Three steps. First, $f_{HV} = 1/(1 + 0.15(3.0 - 1)) = 1/1.30 = 0.769$. Second, $v_p = 3{,}500/(0.92 \times 3 \times 0.769) = 3{,}500/2.122 = 1{,}650$ pc/h/ln. Third, $D = 1{,}650/55 = 30.0$ pc/mi/ln (LOS D). The 23.1 option dropped $f_{HV}$ entirely. The 26.5 option used level-terrain $E_T = 2.0$ instead of rolling terrain $E_T = 3.0$. The 27.6 option forgot PHF.
trans-cl-ex3.hint: Compute fHV first (rolling terrain uses $E_T = 3.0$), then $v_p$, then $D = v_p / S$.
traps: Using level-terrain $E_T = 2.0$ when the problem states rolling terrain ($E_T = 3.0$)
Dropping $f_{HV}$ from the flow-rate equation

trans-cl-ex4.statement: A freeway analysis produces a density of $34\,\text{pc/mi/ln}$. If the heavy-vehicle adjustment factor $f_{HV}$ was accidentally set to $1.0$ instead of its true value of $0.85$, what would happen to the computed density and LOS?

choices.text: The computed density would be lower than actual, potentially understating congestion
The computed density would be higher than actual, overstating congestion
Density would be unchanged because $f_{HV}$ only affects speed
The LOS would improve because passenger cars flow more smoothly

trans-cl-ex4.eli5: $f_{HV}$ appears in the denominator of $v_p = V/(PHF \times N \times f_{HV})$. If you set $f_{HV} = 1.0$ when it should be 0.85, the denominator gets bigger, making $v_p$ smaller. A smaller $v_p$ means a smaller density $D = v_p/S$, which could shift the LOS one or two grades better than reality. You would think the road is less congested than it actually is. The real-world effect of trucks is that they take up more road space, so ignoring their impact makes the analysis unconservative.
trans-cl-ex4.hint: $f_{HV}$ is in the denominator of $v_p$. What happens to $v_p$ when you make the denominator bigger?

steps.text: $v_p = V/(PHF \times N \times f_{HV})$. Setting $f_{HV} = 1.0 > 0.85$ increases the denominator.
Larger denominator means smaller $v_p$, which means smaller $D = v_p/S$.
Smaller density maps to a better LOS grade, underestimating the actual congestion.

traps: Thinking a higher fHV makes density worse -- fHV is in the denominator, so a higher value reduces vp
Confusing the direction of the error -- ignoring trucks underestimates congestion, not overestimates it

trans-pd-ex1.statement: A flexible pavement has: surface $a_1 = 0.44$, $D_1 = 5 \text{ in}$; base $a_2 = 0.14$, $D_2 = 10 \text{ in}$, $m_2 = 0.90$; subbase $a_3 = 0.11$, $D_3 = 8 \text{ in}$, $m_3 = 0.90$. What is the structural number?
trans-pd-ex1.eli5: $SN = a_1D_1 + a_2D_2m_2 + a_3D_3m_3 = 0.44(5) + 0.14(10)(0.90) + 0.11(8)(0.90) = 2.20 + 1.26 + 0.792 = 4.252$, which rounds to 4.26. The 4.58 choice used $m = 1.0$ for all layers: $2.20 + 1.40 + 0.88 = 4.48$ (a near-miss distractor for ignoring drainage coefficients). The 3.46 choice forgot the subbase entirely: $2.20 + 1.26$. The 0.69 choice summed only the coefficients.
trans-pd-ex1.hint: Multiply each layer: coefficient x thickness x drainage, then add them all up.
traps: Ignoring the drainage coefficients and using m = 1.0 for all layers

trans-pd-ex2.statement: In the AASHTO flexible pavement design, the drainage coefficient $m$ for base and subbase layers accounts for:

choices.text: The compaction level achieved during construction
The expected moisture conditions and quality of drainage, which reduce the effective structural contribution of granular layers
The traffic loading applied to each individual layer
The temperature susceptibility of asphalt layers

trans-pd-ex2.eli5: The drainage coefficient $m$ adjusts for how well water drains from the granular base and subbase layers. Poor drainage means water sits in the layer, weakening it and reducing its effective structural contribution. Values of $m < 1.0$ penalize layers with poor drainage; $m = 1.0$ means good drainage. The surface course (layer 1) always uses $m = 1.0$ by convention because asphalt is relatively impermeable. The compaction-level choice describes a construction quality issue, not drainage. The traffic-loading choice is captured by ESALs, not by m. The temperature-susceptibility choice applies to asphalt, not granular layers.
trans-pd-ex2.hint: The drainage coefficient modifies granular layer contributions based on moisture and drainage quality.

steps.text: Drainage coefficients $m$ apply to base and subbase (granular layers), not the surface.
A lower $m$ reduces the effective SN contribution, requiring thicker layers.

traps: Thinking m applies to the asphalt surface layer -- the surface always uses m = 1.0

trans-pd-ex3.statement: A road receives $500$ passes/year of a $32{,}000 \text{ lb}$ tandem-axle load and $200$ passes/year of a $20{,}000 \text{ lb}$ single-axle load. The LEF for a 32,000 lb tandem axle is $1.11$ and the LEF for a 20,000 lb single axle is $1.51$. How many total annual ESALs do these loads produce?
trans-pd-ex3.eli5: For each load type, multiply passes by LEF, then add: Tandem: $500 \times 1.11 = 555$. Single: $200 \times 1.51 = 302$. Total $= 555 + 302 = 857$ ESALs. The 700 option assumed LEF $= 1.0$ for both: $500 + 200 = 700$. The 555 option only counted the tandem axle and forgot the single. The 1,310 option used the wrong LEFs (swapped single and tandem column values).
trans-pd-ex3.hint: ESALs = sum of (passes x LEF) for each load type. Make sure to read the correct column.
traps: Swapping the single-axle and tandem-axle LEF columns in the table
Assuming LEF = 1.0 for all loads

trans-pd-ex4.statement: Two pavement sections have the same required Structural Number ($SN = 4.0$). Section A uses a thicker asphalt surface with a thinner granular base. Section B uses a thinner asphalt surface with a thicker granular base. Which statement is most accurate?

choices.text: Both designs are structurally equivalent per the SN equation, but Section A will likely perform better because asphalt has a higher layer coefficient than granular base
Section B is always the better design because granular base is less expensive
The two sections cannot have the same SN with different layer thicknesses
Section A is overdesigned because thicker asphalt exceeds the SN requirement

trans-pd-ex4.eli5: The SN equation allows different thickness combinations to reach the same total SN. Since asphalt has $a_1 = 0.44$ (much higher than granular base $a_2 = 0.14$), each inch of asphalt provides about 3 times the structural benefit of an inch of base. Section A with more asphalt gets the same SN with less total pavement thickness, and higher-quality materials on top generally provide better performance. Section B may be cheaper in materials but needs much more total thickness. Both satisfy the design SN, so they are structurally equivalent by the AASHTO method. The "granular base is always cheaper/better" choice ignores performance differences. The "cannot have the same SN with different thicknesses" choice misunderstands the SN equation. The "Section A is overdesigned" choice is wrong because both sections hit exactly $SN = 4.0$.
trans-pd-ex4.hint: Multiple layer combinations can produce the same SN. Compare the layer coefficients to understand the tradeoff.

steps.text: Example: Section A with $D_1 = 6$ in asphalt: $0.44 \times 6 = 2.64$. Needs $1.36$ more SN from base.
Section B with $D_1 = 3$ in asphalt: $0.44 \times 3 = 1.32$. Needs $2.68$ more SN from base.
Both reach SN = 4.0, but the asphalt layer coefficient ($a_1 = 0.44$) is much higher than the base ($a_2 = 0.14$), so Section A uses less total material.

traps: Thinking only one layer combination can satisfy a given SN
Ignoring the difference in layer coefficients when comparing designs

trans-ew-ex1.statement: Two cross sections are $50 \text{ ft}$ apart with areas $A_1 = 180 \text{ ft}^2$ and $A_2 = 220 \text{ ft}^2$. What is the earthwork volume using the average end area method, in cubic yards?
trans-ew-ex1.eli5: $V = L(A_1 + A_2)/2 = 50(180 + 220)/2 = 50 \times 400/2 = 50 \times 200 = 10{,}000$ ft$^3$. Convert: $10{,}000/27 = 370$ yd$^3$. The 10,000 yd$^3$ option is in ft$^3$, not yd$^3$ -- forgot to divide by 27. The 741 yd$^3$ option forgot to divide by 2 in the average: $50 \times 400/27 = 741$. The 333 yd$^3$ option used only $A_1$: $50 \times 180/27 = 333$.
trans-ew-ex1.hint: Average the two areas, multiply by L, then divide by 27 for yd^3.
traps: Reporting the answer in ft^3 instead of yd^3 -- always divide by 27

trans-ew-ex2.statement: The average end area method always overestimates the true volume compared to the prismoidal formula (when the two end areas are not equal). Why?

choices.text: The average end area method uses a larger distance $L$ than the prismoidal formula
The average end area method assumes a linear transition between the two cross sections, but the actual shape tapers, so the true mid-section area is smaller than the average of the two ends
The prismoidal formula ignores the mid-section, so it always underestimates
The overestimate occurs only when both areas are very large

trans-ew-ex2.eli5: The average end area method takes $(A_1 + A_2)/2$ as the representative cross section for the entire segment. But when $A_1$ and $A_2$ differ, the actual mid-section area $A_m$ is typically less than $(A_1 + A_2)/2$ because the cross section tapers non-linearly. The prismoidal formula accounts for this by weighting the mid-section $4\times$. Mathematically, $(A_1 + 4A_m + A_2)/6 \leq (A_1 + A_2)/2$ when $A_m < (A_1 + A_2)/2$, which is the typical case. The "larger distance $L$" choice is wrong -- both methods use the same $L$. The "prismoidal ignores the mid-section" choice is backwards -- the prismoidal formula uses $A_m$ and is more accurate. The "only when both areas are very large" choice is wrong because the overestimate depends on the difference between the areas, not their absolute size.
trans-ew-ex2.hint: Compare the representative area used by each method. How does the actual mid-section compare to the simple average?

steps.text: Average end area uses $(A_1 + A_2)/2$ as the representative area.
Prismoidal uses $(A_1 + 4A_m + A_2)/6$, which weights the actual mid-section.
When $A_1 \neq A_2$, the actual $A_m < (A_1 + A_2)/2$, so the prismoidal gives a smaller (more accurate) volume.

traps: Thinking both methods use different distances L -- they use the same station spacing

trans-ew-ex3.statement: Two stations $100 \text{ ft}$ apart have areas $A_1 = 100 \text{ ft}^2$ and $A_2 = 400 \text{ ft}^2$, with mid-section $A_m = 200 \text{ ft}^2$. What is the prismoidal correction (difference between average end area volume and prismoidal volume)?
trans-ew-ex3.eli5: Average end area: $V_{avg} = 100(100 + 400)/2 = 25{,}000$ ft$^3$ $= 926$ yd$^3$. Prismoidal: $V_{prism} = 100(100 + 4 \times 200 + 400)/6 = 100 \times 1{,}300/6 = 21{,}667$ ft$^3$ $= 802$ yd$^3$. Correction $= 926 - 802 = 123$ yd$^3$. The 0 yd³ option assumes both methods give the same answer. The 926 yd³ option is the average end area volume itself, not the correction. The 62 yd³ option halved the correction for no reason.
trans-ew-ex3.hint: Compute both volumes, then subtract. The prismoidal correction is always positive (average end area overestimates).
traps: Confusing the prismoidal correction with the prismoidal volume itself
Forgetting to convert both volumes to the same units before subtracting

trans-ew-ex4.statement: A project has a cut section producing $5{,}000 \text{ yd}^3$ of excavation and a fill section requiring $5{,}000 \text{ yd}^3$ of embankment. An engineer assumes the cut material can directly fill the embankment with no waste or borrow. What critical factor has the engineer overlooked?

choices.text: Shrinkage and swell factors -- excavated soil changes volume when disturbed and recompacted, so equal bank volumes do not mean equal compacted volumes
The two sections may be different soil types, but volume is unaffected by soil type
The hauling cost, which is the only consideration in mass haul analysis
The average end area method was used, which always gives exact volumes

trans-ew-ex4.eli5: When soil is excavated, it expands (swells) because of loosening. When it is placed as fill and compacted, it shrinks below the original bank volume (shrinkage). So 5,000 yd$^3$ of bank cut does not produce 5,000 yd$^3$ of compacted fill. Depending on the soil, you might get only 4,250 yd$^3$ of compacted fill from 5,000 yd$^3$ of bank cut (about 15% shrinkage for typical clay). The engineer would need to borrow additional material. The "different soil types but volume unaffected" choice acknowledges soil differences but incorrectly claims volume is unaffected. The "hauling cost is the only consideration" choice ignores the volume balance issue. The "average end area always gives exact volumes" choice is wrong because that method overestimates, not gives exact volumes.
trans-ew-ex4.hint: Excavated soil does not maintain its original volume when placed and compacted as fill.

steps.text: Bank volume (in-place) is measured before excavation.
Loose volume (after excavation) is typically larger due to swell.
Compacted volume (as fill) is typically smaller than bank volume due to shrinkage. Equal bank volumes of cut and fill do NOT mean balanced earthwork.

traps: Assuming bank volume equals compacted volume -- shrinkage and swell must be applied
Ignoring the distinction between bank, loose, and compacted volumes in mass haul balancing

trans-td-ex1.statement: Zone $i$ produces $P_i = 600$ trips. The trips can go to Zone A ($A_A = 400$, $F = 0.4$) or Zone B ($A_B = 100$, $F = 0.6$), with $K = 1$. How many trips go from Zone $i$ to Zone A?
trans-td-ex1.eli5: Weights A·F: Zone A = 400(0.4) = 160; Zone B = 100(0.6) = 60; sum = 220. Fraction to A = 160/220 = 0.727, so T = 600 × 0.727 = 436 trips. The 164-trip option is the trips to Zone B (60/220 × 600). The 480-trip option uses attractions only (400/500). The 300-trip option splits evenly.
trans-td-ex1.hint: Weight each destination by A×F, normalize by the total, multiply by Pi.
trans-td-ex1.handbookFormula: T_{ij} = P_i[A_j F_{ij} K_{ij}/\sum A_j F_{ij} K_{ij}]
traps: Distributing by attractions alone, ignoring friction factors
Failing to normalize by the sum over all zones

trans-rp-ex1.statement: Compared with flexible pavement, a rigid (PCC) pavement is generally LESS sensitive to subgrade strength. Why?

choices.text: The stiff slab distributes load over a wide area by beam action
Concrete is weaker in bending than asphalt
Rigid pavement transmits all load directly beneath the wheel

trans-rp-ex1.eli5: A rigid slab bends like a beam and spreads each wheel load over a large area of subgrade, so the foundation strength matters less than for flexible pavement. The "concrete is weaker in bending than asphalt" choice is false (concrete carries the bending). The "transmits all load directly beneath the wheel" choice is the opposite of slab behavior. The "rigid pavement has no subgrade" choice is incorrect — there is always a subgrade.
trans-rp-ex1.hint: How does a stiff slab spread load, and what does that imply about subgrade dependence?

steps.text: A rigid slab acts as a beam over the subgrade.
Beam action distributes load over a wide area.
So subgrade strength matters less than for flexible pavement.

traps: Assuming rigid pavement depends heavily on subgrade like flexible does
Thinking a slab concentrates load beneath the wheel

trans-tcd-ex1.statement: Under the MUTCD, a green sign giving the distance to the next town is which category of traffic control device?
trans-tcd-ex1.eli5: Green signs that give directions, distances, and destinations are GUIDE signs. Regulatory signs (white/red) state laws; warning signs (yellow diamonds) alert to conditions; a signal indication is a traffic light, not a sign.
trans-tcd-ex1.hint: Green color + giving directions/distances = which category?

steps.text: Guide signs provide directions and distances and are green.
The sign described matches that purpose and color.
So it is a guide sign.

traps: Confusing guide (green) with regulatory or warning signs
Calling a sign a signal indication

trans-ssd-cp1.statement: A roadway has a design speed of $55 \text{ mph}$ on a $5\%$ upgrade. Using $t = 2.5 \text{ s}$ and $a = 11.2 \text{ ft/sec}^2$, what is the stopping sight distance?
trans-ssd-cp1.eli5: Uphill is positive grade, so $G = +0.05$ and the denominator grows, shortening the braking distance. Reaction distance $= 1.47 \times 55 \times 2.5 = 202.1$ ft. The denominator factor is $a/32.2 + G = 0.3478 + 0.05 = 0.3978$, so braking $= 55^2/(30 \times 0.3978) = 3{,}025/11.93 = 253.5$ ft. Total SSD $= 202.1 + 253.5 = 455.6 \approx 456$ ft. The 202 ft choice is the reaction distance only. The 492 ft choice used a level grade ($G = 0$): $202.1 + 290 = 492$. The 541 ft choice used a downgrade ($G = -0.05$), wrongly making stopping harder.
trans-ssd-cp1.hint: Uphill = positive G in the denominator. Add reaction distance plus the shortened braking distance.
traps: Reversing the grade sign -- uphill is positive G and shortens SSD
Reporting only the reaction distance and omitting the braking component

trans-ssd-cp2.statement: During the peak hour an approach records $2{,}400 \text{ veh/hr}$ with a peak 15-minute count of $700 \text{ veh}$. What is the peak hour factor (PHF)?
trans-ssd-cp2.eli5: $PHF = V/(4 \times V_{15}) = 2{,}400/(4 \times 700) = 2{,}400/2{,}800 = 0.857$. The 0.292 option divided $V_{15}$ by $V$ and forgot the factor of 4 in the wrong place: $700/2{,}400 = 0.292$. The 1.167 option inverted the ratio: $2{,}800/2{,}400$. The 0.750 option used $V_{15} = 800$ by mistake. PHF is always between 0.25 and 1.00.
trans-ssd-cp2.hint: PHF = V / (4 x V15). The peak 15-minute count is multiplied by 4 in the denominator.
traps: Inverting the ratio and reporting a value greater than 1.0
Forgetting to multiply the 15-minute count by 4

trans-vc-cp1.statement: A crest vertical curve must provide a sight distance $S = 700 \text{ ft}$ with $A = 4$. Determine which case ($S \leq L$ or $S > L$) governs and find the minimum curve length.
trans-vc-cp1.eli5: Test the $S \leq L$ case first: $L = AS^2/2{,}158 = 4 \times 700^2/2{,}158 = 1{,}960{,}000/2{,}158 = 908 \approx 909$ ft. Check the assumption: $S = 700 \leq L = 908$ is TRUE, so this branch is valid and governs. Now check the $S > L$ branch: $L = 2S - 2{,}158/A = 1{,}400 - 539.5 = 860.5$ ft, which would require $S > L$ (i.e., $700 > 860.5$) -- that is FALSE, so the $S > L$ branch is invalid here. The minimum length is therefore about 909 ft. The 863 ft choice is approximately the invalid $S > L$ branch value ($2S - 2{,}158/A = 860.5$, rounded). The 1{,}400 ft choice is just $2S$, dropping the second term. The 540 ft choice is the term $2{,}158/A$ alone.
trans-vc-cp1.hint: Try the S <= L crest formula L = AS^2/2158 first, then confirm S <= L holds.

steps.text: Evaluate and check the assumption ($S = 700 \leq L$):

traps: Using the S > L branch when the assumption S > L is not satisfied
Confusing the crest constant (2,158) with the sag denominator

trans-vc-cp2.statement: A vertical curve is designed with a K-value of $K = 160$ connecting a $-2\%$ grade to a $+3\%$ grade. What is the required curve length $L$?
trans-vc-cp2.eli5: $A = |g_2 - g_1| \times 100 = |0.03 - (-0.02)| \times 100 = 0.05 \times 100 = 5$. Then $K = L/A$ rearranges to $L = K \times A = 160 \times 5 = 800$ ft. The 160 ft choice reported $K$ as if it were $L$. The 32 ft choice computed $K/A = 160/5$ instead of $K \times A$. The 320 ft choice used $A = 2$ (only one grade magnitude): $160 \times 2$.
trans-vc-cp2.hint: K = L/A, so L = K x A. Find A from the algebraic grade difference first.
traps: Dividing K by A instead of multiplying
Using only one grade magnitude for A instead of the full algebraic difference

trans-hc-cp1.statement: A horizontal curve has $R = 1{,}000 \text{ ft}$ and intersection angle $I = 40\degree$. What is the middle ordinate $M$?
trans-hc-cp1.eli5: $M = R[1 - \cos(I/2)] = 1{,}000[1 - \cos(20\degree)] = 1{,}000(1 - 0.9397) = 1{,}000 \times 0.0603 = 60.3$ ft. The 234 ft choice used $\cos(I) = \cos(40\degree) = 0.766$ instead of $\cos(I/2)$: $1{,}000(1 - 0.766) = 234$. The 64.2 ft choice is the external distance $E = R[1/\cos(I/2) - 1] = 1{,}000(1/0.9397 - 1) = 64.2$, not the middle ordinate. The 30.2 ft choice halved the correct answer.
trans-hc-cp1.hint: M = R[1 - cos(I/2)]. Halve the intersection angle before taking the cosine.
traps: Using cos(I) instead of cos(I/2)
Confusing the middle ordinate M with the external distance E

trans-hc-cp2.statement: A curve is designed for $V = 60 \text{ mph}$ with a maximum superelevation $e = 8\%$ and a side friction factor $f = 0.12$. What is the minimum allowable curve radius?
trans-hc-cp2.eli5: Rearrange $0.01e + f = V^2/(15R)$ for the minimum radius: $R = V^2/[15(0.01e + f)] = 60^2/[15(0.08 + 0.12)] = 3{,}600/[15 \times 0.20] = 3{,}600/3.0 = 1{,}200$ ft. The 2,000 ft option used only friction ($0.01e + f = 0.12$): $3{,}600/(15 \times 0.12) = 2{,}000$. The 240 ft option forgot to convert $e$: used $0.01e = 0.08$ but then added $e = 8$ giving an inflated denominator. The 600 ft option doubled the denominator factor by using $0.01e + f = 0.40$.
trans-hc-cp2.hint: Solve 0.01e + f = V^2/(15R) for R. Use e as a percent so 0.01e converts it to decimal.
traps: Ignoring the superelevation term and using friction alone
Forgetting the 0.01 factor that converts e from percent to decimal

trans-st-cp1.statement: An intersection approach has a speed of $35 \text{ mph}$ on a $4\%$ upgrade. Using $t = 1.0 \text{ s}$ and $a = 10 \text{ ft/sec}^2$, what is the yellow interval?
trans-st-cp1.eli5: Convert: $v = 35 \times 1.467 = 51.3$ ft/sec. On an upgrade, gravity aids stopping, so the denominator grows: $2a + 64.4G = 2(10) + 64.4(0.04) = 20 + 2.576 = 22.58$. $y = 1.0 + 51.3/22.58 = 1.0 + 2.27 = 3.27 \approx 3.3$ sec. The 3.6 sec option used a level grade ($G = 0$): $1.0 + 51.3/20 = 3.57$. The 3.9 sec option reversed the sign (treated the upgrade as a downgrade): $1.0 + 51.3/17.42 = 3.95$. The 2.6 sec option used mph in the numerator: $1.0 + 35/22.58 = 2.55$.
trans-st-cp1.hint: Upgrade adds to the denominator: 2a + 64.4G. Convert speed to ft/sec first.
traps: Reversing the grade sign -- upgrade adds to the denominator and shortens yellow
Using mph instead of ft/sec in the numerator

trans-st-cp2.statement: Two crosswalks have identical lengths and pedestrian speeds, but Crosswalk A serves $5$ pedestrians per cycle while Crosswalk B serves $25$. Using $G_p = 3.2 + L/S_p + 0.27 N_{\text{ped}}$, how does the required pedestrian green time compare?

choices.text: They are equal because the walking time term $L/S_p$ dominates the calculation
Crosswalk B requires about 5.4 sec more green time because the $0.27 N_{\text{ped}}$ term grows with pedestrian volume
Crosswalk B requires 5 times the green time of Crosswalk A
Crosswalk A requires more green time because fewer pedestrians walk more cautiously

trans-st-cp2.eli5: The only term that differs between the two crosswalks is $0.27 N_{\text{ped}}$. The difference in that term is $0.27(25 - 5) = 0.27 \times 20 = 5.4$ sec, so B needs about 5.4 sec more. The start-up constant (3.2) and the walking time ($L/S_p$) are identical for both. The option that they are equal because the walking time term $L/S_p$ dominates the calculation is wrong because the volume term, while smaller, is not zero. The option that Crosswalk B requires 5 times the green time of Crosswalk A wrongly assumes green time scales linearly with pedestrian count -- only one of three terms depends on $N_{\text{ped}}$. The option that Crosswalk A requires more green time because fewer pedestrians walk more cautiously invents a behavior not in the formula.
trans-st-cp2.hint: Only the 0.27 Nped term changes. Compute the difference in that term.

steps.text: Identical terms: $3.2 + L/S_p$ are the same for both crosswalks.
Difference comes only from the volume term:
Crosswalk B requires about 5.4 sec more green time.

traps: Assuming green time scales linearly with pedestrian count -- only one term depends on N_ped
Ignoring the 0.27 N_ped term entirely

trans-tf-cp1.statement: A roadway has free-flow speed $S_f = 50 \text{ mph}$ and jam density $D_j = 160 \text{ veh/mi/ln}$. Using the Greenshields model, what is the flow when the density is $D = 40 \text{ veh/mi/ln}$?
trans-tf-cp1.eli5: First find speed from Greenshields: $S = S_f - (S_f/D_j)D = 50 - (50/160)(40) = 50 - 0.3125 \times 40 = 50 - 12.5 = 37.5$ mph. Then flow $V = S \times D = 37.5 \times 40 = 1{,}500$ veh/hr/ln. The 2,000 veh/hr/ln choice used the free-flow speed without the density reduction: $50 \times 40 = 2{,}000$. The 1,000 veh/hr/ln choice used the optimum speed $S_f/2 = 25$: $25 \times 40$. The 500 veh/hr/ln choice used only the speed-reduction term ($12.5 \times 40$) as the speed.
trans-tf-cp1.hint: Get speed from Greenshields first, then multiply by density: V = S x D.
trans-tf-cp1.handbookFormula: V = S \times D, \quad S = S_f - \frac{S_f}{D_j} D
traps: Using the free-flow speed directly instead of the reduced Greenshields speed
Multiplying density by the optimum speed instead of the speed at that density

trans-tf-cp2.statement: A $3 \text{ mile}$ rural highway segment carries an ADT of $5{,}000 \text{ veh/day}$ and recorded $27$ crashes over a 5-year study period. What is the crash rate per hundred million vehicle-miles traveled (per $100$ MVM)?
trans-tf-cp2.eli5: $VMT = ADT \times \text{days} \times \text{length} = 5{,}000 \times (365 \times 5) \times 3 = 5{,}000 \times 1{,}825 \times 3 = 27{,}375{,}000$ vehicle-miles. Rate per 100 million VM $= A \times 100{,}000{,}000/VMT = 27 \times 100{,}000{,}000/27{,}375{,}000 = 98.6$. The 0.99 choice used the per-one-million factor instead of per hundred million: $27 \times 1{,}000{,}000/27{,}375{,}000$. The 32.9 choice is the correct rate divided by 3 (e.g., counting the 3-mile length twice in the VMT). The 493 choice used only 1 year instead of the 5-year study period, dividing the VMT by 5 and raising the rate fivefold ($98.6 \times 5 \approx 493$).
trans-tf-cp2.hint: VMT = ADT x total days x length. Then rate = A x 100,000,000 / VMT for a per-100-MVM rate.
traps: Using the per-million factor when the problem asks for a per-hundred-million rate
Using a single year of data instead of the full 5-year study period

trans-cl-cp1.statement: A freeway carries $20\%$ trucks ($P_T = 0.20$) on rolling terrain ($E_T = 3.0$). What is the heavy-vehicle adjustment factor $f_{HV}$?
trans-cl-cp1.eli5: $f_{HV} = 1/[1 + P_T(E_T - 1)] = 1/[1 + 0.20(3.0 - 1)] = 1/[1 + 0.20 \times 2] = 1/1.40 = 0.714$. The 0.625 distractor used $E_T = 3.0$ without subtracting 1: $1/[1 + 0.20 \times 3] = 1/1.60$. The 1.400 distractor reported the denominator itself instead of its reciprocal. The 0.600 distractor computed $1 - P_T \times E_T = 1 - 0.60$.
trans-cl-cp1.hint: fHV = 1/[1 + PT(ET - 1)]. Subtract 1 from ET before multiplying by PT.
traps: Using PT x ET instead of PT x (ET - 1)
Reporting the denominator instead of its reciprocal

trans-cl-cp2.statement: Two freeway segments are analyzed. Segment 1 has a density of $24 \text{ pc/mi/ln}$ and Segment 2 has a density of $40 \text{ pc/mi/ln}$. Using the LOS density boundaries (A $\leq 11$, B $> 11$–18, C $> 18$–26, D $> 26$–35, E $> 35$–45, F $> 45$), which statement is correct?

choices.text: Segment 1 is LOS B and Segment 2 is LOS D
Segment 1 is LOS C and Segment 2 is LOS E
Both segments operate at LOS D
Segment 1 is LOS C and Segment 2 is LOS F

trans-cl-cp2.eli5: LOS is read directly from density. Segment 1 at 24 pc/mi/ln falls in the $> 18$ to $26$ band, which is LOS C. Segment 2 at 40 pc/mi/ln falls in the $> 35$ to $45$ band, which is LOS E. The 'LOS B / LOS D' choice shifts both grades one letter too good. The 'both at LOS D' choice wrongly lumps both into D. The 'LOS C / LOS F' choice pushes Segment 2 to F, but F only begins above 45 pc/mi/ln.
trans-cl-cp2.hint: Match each density to its band. C is >18-26; E is >35-45.

steps.text: Segment 1: $24$ pc/mi/ln is in the $> 18$ to $26$ band.
Segment 2: $40$ pc/mi/ln is in the $> 35$ to $45$ band, which is LOS E.

traps: Shifting the LOS grade by one letter due to misreading the band boundaries
Assigning LOS F to any density above 35 -- F begins only above 45

trans-pd-cp1.statement: A flexible pavement must provide $SN = 5.0$. The base has $a_2 = 0.14$, $D_2 = 10 \text{ in}$, $m_2 = 1.0$; the subbase has $a_3 = 0.12$, $D_3 = 8 \text{ in}$, $m_3 = 1.0$. The asphalt surface has $a_1 = 0.44$. What minimum surface thickness $D_1$ is required?
trans-pd-cp1.eli5: Base contribution: $0.14 \times 10 \times 1.0 = 1.40$. Subbase: $0.12 \times 8 \times 1.0 = 0.96$. Remaining SN for the surface: $5.0 - 1.40 - 0.96 = 2.64$. Then $D_1 = 2.64/a_1 = 2.64/0.44 = 6.0$ in. The 11.4-in choice solved $D_1 = 5.0/0.44$ without subtracting the lower layers. The 2.6-in choice left the remaining SN of 2.64 as a thickness, forgetting to divide by $a_1$. The 7.7-in choice forgot the subbase, dividing $5.0 - 1.40 = 3.60$ by $0.44 \times 1.06$.
trans-pd-cp1.hint: Rearrange SN: D1 = (SN - a2 D2 m2 - a3 D3 m3) / a1.
traps: Dividing the full SN by a1 without subtracting the base and subbase contributions
Using a base or subbase coefficient in place of the surface coefficient

trans-pd-cp2.statement: A pavement carries $300$ passes/day of an $18{,}000 \text{ lb}$ single axle (LEF $= 1.00$) and $150$ passes/day of a $30{,}000 \text{ lb}$ single axle (LEF $= 7.9$). Over a $20$-year design life at $365$ days/year, what is the total design ESALs?
trans-pd-cp2.eli5: Daily ESALs $= 300(1.00) + 150(7.9) = 300 + 1{,}185 = 1{,}485$ ESALs/day. Over the design life: $1{,}485 \times 365 \times 20 = 1{,}485 \times 7{,}300 = 10{,}840{,}500 \approx 10.8 \times 10^6$ ESALs. The $2.2 \times 10^6$ choice counted only the 18-kip axles over the design life: $300 \times 7{,}300 = 2.19 \times 10^6$. The $8.7 \times 10^6$ choice used the heavy axles only: $1{,}185 \times 7{,}300 = 8.65 \times 10^6$. The $0.54 \times 10^6$ choice forgot to multiply by the 20-year life and used only 365 days: $1{,}485 \times 365 = 542{,}025$.
trans-pd-cp2.hint: Compute daily ESALs (sum of passes x LEF), then multiply by 365 days x 20 years.
traps: Forgetting to scale daily ESALs by both 365 days and the 20-year design life
Omitting one of the two axle-load groups from the daily sum

trans-ew-cp1.statement: An embankment requires $9{,}000 \text{ yd}^3$ of compacted fill. The borrow soil has a shrinkage factor such that compacted volume is $0.90$ times the bank (in-place) volume. How many cubic yards of bank material must be excavated from the borrow pit?
trans-ew-cp1.eli5: Compacted volume $= 0.90 \times$ bank volume, so bank volume $=$ compacted volume $/ 0.90 = 9{,}000/0.90 = 10{,}000$ yd^3. Soil shrinks when compacted, so you must dig MORE bank material than the finished fill volume. The 8,100 yd^3 option multiplied by 0.90 instead of dividing: $9{,}000 \times 0.90$. The 9,000 yd^3 option ignored shrinkage entirely. The 9,900 yd^3 option added 10% instead of dividing by 0.90.
trans-ew-cp1.hint: Compacted = shrinkage factor x bank. Solve for bank volume by dividing, not multiplying.
traps: Multiplying by the shrinkage factor instead of dividing -- you need more bank material than fill
Ignoring shrinkage and assuming bank volume equals compacted volume

trans-ew-cp2.statement: Three stations are spaced $100 \text{ ft}$ apart. The cross-sectional areas are $A_1 = 120 \text{ ft}^2$, $A_2 = 200 \text{ ft}^2$, and $A_3 = 160 \text{ ft}^2$. Using the average end area method between consecutive stations, what is the total earthwork volume?
trans-ew-cp2.eli5: Apply the average end area method to each 100-ft span and add. Span 1 ($A_1$ to $A_2$): $V = 100(120 + 200)/2 = 16{,}000$ ft^3. Span 2 ($A_2$ to $A_3$): $V = 100(200 + 160)/2 = 18{,}000$ ft^3. Total $= 34{,}000$ ft^3, then $34{,}000/27 = 1{,}259$ yd^3. The 1,037 yd^3 distractor collapsed the two spans into a single 200-ft span using only the first and last areas: $200(120 + 160)/2 = 28{,}000$ ft^3 $\to 1{,}037$ yd^3. The 1,333 yd^3 distractor wrongly applied the prismoidal formula treating $A_2$ as a mid-section: $200(120 + 4 \times 200 + 160)/6 = 36{,}000$ ft^3 $\to 1{,}333$ yd^3. The 593 yd^3 distractor used only the first span.
trans-ew-cp2.hint: Apply the average end area formula to each 100-ft span, sum the volumes, then divide by 27.
traps: Applying a single long span instead of summing two consecutive average-end-area volumes
Forgetting to convert the summed ft^3 volume to yd^3

trans-td-cp1.statement: A zone produces $P_i = 800$ trips, distributed to two zones with weights $A_1 F_1 = 120$ and $A_2 F_2 = 80$ (K = 1). How many trips go to the first zone?
trans-td-cp1.eli5: Fraction to zone 1 = 120/(120 + 80) = 120/200 = 0.60, so T = 800 × 0.60 = 480 trips. The 320 trips choice is the trips to zone 2 (80/200 × 800). The 400 trips choice splits evenly. The 120 trips choice reports the raw weight, not the trips.

trans-rp-cp1.statement: Which design parameter is used to characterize foundation support specifically in RIGID pavement design?
trans-rp-cp1.eli5: Rigid pavement design uses the modulus of subgrade reaction k (pressure per unit deflection) to describe how the subgrade supports the slab. The structural number (SN) is for flexible pavement; Marshall stability and penetration grade are asphalt-mix and binder properties.

trans-tcd-cp1.statement: An engineer finds that an intersection does not meet any MUTCD signal warrant. What is the appropriate conclusion?

choices.text: A signal is not justified; installing one could worsen safety and delay
Install the signal anyway, since signals always help
Warrants do not apply to existing intersections
A signal must be installed to satisfy the MUTCD

trans-tcd-cp1.eli5: If no warrant is met, a signal is not justified — installing one can increase rear-end crashes and cause unnecessary delay. The "install anyway" option wrongly assumes signals always help. The claim that warrants do not apply to existing intersections is false (warrants apply broadly). The "a signal must be installed" option inverts the purpose of a warrant analysis.

Unwarranted signals can increase crashes and delay.
So a signal should not be installed.

const-cpm-q1.statement: Activity A has a duration of 5 days. Activity B depends on A (finish-to-start) and has a duration of 3 days. If A starts on day 0, what is the early finish of B?
const-cpm-q1.eli5: A starts day 0, finishes day 5 ($ES = 0$, $EF = 0 + 5 = 5$). B starts when A finishes (FS), so $ES_B = 5$. $EF_B = 5 + 3 = 8$. Day 5 is EF of A, not B. Day 3 is just B's duration. Day 15 multiplied $5 \times 3$ instead of adding.
const-cpm-q1.hint: EF = ES + Duration. B's ES equals A's EF in a finish-to-start relationship.
traps: Reporting A's early finish (5) instead of B's early finish (8)
Multiplying durations instead of adding them sequentially

const-cpm-q2.statement: In a CPM network, activity C has two predecessors: A (EF = 6) and B (EF = 9). Both relationships are finish-to-start. What is the early start of C?
const-cpm-q2.eli5: When an activity has multiple predecessors (all FS), its $ES$ = the MAXIMUM of all predecessor EFs. C cannot start until BOTH A and B are done. $\max(6, 9) = 9$. The "Day 6" choice took the minimum — C can't start at day 6 because B isn't done yet. The "Day 15" choice added both EFs. The "Day 7.5" choice averaged them.
const-cpm-q2.hint: ES of an activity = MAX of all predecessor EFs. The activity waits for the LAST predecessor to finish.
traps: Using MIN instead of MAX — the activity must wait for ALL predecessors, not just the first one

const-cpm-q3.statement: A project has 4 activities. A (duration = 4, no predecessors), B (duration = 6, predecessor A), C (duration = 3, predecessor A), D (duration = 2, predecessors B and C). What is the project duration?
const-cpm-q3.eli5: Forward pass: A(0,4). B starts at 4, finishes at 10. C starts at 4, finishes at 7. D starts at max(10,7) = 10, finishes at 12. Project duration = 12 days (the EF of the last activity). Two paths exist: A→B→D = 4+6+2 = 12, and A→C→D = 4+3+2 = 9. The longest path (12) controls. The 9 days option used the shorter path A→C→D. The 15 days option added all durations. The 10 days option forgot activity D.
const-cpm-q3.hint: Run the forward pass for all activities. The project duration = EF of the last activity.

steps.text: Project duration = $EF_D = 12$ days. Critical path: A \u2192 B \u2192 D.

traps: Using the shorter path (A→C→D = 9) instead of the critical (longest) path
Summing ALL durations (4+6+3+2 = 15) instead of finding the longest path

const-fb-q1.statement: Network: A (duration 3, no predecessors), B (duration 4, predecessor A), C (duration 2, predecessor A), D (duration 6, predecessor B), E (duration 3, predecessors B and C). What is the early start and early finish of activity E?
const-fb-q1.eli5: Forward pass: A(0,3). B(3,7). C(3,5). E depends on B and C, so $ES_E = \max(EF_B, EF_C) = \max(7, 5) = 7$. $EF_E = 7 + 3 = 10$. The ES=5,EF=8 option used $EF_C = 5$ as ES (took min instead of max). The ES=3,EF=6 option used $ES = EF_A = 3$ (skipped B and C). The ES=9,EF=12 option used a wrong, larger predecessor finish.
const-fb-q1.hint: E depends on B AND C. Use MAX of their EFs to find ES of E.

traps: Using MIN instead of MAX for the forward pass — E can't start until BOTH predecessors finish

const-fb-q2.statement: Using the same network (A:3, B:4, C:2, D:6, E:3; D predecessor B, E predecessors B\&C), the project duration is $13$ days. What is the late start of activity C?

Choice "Day 3" is $LS_B$ from the backward pass — the question asked for $LS$, not $ES$. Choice "Day 5" is a distractor that does not correspond to a real CPM value for C ($EF_C = 2$). Choice "Day 10" is $LF_C$, not $LS_C$ — forgot to subtract the duration.
const-fb-q2.hint: Run the backward pass: LF of C = LS of its successor (E). Then LS = LF − duration.

steps.text: B feeds D and E: $LF_B = \min(LS_D, LS_E) = \min(7, 10) = 7$, $LS_B = 3$

const-fb-q3.statement: In the same network, what is the late finish of activity B?
const-fb-q3.eli5: B feeds two successors: D ($LS_D = 7$) and E ($LS_E = 10$). The backward pass uses MIN: $LF_B = \min(7, 10) = 7$. B must finish by day 7 so that D can start on time. The Day 10 option used $LS_E$ only, ignoring D. The Day 13 option used the project end date. The Day 4 option is $LS_B + 1$ or confused with duration.
const-fb-q3.hint: When an activity feeds multiple successors, its LF = MIN of all successor LSs. The backward pass uses MIN.
traps: Using MAX instead of MIN on the backward pass — B must finish before its tightest successor

const-fl-q1.statement: Activity C has $ES = 3$, $EF = 5$, $LS = 8$, $LF = 10$. What is the total float?
const-fl-q1.eli5: $TF = LS - ES = 8 - 3 = 5$ days. Or equivalently, $TF = LF - EF = 10 - 5 = 5$ days. Both give the same answer. The 2-day choice is the duration ($EF - ES = 5 - 3 = 2$). The 0-day choice would mean it is critical — it is not. The 7-day choice subtracted wrong values ($LF - ES = 10 - 3 = 7$, but that is not the formula).
const-fl-q1.hint: Total float = LS − ES (or LF − EF). Both formulas give the same result.
traps: Confusing duration (EF − ES) with float (LS − ES)

const-fl-q2.statement: A project has paths: A\u2192B\u2192D (4+6+5 = 15 days), A\u2192C\u2192E (4+3+3 = 10 days), A\u2192C\u2192D (4+3+5 = 12 days). Which is the critical path and what is the project duration?
const-fl-q2.eli5: The critical path is the LONGEST path through the network: A→B→D = 15 days. This is the minimum time to complete the project. A→C→E (10) is the shortest path — not critical. A→C→D (12) is an intermediate path. The "all paths, 37 days" option summed every path, which makes no sense since activities run concurrently.
const-fl-q2.hint: The critical path = the longest path = the path that takes the most time. Compare total durations.
traps: Choosing the shortest path as critical — the critical path is the LONGEST
Summing all paths instead of comparing them — parallel paths overlap

const-fl-q3.statement: In the network from earlier lessons (A:3, B:4, C:2, D:6, E:3; D predecessor B, E predecessors B\&C), activity C has $ES = 3$, $EF = 5$. The earliest successor start is $ES_E = 7$. What is the free float of C?
const-fl-q3.eli5: Free float $= \min(ES_{\text{successors}}) - EF_i = 7 - 5 = 2$ days. C can slip 2 days without pushing E's early start. But C's total float is 5 ($LS - ES = 8 - 3 = 5$). So C has 2 days of free float and 5 days of total float. The extra 3 days of total float would delay E's start (but not the project end). The 5-days choice is total float, not free float. The 0-days choice would mean no free slack. The 3-days choice is $TF - FF$, which is not a standard metric.
const-fl-q3.hint: Free float = (earliest successor ES) − (your EF). It's always ≤ total float.

steps.text: C feeds E. Earliest successor start: $ES_E = 7$
Compare: total float of C = $LS_C - ES_C = 8 - 3 = 5$ days. $FF \leq TF$ \checkmark

traps: Confusing free float (2) with total float (5) — free float only considers the immediate successor
Free float is always ≤ total float — if you get a larger free float, recheck

const-ev-q1.statement: At month 6 of a project: $BCWP = 400{,}000$, $ACWP = 450{,}000$. What is the cost variance, and is the project over or under budget?
const-ev-q1.eli5: $CV = BCWP - ACWP = 400{,}000 - 450{,}000 = -50{,}000$. Negative CV means the project spent more than the work is worth — over budget. The +50,000 (under budget) choice flipped the subtraction order. The -50,000 (under budget) choice got the sign right but misinterpreted it. The +50,000 (over budget) choice got both wrong.
const-ev-q1.hint: CV = Earned − Actual. Negative = over budget (you spent more than you earned).
traps: Subtracting in the wrong order (ACWP − BCWP) — the formula is BCWP − ACWP
Misinterpreting the sign: negative CV = over budget, positive = under budget

const-ev-q2.statement: At week 10: $BCWS = 500{,}000$, $BCWP = 420{,}000$, $ACWP = 480{,}000$. What is the schedule variance?
const-ev-q2.eli5: $SV = BCWP - BCWS = 420{,}000 - 500{,}000 = -80{,}000$. Negative SV means the project earned less value than planned — behind schedule. The $-60{,}000$ choice confused SV with CV: $BCWP - ACWP = 420{,}000 - 480{,}000 = -60{,}000$. That is the cost variance, not the schedule variance. The $+80{,}000$ choice flipped the sign. The $+20{,}000$ choice used $BCWS - ACWP = 500{,}000 - 480{,}000 = 20{,}000$, which is not a standard formula.
const-ev-q2.hint: SV = BCWP − BCWS. Don't confuse it with CV = BCWP − ACWP.

steps.text: Interpretation: $SV < 0$ \u2192 behind schedule (earned less than planned)
For comparison: $CV = BCWP - ACWP = 420{,}000 - 480{,}000 = -60{,}000$ (also over budget)

traps: Computing CV instead of SV — SV uses BCWS, CV uses ACWP
Mixing up the three values: BCWS (planned), ACWP (actual cost), BCWP (earned value)

const-ev-q3.statement: A project reports: planned value (BCWS) = 300,000, earned value (BCWP) = 270,000, actual cost (ACWP) = 250,000. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Ahead of schedule and over budget
Ahead of schedule and under budget

const-ev-q3.eli5: $SV = BCWP - BCWS = 270{,}000 - 300{,}000 = -30{,}000 < 0$ — behind schedule. $CV = BCWP - ACWP = 270{,}000 - 250{,}000 = +20{,}000 > 0$ — under budget. So the project did less work than planned (behind schedule) but spent less than the work is worth (under budget). This combination is common — the crew is efficient but slow. "Ahead of schedule and under budget" has schedule wrong. "Behind schedule and over budget" has cost wrong. "Ahead of schedule and over budget" has both wrong.
const-ev-q3.hint: Compute both CV and SV. CV tells you cost performance, SV tells you schedule performance.

steps.text: Result: behind schedule AND under budget

const-ev-q3.handbookFormula: CV = BCWP - ACWP,\quad SV = BCWP - BCWS
traps: Assuming over budget and behind schedule always go together — they are independent measures
Mixing up the sign interpretation: positive = good (under budget or ahead of schedule)

const-pf-q1.statement: A project has $BCWP = 600{,}000$ and $ACWP = 750{,}000$. What is the CPI?
const-pf-q1.eli5: CPI = BCWP/ACWP = 600,000/750,000 = 0.80. For every dollar spent, only 0.80 of value is earned — the project is over budget. The 1.25 choice inverted the ratio: ACWP/BCWP. The 0.75 choice might come from a different calculation. The 150,000 choice is the cost variance CV, not the index.
const-pf-q1.hint: CPI = Earned / Actual = BCWP / ACWP. Less than 1.0 = over budget.
traps: Inverting the ratio (ACWP/BCWP = 1.25) — CPI = Earned/Actual, not Actual/Earned
Confusing the index (ratio) with the variance (dollar amount)

const-pf-q2.statement: A project has $BAC = 2{,}000{,}000$, $BCWP = 600{,}000$, and $CPI = 0.80$. What is the estimate to complete (ETC)?
const-pf-q2.eli5: ETC = (BAC − BCWP)/CPI = (2,000,000 − 600,000)/0.80 = 1,400,000/0.80 = 1,750,000. The remaining work (1.4M budgeted) will cost more because CPI < 1.0. The 1,400,000 option forgot to divide by CPI — it assumed the remaining work will cost exactly as budgeted. The 1,000,000 option used BAC/2. The 2,500,000 option is the EAC (BAC/CPI), not ETC.
const-pf-q2.hint: ETC = (BAC − BCWP) / CPI. The remaining work is inflated by the cost performance.
traps: Using BAC − BCWP as ETC without dividing by CPI — this ignores the cost overrun trend
Using BAC − ACWP in the numerator instead of BAC − BCWP

const-pf-q3.statement: Continuing: $ACWP = 750{,}000$ and $ETC = 1{,}750{,}000$. The original budget was $BAC = 2{,}000{,}000$. What is the estimate at completion (EAC)?
const-pf-q3.eli5: EAC = ACWP + ETC = 750,000 + 1,750,000 = 2,500,000. The project originally budgeted 2,000,000 but is now forecast to cost 2,500,000 — a 25% overrun. The 2,000,000 option is BAC (the original budget), ignoring the overrun trend. The 1,750,000 option is ETC alone, not EAC. The 2,150,000 option might come from using CPI = 1.0 for ETC: ETC = 1,400,000, EAC = 750,000 + 1,400,000 = 2,150,000.
const-pf-q3.hint: EAC = money already spent (ACWP) + money still needed (ETC).
traps: Reporting ETC (1,750,000) as EAC — EAC includes the money already spent
Using BAC as EAC — BAC is the original budget, EAC is the revised forecast
Using CPI = 1.0 when computing ETC — this assumes the overrun trend stops, giving a falsely optimistic forecast

const-dm-q1.statement: A public agency requires competitive bidding by law and has complete plans and specifications. Which delivery method is most appropriate?
const-dm-q1.eli5: DBB is the standard for public projects that require competitive bidding on complete plans. The agency already has full plans and specs — they just need to advertise for bids. DB and CMAR involve contractor involvement before plans are complete. IPD is a collaborative method rarely mandated by law.

const-dm-q2.eli5: DB is the answer when the owner wants speed (overlapping design and construction) and single-point responsibility. In DB, one entity handles everything. DBB cannot fast-track because design must be complete before bidding. CMAR provides early contractor input but keeps design and construction under separate contracts. const-dm-q3.eli5: The key clues are: (1) contractor input during design → rules out DBB. (2) SEPARATE design professional → rules out DB (where one entity does both). (3) GMP → characteristic of CMAR. In CMAR, the CM joins early, advises on constructability, and later provides a GMP before construction starts. Design-Build puts design and construction under one contract. Design-Bid-Build has no contractor involvement during design. Job Order Contracting is for small, repetitive maintenance work.

const-cs-q1.statement: A contractor is excavating a trench that is $7 \text{ ft}$ deep for a sewer line. No protective system is installed. Is this an OSHA violation?

const-cs-q2.statement: A worker is operating on a scaffold platform $8 \text{ ft}$ above the ground without guardrails, safety nets, or a harness. Is fall protection required?

choices.text: Yes — fall protection is required at 6 ft in construction
No — fall protection is only required above 10 ft
No — scaffolds are exempt from fall protection

const-cs-q3.statement: An excavation is $22 \text{ ft}$ deep. What level of engineering involvement is required for the protective system?

choices.text: Standard OSHA tables can be used without engineering
The contractor's competent person can design it
Must be designed by a registered professional engineer
No protective system is needed at this depth

At 22 ft, a PE must design the shoring, sloping, or shielding system. For excavations 5–20 ft, the contractor's competent person can use OSHA’s standard tables (Appendix A/B).
